The colour of lead is a bluish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, but when it combines with oxygen it assumes a bright yellow or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, in proportion to the quantity of oxygen. Cobalt, which is of a gray colour, when combined with oxygen becomes of a fine blue; and copper, which is red, combined in the same way, exhibits a green colour. 2. Changes in smell. 1. The smell of muriatic acid is highly pungent; ammonia, or the volatile alkali, is not less so; but when these two are combined, forming nitrate of ammonia, or sal ammoniac, the new compound is perfectly inodorous. This last is a remarkable instance of two highly volatile and odorous substances becoming fixed in the compound, and destitute of smell, and thus exhibiting a total change of their properties. 2. The smell of sulphur and of potash is scarcely perceptible in the uncombined state; but when they are united together, and moistened with water, a most fetid and offensive odour is emitted. 3. Changes in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. 1. The taste of sulphur is nearly insipid; and oxygen, which is one of the component parts of the atmosphere, is not only innocent, but necessary for the existence of animals; but when these two enter into union, the compound formed, which is sulphuric acid, is one of the most corrosive substances. 2. Sulphuric acid, which is sour and corrosive, forms a combination with soda, which is also of a corrosive nature; the result, which is Glauber salt, or sulphate of soda, is a compound of a bitter nauseous taste, but possessing none of the properties of its component parts.

BUDDS

Pages 39-39
or **Butt-ends**, in the sea-language, are the fore ends of all planks under water, as they rise, and are joined one end to another.—Butt-ends in great ships are most carefully bolted; for if any one of them should spring or give way, the leak would be very dangerous and difficult to stop.

BURKE

Pages 5-12

EDMUND, a writer, orator, and statesman, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, on the 1st <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, in the year 1730. His father was an attorney, first at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>, and afterwards in Dublin. Young Burke received the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Ballymore, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a>, under the tuition of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Shackleton, a Quaker of considerable celebrity. Committed to the care of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> so admirably qualified for the important business of instruction, young Burke applied to his studies with commendable assiduity, and became one of the numerous examples that might be adduced, to demonstrate the falsehood of that popular but dangerous maxim, that young men of genius are always destitute of application. In this seminary he laid the foundation of his knowledge in the languages of antiquity; whence he was hereafter to borrow the elegance of his style, and the models and imagery of his eloquence. From this source was also, most probably, derived that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, which germinating at certain periods in his bosom, so often pointed his oratory, inflamed his passions, and animated his sentiments; and which in his best days acquired him a reputation almost unequalled in our times. At this respectable school several years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were spent; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of the master, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> of the pupil, reflect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> on both. The former lived to see his scholar attain a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of reputation; and he on his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> was accustomed to spend a portion of his annual visit to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> at Ballymore. From a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> seminary Edmund was sent to the university of Dublin. Here, however, he does not appear to have distinguished himself either by application <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> talents. His character, as a student, was merely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>. He exhibited no symptoms of early genius, obtained no palms in the academic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, and departed even without a degree. During this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, however, he commenced author. His first essays were of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Mr Burke now addicted himself to other pursuits, particularly logic and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>; and is said to have planned a refutation of the systems of Berkeley and Hume. While thus employed in treasuring up the means of attaining a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of celebrity, which far different avocations prevented him afterwards from aspiring to, he was not inattentive to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> object of obtaining a suitable settlement in life; for his family was not opulent, and he already panted after independence. He accordingly became a candidate for a vacant <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> at the university of Glasgow. The immediate reason of his failure is not directly known; but on this he repaired to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, and enrolled his name as a student of the Inner Temple. It appears from his speeches, his writings, and his conversation, that he studied the grand outline of our municipal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a> with particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; but it may be doubted whether he ever entered into the minutiae. Indeed the versatility of his talents, and his avocations, were but little calculated for that dull and plodding circuit which can alone <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to an intimate knowledge of our laws. Besides, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been gifted with the necessary application, both <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and opportunity were wanting; for it is well known that at this period of his life the "res angusta domi" did not permit the student to dedicate his attention solely to this, or indeed to any other single object. The exhausted state of his finances called frequently for a speedy supply, and instead of perusing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> of Bracton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLETA">Fleta</a>, Littleton, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, he was obliged to write essays, letters, and paragraphs, for the periodical publications of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. But if these pursuits diverted his attention from graver studies, they acquired him a facility of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and a command of style and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which proved eminently serviceable in the course of his future life. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, however, became at length impaired, and a nervous fever ensued. This circumstance induced him to call in the aid of Dr Nugent, one of his own countrymen, a medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose manners were more amiable than his practice was extensive. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, who had travelled on the continent, and was an author himself, readily discovered the source of his malady, and, by removing him from books and buffets to his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, soon effected a cure. That event is said to have been hastened, if not entirely completed, by a physician of another kind; the accomplished <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a>. This lady was destined to become his wife; a circumstance particularly fortunate for him, as her disposition was mild and gentle, and she <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, through a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years, and many vicissitudes of fortune, to soothe and tranquillize passions always violent, and often tumultuous. Our student seems at length to have determined once more to endeavour to distinguish himself as an author, Burke, and he accordingly took advantage of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a celebrated peer to write a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> after the manner of that nobleman; in which, by exaggerating his principles, he should be enabled to bring them into contempt: but this effort proved unsuccessful, for the treatise in question was for a long time confined to oblivion, and would never have been heard of, had it not been resuscitated by his future fame. Another performance made ample amends: his "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Sublime and Beautiful" attracted a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of reputation, and acquired him considerable celebrity as a man of letters. In addition to the profits of the publication, he is said on this occasion to have received a present from his father of £100. But his circumstances must have been greatly embarrassed about this time, as he was obliged to sell his books; and surely nothing but the extremity of distress could have forced a man of letters to such a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. The work we have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, having an immediate relation to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, excited a desire in Sir Joshua Reynolds, even then at the head of his profession, to become acquainted with Mr Burke; and a friendship ensued which continued uninterrupted during the life of the painter, and was unequivocally testified by a handsome bequest in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. Dr Johnson also sought and obtained an intimacy with him, and he now became the constant frequenter of two clubs, composed of some of the most celebrated men of that day. One of these met at the Turk's Head tavern in Gerrard-street, and consisted of the following members: Dr Johnson, Mr (afterwards Sir Joshua) Reynolds, Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOLDSMITH">Goldsmith</a>, Mr Topham Beauclerc, Dr Nugent, Sir John Hawkins, Mr Bennet Langton, Mr Chamier, Mr Garrick, and Mr Burke. The other assembled at the St James's coffee-house, and besides many of the above, was composed of the following members: Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, Dr Douglas bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, Dr Bernard <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Derry, Mr Richard Burke, Mr William Burke, Mr Hickey, &c. Dr Goldsmith, who was Mr Burke's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> at Dublin <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, was a member of both, and wrote the epitaphs of those who composed the latter. That on Mr Burke has often been praised. Here lies our good Edmund, whose genius was such, We scarcely can praise it or blame it too much; Who, born for the universe, narrow'd his mind, And to party gave up what was meant for mankind. Though fraught with all learning, yet training his throat To persuade Tommy Townshend to lend him a vote; Who, too deep for his hearers, still went on refining, And thought of convincing while they thought of dining; Though equal to all things, for all things unfit, Too nice for a statesman, too proud for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>; For a patriot too cool; for a drudge disobedient; And too fond of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, to pursue the expedient. In short, 'twas his fate, unemployed or in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, sir, To eat mutton <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and cut blocks with a razor. A literary work on a new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, first suggested in 1750, and by some attributed to the Dodleys, and by others to Mr Burke, became, for some time, a considerable source of emolument to him. This was called the "Annual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a>;" a publication that soon obtained considerable celebrity, and of which he had the superintendence for several years. He was, at length, called off from his literary labours by avocations of a far different kind. A gentleman who afterwards derived the cognomen of "ingle-speech <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>," from a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, having been appointed secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of Ireland, invited his friend Mr Burke to accompany him thither; this offer he readily complied with, and although he acted in no public station, and performed no public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> while he remained in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he was rewarded with a pension of £300 per annum, which he soon after disposed of for a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. On his return to England he amused himself, as usual, with literary composition. A series of essays, written by him in a newspaper, which, at one time, obtained <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celebrity, attracted the notice of the late marquis of Rockingham; and Mr Fitzherbert, a member of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and father of the present Lord St Helen's, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this circumstance, introduced him to that nobleman. From this moment he was destined to become a public man, and to dedicate his studies, his eloquence, and his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, to politics. Lord Rockingham having proved more compliant than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, the former nobleman was brought into power, and seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. On this occasion he selected Mr Burke as his private secretary, an office of no power and very little emolument, but which naturally leads to both. As it was now necessary he should have a seat in parliament, although it cannot be supposed that he was legally qualified in respect to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, he applied to Lord Verney, who was <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WENDOVER">Wendover</a>, a borough at that time dependent on him, and principally occupied by his tenants. Having thus obtained a seat in 1765, he prepared to fit himself for his new situation. He was already provided with all the necessary talents, and was only deficient in the forms of business, and the facility of expressing his sentiments before a public audience. The first of these was mastered by sedulous attention; and as to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, if we are to give <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to those who pretend to be intimately acquainted with this period of his life, he overcame all difficulties by a previous initiation elsewhere. In short he had acquired celebrity at the "Robinhood," before he attempted to speak in the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and vanquished an eloquent "baker" ere he began to cope with the great orators of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Holding a confidential place under the Rockingham administration, he of course supported all its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. A former ministry, anxious to increase its influence by means of increased imposts, had conceived the idea of taxing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> through the medium of a parliament in which she was not represented. Having attempted to carry this into effect by means of the famous stamp <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, the Americans, alarmed at what they conceived to be a flagrant violation of every principle of the English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, made such a spirited resistance to the measure that it was abandoned, and the Rockingham party readily consented to the repeal. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a>, however, of vindicating the honour of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, they unfortunately proposed and carried the declaratory claratory act, by means of which, although the original scheme had been abandoned, the principle on which it was built was asserted anew, and a foundation laid for all the miseries that afterwards ensued. But if this short-lived administration deserved no great credit on this occasion, it is entitled to considerable praise on account of other parts of its conduct; for it repealed the cider act, procured a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the house of commons, condemning the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZURE">seizure</a> of papers, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> against general warrants. The first of these afforded great relief to such of the counties as cultivated orchard grounds, and the two last seemed to be called for by the conduct of their predecessors in respect to Mr Wilkes. On retiring from office they, however, did not carry much popularity along with them, as Lord Chatham and his friends, who in some measure monopolized the public favour, were entrusted with the management of affairs for a short time; and it is extremely probable that they would have sunk into neglect, had not America been driven into resistance. It now fell to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> to enforce the scheme which the Grenville party had projected, and wished to carry boldly into execution; which the Rockingham administration had by an unaccountable blunder at once annihilated and recognized, and which they afterwards manfully, and at length successfully opposed. This forms the most brilliant epoch of Mr Burke's life. He was hostile to the expulsion of Mr Wilkes; an act which the house of commons afterwards rescinded from its records. On the application of the dissenters for relief, he took up their cause, and expressed his resentment, in very animated terms, against that misguided policy, which permits all those not within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> of establishment to enjoy liberty less by right than by connivance. But perhaps the noblest part of his conduct consisted in his steady and uniform opposition to the American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and his marked and declared hostility to the abettors of it. His speech against the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a> Port <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> was one of the most charming specimens of oratory that had ever been exhibited in the British senate; and on the 19th of April, 1774, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> for the repeal of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a> duty, he discovered such talents, that an old and respectable member exclaimed, "Good God! what a man is this!—How could he acquire such transcendant powers?" And when, in reply to another who had said, "That the Americans were our children, and it was horrible to revolt against their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>!" the orator uttered the following passage, the whole house was electrified: "They are our children, it is true; but when children ask for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, we are not to give them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. When those children of ours wish to affiliate with their parent, and to respect the beauteous countenance of British liberty, are we to turn to them the shameful parts of our constitution? Are we to give them our weakness for their strength; our opprobrium for their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; and the flough of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, which we are not able to work off, to serve them for their freedom." The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of which had become rich by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with America, were likely to suffer by its interdiction. This consideration alone rendered many of them hostile to the proceedings of the ministry; but nobler and more exalted motives actuated the bosoms of others, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, Dissenters, and other sectarians, who were moved by zeal against oppression, and a love of liberty imprinted on their minds by a constitution which had remained until then inviolate. Gratified by the exertions of Mr Burke in behalf of civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> freedom, they put him in nomination for their city, and sent into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, to request his immediate personal attendance. After consulting with his patron concerning an offer so flattering and unexpected, accompanied at the same time with assurances most punctually fulfilled, that he should be put to no expense whatever, he immediately set out for the west of England, and found that no less than three candidates had started before him. The first was Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>, afterwards Lord Nugent, one of the former representatives, whose unpopularity was such, that he soon discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of resigning all his pretensions; two, therefore (Mr Cruger and Mr Brickdale), only remained in the field, and the former of these, like Mr Burke himself, was adverse to a rupture with America. The new candidate did not appear on the hustings until the afternoon of the sixth day's poll, on which occasion he addressed the electors in a very able speech, admirably calculated for the occasion. He began by expressing a modest diffidence of his own abilities, and a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the important trust they were assembled to confer. He then boldly declared himself hostile to a contest with America, and asserted, that England had been rendered flourishing by liberty and commerce, the first of which was dear to his heart, while the latter had been a favourite object of his studies, both in its principles and details. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a> was well received by the electors; the contest proved propitious to his wishes; and when the sheriffs had notified, at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the poll, that he was elected, he made the most brilliant <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> on the occasion that had ever been heard within the walls of a city celebrated rather for its opulence than its eloquence. Mr Burke immediately returned from his new constituency to parliament, with increased vigour, reputation, and zeal. The earl of Chatham, having failed, notwithstanding his reputation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, in an attempt to adjust the troubles of the colonies by means of a conciliatory bill introduced by him into the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> for that purpose, the obstinacy of the ministry now became apparent to every one. This circumstance, which would have appalled an inferior man, did not, however, discourage the member for Bristol from a similar attempt in another place; and accordingly, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 22, 1775, he brought forward his thirteen celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, which were intended to close the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>, and heal all the differences between the mother country and her colonies. His plan, on this occasion, embraced not only an immediate conciliation, by a repeal of the late coercive acts, but also the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of an independent judiciary, and the regulation of the courts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. The whole, however, was qualified by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> majority on the side of the minister, who moved the previous question. Mr Burke had hitherto chiefly distinguished himself in opposition to the measures of others; but in 1780, he himself stood forth as the original author and proposer of a scheme which soon engaged the attention of the public, and actually appeared big with the most prosperous results. When he found ministers obstinately persisting in a disastrous war, and perceived that the people began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> beneath the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the taxes for its support, it struck him as advantageous on one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and political on the other, to diminish the public burdens and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of adherents to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> at the same time. Accordingly, on the 11th of February, he brought in a bill "for the regulation of his majesty's civil establishments, and of certain public offices; for the limitation of pensions, and the suppression of sundry useless, expensive, and inconvenient places, and for applying the monies saved thereby, to the public service. This scheme was manifestly founded on the late reforms that had taken place in France; for by an edict of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, registered in the parliament of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, it appeared that he had suppressed no less than 496 places in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> by one regulation. The orator, with great judgement, fastened upon this event, and endeavoured to make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it as an incitement to a similar attempt here; nay, he called in national rivalry itself, by way of an inducement to consent to this sacrifice on the part of the crown. To this bill the minority did not at first give much opposition. Indeed the mover of it contrived to soften those features that appeared harsh to them. Notwithstanding this, it did not prove successful during Lord North's administration; and when it was at length carried, it was much modified and altered. Parliament was dissolved in 1780, but Mr Burke was not re-elected for Bristol, and this is said to have made a deep <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the mind of the orator; but this must have been obliterated by the important events that speedily ensued; for the minister now tottered on the treasury bench, being abandoned by many of his staunchest supporters, and but little confident in his own schemes, all of which had proved eminently unsuccessful. The opposition, having by this time increased to a considerable degree, uneasily assailed him, until at length, March 28, 1782, Lord North assured the house of commons, that his administration was at an end. The day had now arrived when the ministry and opposition were to change places, and the former to be arrayed in the spoils of the latter. Of this rich booty Mr Burke, whose services had been so conspicuous in hunting the enemy into the toils prepared for them, had his portion: for he was made a privy councillor, and invested with the lucrative appointment of paymaster-general of the forces. He was at length now enabled to enforce his plan of political economy, tendered before in vain; and the board of trade, the board of works, the offices of third secretary of state, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the chamber, cofferer of the household, the lords of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> in Scotland, the master of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, the master of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> hounds, the six clerks of the board of green cloth, and the paymaster of the pensions, were abolished. At length the reins of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> were confided to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the marquis of Lansdowne, then earl Shelburne; and this event gave such offence to those who wished to place the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Portland at the head of affairs, that Mr Fox, Lord John Cavendish, and Mr Burke, immediately resigned. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, the critical state of the English East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> had long agitated the public mind, and become occasionally a subject of discussion in parliament. The seizure, imprisonment, and confinement of Lord Pigot, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a>; the conduct of Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, in respect to several of the native powers; the grand question of sovereignty, relative to the territorial possessions of the company in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>: all these subjects had, at different times, excited the attention of the nation. No sooner did Mr Fox behold himself and his friends in possession of power, than he brought in a bill, to remedy the various abuses in the government of British India. Of this bill Mr Burke is well known to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> penman, and upon this occasion he defended its principles and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> with all the zeal of a parent. In a speech of considerable length he exhibited an able retrospect of the system, both political and commercial, of the company. He then proceeded to state the benefit likely to result from the plan under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>, which he considered as calculated to effect "the rescue of the greatest number of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> race that ever were so grievously oppressed, from the greatest tyranny that ever was exercised." In short, he contemplated it as a measure that would "secure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> in his pot to every man in India." "I carry my mind (adds he) to all the people, and all the names and descriptions that, relieved by this bill, will bless the labours of this parliament, and the confidence which the best house of commons has given to him who best deserves it." This celebrated bill, notwithstanding much opposition both within and without, was carried triumphantly through the house of commons: but in the house of peers it experienced a far different fate, and with it fell the power and consequence of its authors, framers, and supporters. In the course of the next year (February 28, 1785), he made a celebrated speech relative to the nabob of Arcot's debts; and depicted one of his creditors, who had taken an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> share in the late elections, "as a criminal who long since ought to have fattened the region kites with his offal; the old betrayer, infilter, oppressor, and scourge, of a country (Tanjore), which had for years been an object of an unremitting, but unhappily unequal, struggle, between the bounties of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> to renovate, and the wickedness of mankind to destroy." But there appeared to Mr Burke to be a still greater delinquent, on whom he was determined to inflict all the wounds of his eloquence, and sacrifice, if possible, the powerful offender himself at the shrine of national vengeance. This was Mr Hastings; and soon after his arrival in England, the orator gave notice of his intentions. On the 17th of February, 1785, he opened the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> by a most eloquent speech; in which he depicted the supposed crimes of the late governor-general, in the most glowing and animated colours. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, however, turned out in the event far different from his hopes and expectations; while the length of it failed not to involve both himself and party in reproach. During the debate on the commercial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with France (January 23, 1787), the member for Malton exhibited an undiminished versatility of talents, and pointed his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> with no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> success at Mr Pitt, who, according to him, contemplated the subject with a narrowness peculiar to limited minds: "He seems to consider it (adds he) as an affair of two little competing-houses, and not of two great nations. He seems to consider it as a contention between the sign of the fleur-de-lis and the sign of the old <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-lion, for which should obtain the best <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>." The next public event of importance in which we find Mr Burke engaged, occurred in consequence of his majesty's indisposition. On this occasion he took an active part in the debates of the house of commons; and supposed to have penned a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> for one, and a speech for another, branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. When Mr Pitt moved his declaratory resolutions relative to the provisional <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the royal authority, he attacked him with much asperity of language, and was particularly severe on the manner in which the royal assent was to be given to all future acts of parliament. The men who held most of the high places under the government were treated as "jobbers, old hacks of the court, and the supporters and betrayers of all parties; and it was a mock crown, a tinsel robe, and a sceptre from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, lacquered over and unreal," which were about to be conferred on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The opposition, lessened indeed by a few occasional defections, had hitherto acted as a great public body, supposed to be united in general principles, for the common welfare and prosperity of the state; but the French revolution thinned their ranks, dispelled their consequence, and, by sowing jealousy between the chiefs, spread consternation and dismay among their followers. It was on the 2d of March 1790, when Mr Fox moved for leave to bring in a bill to repeal the corporation and test-acts, that this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> became evident; and soon after this Mr Burke declared, "that his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> friend and he were separated in their politics for ever. The ministry now seemed anxious to provide for their new associate; and he, on his part, certainly appeared deserving of some remuneration at their hands, for he had abandoned all his old friends, and not a few of his old principles. In addition to this, his "Reflections on the Revolution in France," had afforded some degree of countenance, and even popularity, to the measures of administration; and, not content with his own exertions, he had enlisted his son on the same side, and even sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a>. The royal munificence at length gratified his warmest wishes; for by a warrant, dated September 24, 1795, and made to commence January 5, 1793, he received a pension of £100l. for his own life, and that of his wife, on the civil <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>; while two other pensions of £500l. a-year for three lives, payable out of the four and a half per cent. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a>, dated October 24, 1795, were made to commence from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 24, 1793. Honours as well as wealth now seemed to await him, for he was about to be ennobled, when the untimely death of an only child put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> of ambition, and contributed not a little to hasten his own, which occurred at his house at Beaconsfield, July 8, 1797. Thus died, in the 68th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Edmund Burke, one of the greatest orators, statesmen, and authors, of his age; one whose name will long continue to be celebrated; and who, had he fallen during the meridian of his fame and character, would have scarcely been considered as second to any man, either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. As a man of letters, he ranks high in point of genius, learning, and composition; and his works are attended with this peculiarity, that they are the production of almost the only orator of his day, who could wield his pen with as much fluency as his tongue, and shine equally in the senate and the closet. His dissertation on the "Sublime and Beautiful" acquired him the applause of all, and secured him the friendship and assistance of many men of taste in the nation. His political tracts betoken much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, deep thought, uncommon sagacity; and even those who may be disposed to object to his doctrines, cannot but admire his various talents, his happy allusions, and his acute penetration. There is no species of composition, which he has not attempted; no subject on which he has not occasionally treated: his first and his last days were equally dedicated to literature, and he disdained not any species of it, from the newspaper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, that supplied needful bread to his early youth, to the more elaborate performance that procured unnecessary opulence to his old age. As an orator, notwithstanding some glaring defects, he stands almost unrivalled. His gesticulation was at times violent and repulsive, his manner harsh and overbearing; his epithets coarse and disgusting; on many occasions he made use of assertions which were not bottomed in fact, and on one in particular, toward the latter end of his life, had recourse to stage trick and pantomime, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and argument. But on the other hand, no man was better calculated to arouse the dormant passions, to call forth the glowing affections of the human heart, and to "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> up" the inmost recesses of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. Venality and meanness stood appalled in his presence; he who was dead to the feelings of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, was still alive to his animated reproaches; and corruption for a while became alarmed at the terrors of his countenance. His powers were never more conspicuous than on that memorable day, on which he exposed the enormities of a subaltern <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> of oriental despotism—on which he depicted the tortures inflicted by his orders, the flagrant injustice committed by his authority, the pollution that ensued in consequence of his sanction—when he painted agonizing nature vibrating in horrid suspense between life and destruction—when he described, in the climax of crimes, "death introduced into the very sources of life," the bosoms of his auditors became convulsed with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and those of more delicate organs and weaker frame actually swooned away. Nay, after the storm of eloquence had spent its force, and the captivated ears no longer listened to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, his features still spoke the purpose of his heart, his hand still seemed to threaten <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, and his brow to meditate vengeance. "The qualities of his heart (says one of his biographers) were not less amiable and estimable than his talents were astonishing:—benevolent, just, temperate, magnanimous. He loved his country, loved its constitution, because he believed it the best adapted for its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>: at different times, from the same principle, he supported different members of it, when he thought the one or the other likely to be overbalanced. During the prevalence of the Bute plans, dreading the influence of the crown, he supported the people; and for the same reason, during the American war. "After the overthrow of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, the aristocracy, and the dissemination in Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> of the principles that had destroyed these powers, apprehending similar effects, if not vigourously opposed in England, he strenuously supported the monarchy and aristocracy. Thus discriminatingly patriotic in public life, in his private relations his conduct was highly meritorious. A fond and attentive husband, an affectionate and judiciously indulgent father, a sincere friend, at once fervid and active, a liberal and kind master, an agreeable neighbour, a zealous and bountiful patron, he diffused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and happiness. His principles were as strict, and habits as virtuous, as his dispositions were kind." (Annual Necrology).

BURKITT

Pages 12-12

WILLIAM, a celebrated commentator on the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, was born at Hitcham in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 25, 1650, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He entered young upon the ministry, being ordained by Bishop Reynolds; and the first employment which he had was at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILDENHALL">Mildenhall</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 21 years a constant preacher, first as a curate, and afterwards as rector of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the year 1692, he had a call to the vicarage of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEDHAM">Dedham</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, where he continued to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in the latter end of October 1703. He was a pious and charitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. He made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> collections for the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in the years 1687, &c., and by his great care, pains, and charges, procured a worthy minister to go and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in Carolina. Among other charities, by his last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> and testament, he bequeathed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> wherein he lived, with the lands thereto belonging, to be a habitation for the lecturer that should be chosen from time to time to read the lecture at Dedham. Besides his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> upon the New Testament, written in the same plain, practical, and affectionate manner in which he preached, he wrote a volume, entitled The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> man's help, and the rich man's guide. BURLAW. See BY-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">LAW</a>. BURLEIGH. See CECIL.

BURLESQUE

Pages 12-12

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, which, though a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> engine of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, is not confined to that subject; for it is clearly distinguishable into burlesque that excites <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> merely, and burlesque that excites derision <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ridicule. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> subject, in which there is no impropriety, may be brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by a certain colouring so as to be ridiculous, as in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> tragic; the author first laughs at every turn in order to make his readers laugh. The Lutrin is a burlesque poem of the other sort, laying hold of a low and trifling incident to expose the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, indolence, and contentious spirit, of a set of monks. Boileau, the author, turns the subject into ridicule, by dressing it in the heroic style, and affecting to consider it as of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and importance. Though ridicule is the poet's aim, he always carries a grave <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and never once betrays a smile. The opposition between the subject and the manner of handling it, is what produces the ridicule; and therefore, in a composition of this kind, no image professedly ludicrous ought to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, because such images destroy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>. Though the burlesque that aims at ridicule produces its effects by elevating the style far above the subject; yet the poet ought to confine himself to such images as are lively, and readily apprehended. A strained elevation, soaring above the ordinary reach of fancy, makes not a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. The mind is soon disgusted by being kept <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> on the stretch. Machinery may be employed in a burlesque poem, such as the Lutrin, Dipsenser, or Hudibras, with more success and propriety than in any other species of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. For burlesque poems, though they assume the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, give entertainment chiefly by their pleasant and ludicrous pictures: it is not the aim of such a poem to raise sympathy; and for that reason, a strict <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is not necessary. And hence, the more extravagant the machinery in a ludicrous poem, the more entertainment it affords.

BURLINGTON

Pages 12-12

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in the east riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, situated on the German ocean, about 37 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 10' and N. Lat. 54° 15'. It gave the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to a branch of the noble family of Boyle, but the earldom is now extinct. New-BURLINGTON, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of New-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, in North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; situated in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> river, about 20 miles north of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>. W. Long. 74° 0' N. Lat. 42° 40'.

BURMAN

Pages 12-12

FRANCIS, a Protestant minister, and learned professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1628; and died on the 10th of November 1679, after having published a course of divinity, and several other works. He is not to be confounded with Francis Burman, his son; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Burman, a laborious commentator on Phaedrus, Lucan, Petronius, and other profane authors, who died in 1741.

BURNET

Pages 12-16

GILBERT, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> in the latter end of the 17th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, in 1643, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in the shire of Aberdeen. His father being bred to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, was, at the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, appointed one of the lords of session, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Crimond, in reward for his constant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> party during the troubles of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Our author, the youngest son of his father, was instructed by him in the Latin tongue: at ten years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he was sent to continue his studies at Aberdeen, and was admitted M.A. before he was 14. His own inclination led him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the civil and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal law</a>; and he used to say, that it was from this study he had received more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> notions concerning the foundations of civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, than those which some divines maintain. About the year after, he changed his mind, and began to apply to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, to the great satisfaction satisfaction of his father. He was admitted preacher before he was 18; and Sir Alexander Burnet, his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>-german, offered him a benefice; but he refused to accept of it. In 1663, about two years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he came into England; and after six months stay at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, returned to Scotland; which he soon left again to make a tour for some months, in 1664, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and France. At <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, by the help of a Jewish rabbi, he perfected himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and likewise became acquainted with the leading men of the different persuasions tolerated in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; as Calvinists, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMINIANS">Arminians</a>, Lutherans, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWNISTS">Brownists</a>, Papists, and Unitarians; amongst each of which he used frequently to declare, he met with men of such unfeigned piety and virtue, that he became fixed in a strong principle of universal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, and an invincible abhorrence of all severities on account of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> differences. Upon his return from his travels, he was admitted minister of Saltoun; in which station he served five years in the most exemplary manner. He drew up a memorial, in which he took notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> errors in the conduct of the Scots <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, which he observed not to be conformable to the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>; and sent a copy of it to several of them. This exposed him to their resentments: but, to show he was not actuated with a spirit of ambition, he led a retired course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for two years; which so endangered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, that he was obliged to abate his excessive application to study. In 1669, he published his "Modest and free conference between a conformist and non-conformist." He became acquainted with the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, who communicated to him all the papers belonging to her father and her uncle; upon which he drew up the "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the dukes of Hamilton." The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lauderdale, hearing he was about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, invited him to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and introduced him to King Charles II. He returned to Scotland, and married the lady Margaret Kennedy, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Cassilis; a lady of great piety and knowledge, highly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, to whose sentiments she was strongly inclined. As there was some disparity in their ages, that it might remain past dispute that this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was wholly owing to inclination, and not to avarice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ambition, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> before their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> our author delivered the lady a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, whereby he renounced all pretensions to her fortune, which was very considerable, and must otherwise have fallen into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the herself having no intention to secure it. The same year he published his "Vindication of the authority, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state of Scotland;" which at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> was looked upon as so great a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, that he was again offered a bishopric, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of the next vacant archbishopric; but did not accept of it, because he could not approve of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> view of which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> to be the advancement of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. Mr Burnet's intimacy with the dukes of Hamilton and Lauderdale occasioned him to be frequently sent for by the king and the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, who had conversations with him in private. But Lauderdale conceiving a resentment against him on account of the freedom with which he spoke to him, represented at last to the king, that Dr Burnet was engaged in an opposition to his measures. Upon his return to London, he perceived that these suggestions had entirely thrown him out of the king's favour, though the duke of York treated him with greater civility than ever, and dissuaded him from going to Scotland. Upon this, he resigned his professorship at Glasgow, and sailed at London. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the living at Cripplegate being vacant, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of St Paul's (in whose gift it was), hearing of his circumstances, and the hardships he had undergone, sent him an offer of the benefice; but as he had been informed of their first intention of conferring it on Dr Fowler, he generously declined it. In 1675, at the recommendation of Lord Hollis, whom he had known in France, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> at that court, he was, by Sir Herbotte Grimstone, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the rolls, appointed preacher of the chapel there, notwithstanding the opposition of the court. He was soon after chosen a lecturer of St Clement's, and became one of the preachers that were most followed in town. In 1679, he published his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Reformation, for which he had the thanks of both houses of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it was published in 1679, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1681. Next year he published an abridgement of these two parts. Mr Burnet about this time happened to be sent for to a woman in sickness, who had been engaged in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> with the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>. The manner in which he treated her during her illness, gave that lord a great curiosity for being acquainted with him. Whereupon, for a whole winter, he spent one evening in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> with Dr Burnet, who discoursed with him upon all those topics upon which sceptics and men of loose morals attack the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The happy effects of these conferences occasioned the publication of his account of the life and death of that earl. In 1682, when the administration was changed in favour of the duke of York, being much resorted to by persons of all ranks and parties, in order to avoid returning visits, he built a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a>, and went for above a year through a course of chemical experiments. Not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, he refused a living of 300l. a-year offered him by the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, on the terms of his not residing there, but in London. When the inquiry concerning the popish plot was on foot, he was frequently sent for and consulted by King Charles with relation to the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. His majesty offered him the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, then vacant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would engage in his interests; but he refused to accept it on these terms. He preached at the Rolls till 1684, when he was dismissed by order of the court. About this time he published several pieces. On King James's accession to the throne, having obtained leave to go out of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, he first went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and lived in great retirement, till contracting an acquaintance with Brigadier Stouppé, a Protestant <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in the French service, he made a tour with him into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He met with an agreeable reception at Rome. Pope Innocent XI. hearing of our author's arrival, sent the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the Swiss guards to acquaint him he would give him a private audience in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, to avoid the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of killing his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>'s flipper. But Dr Burnet excused himself as well as he could. Some disputes which our author had here concerning religion, religion, beginning to be taken notice of, made it proper for him to quit the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which, upon an intimation given him by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Borghefe, he accordingly did. He pursued his travels through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and Germany. In 1688, he came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, with an intention to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in some of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> provinces. There he received an invitation from the prince and princess of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> (to whom their party in England had recommended him) to come to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, which he accepted. He was soon made acquainted with the secret of their councils, and advised the fitting out of a fleet in Holland sufficient to support their designs and encourage their friends. This, and the Account of his Travels, in which he endeavoured to blend Popery and tyranny together, and represent them as inseparable, with some papers reflecting on the proceedings of England, that came out in single sheets, and were dispersed in several parts of England, most of which Mr Burnet owned himself the author of, alarmed King James; and were the occasion of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> twice against him to the princes of Orange, and insulting, by his ambassador, on his being forbid the court; which, after much importunity was done, though he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be trusted and employed as before, the Dutch minister consulted him daily. To put an end to these frequent conferences with the ministers, a prosecution for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> was set on foot against him both in England and Scotland. But Burnet receiving the news thereof before it arrived at the States, he avoided the storm, by petitioning for, and obtaining without any difficulty, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of naturalization, in order to his intended marriage with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Scott, a Dutch lady of considerable fortune, who, with the advantage of birth, had some of a fine person and understanding. After his marriage with this lady, being legally under the protection of Holland, when Mr Burnet found King James plainly subverting the constitution, he omitted no method to support and promote the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> the prince of Orange had formed of delivering Great Britain, and came over with him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of chaplain. He was soon advanced to the see of Salisbury. He declared for moderate measures with regard to the clergy who scrupled to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>, and many were displeased with him for declaring for the toleration of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONCONFORMISTS">nonconformists</a>. His pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> concerning the oaths of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy to King William and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Mary, 1689, happening to touch upon the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of conquest, gave such offence to both houses of parliament, that it was ordered to be burnt by the hands of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> executioner. In 1698 he lost his wife by the smallpox; and, as he was almost immediately after appointed preceptor to the duke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> he took great care, this employment, and the tender age of his children, induced him the same year to supply her loss by a marriage with Mrs Berkeley, eldest daughter of Sir Richard Blake, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>. In 1699 he published his Exposition of the 39 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; which occasioned a representation against him in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> in the year 1701; but he was vindicated in the upper house. His speech in the house of lords in 1704 against the bill to prevent occasional conformity was severely attacked. He died in 1715, and was interred in the church of St James, Clerkenwell, where he has a monument erected to him. He formed a scheme for augmenting the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> livings; which he pressed forward with such success, that it ended in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament passed in the second year of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, "for the augmentation of the livings of the poor clergy." Burnet, Thomas, a polite and learned writer in the end of the 17th century, was born in Scotland, but educated in Cambridge under the tuition of Mr John Tillotson, afterwards archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. In the beginning of 1685, he was made master of Sutton's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> in London, after which he entered into holy orders. During the reign of King James, he made a noble stand in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> as master of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a>-house against the encroachments of that monarch, who would have imposed one Andrew Popham, a Papist, as a pensioner upon the foundation of that house. In 1680 he published his Telluris theoria sacra, so universally admired for the purity of the style and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the sentiments, that King Charles gave encouragement to a translation of it into English. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> was, however, attacked by several writers. In 1692 he published his Archaeologia philosophica, dedicated to King William, to whom he was clerk of the closet. He died in 1715. Since his death hath been published, his book De statu mortuorum et reurgentium, and his treatise De fide et officiis Christianorum. Burnet, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> James, Lord Monboddo, a senator of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in Scotland, was born about the year 1714. He was the son of Mr Burnet of Monboddo in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINCARDINESHIRE">Kincardineshire</a>. After passing through the usual course of school education, he prosecuted his studies at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Aberdeen, Edinburgh, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, with distinguished reputation. He was admitted an advocate in 1737, and on the 12th of February 1767, he was raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> by the title of Lord Monboddo, in the room of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, appointed a judge the 4th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1742, and who had succeeded Sir John Lauder of Fountainhall, admitted Nov. 1689; being the third on the bench in succession since the revolution. He married Miss Farquharson, a very amiable woman, by whom he had a son and two daughters. His private life was spent in the practice of all the social virtues, and in the enjoyment of much <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> felicity. Although rigidly temperate in his habits of life, he, however, delighted much in the convivial society of his friends, and among these he could <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> almost all the most eminent of those who were distinguished in Scotland for virtue, literature, or genuine elegance of conversation and manners. One of those who esteemed him the most was the late Lord Gardenstone, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who possessed no <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> portion of the same overflowing benignity of disposition, the same unimpeachable integrity as a judge, the same partial fondness for literature and the fine arts. His son, a very promising boy, in whose education he took great delight, was, indeed, snatched away from his affections by a premature death. But, when it was too late for sorrow and anxiety to avail, the afflicted father stifled the emotions of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and wound up the energies of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> to the firmest tone of stoical fortitude. He was, in like manner, bereaved of his excellent lady, the object of his dearest tenderness; and he endured the loss with a similar firmness, fitted to do <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>... honour either to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> or to religion. In addition to his office as a judge in the court of session, an offer was made to him of a seat in the court of justiciary. But, though the emoluments of this would have made a convenient addition to his income, he refused to accept it; lest its burdens should too much detach him from the pursuit of his favourite studies. To these studies he continued through the whole of a long life to be greatly devoted. His admiration of the manners, literature, and philosophy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was unbounded. Thus strongly prepossessed, it is not to be wondered at, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> which he made between the ancients and moderns, was little favourable to the latter. For among the former he supposed that he saw all that was elegant, manly, and virtuous, all that was praiseworthy and excellent; while the degenerate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the moderns exhibited nothing but effeminacy and corruption. The vacation of the court of session afforded him sufficient leisure to retire every year, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and in autumn, to the country; and he used them to dress in a style of simplicity, as if he had been only a plain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>; and to live among the people upon his estate, with all the kind familiarity and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of an aged father among his grown-up children. Although his estate, from the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a>, afforded comparatively but a moderate income, he would never raise the rents, or displace an old tenant to make room for a new one who offered a higher rent. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the rural economy of some of the ancients, whom he chiefly admired, he accounted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> the true wealth of an estate, and was desirous of no improvement so much as of increasing the number of souls upon his lands, so as to make it greater, in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, than that of those upon the estate of any neighbouring landholder. It was there he had the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of receiving Dr Samuel Johnson, with his friend James Boswell, at the time when these two gentlemen were upon their well-known tour through the Highlands of Scotland. Johnson admired nothing in literature so much as the display of a keen discrimination of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> character, a just <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the principles of moral <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and that vigorous common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> which is the most happily applicable to the ordinary conduct of life. Monboddo delighted in the refinements, the subtleties, the abstractions, the affectations of literature; and in comparison with these, despised the groanings of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and of common affairs. Johnson thought learning and science to be little valuable, except so far as they could be made subservient to the purposes of living usefully and happily with the world, upon his own terms. Monboddo's favourite science taught him to look <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with contempt upon all sublunary, and especially upon all modern things; and to fit life to literature and philosophy, not literature and philosophy to life. James Boswell, therefore, in carrying Johnson to visit Monboddo, probably thought of pitting them one against another, as two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> cocks, and promised himself much sport from the colloquial contest which he expected to ensue between them. But Monboddo was too hospitable and courteous to enter into keen contention with a stranger in his own house. There was much talk between them, but no angry controversy, no exaggeration of that dislike for each other's well-known peculiarities with which they had met. Johnson, it is true, still continued to think Lord Monboddo what he called a prig in literature. Lord Monboddo used frequently to visit London, to which he was allured by the opportunity that great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> affords of enjoying the conversation of a vast number of men of profound erudition. A journey to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> became a favourite amusement of his periods of vacation from the business of the court to which he belonged; and, for a time, he made this journey once a year.
