A carriage, a vehicle that was not in common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the ancients, he considered as an engine of effeminacy and sloth, which it was disgraceful for a man to make use of in travelling. To be dragged at the tail of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, instead of mounting upon his back, seemed, in his eyes, to be a truly ludicrous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of the genuine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of human nature. In all his journeys, therefore, between Edinburgh and London, he was wont to ride on horseback, with a single <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> attending him. He continued this practice, without finding it too fatiguing for his strength, till he was upwards of eighty years of age. Within these few years, on his return from a last visit, which he made on purpose to take leave, before his death, of all his old friends in London, he became exceedingly ill upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and was unable to proceed; and had he not been overtaken by a Scotch friend, who prevailed upon him to travel the remainder of the way in a carriage, he might, perhaps, have actually perished by the way side, or breathed his last in some dirty inn. Since that time, he did not again attempt an equestrian journey to London. In London, his visits were exceedingly acceptable to all his friends, whether of the literary or fashionable world. He delighted to shew himself at court; and the king is said to have taken a pleasure in conversing with the old man with a distinguishing notice that could not but be very flattering to him. A constitution of body, naturally framed to wear well and last long, was strengthened to Lord Monboddo by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, guarded by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and by a tenor of mind too firm to be deeply broken in upon by those passions which consume the principles of life. In the country he always used much the exercises of walking in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and of riding. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> bath was a means of preserving the health, to which he had recourse in all seasons, amidst every severity of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, under every inconvenience of indisposition or business, with a perseverance invincible. He was accustomed, alike in winter and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, to rise at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> in the morning, and, without loss of time, to betake himself to study or wholesome exercise. It is said, that he even found the use of what he called the air bath, or the practice of occasionally walking about, for some minutes, naked, in a room filled with fresh and cool air, to be highly salutary. Lord Monboddo is well known to the world as a man of letters. His first publication was "a Dissertation on the Origin and Progress of Language," in 2 vols. 1773; which were followed by four more vols. the last published not long before his death. In this work, intended chiefly to vindicate the honours of Grecian literature, he attributes the origin of alphabetical writing to the Egyptians; and strenuously maintains, that the ouran-outang is a class of the human <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and that his want of speech is merely accidental. He al- To endeavour to establish the reality of the existence of mermaids, and other fictitious animals. He was induced to undertake another work, for the purpose of defending the cause of Greek philosophy; and published, in five vols. 4to, a work entitled, "Antient <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>," which, like the other, is remarkable for a surprising mixture of erudition and genius, with the most absurd whims and conceits. As a judge, his decisions were found, upright, and learned, and marked with acute discrimination; and free from those paradoxes and partialities which appear in his writings. He attended his judicial duty with indefatigable diligence till within a few days of his death, which happened at his house in Edinburgh, May 26, 1799, at the advanced age of 85. His eldest daughter married some years before his death. His second daughter, in personal loveliness one of the finest women of the age, was beheld in every public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with general admiration, and was sought in marriage by many suitors. Her mind was endowed with all her father's benevolence of temper, and with all his taste for elegant literature, without any portion of his whims and caprices. It was her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> delight to be the nurse and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of his declining age. Her presence contributed to draw around him, in his house, and at his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, all that was truly respectable among the youth of his country. She mingled in the world of fashion, without sharing its follies; and heard those flatteries which are addressed to youth and beauty, without being betrayed to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and selfish vanity which is often the only sentiment that fills the heart of the highly-praised beauty. She delighted in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, in literary conversation, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and in the fine arts, without contracting from this taste, any of that pedantic self-conceit and affectation which usually characterize literary ladies, and whose presence often frightens away the domestic virtues, the graces, the delicacies, and all the more interesting charms of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. When Burns, the well-known Scotch poet, first arrived from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a> to publish his poems in Edinburgh, there was none by whom he was more zealously patronized than by Lord Monboddo and his lovely daughter. No man's feelings were ever more powerfully or exquisitely alive than those of the rustic bard, to the emotions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, or to the admiration of the good and fair. In a poem which he at that time wrote, as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to Edinburgh, he took occasion to celebrate the beauty and excellence of Miss Burnet, in, perhaps, the finest stanza of the whole: "Thy daughters bright thy walks adorn, "Gay as the gilded summer sky, "Sweet as the dewy <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, "Dear as the raptur'd thrill of joy! "Fair Burnet strikes th' adoring eye: "Heaven's beauties on my fancy shine, "I see the Sire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> on high, "And own his work, indeed, divine." She was the ornament of the elegant society of the city in which she resided, her father's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, and the comfort of his domestic life in his declining years. Every amiable and noble sentiment was familiar to her heart, every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> virtue was exemplified in her life. Yet, this woman, thus lovely, thus elegant, thus wise and virtuous, was out off in the flower of her age, and left her father bereft of the last tender tie which bound him to society and to life. She died about six years before him of a consumption; a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> that in Scotland proves too often fatal to the loveliest and most promising among the fair and the young. Neither his philosophy, nor the necessary torpor of the feelings of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old age, were capable of preventing Lord Monboddo from being very deeply affected by so grievous a loss; and from that time he began to droop exceedingly in his health and spirits. Edin. Mag. Burnet. See Poterium and Sanguisorba, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BURNHAM

a market-town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> in England, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 50'. N. Lat. 53°.

BURNING

Pages 16-26

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of fire on some pabulum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, by which the minute parts thereof are put into a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and some of them affuming the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of fire themselves, fly off in orbem, while the rest are dissipated in form of vapour or reduced to ashes. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNITION">Ignition</a>. Extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">Cases</a> of Burning. We have instances of persons burnt by fire kindled within their own bodies. A woman at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, who used to drink brandy to excess, was one night reduced to ashes by a fire from within, all but her head and the ends of her fingers. Signora Corn. Zangari, or, as others call her, Corn. Bandi, an aged lady, of an unblemished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CESENA">Cesena</a> in Romagna, underwent the same fate in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1731. She had retired in the evening to her chamber somewhat indisposed; and in the morning was found in the middle of the room reduced to ashes, all except her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, legs, skull, and three fingers. The stockings and shoes she had on were not burnt in the least. The ashes were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and, on pressing between the fingers, vanished, leaving behind a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tinkling moisture with which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> was smeared; the walls and furniture of the room being covered with a moist cinerious foot, which had not only stained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> in the chests, but had penetrated into the closet, as well as into the room overhead, the walls of which were moistened with the same viscid humour.—We have various other relations of persons burnt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in this unaccountable manner. Sig. Mondini, Bianchini, and Maffei, have written treatises express to account for the cause of so extraordinary an event: <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fire it could not be, since this would likewise have burnt the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> and the room; besides that it would have required many hours, and a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fuel, to reduce a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body to ashes; and, after all, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> would have remained entire, as they were anciently found after the fiercest funeral fires. Some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the effect to a mine of sulphur under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; others to a miracle; while others suppose that art of villainy had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in it. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> maintains, that such a conflagration might have arisen from the inflammable matters wherein the human body naturally abounds. Sig. Bianchini accounts for the conflagration of the lady above-mentioned, from her using a bath or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTION">lotion</a> of camphorated spirit of wine when she found herself out of order. Maffei supposes it owing to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, but to lightning <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in her own body, agreeable to his doctrine, which is, That lightning does not proceed from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, but is always produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it is seen and its effects perceived. We have have had a late attempt to establish the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that these destroying internal fires are caused in the entrails of the body by inflamed effluvia of the blood; by juices and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> in the stomach; by the many combustible matters which abound in living bodies for the purposes of life; and, finally, by the fiery <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> which exhale from the fettlings of spirit of wine, brandies, and other hot liquors, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNICA">tunica</a> villofa of the stomach and other adipose or fat membranes; within which those spirits engender a kind of camphor, which in the night <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, by a full respiration, are put in a stronger motion, and are more apt to be set on fire. Others ascribe the cause of such persons being set on fire to lightning; and their burning so entirely, to the greater quantity of phosphorus and other combustible matters they contained.—For our own part, we can by no means pretend to explain the cause of such a phenomenon: but for the interests of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, we wish it could be derived from something <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> to the human body; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, to the calamities of human life already known, we superadd a suspicion that we may unexpectedly, and without the least warning, be consumed by an internal fire, the thought is too dreadful to be borne. Burning, or Brenning, in our old customs, denotes an infectious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, got in the streets by conversing with lewd women, and supposed to be the same with what we now call the venereal disease. In a manuscript of the vocation of John <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, written by himself, he speaks of Dr Hugh Wotton, who was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> in 1556, but deprived by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Pole for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, thus: "At this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> is lecherous Wotton, who is more practised in the arts of breech-burning, than all the whores of the streets. He not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago burnt a beggar of St Botolph's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>." See Streets. Burning, in antiquity, a way of disposing of the dead, much practised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and still retained by several nations in the East and West Indies. The antiquity of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> rises as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the Theban <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, where we are told of the great solemnity accompanying this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> at the pyre of Menelaus and Archimorus, who were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Jair, the eighth judge of Israel. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> abounds with funeral obsequies of this nature. In the inward regions of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, the practice was of very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, and the continuance long: for we are told, that, in the reign of Julian, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Chionia burnt his son's body, and deposited the ashes in a silver urn. Coeval almost with the first instances of this kind in the east, was the practice in the western parts of the world. The Heruliens, the Getes, and the Thracians, had all along observed it; and its antiquity was as great with the Celts, Sarmatians, and other neighbouring nations. The origin of this custom seems to have been out of friendship to the deceased: their ashes were preserved as we preserve a lock of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>, or a scarf, which had been the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a deceased friend. Kings were burnt in cloth made of the asbestos <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, that their ashes might be preserved pure from any mixture with the fuel and other matters thrown on the funeral pile. The same method is still observed with the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. Among the Greeks, the body was placed on the top of a pile, on which were thrown <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> animals, and even slaves and captives, besides unguents and perfumes. In the funeral of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a> we find a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sheep and oxen thrown in, then four horses, followed by two dogs, and lastly by 12 Trojan prisoners. The like is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> in the funerals of his Trojans; where, besides oxen, swine, and all manner of cattle, we find eight youths condemned to the flames. The first thing was the fat of the beasts, wherewith the body was covered, that it might consume the sooner: it being reckoned great felicity to be quickly reduced to ashes. For the like reason, where numbers were to be burnt at the same time, care was taken to mix with the rest some of humid constitutions, and therefore more easily to be inflamed. Thus we are assured by Plutarch and Macrobius, that for every ten men it was customary to put in one woman. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a> usually had their arms burnt with them. The garments worn by the living were also thrown on the pile, with other ornaments and presents; a piece of extravagance which the Athenians carried to so great a height, that some of their lawgivers were forced to restrain them, by severe penalties, from defrauding the living by their liberality to the dead.—In some cases, burning was expressly forbidden among the Romans, and even looked upon as the highest impiety. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, who died before the breeding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, were interred unburnt in the ground, in a particular place set apart for this purpose, called fugurundarium. The like was practised with regard to those who had been struck dead with lightning, who were never to be burnt again. Some say that burning was denied to suicides.—The manner of burning among the Romans was not unlike that of the Greeks; the corpse, being brought out without the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, was carried directly to the place appointed for burning it; which, if it joined to the sepulchre, was called cibulum; if separate from it, ufrina; and there laid on the rugus or pyra, a pile of wood prepared on which to burn it, built in shape of an altar, but of different height, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the deceased. The wood used was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> from such trees as contain most pitch or rosin; and if any other were used, they split it, for the more easy catching fire: round the pile they set cypresses trees, probably to hinder the noisome smell of the corpse. The body was not placed on the bare pile, but on the couch or bed whereon it lay. This done, the next of blood performed the ceremony of lighting the pile; which they did with a torch, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> their faces all the while the other way, as if it were done with reluctance. During the ceremony, decursions and games were celebrated; after which came the offugium, or gathering of the bones and ashes; also washing and anointing them, and repotting them in urns. Burning, among surgeons, denotes the application of an actual cautery, that is, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, to the part affected; otherwise denominated cauterization. The whole art of physic among the Japanese lies in the choice of places proper to be burnt: which are varied according to the disease. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Mogul, the colic is cured by an iron ring applied red-hot about the patient's navel. Certain it is, that some very extraordinary cures have been performed accidentally by burning. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is recorded in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the academy of sciences by M. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a>. A woman of about 35 became subject to a head- Burning, which at times was so violent that it drove her out of her senses, making her sometimes stupid and foolish, at other times raving and furious. The seat of the pain was in the forehead, and over the eyes, which were inflamed, and looked violently red and sparkling; and the most violent fits of it were attended with nausea and vomitings. In the times of the fits, she could take no food; but out of them, had a very good stomach. Mr Homberg had in vain attempted her cure for three years with all kinds of medicines; only opium succeeded; and that but little, all its effect being only the taking off the pain for a few hours. The redness of her eyes was always the sign of an approaching fit. One night, feeling a fit coming on, she went to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the bed; but first walked up to the glass with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> in her hand, to see how her eyes looked: in observing this, the candle set fire to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>: and as she was alone, her head was terribly burnt before the fire could be extinguished. Mr Homberg was sent for, and ordered bleeding and proper dressings: but it was perceived, that the expected fit this night never came on; the pain of the burning wore off by degrees; and the patient found herself from that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> cured of the headache, which had never returned in four years after, which was the time when the account was communicated. Another case, not less remarkable than the former, was communicated to Mr Homberg by a physician at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>. A woman, who for several years had her legs and thighs swelled in an extraordinary manner, found some relief from rubbing them before the fire with brandy every morning and evening. One evening the fire chanced to catch the brandy she had rubbed herself with, and slightly burnt her. She applied some brandy to her burn; and in the night all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> her legs and thighs were swelled with was entirely discharged by urine, and the swelling did not again return. **Burning-Glass**, Sec. BUSH. **Burning-Glass**, a convex glass commonly spherical, which being exposed directly to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, collects all the rays falling thereon into a very small space called the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>; where wood or any other combustible <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> being put, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be set on fire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> burning-glass is also used to denote those concave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>, whether composed of glass quicksilvered, or of metallic matters, which burn by reflection, condensing the sun's rays into a focus similar to the former. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of burning-glasses appears to have been very ancient. Diodorus Siculus, Lucian, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a>, Zonaras, Galen, Anthemius, Euclidius, Tzetzes, and others, attest, that by means of them <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> set fire to the Roman fleet at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>. Tzetzes is so particular in his account of this matter, that his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> suggested to Kircher the method by which it was probably accomplished. That author says, that "Archimedes set fire to Marcellus's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, by means of a burning glass composed of small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> mirrors moving every way upon hinges; which, when placed in the sun's rays, directed them upon the Roman fleet, so as to reduce it to ashes at the distance of a bow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>." A very particular testimony we have also from Anthemius of Lydia, who takes pains to prove the possibility of setting fire to a fleet, or any other combustible body, at such a distance. That the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were also acquainted with the use of catoptric or refracting burning-glasses, appears from a passage in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of The Clouds, which clearly treats of their effects. The author introduces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> as examining Strephades about the method he had discovered of getting clear of his debts. He replies, that "he thought of making use of a burning-glass which he had hitherto used in kindling his fire;" "for (says he) should they bring a writ against me, I'll immediately place my glass in the sun at some little distance from it, and set it on fire." Pliny and Lactantius have also spoken of glasses that burn by refraction. The former calls them balls or globes of glass or crystal, which, exposed to the sun, transmit a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> sufficient to set fire to cloth, or corrode the dead <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of those patients who stand in need of cauteries; and the latter, after Clemens Alexandrinus, takes notice that fire may be kindled by interposing glasses filled with water between the sun and the object, so as to transmit the rays to it. It seems difficult to conceive how they should know such glasses would burn without knowing they would magnify, which it is granted they did not, till towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 13th century, when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> were first thought on. For as to those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of spectacles, M. de la Hire observes, they do not prove any such thing; and he solves this, by observing, that their burning-glasses being spheres, either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> or full of water, their foci would be one-fourth of their diameter distant from them. If then their diameter were supposed half a foot, which is the most we can allow, an object must be at an inch and a half distance to perceive it magnified; those at greater distances do not appear greater, but only more confused through the glass than out of it. It is no wonder, therefore, the magnifying property of convex glasses was unknown, and the burning one known. It is more wonderful there should be 300 years between the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of spectacles and telescopes. Among the ancients, the burning mirrors of Archimedes and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a> are famous: the former we have already taken notice of; by the other, the navy of Vitellius besieging Byzantium, according to Zonaras, was burnt to ashes. Among the moderns, the most remarkable burning mirrors are those of Settala, of Villette, of Tschirnhausen, of Buffon, of Trudaine, and of Parker. Settala, canon of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, made a parabolic mirror, which, according to Shottus, burnt pieces of wood at the distance of 15 or 16 paces. The following things are noted of it in the Acta Eruditorum. 1. Green wood takes fire instantaneously, so as a strong <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> cannot extinguish it. 2. Water boils immediately; and eggs in it are presently edible. 3. A mixture of tin and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, three inches thick, drops presently; and iron and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> plate becomes red-hot presently, and a little after burns into holes. 4. Things not capable of melting, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, bricks, &c., become soon red-hot, like iron. 5. Slate becomes first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, then a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> glass. 6. Tiles are converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> glass, and shells into a blackish yellow one. 7. A pumice stone, emitted from a volcano, melts into white glass; and 8. A piece of crucible also vitrifies in eight minutes. 9. Bones are soon turned into an opaque glass, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> into a black one. The breadth of this mirror is near three Leipsic cells, its focus two cells from it; it is made of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and and its substance is not above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the thickness of the back of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. Villette, a French <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of Lyons, made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> mirror, which was bought by Tavernier and presented to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, bought by the king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>; a third, presented by the French king to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy; a fourth has been in England, where it was publicly exposed. The effects hereof, as found by Dr Harris and Dr Desaguliers, are, that a silver sixpence is melted in 7½", a King George's halfpenny in 16", and runs with a hole in 34". Tin melts in 3", <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> iron in 16", flate in 3"; a fossil shell calcines in 7"; a piece of Pompey's pillar at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> vitrifies, the black part in 50", the white in 54"; copper ore in 8"; bone calcines in 4", vitrifies in 33". An <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a> melts into a substance like a turquoise stone; a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> weighing four grains loses <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>-eighths of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>: the asbestos vitrifies; as all other bodies will do, if kept long enough in the focus; but when once vitrified, the mirror can go no farther with them. This mirror is 47 inches wide, and is ground to a sphere of 76 inches radius; so that its focus is about 38 inches from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a>. Its substance is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of tin, copper, and tin-glass. Every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENS">lens</a>, whether convex, plano-convex, or concavo-convex, collects the sun's rays, dispersed over its convexity, into a point by refraction; and is therefore a burning glass. The most considerable of this kind is that made by M. de Tschirnhaufen: the diameters of his lenses are three and four feet, the focus at the distance of 12 feet, and its diameter an inch and a half. To make the focus the more vivid, it is collected a second time by a second lens <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the first, and placed in that point where the diameter of the cone of rays formed by the first lens is equal to the diameter of the second: so that it receives them all; and the focus, from an inch and a half, is contracted into the space of eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and its force increased proportionally. This glass vitrifies tiles, flates, pumice-stones, &c., in a moment. It melts sulphur, pitch, and all rosin, under water; the ashes of vegetables, woods, and other matters, are transmuted into glass; and every thing applied to its focus is either melted, turned into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a>, or into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. Tschirnhaufen observes, that it succeeds best when the matter applied is laid on a hard <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> well burnt. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton presented a burning-glass to the royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, consisting of seven concave glasses, so placed as that all their foci join in one physical point. Each glass is about 11 inches and a half in diameter; five of them are placed round the seventh, to which they are all contiguous; and they form a kind of segment of a sphere, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUBTENSE">subtense</a> is about 34 inches and a half, and the central glass lies about an inch farther in than the rest. The common focus is about 22 inches and a half distant, and about an inch in diameter. This glass vitrifies brick or tile in 1", and melts <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in 30". It would appear, however, that glass quicksilvered is a more proper material for burning-glasses than <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; for the effects of that specimen wherewith Mr Macquer melted the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a> seem to have been superior to those above mentioned, though the mirror itself was much smaller. The diameter of this glass was only 22 inches, and its focal distance 28. Black flint, when exposed to the focus, being powdered to prevent its crackling and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> about, and secured in a large piece of charcoal, bubbled up and ran into transparent glass in less than half a minute. Hessian crucibles, and glass-house pots, vitrified completely in three or four seconds. Forged iron smoked, boiled, and changed into a vitreous scoria as soon as it was exposed to the focus. The gypsum of Montmartre, when the flat sides of the plates or leaves of which it is composed were presented to the glass, did not show the least disposition to melt; but, on presenting a transverse <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of it, or the edges of the plates, it melted in an instant, with a hissing noise, into a brownish yellow matter. Calcareous stones did not completely melt: but there was detached from them a circle more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> than the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, and of the size of the focus; the separation of which seemed to be occasioned by the shrinking of the matter which had begun to enter into fusion. The white calx of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, commonly called diaphoretic antimony, melted better than the calcareous stones, and changed into an opaque pretty glossy substance like white enamel. It was observed, that the whiteness of the calcareous stones and the antimonial calx was of great disadvantage to their fusion, by reason of their reflecting great part of the sun's rays; so that the subject could not undergo the full <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of the heat thrown upon it by the burning-glass. The case was the same with metallic bodies; which melted so much the more difficulty as they were more white and polished; and this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> was so remarkable, that in the focus of this mirror, so fusible a metal as silver, when its surface was polished, did not melt at all. Plate CXXXI, fig. 1, represents M. Buffon's burning mirror, which he with great reason supposes to be of the same nature with that of Archimedes. It consists of a number of small mirrors of glass quicksilvered, all of which are held together by an iron frame. Each of these small mirrors is also moveable by a contrivance on the back part of the frame, so that their reflections may all coincide in one point. By this means they are capable of being accommodated to various heights of the sun, and to different distances. The adjusting them in this manner takes up a considerable time; but after they are so adjusted, the focus will continue unaltered for an hour or more. Fig. 2, represents a contrivance of M. Buffon's for diminishing the thickness of very large refracting lenses. He observes, that in the large lenses of this kind, and which are most convenient for many purposes, the thickness of the glass in the middle is so great as very much to diminish their force. For this reason he proposes to form a burning-glass of concentric circular pieces of glass, each resting upon the other, as represented in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. His method is to divide the convex <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the lens into three equal parts. Thus, suppose the diameter to be 26 inches, and the thickness in the middle to be three inches: By dividing the lens into three concentric circles, and laying the one over the other, the thickness of the middle piece needs be only one inch; at the same time that the lens will have the same convexity, and almost the same focal distance, as in the other case; while the effects of it must be much greater, on account of the greater thinness of the glass. M. Trudaine, a French <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, constructed a burning lens on a new principle. It was composed of two circular segments of glass spheres, each four feet in diameter, applied with their concave sides towards each other. The cavity was filled with spirit of wine, of which it contained 40 pints. It was presented by the maker to the royal academy of sciences, but was not long after, broken by accident. The expense of constructing it amounted to about £1000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. After all, it does not appear that the effects of this lens were very great. Mr Magellan informs us, that it could only coagulate the particles of platinum in 20 minutes, while Mr Parker's lens entirely melted them in less than two. A large burning lens, indeed, for the purpose of fusing and vitrifying such substances as resist the fires of ordinary furnaces, and especially for the application of heat in vacuo, and in other circumstances in which heat cannot be applied by any other means, has long been a desideratum among persons concerned in philosophical experiments: And it appears now to be in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> accomplished by Mr Parker. His lens is three feet in diameter, made of flint-glass, and which, when fixed in its frame, exposes a surface two feet eight inches and a half in the clear. In the Elevation represented on Plate CXXXII, A is the lens of the diameter mentioned: thickness in the centre, three inches and one-fourth: weight, 212 pounds: length of the focus, six feet eight inches; diameter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>, one inch. B, a second lens, whose diameter in the frame is 16 inches, and shows in the clear 13 inches: thickness in the centre, one inch five-eighths: weight 21 pounds: length of focus 29 inches: diameter of ditto, three-eighths of an inch. When the two above lenses are compounded together, the length of the focus is five feet three inches: diameter of ditto, half an inch. C, a truncated cone, composed of 21 ribs of wood: at the larger end is fixed the great lens A; at the smaller extremity the lesser lens B: near the smaller end is also fixed a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> D, passing through the pillar L, moveable by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> turning in the said pillar, by means of the handle E, and thus giving a vertical motion to the machine. F, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of wood, fixed between the two lower ribs of the cone at G; having, within a chafed mortice in which it moves, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> H, with the iron plate I, fixed thereto; and this part turning on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> and socket, K, a method is thereby obtained of placing the matter under experiment, so as to be acted upon by the focal rays in the most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and powerful manner. LL, a strong mahogany frame, moving on castors, MM. Immediately under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> N are three friction <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, by which the machine moves horizontally. O, a strong iron bow, in which the lens and the cone hang. Section.—a, The great lens marked A in the elevation. b, The frame which contains the lens. c, The small lens marked B. d, The frame which contains the small lens. e, The truncated cone, marked C. f, The bar on which the apparatus marked F moves. g, The iron plate marked I. h, The cone of rays formed by the refraction of the great lens a, and falling on the lens c. i, The cone of rays formed by the refraction of the lens c. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">Front</a>-view.—k, The great burning lens. l, The frame containing it. m, The strong iron bow in which it hangs. From a great number of experiments made with this lens, in the presence of many scientific persons, the following are selected as specimens of its powers. | Substances fused, with their weight and time of fusion. | Weight in Grains | Time in Seconds | |----------------------------------------------------------|-----------------|----------------| | Gold, pure | 20 | 3 | | Silver, do | 20 | 4 | | Copper, do | 33 | 20 | | Platinum, do | 10 | 3 | | <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICKEL">Nickel</a>, | 16 | 3 | | Bar iron, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> | 10 | 12 | | Cast iron, a cube | 10 | 3 | | Steel, a cube | 10 | 12 | | Scoria of wrought iron | 12 | 2 | | Terra ponderosa, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARYTES">barytes</a> | 10 | 7 | | Topaz, or chrysolite | 3 | 45 | | An oriental emerald | 2 | 25 | | Crystal pebble | 7 | 6 | | White <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> | 10 | 30 | | Flint, oriental | 10 | 30 | | Rough cornelian | 10 | 75 | | Jasper | 10 | 25 | | Onyx | 10 | 20 | | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARNET">Garnet</a> | 10 | 17 | | White rhomboidal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> | 10 | 60 | | Zeolites | 10 | 23 | | Rotten stone | 10 | 80 | | Common slate | 10 | 2 | | Asbestos | 10 | 10 | | Common lime-stone | 10 | 55 | | Pumice-stone | 10 | 24 | | <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">Lava</a> | 10 | 7 | | Volcanic clay | 10 | 60 | | Cornish moor-stone | 10 | 60 | Burning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>. See Etna, Hecla, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, and Volcano, with the plates accompanying them. Burning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">Springs</a>. Of these there are many in different parts of the world; particularly one in Dauphiny near Grenoble; another near Hermannstadt in Transylvania; a third at Chermay, a village near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; a fourth in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Friburg; and a fifth not far from the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. There also is, or was, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the same kind at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIGAN">Wigan</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, which, upon the approach of a lighted candle, would take fire and burn like spirit of wine for a whole day. But the most remarkable one of this kind, or at least that of which we have the most particular description, was discovered in 1711 at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROSELEY">Broseley</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>. The following account of this remarkable spring was given by the reverend Mr Mason, Woodwardian professor at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, dated February 18, 1746. "The well for four or five feet deep is six or seven feet wide; within that is another hole of like depth dug in the clay, in the bottom whereof is placed a cylindric earthen vessel, of about four or five inches diameter at the mouth, having the bottom taken off, and the sides well fixed in the clay." rammed close about it. Within the pot is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> water, thick as puddle, continually forced up with a violent motion beyond that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, and a rumbling hollow noise, rising or falling by fits five or six inches; but there was no appearance of any vapour rising, which perhaps might have been visible, had not the sun shone so bright. Upon putting a candle down at the end of a stick, at about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a yard distance, it took fire, darting and flailing after a very violent manner for about half a yard high, much in the manner of spirits in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>, but with great agitation. It was said, that a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-kettle had been made to boil in about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> minutes time, and that it had been left burning for 48 hours without any sensible diminution. It was extinguished by putting a wet mop upon it; which must be kept there for a little time, otherwise it would not go out. Upon the removal of the mop there arises a sulphurous smoke lasting about a minute, and yet the water is very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> to the touch." In 1755, this well totally disappeared by the sinking of a coal-pit in its neighbourhood. The cause of the inflammable property of such waters is, with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, supposed to be their mixture with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a>, which is a very inflammable substance, and has the property of burning on the surface of water. **Burning of Colours**, among painters. There are several colours that require burning; as, First, Lamp-black, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of so greasy a nature, that, except it is burnt, it will require a long time to dry. The method of burning, or rather drying, lamp black, is as follows: Put it into a crucible over a clear fire, letting it remain till it be red hot, or so near it that no manner of smoke arises from it. Secondly, Umber, which, if it be intended for colour for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, or to be a shadow for gold, then burning fits it for both these purposes. In order to burn umber, you must put it into the naked fire, in large lumps, and not take it out till it is thoroughly red hot; if you have a mind to be more curious, put it into a crucible, and keep it over the fire till it be red hot. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">Ivory</a> also must be burnt to make black, thus: Fill two crucibles with shavings of ivory, then clap their two mouths together, and bind them fast with an iron wire, and lute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> close with clay, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and horse-dung, well beaten together; then set it over the fire, covering it all over with coals; let it remain in the fire till you are sure that the matter enclosed is thoroughly red hot; then take it out of the fire; but do not open the crucibles till they are perfectly cold; for were they opened while hot, the matter would turn to ashes; and so it will be, if the joints are not luted close. **Burnisher**, a round polished piece of steel serving to smooth and give a lustre to metals. Of these there are different kinds of different figures, straight, crooked, &c. Half burnishers are used to folder silver, as well as to give a lustre. Burnishers for gold and silver are commonly made of a dog's or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>'s tooth, set in the end of an iron or wooden handle. Of late, agates and pebbles have been introduced, which many prefer to the dog's tooth. The burnishers used by engravers in copper, usually serve with one end to burnish, and with the other to burnisher scrape. **Burnishing**, the art of smoothing or polishing a metallic body, by a brisk rubbing of it with a burnisher. Book-binders burnish the edges of their books, by rubbing them with a dog's tooth. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BURNLEY">Burnley</a>**, a town of Lancashire in England, situated in W. Long. 2° 5'. N. Lat. 51° 38'. **Burns**, Robert, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a>, one of the western counties of Scotland. He was the son of humble parents; and his father passed through life in the condition of a hired labourer, or of a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>. Even in this situation, however, it was not hard for him to send his children to the parish school, to receive the ordinary instruction in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, and the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. By this course of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> young Robert profited to a degree that might have encouraged his friends to delude him to one of the liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, had not his father's poverty made it necessary to remove him from school, as soon as he had grown up, to earn for himself the means of support as a hired ploughboy or shepherd. The expense of education in the parish-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Scotland is so small, that hardly any parents who are able to labour want the means of giving to their children at least such education as young Burns received. From the spring labours of a ploughboy, from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> employment of a shepherd, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>-youth often returns for a few months, eagerly to pursue his education at the parish-school. It was so with Burns; he returned from labour to learning, and from learning went again to labour, till his mind began to open to the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and knowledge; till he began to feel a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for books, and for the subjects of books, which was to give a colour to the whole thread of his future life. On nature he soon began to gaze with new discernment and with new enthusiasm; his mind's eye opened to perceive affecting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and sublimity, where, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> peasant, there was sought to be seen but water, earth, and sky—but animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. What might perhaps first contribute to dispose his mind to poetical efforts, is one particular in the devotional piety of the Scotch peasantry. It is still common for them to make their children get by heart the Psalms of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, in the version of homely rhymes which is used in their churches. In the morning and in the evening of every day, or at least on the evening of every Saturday and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, these Psalms are sung in solemn family-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> is read, and extemporary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> is fervently uttered. The whole books of the sacred Scriptures are thus continually in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of almost every peasant. And it is impossible that there should not be occasionally some souls among them, awakened to the divine emotions of genius by that rich assemblage which those books present, of almost all that is interesting in incidents, or picturesque in imagery, or affectingly sublime or tender in sentiments and character. It is impossible that those rude rhymes, and the simple artless music with which they are accompanied, should not occasionally excite some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to a fond perception of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. That Burns had felt these impulses, will appear undeniably certain to whoever shall carefully peruse his Cottar's. tar's Saturday's Night; or shall remark, with nice observation, the various fragments of Scripture sentiment, of Scripture imagery, of Scripture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which are scattered throughout his works. Still more interesting to the young peasantry are those ancient ballads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and war, of which a great number are, in the south of Scotland, yet popularly known, and often sung by the rustic maid or matron at her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>-wheel. They are listened to with ravished ears by old and young. Their rude melody; that mingled curiosity and awe which are naturally excited by the very idea of their antiquity; the exquisitely tender and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> complaints sometimes poured forth in them; the gallant deeds of knightly heroism, which they sometimes celebrate; their wild tales of demons, ghosts, and fairies, in whose existence <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> alone has believed; the manners which they represent; the obsolete, yet picturesque and expressive, language in which they are often clothed—give them wonderful power to transport every imagination, and to agitate every heart. To the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of Burns they were like a happy breeze touching the wires of an Æolian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, and calling forth the most ravishing melody. Beside all this, the Gentle Shepherd, and the other poems of Allan Ramsay, have long been highly popular in Scotland. They fell early into the hands of Burns; and while the fond applause which they received drew his emulation, they presented him likewise treasures of phraseology and models of versification. He got acquainted at the same time with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> of Robert Fergusson, written chiefly in the Scottish dialect, and exhibiting many specimens of uncommon poetical excellence. The Seasons of Thomson too, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">Grave</a> of Blair, the far-famed Elegy of Gray, the Paradise Lost of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINSTREL">Minstrel</a> of Beattie, were so commonly read, even among those with whom Burns would naturally associate, that poetical curiosity, although even less ardent than his, could in such circumstances have little difficulty in procuring them.

BURNTWOOD

Pages 31-31

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in England, situated on a hill, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 25', N. Lat. 51° 38'.

BURR-PUMP

Pages 31-31
or BILGE-Pump, differs from the common pump, in having a staff, fix, seven, or eight feet long, with a bar of wood, whereunto the leather is nailed, and this serves instead of a box. So two men, standing over the pump, thrust down this staff, to the middle whereof is fastened a rope, for fix, eight, or ten to hale by, thus pulling it up and down.

BURRE

Pages 31-31

BOUREE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Boree, a kind of a dance composed of three steps joined together in two motions, begun with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROTCHET">crotchet</a> rising. The first couplet contains twice four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> twice eight. It consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> and couplet.

BURROCK

Pages 31-31

a small weir <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, where weels are laid in a river, for the taking of fish.

BURROUGHS'

Pages 31-32

BURR BURR Burrough's BURROUGHS's MACHINE for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> and polishing glass, invented by Mr Burroughs of Southwark; and for which he received from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> for the encouragement of arts a premium of 70l. Plate CXXXI. This machine consists of a cog-wheel A (fig. 3.), 12 feet in diameter, carrying 72 cogs; which turn a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNDLE">trundle</a>-head B, one foot four inches in diameter, and furnished with eight <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>; and also a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> spur-wheel C, of 12 cogs; and one foot eight inches in diameter. The trundle-head B turns a spur-wheel D of 10 cogs, and two feet eight inches in diameter. This spur-wheel has two cranks, a b, in its shaft; one of which a gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to a wooden frame, c, about 34 inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 19 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. On the under side of this frame are fastened by screws 12 pieces of polished metal, each five inches and a half long, and three broad, covered with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; and underneath these polishers a glass-plate cemented in another frame is placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> d, and polished with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">tripoli</a> by the motion given to the upper frame by the crank a. The nuts of the screws which fasten the polishers to the upper frame are not screwed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the wood, in order to give the frame room to play; by which contrivance the perpendicular rise of the crank is avoided, and the motion of the polishers is always <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> and equal. The under frame may be moved by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> without stopping the machine; by which means the plate, when larger than the polishing frame can cover in its motion, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be equally polished in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. The other crank b gives motion to two other polishers marked n, o, which have an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> motion by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> of the crank; they move upon the same plate, and have an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of polishers as that already described. The same crank also gives motion to a contrivance represented at e for polishing spectacle-glasses. It consists of two segments of the same sphere; one concave and the other convex. On the latter the glasses are cemented; and polished by the former, which is moved by the crank b. The convex segment may be moved round by the hand without stopping the machine, so that all the glasses on its superficies will be equally polished. The other spur-wheel C, by means of a crank in its shaft, gives motion to another frame g, employed in grinding the glass plates. The rod h, extended from the crank f to the frame g, is fastened to the latter by means of a pivot, in order to admit of a rotatory motion, as well as that given it by the crank in a longitudinal direction. This rotatory motion is effected by means of a rod of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> i, called a trigger, sharp at the extremity next the frame, where it touches the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a horizontal spur-wheel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> circular piece of wood, fixed on the grinding plate, while the other end is extended three feet two inches to the centre of motion. But this contrivance, in which the merit of the machine principally consists, will be much better conceived from a small delineation of it by itself (fig. 4.), where F is the crank marked f in fig. 3., and turned by the spur-wheel C in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. G is the trigger, three feet two inches long. I, a roll fixed on the trigger for the rod to slide on. H, the horizontal spur-wheel, eleven inches in diameter, fixed on the grinding plate; the teeth of which are touched by the trigger; but with a very unequal force, as it will wholly depend upon the Burrough's grinding-plate's being farther from, or nearer to, the Machine centre of motion of the trigger. By this simple contrivance, the grinding-plate has a very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> motion, never moving exactly in the same track, and therefore must grind the plates equally in every part. Several attempts have been made by others for producing the same effect; but without success; the grinding-plate always follows the same track, and consequently the plates are ground equally.

BURROW

Pages 32-32

Sir James, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> office, was elected F.R.S. and F.A.S. 1751. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mr Wcif in 1772, he was prevailed on to fill the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> till the anniversary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, when he resigned it to Sir John Pringle; and August 10, 1773, when the society presented an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to his majesty, he received the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. He published two volumes of Reports in 1766; two others in 1771 and 1776; and a volume of Decisions of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a> upon settlement <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> from 1732 to 1772 (to which was subjoined An <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNCTUATION">Punctuation</a>), in three parts, 4to, 1768, 1772, 1776. The Essay was also printed separately in 4to, 1773. He published, without his name, "A few Anecdotes and Observations relating to Oliver Cromwell and his family, serving to rectify several errors concerning him," published by Nicol, Comn. Papadopoli, in his Historia Gymnasi Patavini, 1763, 4to. He died in 1782.

BURROWS

Pages 32-32

holes in a warren, serving as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> for rabbits, &c. A coney's coming out of her burrow is called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOLTING">bolting</a>. To catch conies, they sometimes lay purse-nets over the burrows, then put in a terrier <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> muzzled, which making the creature bolt, she is caught in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>.

BURSA

Pages 32-32

Burfe, originally signifies a purse. In middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers it is more particularly used for a little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in a university, for the residence of students, called burfals or burfarii. In the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> it still denotes a foundation for the maintenance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> scholars in their studies. The nomination to burfes is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the patrons and founders thereof. The burfes of colleges are not benefices, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> places assigned to certain countries and persons. A burfe becomes vacant by the burfer's being promoted to a cure. BURSÆ mucose. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BURSAR

Pages 32-32
or Burser, (Burarius), is used in middle-age writers for a treasurer or cash-keeper. In this sense we meet with burfars of colleges. Conventual burfars were officers in monasteries, who were to deliver up their account yearly on the day after Michaelmas. The word is formed from the Latin burfa, whence also the English word purse; hence also the officer, who in a college is called burfar, in a ship is called purser. Bursars, or Burfers, (Burfarii), also denote those to whom stipends are paid out of a burfe or fund appointed for that purpose.

BURSARIA

Pages 32-33

BURSARIA, the bursary, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exchequer of collegiate and coventual bodies; or the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of receiving, paying, and accounting by the bursarii or bursers.

BURSE

Pages 33-33

in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, denotes a public edifice in certain cities, for the meeting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to negotiate bills, and confer on other matters relating to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and trade. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, burse amounts to the same with what we otherwise call an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of this kind to which the name Burse was given, Guiechardin affirms us was at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>; and it took its denomination from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a> adjoining to it, built by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the family de la Bourse, whose arms, which are three purses, are still found on the crowning over the portal of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Catel's account is somewhat different, viz. that the merchants of Bruges bought a house <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment to meet in, at which was the sign of the purse. From this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> the name was afterwards transferred to the like places in others, as in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. This last, anciently known by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> burse of merchants, had the denomination since given it by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> exchange. The most considerable burse is that of Amsterdam, which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, 230 feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 130 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, round which runs a peristyle 20 feet wide. The columns of the peristyle, which are 46, are numbered, for the conveniency of finding people. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> hold 4500 persons. In the times of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> there were public places for the meeting of merchants in most of the trading cities in the empire; that built at Rome, in the 259th year after its foundation, under the consulate of Appius Claudius and Publius Servilius, was denominated the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of merchants; some remains of it are still to be seen, and are known by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Romans under the name loggia. The Hans <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>, after the example of the Romans, gave the name of colleges to their burse. BURSERA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BURSTEN

Pages 33-33

denotes a person who has a rupture. See Rupture. BURTHEN of a Ship. See Burden. BURTON upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, in England. It had formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>; and over the river Trent it has now a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, supported by 37 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. It consists chiefly of one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> street, which runs from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the abbey stood to the bridge, and has a good market for corn and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Burton ale is reckoned the best of any brought to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. Long. 1. 36. N. Lat. 52. 48.

BURTON

Pages 34-34

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a small tackle consisting of two single blocks, and may be made fast anywhere at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, for hoisting small things in and out.

BURY

Pages 34-34

is sometimes used to denote the hole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> den of some animal under ground. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say the bury of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>, a tortoise, or the like. The grillo-talpa, or mole-cricket, digs itself a bury with its fore-feet, which are made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and strong for that purpose. Naturalists speak of a kind of urchins in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Maraguan, which have two entries to their buries, one towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the other to the south, which they open and shut alternately as the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> happens to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>. Bury, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, about 80 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> in the family of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 20'. N. Lat. 53° 36'. Bury St Edmund's, or St Edmund's Bury, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, about 12 miles east of Newmarket, and 70 north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. E. Long. 0° 45'. N. Lat. 52° 20'.

BURYING

Pages 34-34

the same with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">BURIAL</a>. BURYING Alive was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of a vealife who had violated her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of virginity. The unhappy priestess was let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into a deep pit, with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on. But this was only for show; for the moment she was let down, they began to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> upon her till the pit was filled up. Some middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers seem to make burying alive (defolio) the punishment of a woman thief. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> gives instances of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of persons who have been buried alive. The famous Duns Scotus is of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; who, having been seized with a catalepsy, was thought dead, and laid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> among his fathers, but raised again by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> in whose absence he had been buried. Bartholin gives an account of a woman, who, on recovering from an apoplexy, could not be convinced but that she was dead, and solicited so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and so earnestly to be buried, that they were forced to comply; and performed the ceremonies, at least in appearance.
