The ladies of his age were charmed with the prospect of having a dictator whom they might subdue by their attractions. "In vain did the genius of Cato watch for some time to sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It was unequal to contend with that of Cæsar. Of what avail were the eloquence, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and the virtue of this republican, when opposed by a man who had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to debauch the wife of every citizen whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> he meant to engage; who, professing an enthusiasm for glory, wept, because, at the age of 30, he had not conquered the world like Alexander; and who, with the haughty temper of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a>, was more dextrous to be the first man in a village than the second in Rome. "Cæsar had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to exist in times of trouble and civil commotions, when the minds of men are put into a ferment; when opportunities of great actions are frequent; when talents are everything, and those who can only boast of their virtues are nothing. If he had lived a hundred years sooner, he would have been no more than an obscure villain; and, instead of giving laws to the world, would not have been able to produce any confusion in it. "I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> here be bold enough to advance an idea, which may appear paradoxical to those who weakly judge of men from what they achieve, and not from the principle which leads them to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Nature formed in the same mould Cæsar, Mahomet, Cromwell, and Kouli Khan. They all of them united to genius that profound policy which renders it so powerful. They all of them had an evident superiority over those with whom they were surrounded; they were conscious of this superiority, and they made others conscious of it. They were all of them born subjects, and became fortunate usurpers. Had Cæsar been placed in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, he would have made the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, he would have been the founder of a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; in London, he would have stabbed his sovereign, or have procured his assassination under the sanction of the laws. He reigned with glory over men whom he had reduced to be slaves; and, under one aspect, he is to be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>; under another, as a monster. But it would be unfortunate, indeed, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, if the possession of superior talents gave individuals a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to trouble its repose. Usurpers accordingly have flatterers, but no friends; strangers respect them; their subjects complain and submit; it is in their own families that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> finds her avengers. Cæsar was affianced by his son, Mahomet was poisoned by his wife, Kouli Khan was massacred by his nephew, and Cromwell only died in his bed because his son Richard was a philosopher. "Cæsar, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of his country; Cæsar, who destroyed the agents of his crimes, if they failed in addresses; Cæsar, in fine, the husband of every wife, and the wife of every husband, has been accounted a great man by the mob of writers. But it is only the philosopher who knows how to mark the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> between celebrity and greatness. The talents of this singular man, and the good fortune which constantly attended him till the moment of his assassination, have concealed the enormity of his actions." Cæsar, in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> borne by all the emperors, from Julius Cæsar to the destruction of the empire. It was also used as a title of distinction for the intended or presumptive heir of the empire, as king of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> is now used for that of the German empire. This title took its rise from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, C. Julius Cæsar, which, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the senate, all the succeeding emperors were to bear. Under his successor, the appellation of Augustus being appropriated to the emperors, in compliment to that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, the title Cæsar was given to the second person in the empire, though still it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be given to the first; and hence the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Cæsar used simply, and Cæsar with the addition of Imperator Augustus. The dignity of Cæsar remained to the second of the empire, till Alexius Comnenus having elected Nicephorus Melissenus Cæsar by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; and it being necessary to confer some higher dignity on his own <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Isaacius, he created him Sebactocrator with the precedence over Melissenus; ordering, that in all acclamations, &c., Isaacius Sebactocrator should be named the second, and Melissenus Cæsar the third. Cæsar, Sir Julius, a learned civilian, was descended by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> line from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Cesarini in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and was born near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOTTENHAM">Tottenham</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, in the year 1557. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards studied in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where, in the year 1581, he was created <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and two years after was admitted to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> at Oxford, and also became doctor of the canon law. He was advanced to many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> employments, and for the last 20 years of his life was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the rolls. He was remarkable for his extensive bounty and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to all persons of worth, so that he seemed to be the almoner-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. He died in 1639, in the 79th year of his age. It is very remarkable that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of this lawyer were offered (by the executors of some of his descendants) to a cheesemonger for waste <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; but being timely inspected by Mr Samuel Pateron, this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> discovered their worth, and had the satisfaction to find his judgement confirmed by the profession, to whom they were sold in lots for upwards of £500, in the year 1757. Cæsar Augusta, or Cæsarea Augusta, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a Roman colony situated on the river Iberus in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, before called Salduba, in the territories of the Edetans. Now commonly thought to be Saragossa. Cæsarea, the name of several ancient cities, particularly one on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Phoenicia. It was very conveniently situated for trade; but had a very dangerous harbour, so that no ships could be safe in it when the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> was at south-west. Herod the Great, king of Judea, remedied this inconvenience by an immense expense and labour, making it one of the most convenient havens on that coast. He also beautified it with many buildings, and bestowed 12 years on the finishing and adorning it. Cæsarian operation. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>. Cæsarians, Cæsarienses, in Roman antiquity, were officers or ministers of the Roman emperors: They kept the account of the revenues of the emperors; and took possession, in their name, of such things as devolved or were confiscated to them. Cæsarodunum, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Turones in Celtic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, the capital of Touraine. See Tours. Vol. V. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. Cæsaramagus, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Trinobantes in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; by some supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHELMSFORD">Chelmsford</a>, or others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRENTFORD">Brentford</a>, and by others Purfleet. Cæsena, in Ancient Geography, a town of Gallia Cispadana, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Iapris and Rubicon; now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CESENA">Cesena</a>, which see. Cæsia sylva, in Ancient Geography, a wood in Germany, part of the great Sylva Hercynia, situated partly in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>, and partly in Westphalia, between Wefel and Kesfeld. Cæsones, a denomination given to those cut out of their mothers wombs. Pliny ranks this as an auspicious kind of birth; the elder Scipio Africanus, and the first of the family of Cæsars, were brought into the world in this way. Cæstus, in antiquity, a large gauntlet made of raw hide, which the wrestlers made use of when they fought at the public games.—This was a kind of leathern strap, strengthened with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which encompassed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, and a part of the arm, as well to defend these parts as to enforce their blows. Cæstus, or Cæstum, was also a kind of girdle, made of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, which the husband untied for his spouse the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, before they went to bed. This relates to Venus's girdle, which Juno borrowed of her to entice <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> to love her. See Cestus. Cæsura, in the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, is when, in the scanning of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, a word is divided so, as one part seems cut off, and goes to a different foot from the rest: as, Menti[ri no]li, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a>[quam men]dacia/profunt. where the syllables ri, li, quam, and men, are caesuras. Cæsura, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poetry, denotes a rest or pause towards the middle of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> verse, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> are aided, and the verse, as it were, divided into two hemistichs. See Pause. Cæteris paribus, a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in frequent use among mathematical and physical writers. The words literally signify, the rest (or other things) being alike or equal. Thus we say the heavier the bullet, cæteris paribus, the greater the range; i.e., by how much the bullet is heavier, if the length and diameter of the piece and strength of the powder be the same, by so much will the utmost range or distance of a piece of ordnance be the greater. Thus also, in a physical way, we say, the velocity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> circulating in a given time through any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of an artery, will, cæteris paribus, be according to its diameter, and nearness to or distance from the heart. Cætobrix, in Ancient Geography, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>, near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, on the east side; now extinct. It had its name from its fishery; and there are still extant fish ponds on the shore, done with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of Paris, which illustrate the name of the ruined city. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, painted cotton cloths manufactured in the East Indies, and sold at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. Caffa, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAFFA">Kaffa</a>, a city and port town of Crimean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, situated on the south-east part of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>. E. Long. 37°. O. N. Lat. 44°. 55'. It is the most considerable town in the country, and gives gives name to the straits of Caffa, which run from the Euxine or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to the Palus Maeotis, or sea of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASOPH">Asoph</a>.

CAFFILA

Pages 60-60

on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Guzerat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cambaya, signifies a small fleet of merchant ships.

CAFFRARIA

Pages 60-60

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Cafrirs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Hottentots, in the most southerly parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying in the form of a cresent about the inland country of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOMOTAPA">Monomotapa</a>, between 35° south latitude and the tropic of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">Capricorn</a>: and bounded on the east, south, and west, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> and Atlantic oceans. See Hottentots. Most of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coasts of this country are subject to the Dutch, who have built a fort near the most southern promontory called the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope.

CAGANUS

Pages 60-60
or CACANUS, an appellation anciently given by the Huns to their kings. The word appears also to have been formerly applied to the princes of Muscovy, now called czar. From the same also, probably, the Tartar title sham or can, had its origin.

CAGE

Pages 60-60

an enclosure made of wire, wicker, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, interwoven lattice-wise, for the confinement of birds or wild beasts. The word is French, cage, formed from the Italian gaggia, of the Latin cavea which signifies the same: a cavea theatralibus in quibus includebantur feræ. Beasts were usually brought to Rome shut up in oaken or beechen cages artfully formed, and covered or shaded with boughs, that the creatures, deceived with the appearance of a wood, might fancy themselves in their forest. The fiercer sorts were pent in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cages, lest wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> might be broke through. In some prisons there are iron cages for the closer confinement of criminals. The French laws distinguish two sorts of birds cages; viz. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or singing cages, and low or dumb cages; those who expose birds to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> are obliged to put the hens in the latter, and the cocks in the former, that persons may not be imposed on by buying a hen for a cock.

CAGEAN

Pages 60-60
or CAGAYAN, a province of the island of Luzon, or Manila, in the East Indies. It is the largest in the island, being 80 leagues in length and 40 in breadth. The principal city is called New Segovia, and 15 leagues eastward from this city lies Cape Bajador. Doubling that cape, and coasting along 20 leagues from north to south, the province of Cagayan ends, and that of Ilocoos begins. The peaceable Cageans who pay tribute are about 9000; but there are a great many not subdued. The whole province is fruitful: the men apply themselves to agriculture, and are of a martial disposition; and the women apply to several works in cotton. The mountains afford food for a vast number of bees; in consequence of which wax is so plenty, that all the poor burn it instead of oil. They make their candles after the following manner: they leave a small hole at each end of a hollow stick for the wick to run through, and then, stopping the bottom, fill it with wax at the top; when cold, they break the mould and take out the candle. On the mountains there is abundance of brafl, ebony, and other valuable woods. In the woods are store of wild beasts, as boars; but not so good as those of Europe. There are also abundance of deer, which they kill for their skins and horns to sell to the Chinese.

CAGES

Pages 60-60

denote also places in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> amphitheaters, wherein wild beasts were kept, ready to be let out for sport. The caveæ were a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cages different from dens, which were under ground and dark; whereas the caveæ being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, the beasts rushed out of them with more alacrity and fierceness than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been pent under ground.

CAGLI

Pages 60-60

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Urbino, situated at the foot of the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 12. N. Lat. 43. 30.

CAGLIARI

Pages 61-61

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and rich town, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> in the Mediterranean. It is seated on the declivity of a hill; is an university, an archbishopric, and the residence of the viceroy. It has an excellent harbour, and a good trade; but is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength. It was taken, with the whole island, by the English in 1758, who transferred it to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI.; but it was retaken by the Spaniards in 1717, and about two years afterwards ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy in lieu of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and hence he has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sardinia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 14. N. Lat. 39. 12.

CAGUI

Pages 61-61

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a synonyme of two <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of monkeys, viz. the jaeculus and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">oedipus</a>. See SIMIA, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAHORS

Pages 61-61

a considerable town of France, in Quercy in Guienne, with a bishop's see and a university. It is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> made by the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, and built partly on a craggy rock. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> street is very narrow; and terminates in the market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in which is the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a Gothic structure, and has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> steeple. The fortifications are regular, and the town is surrounded with thick walls. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 6. N. Lat. 44. 26.

CAHYS

Pages 61-61

a dry <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for corn, used in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>. It is near a bushel of our measure.

CAIAPHAS

Pages 61-61
high priest of the Jews after Simon, condemned Christ to death; and was put out of his place by the emperor Vitellius, for which disgrace he made away with himself.

CAICOS

Pages 61-61

the name of some American <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of St Domingo, lying from W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 112. 10. to 113. 16. N. Lat. 21. 40.

CAIETA

Pages 61-61

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a port and town of Latium, so called from Enneas's nurse; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAETA">Gaeta</a>, which see.

CAIFONG

Pages 61-61

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and rich town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, seated in the middle of a large and well cultivated plain. It stands in a bottom; and when besieged by the rebels in 1642, they ordered the dykes of the river Hoang-ho to be cut, which drowned the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and destroyed 300,000 of its inhabitants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 113. 27. N. Lat. 35. 0.

CAILLE

Pages 61-62

NICHOLAS <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">LOUIS</a> DE LA, an eminent mathematician and astronomer, was born at a small town in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> in 1713. His father had served in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, which he quitted, and in his retirement studied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and amused himself with mechanic exercises, wherein he proved the happy author of several inventions of considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the public. Nicholas, almost in his infancy, took a fancy to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, which proved of signal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to him in his maturer years. He was sent young to school at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANTES">Mantes</a>-sur-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, where he discovered early tokens of genius. In 1729, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where he studied the classics, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and mathematics. Afterwards, he went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> de Navarre, proposing to embrace an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. At the end of three years he was ordained a deacon, and officiated as such in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the college de Mazarat several years; but he never entered into priests orders, apprehending that his astronomical studies, to which he became most assiduously devoted, might too much interfere with his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duties. In 1739, he was conjoined with M. de Thury, son to M. Cassini, in verifying the meridian of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of France. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of November the same year, whilst he was engaged <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night in the operations which this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> undertaking required; and at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from Paris, he was, without any solicitation, elected into the vacant mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> which the celebrated M. Varignon had so worthily filled. Here he began to teach about the end of 1743; and an observatory was ordered to be erected for his use in the college, and furnished with a suitable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of the best instruments. In May 1741, M. de la Caille was admitted into the Royal Academy of Sciences as an adjoint member for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. Besides the many excellent papers of his dispersed up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, he published Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, Mechanics, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, and Astronomy. Moreover, he carefully computed all the eclipses of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> that had happened since the Christian era, which were printed in a book published by two <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>, entitled l'Art de Varier les Dates, &c. Paris, 1750, in 4to. Besides these he compiled a volume of astronomical ephemerides for the years 1745 to 1755; another for the years 1755 to 1765; a third for the years 1765 to 1775; an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Astronomiae Funda- menta novissimis solis et stellarum observationibus habilita: and the most correct solar tables that ever appeared. Having gone through a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of astronomical observations in his own observatory, he formed a project of going to observe the southern stars at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. This was highly approved by the academy, and by the prime minister Comte de Argençon, and very readily agreed to by the states of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Upon this he drew up a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the method he proposed to pursue in his southern observations; setting forth, that, besides settling the places of the fixed stars, he proposed to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a> of the moon, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> and Venus. But whereas this required correspondent observations to be made in the northern parts of the world, he sent to those of his correspondents who were expert in practical astronomy previous notice, in print, what observations he designed to make at such and such times for the said purpose. At length, on the 21st of November 1750, he sailed for the Cape, and arrived there on the 19th of April 1751. He forthwith got his instruments on shore; and with the assistance of some Dutch artificers, set about <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> an astronomical observatory, in which his apparatus of instruments was properly disposed of as soon as it was in a fit condition to receive them. The sky at the Cape is generally pure and serene, unless when a south-east <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows: But this is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and when it is, it is attended with some strange and terrible effects. The stars look bigger, and seem to caper; the moon has an undulating tremor; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> have a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>. Two hundred and twenty-eight nights did our astronomer survey the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the southern heavens: during which space, which is almost incredible, he observed more than 10,000 stars; and whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> filled the heavens with monsters and old wives tales, the abbé de la Caille chose rather to adorn them with the instruments and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> philosophy has made use of for the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>*. With no less success did he attend to the parallax of the moon, Mars, Venus, and the sun. Having thus executed the purpose of his voyage, and no present opportunity offering for his return, he thought of employing the vacant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in another arduous attempt; no less than that of taking the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, as he had already done that of the heavens. This, indeed, had, through the munificence of the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, been done before by different sets of learned men both in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; some determining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> under the equator, and others under the arctic circles: but it had not as yet been decided whether in the southern parallels of latitude the same dimensions obtained as in the northern. His labours were rewarded with the satisfaction he wished for; having determined a distance of 410,814 feet from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Kap Fontyn to the Cape, by means of a base of 38,832 feet, three times actually measured: whence he discovered a new secret of nature, namely, that the radii of the parallels in south latitude are not the same as those of the corresponding parallels in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. About the 23rd degree of south latitude he found a degree on the meridian to contain 342,222 Paris feet. He returned to Paris the 27th of September 1754; having in his almost four years absence expended no more than 9144 livres on himself and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>; and at his coming into port, he refused a bribe of 100,000 livres, offered by one who thirsted less after <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, to be sharer in his immunity from customhouse searches. After receiving the congratulatory visits of his more intimate friends and the astronomers, he first of all thought fit to draw up a reply to some strictures which Professor Euler had published relative to the meridian, and then he settled the results of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of his own with the observations of other astronomers for the parallaxes. That of the sun he fixed at 94"; of the moon at 56' 56"; of Mars in his opposition, 36"; of Venus, 38". He also settled the laws whereby astronomical refractions are varied by the different density <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rarity of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and dryness or moisture. And, lastly, He showed an easy, and by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> navigators practicable, method of finding the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by means of the moon, which he illustrated by examples selected from his own observations during his voyages. His fame being now established upon so firm a basis, the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> of Europe claimed him as their own: and he was unanimously elected a member of the royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; of the institute of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; of the imperial academy at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>; and of the royal academies at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>. In the year 1760, M. de la Caille was attacked with a severe fit of the gout; which, however, did not interrupt the course of his studies; for he then planned out a new and immense work; no less than the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of astronomy through all ages, with a comparison of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and modern observations, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and use of the instruments employed in making them. In order to pursue the task he had imposed upon himself in a suitable retirement, he obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of apartments in the royal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Vincennes; and whilst his astronomical apparatus was erected there, he began <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> his Catalogue of the Southern Stars, and the third volume of his Ephemerides. The state of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was, towards the end of the year 1763, greatly reduced. His blood grew inflamed; he had pains of the head, obstructions of the kidneys, loss of appetite, with a fulness of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. His mind remained unaffected, and he resolutely persisted in his studies as usual. In the month of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, medicines were administered to him, which rather aggravated than alleviated his symptoms; and he was now sensible, that the same distemper which in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, ten years before, yielded to a few simple remedies, did in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> bid defiance to the best physicians. This induced him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> his affairs: his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> he committed to the care and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of his esteemed friend M. Maraldi. It was at last determined that a vein should be opened; but this brought on an obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a>, of which he died, aged 49.

CAIMACAN

Pages 62-63
or Kaimacam, in the Turkish affairs, a dignity in the Ottoman empire, answering to lieutenant, or rather deputy, amongst us. There are usually two caiamacs; one residing at Constantinople, as governor thereof; the other attends the grand vizir in quality of his lieutenant, secretary of state, and first minister of his council, and gives audience to ambassadors. Sometimes there is a third. CAIMAN or CAYMAN ISLANDS, certain American islands, lying south of Cuba and north-west of Jamaica, between $81^\circ$ and $86^\circ$ of west longitude, and in $21^\circ$ of north latitude. They are most remarkable on account of the fishery of tortoises, which the people of Jamaica catch here and carry home alive, keeping them in pens for food, and killing them as they want them.

CAIN

Pages 63-63

eldest son of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>, killed his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a>; for which he was condemned by God to banishment and a vagabond state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Cain retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Nod, on the east of Eden; and built a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, to which he gave the name of his son Enoch.

CAINITES

Pages 63-63

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the 2nd century, so called on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a>. They pretended that the virtue which produced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a> was of an order inferior to that which had produced Cain, and that this was the reason why Cain had the victory over Abel and killed him; for they admitted a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of genii, which they called virtues, of different ranks and orders. They made profession of honouring those who carry in Scripture the most visible marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>; as the inhabitants of Sodom, Esau, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. They had, in particular, a very great veneration for the traitor Judas, under pretence that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ had saved mankind. They had a forged gospel of Judas, to which they paid great respect.

CAIRNS

Pages 63-63
or CARNES, the vulgar name of those heaps of stones which are to be seen in many places of Britain, particularly Scotland and Wales.—They are composed of stones of all dimensions thrown together in a conical form, a flat stone crowning the apex; (see Plate CXXXV.). Various causes have been assigned by the learned for these heaps of stones. They have supposed them to have been, in times of inauguration, the places where the chieftain elect stood to show himself to best advantage to the people; or the place from whence judgment was pronounced; or to have been erected on the road-side in honour of Mercury; or to have been formed in memory of some solemn compact, particularly where accompanied by standing pillars of stones; or for the celebration of certain religious ceremonies. Such might have been the reasons, in some instances, where the evidences of stone chests and urns are wanting: but these are so generally found that they seem to determine the most usual purpose of the piles in question to have been for sepulchral monuments. Even this destination might render them suitable to other purposes; particularly religious, to which by their nature they might be supposed to give additional solemnity.—According to Toland, fires were kindled on the tops of flat stones, at certain times of the year, particularly on the eve of the 1st of May and the 1st of November, for the purpose of sacrificing; at which time all the people having extinguished their domestic hearths, rekindled them from the sacred fires of the cairns. In general, therefore, these accumulations appear to have been designed for the sepulchral protection of heroes and great men. The stone chests, the repository of the urns and ashes, are lodged in the earth beneath; sometimes only one, sometimes more, are found thus deposited; and Mr Pennant mentions an instance of 17 being discovered under the same pile. Cairns are of different sizes, some of them very large. Mr Pennant describes one in the island of Arran, 114 feet over, and of a vast height. They may justly be supposed to have been proportioned in size to the rank of the person, or to his popularity: the people of a whole district assembled to show their respect to the deceased; and, by an active honouring of his memory, soon accumulated heaps equal to those that afforded us at this time. But these honours were not merely those of the day; as long as the memory of the deceased endured, not a passenger went by without adding a stone to the heap: they supposed it would be an honour to the dead, and acceptable to his manes. Quamquam futilias, non est mora longa: licebit Injetto ter pulvera, curras. To this moment there is a proverbial expression among the Highlanders allusive to the old practice; a suppliant will tell his patron, Curri mi cloch er do charne, “I will add a stone to your cairn;” meaning, When you are no more, I will do all possible honour to your memory. Cairns are to be found in all parts of our islands, in Cornwall, Wales, and all parts of North Britain; they were in use among the northern nations; Dahlberg, in his 323rd plate, has given the figure of one. In Wales they are called carneddau; but the proverb taken from them there, is not of the complimentary kind: Karn ar dy ben, or, “A cairn on your head,” is a token of imprecation.

CAIRO

Pages 63-65
or GRAND CAIRO, the capital of Egypt, situated in a plain at the foot of a mountain, in E. Long. 32°. N. Lat. 30°. It was founded by Jawhar, a Magrebian general, in the year of the Hegira 358. He had laid the foundation of it under the horoscope of Mars; and for that reason gave his new city the name of Al Kahira, or the Victorious, an epithet applied by the Arab astronomers to that planet. In 362 it became the residence of the caliphs of Egypt, and of consequence the capital of that country, and has ever since continued to be so. It is divided into the New and Old cities. Old Cairo is on the eastern side of the river Nile, and is now almost uninhabited. The new, which is properly Cairo, is seated in a sandy plain about two miles and a half from the old city. It stands on the western side of the Nile, from which it is not three quarters of a mile distant. It is extended along the mountain on which the castle is built, for the sake of which it was removed hither, in order, as some pretend, to be under its protection. However, the change is much for the worse, as well with regard to air as water, and the pleasantness of the prospect. Bulack may be called the port of Cairo; for it stands on the bank of the Nile, about a mile and a half from it, and all the corn and other commodities are landed there before they are brought to the city. Some travellers have made Cairo of a most enormous magnitude, by taking in the old city, Bulack, and the new; the real circumference of it, however, is not above ten miles, but it is extremely populous. The first thing that strikes a traveller is the narrowness of the streets, streets, and the appearance of the houses. These are so daubed with mud on the outside, that you would think they were built with nothing else. Besides, as the streets are unpaved, and always full of people, the walking in them is very inconvenient, especially to strangers. To remedy this, there are a great number of alleys, which always stand ready to be hired for a trifle, that is, a penny a mile. The owners drive them along, and give notice to the crowd to make way. And here it may be observed, that the Christians in this, as well as other parts of the Turkish dominions, are not permitted to ride upon horses. The number of the inhabitants can only be guessed at; but we may conclude it to be very great, because in some years the plague will carry off 200,000, without their being much missed. The houses are from one to two or three stories high, and flat at the top; where they take the air, and often sleep all night. The better sort of these have a court on the inside like a college. The common run of houses have very little room, and even among great people it is usual for 20 or 30 to lie in a small hall. Some houses will hold 500 persons of both sexes, among whom are 20 or 30 slaves; and those of ordinary rank have generally three or four. There is a canal, called khuliz, which runs along the city from one end to the other, with houses on each side, which makes a large straight street. Besides this, there are several lakes, which are called birks in the language of the country. The principal of these, which is near the castle, is 500 paces in diameter. The most elegant houses in the city are built on its banks; but what is extraordinary, eight months in the year it contains water, and the other four it appears with a charming verdure. When there is water sufficient, it is always full of gilded boats, barges, and barks, in which people of condition take their pleasure towards night, at which time there are curious fireworks, and variety of music. New Cairo is surrounded with walls built with stone, on which are handsome battlements, and at the distance of every hundred paces there are very fine towers, which have room for a great number of people. The walls were never very high, and are in many places gone to ruin. The basha lives in the castle, which was built by Saladin 700 years ago. It stands in the middle of the famous mountain Moketan, which terminates in this place, after it had accompanied the Nile from Ethiopia hither. This castle is the only place of defence in Egypt; and yet the Turks take no notice of its falling, insomuch that in process of time it will become a heap of rubbish. The principal part in it is a magnificent hall, environed with 12 columns of granite, of a prodigious height and thickness, which sustain an open dome, under which Saladin distributed justice to his subjects. Round this dome there is an inscription in relievo, which determines the date and by whom it was built. From this place the whole city of Cairo may be seen, and above 30 miles along the Nile, with the fruitful plains that lie near it, as well as the mosques, pyramids, villages, and gardens, with which these fields are covered. These granite pillars were the work of antiquity, for they were got out of the ruins of Alexandria. There are likewise in the mosques and in the principal houses no less than 40,000 more, besides great magazines, where all kinds are to be had at very low rates. A janizary happened to find five in his garden, as large as those in the castle; but could not find any machine of strength sufficient to move them, and therefore had them sawed in pieces to make millstones. It is believed that there have been 30 or 40,000 of these pillars brought from Alexandria, where there are yet many more to be had. The gates of Cairo are three, which are very fine and magnificent. There are about 300 public mosques in this city, some of which have six minarets. The mosque of Asher hath several buildings adjoining, which were once a famous university, and 14,000 scholars and students were maintained on the foundation; but it has now not above 1,400, and those are only taught to read and write. All the mosques are built upon the same plan, and differ only in magnitude. The entrance is through the principal gate into a large square, open on the top, but well paved. Round this are covered galleries, supported by pillars; under which they say their prayers, in the shade. On one side of the square there are particular places with basins of water for the convenience of performing the ablutions enjoined by the Koran. The most remarkable part of the mosque, besides the minaret, is the dome. This is often bold, well proportioned, and of an astonishing magnitude. The inside stones are carved like lace, flowers, and melons. They are built so firm, and with such art, that they will last 600 or 700 years. About the outward circumference there are large Arabic inscriptions in relievo, which may be read by those who stand below, though they are sometimes of a wonderful height. The khans or caravanserais are numerous and large, with a court in the middle, like their houses. Some are several stories high, and are always full of people and merchandise. The Nubians, the Abyssinians, and other African nations, which come to Cairo, have one to themselves, where they always meet with lodging. Here they are secure from insults, and their effects are all safe. Besides these there is a bazaar, or market, where all sorts of goods are to be sold. This is in a long broad street; and yet the crowd is so great, you can hardly pass along. At the end of this street is another short one, but pretty broad, with shops full of the best sort of goods and precious merchandise. At the end of this short street there is a great khan, where all sorts of white slaves are to be sold. Farther than this is another khan, where a great number of blacks, of both sexes, are exposed to sale. Not far from the best market place is a mosque, and an hospital for mad people. They also receive and maintain sick people in this hospital, but they are poorly looked after. Old Cairo has scarce anything remarkable but the granaries of Joseph; which are nothing but a high wall, lately built, which includes a square spot of ground where they deposit wheat, barley, and other grain, which is a tribute to the basha, paid by the owners of land. This has no other covering but the heavens, and therefore the birds are always sure to have their share. There is likewise a tolerably handsome church, which is made use of by the Copts, who are Christians and the original inhabitants of Egypt. Joseph's Joseph's well is in the castle, and was made by King Mohammed about 700 years ago. It is called Joseph's well, because they attribute every thing extraordinary to that remarkable person. It is cut in a rock, and is 280 feet in depth. The water is drawn up to the top by means of oxen, placed on platforms, at proper distances, which turn about the machines that raise it. The descent is so sloping, that, though there are no steps, the oxen can descend and ascend with ease. The river Nile, to which not only Cairo, but all Egypt is so much indebted, is now known to have its rise in Abyssinia. The increase of the Nile generally begins in May, and in June they commonly proclaim about the city how much it is risen. Over against old Cairo the batha has a house, wherein the water enters to a column, which has lines at the distance of every inch, and marks at every two feet as far as 30. When the water rises to 22 feet, it is thought to be of a sufficient height; when it rises much higher, it does a great deal of mischief. There is much pomp and ceremony used in letting the water into the canal above mentioned. See EGYPT. The inhabitants of Cairo are a mixture of Moors, Turks, Jews, Greeks, and Copts or Coptics. The only difference between the habit of the Moors and Copts is their turbans; those of the Moors being white, and of the Copts white striped with blue. The common people generally wear a long black loose frock, sewed together all down before. The Jews wear a frock of the same fashion, made of cloth; and their caps are like a high-crowned hat, without brims, covered with the same cloth, but not so taper. The Jewish women's are not very unlike the men's, but more light and long. The Greeks are habited like the Turks, only their turbans differ. Provisions of all kinds are exceedingly plenty; for 20 eggs may be bought for a parah or penny, and bread is six times as cheap as with us. They have almost all sorts of flesh and fish; and in particular have tame buffaloes, which are very useful. They bring goats into the streets in great numbers, to sell their milk. Their gardens are well stocked with fruit trees of various kinds, as well as roots, herbs, melons, and cucumbers. The most common flesh meat is mutton. The goats are very beautiful, and have ears two feet in length; but their flesh is in no great esteem. See farther the article EGYPT.

CAIROAN

Pages 65-65
or CAIRWAN, a city of Africa, in the kingdom of Tunis, seated in a sandy barren soil, about five miles from the gulf of Capres. It has neither spring, well, nor river; for which reason they are obliged to preserve rain water in tanks and cisterns. It was built by the Aglabites; and is the ancient Cyrene*, but hath now lost its splendour. There is still, however, a very superb mosque, and the tombs of the kings of Tunis are yet to be seen. E. Long. 9. 12. N. Lat. 35. 40.

CAISSON

Pages 65-65

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, into which several bombs are put, and sometimes filled only with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder: this is buried under some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> whereof the enemy intend to possess themselves, and, when they are masters of it, is fired, in order to blow them up. CAISSON is also used for a wooden frame <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chest used in laying the foundations of the piers of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>.

CAITHNESS

Pages 65-66

otherwise called the shire of Wick, is the most northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of all Scotland; bounded on the east by the ocean, and by Strathnaver and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a> on the south and south-west: from these it is divided by the mountain of Orde, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ridge of hills as far as Knockfin, then by the whole course of the river Hallowdale. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it is washed by the Pentland <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Picland frith, which flows between this county and the Orkneys. It extends 35 miles from north to south, and about 20 from east to west. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is rocky, and remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bays and promontories. Of these, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are Sandside-head to the west, pointing to the opening of Pentland frith; Orcas, now Holborn-head, and Dunnet-head, both pointing northward to the frith. Dunnet-head is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in compass; affording several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, good pasture, excellent mill-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> mine. Scribster <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, on the north-west is a good harbour, where ships may ride securely. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">Rice</a>-bay, on the east side, extends three miles in breadth; but it is of dangerous access, on account of some sunk rocks at the entrance. At the bottom of this bay appear the ruins of two strong castles, the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Caithness, called Castle Sinclair, and Gernego, joined to each other by a draw-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. Duncan's bay, otherwise called Dunby-head, is the north-east point of Caithness, and the extremest promontory in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the breadth of the frith does not exceed 12 miles, and in the neighbourhood is the ordinary ferry to the Orkneys. Here is likewise Clythene's point east, and Northhead pointing north-east. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in this place is very impetuous, being in continual agitation from violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, currents, and vortices. The only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> belonging to this county is that of Strom, in the Pentland frith, at the distance of two miles from the main <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, extending about a mile in length, and producing good corn. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> is here rendered very difficult by conflicting tides and currents, which at both ends of the island produce a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> agitation in the sea. At the south end, the waves dance so impetuously, that the sailors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> them the merry men of May, from the name of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s seat on the opposite shore of Caithness, which served them as a landmark, in the dangerous passage between the island and the continent. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this island was once disputed between the earls of Orkney and Caithness; but adjudged to the latter, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an experiment, by which it appeared, that venomous creatures <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> live in Strom, whereas they die immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> transported to the Orkneys. The county of Caithness, though chiefly mountainous, flattens towards the sea coast, where the ground is arable, and produces good harvests of oats and barley, sufficient for the natives, and yielding a surplus for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Caithness is well watered with small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, brooks, lakes, and fountains, and affords a few woods of birch, but is in general bare of trees; and even those the inhabitants plant are stunted in their growth. Lead is found at Dunnet, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> at Old Urk, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore at several places; but these advantages are not improved. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of Caithness is temperate, though in the latitude of 58°, where the longest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is computed at 18 hours; and when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> sets, he makes Caithness, so small an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of a circle below the horizon, that the people enjoy a twilight until he rises again. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> used by the inhabitants of Caithness consists of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEAT">peat</a> and turf, which the ground yields in great plenty. The forests of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAYSHIRE">Morayshire</a> and Berridale afford abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> deer and roe-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">bucks</a>; the county is well stored with hares, rabbits, grouse, heathcocks, plover, and all sorts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, comprehending a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> called snow-fleet, about the size of a sparrow, exceedingly fat and delicious, that comes hither in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flights about the middle of February, and takes its departure in April. The hills are covered with sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle; so numerous, that a fat cow has been sold at market for 4s. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The rocks along the coasts are frequented by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, hawks, and all manner of sea fowl, whose eggs and young are taken in vast quantities by the natives. The rivers and lakes abound with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, salmon, and eels; and the sea affords a very advantageous fishery. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">obelisks</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments appear in this district, and several Roman chapels are still standing. Caithness is well peopled with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of hardy inhabitants, who employ themselves chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, and breeding sheep and black cattle: they are even remarkably industrious; for between Wick and Dunbeath, one continued tract of rugged rocks, extending 12 miles, they have formed several little harbours for their fishing boats, and cut <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> steps from the beach to the top of the rocks, where they have erected houses, in which they cure and dry the fish for market. According to Mr Pennant, this county is supposed to send out in some years about 20,000 head of black cattle, but in bad seasons the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> kills and sells great numbers for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. Great numbers of swine are also reared here. These are short, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> backed, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> bristled, sharp, slender, and long nosed; have long erect ears, and most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> looks. Here are neither barns nor granaries; the corn is threshed out, and preserved in the chaff in byks; which are stacks, in the shape of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a> hives, thatched quite round, where it will keep good for two years. Vast numbers of salmon are taken at Cattle-hill, Dunnet, Wick, and Thurso. A miraculous draught at this last place is still talked of, not less than 2500 being taken at one tide within the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and Mr Smollett informs us, that, in the neighbourhood, above 300 good salmon have been taken at one draught of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of November, great numbers of seals are taken in the caverns that open into the sea, and run some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of yards underground. The entrance of these caverns is narrow, but the inside lofty and spacious. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> hunters enter these in small boats with torches, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> as soon as they land, and then with loud shouts alarm the animals, which they kill with clubs as they attempt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. This is a hazardous employment; for should the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blow hard from sea, these adventurers are inevitably lost. Sometimes a large <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of seals, 12 feet long, have been killed on this coast; and it is said the same kind are found on the rock Hiskir, one of the Western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. During the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, great quantities of lump fish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to this coast, and are the prey of the seals, as appears from the number of skins of those fishes which at that season float ashore. At certain times also the seals seem to be visited by a great mortality; for, at those times, multitudes of them are seen dead in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Much <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> is found in this Caithness, county, which when burnt is made into a compost with turf and sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The discovery of coal has long been an object of great importance in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Scotland. In the years 1801 and 1802 some attempts were made for this purpose at the expense of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. But although the business was conducted by persons well skilled in such matters, and long persevered in, it has entirely failed, which leaves little hope of future success. The following is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the county of Caithness according to the parishes, taken at two different periods, namely in 1755 and in 1798, and extracted from the Statistical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. | <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a> | Population in 1755 | Population in 1798—1798 | |----------|-------------------|------------------------| | Bower | 1287 | 1592 | | Canisbay | 1481 | 1950 | | Dunnet | 1235 | 1399 | | Halkirk | 3575 | 3180 | | Latheron | 3675 | 4006 | | Olrick | 875 | 1001 | | Reay | 2262 | 2208 | | Thurso | 2963 | 3146 | | Wattin | 1424 | 1230 | | Wick | 3938 | 5000 | Total 22,215 24,802 22,215

CAIUS

Pages 66-67

KAYE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Keye, Dr John, the founder of Caius <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a> in 1510. He was admitted very young a student in Gonville <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in the above-mentioned university; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21 translated from Greek into Latin some pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and into English Erasmus's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> on Jude, &c. From these his juvenile labours, it seems probable that he first intended to prosecute the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of divinity. Be that as it may, he travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, studied physic under the celebrated Montanus. In that university he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, where we are told he read Greek lectures with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. In 1543, he travelled through <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Italy, Germany, and France; and returning to England commenced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic at Cambridge. He practised first at Shrewsbury, and afterwards at Norwich; but removing to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in 1547, he was admitted fellow of the college of physicians, to which he was several years <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. In 1557, being then physician to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, and in great favour, he obtained a license to advance Gonville-hall, where he had been educated, into a college; which he endowed with several considerable estates, adding an entire new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at the expense of 1834l. Of this college he accepted the mastership, which he kept till within a short time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was physician to Edward VI. Queen Mary, and Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. Towards the latter end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he retired to his own college at Cambridge; where, having resigned the mastership to Dr Legge of Norwich, he spent the remainder of his life as a fellow <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a>. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1573, aged 63; and was buried in the chapel of his own college. Dr Caius was a learned, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. In 1557, he erected a monument in St Paul's to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the famous Linacre. In 1563, he obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> for the college of physicians to take the bodies of two malefactors annually for dissection; and he was the inventor of the insignia which distinguish the president from the rest of the fellows. He wrote, 1. Annals of the college from 1555 to 1572. 2. Translation of several of Galen's works. Printed at different times abroad. 3. Hippocratis de Medicamentis; first discovered and published by our author: also De ratione victus, Lov. 1556, 8vo. 4. De Medendi Methodo. Bafli, 1554, Lond. 1556, 8vo. 5. Account of the sweating sicknesses in England. Lond. 1556, 1721. It is entitled De ephemera Britannica. 6. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the university of Cambridge. Lond. 1568, 8vo. 1574, 4to, in Latin. 7. De thermis Britannicis. Doubtful whether ever printed. 8. Of some rare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and animals. Lond. 1570. 9. De canibus Britannicis, 1570, 1729. 10. De pronunciatio Graeca et Latinae Linguae. Lond. 1574. 11. De libris propriis. Lond. 1570. Besides many other works which never were printed.

CAJETAN

Pages 61-61
CARDINAL, was born at Cajeta in the kingdom of Naples in the year 1469. His proper name was Thomas de Vio; but he adopted that of Cajetan from the place of his nativity. He defended the authority of the pope, which suffered greatly at the council of Nice, in a work entitled Of the power of the Pope; and for this work he obtained the bishopric of Cajeta. He was afterwards raised to the archiepiscopal see of Palermo, and in 1517 was made a cardinal by Pope Leo X. The year after, he was sent as legate into Germany, to quiet the commotions raised against indulgences by Martin Luther; but Luther, under protection of Frederic elector of Saxony, set him at defiance; for though he obeyed the cardinal's summons, in repairing to Augsburg, yet he rendered all his proceedings ineffectual. Cajetan was employed in several other negotiations and transactions, being as ready at buffets as at letters. He died in 1534. He wrote Commentaries upon Aristotle's philosophy, and upon Thomas Aquinas's theology; and made a literal translation of the Old and New Testaments.

CAKET

Pages 67-67

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Curdistan near Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>. Its trade consists chiefly in silks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 46. 15. N. Lat. 43. 32.

CALABASH

Pages 67-67

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> kind of vessel formed of the shell of a gourd, emptied and dried, serving to put <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of goods in, as pitch, rofe, and the like. The word is Spanish, Calabacce, which signifies the same. The Indians also, both of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, put the pearls they have fished in calabashes, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> do the same by their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust. The smaller calabashes are also frequently used by these people as a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, by which they sell these precious commodities to the Europeans. The same vessels likewise serve for putting liquors in; and do the office of cups, as well as bottles, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, pilgrims, &c. CALABASH-Tree. See Crescentia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. African CALABASH-Tree. See ADANSONIA, Botany Index.

CALABRIA

Pages 67-68

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, divided into Calabria Ultra and Calabria Citra, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Ulterior and Citerior; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Farther and Hither Calabria. Calabria Citerior is one of the 12 provinces of the kingdom of Naples; and bounded on the south by Calabria Ultra, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BASILICATA">Basilicata</a>, and on the west and east by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: Cosenza is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Calabria Ultra is washed by the Mediterranean sea on the east, south, and west, and bounded by Calabria Citra on the north. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a> is the capital town. This country has been almost entirely defoliated by the earthquakes of 1783. The reiterated shocks extended from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Spartivento to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMANTEA">Amantea</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of St Eufemia, and also affected that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> which lies opposite to the southern extremity of Italy. Those of the 5th and 7th of February, and of the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, were the most violent, and completed the destruction of every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> throughout the abovementioned space. Not one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was left upon another south of the narrow isthmus of Squillace: and what is more disastrous, a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of the inhabitants was killed by the falling of their houses, near 40,000 lives being lost. Some persons were dug out alive after remaining a surprising length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> buried among the rubbish. Messina became a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of ruins; its beautiful palazzata was thrown in upon the town, and its quay cracked into ditches full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Reggio was almost destroyed; Tropea greatly damaged; and every other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> levelled to the ground. Before and during the concussion the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> gathered, and then hung immovable and heavy over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. At Palmi the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> wore so fiery an aspect, that many people thought part of the town was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>.
