A few of the streets are paved with brick. The houses are built, some with brick, others with mud, and a still greater number with bamboos and mats; all which different kinds of fabrics standing intermixed with one another, form a very uncouth appearance. The brick houses are seldom above two stories <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, but those of mud and bamboos are only one, and are covered with thatch. The roofs of the brick houses are flat and terraced. These, however, are much fewer in number than the other two kinds; so that fires, which often happen, do not sometimes meet with a brick <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to obstruct their progress in a whole street. Within these 20 or 25 years Calcutta has been greatly improved both in appearance and in the salubrity of its air: the streets have been properly drained, and the ponds filled; thereby removing a vast surface of stagnant water, the exhalations of which were particularly hurtful. The citadel is named Fort William, and is superior as a fortress to any in India; but is now on too extensive a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> to answer the purpose for which it was intended, viz. the holding a post in case of extremity. It was begun on this extended plan by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clive immediately after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASSEY">Plassey</a>. The expense attending it was supposed to amount to two millions <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Calcutta is the emporium of Bengal, and the residence Calcutta. dence of the governor general of India. Its flourishing state may in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be supposed owing to the unlimited toleration of all religions allowed here; the Pagans being suffered to carry their idols in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, the Mahomedans not being discomfited, and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> being allowed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. At about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>'s distance from the town is a plain where the natives annually undergo a very strange kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> on the 9th of April; some for the sins they have committed, others for those they may commit, and others in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> made by their parents. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is performed in the following manner: Thirty bamboos, each about the height of 20 feet, are erected in the plain above mentioned. On the top of these they contrive to fix a swivel, and another bamboo of thirty feet or more crosses it, at each end of which hangs a rope. The people pull <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> one end of this rope, and the devotee placing himself under it, the brahmin pinches up a large piece of skin under both the shoulder-blades, sometimes in the breasts, and thrusts a strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> hook through each. These hooks have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> grass hanging to them, which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> makes fast to the rope at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bamboo, and at the same time puts a fathom round the body of the devotee, laying it loosely in the hollow of the hooks, lest by the skin's giving way, he should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the ground. When this is done, the people haul down the other end of the bamboo; by which means the devotee is immediately lifted up 30 feet or more from the ground, and they run round as fast as their legs can carry them. Thus the devotee is thrown out the whole length of the rope, where, as he swings, he plays a thousand antic tricks; being painted and dressed in a very particular manner, on purpose to make him look more ridiculous. Some of them continue swinging half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, others less. The devotees undergo a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of four days for this ceremony. On the first and third they abstain from all kinds of food; but eat fruit on the other two. During this time of preparation they walk about the streets in their fantastic dresses, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of drums and horns; and some to express the greater ardour of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, run a rod of iron quite through their tongues, and sometimes through their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> also. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 1755, Calcutta was commonly garrisoned by 300 Europeans, who were frequently employed in conveying the company's vessels from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATNA">Patna</a>, loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, piece goods, opium, and raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. The trade of Bengal alone supplied rich cargoes for 50 or 60 ships annually, besides what was carried on in small vessels to the adjacent countries. It was this flourishing state of Calcutta that probably was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> for the nabob Surajah Dowlah to attack it in the year 1756. Having had the fort of Cossimbazar delivered up to him, he marched against Calcutta with all his forces, amounting to 70,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot, with 400 elephants, and invested the place on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. Previous to any hostilities, however, he wrote a letter to Mr Drake the governor, offering to withdraw his troops, on condition that he would pay him his duty on the trade for 15 years past, defray the expense of his army, and deliver up the black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> who were in the fort. This being refused, he attacked one of the redoubts at the entrance of the town; but was repulsed with great slaughter. On the 16th he attacked another advanced post, but was likewise repulsed with great loss. Notwithstanding this disappointment, however, the attempt was renewed on the 18th, when the troops abandoned these posts, and retreated into the fort; on which the nabob's troops entered the town, and plundered it for 24 hours. An order was then given for attacking the fort; for which purpose a small breastwork was thrown up; and two twelve-pounders mounted upon it; but without firing oftener than two or three times an hour. The governor then called a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of war, when the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the train informed them, that there was not ammunition in the fort to serve three days; in consequence of which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ladies were sent on board the ships lying before the fort. They were followed by the governor, who declared himself a Quaker, and left the place to be defended by Mr Holwell the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in council. Besides the governor, four of the council, eight gentlemen of the company's service, four officers, and 100 soldiers, with 52 free merchants, captains of ships, and other gentlemen, escaped on board the ships, where were also 59 ladies, with 33 of their children. The whole number left in the fort was about 250 effective men, with Mr Holwell, four captains, five lieutenants, six ensigns, and five sergeants; as also 14 sea captains, and 29 gentlemen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>. Mr Holwell then having held a council of war, divided three chests of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> among the discontented soldiers, making them large promises also, if they behaved with courage and fidelity; after which he boldly stood on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the place, notwithstanding the immense force which opposed him. The attack was very vigorous; the enemy having got possession of the houses, galled the English from thence, and drove them from the bastions; but they themselves were several times dislodged by the fire from the fort, which killed an incredible number, with the loss of only five English soldiers the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The attack, however, was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the afternoon of the 27th; when many of the garrison being killed and wounded, and their ammunition almost exhausted, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> of truce was hung out. Mr Holwell intended to have availed himself of this opportunity to make his escape on board the ships, but they had fallen several miles down from the fort, without leaving even a single <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> to facilitate the escape of those who remained. In the meantime, however, the back-gate was betrayed by the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and the enemy, entering the fort, killed all they first met, and took the rest prisoners. The fort was taken before six in the evening; and, in an hour after, Mr Holwell had three audiences of the nabob, the last being in the durbar or council. In all of these the governor had the most positive assurances that no harm should happen to any of the prisoners; but he was surprized and enraged at finding only 500l. in the fort, instead of the immense treasures he expected; and to this as well as perhaps to the resentment of the jemmidars or officers, of whom many were killed in the siege, we may impute the catastrophe that followed. As soon as it was dark, the English prisoners, to the number of 146, were directed by the jemmidars who guarded them, to collect themselves into one body, and sit down quietly under the arched veranda, Besides the guard over them, another was placed at the fourth end of this veranda, to prevent the escape of any of them. About 500 gunmen, with lighted matches, were drawn up on the parade; and soon after the factory was in flames to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left of the prisoners, who had various conjectures on this appearance. The fire advanced with rapidity on both sides; and it was the prevailing opinion of the English, that they were to be suffocated between the two fires. On this they soon came to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of rushing on the guard, seizing their fezimars, and attacking the troops upon the parade, rather than be thus tamely roasted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but Mr Holwell advanced, and found the Moors were only searching for a place to confine them in. At this time Mr Holwell might have made his escape, by the assistance of Mr Leech, the company's smith, who had escaped when the Moors entered the fort, and returned just as it was dark, to tell Mr Holwell he had provided a boat, and would ensure his escape, if he would follow him through a passage few were acquainted with, and by which he then entered. This might easily have been accomplished, as the guard took little notice of it; but Mr Holwell told Mr Leech, he was resolved to share the fate of the gentlemen and the garrison; to which Mr Leech gallantly replied, that "then he was resolved to share Mr Holwell's fate, and would not leave him." The guard on the parade advanced, and ordered them all to rise and go into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. Then, with their muskets presented, they ordered them to go into the Black Hole prison; while others, with clubs and fezimars, pressed upon them so strong, that there was no resisting it; but, like one agitated wave impelling another, they were obliged to give way and enter; the rest following like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>. Few among them, the soldiers excepted, had the least idea of the dimensions or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a place they had never seen; for if they had, they should at all events have rushed upon the guard, and been cut to pieces by their own choice as the lesser evil. It was about eight o'clock when these 146 unhappy persons, exhausted by continual <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and fatigue, were thus crammed together into a dungeon about eighteen feet square, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> sultry night in Bengal; shut up to the east and south, the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> from whence air could reach them; by dead walls, and by a wall and door to the north; open only to the west by two windows, strongly barred with iron, from which they could receive scarce any circulation of fresh air. They had been but few minutes confined before every one fell into a perspiration so profuse, that no idea can be formed of it. This brought on a raging thirst, which increased in proportion as the body was drained of its moisture. Various expedients were thought of to give more room and air. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was stripped, and every hat put in motion: they several times sat down on their hams; but at each time several of the poor creatures fell, and were instantly suffocated or trode to death. Before <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> o'clock every man's thirst grew intolerable, and respiration difficult. Efforts were again made to force the door; but still in vain. Many insults were used to the guards, to provoke them to fire in upon the prisoners, who grew outrageous, and many delirious. "Water, water," became the general cry. Some water was brought: but these supplies like sprinkling water on fire, only served to raise and feed the flames. The confusion became general and horrid from the cries and ravings for water; and some were trampled to death. This <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of misery proved entertainment to the brutal wretches without, who supplied them with water, that they might have the satisfaction of seeing them fight for it, as they phrased it; and held up lights to the bars, that they might lose no part of the inhuman diversion. Before eleven o'clock, most of the gentlemen were dead, and one-third of the whole. Thirst grew intolerable: but Mr Holwell kept his mouth moist by sucking the perspiration out of his shirt sleeves, and catching the drops as they fell, like heavy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, from his head and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. By half an hour after eleven, most of the living were in an outrageous delirium. They found that water heightened their uneasiness; and "Air, air," was the general cry. Every insult that could be devised against the guard; all the opprobrious names that the viceroy and his officers could be loaded with, were repeated, to provoke the guard to fire upon them. Every man had eager hopes of meeting the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. Then a general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> to heaven, to hasten the approach of the flames to the right and left of them, and put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to their misery. Some expired on others; while a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> arose as well from the living as the dead, which was very offensive. About two in the morning, they crowded so much, to the windows, that many died standing, unable to fall by the throng and equal pressure round. When the day broke, the stench arising from the dead bodies was intolerable. At that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, the loubah, who had received an account of the havoc death had made among them, sent one of his officers to inquire if the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> survived. Mr Holwell was shown to him; and near six, an order came for their release. Thus they had remained in this infernal prison from eight at night until six in the morning, when the poor remains of 146 souls, being only 23, came out alive; but most of them in a high putrid fever. The dead bodies were dragged out of the hole by the soldiers, and thrown promiscuously into the ditch of an unfinished ravelin, which was afterwards filled with earth. The injuries which Calcutta suffered at this time, however, were soon repaired. The place was retaken by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Watson and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Clive, early in 1737; Surajah Dowlah was defeated, deposed, and put to death; and Meer Jaffier, who succeeded him in the nabobship, engaged to pay an immense sum for the indemnification of the inhabitants. Since that time, the immense acquisition of territory by the British in this part of the world, with the constant state of security enjoyed by this city, have given an opportunity of embellishing and improving it greatly beyond what it was before.—Among these improvements we may reckon that of Sir William Jones, who on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, 1784, instituted a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> for inquiring into the history civil and natural, the antiquities, arts, sciences, and literature of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and thus the literature CALCUTTA of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and along with it, it is to be hoped, the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, beneficence, and peace, have at length obtained a footing in the rich empire of Indostan, so long a prey to the rapine and violence of tyrants and usurpers.

CALDARIUM

Pages 78-78

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, denoted a brazen vessel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cistern, placed in the hypocaustum, full of hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to be drawn thence into the pila or bath, to give it the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the caldarium stood distinguished from the tepidarium and frigidarium. Caldarium, also denoted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUDATORY">sudatory</a>, being a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vaulted room, wherein by hot dry fumes, without water, people were brought to a profuse sweat. In which sense, caldarium was the same with what was otherwise denominated vaporarium, sudatorium, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LACONIUM">laconium</a>; in the Greek baths, hypocaustum, hypocauston.

CALDERINUS

Pages 78-78

DOMITIUS, a learned critic, born at Calderia near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>. He read lectures upon polite literature at Rome with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; and was the first who ventured to write upon the most difficult of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets. He died very young in 1477.

CALDERON

Pages 78-78

DE LA <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCA">BARCA</a>, DOM PEDRO a Spanish officer, who after having signalized himself, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> profession, quitted it for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, and then commenced dramatic writer. His dramatic works make 9 vols. in 4to, and some Spanish authors have compared him to Shakespeare. He flourished about the year 1640.

CALDERWOOD

Pages 78-79
DAVID, a famous divine of the church of Scotland, and a distinguished writer in behalf of the Presbyterians, was descended of a good family in that kingdom; and being early designed for the ministry, he applied with great diligence to the study of the Scriptures in their original tongues, the works of the fathers, the councils, and the best writers on church history. He was settled about the year 1624 at Creling near Jedburgh. King James I. of Great Britain, being desirous of bringing the church of Scotland nearer to a conformity with that of England, laboured earnestly to restore the episcopal authority, and enlarge the powers of the bishops who were then in Scotland. This design was very warmly opposed by many of the ministers, and particularly by Mr David Calderwood; who, when Mr James Law, bishop of Orkney, came to visit the presbyteries of Merle and Tiviotdale, declined his jurisdiction by a paper under his hand, dated May 5, 1658. But the king having its success much at heart, sent the earl of Dunbar, the high-treasurer of Scotland, with Dr Abbot, afterward archbishop of Canterbury, and two other divines, into that kingdom, with instructions to employ every method to persuade both the clergy and laity of his majesty's sincere desire to promote the good of the church, and of his zeal for the Protestant religion. Mr Calderwood did not attend at the general assembly held at Glasgow June 8, 1610, in which Lord Dunbar presided as commissioner; and it appears from his writings, that he looked upon every thing transacted in it as null and void. In May following, King James went to Scotland; and on the 17th of June held a parliament at Edinburgh. At that time the clergy met in one of the churches, to hear and advise with the bishops, which kind of assembly, it seems, was contrived in order to resemble the English convocation. Mr Calderwood was present at it, but declared publicly that he did not take any such meetings to resemble a convocation; and being opposed by Dr Whitford and Dr Hamilton, who were friends to the bishops, he took his leave of them in these words: "It is absurd to see men fitting in silks and satins, and to cry poverty in the kirk, when purity is departing." The parliament proceeded in the meanwhile in the dispatch of business; and Mr Calderwood, with several other ministers, being informed that a bill was depending to empower the king, with the advice of the archbishops, bishops, and such a number of the ministry as his majesty should think proper, to consider and conclude as to matters decent for the external policy of the church, not repugnant to the word of God; and that such conclusions should have the strength and power of ecclesiastical laws: against this they protested, for four reasons: 1. Because their church was so perfect, that, instead of needing reformation, it might be a pattern to others. 2. General assemblies, as now established by law, and which ought always to continue, might by this means be overthrown. 3. Because it might be a means of creating schism, and disturb the tranquility of the church. 4. Because they had received assurances, that no attempts should be made to bring them to a conformity with the church of England. They desired therefore, that, for these and other reasons, all thoughts of passing such a law might be laid aside: but in case this be not done, they protest for themselves and their brethren who shall adhere to them, that they can yield no obedience to this law, when it shall be enacted, because it is destructive of the liberty of the church; and therefore shall submit to such penalties, and think themselves obliged to undergo such punishments, as may be inflicted on them for disobeying that law. This protest was signed by Mr Archibald Simson on behalf of the members, who subscribed another separate roll, which he kept for his justification. This protest was presented to the clerk register, who refused to read it before the estates in parliament. However, though not read, it had its effect; for although the bill had the consent of parliament, yet the king thought fit to cause it to be laid aside, and not long after called a general assembly at St Andrew's. Soon after the parliament was dissolved, and Mr Calderwood was summoned to appear before the high-commission court at St Andrew's, on the 8th of July following, to answer for his mutinous and seditious behaviour. July 10th, the king came to that city in person; when Mr Calderwood, being called upon, and refusing to comply with what the king in person required of him, was committed to prison. Afterwards the privy s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council, according to the power exercised by them at that time, directed him to banish himself out of the king's dominions before Michaelmas next; and not to return without licence. Having applied to the king for a prorogation of his sentence without success, because he would neither acknowledge his offence, nor promise conformity for the future, he retired to Holland, where, in 1623, he published his celebrated piece entitled Altare Domini. Mr Calderwood having in the year 1624 been afflicted with a long fit of sickness, and nothing having been heard of him for some time, one Mr Patrick Scot, as Calderwood himself informs us, took it for granted that Calderwood he was dead; and thereupon wrote a recantation in his name, as if, before his decease, he had changed his sentiments. This impudence being detected, Scott went over to Holland, and laid three weeks at Amsterdam, where he made a diligent search for the author of Altare Damascenum, with a design to have despatched him. But Calderwood had privately retired into his own country, where he lived several years. Scott gave out that the king had furnished him with the matter for the pretended recantation, and that he only put it in order. During his retirement, Mr Calderwood collected all the memorials relating to the ecclesiastical affairs of Scotland, from the beginning of the reformation there down to the death of King James; which collection is still preserved in the university library of Glasgow; that which was published under the title of "The True History of Scotland," is only an extract from it. In the advertisement prefixed to the last edition of his Altare Damascenum mention is made of his being minister of Pencaitland near Edinburgh in 1638, but we find nothing said there, or anywhere else, of his death.

CALDRON

Pages 79-79

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> utensil, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; having a moveable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> handle, whereby to hang it on the chimney hook. The word is formed from the French chaudron, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALDARIUM">caldarium</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">Boiling</a> in CALDRONS (caldariis decoquere), is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> spoken of in the middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, decreed to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sort of criminals, but chiefly to defilers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. One of the torments inflicted on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian martyrs, was boiling in caldrons of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, &c.

CALDWALL

Pages 79-79

RICHARD, a learned English physician, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> about the year 1573. He studied physic in Brazen-nose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and was examined, admitted into, and made censor of, the College of Physicians at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, all in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Six weeks after he was chosen one of the elects; and in the year 1570, he was made <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of that college. Mr Wood tells us, that he wrote several pieces in his profession; but he does not tell us what they were, only that he translated a book on the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, written by one Horatio More, a Florentine physician. We learn from Camden, that Caldwell founded a surgical lecture in the College of Physicians, and endowed it with a handsome salary. He died in 1585. CALEA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CALEB

Pages 79-79

one of the deputies sent by the Israelites to take a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>. He made a good report of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and by this means revived the spirits of the dejected people; on which account, he and Joshua were the only persons who, after their leaving <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, settled in the land of Canaan. Caleb had for his share the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEBRON">Hebron</a>, from which he drove three kings. Othniel his nephew having taken the city of Debir, Caleb gave him his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Achsah in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; and died, aged 114.

CALEDONIA

Pages 79-81

the name of a settlement made by the Scots on the west side of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>, in 1698; out of which they were starved at the request of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>; for the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> prohibited the other colonies feeding them any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; so they were obliged to leave it in 1700. New CALEDONIA, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lately discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, and next to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, is the largest island that hath yet been discovered in that sea. It extends from 19° 37' to 22° 30' S. Lat. and from 163° 37' to 167° 14' E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. Its length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west to south-east is about 82 leagues; but its greatest breadth does not exceed ten leagues. This island is diversified with hills and valleys of various size and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. From the hills issue abundance of rivulets, which contribute to fertilize the plains. Along its north-east shore the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is flat; and being well watered, and cultivated by the inhabitants after their manner, appeared to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage to Captain Cook's people. Was it not, indeed, for those fertile spots on the plains, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> might be called a dreary waste: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and higher parts of the land are in general incapable of cultivation. They consist chiefly of rocks, many of which are full of mud; the little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> that is upon them is scorched and burnt up by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>: it is, however, covered with coarse grass and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and here and there covered with trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>. The country in general bears a great resemblance to those parts of New South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> under the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> of latitude. Several of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions are the same, and the woods are without underwood as well as in that country. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> seems to be surrounded by reefs and shoals, which render all access to it extremely dangerous; but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the coasts against the attacks of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and sea; rendering it easily navigable along the coast by canoes, and caulking it about with fish. Every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the coast seems to be inhabited: the plantations in the plains are laid out with great judgment, and cultivated with much labour. They begin their cultivation by setting fire to the grass, &c., with which the ground is covered, but have no notion of preserving its vigour by manure; they, however, recruit it by letting it lie for some years untouched. On the beach was found a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of rock, not less than a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> of ten feet, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-grained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> speckled full of granites somewhat bigger than pine heads, from whence it seems probable that some valuable minerals may be found on this island. It differs from all the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> yet discovered in the South Sea, by being entirely destitute of volcanic productions. Several plants of a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> were found here; and a few young <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit trees, not then sufficiently grown to bear fruit, seemed to have come up without culture; plantains and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes are here in small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, and the cocoanut trees are small and thinly planted. A new species of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> flower was likewise met with, which was never known to grow wild anywhere but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Several Caputi (Melaleuca) trees were also found in flower. Mulquetos here are very numerous. A great variety of birds was seen of different classes, which were for the most part entirely new; particularly a beautiful species of parrot before unknown to zoologists. A new species of fish, of the genus called by Linnaeus Tetraodon, was caught here; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, which was very large, presented at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. Several species of this genus being reckoned poisonous, and the present species being remarkably ugly, Mr. Forsters hinted their suspiciousness of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; but the temptation of a fresh <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and the assurances of Captain Cook that he had formerly eaten this identical sort of fish without harm, got the better of their scruples, and they ate of it. Its oiliness, however, though it had no other bad <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> than what proceeded from this, prevented them from taking more than a morsel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two. In a few hours after they had retired to rest, they were awakened by very alarming symptoms, being all seized with an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> giddiness; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet were numb, so that they were fearlessly able to crawl; and a violent languor and oppression seized them. Emetics were administered with some success, but sudorifics gave the greatest relief. Some dogs who had eaten the remainder of the liver were likewise taken ill; and a pig which had eaten the entrails died soon after, having swelled to an unusual size. The effects of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> on the gentlemen did not entirely go off in less than six weeks.—Abundance of turtle was seen here. The natives had not the least notion of goats, hogs, dogs, or cats, and had not even a name for any of them. The inhabitants are very stout, tall, and in general well proportioned; their features mild; their beards and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and strongly frizzled, so as to be somewhat woolly in some individuals: their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is fawny, or a dark chestnut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. A few were seen who measured five feet four inches. They are remarkably courteous, not at all addicted to pilfering and stealing: in which character of honesty they are singular, all the other nations in the South Sea being remarkably thieves. Some wear their hair long, and tie it up to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of their heads; others suffer only a large lock to grow on each side, which they tie up in clubs; many others, as well as all the women, wear it cropped short. They make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a kind of comb made of sticks of hard wood, from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten inches long, and about the thickness of knitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these, seldom exceeding twenty, but generally fewer, are fastened together at one end, parallel to and near one-tenth of an inch from each other; the ends, which are a little pointed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> spread out or open like the sticks of a fan. These combs they always wear in their hair on one side of their head. Some had a kind of concave cylindrical stiff black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, which appeared to be a great ornament among them, and was supposed to be worn only by the chiefs and warriors. A large sheet of strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, whenever they got one in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> applied to this purpose. The men go naked; only tying a string round their middle, and another round their neck. A little piece of a brown cloth made of the bark of a fig tree, sometimes tucked up to the belt, and sometimes pendulous, scarcely deserves the name of a covering; nor indeed does it seem at all intended for that purpose. This piece of cloth is sometimes of such a length, that the extremity is fastened to the string round the neck; to this string they likewise hang small round beads of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> green nephritic stone. Coarse garments were seen among them made of a sort of matting; but they seemed never to wear them, except when in their canoes and unemployed. The women seemed to be in a servile state: they were the only persons of the family who had any employment, and several of them brought bundles of sticks and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> on their backs; those who had children carried them on their backs in a kind of satchel. The women also were seen to dig up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in order to plant it. They are in general of a dark chestnut, and sometimes mahogany brown; their stature middle-sized, some being rather tall, and their whole form rather stout and somewhat clumsy. Their dress is the most disfiguring that can be imagined, and gives them a thick squat shape; it is a short petticoat or fringe, consisting of filaments or little cords, about eight inches long, which are fastened to a very long string, which they have tied several times round their waist. The filaments, or little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, therefore, lie above each other in several layers, forming a kind of thick... Caledonia, thick thatch all round the body, but which does not near cover the thigh; these filaments were sometimes dyed black; but frequently those on the outside only were of that colour, the rest being of a dirty gray. There was not a single instance, during the ship's stay in this island, of the women permitting any indecent familiarity with an European: they took <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in practising the arts of a jilting coquette, but never became <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> wantons. The general ornaments of both sexes are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings of tortoise shells; necklaces, or amulets, made of both shells and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and bracelets made of large shells, which they wear above the elbows. The houses, or huts, in New Caledonia, are circular, something like a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a>-hive, and full as close and warm; the entrance is by a small door, or long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> big enough to admit a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> bent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>: the side walls are about four feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is lofty, and peaked to a point at the top, above which is a pott or stick of wood, which is generally ornamented either with carving or shells, or both. The framing is of small spars, reeds, &c., and both sides and roof are thick, and close covered with thatch made of coarse long grass. In the inside of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> are set up pots, to which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> spars are fastened, and platforms made for the convenience of laying anything on. Some houses have two floors, one above another; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is laid with dried grass, and here and there mats are spread for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> people to sit or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on. In these houses there was no passage for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> but through the door; they were intolerably smoky, and so hot as to be insufficiently to those unaccustomed to them: probably the smoke is intended to drive out the musquitoes which swarm here. They commonly erect two or three of these huts near each other under a clump of lofty fig trees, whose leaves are impervious to the rays of the sun. The canoes used here are very heavy clumsy vessels; they are made of two trees hollowed out, having a raised gunnel about two inches high, and closed at each end with a bulk head of the same height; so that the whole is like a long square trough about three feet shorter than the body of the canoe. Two canoes thus fitted are fastened to each other about three feet under, by means of cross spars, which project about a foot over each side. Over these is laid a deck or heavy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> made of plank and small round spars, on which they have a fire-hearth, and generally a fire <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>; they are navigated by one or two lateen sails, extended to a small lateen yard, the end of which is fixed in a notch or hole in the deck. Notwithstanding the inoffensive disposition of the inhabitants of New Caledonia, they are well provided with offensive weapons; as clubs, spears, darts, and flings for throwing stones. Their clubs are about two feet and a half long, and variously formed; some like a scythe, others like a pick-axe; some have a head like a hawk, and others have round heads; but all are neatly made; many of their darts and spears are no less neat and ornamented with carvings. The flings are as simple as possible; but they take some pains to form the stones that they use into a proper shape, which is something like an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, supposing both ends to be like the small one. They drive the dart by the assistance of short cords knotted at one end and looped at the other, called by the seamen beackets. These contain a quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> taken from the vampire, or great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> bat. Bows and arrows are wholly unknown among them. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> bears no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to that spoken in the other South sea islands, the word arrakee and one or two more excepted. This is the more extraordinary, as different dialects of one language were spoken not only in the easterly islands, but at New Zealand. A musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, a kind of whistle, was procured here. It was a little polished piece of brown wood about two inches long, shaped like a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, though apparently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, with a rope fixed at the small end; two holes were made in it near the base, and another near the insertion of the rope, all which communicated with each other; and by blowing in the uppermost, a shrill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> like whistling was produced: no other instrument was seen among them that had the least relation to music. Many of the New Caledonians were seen with prodigiously thick legs and arms, which seemed to be affected with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>; the swelling was found to be extremely hard, but the skin was not alike harsh and scaly in all those who were afflicted with the disorder. The preternatural expansion of the arm or leg did not appear to be a great inconvenience; and they seemed to intimate that they very rarely felt any pain in it; but in some the disorder began to form blisters, which are marks of a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of virulence. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is probably elephantiasis. Here they <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead in the ground. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> who had been slain in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> here resembled a large <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>-hill, and was decorated with spears, darts, paddles, &c., all stuck upright in the ground round about it. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Pickering was showed a chief whom they named Tra-booma, and styled their arrakee or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; but nothing further is known of their government, and nothing at all of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

CALEFACTION

Pages 81-81

the production of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in a body from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of fire, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that impulse impressed by a hot body on others around it. This word is used in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>, by way of distinction from cælium, which implies <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>; whereas calefaction is only heating a thing.

CALENBERG

Pages 81-81

a principality of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and one of the three parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the duchy of Verden, on the east by the principality of Zell, on the south by the principalities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRUBENHAGEN">Grubenhagen</a> and Wolfenbuttle, and on the west by Westphalia. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>.

CALENDAR

Pages 81-81

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>. See KALENDER. CALENDAR of prisoners, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of all the prisoners names in the custody of each respective <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>*.

CALENDER

Pages 82-82

a machine used in manufactories to press certain woollen and filken stuffs and linens, to make them smooth, even, and glossy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to give them waves, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> them, as may be seen in mohairs and tabbies. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is composed of two thick cylinders, or rollers, of very hard and well polished wood, round which the stuffs to be calendered are wound; these rollers are placed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-wise between two very thick boards, the lower serving as a fixed base, and the upper moveable by means of a thick screw with a rope fastened to a spindle, which makes its axis: the uppermost board is loaded with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> weighing 20,000 lb. or more. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> they have an extraordinary machine of this kind, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> calender, made by order of M. Colbert. The lower <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> or plank is made of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of smooth marble, and the upper is lined with a plate of polished <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the upper board sometimes one way and sometimes another, together with the prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> laid upon it, gives the stuffs their glofs and smoothness; or gives them the waves, by making the cylinders on which they are put roll with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force over the undermost board. When they would put a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a> from under the calender, they only incline the undermost board of the machine. The dressing alone, with the many turns they make the stuffs and linens undergo in the calender, gives the waves, or waters them, as the workmen call it. It is a mistake to think, as some have asserted, and Mr Chambers among others, that they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> rollers with a shallow indenture or engraving cut in them. CALENDER of Monteith, a district in the southwest corner of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a> in Scotland, from which a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of Livingstone had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> seat of the family near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a> is also called Calender. Both estate and title were forfeited in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the possessor being engaged in the rebellion 1715.

CALENDERS

Pages 82-83

a sort of Mahometan friars, so called from Santon Calenderi their founder. This Santon went bareheaded, without a shirt, and with the skin of a wild beast thrown over his shoulders. He wore a kind of apron before, the strings of which were adorned with counterfeit precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. His disciples are rather a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of epicures than a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. They <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> a tavern as much as they do a mosque; and think they pay as acceptable worship to God by the free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his creatures, as others do by the greatest austerities and acts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. They are called, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, Abdals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Abdallet, i.e. persons consecrated to the honour and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of God. Their garment is a single coat, made up of a variety of pieces, and quilted like a rug. They preach in the market places, and live upon what their auditors bestow on them. They are generally very vicious persons: for which reason they are not admitted into any houses. per <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. About <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> almost all the calves are fattened for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>. The reason of this is, that there is a good market for them, and the lands there are not so profitable to breed upon as in cheaper countries. The way to make calves fat and fine, is the keeping them very clean; giving them fresh litter every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and the hanging a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> chalk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in some corner where they can easily get at it to lick it, but where it is out of the way of being fouled by their dung and urine. The coops are to be placed so as not to have too much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> upon them, and so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> above the ground that the urine may run off. They also bleed them once when they are a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> old, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before they kill them; which is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> addition to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and whiteness of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>: the bleeding is by some repeated much oftener, but this is sufficient. Calves are very apt to be loose in their bowels; which wastes and very much injures them. The remedy is to give them chalk scraped among <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, pouring it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this does not succeed, they give them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">bale</a> armenic in large doses, and use the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> bath every morning. If a cow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not let a strange calf suck her, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method is to rub both her nose and the calf's with a little brandy; this generally reconciles them after a few feedings. Golon CALF, an idol set up and worshipped by the Israelites at the foot of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>, in their passage through the wilderness to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>. Our version makes <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> fashion this calf with a graving tool after he had <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> it in a mould: the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> translation makes him engrave it first, and cast it afterwards. Others, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, render the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> thus: "And Aaron received them (the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> earrings), and tied them up in a bag, and got them cast into a molten calf," which version is authorised by the different senses of the word tsur, which signifies to tie up or bind, as well as to shape or form; and of the word cheret, which is used both for a graving tool and a bag. Some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fathers have been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this idol had only the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a calf, and the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> from the neck downwards, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Egyptian Ibis. Others have thought it was only the head of an ox without a body. But the most general opinion is, that it was an entire calf in imitation of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> worshipped by the Egyptians; among whom, no doubt, the Israelites had acquired their propensity to idolatry. This calf Moses is said to have burnt with fire, reduced to powder, and threw upon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which the people were to drink. How this could be accomplished hath been a question. Most people have thought, that as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> is indestructible, it could only be burnt by the miraculous power of God; but M. Stahl conjectures that Moses dissolved it by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> of sulphur. The Rabbins tell us that the people were made to drink of this water in order to distinguish the idolaters from the rest; for that as soon as they had drunk of it, the beards of the former turned <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. The Cabbalists add, that the calf weighed 125 quintals; which they gather from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word maffakah, whose numerical letters make 125.

CALENTIUS

Pages 82-82

Elisius, a Neapolitan poet and prose author. He was preceptor to Frederick the son of Ferdinand <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and the earliest writer on the illegality of putting criminals to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, except for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. He died in 1593.

CALENTURE

Pages 82-82

a feverish disorder incident to sailors in hot countries; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> symptom of which is their imagining the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to be green fields: hence, attempting to walk abroad in these imaginary places of delight, they are frequently lost. Vomiting, bleeding, a spare diet, and the neutral salts, are recommended in this disorder; a single vomit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> removing the delirium, and the cooling medicines completing the cure.

CALEPIN

Pages 82-82

Ambrosius, an Augustinian monk of Calepio, whence he took his name, in the 16th century. He is author of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of eight languages, since augmented by Paffert and others.

CALES

Pages 82-82

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a municipal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in Campania, at no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from Caflinum. The epithet Calenus is by Horace and Juvenal applied to a generous wine which the territory produced.

CALETES

Pages 82-82

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a people of Gallia Celtica, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, situated between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and the Sequana. Now called le Paix de Caux, in Normandy.

CALETURE

Pages 82-82

a fort on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon, at the mouth of a river of the same name. The Dutch became masters of it in 1655; but were afterwards obliged to leave it. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80. 51. N. Lat. 6. 38.

CALF

Pages 82-82

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the young of the ox kind. There are two ways of breeding calves that are intended to be reared. The one is to let the calf run about with its <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> all the year round; which is the method in the cheap breeding countries, and is generally allowed to make the best cattle. The other is to take them from the dam after they have sucked about a fortnight; they are then to be taught to drink flat <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, which is to be made but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> warm for them, it being very dangerous to give it them too hot. The best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of weaning calves is from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> to May: they should have milk for 12 weeks after; and a fortnight before that is left off, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> should be mixed with the milk in larger and larger quantities. When the calf has been fed on milk for about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, little wafers of hay should be placed all about him in cleft sticks to induce him to eat. In the beginning of April they should be turned out to graze; only for a few days they should be taken in for the night, and have milk and water given them: the same may also be given them in a pail sometimes in the field, till they are so able to feed themselves that they do not regard it. The grazes they are turned into must not be too <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, but short and sweet, that they may like it, and yet get it with some labour. Calves should always be weaned at grazes; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be done with hay and water, they often grow big-bellied on it, and are apt to rot. When those among the males are selected which are to be kept as bulls, the rest should be kept for oxen: the sooner the better. Between 10 and 20 days is a pro-

CALF-SKIN

Pages 83-83

in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> manufacture, are prepared and dressed by the tanners, skinners, and curriers, who sell them for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the shoemakers, saddlers, bookbinders, and other artificers, who employ them in their several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. CALF-SKIN draped in fumach, denotes the skin of this animal curried <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> side, and dyed of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> side, by means of fumach, chiefly used in the making of belts. The English calf-skin is much valued abroad, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> thereof very considerable in France and other countries; where <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> attempts have been made to imitate it, but hitherto in vain. What is like to baffled all endeavours for imitating the English calf in France is, the smallness and weakness of the calves about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; which at 15 days old are not so big as the English ones when they come into the world. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-CALF. See PHOCA, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> LIV.

CALIBER

Pages 83-83
or CALLIPER, properly denotes the diameter of any body; thus we say, two columns of the same caliber, the caliber of the bore of a gun, the caliber of a bull's eye, &c. CALIBER Compasses, a sort of compasses made with arched legs to take the diameter of round or swelling bodies. See COMPASSES. Caliber compasses are chiefly used by gunners for taking the diameters of the several parts of a piece of ordnance, or of bombs, bullets, &c. Their legs are therefore circular; and move on an arch of brass, wherein is marked the inches and half inches, to show how far the points of the compasses are opened or closed. Some are also made for taking the diameter of the bore of a gun or mortar. The gaugers also sometimes use calibers, to embrace the two heads of any cask, in order to find its length. The caliber used by carpenters and joiners, is a piece of hard notched triangular-wood in the middle for the taking of measure.

CALIBER RULE

Pages 83-87
or Gunners CALLIPERS, is an instrument wherein a right line is so divided as that the first part being equal to the diameter of an iron or leaden ball of one pound weight, the other parts are to the first as the diameters of balls of two, three, four, &c., pounds are to the diameter of a ball of one pound. The caliber is used by engineers, from the weight of the ball given, to determine its diameter or caliber, or vice versa. The gunners callipers consist of two thin plates of brass joined by a rivet, so as to move quite round each other: its length from the centre of the joint is between six inches and a foot, and its breadth from one to two inches; that of the most convenient size is about nine inches long. Many scales, tables, and proportions, &c. may be introduced on this instrument; but none are essential to it, except those for taking the caliber of shot and cannon, and for measuring the magnitude of salient and entering angles. The most complete callipers is exhibited Plate CXXXIII. The furniture and use of which we shall now briefly describe. Let the four faces of this instrument be distinguished by the letters A, B, C, D: A and D consist Caliber. On the circular head adjoining to the leg of the face A are divisions denominated *shot diameters*; which show the distance in inches and tenths of an inch of the points of the callipers when they are opened; so that if a ball not exceeding ten inches be introduced between them, the bevil edge E marks its diameter among these divisions. On the circular bevil part E of the face B is a scale of divisions distinguished by *lb., weight of iron shot*. When the diameter of any shot is taken between the points of the callipers, the inner edge of the leg A shows its weight in avoirdupois pounds, provided it be lb. \( \frac{1}{2}, 1, \frac{3}{4}, 2, 3, 4, \frac{5}{4}, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, 24, 26, 32, 36, \) or \( 42 \); the figures nearest the bevil edge answering to the short lines in the scale, and those behind them to the longer strokes. This scale is constructed on the following geometrical theorem, viz. that the weights of spheres are as the cubes of their diameters. On the lower part of the circular head of the face A is a scale of divisions marked *bores of guns*; for the use of which, the legs of the callipers are flipped across each other, till the steel points touch the concave surface of the gun in its greatest breadth; then the bevil edge F of the face B will cut a division in the scale showing the diameter of the bore in inches and tenths. Within the scales of *shot* and *bore* diameters on the circular part of A, are divisions marked *pounders*: the inner figures \( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, 3, \frac{5}{4}, 8, 12, 18, 26, 36 \), correspond to the longest lines; and the figures, 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 16, 24, 32, 42, to the short strokes. When the bore of a gun is taken between the points of the callipers, the bevil edge F will either cut or be near one of these divisions, and show the weight of iron shot proper for that gun. On the upper half of the circular head of the face A are three concentric scales of degrees; the outer scale consisting of 180 degrees numbered from right to left, 10, 20, &c. the middle numbered the contrary way, and the outer scale beginning at the middle, with 0, and numbered on each side to 90 degrees. These scales serve to take the quantity of an angle, either entering or salient. For an entering or internal angle, apply the legs of the callipers so that its outward edges coincide with the legs of the given angle, the degree cut by the bevil edge F in the outer scale shows the measure of the angle sought; for a salient or external angle, slip the legs of the callipers across each other, so that their outward edges may coincide with the legs forming the angle, and the degree marked on the middle scale by the bevil edge E will show the measure of the angle required. The inner scale will serve to determine the elevation of cannon and mortars, or of any oblique plane. Let one end of a thread be fixed into the notch on the plate B, and any weight tied to the other end: apply the straight side of the plate A to the side of the body whose inclination is sought; hold it in this position, and move the plate B, till the thread falls upon the line near the centre marked *perp.* Then will the bevil edge F cut the degrees on the inner scale, showing the inclination of that body to the horizon. On the face C near the point of the callipers is a little table showing the proportion of troy and avoirdupois weights, by which one kind of weight may be easily reduced into another. Near the extreme of the face D of the callipers are two tables showing the proportion between the pounds weight of London and Paris, and also between the lengths of the foot measure of England and France. Near the extreme on the face A is a table containing four rules of the circle and sphere; and geometrical figures with numbers annexed to them: the first is a circle including the proportion in round numbers of the diameter to its circumference; the second is a circle, inscribed in a square, and a square within that circle, and another circle in the inner square: the numbers 28, 22, above this figure exhibit the proportion of the outward square to the area of the inscribed circle; and the numbers 14, 11, below it, show the proportion between the area of the inscribed square and the area of its inscribed circle. The third is a cube inscribed in a sphere; and the number 89\(\frac{1}{2}\) shows that a cube of iron, inscribed in a sphere of 12 inches in diameter, weighs 89\(\frac{1}{2}\)lb. The fourth is a sphere in a cube, and the number 243 expresses the weight in pounds of a sphere inscribed in a cube whose side is 12 inches; the fifth represents a cylinder and cone of one foot diameter and height: the number in the cylinder shows, that an iron cylinder of that diameter and height weighs 364.5 lb, and the number 121.5 in the cone expresses the weight of a cone, the diameter of whose base is 12 inches, and of the same height: the fifth figure shows that an iron cube, whose side is 12 inches, weighs 464lb, and that a square pyramid of iron, whose base is a square foot and height 12 inches, weighs 154\(\frac{1}{2}\)lb. The numbers which have been hitherto fixed to the four last figures were not strictly true; and therefore they have been corrected in the figure here referred to; and by these the figures on any instrument of this kind should be corrected likewise. On the leg B of the callipers, is a table showing the weights of a cubic inch or foot of various bodies in pounds avoirdupois. On the face D of the circular head of the callipers is a table contained between five concentric segments of rings: the inner one marked *Gun* shows the nature of the gun or the weight of ball it carries; the two next rings contain the quantity of powder used for proof and service to brass guns, and the two outermost rings show the quantity for proof and service in iron cannon. On the face A is a table exhibiting the method of computing the number of *lbs* or *balls* in a triangular, square, or rectangular pile. Near this is placed a table containing the principal rules relative to the fall of bodies, expressed in an algebraic manner: nearer the centre we have another table of rules for raising water, calculated on the supposition, that one horse is equal in this kind of labour to five men, and that one man will raise a hoghead of water to eight feet of height in one minute, and work at that rate for some hours. N.B. Hogheads are reckoned at 60 gallons. Some of the leading principles in gunnery, relating to *firing* in cannon and mortars, are expressed on the face B of the callipers. Besides the articles already enumerated, enumerated, the scales usually marked on this sector are laid down on this instrument; thus the line of inches is placed on the edge of the callipers, or on the straight borders of the faces C, D: the logarithmic scales of numbers, fines, versed fines, and tangents, are placed along these faces near the straight edges: the line of lines is placed on the same faces in an angular position, and marked Lin. The lines of planes or surfaces are also exhibited on the faces C and D, tending towards the centre, and marked Plan. Finally, the lines of solids are laid on the same faces tending towards the centre, and distinguished by Sol.

CALICOUAN

Pages 87-87
or Quillon, a town of Asia, in the East Indies, on the coast of Malabar, and in the peninsula on this side the Ganges, where the Dutch have a factory. E. Long. 75. 21. N. Lat. 9.

CALICUT

Pages 87-87

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of that name on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar. It contains a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> low houses, each of which has a garden. The English had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> here, but it is removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TELLICHERRY">Tellicherry</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76. 4. N. Lat. 11. 21. CALIDÆ PLANTÆ (from calor, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>); <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> that are natives of warm climates. Such are those of the East Indies, South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and the Canary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. These plants, says Linnæus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat which is as 40 on a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> in which the freezing point is 0, and 100 the heat of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. In the 10th degree of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> they cease to grow, lose their leaves, become barren, are suffocated, and perish.

CALIDUCT

Pages 87-87
