Oath of CALUMNY, Juramentum (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather Jucurandum) Calumniae, among civilians and canonists, was an oath which both parties in a cause were obliged to take; the plaintiff that he did not bring his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, and the defendant that he did not deny it, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to abuse each other, but because they believed their cause was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and good; that they would not deny the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, nor create unnecessary delays, nor offer the judge or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> any gifts or bribes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the plaintiff refused this oath, the complaint or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> was dismissed; if the defendant, it was taken pro confesso. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was taken from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol2.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a>; who, before they engaged, were to swear that they had no malice, nor would <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> any unfair means for overcoming each other. The juramentum calumniae is much disused, as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> occasion of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>. Anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> and proctors also took this oath; but of late it is dispensed with, and thought sufficient that they take it once for all at their first admission to practice. See also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">LAW</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. N° clxxxiv. 7.

CALVARIA

Pages 94-94

in Anatomy, the hairy scalp <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head, which, either by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> or old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, grows bald first.

CALVART

Pages 94-94

Denis, a celebrated painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1552; and had for his masters Prospero Fontana and Lorenzo Sabbatini. He opened a school at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, which became celebrated; and from which proceeded Guido, Albani, and other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> masters. Calvart was well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, and anatomy, which he considered as necessary to a painter, and taught them to his pupils. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are at Bologna, Rome, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>. He died at Bologna in 1619.

CALVARY

Pages 94-94

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> so called, because it resembles the cross on which our Saviour suffered. It is always set upon steps.

CALVERT

Pages 94-94

GEORGE, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a>, was born at Kipling in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> about the year 1582, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts, and afterwards travelled. At his return, he was made secretary to Sir Robert Cecil: he was afterwards knighted, and in 1618 appointed one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretaries of state. But after he had enjoyed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> about five years, he willingly resigned it; freely owning to his majesty that he was become a Roman Catholic, so that he must either be wanting to his trust, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> violate his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> in discharging his office. This ingenuous confession so affected <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James, that he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> him privy counsellor all his reign, and the same year created him baron of Baltimore in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. He had before obtained a patent for him and his heirs, for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Avalon in Newfoundland: but that being exposed to the insults of the French, he abandoned it, and afterwards obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., who called it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>: but he died in April 1632 (aged 50), before the patent was made out. It was, however, filled up to his son Cecil Calvert Lord Baltimore; and bears <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 20, 1632. It is held from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> as part of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, on one very singular condition, viz., to present two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> arrows yearly, on Easter Tuesday, at the castle, where they are kept and shown to visitors.—His lordship wrote, 1. A Latin poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir Henry Upton. 2. Speeches in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. 3. Various letters of state. 4. The answer of Tom Tell-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. 5. The Practice of Princes. And, 6. The Lamentation of the Kirk.

CALVI

Pages 94-94

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lavoro, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, situated near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, about fifteen miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Naples. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 45'. N. Lat. 41° 15'. Calvi is also the name of a sea port in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Corsica, situated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, on the west side of the island, about 40 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTIA">Bastia</a>. E. Long. 9° 5'. N. Lat. 42° 16'.

CALVIN

Pages 94-95

JOHN, the celebrated reformer of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> from Romish superstitions and doctrinal nal errors, and founder of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> since called Calvinists, was born in 1509. He was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">cooper</a> of Noyon in Picardy; and his real name was Chauvin, which he chose to latinize into Calvinus, styling himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> page to his first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> (a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on Seneca de Clementia), "Lucius Calvinus, Civis Romanus;" an early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, at about 24 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In 1529, he was rector of Puy l'Eveque; and in 1534 he threw up this benefice, separating himself entirely from the Roman church. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in France (with whom he was now associated) obliged him to retire to Basle in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; here he published his famous Institutes of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in 1536. The following year he was chosen professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and one of the ministers of the church at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. The next year, viz. 1537, he made all the people solemnly swear to a body of doctrines; but finding that religion had not yet had any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence on the morals of the people, he, afflicting by other ministers, declared, that since all their admonitions and warnings had proved unsuccessful, they could not celebrate the holy sacrament as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as these disorders reign; he also declared, that he could not submit to some regulations made by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>. Upon which the syndics having summoned the people, it was ordered that Calvin and two other ministers should leave the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> within two days. Upon this Calvin retired to Straßburg, where he established a French church, of which he was the first minister, and was also chosen professor of divinity there. Two years after he was chosen to assist at the diet appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> to meet at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a> and at Ratibon in order to appease the troubles occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of religion. He went with Beucer, and entered into a conference with Melanchthon. The people of Geneva now entreated him to return; to which he consented, and arrived at Geneva, September 13, 1541. He began with establishing a form of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and a consistorial jurisdiction, with the power of inflicting all kinds of canonical punishments. This was greatly disliked by many persons, who imagined that the papal tyranny would soon be revived. Calvin, however, asserted on all occasions the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of his consistory with inflexible strictness; and he caused Michael Servetus to be burnt at the stake for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> against the doctrine of the Trinity. But though the rigour of his proceedings sometimes occasioned great tumults in the city, yet nothing could shake his tenacity and inflexibility. Amongst all the disturbances of the commonwealth, he took care of the foreign churches in England, France, Germany, and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; and did more by his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> than his presence, sending his advice and instructions by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and writing a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books. This great reformer died on the 27th of May 1564, aged 55. His works were printed together at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1671, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> volumes folio; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are his Institutions, in Latin, the best edition of which is that of Robert Stephens in 1553, in folio; and his Commentaries on the Holy Scriptures.—Calvin is universally allowed to have had great talents, an excellent genius, and profound learning. His style is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and polite. Independent of his spiritual pride, his morals were exemplary; for he was pious, sober, chaste, laborious, and disinterested. But his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> can never be purified from the stain of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> Servetus; it ill became a reformer, to adopt the most odious practice of the corrupt church of Rome.

CALVINISM

Pages 95-95

the doctrine and sentiments of Calvin and his followers. Calvinism subsists in its greatest purity in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; and from thence it was first propagated into Germany, France, the United Provinces, and England. In France it was abolished by the revocation of the edict of Nantes in 1685. It has been the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in the United Provinces ever since the year 1571. The theological system of Calvin was adopted, and made the public rule of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in England, under the reign of Edward VI. and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland was modelled by John Knox, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Calvin, agreeably to the doctrine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, and form of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, established at Geneva. In England, it has declined since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; though it still subsists, some say a little alloyed, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the established church; and in its rigour in Scotland. The distinguishing theological tenets of Calvinism, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is now generally applied, respect the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREDESTINATION">Predestination</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">Election</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">Reprobation</a>, original Sin, particular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">Redemption</a>, effectual, or, as some have called it, irresistible <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> in regeneration, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">Justification</a> by faith, Perseverance, and the Trinity. See each of these articles. Besides the doctrinal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Calvin's system, which, so far as it differs from that of other reformers of the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, principally regarded the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of God, whereby the future and eternal condition of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> was determined out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> sovereign <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>; it extended likewise to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and government of the Christian church, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the Eucharist, and the qualification of those who were entitled to the participation of it. Calvin considered every church as a separate and independent body, invested with the power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a> for itself. He proposed that it should be governed by presbyteries and synods, composed of clergy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>, without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, or any clerical subordination; and maintained, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> extended only to its protection and outward accommodation. In order to facilitate an union with the Lutheran church, he acknowledged a real, though spiritual, presence of Christ, in the Eucharist; that true <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were united to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> Christ in this ordinance, and that divine grace was conferred upon them, and sealed to them, in the celebration of it; and he confined the privilege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> to pious and regenerate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>. In France the Calvinists are distinguished by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>; and, among the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, by that of Parpaillois. In Germany they are confounded with the Lutherans, under the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>; only sometimes distinguished by the name Reformed.

CALVINISTS

Pages 95-96

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, those who follow the opinions of Calvin. See the two preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Crypto-Calvinists, a name given to the favourers of Calvinism in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, on account of their secret <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Genevan doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. Many of them suffered by the decrees of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> of Torgau, held in 1576. The Calvinists in their progress... CALVINISTS have divided into various branches, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lesser sects.

CALVISIUS

Pages 96-96

Seth, a celebrated German chronologer in the beginning of the 17th century. He wrote *Elenchus calendarii Gregoriani*, et *duplex calendarii melioris forma*, and other learned works, together with some excellent treatises on music. He died in 1617, aged 61.

CALVITES

Pages 96-96
or CALVITIUM, in Medicine, baldness, or a want of hair, particularly on the fisciput, occasioned by the moisture of the head, which should feed it, being dried up, by some disease, old age, or the immoderate use of powder, &c. See ALOPECIA.

CALVUS

Pages 96-96

Cornelius Licinius, a celebrated Roman orator, was the friend of Catullus; and flourished 64 B.C. Catullus, Ovid, and Horace, speak of him.

CALX PROPERLY

Pages 96-97

X properly signifies lime, but has been used by chemists and physicians for a fine powder remaining after the calcination of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. All metallic calces are found to weigh more than the metal from which they were originally produced. This arises from the metal having combined with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of calcination <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>; and hence in the present chemical nomenclature they are called oxides. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">CALX</a> Nativa, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARLY">marly</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, of a dead whitish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> thrown into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, water, makes a considerable bubbling and hissing noise, and has, without previous burning, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of making a cement like lime or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. CALX Viva, or Quicklime, that whereon no water has been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to lime which has been flaked by pouring water on it.

CALYBITES

Pages 97-97

the inhabitants of a cottage, an appellation given to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> saints on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> residence in some hut by way of mortification. The word is formed from καλύπτω, tigo, I cover; whence καλύπτον, a little cot. The Cumbish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> commemorates St John the Calybite on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. CALYCANTHEMÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in the Fragmenta methodi naturalis of Linnaeus, in which are the following genera, viz. epilobium, cænotha, jujfæa, ludwigia, oldenlandia, infarda, &c. See BOTANY, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Orders. CALYCANTHUS. See BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CALYCIFLORÆ, in Botany, the 16th order in Linnaeus's Fragmenta methodi naturalis, consisting of plants which, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> imports, have the stamens (the flower) inserted into the calyx. This order contains the following genera, viz. elegans, hippophae, osyris, and tropis. See BOTANY. CALYCISTÆ, (from calyx, the flower-cup), systematic botanists, so named by Linnaeus, who have arranged all vegetables from the different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, structure, and other circumstances, of the calyx <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flower-cup. The only systems of this kind are the Character Plantarum Novus, a posthumous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Magnolius, professor of botany at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a>, published in 1720; and Linnaeus's Methodus Calycina, published in his Claves Plantarum, at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in 1738. See BOTANY, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>.

CALYDON

Pages 97-97

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Aetolia, situated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles and a half from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and divided by the river Evenus; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was anciently called Aolir, from the Aeolians its inhabitants. This country was famous for the story of Meleager and the Calydonian boar.

CALYPSO

Pages 97-97

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> who was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Oceanus and Tethys, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as others say, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. She was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ogygia, which from her was called the island of Calypso. According to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Ulysses suffered shipwreck on her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and staid with her several years.

CALYPTRA

Pages 97-97

among botanists, a thin membranaceous involucrum, usually of a conic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, which covers the parts of fructification. The capsules of most of the mosses have calyptrae.

CALYX

Pages 97-97

among botanists, a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, expressing the cup of a flower, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a plant which surrounds and supports the other parts of the flower. The cups of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are very various in their structure, and on that account distinguished by several names, as perianthium, involucrum, spathe, gluma, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>.

CALZADA

Pages 97-97

a town of Old Castile in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated on the river Leglera. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 47'. N. Lat. 42° 12'. CAMÆA, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of the semi-pellucid gems, approaching to the onyx structure, being composed of zones, and formed on a crystalline basis: but having their zones very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and thick, and laid alternately one on another, with no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> between; usually less transparent, and more debased with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, than the onyxes. 1. One <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the camæa is the dull-looking onyx, with broad, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> zones; and is the camæa of the moderns, and the Arabian onyx. This species is found in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and the East Indies. 2. Another species of the camæa is the dull broad-zoned, green and white camæa, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the jalpi-camæa of the Italians: it is found in the East Indies, and in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. 3. The third is the hard camæa, with broad white and chestnut-coloured veins. 4. The hard camæa, with bluish, white, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-coloured broad veins, being the sardonyx of Pliny's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, only brought from the East Indies.

CAMAIEU

Pages 97-97
or CAMAYEU, a word used to express a peculiar sort of onyx; also by some to express a stone, whereon are found various figures, and representations of landscapes, &c., formed by a kind of lytus nature, so as to exhibit pictures without painting. The word comes from camaius, a name the Orientals give to the onyx, when they find, in preparing it, another colour; as who should say, a second stone. It is of these camaius Pliny is to be understood when he speaks of the manifold picture of gems, and the party-coloured spots of precious stones: Gemmarum pictura tam multiplex lapidumque tam discolores macule. Camaieu is also applied by others to those precious stones, as onyxes, cornelian, and agates, whereon the lapidaries employ their art to aid nature, and perfect these representations. See CAMÆA. Camaieu is also frequently applied to any kind of gem, whereon figures may be engraved either indentedly or in relievo. In this sense the lapidaries of Paris are called in their statutes, cutters of camayeu. A society of learned men at Florence undertook to procure all the cameos or camayeu and intaglios in the great duke's gallery to be engraved; and began to draw the heads of divers emperors in cameos. Camaieu is also used for a painting, wherein there is only one colour; and where the lights and shadows are of gold, wrought on a golden or azure ground. When the ground is yellow, the French call it cirage; when gray, griffaille. This kind of work is chiefly used to represent baso relievos: the Greeks call pieces of this sort περιγραμματα.

CAMALDULIANS

Pages 97-98

Camaldunians, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Camaldolites, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, founded by Romuald, an Italian fanatic, in 1023, in the horrible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Camaldoli, otherwise called Campo Malduli, situated in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, on the Appennines. Their rule is that of St Benedict; and their houses, by the statutes, are never to be less than five leagues from cities. The Camaldulians have not borne that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> from the beginning of their order; till the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the eleventh century they were called Romualdinis, from the name of their founder. Till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, Camaldulian was a particular name for those of the desert Camaldoli; and D. Grandi observes, was not given to the whole order in regard it was in this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> that the order commenced, but because the regulation was best maintained here. Guido Grandi, mathematician of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>. Camaldulans, and a monk of this order, has published Camaldulian Dissertations, on the origin and establishment of it. The Camaldulites were distinguished into two classes, of which the one were Coenobites, and the other Eremites.

CAMALODUNUM

Pages 98-98

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Trinobantes, the first Roman colony in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, of veterans under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. From the Itineraries it appears to have stood where now Malden stands. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be an open <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; a place of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> rather than strength; yet not unadorned with splendid works, as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> and a temple of Claudius: which the Britons considered as badges of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, and which gave rise to several seditions and commotions. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the mouth of the Chelmer, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name is curtailed from the ancient.

CAMARANA

Pages 98-98

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, whose inhabitants are little and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. It is the best of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in this sea, and here they fish for coral and pearls. N. Lat. 15°.

CAMARCUM

Pages 98-98

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Nervii, a people of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, (Antonine, Peutinger); before whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> no mention was made of it. Now Cambrai, capital of the Cambresis, in French <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3°. Lat. 50°.

CAMARINA

Pages 98-98

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, built by the Syracusans on an eminence near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in the south of Sicily, to the west of the promontory Pachynum, between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the Hipparis and Oanus. Of so famous a city nothing now remains but its name and ancient walls, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in compass, with the slight remains of houses: now called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMARANA">Camarana</a>. CAMARINA Palus, a marsh <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lake, near the city Camarina, and from which it took its name. In a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of drought, the fench of the lake produced a pestilence; upon which the inhabitants consulted the oracle, whether they should not quite drain it. The oracle dissuaded them: they notwithstanding drained it, and opened a way for their enemies to come and plunder their city: hence the proverb Ne moveas Camarinam, that is, not to remove one evil to bring on a greater. Lago di Camarano, situated in a beautiful plain, under the very walls of Camarina, and of a triangular form. CAMAYEU. See CAMAIEU.

CAMASSEI

Pages 98-98
or CAMACE, ANDREA, painter of history and landscape, was born at Bevagna, and at first learned the principles of design and colouring from Domenichino; but afterwards he studied in the school of Andrea Sacchi, and proved a very great painter. He was employed in St Peter's at Rome, as also at St John Lateran; and his works are extremely admired, for the sweetness of his colouring, the elegance of his thoughts and design, and likewise for the delicacy of his pencil. Sandrart laments that the world was deprived of so promising a genius, in the very bloom of life, when his reputation was daily advancing. He died in 1657. At St John Lateran are to be seen, the Battle of Constantine and Maxentius; and the Triumph of Constantine; which are noble and grand compositions; and they afford sufficient proofs of the happiness of his invention, and the correctness of his execution. Also at Wilton, the seat of the earl of Pembroke, there is a picture of Venus with the Graces, said to be by the hand of Camassei.

CAMBAIA

Pages 98-98
or CAMPAT, a town of Asia, in India, and in the peninsula on this side the Ganges; capital of a province of the same name; but more commonly called Guzerat. It is seated at the bottom of a gulf of the same name, on a small river; is a large place with high walls, and has a pretty good trade. The product and manufactures are inferior to few towns in India, for it abounds in corn, cattle, and silk; and cornelian and agate stones are found in its rivers. The inhabitants are noted for embroidery; and some of their quilts have been valued at 40l. It is subject to the Great Mogul. E. Long. 72°. 15°. N. Lat. 22°. 30'.

CAMBAYES

Pages 98-98

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, cotton cloths made at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a>, and some other places on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Coromandel. They are proper for the trade of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, whither the English at Madras send <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of them. Many are also imported into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>.

CAMBER

Pages 98-98

according to our monkish historians, one of the three sons of Brutus, who, upon his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, had that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> assigned him for his share, called from him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIA">Cambria</a>, now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. CAMBER-Beam, among builders, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> in an edifice cut archwise, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with an obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> in the middle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in platforms, as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> leads, and on other occasions where <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and strong beams are required.

CAMBERED DECKS

Pages 98-98

among ship-builders. The deck <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flooring of a ship is said to be cambered, or to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> cambering, when it is higher in the middle of the ship's length, and droops towards the stem and stern, or the two ends. Also when it lies <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; a circumstance which renders the ship very unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

CAMBIO

Pages 98-98

an Italian word which signifies <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in Provence, and in some other countries, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>.

CAMBIT

Pages 98-98

a name given in France to those who trade in notes and bills of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. The word cambio, though a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of antiquity, is even now a technical word, of some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, traders, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>. Some derive it from the Latin cambium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather cambio.

CAMBLET

Pages 98-99
or Chamblet, a stuff sometimes of wool, sometimes silk, and sometimes hair, especially that of goats, with wool or silk: in some, the Cambray warp is silk and wool twisted together, and the woof hair. The true or oriental cambray is made of the pure hair of a sort of goat, frequent about Angora, and which makes the riches of that city, all the inhabitants whereof are employed in the manufacture and commerce of cambrays. It is certain we find mentioned in middle-age writers stuffs made of camel's hair, under the denominations of caneletum and camelinum; whence probably the origin of the term; but these are represented as strangely coarse, rough, and prickly, and seem to have been chiefly used among the monks by way of mortification, as the hair shirt of latter times. We have no cambrays made in Europe of the goats' hair alone; even at Bruxelles, they find it necessary to add a mixture of woollen thread. England, France, Holland, and Flanders, are the chief places of this manufacture. Bruxelles exceeds them all in the beauty and quality of its cambrays; those of England are reputed the second. Figured CAMBRAYS, are those of one colour, whereon are stamped various figures, flowers, foliage, &c., by means of hot irons, which are a kind of moulds, patted together with the stuff under a press. These are chiefly brought from Amiens and Flanders; the commerce of these was anciently much more considerable than at present. Watered CAMBRAYS, those which, after weaving, receive a certain preparation with water; and are afterwards passed under a hot press, which gives them a smoothness and lustre. Waved CAMBRAYS, are those wherein waves are impressed, as on tabbies; by means of a calender, under which they are patted and repatted several times. The manufacturers, &c., of cambrays are to take care they do not acquire any false and needleless plait; it being almost impossible to get them out again. This is notorious even to a proverb; we say a person is like cambray he has taken his plait.

CAMBODIA

Pages 99-99

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the kingdom of Laos, on the east by Cochin-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and Chiapa, and on the south and west by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> and kingdom of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>; divided by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river called Mecoon. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town is of the same name, seated on the western shore of the said river, about 150 miles north of its mouth. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is annually overflowed in the rainy season, between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and October; and its productions and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are much the same with those usually found between the tropics. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 104° 15' N. Lat. 12° 42'.

CAMBODUNUM

Pages 99-99

(Itinerary); a town of the Brigantes in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; now in ruins near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALMONBURY">Almonbury</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. Weltechester, (Talbot.) Also a town of Vindelicia, on the Cambus; now Kempton in Swabia.

CAMBOGIA

Pages 99-99

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the polyandria class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricoceae. The corolla is tetrapetalous; the calyx tetraphyllous; and the fruit is a pome with eight cells, and solitary seeds. There is but one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUTTA">gutta</a>, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, which yields the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-resin known by the name of gamboge in the shops. See GAMBOGE.

CAMBRASINES

Pages 99-99

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> made in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, of which there is a considerable trade at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROSETTA">Rosetta</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Raschit. They are called cambrafines from their resemblance to cambrics.

CAMBRAY

Pages 99-99

an archiepiscopal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Cambresis, in the Low Countries, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a>. It is defended by good fortifications, and has a fort on the side of the river; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is low on that side, they can lay the adjacent parts under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> by means of sluices. Its ditches are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and deep, and those of the citadel are cut into a rock. Clovis became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Cambrey in 445. The Danes burnt it afterwards; since which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it became a free imperial city. It has been the subject of contest between the emperors, the kings of France, and the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. Francis I. let it remain neutral during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V.; but this last took possession of it in 1543. After this it was given to John of Montluc by Henry III. of France, whom he created <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Cambrey; but the Spaniards took it from Montluc in 1593, which broke his heart. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> till 1677, when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France became master of it, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it has continued ever since. The buildings of Cambrey are tolerably handsome, and the streets fine and spacious. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> for arms is of an extraordinary largeness, and capable of receiving the whole garrison in order of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> is one of the finest in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The body of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is very large, and there are rich chapels, the pillars of which are adorned with marble tombs that are of exquisite workmanship, and add greatly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the place. There are two galleries, one of which is of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, finely wrought. The door of the choir is of the same metal, and well carved. The steeple of this church is very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>; and from its top you have a view of the city, which is one of the finest and most agreeable in the Low Countries. There are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> parishes, four abbeys, and several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> for both sexes. The citadel is very advantageously situated on the high ground, and commands the whole city. Cambrey is one of the most opulent and commercial cities in the Low Countries; and makes every year a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIC">cambric</a>, with which the inhabitants drive a great trade. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 20' N. Lat. 50° 11'.

CAMBRESIS

Pages 99-99

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, about 25 miles in length. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and east by Hainault, on the south by Picardy, and on the west by Artois. It is a very fertile and populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and the inhabitants are industrious, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, and ingenious. The trade consists principally in corn, sheep, very fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth. Cambrey is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

CAMBRIC

Pages 99-100

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, very fine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; the name of which was originally derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Cambrey, where they were first manufactured. They are now made at other places in France. The manufacture of cambrics hath <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> since proved of extraordinary advantage to France. For many years it appeared that England did not in this article contribute less than 200,000l. per annum to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of France. This proved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> sufficient to induce the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> to enact many salutary laws to prevent this great loss of our wealth. See 18 Geo. II. c. 38. and 21 Geo. II. c. 26. See also stat. 32 Geo. II. c. 32. and 4 Geo. III. c. 37. which regulates the cambric manufactory, not long since introduced into Winchelsea in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>; but very soon abolished. The cambrics now allowed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are manufactured in Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Any persons convicted of wearing, selling (except for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making up for hire any cambric or French lawns, are liable to a penalty of 5l. by the two first statutes cited above.

CAMBRIDGE

Pages 100-102

a town of England, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of that name. It takes the name of Cambridge from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Cam, which divides the town into two parts. Either it <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the neighbourhood was styled Camborium, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It suffered much during the wars with the Danes. Here was a castle built by William the Conqueror, of which the gatehouse yet remains, and is now the county gaol. By Doomsday-book it appears that it then had ten wards, containing 387 houses. In William Rufus's reign it was quite destroyed by Roger de <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a>; but Henry I. bestowed many privileges upon it to encourage its restoration, particularly an exemption from the power of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, on condition of its paying yearly into the exchequer 100 marks (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 1000 pounds now), and from tolls, lassage, pontage, passage, and stallage, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> of his dominions. It was afterwards often plundered in the barons wars by the outlaws from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, till Henry III. secured it by a deep ditch. In 1388, Richard II. held a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> there. In the rebellion of Wat Tyler and Jack Straw against that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, the university records were taken and burnt in the market place. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> town is about one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and about half a mile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in the middle, diminishing at the extremities. It has 14 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches, of which two are without any towers. It contains above 1200 houses; but the private buildings are neither elegant nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, owing chiefly to their being held on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> or corporation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a>. It is governed by a mayor, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, recorder, 13 aldermen and 24 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men, a town clerk, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> trade is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> carriage from hence to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNHAM">Downham</a>, Lynn, Ely, &c. The Jews, being encouraged to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in England by William I. and II. were very populous here for several generations, and inhabited that street now called the Jewry. They had a synagogue, since converted to a parish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, called from the shape of its tower Round Church; though others are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it was built by the Knights <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPLARS">Templars</a>, it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a resemblance to the Temple church in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The market place is situated in the middle of the town, and consists of two spacious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> squares united together; at the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> stands the shire <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, lately erected at the expense of the county. At the back of the shire hall is the town hall and gaol. In the market place, fronting the shire hall, is a remarkably handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> conduit, to which water is conveyed by an aqueduct, which was the benefaction of the celebrated Hobson, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a> in the reign of James I. who was a native of this town. A fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for the benefit of the inhabitants and students was made a few years since for four miles, from this town to Gogmagog hills, pursuant to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of Mr Worts. The late Dr Adenbrooke also left it 400l. towards <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and furnishing an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for the cure of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> diseased people gratis; of which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Catharine hall is a trustee; which hospital has been erected at the south-east end of the town. At a little distance from Bennet college is the botanic garden of five acres, and a large <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the governors and the residence of the curator, given to the university by the late Dr Walker, who settled an estate on it towards its support, to which the late Mr Edward Betham added a very considerable benefaction. The town has fairs on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 24. and August 14. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of Cambridge is its university; but when it had its beginning is uncertain. At first there was no public provision for the accommodation or maintenance of the scholars; but afterwards inns began to be erected by pious persons for their reception, and in the time of Edward I. colleges began to be built and endowed. This university, not inferior to any in Christendom, consists of 12 colleges and 4 halls, which have the same privileges as the colleges. The whole body, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> about 1500, enjoys very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> privileges granted by several of our sovereigns; but it was James I. who empowered it to send two members to parliament, as the town had done from the first. The university is governed, 1. By a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, who is always some nobleman, and may be changed every three years, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> longer by the tacit consent of the university. 2. By a high steward, chosen by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and holding his place by patent from the university. 3. By a vice-chancellor, who is the head of some college or hall, and chosen yearly by the body of the university, the heads of the colleges naming two. 4. By two proctors chosen every year, according to the cycle of colleges and halls; as are two taxors, who with the proctors regulate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, as clerks of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. The proctors also inspect the behaviour of the scholars, who must not be out of their colleges after <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> at night. Here are also 2 moderators, 2 scrutators, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>, public orator, 2 librarians, a registrar, a school-keeper, 3 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESQUIRE">esquire</a> beadles and a yeoman beadle, 18 professors, and the caput, consisting of the vice-chancellor, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, a doctor of laws, a doctor of physic, a regent and a non-regent master of arts. Henry VI. granted it the power to print all books of any kind within itself, a privilege which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> had not. The senate house of the university is an elegant building of the Corinthian order, cost near 16,000l. building; in which on the north side is a fine statue of George I. erected in 1739 at the expense of the late <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Townshend; opposite to this on the south side is another of George II. erected in 1765 at the expense of the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>; at the east end, on each side of the entrance, are two others; one, the late duke of Somerset, after the Vandyke <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; the other, an Italian emblematical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of Gloria. This is allowed to be the most superb room in England, being 101 feet long, Cambridge, long, 42 broad, and 32 high; and it has a gallery which can contain 1000 persons. This building forms the north side of the quadrangle, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and public library do the west, the schools being the ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, and the library over them surrounding a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. North of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> school is the repository of Dr Woodward's fossils, ores, shells, &c. The doctor, together with that collection, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his library, left a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to this university for erecting a professorship for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, with a provision of £500 a-year for ever. At the fourth-east corner of this building is an elegant geometrical stone staircase which leads to the old library, and consists of 18 classes; at the end of which is an elegant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> room, in which are deposited the MSS, and a valuable cabinet of oriental books and curiosities, &c. This room opens to two other rooms, containing 26 large classes, consisting of 30,000 volumes presented to the university by George I., being the entire collection of Dr Moore, bishop of Ely, and purchased of the doctor's executors by his majesty for 6000 guineas; before which his majesty gave the university £2000, to defray the expense of fitting up the apartments, and erecting classes for their reception; they consist of the first editions of the Greek and Latin classics and historians, and the greatest part of the works of the first printers; large collections of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> by the greatest masters; and a valuable MS. of the Gospels and Acts of the Apostles, on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, in Greek and Latin capitals, given to the university by Theodore Beza, supposed to be as old as any MS. extant. The other part of the library has been rebuilt in an elegant manner, and forms the west side of the intended quadrangle. The books which are contained in the last room are part of the old library, augmented with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the best modern books, several of which are presents from foreign sovereigns and eminent men. The south side of the quadrangle is designed for a building to contain the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-office, &c. of the university, for which preparations began lately to be made by pulling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the old buildings on the spot. St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s church forms the east side of this quadrangle: here the university have their public sermons; and the pulpit, which stands in the centre of the church, and faces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a>, has no soundingboard. In a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> gallery over part of the chancel is a seat for the chancellor, vice-chancellor, &c. George I., when he gave the books, also established a professor of modern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and modern languages in this university, with a salary of £400. for himself and two persons under him, qualified to instruct in that branch 20 scholars, to be nominated by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, each of whom is obliged to learn at least two of the languages. A fellowship is founded at Magdalen college, appropriated to the gentlemen of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, and called the travelling Norfolk fellowship. All the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in Cambridge, except that of King's college, are lending libraries; and those at Oxford are studying libraries. The different colleges are as follow: 1. St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and the first on entering the town from London, consisting of two courts, separated by a cloister and gallery. The largest is 144 feet long, and 84 broad. The buildings in this court have been lately repaired in an elegant manner. The lesser court is divided by the chapel, which is a fine old building, 54 feet long, 27 broad, and 27 high. This college was founded in 1257. There are three colleges in Oxford, which dispute the antiquity with this. Cambridge and Oxford were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> long before they were possessed of any colleges in their own <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the students then lodging and boarding with the townsmen, and they then hired hotels for their exercises and disputations. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a> or hall, now denominated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>'s school, situated on the west side of the river, is one of the ancient hotels that remain undemolished, and in which Erasmus read his first Greek lectures in England. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a> hall, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river, over which it has an elegant stone bridge, was founded in 1326, consisting of one grand court, 150 feet long, and 111 broad. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of this building that faces the fields has the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. To this college a new chapel has been added. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> hall is near St Peter's college, and was founded in 1343; it consists of two courts. It has an elegant chapel, built by Sir Christ Wren. 4. Corpus Christi or Bennet college, founded in 1350, has but a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> appearance, but is possessed of a remarkably large collection of valuable and curious ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. 5. Trinity hall, on the north of Clare hall, near the river, was founded in 1351; it is a small but remarkably neat building. 6. Gonvil and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> college is near the middle of the town, north of the senate house, and has three courts. It was founded in 1348, and augmented in 1557. 7. King's college, the most noble foundation in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, was first endowed by Henry VI. The old court resembles a decayed castle, more than a college. The new building is very magnificent, near 300 feet long. The chapel is one of the finest pieces of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> now remaining in the world. It is 304 feet long, 73 broad on the outside, and 40 within, and 91 high; and yet not a single pillar to sustain its ponderous roofs, of which it has two: the first is of stone, most curiously carved; the other of wood, covered with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, between which is a vacancy of 10 feet. There is such a profusion of carvings, both within and without, as is nowhere to be equalled. Henry VII. enlarged it 188 feet in length, and Henry VIII. gave the elegant stalls and organ gallery, with its inimitable carvings, where are the coats of arms of that king and those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Boleyn quartered. He gave also the elegant painted glass windows, which are in fine preservation, and were permitted by Cromwell to be preserved when almost every other in England was destroyed, as he had a particular regard for this university, where he had his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and for the town which he had represented in parliament. A new altar has been lately erected, which corresponds with the architecture of the building, embellished with an antique <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of Christ taking down from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, purchased in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and presented to the college by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Carlisle. In this chapel are put-up the Spanish colours taken at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANILLA">Manilla</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Draper, a member of this college. This college has an ancient stone bridge over the Cam. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s college, near the river, south of King's, was founded in 1448, and consists of two courts, with a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, and gardens on both sides of the river, connected with each other and the college by two wooden bridges, one of which is of a curious structure. 9. Catharine hall is east of Queen's, and its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> front on the weft, Cambridge, west, the most extensive and regular in the university. It contains only one court, 180 feet long, and 120 broad, and was founded in 1475. 10. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> college is at the east end of the town, surrounded by groves and gardens. The principal front faces the south, 180 feet long, regularly built and sashed: it was originally a Benedictine convent, and converted to the present use in 1576. 11. Christ's college is opposite to St Andrew's church, on the east side of the town; and was founded by Henry VIIth's mother, in 1505. It has lately had a thorough repair, and is now a neat and beautiful structure. 12. St John's college was founded by the same lady, in 1509, on the site of a dissolved priory. It consists of three courts, and has a large library filled with scarce and valuable books. To this college belongs a fine stone bridge over the river, which leads to their grand walks. 13. Magdalen college, the only one that stands on the north side of the river, near the great bridge, consists of two courts, and was founded in 1519. 14. Trinity college is east of the river, having St John's college on the north, and Caius's college and Trinity hall on the south. It contains two large quadrangles, the first of which is 344 feet long, and 280 broad. It has two noble entrances; and on the north side of it is the chapel, 204 feet long, 34 broad, and 44 high. It has every grand ornament, and the much admired statue of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, who was a student in this college. The hall is above 100 feet long, 40 broad, and 50 high. The inner court is effected the finest in the university, and surpasses any in Oxford. It is very spacious, and has an elegant cloister of stone pillars, supporting grand apartments; on the west is the library, the most elegant structure of the kind in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, 190 feet long, 40 broad, and 38 high within. Its entrance is by a staircase, the steps <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, and the walls incrusted with ancient Roman monuments. The entrance into the library is by folding doors at the north end. Its inside appearance is inexpressibly grand, having at the south end (lately erected) a beautiful painted glass window of his present majesty in his robes; and the classes are large, beautiful, and noble, well stocked with books, manuscripts, &c. Its outside has every suitable embellishment, and was erected by Sir Christopher Wren, at the expense of near £2,000. Under this building is a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a> of equal dimensions; out of which open three gates to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> that leads to the river, over which is a new elegant cycloidal bridge of three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, leading to extensive walks. In the middle is a remarkable vista. This college was founded on the site of two other colleges and a hall in 1546, by Henry VIII. 15. Emmanuel college is at the south-east end of the town; consists of two courts, the principal of which is very neat; and was built on the site of a Dominican convent. It has been lately in great part rebuilt and elegantly embellished. 16. Sidney-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> college is in Bridge-street. Its hall is elegant, but the chapel remarkable only for standing north and south, as others do east and west. The number of inhabitants in the town of Cambridge in 1801, was 10,087.

CAMBRIDGESHIRE

Pages 102-103

an inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a> and Huntingdonshire, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Cambridgeshire, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> to the arrival of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> it was included in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Iceni; and New <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, after their conquest, in the third <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Flavia Caesariensis, which reached from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> to the Humber. During the Heptarchy it belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the East <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a>, the fifth kingdom, which began in 575, and ended in 792, having had 14 kings; and it is now included in the Norfolk circuit, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, and province of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, except a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which is in the diocese of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>. It is about 40 miles in length from north to south, and 25 in breadth from east to west, and is 130 miles in circumference, containing near 570,000 acres. It has about 17,400 houses, 140,000 inhabitants; is divided into 17 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, in which are one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, Ely; 8 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. Cambridge, which is the shire town, and a celebrated university, Caxton, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINTON">Linton</a>, Merch, Newmarket, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOHAM">Soham</a>, Wisbech, Thorney, and part of Royton; 220 villages, 64 parishes: sends 2 members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> (exclusive of 2 for the town, and 2 for the university), pays one part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax, and provides 480 men in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. Its only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Cam, the Nene, and the Ouse. A considerable tract of land in this county is distinguished by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Ely. It consists of fenny ground, divided by innumerable channels and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>: and is part of a very spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, containing 300,000 acres of land, extending into Norfolk, Suffolk, Huntingdonshire, and Lincolnshire. The Isle of Ely is the north division of the county, and extends south almost as far as Cambridge. The whole level of which this is part, is bounded on one side by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the others by uplands; which taken together, form a rude kind of fen-micircle, resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very different in different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.
