In the fens it is moist and foggy, and therefore not so wholesome; but in the south and east parts it is very good, these being much drier than the other: but both, by late improvements, have been rendered very fruitful, the former by draining, and the latter by cinquefoil: so that it produces plenty of corn, especially barley, saffron, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and affords the richest pastures. The rivers abound with fish, and the fens with wild fowl. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the county are malt, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and baskets. As the above tract appears to have been dry land formerly, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> change it has undergone must have been owing either to a violent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> and inundation of the sea, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to earthquakes. As the towns in and about the fens were great sufferers by the stagnation of the waters in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in winter, many attempts were made to drain them, but without success, until the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., in which, and that of his son, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was happily completed, and an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament passed, by which a corporation was established for its preservation and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. By the same act, 83,000 acres were vested in the corporation, and 10,000 in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. In these fens are a great many decoys, in which incredible numbers of ducks, and other wild fowl, are caught during the season. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the county of Cambridge, as it was taken in 1801, amounted to 89,349 persons. New CAMBRIDGE, a town of New England, about three New Cambridge three miles from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a>, remarkable for an university consisting of three colleges. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 70.4. N. Lat. 42.0. Cambridge Manuscript, a copy of the Gospels and Acts of the Apostles in Greek and Latin. Beza found it in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Irenaeus at Lyons in the year 1562, and gave it to the university of Cambridge in 1582. It is a quarto size, and written on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>; 66 leaves of it are much torn and mutilated, ten of which are supplied by a later transcriber. Beza conjectures, that this manuscript might have existed so early as the time of Irenaeus: Wetstein apprehends that it either returned or was first brought from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> into France; that it is the same copy which Druthmar, an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSITOR">expositor</a> who lived about the year 840, had seen, and which, he observes, was ascribed to St Hilary; and that R. Stephens had given a particular account of it in his edition of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> in 1550. It is usually called Stephens's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Manuscript. Mill agrees with F. Simon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it was written in the western part of the world by a Latin scribe, and that it is to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> interpolated and corrupted: he observes that it agrees so much with the Latin Vulgate, as to afford reason for concluding, that it was corrected or formed upon a corrupt and faulty copy of that translation. From this and the Clermont copy of St Paul's Epistles, Beza published his larger Annotations in 1582. CAMBYSÉS. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>.

CAMDEN

Pages 103-104

WILLIAM, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquarian, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the year 1551. His father was a native of Lichfield in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, who settling in London, became a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-makers, and lived in the Old Bailey. His mother was of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of Curwen, of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-WORKINGTON">Workington</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>. He was educated first at Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and afterwards at St Paul's school: from thence he was sent, in 1566, to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and entered servitor of Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; but being disappointed of a demy's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he removed to Broadgate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, and somewhat more than two years after to Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, where he was supported by his kind friend and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Dr Thornton. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was a candidate for a fellowship of All-souls college, but lost it by the intrigues of the Popish party. In 1570, he supplicated the regents of the university to be admitted bachelor of arts; but in this also he miscarried. The following year Mr Camden came to London, where he prosecuted his favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of antiquity, under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Dr Goodman, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Westminster, by whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> he was made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Westminster school in 1575. From the time of his leaving the university to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he took several journeys to different parts of England, with a view to make observations and collect materials for his Britannia, in which he was now deeply engaged. In 1581 he became intimately acquainted with the learned <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> Brison, who was then in England; and in 1586 he published the first edition of his Britannia; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which, though much enlarged and improved in future editions, was even then esteemed an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to its author, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In 1593 he succeeded to the head mastership of Westminster school on the resignation of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">Grant</a>. In this office he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till 1597, when he was promoted to be Clarenceux <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> at arms. In the year 1600 Mr Camden made a tour to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, as far as Carlisle, accompanied by his friend Mr (afterwards Sir Robert) Cotton. In 1606 he began his correspondence with the celebrated President de Thou, which continued to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that faithful historian. In the following year he published his last edition of the Britannia, which is that from which the several English translations have been made; and in 1608, he began to digest his materials for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. In 1609, after recovering from a dangerous illness, he retired to Chislehurst in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, where he continued to spend the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months during the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his Annals of the queen did not appear till the year 1615, and he determined that the second volume should not appear till after his death (A). The work was entirely finished in 1617; and from that time he was principally employed in collecting more materials for the further improvement of his Britannia. In 1622, being now upwards of 70, and finding his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> decline apace, he determined to lose no time in executing his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of founding a history lecture in the university of Oxford. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of gift was accordingly transmitted by his friend Mr Heather to Mr Gregory Wheare, who was, by himself, appointed his first professor. He died at Chislehurst in 1623, in the 73rd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and was buried with great solemnity in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, in the south aisle, where a monument of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble was erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Camden was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of singular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and integrity; profoundly learned in the history and antiquities of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and a judicious and conscientious historian. He was reverenced and esteemed by the literati of all nations, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be ever remembered as an honour to the age and country wherein he lived. Besides the works already mentioned, he was author of an excellent Greek <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, and of several tracts in Hearne's collection. But his great and most useful work, the Britannia, is that upon which his fame is chiefly built. The edition above mentioned, to which he put his last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, was correctly printed in folio, much augmented, amended where it was necessary, and adorned with maps. It was first translated into English, and published in folio at London, in 1611, by the laborious Dr Philemon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, who is thought to have consulted our author himself; and therefore great respect has been paid to the additions and explanations that occur. (A) The reign of Queen Elizabeth was so recent when the first volume of the Annals was published, that many of the persons concerned, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> their dependents, were still living. It is no wonder, therefore, that the honest historian should offend those whose actions would not bear inquiry. Some of his enemies were clamorous and troublesome; which determined him not to publish the second volume during his life; but that posterity might be in no danger of disappointment, he deposited one copy in the Cotton library, and transmitted another to his friend Dupuy at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It was first printed at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1625. CAM occur therein, on a supposition that they may belong to Camden. But in a later edition of the same translation, published in 1636, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> has taken liberties which cannot either be defended or excused. A new translation, made with the utmost fidelity from the last edition of our author's work, was published in 1695, by Edmund Gibbon of Queen's college in Oxford, afterwards bishop of London; in which, besides the addition of notes, and of all that deserved to be taken notice of in Dr Holland's first edition, which, though thrown out of the text, is preserved at the bottom of the page, there are many other augmentations and improvements, all properly distinguished from the genuine work of the author, as they ought to be: and the same judicious method obtained in the next edition of the same performance, which was justly considered as the very best book of its kind that had been hitherto published. But the public has been recently put in possession of a new translation, and still more improved edition, by that learned and industrious topographer Mr Gough, under whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it has been enlarged to near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the size of the last of the preceding editions.

CAMEL

Pages 104-104

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>. See Camelus. Camel, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a kind of machine used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> for raising <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lifting ships, in order to bring them over the Pampus, which is at the mouth of the river Y, where the shallowness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> hinders <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships from passing. It is also used in other places, particularly at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>, the vessels built here being in their passage to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a> lifted over the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> by means of camels. These <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> were originally invented by the celebrated De <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">Wit</a>, for the purpose above mentioned; and were introduced into Russia by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, who obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of them when he worked in Holland as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> shipwright. A camel is composed of two separate parts, whose outsides are perpendicular, and whose insides are concave, shaped so as to embrace the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> of a ship on both sides. Each <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> has a small cabin with fifteen pumps and ten plugs, and contains 20 men. They are braced to a ship underneath by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, and entirely enclose its sides and bottom; being then towed to the bar, the plugs are opened, and the water admitted until the camel sinks with the ship and runs <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>. Then, the water being pumped out, the camel rises, lifts up the vessel, and the whole is towed over the bar. This machine can raise the ship eleven feet, or, in other words, make it draw eleven feet less water.

CAMELFORD

Pages 104-104

a borough town of Cornwall in England, consisting of about 100 houses, badly built; but the streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and well paved. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 4. N. Lat. 50. 40. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron to Thomas Pitt, elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>. CAMELLIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CAMELODUNUM. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMALODUNUM">Camalodunum</a>.

CAMELOPARDALIS

Pages 104-104

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Cervus. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAMELUS

Pages 104-104
or Camel, in Zoology, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of pinnipeds. See Mammalia Index. CAMEO. See Cameo.

CAMERA AEOLIA

Pages 104-104

a contrivance for blowing the fire, for the fusion of ores, without bellows; by means of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> falling through a funnel into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vessel, which sends from it so much <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vapour as continually blows the fire: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be the space of another vessel for it to expiate in by the way, it there lets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> its humidity, which otherwise might hinder the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. This contrivance was named camera aeolia by Kircher.

CAMERA LUCIDA

Pages 104-104

a contrivance of Dr Hook for making the image of any thing appear on a wall in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> room, either by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> night. Opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or wall where the appearance is to be, make a hole of at least a foot in diameter, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> window with a casement of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> in it, this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> do much better without such hole or casement opened. At a convenient distance, to prevent its being perceived by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in the room, place the object or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> intended to be represented, but in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> situation. If the picture be transparent, reflect the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays by means of a looking glass, so as that they may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it towards the place of representation; and, to prevent any rays from passing aside it, let the picture be encompassed with some board or cloth. If the object be a statue, or a living creature, it must be much enlightened by casting the sun's rays on it, either by reflection, refraction, or both. Between this object and the place of representation put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> convex glass, ground to such a convexity as that it may represent the object distinctly in such place. The nearer this is situated to the object, the more will the image be magnified on the wall, and the further the less: such diversity depending on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the spheres of the glasses. If the object cannot be conveniently inverted, there must be two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> glasses of proper spheres, situated at suitable distances, easily found by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, to make the representations erect. This whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of object, glasses, &c., with the persons employed in the management of them, are to be placed without the window or hole, so that they may not be perceived by the spectators in the room, and the operation itself will be easily performed. Phil. Trans. No. 38. p. 741. seq.

CAMERA OBSCURA

Pages 104-104
or Dark Chamber, in Optics, a machine, or apparatus, representing an artificial eye; whereon the images of external objects, received through a double convex glass, are exhibited distinctly, and in their native colours, on a white matter placed within the machine, in the focus of the glass. The first invention of this instrument is ascribed to Baptista Porta. See his Magia Naturalis, lib. xvii. cap. 6. first published at Frankfort about the year 1580 or 1591; the first four books of this work were published at Antwerp in 1560. The camera obscura affords very diverting spectacles; both by exhibiting images perfectly like their objects, and each clothed in their native colours; and by expressing, at the same time, all their motions; which latter no other can imitate. By means of this instrument, a person unacquainted with designing will be able to delineate objects with the greatest accuracy and justness, and another well versed in painting will find many things herein to perfect his art. See the construction under Dioptrics.

CAMERARIA

Pages 104-105

CAMERARIUS, Joachim, one of the most learned writers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born in 1500, at Bamberg, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Franconia; and obtained <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by his writings. He translated into Latin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, Xenophon, Euclid, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, Sophocles, Lucian, Theodoret, Nicephorus, &c. He published a catalogue of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sees; Greek epistles; Accounts of his journeys, in Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on Plautus; the Lives of Helius Eobanus Hessus, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Melancthon, &c. He died in 1574.

CAMERARIUS

Pages 105-105

Joachim, son of the former, and a learned physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> in 1534. After having finished his studies in Germany, he went into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he obtained the esteem of the learned. At his return he was courted by several princes to live with them; but he was too much devoted to books, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, to comply. He wrote a Hortus Medicus, and several other works. He died in 1598.

CAMERET BAY

Pages 105-105

in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Brittany in France, forms the harbour of Breft. See BREST.

CAMERINO

Pages 105-105

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> State in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 7' N. Lat. 45° 5'.

CAMERLINGO

Pages 105-105

according to Du Cange, signified formerly the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>: at present, camerlingo is nowhere used but at Rome, where it denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> who governs the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> State, and administers <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. It is the most eminent office at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, because he is at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. During a vacation of the papal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, the cardinal camerlingo publishes edicts, coins <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and exerts every other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of a sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; he has under him a treasurer-general, auditor-general, and 12 prelates called clerks of the chamber.

CAMERON

Pages 105-105

John, one of the most famous divines among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> of France in the 17th century, was born at Glasgow in Scotland, where he taught the Greek tongue; and having read lectures upon that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> for about a year, travelled, and became professor at several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and minister at Bordeaux. He published, 1. Theological lectures; 2. Icon Johannis Cameronis; and some miscellaneous pieces. He died in 1625, aged 62.

CAMERONIANS

Pages 105-105
or Cameronites, is also the denomination of a party of Calvinists in France, who asserted that the will of a man is only determined by the practical judgment of the mind; that the cause of men's doing good or evil proceeds from the knowledge which God infuses into them; and that God does not move the will physically, but only morally, in virtue of its dependence on the judgment of the mind. They had this name from John Cameron, a famous professor, first at Glasgow, where he was born, in 1580, and afterwards at Bourdeaux, Sedan, and Saumur; at which last place he preached his new doctrine of grace and free will, which was formed by Amyraut, Cappel, Bohart, Daille, and others of the more learned among the reformed ministers, who judged Calvin's doctrines on these points too harshly. The Cameronians are a sort of mitigated Calvinists, and approach to the opinion of the Arminians. They are also called Universalists, as holding the universality of Christ's death; and sometimes Amyraldists. The rigid adherents to the synod of Dort accused them of Pelagianism, and even of Manicheism. The controversy between the parties was carried on with a zeal and subtlety scarcely conceivable; yet all the question between them was only, Whether the will of man is determined by the immediate action of God upon it, or by the intervention of a knowledge which God imprest into the mind? The synod of Dort had defined that God not only illuminates the understanding, but gives motion to the will by making an internal change therein. Cameron only admitted the illumination, whereby the mind is morally moved; and explained the sentiment of the synod of Dort so as to make the two opinions consistent.

CAMES

Pages 105-105

a name given to the small slender rods of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> of which the glaziers make their turned lead. Their lead being cast into slender rods of twelve <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fourteen inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> each, is called the came; sometimes also they call each of these rods a came, which being afterwards drawn through their vice, makes their turned lead.

CAMILUS

Pages 105-117

Marcus Furius, was the first who rendered the family of Furius illustrious. He triumphed four times, was five times <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, and was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> founder of Rome. In a word, he acquired all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Lucius Apuleius, one of the tribunes, prosecuted him to make him give an account of the spoils taken at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VEII">Veii</a>. Camillus anticipated judgment, and banished himself voluntarily. During his banishment, instead of rejoicing at the devastation of Rome by the Gauls, he exerted all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and bravery to drive away the enemy; and yet kept with the utmost strictness the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Rome, in refusing to accept the command, which several private persons offered him. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> who were besieged in the capitol, created him dictator in the year 393; in which office he acted with so much bravery and conduct, that he entirely drove the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the Gauls out of the territories of the commonwealth. He died in the 81st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, 365 years before the Christian era. CAMILLI and CAMILLAE, in antiquity, boys and girls of ingenious birth, who ministered in the sacrifices of the gods; and especially those who attended the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMEN">flamen</a> dialis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. The word seems borrowed. borrowed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hetrurians, where it signified minister, and was changed from *cafil- millus*. The Tuscans also gave the appellation *Camil- lus* to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of minister of the gods. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMINHA">Caminha</a>**, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Entre-Duero-e-Minho, with the title of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is situated at the mouth of the river Minho, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 15', N. Lat. 41° 44'. **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAMIS">Camis</a>**, or **Kamis**, in the Japanese <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, denote deified souls of ancient heroes, who are supposed still to interfect themselves in the welfare of the people whom they anciently commanded. The camis answer to the heroes in the ancient Greek and Roman theology, and are venerated like the saints in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Besides the heroes or camis beatified by the consent of antiquity, the *mikaddos*, or pontiffs, have deified many others, and continue still to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> to new worthies; so that they swarm with *camis*: the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> one is *Tenso Dai Sin*, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> father of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, to whom are paid devotions and pilgrimages extraordinary. **Camisaide**, in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, an attack by surprise in the night, or at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when the enemy is supposed to be asleep. The word is said to have taken its rise from an attack of this kind; wherein, as a badge or signal to know one another by, they bore a shift, in French called *chemise*, or *chamise*, over their arms. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMISARDS">Camisards</a>**, a name given by the French to the Calvinists of the Cevennes, who formed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, and took up arms in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, in 1688. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMLETINE">Camletine</a>**, a slight stuff, made of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, in the manner of camlet. It is now out of fashion. **Camma**, and **Gobbi**, two provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Loango in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The inhabitants are continually at war with each other. The weapons they formerly used in their wars were the short pike, bows and arrows, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and dagger; but since the Europeans have become acquainted with that coat, they have supplied them with fire-arms. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of Gobbi lies about a day's journey from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.—Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with a variety of fish; but are infested with sea-horses, which do <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mischief both by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the natives is in logwood, elephants <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and tails, the hair of which is highly valued, and used for several curious purposes. **Cammin**, a maritime town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> Pomerania, situated in E. Long. 15°, N. Lat. 54°. **Camoens**, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> de, a famous Portuguese poet, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of whose birth is claimed by different cities. But according to N. Antonio, and Manuel Correa, his intimate friend, this event happened at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> in 1517. His family was of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and originally Spanish. In 1370, Vasco Perez de Caamans, disgusted at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Castile, fled to that of Lisbon, where <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Ferdinand immediately admitted him into his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and gave him the lordships of Sardoal, Punete, Marano, Amendoe, and other considerable lands; a certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the eminence of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and abilities. In the war for the succession, which broke out on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Ferdinand, Camoens sided with the king of Castile, and was killed in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Aljabarota. But though John I., the victor, seized a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his estate, his widow, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Gonfalo Tereyro, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the order of Christ, and general of the Portuguese army, was not reduced beneath her rank. She had three sons who took the name of Camoens. The family of the eldest intermarried with the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of Portugal; and even, according to Cafera, with the blood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>. But the family of the second <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, whose fortune was slender, had the superior honour to produce the author of the *Lusiad*. Early in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the misfortunes of the poet began. In his infancy, Simon Vaz de Camoens, his father, commander of a vessel, was shipwrecked at Goa, where, with his life, the greatest part of his fortune was lost. His mother, however, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> de Macedo of Santarene, provided for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of her son Louis at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>. What he acquired there, his works discover; an intimacy with the classics, equal to that of a Scaliger, but directed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> or a Pope. When he left the university, he appeared at court. He was handsome; had speaking eyes, it is said; and the finest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. Certain it is, however, he was a polished scholar, which, added to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> ardour and gay vivacity of his disposition, rendered him an accomplished <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. Courts are the scenes of intrigue; and intrigue was fashionable at Lisbon. But the particulars of the amours of Camoens rest unknown. This only appears: he had aspired above his rank, for he was banished from the court; and in several of his sonnets he ascribes this misfortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. He now retired to his mother's friends at Santarene. Here he renewed his studies, and began his poem on the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. John III. at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prepared an armament against Africa. Camoens, tired of his inactive obscure life, went to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEUTA">Ceuta</a> in this expedition, and greatly distinguished his valour in several encounters. In a naval engagement with the Moors in the straits of Gibraltar, in the conflict of boarding, he was among the foremost, and lost his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> eye. Yet neither hurry of actual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> nor the dissipation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> could stifle his genius. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his *Lusiad*, and several of his most beautiful sonnets were written in Africa, while, as he expressed it, One <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, and one the sword, employ'd. The fame of his valour had now reached the court, and he obtained permission to return to Lisbon. But, while he solicited an establishment which he had merited in the ranks of battle, the malignity of evil tongues, as he calls it in one of his letters, was injuriously poured upon him. Though the bloom of his early youth was effaced by several years residence under the scorching heavens of Africa, and though altered by the loss of an eye, his presence gave uneasiness to the gentlemen of some families of the first rank where he had formerly visited. Jealousy is the characteristic of the Spaniards and Portuguese; its resentment knows no bounds, and Camoens now found it prudent to banish himself from his native country. Accordingly, in 1553, he failed for India, with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> never to return. As the ship left the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, he exclaimed, in the words of the sepulchral monument of Scipio Africarum, canus, ingrata patria, non possitis offa mea! "Ungrateful country, thou shalt not possess my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>!" But he knew not what evils in the east would awake the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of his native fields. When Camoens arrived in India, an expedition was ready to sail to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the king of Cochin on the king of Pimenta. Without any rest on shore after his long voyage, he joined this armament, and in the conquest of the Alagada <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> displayed his usual bravery. In the year following, he attended Manuel de Vafconcello in an expedition to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea. Here, says Faria, as Camoens had no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for his sword, he employed his pen. Nor was his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> confined to the fleet or camp. He visited Mount Felix and the adjacent inhospitable regions of Africa, which he so strongly pictures in the Lusiad, and in one of his little pieces where he laments the absence of his mistress. When he returned to Goa, he enjoyed a tranquillity which enabled him to bestow his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on his epic poem. But this serenity was interrupted, perhaps by his own imprudence. He wrote some satires which gave offence; and by order of the viceroy Francisco Barreto, he was banished to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. The accomplishments and manners of Camoens soon found him friends, though under the disgrace of banishment. He was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> of the defunct in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACAO">Macao</a>, a Portuguese settlement in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a>. Here he continued his Lusiad; and here also, after five years residence, he acquired a fortune, though small, yet equal to his wishes. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Constantine de <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a> was now viceroy of India; and Camoens, desirous to return to Goa, resigned his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. In a ship, freighted by himself, he set sail; but was shipwrecked in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> near the mouth of the river Mehon, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of China. All he had acquired was lost in the waves; his poems, which he held in one hand, while he swammed with the other, were all he found himself possessed of when he stood friendless on the unknown shore. But the natives gave him a most humane reception: this he has immortalized in the prophetic song in the tenth Lusiad; and in the seventh, he tells us, that here he lost the wealth which satisfied his wishes. Agora da esperança ja adquirida, &c. Now blest with all the wealth fond hope could crave, Soon I behold that wealth beneath the wave For ever lost; My life, like Judah's heaven-doom'd king of yore, By miracle prolong'd— On the banks of the Mehon he wrote his beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> of the psalm, where the Jews, in the finest strain of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, are represented as hanging their harps on the willows, by the rivers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, and weeping their exile from their native country. Here Camoens continued some time, till an opportunity offered to carry him to Goa. When he arrived at that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, Don Constantine de Braganza, the viceroy, whose characteristic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> admitted him into intimate friendship, and Camoens was happy till <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Redondo assumed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Those who had formerly procured the banishment of the satirist, were silent while Constantine was in power; but now they exerted all their arts against him. Redondo, when he entered on office, pretended to be the friend of Camoens; yet, with all that unfeeling indifference with which he made his most horrible witticism on the Zamorin, he suffered the innocent man to be thrown into the common prison. After all the delay of bringing witnesses, Camoens, in a public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, fully refuted every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of his conduct while commissary at Macao, and his enemies were loaded with ignominy and reproach. But Camoens had some creditors, and these detained him in prison a considerable time, till the gentlemen of Goa began to be ashamed that a man of his singular merit should <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> such treatment among them. He was set at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; and again he assumed the profession of arms, and received the allowance of a gentleman volunteer, a character at this time common in Portuguese India. Soon after, Pedro Barreto, appointed governor of the fort at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOFALA">Sofala</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> promises, allured the poet to attend him thither. The governor of a distant fort, in a barbarous country, shares in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the fate of an exile. Yet, though the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of Barreto was, in this unpleasant situation, to retain the conversation of Camoens at his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, it was his least care to render the life of his guest agreeable. Chagrined with his treatment, and a considerable time having elapsed in vain dependence upon Barreto, Camoens resolved to return to his native country. A ship, on the homeward voyage, at this time touched at Sofala, and several gentlemen who were on board, were desirous that Camoens should accompany them. But this the governor ungenerously endeavoured to prevent, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> him with a debt for board. Anthony de <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CABRA">Cabra</a>, however, and Hector de Sylveira, paid the demand; and Camoens, says Faria, and the honour of Barreto, were sold together. After an absence of 16 years, Camoens, in 1569, returned to Lisbon, unhappy even in his arrival, for the pestilence then raged in that city, and prevented his publication for three years. At last, in 1572, he printed his Lusiad, which, in the opening of the first book, in a most elegant turn of compliment, he addressed to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, King Sebastian, then in his 18th year. The king, says the French translator, was so pleased with his merit, that he gave the author a pension of 4000 reals, on condition that he should reside at court. But this salary, says the same writer, was withdrawn by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Henry, who succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Portugal, lost by Sebastian at the battle of Alcazar. Though the great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of literature, a species the reverse of that of Camoens, certain it is, that the author of the Lusiad was utterly neglected by Henry, under whose inglorious reign he died in all the misery of poverty. By some, it is said, he died in an almshouse. It appears, however, that he had not even the certainty of subsistence which these houses provide. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, who had grown old with him, and who had long experienced his master's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. This grateful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, who, according to some writers, saved his master's life in the unhappy shipwreck where he lost his effects, begged in the streets of Lisbon for the only man in Portugal on whom God had bestowed those talents which have a tendency to erect the spirit of a downward age. To the eye of a faithful observer, the fate of Camoens throws throws great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on that of his country, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear strictly connected with it. The same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, the same degenerated spirit, which suffered Camoens to depend on his share of the alms begged in the streets by his old hoary servant, the same spirit which caused this sunk the kingdom of Portugal into the most abject vassalage ever experienced by a conquered <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. While the grandees of Portugal were <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> to the ruin which impended over them, Camoens beheld it with a pungency of grief which hastened his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a>. In one of his letters he has these remarkable words: *Em fim acabarey á vida, e verram todos que fui eficacada a minho patria, &c.* "I am ending the course of my life; the world will witness how I have loved my country. I have returned, not only to die in her bosom, but to die with her." In this unhappy situation, in 1579, in his 62d year, the year after the fatal defeat of Don Sebastian, died Louis de Camoens, the greatest literary genius ever produced by Portugal; in martial courage and spirit of honour, nothing inferior to her greatest heroes. And in a manner suitable to the poverty in which he died, was he buried. **CAMOMILE.** See Anthemis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **CAMP,** the ground on which an army pitch their tents. It is marked out by the quartermaster general, who appoints every regiment their ground. The chief advantages to be minded in choosing a camp for an army, are, to have it near the water, in a country of forage, where the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> may find wood for dressing their victuals; that it have a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with garrisons, and with a country from whence it may be supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, that it be situated on a rising ground, in a dry gravelly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. Besides, the advantages of the ground ought to be considered, as marshes, woods, rivers, and enclosures; and if the camp be near the enemy, with no river or marsh to cover it, the army ought to be intrenched. An army always encamps facing the enemy; and generally in two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, running <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> about 300 yards distance; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and dragoons, on the wings; and the foot, in the centre: sometimes a body of two, three, or four brigades, is encamped behind the two lines, and is called the body of reserve. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-waggons are generally encamped in the rear of the two lines. A battalion of foot is allowed 80 or 100 paces for its camp; and 30 or 40 for an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between one battalion and another. A squadron of horse is allowed 30 for its camp, and 30 for an interval, and more if the ground will allow it. Where the grounds are equally dry, those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a> are always the most healthful that are pitched on the banks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rivers; because, in the hot season, situations of this kind have a stream of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> from the water, serving to carry off the moist and putrid exhalations. On the other hand, next to marshes, the worst encampments are on low grounds <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> befet with trees; for then the air is not only moist and hurtful in itself, but by stagnating becomes more susceptible of corruption. However, let the situation of camps be ever so good, they are frequently rendered infectious by the putrid effluvia of rotten straw, and the privies of the army, more especially if the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> prevails; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the best method of preventing a general infection, is to leave the ground with the privies, foul straw, and other filth, of the camp behind. This must be frequently done, if consistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations; but when these render it improper to change the ground often, the privies should be made deeper than usual, and once a day a thick layer of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> thrown into them till the pits are near full; and then they are to be well covered, and supplied by others. It may also be a proper caution to order the pits to be made either in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> or the rear, as the then <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> winds may best carry off their effluvia from the camp. Moreover, it will be necessary to change the straw frequently, as being not only apt to rot, but to retain the infectious fleas of the sick. But if fresh straw cannot be procured, more care must be taken in airing the tents, as well as the old straw. The disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> encampment was at first laid out by God himself. Their camp was of a quadrangular form, surrounded with an enclosure of the height of 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>-breadth. It made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of 12 miles in compass about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>; and within this was another called the Levites camp. The Greeks had also their camps, fortified with gates and ditches. The Lacedemonians made their camp of a round <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, looking upon that as the most perfect and defensible of any form: we are not, however, to imagine, that they thought this form so essential to a camp, as never to be dispensed with when the circumstances of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> required it. Of the rest of the Grecian camps, it may be observed, that the most valiant of the soldiers were placed at the extremities, the rest in the middle. Thus we learn from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> and Ajax were posted at the ends of the camp before <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, as bulwarks on each side of the rest of the princes. The figure of the Roman camp was a square divided into two principal parts: in the upper part were the general's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>, or praetorium, and the tents of the chief officers; in the lower, those of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> were placed. On one side of the praetorium stood the quaestorium, or apartment of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the army; and near this the forum, both for a market place and the assembling of councils. On the other side of the praetorium were lodged the legati; and below it the tribunes had their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, opposite to their respective legions. Aside of the tribunes were the praefecti of the foreign troops, over against their respective wings; and behind these were the lodgments of the evocati, then those of the extraordinarii and ablesti equites, which concluded the higher part of the camp. Between the two partitions was a spot of ground called principia, for the altars and images of the gods, and probably also for the chief ensigns. The middle of the lower partition was assigned to the Roman horse: next to them were quartered the triarii; then the principes, and close by them the hastati; afterwards the foreign horse, and lastly, the foreign foot. They fortified their camp with a ditch and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, which they termed fossa and vallum; in the latter some distinguishing two parts, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGGER">agger</a> or earth, and the fides or wooden stakes driven in to secure it. The camps were sometimes surrounded by walls made of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and the tents themselves formed of the same <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. In the front of the Turkish camp are quartered the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a> and other foot, whose tents encompass their aga: in the rear are the quarters of the sipahis and other other horsemen. The body of the camp is possessed by the stately tents or pavilions of the vizier or general, rais effendi or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, khaija or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, the teztedar bafhaw or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> treasurer, and kapilar kahiafer or master of the ceremonies. In the middle of these tents is a spacious field, wherein are erected a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVAN">divan</a>, and a hafna or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. When the ground is marked out for a camp, all wait for the pitching of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> lailac, the place where the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> are held; it being the disposition of this that is to regulate all the rest. The Arabs still live in camps, as the ancient Scenites did. The camp of the Aflyne Emir, or king of the country about Tadmor, is described by a traveller who viewed it, as spread over a very large plain, and professing to vast a space, that though he had the advantage of a rising ground, he could not see the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of it. His own tent was near the middle; scarce distinguishable from the rest, except that it was bigger, being made, like the others, of a fort of haircloth. Camp, is also used by the Siamese, and some other nations in the East Indies, as the name of the quarters which they assign to foreigners who come to trade with them. In these camps, every nation forms, as it were, a particular town, where they carry on all their trade, not only keeping all their warehouses and shops there, but also living in these camps with their whole families. The Europeans, however, are so far indulged, that at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, and almost everywhere else, they may live either in the cities or suburbs, as they shall judge most convenient. Camp-fight, or Kamp-fight, in law writers, denotes the trial of a cause by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>, or a legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> of two champions in the field, for decision of some controversy. In the trial by camp-fight, the accuser was, with the peril of his own body, to prove the accused guilty; and by offering him his glove, to challenge him to this trial, which the other must either accept of, or acknowledge himself guilty of the crime whereof he was accused. If it were a crime deserving death, the camp-fight was for life and death: if the offence deserved only imprisonment, the camp-fight was accomplished when one combatant had subdued the other, so as either to make him yield or take him prisoner. The accused had liberty to choose another to fight in his stead, but the accuser was obliged to perform it in his own person, and with equality of weapons. No women were permitted to be spectators, nor men under the age of thirteen. The priest and the people who looked on, were engaged silently in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, that the victory might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to him who had right. None might cry, shriek, or give the least sign; which in some places was executed with so much strictness, that the executioner stood ready with an axe to cut off the right hand or foot of the party that should offend therein. He that, being wounded, yielded himself, was at the other's mercy either to be killed or suffered to live. But if life were granted him, he was declared infamous by the judge, and disfabled from ever <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms, or riding on horseback. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a>. See Campania. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">Campaign</a>, in the art of war, denotes the space of time that an army keeps the field, or is encamped.—Campaign The beginning of every campaign is considerably more unhealthy than if the men were to remain in quarters. After the first fortnight or three weeks encampment, the sickness decreases daily; the most infirm being by that time in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> daily growing warmer. This healthy state continues throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, unless the men get wet clothes or wet beds; in which case, a greater or less degree of the dysentery will appear in proportion to the preceding heats. But the most sickly part of the campaign begins about the middle or end of August, whilst the days are still hot, but the nights cool and damp, with fogs and dews: then, and not sooner, the dysentery prevails; and though its violence is over by the beginning of October, yet the remitting fever gaining ground, continues throughout the rest of the campaign, and never entirely ceases, even in winter-quarters, till the frosts begin. At the beginning of a campaign the sickness is so uniform, that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> may be nearly predicted; but for the rest of the season, as the diseases are then of a contagious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and depend so much upon the heats of summer, it is impossible to foresee how many may fall sick from the beginning to the end of autumn. It is also observed, that the last fortnight of a campaign, if protracted till the beginning of winter, is attended with more sickness than the first two months encampment; so that it is better to take the field a fortnight sooner, in order to return into winter-quarters so much the earlier. As to winter expeditions, though severe in appearance, they are attended with little sickness, if the men have strong shoes, quarters, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and provisions. Long marches in summer are not without danger, unless made in the night, or so early in the morning as to be over before the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the day. Campanaceae, in Botany, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in the Fragments methodi naturalis of Linnaeus, in which are the following genera, viz. convolvulus, ipomoea, polemonium, campanula, roella, viola, &c.* Campanella, Thomas, a famous Italian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Stilo in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, in 1568. He distinguished himself by his early proficiency in learning; for at the age of 13 he was a perfect master of the ancient orators and poets. His peculiar inclination was to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, to which he at last confined his whole time and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. In order to arrive at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, he shook off the yoke of authority: by which means the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of some of his opinions exposed him to many inconveniences; for at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> he was thrown into prison, in which he remained 27 years, and during this confinement wrote his famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Athelstamus triumphatus. Being at length set at liberty, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he was graciously received by Louis XIII. and Cardinal Richelieu; the latter procured him a pension of 2000 livres, and often consulted him on the affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Campanella passed the remainder of his days in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> at Paris, and died in 1639. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPION">Campion</a>, Matthew, of Spoleto, curate at Rome, wrote a curious treatise on the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> glasses for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a>, and made several improvements in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, assisted by his brother and pupil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. He died after 1678. Campania, a town of Italy, in the kingdom of Naples, Campania, Naples, and in the Farther Principato, with a bishop's see. E. Long. 15° 30'. N. Lat. 40° 40'. Campania, or Campagna di Roma, anciently Latium, a province of Italy, bounded on the west by the Tiber and the sea, on the south-west by the sea, on the south by Terra di Lavoro, on the east by Abruzzo, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Sabina. Though the soil is good, it produces little or nothing, on account of the heavy duties on corn; and though the waters are good, the air is unwholesome. It is subject to the Pope, and is about 60 miles in length on the Mediterranean sea. It has been generally thought that the air of this country hath something in it peculiarly noxious during the summer-time; but Mr Condamine is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it is not more unhealthy than any other marshy country. His account follows. "It was after the invasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> in the fifth and sixth centuries that this corruption of the air began to manifest itself. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the Tiber being covered by the accumulated ruins of the edifices of ancient Rome, could not but raise itself considerably. But what permits us not to doubt of this fact is, that the ancient and well-preserved pavement of the Pantheon and its portico is overflowed every winter; that the water even rises there sometimes to the height of eight or ten feet: and that it is not possible to suppose that the ancient Romans should have built a temple in a place so low as to be covered with the waters of the Tiber on the least inundation. It is evident, then, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the bed of this river is raised several feet; which could not have happened without forming there a kind of dikes or bars. The choking up of its canal necessarily occasioned the overflow and reflux of its waters in such places as till then had not been subject to inundations: to these overflows of the Tiber were added all the waters that escaped out of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, the ruins of which are still to be seen, and which were entirely broken and destroyed by Totila. What need, therefore, of anything more to infect the air, in a hot <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, than the exhalations of such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of stagnating waters deprived of any discharge, and become the receptacle of a thousand impurities, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> of several millions both of men and animals? The evil could not but increase from the same causes while Rome was exposed to the incursions and devastations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, the Normans, and the Saracens, which lasted for several centuries. The air was become so infectious there at the beginning of the 13th century, that Pope Innocent III. wrote, that few people at Rome arrived at the age of forty years, and that nothing was more uncommon there than to see a person of sixty. A very short time after, the popes transferred the seat of their residence to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>: during the seventy-two years they remained there, Rome became a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>; the monasteries in it were converted into stables; and Gregory XI. on his return to Rome, in 1376, hardly counted there 30,000 inhabitants. At his death began the troubles of the great schism in the west, which continued for upwards of 50 years. Martin V., in whom this schism ended in the year 1429, and his first successors, were able to make but feeble efforts against so prevalent an evil. It was not till the beginning of the 16th century that Leo X., under whom Rome began to resume her wonted splendour, gave himself some trouble about re-establishing the salubrity of the air; but the city, being shortly after besieged twice successively by Campania the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> itself plunged again into all its old calamities; and from 85,000 inhabitants, which it contained under Leo X. it was reduced under Clement VIII. to 32,000. In short, it is only since the time of Pius V. and Sixtus V. at the end of the 16th century, that the popes have constantly employed the necessary methods for purifying the air of Rome and its environs, by procuring proper discharges for the waters, drying up the humid and marshy grounds, and covering the banks of the Tiber and other places reputed uninhabitable with superb edifices. Since that time a person may dwell at Rome, and go in or out of it at all seasons of the year. At the beginning, however, of the present century, they were still afraid to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> out of the city in summer, when they had resided there; as they were also to return to it, when once they had quitted it. They never ventured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> at Rome, even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> day, in any other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> than their own. They are greatly relaxed at present from these ancient scruples: I have seen cardinals, in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August, go from Rome to lie at Frascati, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>, &c. and return the next or the following days to the city, without any detriment to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>: I have myself tried all these experiments, without suffering the least inconvenience from them: we have even seen, in the last war in Italy, two armies encamped under the walls of Rome at the time when the heats were most violent. Yet, notwithstanding all this, the greater part of the country people dare not still venture to lie during that season of the year, nor even so much as sleep in a carriage, in any part of the territory comprehended under the name of the Campagna of Rome." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPANIFORM">Campaniform</a>, or Campanulated, an appellation given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPANINI">Campanini</a>, a name given to an Italian marble dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRARA">Carrara</a>, because, when it is worked, it looks like a bell. Campanula, or Bell-flower. See Botany Index. Campbell, Archibald, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> and marquis of Argyle, was the son of Archibald earl of Argyle, by the lady Anne Douglas, daughter of William earl of Morton. He was born in the year 1598; and educated in the profession of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, according to the strictest rules of the church of Scotland, as it was established immediately after the reformation. During the commonwealth he was induced to submit to its authority. Upon the restoration, he was tried for his compliance; a crime common to him with the whole nation, and such a one as the most loyal and affectionate subject might frequently by violence be induced to commit. To make this compliance appear the more voluntary and hearty, there were produced in court letters which he had wrote to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>, while that general governed Scotland, and which contained expressions of the most cordial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the established government. But, besides the general indignation excited by Albemarle's discovery of this private correspondence, men thought, that even the highest demonstrations of affection might, during jealous times, be exacted as a necessary mark of compliance from a person of such distinction as Argyle; and could not, by any equitable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, imply the crime of trea- The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, however, scrupled not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon him, and he suffered with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> and courage. Campbell, Archibald, earl of Argyle, son to the former, had from his youth distinguished himself by his loyalty and his attachment to the royal family. Though his father was head of the covenanters, he himself refused to concur in any of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>; and when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> was given him by the convention of states, he forbore to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon it till it should be ratified by the king. By his respectful behaviour, as well as by his services, he made himself acceptable to Charles when that prince was in Scotland; and even after the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, all the misfortunes which attended the royal cause could not engage him to desert it. Under Middleton he obstinately persevered to harass and infest the victorious English; and it was not till he received orders from that general, that he would submit to accept of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. Such jealousy of his loyal attachments was entertained by the commonwealth and protector, that a pretence was soon after fallen upon to commit him to prison; and his confinement was rigorously continued till the restoration. The king, sensible of his services, had remitted to him his father's forfeiture, and created him earl of Argyle; and when a most unjust sentence was passed upon him by the Scots parliament, Charles had anew remitted it. In the subsequent part of this reign Argyle behaved himself dutifully; and though he seemed not disposed to go all lengths with the court, he always appeared, even in his opposition, a man of mild dispositions and peaceable deportment. A parliament was summoned at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in summer 1681, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>.
