Besides granting <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the king, and voting the indefeasible right of succession, this parliament enacted a test, which all persons possessed of offices, civil, military, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, were bound to take. In this test the king's supremacy was affected, the covenant renounced, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> obedience attested to, and all obligations disclaimed of endeavouring any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in civil or ecclesiastical establishments. This was the state of the test as proposed by the courtiers; but the country party proposed also a clause of adherence to the Protestant religion, which could not with decency be rejected. The whole was of an enormous length, considered as an oath; and, what was worse, a confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> was there ratified which had been imposed a little after the reformation, and which contained many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> altogether forged by the parliament and nation. Among others, the doctrine of resistance was inculcated; so that the test being voted in a hurry, was found on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> to be a medley of absurdity and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>. Though the courtiers could not reject the clause of adhering to the Protestant religion, they proposed, as a requisite mark of respect, that all princes of the blood should be exempted from taking that oath. This exception was zealously opposed by Argyle; who observed that the sole danger to be dreaded for the Protestant religion must proceed from the perversion of the royal family. By insisting on such topics, he drew on himself the secret indignation of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, of which he soon felt the fatal consequences. When Argyle took the test as a privy counsellor, he subjoined, in the duke's presence, an explanation which he had beforehand communicated to that prince, and which he believed to have been approved by him. It was in these words, "I have considered the test, and am very desirous of giving obedience as far as I can; I am confident that the parliament never intended to impose contradictory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>: therefore I think no man can explain it but for himself. Accordingly I take it as far as it is consistent with itself and the Protestant religion. And I do declare that I <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> not to bind myself, in my station, and in a lawful way, from willing and endeavouring any alteration, which I think to the advantage of church or state, and not repugnant to the Protestant religion and my loyalty: and this I understand as a part of my oath." The duke, as was natural, heard it with great tranquillity: no one took the least offence: Argyle was admitted to sit that day in council: and it was impossible to imagine that a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offence had been committed where occasion seemed not to have been given so much as for a frown or reprimand. Argyle was much surprized a few days after, to find that a warrant was issued for committing him to prison; that he was indicted for high <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, leafling-making, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>; and that from the innocent words above mentioned an accusation was extracted, by which he was to forfeit life, honours, and fortune. It is needless to enter into particulars, where the iniquity of the whole is so evidently apparent. Though the sword of justice was displayed, even her semblance was not put on; and the forms of law were preferred to sanctify, or rather aggravate, the oppression. Of five judges, three did not scruple to find the guilt of treason and leafling-making to be incurred by the prisoner: a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of fifteen noblemen gave verdict against him; and the king being consulted, ordered the sentence to be pronounced, but the execution of it to be suspended till further orders. Argyle, however, saw no reason to trust to the justice or mercy of such enemies: He made his escape from prison, and till he could find a ship for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> he concealed himself during some time in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The king heard of his lurking place, but would not suffer him to be arrested. All the parts, however, of his sentence, so far as the government in Scotland had power, were rigorously executed; his estate confiscated, his arms reversed and torn. Having got over to Holland, he remained there during the remaining part of the reign of Charles II. But thinking himself at liberty, before the coronation of James II. to exert himself in order to recover the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> by force of arms, he concerted measures with the duke of Monmouth, and went into Scotland, to assemble his friends: but not meeting with the success he expected, he was taken prisoner; and being carried to Edinburgh, was beheaded upon his former unjust sentence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 30, 1685. He showed great constancy and courage under his misfortunes; on the day of his death he ate his dinner very cheerfully; and, according to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, slept after it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> or more, very soundly. At the place of execution, he made a short, grave, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> speech; and, after solemnly declaring that he forgave all his enemies, submitted to death with great firmness. Campbell, Archibald, first duke of Argyle, son to the preceding, was an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> promoter of the revolution. He came over with the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>; was admitted into the convention as earl of Argyle, though his father's attainder was not reversed; and in the claim of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> the sentence against him was declared to be, what most certainly it was, a reproach upon the nation. The establishment of the crown upon the prince and princesses of Orange being carried by a great majority in the Scottish convention, the earl was sent from the nobility, with Sir James <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a> and Sir John Dalrymple from the barons and boroughs, to offer the crown, in the name of the convention, to their majesties, and tendered them the coronation oath; for which, and many other eminent services, he was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, and, in 1690, made one of the lords of the treasury. He was afterwards made a colonel of the Scots horse guards; and, in 1694, one of the extraordinary lords of petition. He was likewise created duke of Argyle, marquis of Kintyre and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LORN">Lorn</a>, earl of Campbell and Cowal, viscount of Lochow and Glenila, Lord <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERARY">Inverary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, Morvern, and Terrey, by letters-patent, bearing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENNINGTON">Kennington</a> the 23d of June 1701. He sent over a regiment to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> for King William's service, the officers of which were chiefly of his own name and family, who bravely distinguished themselves through the whole course of the war. He married <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, daughter of Sir Lionel Talman of Helmingham in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, by Elizabeth duchess of Lauderdale his wife, daughter and heiress of William Murray, earl of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol8.html#article-DYSART">Dysart</a>, by whom he left issue two sons and a daughter; namely, John duke of Argyle, the subject of the next article; Archibald, who succeeded his brother as duke of Argyle; and Lady Anne, married to James Stuart, second earl of Bute, by whom she had a son afterwards earl of Bute. Campbell, John, second duke of Argyle, and also duke of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> and baron of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, son to the subject of the preceding article, was born on the 10th of October 1680; and, on the very day when his grandfather suffered at Edinburgh, fell out of a window three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of stairs high without receiving any hurt. At the age of 15, he had made a considerable progress in classical learning. His father then perceived and encouraged his military disposition, and introduced him to King William, who appointed him to the command of a regiment. In this situation he remained till the death of his father in 1723; when becoming duke of Argyle, he was soon after sworn of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Anne's privy council, made <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the Scotch horse guards, and appointed one of the extraordinary lords of petition. In 1724, her majesty's reviving the Scottish order of the Thistle, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> was invested one of the knights of that order, and was soon after appointed high-commissioner to the Scotch parliament; where, being of great service in promoting the intended union, he was on his return created a peer of England, by the titles of baron of Chatham and earl of Greenwich, and in 1710 was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>. His grace first distinguished himself in his military capacity at the battle of Oudenarde; where he commanded as brigadier-general, with all the bravery of youth and the conduct of a veteran officer. He was present under the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> at the siege of Ghent, and took possession of the town. He had also a considerable share in the victory obtained over the French at the battle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALPLAQUET">Malplaquet</a>, by dislodging them from the wood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SART">Sart</a>, Campbell and gaining a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. In this sharp engagement, several musket-balls passed through the duke's clothes, hat, and periwig. Soon after this hot <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, he was sent to take the command in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a>, he returned to England. His grace having now a seat in the house of lords, he censured the measures of the ministry with such freedom, that all his places were disposed of to other noblemen; but at the accession of George I, he recovered his influence. At the breaking out of the rebellion in 1715, he was made commander in chief of his majesty's forces in North <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; and was the principal means and cause of the total extinction, at that time, of the rebellion in Scotland, without much bloodshed. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition to him, or that part of the army he commanded, at the head of all his Campbells was placed Campbell earl of Braidalbin, of the same family and kindred, by some fatal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> that ever misguided and misled that unhappy family of the Stuarts and all its adherents. The consequence was, that both sets of Campbells, from family affection, refused to strike a stroke, and retired out of the battle. He arrived at London <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 6th 1716, and was in high favour; but, to the surprize of people of all ranks, he was in a few months divested of all his employments; and from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to the year 1718, he signalized himself in a civil capacity, by his uncorrupted <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> and manly eloquence. In the beginning of the year 1719, he was again admitted into favour, appointed lord-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and in April following was created duke of Greenwich. He continued in the administration during all the remaining part of that reign; and, after his late majesty's accession, till April 1740; when he delivered a speech with such warmth, that the ministry being highly offended, he was again dismissed from his employments. To these, however, on the change of the ministry, he was soon restored; but not approving of the measures of the new ministry more than those of the old, he gave up all his posts for the last time, and never after engaged in affairs of state. He now enjoyed privacy and retirement; and died of a paralytic disorder on the 4th of October 1743. To the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his grace a very noble monument was erected in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, executed by the ingenious Rouilliac. The duke of Argyle, though never first minister, was a very able statesman and politician, most steadily fixed in those principles he believed to be right, and not to be shaken or changed. His delicacy and honour were so great, that it hurt him to be even suspected; witness that application said to be made to him by one of the adherents of the Stuart family before the last rebellion in order to gain his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, which was considerable both in Scotland and England. He immediately sent the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the secretary of state; and it vexed him much even to have an application made him, lest any person should think him capable of acting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> part. When he thought measures wrong or corrupt, he cared not who was the author, however great or powerful he might be; witness his boldly attacking the great duke of Marlborough in the house of lords, about his forage and army contracts in Flanders, in the very zenith of his power and popularity. Campbell. popularity, though in all other respects he was the most able general of his time. The duke of Argyle on all occasions spoke well, with a firm, manly, and noble eloquence; and seems to deserve the character given of him by Pope: Argyle the state's whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> born to wield, And shake alike the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and the field. In private life, the duke's conduct was highly exemplary. He was an affectionate husband and an indulgent master. He seldom parted with his servants till age had rendered them incapable of their employments; and then he made provision for their subsistence. He was liberal to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and particularly to persons of merit in distress: but though he was ready to patronize deserving persons, he was extremely cautious not to deceive any by lavish promises or leading them to form vain expectations. He was a strict economist, and paid his tradesmen punctually every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; and though he maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his rank, he took care that no part of his income should be wasted in empty pomp or unnecessary expenses. He was twice married, and left five daughters, but no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue. The titles of duke and earl of Greenwich and baron of Chatham became extinct at his death; but in his other titles he was succeeded by his brother Archibald earl of Isla, the subject of the next article. Campbell, Archibald, third duke of Argyle, brother to the subject of the preceding article, was born at Hamhoufe, in England, in June 1682, and was educated at the university of Glasgow. He afterwards applied himself to the study of the law at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; but, upon his father's being created a duke, he betook himself to a military life, and served some time under the duke of Marlborough. Upon quitting the army, in which he did not long remain, he applied to the acquisition of that knowledge which would enable him to make a figure in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> world. In 1705, he was constituted treasurer of Scotland, and made a considerable figure in parliament, though he was not more than 23 years of age. In 1706, he was appointed one of the commissioners for treating of the Union; and the same year was created Lord Oronlay, Dunoon, and Arrois, viscount and earl of Illay. In 1708, he was made an extraordinary lord of session; and when the Union was effected, he was chosen one of the Sixteen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">Peers</a> for Scotland, in the first parliament of Great Britain; and was constantly elected to every future parliament till his death, except the fourth. In 1710, he was made justice-general of Scotland. In 1711, he was called to the privy council; and upon the accession of George I, he was nominated lord <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of Scotland. When the rebellion broke out in 1715, he again betook himself to arms, in defence of the house of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and by his prudent conduct in the West Highlands, he prevented General Gordon at the head of three thousand men, from penetrating into the country and raising levies. He afterwards joined his brother at Stirling, and was wounded at the battle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>. In 1725, he was appointed keeper of the privy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; and from this time, he was entrusted with the management of Scotch affairs. In 1734, upon his resigning the privy seal, he was made keeper of the great seal, which office he enjoyed till his death. Upon the decease of his brother, he became duke of Argyle, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> justice-general, lieutenant, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, and commissary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARGYLESHIRE">Argyleshire</a> and the Western Isles, hereditary great master of the household, hereditary keeper of Duntaffnage, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a>, and several other castles. He was also chancellor of the university of Aberdeen; and laboured to promote the interest of that, as well as of the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Scotland. He particularly encouraged the school of physic at Edinburgh, which has now acquired so high a reputation. Having the chief management of Scotch affairs, he was also extremely attentive to promote the trade, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and improvements of his country. It was by his advice that, after the rebellion in 1745, the Highlanders were employed in the royal army. He was a man of great endowments both natural and acquired, well versed in the laws of his country, and possessed considerable parliamentary abilities. He was likewise eminent for his skill in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, had great talents for conversation, and had collected one of the most valuable private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in Great Britain. He built himself a very magnificent seat at Inverary. The faculties of his mind continued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and vigorous till his death, which happened suddenly on the 15th of April 1761, in the 79th year of his age. He was married, but had no issue; and was succeeded in his titles and the estates of the family by John Campbell, fourth duke of Argyle, son of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> John Campbell of Mammore, who was the second son of Archibald the ninth earl of Argyle. The family of Argyle were heritable justice generals for Scotland till abolished by the jurisdiction act. They are still heritable masters of the king's household in Scotland, and keepers of Duntaffnage and Carrick. Campbell, John, an eminent historical, biographical, and political writer, was born at Edinburgh, March 8, 1707-8. His father, Robert Campbell of Glenlyon, Esq., was captain of horse in a regiment commanded by the then earl of Hyndford; and his mother, Elizabeth, daughter of Smith, Esq., of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, had the honour of claiming a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the poet Waller. Our author, their fourth son, was at the age of five years carried from Scotland to Windsor, where he received the first principles of his education; and at a proper age, he was placed out as clerk to an attorney, being intended for the law. This profession, however, he never followed; but by a close application to the acquisition of knowledge of various kinds, became qualified to appear with great advantage in the literary world. In 1736, before he had completed his 30th year, he gave to the public, in two volumes folio, "The Military <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Prince Eugene and the duke of Marlborough," enriched with maps, plans, and cuts. The reputation hence acquired, occasioned him soon after to be solicited to take a part in the "Ancient Universal History." Whilst employed in this capital work, Mr Campbell found leisure to entertain the world with other productions. In 1739, he published the "Travels and Adventures of Edward <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, Esq." 8vo. In the same year appeared his "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">Bashaw</a> Duke de Ripperda," 8vo, reprinted, with improvements, in 1740. These memoirs were followed... Campbell followed, in 1741, by the "Concise History of Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>," 8vo. In 1742, he was the author of "A Letter to a friend in the Country, on the Publication of Thurlow's State Papers; giving an account of their discovery, importance, and utility." The same year was distinguished by the appearance of the 1st and 2d volumes of his "Lives of the English Admirals, and other eminent British Seamen." The two remaining volumes were completed in 1744; and the whole, not long after, was translated into German. This was the first of Mr Campbell's works to which he prefixed his name; and it is a performance of great and acknowledged merit. In 1743, he published "Hermippus revived;" a second edition of which, much improved and enlarged, came out in 1749, under the following title: "Hermippus Redivivus: or, the Sage's Triumph over Old Age and the Grave. Wherein a method is laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for prolonging the life and vigour of man. Including a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> upon an ancient Inscription, in which this great secret is revealed; supported by numerous authorities. The whole interposed with a great variety of remarkable and well-attested relations." This extraordinary tract had its origin in a foreign publication; but it was wrought up to perfection by the additional ingenuity and learning of Mr Campbell. In 1744 he gave to the public, in two volumes folio, his "Voyages and Travels," on Dr Harris's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, being a very distinguished improvement of that collection which had appeared in 1705. The time and care employed by Mr Campbell in this important undertaking did not prevent his engaging in another great work, the "Biographia Britannica," which began to be published in weekly numbers in 1745, and extended to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes folio; but our author's articles were only in the first four volumes; of which Dr Kippis observes, they constitute the prime merit. When the late Mr Dodley formed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of "The Preceptor," which appeared in 1748, Mr Campbell was to assist in the undertaking; and the parts written by him were the Introduction to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, and the discourse on Trade and Commerce, both of which displayed an extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of knowledge upon these subjects. In 1750 he published the first separate edition of his "Prefect State of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>;" a work which had been originally begun in 1746, in the "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>," a very valuable periodical performance, printed for Doddley. There is no production of our author's that hath met with a better reception. It has gone through six editions, and fully deserved this encouragement. The next great undertaking which called for the exertion of our author's abilities and learning, was "The Modern Universal History." This extensive work was published, from time to time, in detached parts, till it amounted to 16 volumes folio; and a second edition of it, in 8vo, began to make its appearance in 1759. The parts of it written by Mr Campbell were, the histories of the Portuguese, Dutch Spanish, French, Swedish, Danish, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a> Settlements in the East-Indies; and the Histories of the Kingdoms of Spain, Portugal, Algarve, Navarre, and that of France, from Clovis to 1656. As our author had thus distinguished himself in the literary world, the degree of LL.D. was very properly and honourably conferred upon him, June 18, 1754, by the university of Glasgow. His principal and favourite work was, "A Political Survey of Great Britain," 2 vol. 4to, published a short time before his death; in which the extent of his knowledge, and his patriotic spirit, are equally conspicuous. Dr Campbell's reputation was not confined to his own country, but extended to the remotest parts of Europe. As a striking instance of this, it may be mentioned, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1774, the empress of Russia was pleased to honour him with the present of her <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, drawn in the robes worn in that country in the days of John Bafflowitz, grand duke of Mulcovy, who was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Queen Elizabeth. To manifest the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of her imperial majesty's goodwills, a set of the "Political Survey of Britain," bound in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, highly ornamented, and accompanied with a letter descriptive of the triumphs and felicities of her reign, was forwarded to St Petersburg, and conveyed into her hands by Prince Orloff, who had resided some months in this kingdom. Dr Campbell in 1736 married Elizabeth, daughter of Benjamin Vobe, of Leominster, in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, gentleman, with whom he lived nearly 40 years in the greatest conjugal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. So wholly did he dedicate his time to books, that he seldom went abroad; but to relieve himself as much as possible from the inconveniences incident to a sedentary life, it was his custom, when the weather would admit, to walk in his garden; or otherwise in some room of his house, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. By this method, united with the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> in eating, and an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from drinking, he enjoyed a good state of health, though his constitution was delicate. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> manner of living did not preclude him from a very extensive and honourable acquaintance. His house, especially on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> evening, was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the most distinguished persons of all ranks, and particularly of such as had rendered themselves eminent by their knowledge or love of literature. He received foreigners, who were fond of learning, with an affability and kindness which excited in them the highest respect and veneration; and his instructive and cheerful conversation made him the delight of his friends in general. He was, during the latter part of his life, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> for the province of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> in North America; and died at the close of the year 1775, in the 67th year of his age. The doctor's literary knowledge was by no means confined to the subjects on which he more particularly treated as an author; he was well acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and had read much in medicine. It hath been with great reason believed, that if he had dedicated his studies to this last science, he would have made a very conspicuous figure in the medical profession. He was eminently versed in the different parts of sacred literature; and his acquaintance with the languages extended not only to the Hebrew, Greek and Latin among the ancient, and to the French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, and Dutch, among the modern; but likewise to the Oriental tongues. He was particularly fond of the Greek language. His attainment of such a variety of knowledge was exceedingly assisted by a memory surprisingly retentive, and which indeed astoni... Campbell. nished every person with whom he was conversant. In communicating his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, he had an uncommon readiness and facility; and the style of his works, which had been formed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that of the celebrated Bishop Sprat, was perspicuous, easy, flowing, and harmonious. To all these accomplishments of the understanding, Dr Campbell joined the more important virtues of a moral and pious character. His disposition was gentle and humane, and his manners kind and obliging. He was the tenderest of husbands, a most indulgent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, a kind master, a firm and sincere friend. To his great Creator he paid the constant and ardent tribute of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, duty, and reverence; and in his correspondences he showed that a sense of piety was always nearest his heart. Campbell, George, D.D., was born at Aberdeen in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1719. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school in the same town, and intended for the employment of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a>-writer, an occupation similar to that of an English attorney, in which he was bound an apprentice. The love of study, however, prevailed over every opposition: in 1741 he attended <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> lectures at Edinburgh before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> was fully completed, and soon after became a regular student in the university of Aberdeen, attending the lectures of Professor Lumden in King's, and Professor Chalmers in Marischal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. In 1746 he was licensed to preach by the presbytery of Aberdeen. In 1748 he obtained the living of Banchory Ternan, in which situation he became a married man, and was fortunate in possessing a lady "remarkable for the sagacity of her understanding, the integrity of her heart, the general propriety of her conduct, and her skill in the management of domestic economy." Mutual happiness was the consequence of this union, which was not terminated till her death in 1792. In 1757 he was translated to Aberdeen, to be one of the ministers of that town, and in 1759 was presented to the office of principal of Marischal college. Mr Hume's Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a> gave the new principal an opportunity of evincing that he was not unworthy of his office. He opposed it in a sermon preached before the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of Aberdeen, in 1762, which he was requested to publish; but he preferred the form of a dissertation, and in that state sent the manuscript to Dr Blair, to be by him communicated to the metaphysician. Availing himself then of the remarks of his friends, and his opponent, he gave it to the world in 1763, with a dedication to Lord Bute: but however desirable the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the minister might be in other respects, it was of very little assistance in giving circulation, in the literary world, to an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> which, from the favourable impressions of Blair and Hume, was eagerly read, and universally admired. In 1771 he was elected professor of divinity in Marischal college, on which he resigned his office as one of the ministers of Aberdeen: but as "minister of Gray Friars, an office conjoined to the professorship about a century ago, he was obliged to preach once every Sunday in one of the established churches." Few persons seem to have entertained truer notions of the office of a teacher in an university than our new professor; and the plan he had in view, on entering upon his lectures, though expressed in rather too strong language, may be recommended to every one who undertakes a similar employment. "Gentlemen, (he thus addresses his pupils) the nature of my office has been much misunderstood. It is supposed, that I am to teach you everything connected with the study of divinity. I tell you honestly, that I am to teach you nothing. Ye are not school-boys. Ye are young men, who have finished your courses of philosophy, and ye are no longer to be treated as if ye were at school. Therefore, I repeat it, I am to teach you nothing; but, by the grace of God, I will assist you to teach yourselves everything." In 1771 he published his excellent sermon on the Spirit of the Gospel; and, in 1776, his Philosophy of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>. In this latter year, also, he acquired the friendship of Dr Tucker by a sermon, then much admired, and very generally read, on the Duty of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">Allegiance</a>, in which he endeavours to show "that the British colonies in America had no right, either from reason or from Scripture, to throw off their allegiance;" and he uses those vulgar arguments, which, as being purely political, and more especially adapted to the sentiments of the majority of that day, were very improper topics for the pulpit. It is so much the fashion for divines to make the varying politics of the hour the subject of their discourses, and in them to follow the sentiments of those whose patronage is deemed most advantageous, that we must not be very severe in our animadversions on the present occasion. In 1777 he chose a better subject for a discourse, which he published at the request of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for propagating Christian Knowledge, and in which the success of the first publishers of the Gospel is ably treated as a proof of its truth. In 1779, when many of his countrymen, led away by the madness of enthusiasm and fanaticism, were rushing headlong into the most antichristian practice of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, he published a very seasonable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to the people of Scotland, on the alarms which had been raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> in favour of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. In the same year, also, he published a sermon on the Happy Influence of Religion on Civil Society. The last work which he lived to bring before the public was his Translation of the Four Gospels, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> dissertations, and explanatory notes, of which it is unnecessary to say anything farther in this place than that it is worthy of his talents and character. In 1795 he resigned his professorship, in a letter to the moderator of the presbytery of Aberdeen, which they voted to be inserted in their records. Soon after the resignation of his professorship, he resigned also the principalship, on a pension of £300 a-year being conferred on him by government; but this pension he possessed for a very short time; for, on the 31st of March, 1796, his last illness seized him, and on the next morning it was followed by a paroxysm of the palsy, which destroyed his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of speech, and under which he languished till he died. His funeral sermon was preached on the 17th of April by Dr Brown, who had succeeded him in the offices of principal and professor. His character, very justly drawn by the same gentleman, we shall now lay before our readers. "Dr Campbell, as a public teacher, was long admired for the clearness and copiousness with which he illustrat- Campbell ed the great doctrines and precepts of religion, and the strength and energy with which he enforced them. Intimately persuaded of the truth and infinite consequence of what <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> teaches, he was strongly dexterous of carrying the same conviction to the minds of his hearers, and delivered his discourses with that zeal which flows from strong impressions, and that power of persuasion which is the result of fineness of heart, combined with clearness of understanding. He was satisfied, that the more the pure dictates of the gospel were studied, the more they would approve themselves to the mind, and bring forth, in the affections and conduct, all the peaceable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of righteousness. The unadulterated dictates of Christianity, he was, therefore, only studious to recommend and inculcate; and knew perfectly to discriminate them from the inventions and traditions of men. His chief study ever was, to direct <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> to the great objects of practice; and, without these, he viewed the most orthodox profession as "a sounding brafs, and a tinkling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYMBAL">cymbal</a>." But, besides the character of a preacher of righteousness, he had also that of a teacher of the science of divinity to sustain. How admirably he discharged this duty, and with what effect he conveyed the soundest and most profitable instruction to the minds of his scholars, let those declare who are now in various congregations of this country, communicating to their fellow <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> the fruits of their studies under so able and judicious a teacher. Discarding all attachment to human systems, merely considered as such, he tied his faith to the Word of God alone, possessed the happiest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> in investigating its meaning, and communicated to his hearers the result of his own inquiries, with a precision and perspicuity which brought light out of obscurity, and rendered clear and simple what appeared intricate and perplexed. He exposed, without reserve, the corruptions which ignorance, craft, and hypocrisy had introduced into religion, and applied his talent for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> to the best of all purposes, to hold up to contempt the absurdities with which the purest and sublimest truths had been loaded. "Placed at the head of a public seminary of learning, he felt all the importance of such a situation, and uniformly directed his influence to public utility. His enlarged and enlightened mind justly appreciated the extensive consequence of the education of youth. He anticipated all the effects resulting to the great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of mankind, from numbers of young men issuing, in regular succession, from the university over which he presided, and occupying the different departments of social life. "His benevolent heart delighted to represent to itself the students under his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> usefully and honourably discharging the respective duties of their different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>; and some of them, perhaps, filling the most distinguished stations of civil society. With these prospects before him, he constantly directed his public conduct to their attainment. He never suffered his judgement to be warped by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> or partiality, or his heart to be seduced by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> or private interest. Those mean and ignoble motives by which many are actuated in the discharge of important trusts, approached not his mind. A certain honourable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, if pride it may be called, diffused an uniform dignity over the whole of his behaviour. He felt the man degraded by the perversion of public character. His understanding also clearly showed him even personal advantage attached to such principles and practice, as he adopted from a sense of obligation, and those elevated conceptions of real worth which were so congenial to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. He saw, he experienced, esteem, respect, and influence, following in the train of integrity and beneficence; but contempt, disgrace, aversion, and complete insignificance, closely linked to corruption and selfishness. Little minds are seduced and overpowered by selfish considerations, because they have not the capacity to look beyond the present advantage, and to extend to the misery that stands on the other side of it. The same circumstance that betrays the perversity of their hearts, also evinces the weakness of their judgements. "His reputation as a writer is as extensive as the present intercourse of letters; not confined to his own country, but spread through every civilized nation. In his literary pursuits, he aimed not, as is very often the case, with men of distinguished literary abilities, merely at establishing his own celebrity, or increasing his fortune; but had chiefly at heart the defence of the great cause of Religion, or the elucidation of her dictates. "At an early period he entered the lists as a champion for Christianity against one of its acutest opponents. He not only triumphantly refuted his arguments, but even conciliated his respect by the handsome and dextrous manner in which his defence was conducted. While he refuted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a>, he spared the man, and exhibited the uncommon spectacle of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> writer possessing all the moderation of a Christian. But while he defended Christianity against its enemies, he was dexterous of contributing his endeavours to increase, among its professors, the knowledge of the sacred writings. Accordingly, in the latter part of his life, he favoured the world with a work, the fruit of copious erudition, of unwearied application for almost thirty years, and of a clear and comprehensive judgement. We have only to regret, that the other writings of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> have not been elucidated by the same pen that translated the Gospels. Nor were his literary merits confined to theology, and the studies more immediately connected with it. Philosophy, and the fine arts, are also indebted to his genius and labours; and in him the polite scholar was eminently joined to the deep and liberal divine. "Political principles will always be much affected by general character. This was also the case with Dr Campbell. In politics, he maintained that moderation which is the surest criterion of truth and rectitude, and was equally distant from those extremes into which men are so apt to run in great political questions. He cherished that patriotism which consists in wishing, and endeavouring to promote, the greatest happiness of his country, and is always subordinate to universal benevolence. Firmly attached to the British constitution, he was animated with that genuine love of liberty which it inspires and invigorates. He was equally adverse to despotism and to popular anarchy; the two evils into which political parties are so frequently hurried, to the destruction of all that is valuable to government. Party-spirit, of whatever <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, he considered as having an unhappy tendency to pervert, to the most pernicious purposes, the best principles of the human mind, and to clothe the most iniquitous actions with the most specious appearances. Although tenacious of those sentiments, whether in religion or politics, which he was convinced to be rational and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, he never suffered more <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of opinion to impair his good will, to obstruct his good offices, or to cloud the cheerfulness of conversation. His own conversation was enlivened by a vein of the most agreeable pleasantry."

CAMPBELTOWN

Pages 117-117

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> town of Argyllshire in Scotland, seated on the eastern shore of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Kintyre <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTYRE">Cantyre</a>, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It hath a good harbour; and is now a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though within these 50 years only a petty <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> town. It has in fact been created by the fishery: for it was appointed the place of rendezvous for the buffes; and above 260 have been seen in the harbour at once. The inhabitants are reckoned at upwards of 8000 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 10. N. Lat. 54.

CAMPDEN

Pages 117-117

a small town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> in England, containing about 200 houses. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Viscount, by courtesy, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAINSBOROUGH">Gainsborough</a> his son. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 50. N. Lat. 52.

CAMPEACHY

Pages 117-117

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, seated on the east <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, on the west of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Yucatan. It is defended by a good wall and strong forts; but is neither so rich, nor carries on such a trade, as formerly; it having been the port for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of logwood, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it is cut being about 30 miles distant. It was taken by the English in 1596; by the Buccaneers in 1678; and by the Flibutters of St Domingo in 1685, who set it on fire and blew up the citadel. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 93. 7. N. Lat. 19. 20. CAMPEACHY-Wood. See HEMATOXYLUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAMPEN

Pages 117-117

a strong town of Overijssel in the United Provinces. It hath a citadel and a harbour; but the latter is almost choked up with sand. It was taken by the Dutch in 1578, and by the French in 1672: but they abandoned it the following year. It is seated near the mouth of the river Yssel and Zuyder Zee. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 35. N. Lat. 52. 38.

CAMPESTRE

Pages 117-117

in antiquity, a fort of cover for the privacies, worn by the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in their field exercises; being girt under the navel, and hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. The name is supposed to be formed from campus, the field <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the Roman soldiers performed their exercises.

CAMPHORA

Pages 117-117
or CAMPHIRE, a solid concrete substance extracted from the wood of the laurus camphora. See Chemistry, and Materia Medica Index. Pure camphire is very white, pellucid, somewhat unctuous to the touch; of a bitterish aromatic taste, yet accompanied with a sense of coolness; of a very fragrant smell, somewhat like that of rosemary, but much stronger. It has been very long esteemed one of the most efficacious diaphoretics; and has been celebrated in fevers, malignant and epidemical distempers. In deliria, also, where opiates could not procure sleep, but rather aggravated the symptoms, this medicine has often been observed to procure it. All these effects, however, Dr Cullen attributes to its sedative property, and denies that camphire has any other medicinal virtues than those of an antipathodic and sedative. He allows it to be very powerful, and capable of doing much good or much harm. From experiments made on different brute creatures, camphire appears to be poisonous to every one of them. In some it produced sleep followed by death, without any other symptom. In others, before death, they were awakened into convulsions and rage. It seems, too, to act chiefly on the stomach; for an entire piece swallowed, produced the above-mentioned effects with very little diminution of weight.

CAMPHUISEN

Pages 117-117

DIRK THEODORE RAPHAEL, an eminent painter, was born at Gorcum in 1586. He learned the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> from Diederic Govertze; and by a studious application to it, he very soon not only equalled, but far surpassed his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He had an uncommon genius, and studied <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with care, judgment, and affluency. His subjects were landscapes, mostly small, with ruinous buildings, huts of peasants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> views of villages on the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, with boats and hogs, and generally he represented them by moonlight. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> is remarkably tender and soft, his colouring true nature and very transparent, and his expertise in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> is seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> distances of his objects, which are excellently contrived, and have a surprising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of nature and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. As he left off painting at an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> when others are scarcely qualified to commence artifices, few of his works are to be met with, and they bring considerable prices; as they cannot but give <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to the eye of every observer. He painted his pictures with a thin body of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, but they are handled with singular neatness and spirit. He practised in his profession only till he was 18 years of age, and being then recommended as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the sons of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Nieuport, he undertook the employment, and discharged it with so much <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that he was appointed secretary to that nobleman. He excelled in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>; and the designs which he finished in that manner are exceedingly valued.

CAMPION

Pages 117-119

EDMUND, an English Jesuit, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, of indigent parents, in the year 1540; and educated at Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, where he had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to speak an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> on her accession to the throne. He was admitted a scholar of St John's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> at its foundation, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts in 1564. About the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was ordained by a bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, and became an eloquent Protestant preacher. In 1566, when Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> was entertained by the university of Oxford, he spoke an elegant oration before her majesty, and was also <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESPONDENT">respondent</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in St Mary's church. In 1568, he was junior proctor of the university. In the following year, he went over to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where he wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and turned Papist; but being found rather too affluent in persuading others to follow his example, he was committed to prison. He soon, however, found means to make his escape. He landed in England in 1571; and thence proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, where he publicly recanted his former <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, and was created bachelor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He went soon after to Rome, where, in 1573, he was admitted of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, and was sent by the general of that order to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, where he wrote his tragedy cal... led <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECTAR">Nectar</a> et Ambrosia, which was acted before the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. From Vienna he went to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, where he resided in the Jesuits' college about six years, and then returned to Rome. From thence, in 1580, he was sent by Pope Gregory XIII. with the celebrated Father Parsons, to convert the people of England. From Pitts we learn, that some time before, several English priests, inspired by the Holy Ghost, had undertaken to convert their countrymen; that 80 of these from foreign seminaries, besides several others who by God's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> had been converted in England, were actually engaged in the pious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with great success; that some of them had suffered imprisonment, chains, tortures, and ignominious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, with becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; but seeing at last that the labour was abundant, and the labourers few, they solicited the assistance of the Jesuits; requesting, that though not early in the morning, they would at least in the third, fifth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ninth <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, send labourers into the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s vineyard. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this solicitation, the above two were sent to England. They arrived in an evil hour for Campian, at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>; and were next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> joyfully received by their friends at London. He had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in England, before <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALSINGHAM">Walsingham</a> the secretary of state, being informed of his uncommon affability in the cause of the church of Rome, used every means in his power to have him apprehended, but for a long time without success. However, he was at last taken by one Eliot, a noted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>-taker, who found him in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Edward Yates, Esq. at Lyford in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, and conducted him in triumph to London, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on his hat, on which was written Campian the Jesuit. He was imprisoned in the Tower; where Wood says, "he did undergo many examinations, abuses, wrackings, tortures; exquisitissimus cruciatus tortus," says Pitts. It is hoped, for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of our reformers, this torturing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the story is not true. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> wretch, however, was condemned, on the statute 25 Ed. III. for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; and butchered at Tyburn, with two or three of his fraternity. Howsoever criminal in the eye of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or of the English gospel, might be the zeal of this Jesuit for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of the poor heretics of this kingdom, biographers of each persuasion unite in giving him a great and amiable character. "All writers (says the Oxford antiquary), whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> or Popish, say, that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of admirable parts; an elegant orator, a subtle <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and disputant, and an exact preacher whether in English or the Latin tongue; of a sweet disposition, and a well-polished man," Fuller, in his church-history, says, "he was of a sweet <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, constantly carrying about him the charms of a plausible behaviour, of a fluent tongue, and good parts." His History of Ireland, in two books, was written in 1579; and published, by Sir James <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">Ware</a>, from a manuscript in the Cotton library, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, 1633, folio. He wrote also Chronologia Universalis, a very learned work; and various other tracts. Campicursio, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of armed men for several miles, from and back again to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, to instruct them in the military pace. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> was nearly akin to the decurio, from which it only differed, in that the latter was performed by horsemen, the former also by foot. Campidoctores, or Campiductores, in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, were officers who instructed the soldiery in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and exercises of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and the art of handling their weapons to advantage. These are also sometimes called campigni, and armiductores. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPIDUCTOR">Campiductor</a>, in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, signifies the leader or commander of an army, or party. Campion, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the English name of the Lychinis. Campion, a town of the kingdom of Tangut in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. It was formerly remarkable for being a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> through which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> passed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Bukhara to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. E. Long. 104° 53'. N. Lat. 40° 25'. Campistron, a celebrated French dramatic author, was born in 1656. Racine directed his poetical talents to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and assisted him in his first pieces. He died in 1723. Campitae, in church history, an appellation given to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DONATISTS">Donatists</a>, on account of their assembling in the fields for want of churches. For a similar reason, they were also denominated Montefeces and Rupitani. Campli, or Campli, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the farther Abruzzo, situated in E. Long. 13° 55'. N. Lat. 42° 38'. Campo <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. W. Long. 7° 24'. N. Lat. 38° 50'. Campredon, a town of Catalonia in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated at the foot of the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The fortifications were demolished by the French in 1691. W. Long. 1° 56'. N. Lat. 42° 20'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">Camps</a>, Francis de, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Notre Dame at Sigl., was born at Amiens in 1643; and distinguished himself by his knowledge of medals, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a history of France, and several other works. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1723. Campvere. See Veer. Campus, in antiquity, a field or vacant plain in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, not built upon, left vacant on account of shows, combats, exercises, or other uses of the citizens. Campus Maii, in ancient customs, an annual fair <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> held on May-day, when they confederated together for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the kingdom against all its enemies. Campus Martius, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain in the suburbs of ancient Rome, lying between the Quirinal and Capitoline mounts and the Tiber; thus called because consecrated to the god <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, and set apart for military sports and exercises to which the Roman youth were trained, as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and handling of arms, and all manner of feats of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Here were the races run, either with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> or single horses; here also stood the villa publica, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for the reception of ambassadors, who were not permitted to enter the city. Many of the public <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> were held in the same field, part of which was for that purpose cantoned out. The place was also nobly decorated with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, columns, porticoes, and the like structures. Campus Sceleratus, a place without the walls of ancient Rome, where the Veletas who had violated their vows of virginity were buried alive. Camul, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, on the eastern extremity of the kingdom of Chalos, on the frontiers of Tangut. E. Long. 98° 5'. N. Lat. 37° 15'. Camus, a person with a low flat nose, hollowed in the middle. The Tartars are great admirers of camus beauties. Rubruquis observes, that the wife of the great Jenghiz Khan, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, had only two holes for a nose. Camus, John <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, a French prelate born in 1582. He was author of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pious romances (the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of his time), and other theological works, to the amount of 200 vols. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of politics is remarkable: *Ars non tam regendi, quam fallendi, homines*; "The art not so much of governing, as of deceiving mankind." He died in 1652.

CANAAN

Pages 119-120

the fourth son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>. The irreverence of Ham towards his father <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> is recorded in Gen. ix. Upon that occasion the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> cursed him in a branch of his posterity: "Curse," says he, "be Canaan; a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of servants shall he be unto his brethren." This curse being pronounced, not against Ham the immediate transgressor, but against his son, who does not appear, from the words of Moses, to have been anywise concerned in the crime, hath occasioned several conjectures. Some have believed that Noah cursed Canaan, because he could not well have cursed Ham himself, whom God had not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before blessed. Others think Moses's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> intent in recording this prediction was to raise the spirits of the Israelites, then entering on a terrible <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the children of Canaan, by the assurance, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the curse, that people were destined by God to be subdued by them. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of those who imagine all Ham's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> were here accursed, seems repugnant to the plain words of Scripture, which confines the malediction to Canaan and his posterity; and is also contrary to fact. Indeed, the prophecy of Noah, that "Canaan should be a servant of servants to his brethren," seems to have been wholly completed in him. It was completed with regard to Shem, not only in that a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> nations of the Canaanites were made slaves to the Hiraclites, when they took possession of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, as part of the remainder of them were afterwards enslaved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>; but also by the subsequent expeditions, of the Assyrians and Persians, who were both descended from Shem; and under whom the Canaanites suffered subjection, as well as the Hiraclites; not to mention the conquest of part of Canaan by the Elamites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Persians, under Chedorlaomer, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to them all. With regard to Japhet, we find a completion of the prophecy, in the successive conquests of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> and Phoenicia, where the Canaanites were settled; but especially in the total subversion of the Carthaginian power by the Romans; besides some invasions of the northern nations, as the posterity of Thorgarma and Magog; wherein many of them, probably, were carried away captive. The posterity of Canaan were very numerous. His eldest son was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>, who at least founded and peopled the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Sidon, and was the father of the Sidonians and Phoenicians. Canaan had besides ten sons, who were the fathers of so many peoples, dwelling in Palestine, and in part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; namely, the Hittites, the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgaites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and Hamathites. Land of CANAAN, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> so named from Canaan the son of Ham. It lies between the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and extends from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to Phoenicia. It is bounded to the east by the mountains of Arabia; to the south by the wilderness of Paran, Idumæa, and Egypt; to the west by the Mediterranean, called in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> sea; to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the mountains of Libanus. Its length from the city of Dan (since called Cæsarea Philippi, or Paneadis, which stands at the foot of these mountains) to Beer-sheba, is about 70 leagues; and its breadth from the Mediterranean sea to the eastern borders, is in some places 30. This country, which was first called Canaan, from Canaan the son of Ham, whose posterity possessed it, was afterwards called Palestine, from the people which the Hebrews call <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, and the Greeks and Romans corruptly Palestinians, who inhabited the sea coasts, and were first known to them. It likewise had the name of the Land of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">Promise</a>, from the promise God made to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> of giving it to him; that of the Land of Israel, from the Israelites having made themselves masters of it; that of Judah, from the tribe of Judah, which was the most considerable of the twelve; and lastly, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> it had of being sanctified by the presence, actions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, has given it the name of the Holy Land, which it retains to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The first inhabitants of this land therefore were the Canaanites, who were descended from Canaan, and the eleven sons of that patriarch. Here they multiplied extremely; trade and war were their first occupations; these gave rise to their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and the several colonies scattered by them over almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> provinces of the Mediterranean. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of their idolatry and abominations was completed, when God delivered their country into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Israelites. In St Athanasius's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the Africans still said they were descended from the Canaanites; and it is said, that the Punic tongue was almost entirely the same with the Canaanitish and Hebrew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The colonies which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a> carried into Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Cilix into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, came from the stock of Canaan. The isles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, Cyprus, Corfu, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GADES">Gades</a> and Ebusus, are thought to have been peopled by the Canaanites. Bocart, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Canaan, has set all this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Many of the old inhabitants of the north-west of the land of Canaan, however, particularly on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> or territories of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> and Sidon, were not driven out by the children of Israel, whence this tract seems to have retained the name of Canaan a great while after those other parts of the country, which were better inhabited by the Israelites, had lost the said name. The Greeks called this tract, inhabited by the old Canaanites along the Mediterranean sea, Phoenicia; the more inland parts, as being inhabited partly by Canaanites, and partly by Syrians, Syrophoenicia: and hence the woman said by St Matthew (xv. 22.) to be a woman of Canaan, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Jesus cured, is said by St Mark (vii. 26.) to be a Syrophoenician by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, as she was a Greek by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and language.

CANABAC

Pages 120-120

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> which lies contiguous to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULAM">Bulam</a> on the western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and is inhabited by a fierce people, governed by two kings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chiefs. It would appear that the Canabacs had been very troublesome to their neighbours; for the inhabitants of some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in that cluter rejoiced at the settlement of the English in Bulam, hoping to find in them a defense against the usurpations of this people.

CANAL

Pages 128-131

canal and that in the coffer. As it was impossible to represent this part of the apparatus on so small a scale, for the sake of illustration it is represented more at large in fig. 9, where A, as before, represents the upper reach of the

CANAL

Pages 131-131
