an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to hold a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, made in different forms, and of all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> candlestick was one of the sacred utensils made by Moses to be placed in the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>. It was made of hammered <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. It consisted of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> branches supported by a base <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foot. These branches were adorned at equal distances with five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> like lilies, and with as many bowls and knobs placed alternately. Upon the stock and six branches of the candlestick were the golden lamps, which were immovable, wherein were put <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and cotton. These seven lamps were lighted every evening, and extinguished every morning. The lamps had their tongs or snuffers to draw the cotton in or out, and dishes underneath them to receive the sparks or droppings of the oil. This candlestick was placed in the antechamber of the sanctuary on the south side, and served to illuminate the altar of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> and the tabernacle of the shew-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> had built the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, he placed in it ten golden candlesticks of the same form as that described by Moses, five on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and five on the south side of the holy: But after the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, the golden candlestick was again placed in the temple, as it had been before in the tabernacle by Moses. This sacred utensil, upon the destruction of the temple by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was lodged in the temple of Peace built by Vespasian; and the representation of it is still to be seen on the triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> at the foot of Mount Palatine, on which Vespasian's triumph is delineated.

CANDY

Pages 144-145

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon. It contains about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the island; and as it is encompassed with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and covered with thick forests, through which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> and paths are narrow and difficult, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> has them guarded to prevent his subjects from going into other countries. It is full of hills, from whence rivulets proceed which are full of fish; but as they run among the rocks, they are not fit for boats: however, the inhabitants are very dexterous in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> them to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which is fruitful in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. Since the island of Ceylon fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, we have obtained fuller information respecting it. Mr Percival, who has published an account of this island, mentions the jealousy, both of the Dutch and of the natives, as difficulties which could not have been easily surmounted by travellers while it remained subject to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The interior of the island (he says), owing to the jealousy of the Dutch, has been little explored by Europeans; and any traveller who might have obtained the permission of the Dutch to visit it, could not have executed his purpose from the jealousy of the natives. Since the Candians have been driven by their invaders into the mountains of the interior, it has been their policy carefully to prevent any European from seeing those objects which might tempt the avarice of his countrymen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from observing the approaches by which an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> could penetrate their mountains. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> an European by any accident was carried into their territories, they took every precaution to prevent him from escaping; and the guards, stationed everywhere at the approaches, joined to the wide and pathless woods which divide the interior from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, rendered such an attempt almost completely desperate. When an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> was sent from any European <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to the king of Candy, he was watched with all that strictness and jealousy, which the suspicious temper of uncivilized nations dictates. In an embassy which I attended to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of that monarch, I had an opportunity of observing how careful the natives were to prevent strangers from making any observations. Mr Boyd, who about twenty years ago went on a similar embassy, was watched with the same particular circumspection; and has therefore been able to add little to our stock of knowledge concerning the interior. "The dominions of the native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> are completely cut off on all sides from those of the Europeans by almost impenetrable woods and mountains. The paths which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> through these to the coasts are extremely steep and difficult, and scarcely known even by the natives themselves. As soon as we advance from ten to twenty miles from the coasts, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> presents itself greatly differing from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coast, both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and appearance. After ascending the mountains and passing the woods, we find ourselves in the midst of a country not advanced many stages beyond..." the first state of improvement, and which we are astonished to find in the neighbourhood of the highly cultivated fields which surround Columbo. As we advance towards the centre of the island, the country gradually rises, and the woods and mountains which separate the several parts of the country become more steep and impervious. "It is in the midst of these fastnesses that the native prince still preserves those remains of territory and power which have been left him by succedane invaders. His dominions are now much reduced in size; for besides the whole of the sea coasts which were of any value, the Dutch, in their various attacks during the last century, have contrived to get into their power every tract from which they could derive either emolument or security. Those provinces which still remain to him, are Nourecalva and Hotcourly towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-west; while Matuly, comprehending the districts of Bintana, Velas, and Panoa, with a few others, occupy those parts more to the eastward. To the south-east lies Ouvvah, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and giving the king one of his titles. The western parts are chiefly included in the provinces of Cotemal and Hotteracoryl. These different provinces are subdivided into cortes or districts, and entirely belong to the native prince. It is needless to recount the names of those divisions which stretch towards the sea-coast, and are now chiefly in our possession. "In the highest and most central <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the native king's dominions <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> the cortes or counties of Oudanor and Tatanour, in which are situated the two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities. Those counties take the pre-eminence of all the rest, and are both better cultivated, and more populous, than any of the other districts, and are distinguished by the general name of Condé Udda; condé or candé in the native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifying a mountain, and udda the greatest or highest. "This province of Condé Udda is even more inaccessible than the others, and forms as it were a separate kingdom of itself. On every side it is surrounded by lofty mountains covered with wood, and the paths by which it is entered seem little more than the tracks of wild beasts. Guards are stationed all around to prevent both entrance and escape; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> they might seem entirely superfluous, did not recollect that the perseverance of the Dutch overcame all these obstacles, and forced a way into the very centre of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fortification." Candy, a town of Asia, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a kingdom of the same name, in the island of Ceylon. It has been often burnt by the Portuguese, when they were masters of the coasts. It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 79. 12. N. Lat. 7. 35. We have the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Candy by Mr Percival, whom we have already quoted, and who attended an embassy to the king. "In the district of Tatanour lies Candy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence and the capital of the native prince's dominions. It is situated at the distance of 80 miles from Columbo, and twice as far from Trincomalee, in the midst of lofty and steep hills covered with thick jungle. The narrow and difficult passes by which it is approached are intersected with thick hedges of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>; and hedges of the same sort are drawn round the hills in the vicinity of Candy like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of circumvallation. Through them the only passage is by gates of the same thorny materials, so contrived as to be drawn up and let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>. When the Candians are obliged to retreat within these barriers, they cut the ropes, and then it is impossible to force a passage except by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> down the gates, which from their green state, and the constant annoyance of the enemy sheltered behind them, would prove an enterprise of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and difficulty. These hedge-rows form the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> fortifications of Candy. The Malivagonga also nearly surrounds the hill on which it stands: that river is here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, rocky, and rapid; a very strict <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> is kept on it, and every one who passes or repasses is closely watched and examined. "The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> itself is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> miserable-looking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, surrounded by a mud wall of no strength whatever. It has been several times burnt by Europeans, and was once deserted by the king, who retired to a more inaccessible part of his dominions. It is upon occasion of the embassy of General Macdowall, that any information concerning the present state of Candy has been obtained; and even then it could be little more than guessed at, as the ambassador and his suite were admitted only by torch-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and always retired before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. From what could then be observed, the city consists of a long straggling street built on the declivity of a hill; the houses <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and low, but with their foundations raised in such a manner above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the street that they appear quite lofty to passengers. The reason of this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is to enable the king to hold his assemblies of the people and to have his elephant and buffalo fights in the street, without interfering with the houses. When the king passes along the street, none of the inhabitants are allowed to appear before their houses, or the paths on a level with them, as that would be attended with the heinous indecorum of placing a subject higher than the prince defended of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. "At the upper end of this street, stands the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, a poor mansion for the abode of a king. It is surrounded with high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls, and consists of two squares, one within the other. In the inner of these are the royal apartments, and it is there that the court is held and audiences given. The exterior of the palace and the rest of the city could be but very partially observed by those who attended General Macdowall, owing to the pressure of the crowd, and the dazzling glare of the torches. By every account indeed which I have heard, Candy contains nothing worthy of notice, and from the want of either wealth or industry among the inhabitants, it is not indeed to be expected that any thing could be met with in this straggling village to attract the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the traveller." Candy, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>-Candy, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of sugar made by melting and crystallizing it five or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times over, to render it hard or transparent. It is of three kinds, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. The white comes from the loaf-sugar, the yellow from the caffonado, and the red from the muscovado.

CANDYING

Pages 145-146

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of preserving simples in substance, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. The performance <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">CANE</a>. See ARUNDO and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAMUS">CALAMUS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CANE

Pages 146-146

e denotes also a walking stick. It is customary to adorn it with a head of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, &c. Some are without knots, and very smooth and even; others are full of knots about two inches distance from one another. These last have very little elasticity, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> so well as the others. Canes of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> are the most beautiful which the Europeans bring into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Some of them are so fine, that people <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> them into bowls <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessels, which being varnished over in the inside, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> lacca, will hold liquors as well as glass or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> does; and the Indians <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them for that purpose. Cane is also the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, which differs according to the several countries where it is used. At <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> the cane is equal to 7 feet 3½ inches English measure: the cane of Thoulouse and the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, is equal to the varre of Arragon, and contains five feet 8½ inches; at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a>, Provence, Dauphiny, and the Lower Languedoc, to fix English feet 5½ inches.

CANEA

Pages 146-146

a considerable town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Candia, where a bafaw resides. It was built by the Venetians, and occupies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the site of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CYDONIA">CYDONIA</a>. It is but about two miles in compass; encircled on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side with a single wall, extremely thick; and defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and deep ditch, cut through a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of rock, which extends all around the wall. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it still deeper, they might cause the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to flow round its ramparts; on which they have raised <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> platforms, that their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns might command a wider <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the adjacent plain. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> has only one gate, the gate of Retimo, protected by a half-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, which is the only exterior fort. The side which faces the sea is the best fortified. On the left of the harbour are four batteries, rising one above another, and planted with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cannons of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> metal, marked with the arms of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The first of these batteries stands <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> on the brink of the sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of the harbour is defended only by a strong wall, extending along a chain of pointed rocks which it is dangerous for ships to approach. At the extremity of this wall, there is an old castle, falling into ruins. Beneath that castle, the Venetians had immense arsenals, vaulted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Each of these vaults was of sufficient length, breadth, and height, to serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>-shop for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a ship of the line. The ground is sloping, and the outermost part of these capacious arsenals is on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the sea; so that it was very easy to launch the ships built there into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The Turks are suffering that magnificent work to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into ruins. The city of Canea is laid out on a fine <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. The streets are large and straight; and the squares adorned with fountains. There are no remarkable buildings in it. Most of the houses are flat-roofed, and have only one story. Those contiguous to the harbour are adorned with galleries, from which you enjoy a delightful prospect. From the windows you discover the large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> formed between <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Spada and Cape Melec, and all the ships that are entering in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> passing out. The harbour, at present, receives ships of 200 tons burden; and it might be enlarged so as to admit the largest frigates. Its mouth is exposed to the violence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> winds, which sometimes swell the billows above the ramparts. But, as it is narrow, and the bottom is good, ships that are well moored run no danger. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when Tournefort visited <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, Canea did not contain more than five or six thousand inhabitants. But, at present, when the gates of Gira-Petra, Candi, and Retimo, are choked up, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> have retired to Canea; and it is reckoned to contain 16,000 souls. The environs of the town are admirable; being adorned with forests of olive-trees mixed with fields, vineyards, gardens, and brooks bordered with myrtle-trees and laurel-roses. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> revenue of this town consists in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-olive. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 24. 15. N. Lat. 35. 28. CANELLA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CANELLE

Pages 146-146
or CANE LAND, a large country in the island of Ceylon, called formerly the kingdom of Cota. It contains a great number of cantons, the principal of which are occupied by the Dutch. The chief riches of this country consist in cinnamon, of which there are large forests. There are five towns on the coast, some forts, and a great number of harbours. The rest of the country is inhabited by the natives; and there are several rich mines, from whence they get rubies, sapphires, topazes, cats eyes, and several other precious stones. CANEPHORÆ, in Grecian antiquity, virgins who when they became marriageable, presented certain baskets full of little curiosities to Diana, in order to get leave to depart out of her train, and change their state of life.

CANEPHORIA

Pages 146-146

in Grecian antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> which made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a feast, celebrated by the Athenian virgins on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> the canephoria consisted in this, that the maid, conducted by her father and mother, went to the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, carrying with her a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> full of presents to engage the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> to make the marriage-state happy; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as the scholiast of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a> has it, the basket was intended as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> amends made to that goddess, the protectrix of virginity, for abandoning her party; or as a ceremony to appease her wrath. Suidas calls it a festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>. CANEPHORIA is also the name of a festival in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, celebrated particularly by the Athenians, on which the young maids carried <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> baskets full of fruit, which baskets were covered, to conceal the mystery from the uninitiated.

CANES

Pages 146-146

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and other eastern countries, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> sort of buildings for the reception of strangers and travellers. People are accommodated in these with a room at a small price, but with no other necessaries; so that, excepting the room, there are no greater accommodations in these housetops than in the deserts, only that there is a market near. CANES Venatici, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the Greyhounds, two new <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>, first established by Hevelius, between the tail of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bear and Bootes's arms, above the Coma Berenices. The first is called asterion, being that next the Bear's tail; the other chara. They comprehend

CANETO

Pages 146-147

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, seated on the river Oglio, which was taken by the Imperialists in 1701, by the French in 1702, afterwards by the Imperialists, and then by the French in 1705. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 45'. N. Lat. 4° 55'.

CANGA

Pages 147-147

in the Chinese affairs, a wooden clog borne on the neck, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> offences. The canga is composed of two pieces of wood notched, to receive the criminal's neck; the load lies on his shoulders, and is more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less heavy according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of his offence. Some cangas weigh 200 lb.; the generality from 50 to 60. The mandarins condemn to the punishment of the canga. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">Sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is sometimes changed for this kind of punishment.

CANGE

Pages 147-147
Charles du Fresne, Sieur du, one of the most learned writers of his time, was born at Amiens in 1663, and studied at the Jesuits college in that city. Afterwards he applied himself to the study of the law at Orleans, and gained great reputation by his works; among which are, 1. The history of the empire of Constantinople under the French emperors. 2. John Cinnamus's five books of the history of the affairs of John and Manuel Comnenus, in Greek and Latin, with historical and philological notes. 3. Gieffarium ad Scriptores medice et infimae Latinae.

CANGI

Pages 147-147

Ceangi, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cangani, anciently a people of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, concerning whose situations antiquaries have been much perplexed. They are all the same people. Camden discovered some traces of them in many different and distant places, as in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, and Cheshire; and he might have found as plain vestiges of them in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, Wiltshire, &c. Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSLEY">Horsley</a> and others are no less perplexed and undetermined in their opinions on this subject. But Mr Baxter seems to have discovered the true cause of all this perplexity, by observing that the Cangi or Ceangi were not a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> located in one particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but such of the youth of many different nations as were employed in pasturage, in feeding the flocks and herds of their respective tribes. Almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> nations of Britain had their ceangi, their pastoralia pubes, the keepers of their flocks and herds, who ranged about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers, as they were invited by the season and plenty of pasture for their cattle. This is the reason that vestiges of their name are to be found in so many different parts of Britain; but chiefly in those parts which are most fit for pasturage. These ceangi of the different British nations, naturally brave, and rendered still more hardy by their way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, were constantly armed for the protection of their flocks from wild beasts; and these arms they occasionally employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of their country and their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>.

CANGIAGIO

Pages 147-147
or Cambiaso Ludovico, one of the most eminent of the Genoese painters, was born in 1527. His works at Genoa are very numerous; and he was employed by the king of Spain to adorn part of the Escorial. It is remarked of him, that he was not only a most expeditious and rapid painter, but also that he worked equally well with both hands; and by that unusual power he executed more designs, and finished more grand works with his own pencils, in a much shorter time, than most other artists could do with several assistants. He died in 1585. In the royal collection at Paris there is a Sleeping Cupid, as large as life, and likewise Judith with her attendant, which are painted by Cangiagio, and are an honour to that master. And in the Pembroke collection at Wilton is a picture, reputed the work of Cangiagio, representing Christ bearing his cross.

CANICULA

Pages 147-147

is a name proper to one of the stars of the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">Canis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, called also simply the dog <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>; by the Greeks Σειρος, Sirius. Canicula is the tenth in order in the Britannic catalogue; in Tycho's and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s it is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. It is situated in the mouth of the constellation; and is of the first magnitude, being the largest and brightest of all the stars in the heavens. From the rising of this star not comically, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, but heliacally, that is, its emergence from the sun's rays, which now happens about the 15th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of August, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> reckoned their dies canicularis, or dog days. The Egyptians and Ethiopians began their year at the rising of the Canicula, reckoning to its rise again the next year, which is called the annus canarius, or canicular year. This year consisted ordinarily of 365 days, and every fourth year of 366, by which it was accommodated to the civil year. The reason of their choice of the Canicula before the other stars to compute their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by, was not only the superior brightness of that star, but because its heliacal rising was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> a time of singular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, as falling on the greatest augmentation of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, the reputed father of Egypt. Ephesius adds, that, from the aspect and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of Canicula, the Egyptians drew prognostics concerning the rise of the Nile; and, according to Florus, predicted the future state of the year; so that the first rising of this star was annually observed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>.

CANICULUM

Pages 147-147
or CANICULUS, in the Byzantine antiquities, a golden standish or ink vessel, decorated with precious stones, wherein was kept the sacred encaytum, or red ink, wherewith the emperors signed their decrees, letters, &c. The word is by some derived from canis, or caniculus; alluding to the figure of a dog, which it represented, or rather because it was supported by the figures of dogs. The caniculum was under the care of a particular officer of state.

CANINA

Pages 147-147

the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Epirus, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, which now belongs to the Turks, and lies off the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is of the same name, and is seated on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Chimera. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 25'. N. Lat. 4° 55'.

CANINANA

Pages 147-147

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and esteemed one of the least poisonous kinds. It grows to about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and is green on the back, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> on the belly. It feeds on eggs and small birds; the natives cut off the head and tail, and eat the body as a delicate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a>.

CANINE

Pages 147-149

whatever partakes of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> has any relation to, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a dog. CANINE Appetite, amounts to much the same with Bulimy. CANINE Madness. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Canine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">Teeth</a>, are two sharp-edged teeth in each jaw; one on each side, placed between the incisors and molars. Canini, John Angelo and Marc Anthony, brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, celebrated for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of antiquities. John excelled in designs for engraving on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, particularly heads; Marc engraved them. They were encouraged by Colbert to publish a succession of heads of the heroes and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men of antiquity, designed from medals, antique stones, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> remains; but John died at Rome soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was begun: Marc Anthony, however, procured assistance, finished and published it in Italian in 1669. The cuts of this edition were engraved by Canini, Piccard, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">Valet</a>; and a curious explanation is given, which discovers the skill of the Caninis in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. The French edition of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in 1731, is spurious. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">Canis</a>, or Dog. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. Canis <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, the Great Dog, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the southern hemisphere, below <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORION">Orion</a>'s feet, though somewhat to the westward of him; whose stars <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> makes 29; Tycho observed only 13; Hevelius 21; in the Britannic catalogue they are 31. Canis <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, the Little Dog, in Astronomy, a constellation of the northern hemisphere; called also by the Greeks, Procyon, and by the Latins Antecanis and Canicula. The stars in the constellation Canis Minor, are in Ptolemy's catalogue, 2; in Tycho's, 5; in Hevelius's, 13; and in the British catalogue, 14. Canisius, Henry, a native of Nimeguen, and one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was professor of canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> at Ingolstadt; and wrote a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Summa Juris Canonici. 2. Antique Lectiones, a very valuable work. He died in 1609. Canitz, the baron of, a German poet and statesman, was of an ancient and illustrious family in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in 1634, five months after his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. After his early studies, he travelled to France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and England; and upon his return to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with important negotiations by Frederic II. Frederic III. employed him also. Canitz united the statesman with the poet; and was conversant in many languages, dead as well as living. His German poems were published for the tenth time, 1750, in 8vo. He is said to have taken Horace for his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, and to have written purely and delicately. But he did not content himself with barely cultivating the fine arts in himself; he gave all the encouragement he could to them in others. He died at Berlin, in 1699, privy counsellor of state, aged 45. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANKER">Canker</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> incident to trees, proceeding chiefly from the nature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It makes the bark rot and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the canker be in a bough, cut it off; in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bough, at some distance from the item; in a small one, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it: but for over hot strong ground, the ground is to be cooled about the roots with pond mud and cow dung. Canker, among farriers. See Farriery Index. Canna, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> reed. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Cannabis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">Hemp</a>. See Botany Index. From the leaves of hemp pounded and boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the natives of the East Indies prepare an intoxicating liquor of which they are very fond. The plant, when fresh, has a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> narcotic smell; the water in which the stalks are soaked, in order to separate the tough rind for mechanic uses, is said to be violently poisonous, and to produce its effects almost as soon as drunk. The seeds also have some smell of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is unctuous and sweetish: they are recommended, boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, or triturated with water into an emulsion, against coughs, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of urine, and the like. They are also said to be useful in incontinence of urine, and for restraining venereal appetites; but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> does not warrant their having any virtues of that kind. Cannae, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Apulia on the Adriatic, at the mouth of the river Aufidus, rendered famous by a terrible overthrow which the Romans here received from the Carthaginians under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>. The Roman consuls, Aemilius Paulus and Terentius Varro, being authorized by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> to quit the defensive <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and stake the fortunes of the republic on the chance of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, marched from Cannae, and encamped a few miles east, in two unequal divisions, with the Aufidus between them. In this position they meant to wait for an opportunity of engaging to advantage; but Hannibal, whose critical situation in a deflated country, without refuge or allies, could admit of no delay, found means to inflame the vanity of Varro by some trivial advantages in skirmishes between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. The Roman elated with this success, determined to bring matters to a speedy conclusion; but, finding the ground on the south side too confined for the operations of so large an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, crossed the river; and Varro, raising his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing upon the Aufidus, drew out his forces in the plain. Hannibal, whose head-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> were at Cannae, no sooner perceived the enemy in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, than he forded the water below, and marshalled his troops in a line opposite to that of his adversaries. The Romans were vastly superior in number to the Carthaginians; but the latter were superior in cavalry. The army of the former, consisting of 87,000 men, was drawn up in the usual manner; the hastati in the first line, the principes in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and the triarii in the third. The cavalry were posted on the wings.—On the right, the Roman knights flanked the legions; on the left, the cavalry of the allies covered their own infantry. The two consuls commanded the two wings, Aemilius the right, and Terentius the left; and the two proconsuls, Servilius and Attilius, the main body. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Hannibal, whose army consisted of 40,000 foot and 10,000 horse, placed his Gaulish and Spanish cavalry in his left wing, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> the Roman knights; and the Numidian horse in his right, over-against the cavalry of the allies of Rome. As to his infantry, he divided the African battalions into two bodies; one of which he posted near the Gaulish and Spanish horse, the other near the Numidian. Between these two bodies were placed on one side the Gaulish, on the other the Spanish infantry, drawn up in such a manner as to form an obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, projecting a considerable way beyond the two wings. Behind this line he drew up a second which had no projection. Africrual commanded the left wing; Maharbal the right; and Hannibal himself, with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGO">Mago</a>, Mago, the main body. He had also taken care to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> himself in such a manner, that the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> Vulturnus, which rises at certain stated times, should blow directly in the faces of the Romans during the fight, and cover them with dust. The onset was begun by the light-armed infantry; the Romans discharging their javelins, and the balistae their stones, with pretty equal success; nevertheless, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Æmilius was wounded. Then the Roman cavalry in the right wing advanced against the Gaulish and Spanish in Hannibal's left. As they were shut in by the river Aufidus on one side, and by their infantry on the other, they did not fight as usual, by charging and wheeling off, and then returning to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> fighting each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> against his adversary, till one of them was killed or retired. After they had made prodigious efforts on both sides to overpower each other, they all on a sudden dismounted, and fought on foot with great fury. In this attack the Gauls and Spaniards soon prevailed; put the Romans to the rout; and, pursuing them along the river, strewed the ground with their dead bodies, Afrunbal giving no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was scarce over, when the infantry on both sides advanced. The Romans first fell upon the Spaniards and Gauls, who, as already observed, formed a kind of triangle projecting beyond the two wings. These gave ground, and, pursuant to Hannibal's directions, sunk into the void space in their rear, by which means they insensibly brought the Romans into the centre of the African infantry; and then the fugitives rallying, attacked them in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, while the Africans charged them in both flanks. The Romans being, by this artful retreat, drawn into the snare and surrounded, no longer kept their ranks, but formed several platoons in order to face every way. Æmilius, who was on the right wing, seeing the danger of the main body, at the head of his legionaries acted the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> both of a solderer and general, penetrating into the heart of the enemy's battalions, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> great numbers of them in pieces. All the Roman cavalry that were left, attended the brave consul on foot; and, encouraged by his example, fought like men in despair. But, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Afrunbal, at the head of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of Gaulish and Spanish infantry brought from the centre, attacked Æmilius's legionaries with such fury, that they were forced to give ground and fly: the consul, being all covered with wounds, was at last killed by some of the enemy who did not know him. In the main body, the Romans, though invested on all sides, continued to fall their lives dear; fighting in platoons, and making a great slaughter of the enemy. But being at length overpowered, and disheartened by the death of the two proconsuls, Servilius and Attilius, who headed them, they dispersed and fled, some to the right, and others to the left, as they could find opportunity; but the Numidian horse cut most of them in pieces: the whole plain was covered with heaps of dead bodies, insomuch that Hannibal himself, thinking the butchery too terrible, ordered his men to put a stop to it.—There is a great disagreement among authors as to the number of Romans killed and taken at the battle of Cannæ. According to Livy, the republic lost 50,000 men, including the auxiliaries. According to Polybius, of 6000 Roman horse, only 70 escaped to Venetia with Terentius Varro, and 300 of the auxiliary horse. As to the infantry, that writer tells us, that 72,000 of the Roman foot died on the field of battle fighting like brave men; and that 13,000 were made prisoners. According to Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>, of 6000 horse, only 370 escaped the general slaughter, and of 80,000 foot, 3000 only were left. The most moderate computation makes the number of Romans killed to amount to 45,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of action is marked out to posterity, by the name of Pezzo di Sangue, "Field of Blood." These plains have more than once, since the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, afforded room for men to accomplish their mutual destruction. Melo of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, after raising the standard of revolt against the Greek emperors, and defeating their generals in several engagements, was at last routed here in 1019, by the Catapan Bolanos. Out of 250 Norman adventurers, the flower of Melo's army, only ten escaped the slaughter of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. In 1201, the archbishop of Palermo and his rebellious associates, who had taken advantage of the nonage of Frederick of Swabia, were cut to pieces at Cannæ by Walter de Brienne, sent by the Pope to defend the young <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s dominions. The traces of the town of Cannæ are very faint, consisting of fragments of altars, cornices, gates, walls, vaults, and under-ground granaries. It was destroyed the year before the battle; but, being rebuilt, became an episcopal see in the infancy of Christianity. It was again ruined in the sixth century, but seems to have subsisted in a humble state many ages later; for we read of its contending with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARLETTA">Barletta</a> for the territory which till then had been enjoyed in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> by them; and in 1284, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. issued an edict for dividing the lands, to prevent all future litigation. The prosperity of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, which increased in wealth and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> by embarkations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSADES">crusades</a> and by traffic, proved the annihilation of the great inland cities; and Cannæ was probably abandoned entirely before the end of the thirteenth century. CANNELL COAL. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> Index.

E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. N. Lat. 43. 34.

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for an anthropophagus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>-eater, more especially in the West Indies. See ANTHROPOPHAGI.

CANNON

Pages 150-150

with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-founders and printers, the name of the largest size of letters they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>.

CANNONADE

Pages 150-150

the application of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> to the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of its efforts against some distant object intended to be seized or destroyed, as a ship, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, or fortresses. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">GUNNERY</a>. Since a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ship of war may be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of floating batteries, it is evident that the efforts of her artillery must be greatly superior to those of a fortress on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; that is to say, in general; because, on some particular occasions, her situation may be extremely dangerous, and her cannonading ineffectual. Her superiority consists in several circumstances, as the power of bringing her different batteries to converge to one point; or shifting the line of her attack so as to do the greatest possible execution against the enemy, or to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> where she <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the least exposed to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>; and chiefly because, by employing a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cannon against a fort than it can possibly return, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of her artillery against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls soon becomes decisive and irresistible. Besides these advantages in the attack, she is also greatly superior in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; because the cannon shot, passing with rapidity through her sides seldom do any execution out of the line of their flight, or occasion much mischief by their splinters; whereas they very soon shatter and destroy the faces of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and produce incredible havoc among the men by the fragments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, &c. A ship may also retreat when she finds it too dangerous to remain longer exposed to the enemy's fire, or when her own fire cannot produce the desired effect. Finally, the fluctuating situation of a ship, and of the element on which she rests, renders the effects of bombs very uncertain, and altogether destroys the effect of the ricochet, or rolling and bounding shot, which is so pernicious and destructive in a fortress or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> engagement. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> inconvenience to which a ship is exposed, on the contrary, is, that the low-laid cannon in a fort near the brink of the sea, may strike her repeatedly on or under the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so as to sink her before her cannonade can have any considerable efficacy.

CANO

Pages 150-150

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in Negroland, with a town of the same name. It is bounded by Zaza on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a> on the south, the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGADES">Agades</a> on the west, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a> on the east. Some of the inhabitants are herdsmen, and others till the ground and dwell in villages. It produces corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and cotton. Here are also many deserts, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> covered with woods, in which are wild citrons and lemon trees. The walls and houses of the town are made of clay, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 18. N. Lat. 21. 5.

CANOBIA

Pages 150-150

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, seated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Lago Maggiore, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Greater Lake. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 47. N. Lat. 45. 55.

CANOE

Pages 150-150

a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessel, formed of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree hollowed, and sometimes of several pieces of the bark put together. Canoes are of various sizes, according to the uses for which they may be designed, or the countries wherein they are formed. The largest are made of the cotton tree; some of them <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry between 20 and 30 headloads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> or molasses. Some are made to carry sail; and for this purpose are steeped in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> till they become pliant; after which their sides are extended, and strong beams placed between them, on which a deck is afterwards laid that serves to support their sides. The other sorts very rarely carry sail, unless when going before the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; their sails are made of a sort of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a> or rushes. They are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> rowed with paddles, which are pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> wood somewhat resembling a corn shovel; and, instead of rowing with it horizontally like an oar, they manage it perpendicularly. The smallest canoes are very narrow, having only room for one person in breadth, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight lengthwise. The rowers, who are generally American savages, are very expert in managing their paddles uniformly, and in balancing the canoes with their bodies; which would be difficult for a stranger to do, how well accustomed forever to the conducing of European boats, because the canoes are extremely light, and liable to be overturned. The American Indians, when they are under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of landing to avoid a water-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, or of crossing the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> from one river to another, carry their canoes on their heads, till they arrive at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they can launch them again. This is the general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of canoes, and method of managing them: but some nations have vessels going under the name of canoes, which differ considerably from the above; as the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, Otaheite, &c.

CANON

Pages 150-154

a person who possesses a prebend, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> revenue allotted for the performance of divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, or collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Canons are of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity: Paschier observes, that the name canon was not known before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>; at least the first we hear of are in Gregory de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, who mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of canons instituted by Baldwin XVI., archbishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Clotharius I. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> attributes the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of this order to Chrodegangus, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a> about the middle of the eighth century. Originally canons were only priests, or inferior <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, who lived in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; residing by the cathedral church, to assist the bishop; depending entirely on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>; supported by the revenues of the bishopric; and living in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, as his domestics, or counsellors, &c. They even inherited his moveables, till the year 817, when this was prohibited by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, and a new rule substituted Canons. Situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of that which had been appointed by Chrodegangus, and which was observed for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in the west till the 12th century. By degrees, these communities of priests, shaking off their dependence, formed separate bodies; whereof the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, however, were still heads. In the tenth century, there were communities or congregations of the same kind, established even in cities where there were no bishops: these were called collegiates, as they used the terms <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> and college indifferently: the name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, now given to these bodies, being much more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. Under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the French kings, the canonical or collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> had spread itself all over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and each cathedral had its chapter, distinct from the rest of the clergy. They had the name canon from the Greek κανών, which signifies three different things; a rule, a pension or fixed revenue to live on, and a catalogue or matricula; all which are applicable to them. In time, the canons freed themselves from their rules, the observance relaxed, and, at length, they ceased to live in community: yet they still formed bodies; pretending to other functions besides the celebration of the common office in the church; yet assuming the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the rest of the clergy: making themselves as a necessary council of the bishop; taking upon them the administration of a fee during a vacancy, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a bishop to supply it. There are even some chapters exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop, and owning no head but their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>. After the example of cathedral chapters, collegiate ones also <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to form bodies, after they had abandoned living in community. Canons are of various kinds; as: <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Canons, which are those attached, and, as the Latins call it, incardinati, to a church, as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> is to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. Domiciliary Canons, were young canons, who, not being in orders, had no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in any particular chapters. Expectative Canons, were such as, without having any revenue or prebend, had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and dignities of canons, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the chapter, and a place in the choir; till such time as a prebend should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. Foreign Canons, were such as did not officiate in the canonries to which they belonged. To these were opposed manonary canons, or canons residentiary. Lay or honorary Canons, are such among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> as have been admitted, out of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and respect, into some chapter of canons. Regular Canons, are canons that still live in community; and who, like <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, have, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, to the practice of their rules, added the solemn profession of vows. They are called regulars, to distinguish them from those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> canons who abandon living in community, and at the same time the observance of the canons made as the rule of the clergy, for the maintenance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. The canons subsisted in their simplicity till the eleventh, some say the twelfth century, when some of them, separating from the community, took with them the name of canons, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACEPHALOUS">acephalous</a> priests, because they declined to live in community with the bishop; and those who were left thenceforth acquired the denomination of canons regular, and adopted most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> of the rule of St Augustine. This order of regular canons of St Augustine was brought into England by Adelwald, confessor to Henry I. who erected a priory at Nottel in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; and obtained for them the church of Carlisle as an episcopal see, with the privilege of choosing their own bishop. They were singularly protected and encouraged by Henry I. who gave them the priory of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNSTABLE">Dunstable</a> in 1107, and by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Maud, who, in the following year, gave them the priory of the Holy Trinity in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It appears, that under the reign of Edward I. they had fifty-three priories. Tertiary Canons, those who had only the third part of the revenues of the canonicate. Canon, in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> or rule, either of doctrine or discipline, enacted especially by a council, and confirmed by the authority of the sovereign. Canons are properly decisions of matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; or regulations of the policy and discipline of a church, made by councils, either general, national, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a>. Such are the canons of the council of Nice, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, &c. There have been various collections of the canons of the eastern councils; but four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ones, each ampler than the preceding. The first, according to Uthier, A.D. 382, containing only those of the first ecumenical council, and the first provincial ones: they were but 164 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. To these, Dionysius Exiguus, in the year 520, added the 50 canons of the apostles, and those of the other general councils. The Greek canons in this second collection end with those of the council of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>; to which are subjoined those of the council of Sardica, and the African councils. The fourth and last collection comes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as low as the second council of Nice; and it is on this that Balmamon and Zonaras have commented. Apostolical Canons, are those which have been usually ascribed to St Clement. Bellarmine, Baronius, &c. will have them to be genuine canons of the apostles: Catechism observes, that they cannot be ascribed to the apostles or Clement, because they are not received with other books of Scripture, are not quoted by the writers of the first ages, and contain many things not agreeable to the apostolical times: Hincmar, De Marca, Beveridge, &c. take them to be framed by the bishops who were the apostles disciples in the second or third century; S. Balmamon is of opinion that they were collected by an anonymous writer in the fifth century; but Daillé, &c. maintain them to have been forged by some heretic in the sixth century; and S. Balmamon conjectures that some of them are ancient, and others not older than the seventh century. The Greek church allows only 85 of them, and the Latins only 50; though there are 84 in the edition given of them in the Corpus Juris Canonici. Canon is also used for the authorized catalogue of the sacred writings. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. The ancient canon, or catalogue of the books of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, was made by the Jews, and is ordinarily attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>; who is said to have distributed them into the law, the prophets, and the hagiographa, to which our Saviour refers, Luke, chap. xxiv. ver. 44. The same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is also mentioned by Josephus, cont. Appion. This is the canon allowed to have been followed by the primitive church, till the council of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>; and, according to St Jerome, this consisted of no more than 22 books; answering to the number of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>; though at present they are classified into 24 divisions, containing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEUTERONOMY">Deuteronomy</a>, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> prophets, the Psalms, the Proverbs, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, Canticles, Ruth, Lamentations, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTES">Ecclesiastes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>, Daniel, Ezra, comprehending the book of Nehemiah and the Chronicles. However, this order is not universally observed either among Jews or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; nor were all the books above enumerated admitted into the canon in Ezra's time. It is most likely, says Dr Prideaux, that the two books of Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>, were added in the time of Simon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, when the canon was completed. But that council enlarged the canon very considerably, taking into it the books which we call apocryphal; which the council of Trent has further enforced, enjoining all these to be received as books of Holy Scripture, upon pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a>, and being attainted of hereby. The Romanists, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this canon, say, that it is the same with that of the council of Hippo, held in 393; and with that of the third council of Carthage, in 397, at which were present 46 bishops, and, among the rest, St Augustine; who declared that they received it from their fathers. Their canon of the New Testament perfectly agrees with ours. It consists of books that are well known; some of which have been universally acknowledged; such are the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, thirteen Epistles of St Paul, one Epistle of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and one Epistle of St John; and others, concerning which doubts were entertained, but which were afterwards received as genuine; such are the epistle to the Hebrews, that of James, the second of Peter, the second and third of John, that of Jude, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. These books were written at different times; and they are authenticated, not by the decrees of councils, or infallible authority, but by such kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> as is thought sufficient in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any other ancient writings. They were very extensively diffused; they were read in every Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; they were valued and preserved with care by the first Christians; they were cited by Christian writers of the second, third, and fourth century, as by Irenaeus, Clement the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a>, Tertullian, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, Eusebius, &c., and their genuineness is proved by the testimony of those who were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the apostles themselves, and by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. The four Gospels, and most of the other books of the New Testament, were collected either by one of the apostles, or some of their disciples and successors, before the end of the first century. The catalogue of canonical books furnished by the more ancient Christian writers, as Origen about the year 210, Eusebius and Athanasius in 315, Epiphanius in 370, Jerome in 382, Aelfin in 394, and many others, agrees with that which is now received among Christians. For the time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the several books of the New Testament, see the titles of the books themselves; as the Gospel of St Matthew, Mark, &c. Some of the fathers distinguish the inspired writings into three classes; proto-canonical, deutero-canonical, and apocryphal. Paschal Canon, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the moveable feasts, showing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of Easter, and the other feasts depending on it, for a cycle of 19 years. The paschal canon is supposed to be the calculation of Eusebius of Cesarea, and to have been done by order of the council of Nice. Canon, in monastic orders, a book wherein the religious of every convent have a fair transcript of the rules of their order, frequently read among them as their local statutes. This is also called regula, as containing the rule and institution of their order. The canon differs from the missale, martyrologium, and necrologium. Canon, again, is used for the catalogue of saints acknowledged and canonized in the Roman church. Canon is also used, by way of excellence, in the Roman church, for the secret words of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the Pater; in the middle of which the priest consecrates the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a>. The common opinion is, that the canon of the mass commences with Te igitur, &c. The people are to be on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, hearing the canon; and are to rehearse it to themselves, so as not to be heard. Canon, in the ancient music, is a rule or method of determining the intervals of notes. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, rejecting the Aristoxenian way of measuring the intervals in music, by the magnitude of a tone (which was supposed to be formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a diapente and a diatessaron), thought that musical intervals should be distinguished, according to the ratios or proportions which the sounds terminating those intervals bear to one another, when considered according to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of acuteness or gravity; which, before Aristoxenus, was the old Pythagorean way.
