He therefore made the diapason consist in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> ratio; the diapente, in a sesquialterate; the diatessaron, in a sesquiterian; and the tone itself, in a sesqui <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>; and all the other intervals, according to the proportion of the sounds that terminate them; wherefore taking the canon (as it is called) for a determinate line of any length, he shows how this canon is to be cut accordingly, so that it may represent the respective intervals: and this method answers exactly to experiment, in the different lengths of musical chords. From this canon, Ptolemy and his followers have been called Canonici; as those of Aristoxenus were called Musici. Canon, in modern music, is a kind of fugue, which they call a perpetual fugue, because the different parts beginning one after another, repeat incessantly the same <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Formerly, says Zarlino, they placed, at the head of perpetual fugues, particular directions which showed how this kind of fugues was to be sung; and these directions, being properly the rules by which perpetual fugues were composed, were called canoni, rules or canons. From this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, others taking the title for the thing signified, by a metonymy, termed this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> canon. Such canons as are composed with the greatest facility, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> most generally used, begin the fugue either with the octave or the unison; that is to say, that every part repeats in the same tone the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of the preceding. In order to form a canon of this kind, it is only necessary for the composer to make an air according to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; to add in score as many parts as he chooses, where the voices in octave or uniform repeat the same melody; then forming a single air from all these parts successively executed, to try whether this succession may form an entire piece, which will give <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> as well in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> as the melody. In order to execute such a canon, he who sings the first part begins alone, and continues till the air is finished; then recommences immediately, without any suspense of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> or interruption of time; as soon as he has ended the first couplet, which ought to serve for the perpetual subject upon which the whole canon has been composed, the second part begins and repeats the same couplet, whilst the first who had begun pursues the second: others in succession begin and proceed the same way, as soon as he who precedes has reached the end of the first couplet. Thus, by incessantly recommencing, an universal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> can never be found, and the canon may be repeated as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the fingers please. A perpetual fugue may likewise consist of parts which begin with the intervals of a fourth or fifth; or, in other words, every part may repeat the melody of the first, a fourth or a fifth higher or lower. It is then necessary that the whole canon should be invented di prima intensione, as the Italians say; and that sharps or flats should be added to the notes, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> gradations do not answer exactly, by a fourth or fifth, to the melody of the preceding part, and produce the same intervals with itself. Here the composer cannot pay the least regard to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>; his only care is, that the melody may be the same, which renders the formation of a canon more difficult; for at every time when any part returns the fugue, it takes a new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>; it changes the tone almost at every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and, what is still worse, no part is at the same time found in the same tone with another; hence it is that this kind of canons, in other respects far from being easy to be perused, never produce a pleasing effect, however good the harmony may be, and however properly it may be sung. There is a third kind of canon, but very scarce, as well because it is extremely difficult, as because it is for the most part incapable of giving pleasure, and can boast no other merit but the pains which have been thrown away in its composition. This may be called a double canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, as well by the inversions which are practised in it with respect to the melody of the parts, as by those which are found among the parts themselves in singing. There is such an artifice in this kind of canon, that whether the parts be sung in their natural order, or whether the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in which they are set be turned the contrary way, to sing them backward from the end to the beginning, in such a manner that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> becomes the upper part, and the rest undergo a similar change, still you have pretty harmony, and still a regular canon. The reader may consult Rousseau's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> in this article, where he is referred to Plate D, fig. 11, for two examples of canons of this sort extracted from Bontempi, who likewise gives rules for their composition. But he adds, that the true principle from which this rule is deduced will be found at the word Système, in his account of the system of Tartini, to which we must likewise once more refer the reader; as a quotation of such length must have protracted our article to an enormous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. To form a canon, in which the harmony may be a little varied, it is necessary that the parts should not follow each other in a succession too rapid, and that the one should only begin a considerable time after the other. When they follow one another so immediately as at the distance of a semibreve or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIM">minim</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> is not sufficient to admit a great number of chords, and the canon must of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> exhibit a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a>; but it is a method of composing, without much difficulty, a canon in as many parts as the composer chooses. For a canon of four bars only, will consist of eight parts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they follow each other at the distance of half a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; and by each bar which is added, two parts will constantly be gained. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI, who was a great musician, and composed extremely well, took much pleasure in composing and singing canons. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> is still replete with most beautiful canons composed for this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, by the best masters in that country. To what has been said by Rousseau, we need only subjoin, that the English catch and the Italian canon are much the same; as any intelligent reader may perceive, from comparing the structure and execution of the English catch with the account of canons which has now been given. Canon, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, a general rule for the solution of all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of a like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with the present inquiry. Thus every last step of an equation is a canon; and, if turned into words, becomes a rule to solve all questions of the same nature with that proposed. Canon Law, a collection of ecclesiastical laws, serving as the rule and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of church-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The power of making laws was exercised by the church before the Roman empire became Christian. The canon law that obtained throughout the west, till the 12th century, was the collection of canons made by Dionysius Exiguus in 529, the capitularies of Charlemagne, and the decrees of the popes from Siricius to Anastasius. The canon law, even when papal authority was at its height in England, was of no force when it was found to contradict the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, the laws, statutes, and customs of the realm, or the doctrine of the established church. The ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the see of Rome in England was founded on the canon law; and this created quarrels between kings and several archbishops and prelates who adhered to the papal usurpation. Besides the foreign canons, there were several laws and constitutions made here for the government of the church; but all these received their force from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> assent; and if, at any time, the ecclesiastical courts did, by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, endeavour to enforce obedience to such canons, the courts at common law, upon complaints made, would <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> prohibition. The authority vested in the church of England of making canons, was ascertained by a statute of Henry VIII, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the clergy's submission; by which they acknowledged, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> had always been assembled by the king's writ; so that, though the power of making canons resided in the clergy met in convocation, their force was derived from the authority of the king's assenting to and confirming them. The old canons continued in full force till the reign of James I., when the clergy being assembled in convocation, the king gave them leave to treat and consult upon canons; which they did, and presented them to the king, who gave them the royal assent: these were a collection out of several preceding canons, and injunctions. Some of these canons are now obsolete. In the reign of Charles I., several canons were passed by the clergy in convocation.

CANONESS

Pages 154-154

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a woman who enjoys a prebend, affixed, by the foundation, to maids, without their being obliged to renounce the world, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> make any vows.

CANONICA

Pages 154-154

in philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an appellation given by Epicurus to his doctrine of logic. It was called canonica, as consisting of a few canons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rules for directing the understanding in the pursuit and knowledge of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Epicurus's canonica is represented as a very slight and insufficient logic by several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who put a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value on his ethics and physics. Laertius even affirms us, that the Epicureans rejected logic as a superfluous science; and Plutarch complains that Epicurus made an unskilful and pernicious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of syllogisms. But these cautions seem too severe. Epicurus was not adverse to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of logic, but even gave better rules in this art than those philosophers who aimed at no <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> but that of logics. He only seems to have rejected the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALECTICS">dialectics</a> of the Stoics, as full of vain subtleties and deceits, and fitted rather for parade and disputations than real use. The stress of Epicurus's canonica consists in his doctrine of the criteria of truth. All questions in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> are either concerning words or things: concerning things, we seek their truth; concerning words, their signification: things are either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or moral; and the former are either perceived by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> or by the understanding. Hence, according to Epicurus, arise three criterions of truth, viz. sense, anticipation or premonition, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The great canon or principle of Epicurus's logic is, that the senses are never deceived; and therefore, that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> or perception of an appearance is true.

CANONICAL

Pages 154-154

something that belongs to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> partakes of, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a rule or canon. CANONICAL Hours, are certain stated times of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, confirmed, more especially by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, to the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Such are matins, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUDS">lauds</a>, sixth, ninth vespers. In our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> the canonical hours are from eight to twelve in the forenoon, before or after which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> cannot be legally performed in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church. CANONICAL Obedience, is that submission which, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> laws, the inferior clergy are to pay to their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> to their superiors. CANONICAL Sins, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church, those which were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> or mortal. Such especially were idolatry, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, and schism. CANONICAL Punishments, are those which the church may inflict; such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, in Roman Catholic countries, also fasting, alms, whipping, &c. CANONICAL <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, the method or rule of living prescribed by the ancient clergy who lived in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. The canonical life was a kind of medium between the monastic and clerical lives. Originally the orders of monks and clerks were entirely distinct; but pious persons, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, instituted colleges of priests and canons, where clerks, brought up for the ministry, as well as others already engaged therein, might live under a fixed rule, which, though somewhat more easy than the monastic, was yet more restrained than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a>. This was called the canonical life, and those who embraced it canons. Authors are divided about the founder of the canonical life. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to be founded by the apostles; others ascribe it to Pope Urban I., about the year 1239, who is said to have ordered bishops to provide such of their clergy as were willing to live in community, with necessaries out of the revenues of their churches. The generality <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> it to St Augustine; who, having gathered a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of clerks to devote themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, instituted a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> within the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, where he lived in community with them. Onuphrius Panvinus brings the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> somewhat lower; according to him, Pope Gelasius I., about the year 495, placed the first regular canons of St Augustine in the Lateran church. CANONICAL Letters, in the ancient church, were a sort of testimonials of the orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, which the bishops and clergy sent each other to keep up the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, and distinguish orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> and other heretics. They were denominated canonical, either as being composed according to a certain rule or form, or because they were given to the canonicum, that is, those comprehended in the canon or catalogue of their church. When they had occasion to travel into other dioceses or countries, diplomatic and recommendatory letters, also letters of peace, &c. were so many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of canonical letters. CANONICAL is also an appellation given to those epistles in the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, more frequently called catholic or general epistles. CANONICUM in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes a tax or tribute. CANONICUM is more particularly used in the Greek church for a fee paid by the clergy to bishops, archbishops, and metropolitans, for degrees and promotions.

CANONICUM ALSO

Pages 154-154

M also denotes a due of first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, paid by the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> to their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to Du Cange, to their priests. The canonicum is assessed according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of houses or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Comnenus made a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> for regulating the canonicum of bishops, which was confirmed by another made in 1086, by his nephew <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Comnenus. A village containing thirty fires, was to pay for its canonicum one piece of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, two of silver, one sheep, six bushels of barley, six of wheat flour, six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of wine, and thirty hens.

CANONIST

Pages 154-154

a person skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who makes profession of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and practice of the canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Canonists and civilians are usually combined in the same persons: and hence the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> juris utrinque, or legum doctor, usually expressed in abbreviation, L. L. D. or J. U. D.

CANONIZATION

Pages 154-155

CANONIZATION, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, by which persons deceased are ranked in the catalogue of the saints. It succeeds beatification. Before a beatified person is canonized, the qualifications of the candidate are strictly examined into, in some consistories held for that purpose; after which, one of the consistorial <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>, in the presence of the pope and cardinals, makes the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> of the person who is to be proclaimed a saint, and gives a particular detail of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>: which done, the holy father decrees his canonization, and appoints the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. On the day of canonization the pope officiates in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and their eminences are drest in the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s church is hung with rich <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, upon which the arms of the pope, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state requiring the canonization, are embroidered in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver. An infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lights blaze all round the church, which is crowded with pious souls, who wait with devout impatience till the new saint has made his public entry as it were into paradise, that they may offer up their petitions to him without danger of being rejected. The following maxim with regard to canonization is now observed, though it has not been followed above a century, viz. not to enter into the inquiries <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to canonization, till 50 years, at least, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the person to be canonized. By the ceremony of canonization, it appears that this rite of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> has something in it very like the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> or deification of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Romans, and, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, takes its rise from it; at least several ceremonies of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are conspicuous in both.

CANONRY

Pages 155-155

the benefice filled by a canon. It differs from a prebend, in that the prebend may subsist without the canonicate, whereas the canonicate is inseparable from the prebend: again, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of suffrages, and other privileges, are annexed to the canonicate, and not to the prebend.

CANOPUS

Pages 155-155

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the first magnitude in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> of Argo, a constellation of the southern hemisphere. Canopus, in Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, one of the deities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians, and, according to some, the god of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is said, that the Chaldeans, who worshipped fire, carried their fancied deity through other countries to try its powers, in order that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it obtained the victory over the other gods, it might be acknowledged as the true object of worship; and it having easily subdued the gods of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, its priests declared that all gods did it homage. This the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Canopus hearing, and finding that the Chaldeans had brought their god to contend with Canopus, they took a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> earthen vessel, in which they bored several holes, which they afterwards stopped with wax, and having filled the vessel with water, painted it of several colours, and fitting the head of an idol to it, brought it out, in order to contend with the Chaldean deity. The Chaldeans accordingly kindled their fire all around it; but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> having melted the wax, the water gushed out through the holes, and extinguished the fire; and thus Canopus conquered the god of the Chaldeans. Canopus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Canobus, according to Strabo, had been Menelaus's pilot, and had a temple erected to him in a town called Canopus, near one of the mouths of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Dionysius mentions it: καὶ τοῖς πιστεύοντι Ἀμυκλαῖ ὑπὸ Κανόπου. There stands Canobus' temple known to fame: The pilot who from fair Amycla came. Vossius remarks, on this occasion, the vanity of the Greeks, who, as he conjectures, hearing of an Egyptian deity named Canopus, took from thence an opportunity of deifying the pilot of Menelaus who bore the same name, and giving out that the Egyptian god Canopus had been a Greek. F. Montfaucon gives several representations of this deity. One, in allusion to the victory above-mentioned, throws out water on every side through little holes. Canopus, or Canobus, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the Mediterranean, a hundred and twenty stadia, or fifteen miles, to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; as old as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, Canopus, or Canobus, Menelaus's steersman, being there buried. Canopei the gentilious name; famous for their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and debauchery, (Strabo, Juvenal.) See Aboukir.

CANOPY

Pages 155-155

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, a magnificent kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>, serving to cover and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> an altar, throne, tribunal, pulpit, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. The word is formed from the barbarous Latin canopeum, of ναυωπεύων, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> spread over a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> to keep off the gnats, from ναῦς, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. Canopies are also borne over the head in processions of state, after the manner of umbrellas. The canopy of an altar is more peculiarly called ciborium. The Roman grandees had their canopies, or spread veils, called themselves, over their chairs; the like were also in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> over the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of their gods. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> cardinals still retain the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of canopies.

CANOSA

Pages 155-156

a town of Puglia in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, occupying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the site of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Camplum. The old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was founded by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>, according to Strabo. It afterwards became a Roman colony, and one of the most considerable cities of this part of Italy for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and magnificence of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The era of Trajan seems to have been that of its greatest splendour: but this pomp only served to mark it as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> object for the avarice and fury of the Barbarians. Genseric, Totila, and Autharis, treated it with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> cruelty. The deplorable state to which this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was reduced in 590 is concisely described by Gregory the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> in these terms: "On every side we hear groans; on every side we behold crowds of mourners, cities burnt, castles razed to the ground, countries laid waste, provinces become deserts, some citizens led away captives, and others inhumanly massacred." No town in Puglia suffered more than Canosa from the outrages of the Saracens; the contests between the Greeks and Normans increased the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of its woes, which was filled by a conflagration that happened when it was stormed by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Robert. In 1090, it was assigned, by agreement, to Bohemund <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Antioch, who died here in 1111. Under the reign of Ferdinand the Third, this estate belonged to the Grimaldis. On their forfeiture, the Affaititi acquired it, and still retain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquis, though the Capeci are the proprietors of the fief. The ancient city stood in a plain between the hills and the river Ofanto, and covered a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tract of ground. Many brick monuments, though degraded and stripped of their marble casing, still attest its ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. Among them may be traced the fragments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, tombs, amphitheatres, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> columns, and two triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which, by their position, seem to have been two city gates. The present town stands above, on the foundations of the old citadel, and is a most pitiful remnant of so great a city, not containing above three hundred houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Sabinus, built, as is said, in the fifth century, is now without the enclosure. It is astonishing that any part of this ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> should have withstood so many calamities. Its altars and pavements are rich in marble; and in a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> adjoining, under an octagonal cupola, is the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Bohemund, adorned in a minute Gothic style.

CANSO

Pages 156-156

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of Acadia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, seated on a narrow strait which separates Nova Scotia from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Breton. Near this town is a fine fishery for cod. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 62° N. Lat. 46°.

CANSTAT

Pages 156-156

a town of Swabia, in Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>, situated on the river Neckar, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 9° 9' N. Lat. 48° 51'.

CANT

Pages 156-156

a quaint affected manner of speaking, adapted chiefly to the lower sort. Skinner racks his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> for the origin of this word; which he successively deduces from the German, Flemish, and Saxon tongues. According to the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, Cant is originally the proper name of a Cameronian preacher in Scotland, who by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> had attained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of talking in the pulpit in such a tone and dialect as was understood by none but his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>: since Andrew Cant's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the word has been extended to signify all sudden exclamations, and whining unmusical tones, especially in praying and preaching. But this origin of the word has been disputed by others; and perhaps the true derivation is from the Latin cantare "to sing." Cant is also applied to words and phrases affected by particular persons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> for low ends, and not authorized by the established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>*. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between cant and technical seems to be this: the former is restrained to words introduced out of folly, affectation, or imposition; the latter is applied to such as are introduced for the sake of clearness, precision and significance. Cant is also used to denote a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> by auction. The origin of the word in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is dubious; it may come, according to some, from quantum, how much; according to others, from cantare, to sing or cry aloud; agreeably to which, we sometimes also call it an outcry. Cant-Timbers, in ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, those timbers which are situated at the two ends of a ship. They derive their name from being canted, or raised obliquely from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> from those whose planes are perpendicular to it. The upper ends of those on the bow, or fore <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship, are inclined to the stern; as those in the after or hind part, incline to the stern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> above. See Ship-Building.

CANTABRIA

Pages 156-156

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district of Tarraconensis, on the Oceanus Cantabricus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>; now Biscay. The inhabitants were famous for their warlike character. In conjunction with the Asturians†, they carried on desperate wars with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; but were subdued by them about 25 years before Christ. Being impatient, however, of a foreign yoke, they in a few years revolted. Most of their youth had been already taken prisoners by the Romans, and sold for slaves to the neighbouring nations: but having found means to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their chains, they cut the throats of their masters; and returning into their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, attacked the Roman garrisons with incredible fury. Agrippa marched against them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expedition; but on his arrival, met with so vigorous a resistance, that his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> began to despair of ever being able to reduce them. As the Cantabrians had waged <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Romans for upwards of 200 years, they were well acquainted with their manner of fighting, no way inferior to them in courage, and were now become desperate; well knowing, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were conquered, after having so often attempted to recover their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, they must expect the most severe outrage, and cruel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Animated with this reflection, they fell upon the Romans with a fury hardly to be expressed, routed them in several engagements, and defended themselves when attacked by the enemy with such intrepidity, that Agrippa afterwards owned that he had never, either by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, been engaged in a more dangerous enterprise. That brave commander was obliged to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> entreaties, menaces, and to brand some of his legionaries with ignominy, before he could bring them to enter the lists with such a formidable enemy. But having at last, with much ado, prevailed upon them to try the chance of an engagement in the open field, he so animated them by his example, that after a most obstinate dispute, he gained a complete victory, which indeed cost him dear, but put an end to that destructive war. All the Cantabrians fit to bear arms were cut in pieces; their castles and strong holds taken and razed; and their women, children, and old men (none else being left alive), were obliged to abandon the mountainous places, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the plain. Dr Wallis seems to make the Cantabrian the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; which, according to him, like the Gaulish, give way to a kind of broken Latin called <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, romanis; which by degrees was refined into the Castilian or present Spanish. But we can hardly suppose that so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a country, inhabited by such a variety of people, spoke all the same language. The ancient Cantabrian, in effect, is still found to subsist in the more barren and mountainous parts of the provinces of Biscay, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, and Navarre, as far as Bayonne, much as the British does in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; but the people only talk it: for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, they use either the Spanish or French, as they happen to live under the one or the other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this to a jealousy of foreigners learning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of their language; others to a poverty of words and expressions. The Cantabrian does not appear to have any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with any other known language, abating that some Spanish words have been adopted in it for things whose use the Biscayans were anciently unacquainted with. Its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> is not disagreeable. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, in the Cantabrian tongue, runs thus: Gure aita ceruetan aiçena, santifica bedi hire icena, ethor ledi hire refuma,

CANTABRUM

Pages 157-157

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> used by the Roman emperors, distinguished by its peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> on it some word <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> motto of good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>, to encourage the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>.

CANTACUZENUS

Pages 157-157

Johannes, of Constantinople, a celebrated statesman, general, and historian, was born in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family. He was bred to letters and to arms, and admitted to the highest offices in the state. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Andronicus loaded him with wealth and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; made him <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a> of his forces; and was desirous of having him join him in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, but this he refused. Andronicus dying in 1341, left to Cantacuzenus the care of the empire, till his son John Paleologus, who was then but <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, should be fit to take it upon himself. This trust he faithfully discharged; till the empress-dowager and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> forming a party against him, declared him a traitor. On this the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> befought him to ascend the throne; and accordingly he was crowned on the 21st of May 1342. This was followed by a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which lasted five years; when he admitted John a partner with him in the empire, and their union was confirmed by his giving him his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Suspicions and enmities, however, soon arising, the war broke out again, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till John took Constantinople in 1355. A few days after, Cantacuzenus, unwilling to continue the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood, abdicated his share of the empire, and retiring to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a monk, and the name of Joasaphus. His wife also retired to a nunnery, and changed her name of Irene for that of Eugenia. In this retirement he lived till the year 1411, when he was upwards of 100 years of age. Here he wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his own times, a Latin translation of which, from the Greek manuscript, was published by Pontanus at Ingolstadt, in 1603; and a splendid edition was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1645, in three volumes folio, of the original Greek, and Pontanus's Latin version. He also wrote an apology for the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> against that of Mahomet, under the name of Chrysostomus.

CANTALIVERS

Pages 157-157

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, pieces of wood framed into the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sides of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to suspend the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> and eyes over it.

CANTAR

Pages 157-157
or CANTARO, an eastern weight, of different value in different places, equal at Accra in Turkey to 603 pounds, at Tunis and Tripoli to 114 pounds. CANTARO is also an Egyptian weight, which is denominated a quintal, and consists of a hundred or of an hundred and fifty rotolos, according to the goods they are to weigh. CANTARO is also an Egyptian weight, which at Naples is equivalent to 25 pounds, at Genoa to 150 pounds. At Leghorn there are three kinds of cantaros, one weighing 150 pounds, another 151, and a third 162 pounds. CANTARO is also a Spanish liquid measure, in use especially at Alicante, containing three gallons. CANTARO is also a measure of capacity, used at Cochin, containing four rubis, the rubi 32 rotolos.

CANTARINI

Pages 157-157

Simon, a famous painter, called the Peferefe, from his being born at Pefaro, was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Guido; and copied the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> so happily, that it is often difficult to distinguish between their works. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> in 1648.

CANTATA

Pages 157-157

in Music, a song <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, intermixed with recitatives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, and different movements, chiefly intended for a single <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, with a thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>, though sometimes for other instruments. The cantata, when performed with judgement, has something in it very agreeable; the variety of the movement not clogging the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, like other compositions. It was first used in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, then in France, whence it passed to us.

CANTAZARO

Pages 157-157

an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>-Interior. It is the residence of the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and is seated near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17°. N. Lat. 38°. 59'.

CANTECOIX

Pages 157-157

a small territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Brabant, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality; there is a small town of the same name, but Lire is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

CANTEMIR

Pages 157-157

Antiochus, esteemed the founder of the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, was the youngest son of the preceding. Under the most ingenious professors, whom the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> had invited to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>, he learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, physic, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and polite literature; without neglecting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Holy Scriptures, to which he had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> inclination. Scarce had he finished his academic course, when he printed a Concordance of the Psalms in the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and was elected member of the academy. The affairs of state in which he was soon after engaged, did not make him neglect his literary pursuits. In order to make himself useful to his fellow citizens, he composed his satires, to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> certain prejudices which had got footing among them. When but 24 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was nominated minister at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; and his dexterity in the management of public affairs was as much admired as his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the sciences. He had the same reputation in France, whither he went in 1738 in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of minister plenipotentiary, and soon after was invested with the character of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> extraordinary. The wise and prudent manner in which he conducted himself during the different revolutions which happened in Russia during his absence, gained him the confidence and esteem of three successive princes. He died of a dropy, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 1744, aged 44. Besides the pieces already mentioned, he wrote, 1. Some Fables and Odes. 2. A translation of Horace's Epistles in Russian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. 3. A

CANTERBURY

Pages 157-158

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of England, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 15. N. Lat. 51. 16. It has the names of Durovernum and Darvernum given it by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Durobernia by Bede, which are thought to be derived from Durwheam, signifying a rapid stream, such as the Stour, on which it stands, is. The Britons call it Caer Kent, i.e. the city of Kent; and its present English name is of the same import, derived from the Saxon. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> writers in Latin call it Cantuaria. Its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity appears not only from Antoninus's Itinerary, but from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> way which has been discovered here, and the causeways leading to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> and Lymne, besides the coins and other curiosities found about it. The archiepiscopal and metropolitan <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> seems to have been settled here very early; and to prevent its being removed, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> was decreed against any who should attempt it. After that, the city flourished greatly; though it suffered in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> during the Danish invasions, and at other times by the casualities of fire. The city was given entirely to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> by William Rufus, and was held in the utmost veneration in the Popish times, especially after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Becket in the reign of Henry II., to whose shrine so great was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, and so rich were the offerings, that Erasmus, who was an eye-witness of its wealth, says the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and chapel in which he was interred glittered with jewels; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, the plate and jewels filled two great chests, each of which required eight strong men to carry out. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> was granted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Kent, upon his conversion, to Austin the monk, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and the royalty of the city and its territories. This Austin founded a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> for monks, called from him Augustine. After the cathedral had been several times destroyed by fire and rebuilt, the present was begun about the year 1174, and augmented and embellished by the succeeding archbishops, till it was completed in the reign of Henry V. It is a noble Gothic pile, and before the Reformation had 37 altars. A great many kings, princes, cardinals, and archbishops are buried in it. At the dissolution, Henry VIII. seized all the revenues both of the church and monastery, except what he allotted for the maintenance of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, 12 prebendaries, and five preachers, whom he established in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the monks. During the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> rebellion, it suffered much; the usurper Cromwell having made a stable of it for his dragoons. After the Restoration, it was repaired, and made what it now appears. Besides the cathedral and other churches, as well as a monastery, the city had anciently a castle on the south side, and strong walls, with towers, a ditch, and rampart; it had also a mint and an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. As to its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, it seems to have been entirely subject to the archbishop, both in spirituals and temporals; at least from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that William Rufus gave it solely to Bishop <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a>, till the Reformation. It is now a county of itself: and the corporation consists of a mayor, recorder, 12 aldermen, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, 24 common councilmen, a mace-bearer, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer, and four ferjeants at mace. Every Monday a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> is held at Guildhall Canterbury for civil and criminal causes: and every other Tuesday for the government of the city. Here were formerly 2000 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 3000 French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> manufacture; but this branch is now greatly decayed in the place, since Spitalfields became so flourishing. Besides the cathedral, it contains 15 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, a free school, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of correction, a gaol for criminals, and sumptuous conduit for supplying the inhabitants with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It consists of four streets, disposed in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and divided into six wards, which are about three miles in circumference. It is surrounded on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> with hop grounds much to its advantage, and is famed for its excellent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Canterbury contains 257 parishes, besides chapels, in Kent, and about 100 more in other dioceses. These are called Peculiars; it being an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> privilege of this fee, that, wheresoever the archbishop had either manors or advowsons, the place was exempted from the jurisdiction of the ordinary of the diocese where it was situated, and was deemed in the diocese of Canterbury. This fee is valued in the king's books at £816l. 17s. 9½d., but is reckoned to produce a clear revenue of £8000 a year. The clergy's tenths come to £615l. 18s. 2½d. This fee had many great privileges in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>, some of which it still retains. The archbishop is accounted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> and metropolitan of all England, and is the first peer in the realm; having the precedence of all dukes not of the blood-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and of all the great officers of state. In common speech he is styled His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>, and he writes himself Divina Providentia; whereas other bishops style themselves Divina Permissione. At coronations, he places the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on the king's head; and, wherever the court may be, the king and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> are the proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> parishioners of the archbishop of Canterbury. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is accounted his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> dean, the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a> his sub-dean, the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> his chaplain. This fee hath yielded to the church 18 saints; to the church of Rome, 9 cardinals; to the civil state of England, 12 <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chancellors, 4 lord treasurers, and 1 lord <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and 9 chancellors to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. To this fee belongs only one archdeacon, viz. of Canterbury. To the cathedral belongs an archbishop, a dean, a chancellor, an archdeacon, 12 prebends, 6 preachers, 6 <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> canons, 6 substitutes, 12 lay clerks, 10 choristers, 2 masters, 50 scholars, and 12 almsmen. CANTERBURY <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Campanula. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CANTERUS

Pages 158-158

WILLIAM, an eminent linguist and philologer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, in 1541. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and gave surprising proofs of his progress in Greek and Latin literature. He afterwards visited the several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and died at Louvain, in 1575, aged 33. He understood five languages, besides that of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and, notwithstanding his dying too young, wrote several philological and critical works, among which are, Notae, Scholi, Emendationes, et Explicationes, in Euripidem, Sophoclem, Ephylem, Ciceronem, Perpetium, Aesopum, &c. and many translations of Greek authors.

CANTHARIDES

Pages 158-159

CANTHARIDES, in the *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>*, flies which are employed to produce blisters on the skin.

CANTHARIS

Pages 159-159

in *<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>*, a genus of insects belonging to the order of *insecta coleoptera*. Linnæus enumerates 27 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the cantharis, most of them to be found in different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The cantharis used in making blistering plasters is ranked under the genus *Meloe*. See *Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*.

CANTHI

Pages 159-159

in *Anatomy*, cavities at the extremities of the eyelids, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the corners of the eye; the greater of them, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> canthus, is next the nose; the lesser of them, or the little canthus, lies towards the temple.

CANTICLES

Pages 159-159

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, otherwise called the *Song of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>*; by the Jews the *Song of Songs*, *Canticum Canticorum*. The book of Canticles is usually supposed to be an epithalamium composed by Solomon, on occasion of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. But those who penetrate further into the mystery, find in it the marriage of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and good men. On this principle the Canticles is held to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> allegory, wherein under the terms of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wedding, a divine and spiritual marriage is expressed. This song contains the adventures of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days and seven nights; the exact <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> allowed for the celebration of marriage among the Hebrews. The Jews themselves, apprehending the book liable to be understood in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and carnal manner, prohibited the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of it before the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 30, and the same usage anciently obtained in the Christian church. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, Theodore Mopsuetianus rejected the book of Canticles as not divine. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a> rabbins have also questioned its being written by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. It is alleged, that the name of God is not once found in it. Mr Whilton has a discourse expressly to prove that the Canticles is not a sacred book of the Old Testament. He alleges it indeed to have been written by King Solomon the son of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>; but affirms that it was composed at the time when that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, blinded by his concubines, was sunk in lust and idolatry. This he chiefly infers from the general character of vanity and dissoluteness which reigns through the Canticles; in which there is not, according to Whilton, one thought that leads the mind towards <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, but all is worldly and carnal, to say no worse. For the mystic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, he affirms it to be without foundation; and that the book is not cited as canonical by any writer before the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Mr Whilton <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to have been taken into the canon between the years 77 and 128, when allegories came into vogue, and the rabbins began to corrupt the text of Scripture. Grotius, Nierembergius, the Dutch divines who criticised F. Simon, Menetrier, Bafnage, and some others, seem also to take the Canticles for a profane <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, on a footing with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> pieces of Catullus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ovid. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is refuted by Michaelis, Majus, Witsius, Nat. Alexander, Outrein, Francius, and others. Mr Whilton's arguments have been particularly considered by Itchener, and also by Dr Gill. R. Akiba finds the book of Canticles more divine than the rest: the whole world, according to this rabbin, is not worth that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the Canticles was given to Israel; for, whereas all the hagiographers are holy, the Canticles is the holy of holies.

CANTIMARONS

Pages 159-159
or CATIMARONS, a kind of floats or rafts, used by the inhabitants of the coast of Coromandel to go a fishing in, and to trade along the coast. They are made of three or four small canoes, or trunks of trees dug hollow, and tied together with cacao ropes, with a triangular sail in the middle, made of mats. The persons who manage them are almost half in the water, there being only a place in the middle a little raised to hold their merchandise: which last particular is only to be understood of the trading cantimarons, and not of those that go a-fishing.

CANTIN

Pages 159-159
CAPE, a promontory of the coast of Morocco in Africa, situated in W. Long. 10° 2' N. Lat. 33° 9'.

CANTING

Pages 159-159

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> phrase, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> anything about. CANTING <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dialect, is a mysterious sort of jargon used by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GYPSIES">gypsies</a>, thieves, and trolling beggars, to express their sentiments to each other, without being understood by the rest of mankind. This dialect is not founded on any rules; yet even out of that irregularity many words seem to retain something of scholarship; as *togan*, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, from *toga* in the Latin; *pannum*, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, from *panis*; *cafán*, cheese, from *cafrus*, &c. It is observable, that, even unknown to ourselves, we have adopted some of their terms into our vulgar language; as *bite* and *bilk*, to cheat; *bounce*, to vapour; *bouye*, strong drink; *fitch*, to steal; *flog*, to whip; *rig*, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; *roak*, to rally; *rhino*, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. From the same source proceed the words *flam*, *banter*, *bubble*, *bully*, *sharp*, *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>*, *fluffing*, *polting*, &c. An anonymous author has given a canting <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, comprehending all the terms used by the several tribes of gypsies, beggars, tholifters, highwaymen, foot-pads, and other clans of cheats and villains, with a collection of songs in the canting dialect: <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1725, 8vo.

CANTIUM

Pages 159-160

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, literally denoting a headland: giving name to a territory called *Cantium*, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; and to a people called *Cantii* (Caesar), commended for their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>. The promontory now the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Foreland. It is supposed that this was the first district in Britain which received a colony from the continent; and that it had frequently changed its masters, by new colonies coming over from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and driving the inhabitants further north. In the midst of all these revolutions it still retained its ancient name (which was so agreeable to its shape and situation), and gave the same name to all the successive tribes by which it was inhabited. Those who possessed it at the time of the first Roman invasion were evidently of Belgic origin, and had come over lately, that they differed in nothing from their countrymen on the continent. "The inhabitants of Kent (says Caesar) are the most civilized of all the Britons, and differ but very little in their manners from the Gauls." This great resemblance between the people of Kent and their neighbours on the continent, might be partly owing to the situation of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which being nearest to the continent, was most frequented by strangers from thence. It was this situation also which exposed them to the first assaults of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. For Caesar, in both his expeditions into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, landed in Kent; and therefore we may conclude, that the Cantii had a great share in the vigorous opposition that was made to his landing, and in the several battles and skirmishes which were fought against him after his landing; particularly, they made a very bold, but unsuccessful attempt, upon his naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The Cantii did not make the same vigorous resistance to the Romans on their next invasion in the reign of Claudius. For Aulus Plautius, the Roman general in that expedition, traversed their country without seeing an enemy; and as they now submitted to the power of Rome without a struggle, so they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a state of quiet submission to it to the very last. The situation of Cantium occasioned its being much frequented by the Romans, who generally took their way through it in their marches to and from the continent. Few places in Britain are more frequently mentioned by the Roman writers than Rutupium and Portus Rutupensis, most probably Richborough and Stonar. Rutupium was the same in those times that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> is ours; the usual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of embarking for, and landing from, the continent. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> departure of the Romans out of Britain, Portus Dubris, now Dover, had become a considerable place, and a well frequented harbour, where the third iter of Antoninus ends, and from whence they often embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. Portus Lemanus, supposed to be Lime near West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-HYTHE">Hythe</a>, was also a noted seaport in these times, and the termination of the fourth iter of Antoninus. Duovriæ and Durovernum, now <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, were both Roman <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and stations, and are often mentioned in the Itinerary and other books. Besides these, there were several other Roman stations, towns, and ports in Cantium, which need not be particularly enumerated here. Cantium, in the most perfect state of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> which was called Flavia Caesariensis.

CANTO

Pages 160-160

denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of a poem, answering to what is otherwise called a book. The word is Italian, where it properly signifies song. Tasso, Ariosto, and several other Italians, have divided their longer or heroic poems into cantos. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of them, Scarron has also divided his Gigantomachia, and Boileau his Lutrin, into chants or songs. The like usage has been adopted by some English writers, as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a>, who divides his Hudibras, and Dr Garth his Dunciad, into cantos. A late translator of part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Aeneid has even subdivided a book of Virgil into several cantos. Canto, in the Italian music, signifies a song: hence canto simplex is where all the notes or figures are equal, and called also canto <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERMO">fermo</a>; canto figurato, that where the figures are unequal, and express different motions.

CANTO ALSO

Pages 160-160

o also signifies the treble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a song: hence <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> concertante, the treble of the little chorus; canto ripieno, the treble of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> chorus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which sings only now and then in particular places. Canto signifies the first treble, unless some other word be added to it, as secondo; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it denotes the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> treble.

CANTON

Pages 160-163

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, denotes a small district <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> constituting a distinct <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: such are the cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. Canton, Quang-tong, or Koanton, one of the southern provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by Fokien, on the north by Kiang-si, on the west by Quang-si and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tonking, and everywhere else by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The country is diversified with hills and plains, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general so fertile that it produces two crops annually. Besides many of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and those <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in other parts of the Indies, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Canton produces some peculiar to itself. Abundance of valuable aromatic woods is also to be met with in this province, as well as eagle wood, ebony, &c., and in the mineral kingdom the province furnishes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, tin, quicksilver, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> are also cultivated here, and pearls are fished upon the coasts; so that every thing which can contribute to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or convenience of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is to be met with in Canton. "One begins (says F. Premare) to have an idea of China, on entering the river Canton. Both sides of it present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fields of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> which resemble green meadows, and extend beyond the reach of sight. They are intersected by an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, in such a manner that the barks which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and repass in them seem at a distance, while the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which carries them is concealed, to glide along the groats.
