Farther inland the country appears covered with trees, and cultivated along the valleys; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is interlarded with villages, rural seats, and such a variety of delightful prospects, that one is never tired of viewing them, and regrets to be obliged to pass them so quickly. All the coasts of this province abound with fish, and furnish vast numbers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, oysters, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TORTOISES">tortoises</a> of an immense size. The inhabitants keep a prodigious number of tame ducks, which they <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> in ovens or dunghills, though it does not appear that they borrowed this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> from the Egyptians. The docility of these creatures exceeds what we should be apt at first to imagine. The inhabitants load a number of small barks with them, and carry them in flocks to feed on the sea shore, where they find shrimps and other animals proper for their nourishment. But though the ducks from the different barks are thus unavoidably mixed together in the daytime, they are easily collected by only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> on a basin, on which they immediately collect themselves into different flocks, and each returns to its proper bark. In this province the Chinese have also a method of preserving not only the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of the ducks in such a manner that it loses nothing of its original flavour, but their eggs also. The latter operation is performed by covering the eggs with a coat of clay mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. When mixed in this manner, it seems that the salt has the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of penetrating through the pores of the shell, and thus impregnating the substance in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, which it could not do by simple solution in water. Canton, though it suffered much in the Chinese wars, is at present one of the most flourishing provinces of the empire; and being at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, its government is one of the most important. A great number of fortresses, many of which are cities, provided with numerous garrisons, have been built along the coasts for the suppression of pirates and robbers; for which purpose also a certain number of troops are kept properly posted in different parts of the province. It is divided into ten districts, which contain as many cities of the first class, and 84 of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> in general is warm but healthy, healthy, and the people are very industrious. They possess in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are only shown any European <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, they can execute others like it with surprising exactness. The most remarkable cities in the province besides Canton the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> are, 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHAO_TCHEOU_FOU">Chao-tcheou-fou</a>, chiefly noted for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of bonzes in its neighbourhood, to which the adjacent country belongs, and the origin of which is traced back for 800 or 900 years. It has under its jurisdiction six cities of the third class; near one of these grows a reed of which several instruments are made, which cannot be distinguished from real ebony. The air of Chao-tcheou-fou, however, is unhealthy; and great numbers of the inhabitants are carried off annually by contagious distempers, which prevail from the middle of October to the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. 2. Kao-tcheou-fou, situated in a delightful and plentiful country. In the neighbourhood is found a singular kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> much resembling marble, on which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> representations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, landscapes, and trees. These stones are cut into slabs, and made into tables, &c. Crabs are also caught on the coasts here, which very much resemble those of Europe; but, says M. Grolier, they have this singularity, that when taken out of the water, they become petrified without losing anything of their natural <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. 3. Kiun-tcheou-fou, the capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Hai-nan. See Hai-nan. Canton, a large, populous, and wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of China, capital of the province of that name, stands on the banks of the river Taa, or great river, which, near the city, is wide and spacious. The wall of the city is pretty <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and about six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in circumference, though not more than one-third of the ground is occupied by buildings, the other parts being appropriated to pleasure grounds or to fish ponds. The country is extremely pleasant, and towards the east hilly, so as to command a beautiful prospect of the city and suburbs, the compass of which, together, is about ten miles. The buildings of Canton are in general low, consisting of one story and a ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, which is covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> tiles in order to keep it cool; but the houses of the most respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and mandarins are comparatively lofty and well built. In different parts of the city and suburbs are joss houses or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, in which are placed the images worshipped by the Chinese: before whom are placed, at particular seasons, a vast variety of sweetmeats, oranges, great plenty of food ready dressed, and also incense, which is kept perpetually <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. The streets of Canton are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, paved with flat stones, adorned at intervals with triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which have a pleasing effect, and much crowded with people. On both sides are shops as in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, appropriated to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of different commodities; and a kind of awning is extended from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to house, which prevents the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays from incomming either inhabitants or passengers. At the end of every street is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, which, with the gates of the city, is shut in the evening. In China Street, which is pretty long and considerably wider than the rest, reside merchants; whose trade, so far as respects china, lacquered <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, fans, &c., is wholly confined to Europeans. Most of them speak the foreign languages tolerably well, or at least sufficiently intelligible to transact business. Besides these merchants, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of twelve or thirteen, called the Cohong; who have an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> by appointment from authority to purchase the cargoes from the different ships, and also to supply them with teas, raw silks, &c., in return. The establishment of the Cohong, though injurious to private trade, is admirably well adapted for the security of the different companies with which they traffic; because each individual becomes a guarantee for the whole; so that if one fail, the others consider themselves as responsible. In Canton there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>; all burdens are carried by porters across their shoulders on bamboos; as are also the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> people in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">sedan</a> chairs, and the ladies always. The streets of Canton may be traversed from morning till evening without seeing a woman, those excepted who are Tartars, and even these but very seldom. On the wharf of the river, which is commodious and pleasant, stand the factories of the different European nations, viz., the Dutch, French, Swedes, Danes, English, &c. In those reside the supercargoes belonging to their respective companies, who are appointed to dispose of the cargoes brought to market; to supply the ships with others from Europe in return; and, during their absence, to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with the merchants for such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as may be judged necessary for the next fleet. Between the residents of the factories the most perfect cordiality subsists; in each a common and splendid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> is kept at the company's expense, and visits are reciprocally exchanged; so that nothing is wanting to make residence at Canton agreeable to an European, but the pleasure naturally resulting from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of women. The side of the river next the city is covered with boats, which form a kind of town or streets, in which live the poorer sort of the Chinese, or rather the descendants of the Tartars. Some of the men come on shore in the morning to their respective employments, and in those sampans, or boats which are not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, the women and also the men carry passengers from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place in the same manner as is done by wherries on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. On this river live many thousand souls who never were permitted to come on shore; whose only habitation is their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>; in which they eat, drink, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, carry on many occupations, keep ducks, &c., and occasionally a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Canton are principally carried on in the suburbs; though it has been frequently supposed that they were confined to the city; and this, by some writers, has been given as a reason why Europeans are not permitted to enter within the gates. But this is a mistake; and perhaps the true reason for this very singular restraint is, that the houses in which they keep their women are chiefly within the city. At Wampo, a large commodious place for anchorage, and which is about 12 or 14 miles from Canton, the European vessels <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> and unload their cargoes, which are transmitted by lighters to the factories; and by the same conveyance receive their respective freights. Between this place and the city are three hoppo, or customhouses, at which the boats passing and repassing are obliged to stop, and undergo with their passengers an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, in order to prevent smuggling. The lighters <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, and also the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>'s pinnace, are, however, excepted; the former having proper officers on board for the purpose, and the latter being narrowly watched and examined at the landing. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> at Canton is, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, extremely hot; and in the months of December, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, and February, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>: the country is nevertheless pleasant and healthful, abounding with all the necessaries and delicacies of life, which may be procured on terms much cheaper than in Europe. The number of inhabitants has been estimated at one million; but later calculations have made the number considerably less. N. Lat. 23° 30'. E. Long. 113° 20'. Canton, John, an ingenious natural <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Stroud, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, in 1718; and was placed, when young, under the care of a Mr Davis of the same place, a very able mathematician, with whom, before he had attained the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years, he had gone through both vulgar and decimal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. He then proceeded to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and particularly to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, wherein he had made a considerable progress, when his father took him from school, and put him to learn his own business, which was that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-cloth weaver. This circumstance was not able to damp his zeal for the acquisition of knowledge. All his leisure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was devoted to the assiduous cultivation of astronomical science; and, by the help of the Caroline tables annexed to "Wing's Astronomy," he computed eclipses of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> and other phenomena. His acquaintance with that science he applied likewise to the constructing of several kinds of dials. But the studies of our young philosopher being frequently pursued to very late hours, his father, fearing that they would injure his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, forbade him the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> in his chamber any longer than for the purpose of going to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and would himself often see that his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> was obeyed. The son's thirst of knowledge was, however, so great, that it made him attempt to evade the prohibition, and to find means of secreting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> till the family had retired to rest, when he rose to prosecute undisturbed his favourite pursuits. It was during this prohibition, and at these hours, that he computed, and cut upon stone, with no better an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> than a common <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of a large upright sun <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>, on which, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, was shown the rising of the sun, his place in the ecliptic, and some other particulars. When this was finished, and made known to his father, he permitted it to be placed before the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of his house, where it excited the admiration of several gentlemen in the neighbourhood, and introduced young Mr Canton to their acquaintance, which was followed by the offer of the use of their <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>. In the library of one of these gentlemen, he found "Martin's Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>," which was the first book that gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In the possession of another <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, a few miles from Stroud, he first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of globes; an object that afforded him uncommon pleasure, from the great ease with which he could solve those problems he had hitherto been accustomed to compute. The dial was beautified a few years ago at the expense of the gentlemen at Stroud, several of whom had been his schoolfellows, and who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> fill to regard it as a very distinguished performance. Among other persons with whom he became acquainted in early life, was the late reverend and ingenious Dr Henry Miles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOOTING">Tooting</a>, a learned and respectable member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society, and of approved eminence in natural knowledge. This gentleman perceiving that Mr Canton possessed abilities too promising to be confined within the narrow limits of a country town, prevailed on his father to permit him to come to London. Accordingly he arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 4, 1737, and resided with Dr Miles at Tooting till the 6th of May following; when he articled himself for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of five years, as a clerk to Mr Samuel Watkins, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the academy in Spital-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. In this situation, his ingenuity, diligence, and good conduct, were so well displayed, that on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his clerkship in May 1742, he was taken into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with Mr Watkins for three years; which gentleman he afterwards succeeded in Spital-square, and there continued during his whole life. In 1744, he married Penelope, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Mr Thomas Colbrooke, and niece to James Colbrooke, Esq. banker in London. Towards the end of 1745, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, which seems early to have engaged Mr Canton's notice, received a very capital improvement by the discovery of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> Phial. This event turned the thoughts of most of the philosophers of Europe to that branch of natural philosophy; and our author, who was one of the first to repeat and to pursue the experiment, found his affluency and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> rewarded by many capital discoveries. Towards the end of 1749, he was concerned with his friend, the late Mr Benjamin Robins, in making experiments in order to determine to what height rockets may be made to ascend, and at what distance their light may be seen. In 1750 was read at the Royal Society Mr Canton's "Method of making <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> magnets, without the use of, and yet far superior to, any natural ones." This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> procured him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being elected a member of the society, and the present of their gold medal. The same year he was complimented with the degree of M.A. by the university of Aberdeen; and, in 1751, was chosen one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the Royal Society. In 1752, our philosopher was so fortunate as to be the first person in England, who, by attracting the electric fire from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> during a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> storm, verified Dr Franklin's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of the similarity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> and electricity. Next year, his paper entitled, "Electrical Experiments, with an attempt to account for their several Phenomena," was read at the Royal Society. In the same paper Mr Canton mentioned his having discovered by a great number of experiments, that some clouds were in a positive, and some in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, state of electricity. Dr Franklin, much about the same time, made the like discovery in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. This circumstance, together with our author's constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s hypothesis, induced that excellent philosopher, immediately on his arrival in England, to pay Mr Canton a visit, and gave rise to a friendship which ever after continued without interruption or diminution. In the "Lady's Diary, for 1756," our author answered the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> question that had been proposed in the preceding year. The ques- CANTON was, "How can what we call the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> of stars be best accounted for; what is the substance of this phenomenon; and in what state of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> doth it most frequently show itself?" The solution, though anonymous, was so satisfactory to his friend, Mr Thomas Simpson, who then conducted that work, that he sent Mr Canton the prize, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, in which he said, he was sure that he was not mistaken in the author of it, as no one besides, that he knew of, could have answered the question. Our philosopher's next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> to the public, was a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in the "Gentleman's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, for September 1759," on the electrical properties of the tourmaline, in which the laws of that wonderful stone are laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a very concise and elegant manner. On December 13, in the same year, was read at the Royal Society, "An attempt to account for the regular diurnal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">Horizontal</a> Magnetic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>; and also for its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> variation at the time of an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> Borealis." A complete year's observations of the diurnal variations of the needle are annexed to the paper. On Nov. 5, 1761, our author communicated to the Royal Society an account of the Transit of Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 6, 1761, observed in Spital-square. Mr Canton's next communication to the Society, was a letter addressed to Dr Benjamin Franklin, and read Feb. 4, 1762; containing some remarks on Mr Delaval's electrical experiments. On Dec. 16, in the same year, another curious addition was made by him to philosophical knowledge, in a paper entitled, "Experiments to prove that water is not incompreffible." These experiments are a complete refutation of the famous Florentine experiments, which so many philosophers have mentioned as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the incompreffibility of water. On St Andrew's day, 1763, our author was the third time elected one of the council of the Royal Society; and on Nov. 8, in the following year, were read before that learned body, his farther "Experiments and observations on the compressibility of water, and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>." The establishment of this fact, in opposition to the received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, formed on the hasty decision of the Florentine Academy, was thought to be deserving of the society's gold medal. It was accordingly moved for in the council of 1764; and after several invidious delays, which terminated much to the honour of Mr Canton, it was presented to him Nov. 30, 1766. The next communication of our ingenious author to the Royal Society, which we shall take notice of in this place, was on Dec. 22, 1763, being "An easy method of making a Phosphorus that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> imbibe and emit light like the Bolognian stone; with experiments and observations." When he first showed to Dr Franklin the instantaneous light acquired by some of this phosphorus from the near discharge of an electrified bottle, the doctor immediately exclaimed, "And God said, Let there be light, and there was light." The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of St Paul's having, in a letter to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, dated March 5, 1769, requested the opinion of the Royal Society relative to the best and most effectual method of fixing electrical conductors to preserve that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> from damage by lightning, Mr Canton was one of the committee appointed to take the letter into consideration, and to report their opinion upon it. The gentlemen joined with him in this business were, Dr Watson, Dr Franklin, Mr Delaval, and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a>. Their report was made on the 8th of June following; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> recommended by them has been carried into execution. The last paper of our author's, which was read before the Royal Society, was on Dec. 21, 1769; and contained "Experiments to prove that the Luminousness of the Sea arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> of its animal substances." In the account now given of his communications to the public, we have chiefly confined ourselves to such as were the most important, and which threw new and distinguished light on various objects in the philosophical world. Besides these he wrote a number of papers both in earlier and in later life, which appeared in several different publications, and particularly in the Gentleman's Magazine. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and sedentary life of Mr Canton, arising from an unremitting attention to the duties of his profession, and to the prosecution of his philosophical inquiries and experiments, probably contributed to shorten his days. The disorder into which he fell, and which carried him off, was a drophy. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happened on March 22, 1772, in the 54th year of his age.

CANTONING

Pages 163-163

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, is the allotting distinct and separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> to each regiment; the town where they are quartered being divided into as many cantons as there are regiments.

CANTRED

Pages 163-163
or CANTRETH, signifies a hundred villages. It is a British word, compounded of the adjective cant, i.e., hundred; and trey, a town or village. In Wales some of the counties are divided into cantreds, as in England into hundreds.

CANTYRE

Pages 163-163

from Cantierre, signifying a "headland;" the southern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the shire of Argyle in Scotland. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, stretching 27 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in breadth. It is mostly plain, arable, and populous; inhabited promiscuously by Highlanders and Lowlanders, the latter being invited to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by the Argyle family, that the lands might be the better cultivated. It gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquis to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, and is by Lochfyn divided from Argyle Proper. This loch is an inlet from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, about 60 miles in length and four in breadth, celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> fishery. There are many paltry villages in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but no town of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> except Campbelltown. Cantyre was granted to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Argyle after the suppression of a rebellion of the Macdonalds of the Isles (and it is supposed of this peninsula) in the beginning of the last century, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> was afterwards ratified by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants were the Macdonalds, Mac-eachrains, Mac-kays, and Mac-maths. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a> of CANTYRE, the south <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> promontory of the peninsula. There is here a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> 235 feet above the sea at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, situated on the rocks called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a>. Lat. 55° 22'. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 42' west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The found of Illa from the lighthouse <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, by the compass, N. by E. distant 27 miles; the south end of Illa N. W. distant 25 miles; the north end of Rathlin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, N. W. by W. one half W.; the Maiden Rocks, S. by W. one half W. distant 14 miles; Copland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, S. by W. one half W.

CANTZ

Pages 163-164

a town of Silea in Germany. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16° 36'. N. Lat. 51° 6'.

CANULA

Pages 164-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a tube made of different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, principally of silver and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, but sometimes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. They are introduced into hollow ulcers, in order to facilitate a discharge of pus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other substance; or into wounds, either accidental or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cavities, as the thorax or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>; they are used in the operation of bronchotomy; and by some, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, as a drain for urine. Other canulas are used for introducing cauteries, either actual or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">potential</a>, into hollow parts, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the parts adjacent to that to be cauterized, from injury. They are of various figures; some being oval, some round, and others crooked.

CANUSIUM

Pages 164-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Apulia, on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> south side of the Ausidus, to the west of Cannae, whither the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> fled after the defeat sustained there. It was famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> shining <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; whence those who wore clothes made of it were called Canusinati. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANOSA">CANOSA</a>; which see.

CANUTE

Pages 164-165

the first Danish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England after Ironside. He married Emma widow of King <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>; and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> several persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> who stood in his way to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Having thus settled his power in England, he made a voyage to his other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in order to resist the attacks of the king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>; and he carried along with him a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> body of the English under the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Godwin. This nobleman had here an opportunity of performing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> by which he both reconciled the king's mind to the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and, gaining to himself the friendship of his sovereign, laid the foundation of that immense fortune which he acquired to his family. He was stationed next the Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and observing a favourable opportunity which he was obliged suddenly to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a>, he attacked the enemy in the night, drove them suddenly from their trenches, threw them into disorder, pursued his advantage, and obtained a decisive victory over them. Next morning, Canute, seeing the English camp entirely abandoned, imagined that these disaffected troops had deserted to the enemy; and he was agreeably surprised to find that they were at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> engaged in pursuit of the discomfited Swedes. He was so pleased with this success, and the manner of obtaining it, that he bestowed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> upon Godwin, and treated him ever after with the most entire confidence and regard. In another voyage which he afterwards made to Denmark, Canute attacked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> but unworthy Olaf from his kingdom, of which he kept possession till the death of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. He had now by his conquests and valour attained the utmost height of his ambition, and having leisure from wars and intrigues, he felt the unsatisfactory <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> enjoyments; and equally weary of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and turmoils of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he began to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his view towards that future existence, which it is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for the human mind, whether satiated by prosperity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disgusted with adversity, to make the object of its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Unfortunately the spirit which prevailed in that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> gave a wrong <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; and, instead of making atonement to those whom he had formerly injured by his acts of violence, he entirely employed himself in those exercises of piety, which the monks represented as most meritorious. He built churches; he endowed monasteries; he enriched <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>; and he bestowed revenues for the support of chantries at Assington and other places, where he appointed prayers to be said for the souls of those who had there fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against him. He even undertook a pilgrimage to Rome, where he sojourned a considerable time; and, besides obtaining from the pope some privileges for the English school erected there, he engaged all the princes through whose dominions he was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, to desist from those heavy impositions and tolls which they were accustomed to exact from the English pilgrims. By this spirit of devotion, no less than by his equitable and politic administration, he gained in a good <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the affections of his subjects. Canute, who was the greatest and most powerful prince of his time, sovereign of Denmark and Norway as well as of England, could not fail to meet with adulation from his courtiers; a tribute which is liberally paid even to the meanest and weakest of princes. Some of his flatterers breaking out one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in admiration of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, exclaimed that every thing was possible for him; upon which the monarch, it is said, ordered a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> to be set on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shore while the tide was making; and as the waters approached, he commanded them to retire, and obey the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of him who was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the ocean. He feigned to sit some time in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of their submission; but when the sea still advanced towards him, and began to wash him with its billows, he turned to his courtiers, and remarked to them, That every creature in the universe was feeble and impotent, and that power reposed with one Being alone, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> were all the elements of nature, who could say to the ocean, "Thus far shalt thou go, and no farther," and who could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with his nod the most towering piles of human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and and ambition. From that time, it is said, he never would wear a crown. He died in the 20th year of his reign, and was interred at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, in the old <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>.

CANVAS

Pages 164-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a very clear unbleached cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, wove regularly in little squares. It is used for working <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, by passing the threads of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, through the intervals or squares. Canvas is also a coarse cloth of hemp, unbleached, somewhat clear, which serves to cover women's stays, also to stiffen men's clothes, and to make some other of their wearing apparel, &c. Canvas is also used among the French for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> or first words whereon an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> or piece of music is composed, and given to a poet to regulate and finish. The canvas of a song contains certain notes of the composer, which show the poet the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the verses he is to make. Thus Du <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> says, he has canvassed for ten sonnets against the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>. Canvas is also the name of a cloth made of hemp, and used for ship sails. Canvas, among painters, is the cloth on which they usually draw their pictures; the canvas being smoothed over with a slick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, then fixed, and afterwards whitened over, makes what the painters called their primed cloth, on which they draw their first sketches with coal or chalk, and afterwards fill in with colours.

CANZONE

Pages 165-165

in Music, signifies, in general, a song, where some little fugues are introduced; but it is sometimes used for a sort of Italian poem, usually pretty <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, to which music may be composed in the style of a cantata. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> be added to a piece of instrumental music, it signifies much the same as cantata; if placed in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a sonata, it implies the same meaning as allegro, and only denotes that the part to which it is prefixed is to be played <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sung in a brisk and lively manner.

CANZONETTA

Pages 165-165

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of canzone, denoting a little short song. The canzonette Neapolitan has two strains, each whereof is sung twice over, as the vaudevilles of the French. The canzonette Siciliane is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of jig, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> whereof is usually twelve eighths, and six eighths, and sometimes both, as rondeaus.

CAORLO

Pages 165-165

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Friuli, 20 miles south-west of Aquileia, subject to Venice. It has a town of the same name, with a bishop's see.

CAOUTCHOUC

Pages 165-167
Elastic Resin, or India rubber, a substance produced from the syringe tree of Cayenne and other parts of South America, and polished of the most singular properties. No substance is yet known which is so pliable, and at the same time so elastic; and it is farther a matter of curiosity, as being capable of resisting the action of very powerful menstrua. From the account of M. de la Condamine, we learn that this substance oozes out, under the form of a vegetable milk, from incisions made in the tree; and that it is gathered chiefly in time of rain, because, though it may be collected at all times, it flows then most abundantly. The means employed to infuse and indurate it, M. de la Borde says, are kept a profound secret. M. Bemare, and others, affirm, that it thickens and hardens gradually by being exposed to the air; and as soon as it acquires a solid consistence it manifests a very extraordinary degree of flexibility and elasticity. Accordingly the Indians make boots of it which water cannot penetrate, and which, when smoked, have the appearance of real leather. Bottles are also made of it, to the necks of which are fastened hollow reeds, so that the liquor contained in them may be squirted through the reeds or pipes by pressure. One of these filled with water is always presented to each of the guests at their entertainments, who never fail to make use of it before eating. This whimsical custom led the Portuguese in that country to call the tree that produces the resin pao di xirringe; and hence the name of feringa is given both to the tree and to its resinous production. Flambeaux, an inch and a half in diameter, and two feet long, are likewise made of this resin, which give a beautiful light, have no bad smell, and burn twelve hours. A kind of cloth is also prepared from it, which the inhabitants of Quito apply to the same purpose as our oil cloth and sail cloth. It is formed, in fine, by means of moulds, into a variety of figures for use and ornament; and the proceeds is said to be thus:—The juice, which is obtained by incision, is spread over pieces of clay formed into the desired shape; and as fast as one layer is dry, another is added, till the vessel be of the proper thickness: the whole is then held over a strong smoke of vegetables on fire, whereby it hardens into the texture and appearance of leather; and before the finishing, while yet soft, is capable of having any impression made on the outside, which remains for ever after. When the whole is done, the inside mould is picked out. Since this resin has been known in Europe, its chemical qualities and other interesting properties have been very diligently investigated. In particular, it has been endeavoured to discover some method of dissolving it in such a manner that it would assume different figures, with equal ease as when in its original fluid state. In the memoirs of the Academy of Sciences for 1768, we have an account of several attempts for this purpose, and how it may be effected.—The state of vegetable milk in which the caoutchouc resin is found when it comes from the tree, led M. Macquer to imagine that it was composed of an oil and a watery matter. From its wanting aromatic flavour, from its little volatility, and from its being incapable of solution in spirit of wine, he concluded that the oil which entered its composition was not an essential, but a fatty, one. Hence he thought it probable that it passed from a fluid to a solid form by the evaporation of the watery part, and that the oily solvents would reduce it to a soft state. The first trials he made for dissolving it were with linseed oil, essence of turpentine, and several others. But all he could obtain by means of these menstrua was a viscid substance incapable of being hardened, and totally void of elasticity. The rectified essential oil of turpentine was employed seemingly with greater success. To separate from this menstruum the caoutchouc which it had dissolved, M. Macquer added spirit of wine; but the consequence was, that part only of the oil united with the spirit; the rest remaining obstinately attached to the resin which it had dissolved, and thus preventing it from assuming a solid consistence. The author next endeavoured to dissolve it by means of heat in Papin's digester. But neither water, nor spirit of wine, although in this way capable of dissolving the hardest bones, could produce any other effect upon it than to render it more firm than before. After this, he tried what effect the milky juice of other vegetables would have upon it. He used several kinds, particularly that of the fig. But, in this way, he could obtain no solution. From the great volatility of ether, he was next induced to try it as a menstruum; and, for this purpose, he prepared some with great attention. The caoutchouc, cut into little bits, and put into a proper vessel with as much ether as was sufficient to cover it, was perfectly dissolved without any other heat than that of the atmosphere. This solution was transparent and of an amber colour. It still preserved the smell of ether, but mixed with the disagreeable odour of the caoutchouc, and it is a little less fluid than pure ether. Upon its being thrown into water, no milky liquor was produced; but there arose to the surface a solid membrane, which possessed the great elasticity and other peculiar properties of the caoutchouc. He observes, however, that two pints of the best ether, obtained by rectifying eight or ten pints of the common ether by a gentle heat, must be used, in order to the success of the operation. The distinguishing properties of this substance, viz. its solidity, flexibility, and elasticity, and its quality of resisting the action of aqueous, spirituous, saline, oily, and other common solvents, render it extremely fit for the construction of tubes, catheters, and other instruments, in which these properties are wanted. In order to form this resin into small tubes, M. Macquer prepared a solid cylindrical mould of wax, of the desired size and shape; and then dipping a pencil into the ethereal solution of the resin, daubed the mould over with it, till he had covered it with a coat of resin of sufficient thickness. The whole piece is then thrown into boiling water; by the heat of which the wax is soon melted, and rises to the surface, leaving the resinous tube completely formed behind. Grosart informs us, that he has succeeded very well in employing the essential oils of turpentine and lavender as a solvent for the elastic gum, and thus forming it into tubes or giving it any shape that is wanted. When the elastic tube is prepared with oil of lavender, the latter may be separated by immersing the tube in alcohol, which charges itself with the oil, and becomes a good lavender water. Alcohol serves another purpose before taking up the essential oil. It accelerates very much the drying of caoutchouc instruments which are thus formed. Oil of turpentine appeared always to have a kind of stickiness; and the smell which could not be got rid of, by any means yet discovered, was another inconvenience. Grosart proposes another solvent, which is easily procured, and is not liable to the inconvenience just mentioned. This solvent is water. "I conceive (says he) it will appear strange to mention water as a solvent of elastic gum, that liquid having been always supposed to have no action upon it. I myself resisted the idea; but reflecting that ether, by being saturated with water, is the better enabled to act on caoutchouc, and that this gum when plunged into boiling water becomes more transparent at the edges, I presumed that this effect was not due simply to the dilatation of its volume by the heat. I thought that, at that temperature, some action might take place, and that a long-continued ebullition might produce more sensible effects. I was not disappointed in my expectations, and one of those tubes was prepared without any other solvent than water and heat. I proceeded in the same manner as with ether: the elastic gum dilates but very little in boiling water; it becomes whitish, but recovers its colour again by drying it in the air and light. It is sufficiently prepared for use when it has been a quarter of an hour in boiling water; by this time its edges are somewhat transparent. It is to be turned spirally round the mould, in the manner we described before, and replunged frequently into the boiling water, during the time that is employed in forming the tube, to the end that the edges may be disposed to unite together. When the whole is bound with packthread, it is to be kept some hours in boiling water; after which it is to be dried, still keeping on the binding. "If we wish to be more certain that the connexion is perfect, the spiral may be doubled; but we must always avoid placing the exterior surfaces of the flips one upon the other, as those surfaces are the parts which most resist the action of solvents. This precaution is necessary when ether is employed, on account of its great action upon the caoutchouc. "It might be feared that the action of water upon caoutchouc would deprive us of the advantages which might otherwise be expected; but these fears will be removed, if we consider that the affinities differ according to the temperatures; that it is only at a very high temperature that water exercises any sensible action upon caoutchouc. I can affirm, that at 120° of Reaumur's thermometer (302° of Fahrenheit) this affinity is not such as that the water can give a liquid form to caoutchouc; and it does not appear that we having anything to fear in practice from a combination between these two bodies, which, though it really is a true solution, does not take place in any sensible degree but at a high temperature. It is therefore at present easy to make of caoutchouc whatever instruments it may be advantageous to have of a flexible, supple, and elastic substance, which is impermeable to water at the temperature of our atmosphere, and resists the action of acids as well as that of most other solvents. As to the durability of these instruments, few substances promise more than this, because it may be foldered afresh in a damaged part. Any woven substance may be covered with it; it is only required that the substance should be of a nature not to be acted upon during the preparation, either by ether or by boiling water; for these two agents are those which appear to me to merit the preference. Artists will frequently find an advantage in employing ether, as it requires less time; so that a person may make, in a single day, any tube he may have occasion for. The expense of ether is very little, since it is needful only to dispose the caoutchouc to adhere; and being brought into that state, the caoutchouc may be kept in a vessel perfectly well closed. It would also diminish the expense of the ether, if, instead of wasting it with a large quantity of water, there should be added to it only as much water as it can take up." Annales de Chimie, vol. xi. p. 149. A resin similar to this was some years ago discovered by M. Poivre, in the isle of France; and there are various milky juices extracted from trees in America and elsewhere, which by previous mixtures and preparations are formed into an elastic resin, but of an inferior quality to that of Cayenne; such, for instance, are the juices obtained from the Cecropia peltata, the Ficus religiosa and Indica, &c. Of the genuine trees, those growing along the banks of the river of the Amazons are described by M. Condamin as attaining a very great height, being at the same time perfectly straight, and having no branches except at top, which is but small, covering no more than a circumference of ten feet. Its leaves bear some resemblance to those of the maniac: they are green on the upper part, and white beneath. The seeds are three in number, and contained in a pod consisting of three cells, not unlike those of the ricinus or palma Christi; and in each of them there is a kernel, which being stripped and boiled in water produces a thick oil or fat, answering the purpose of butter in the cookery of that country. A method of dissolving this elastic gum without ether, for the purposes of a varnish or the like, is as follows: Take one pound of the spirit of turpentine, and a pound of the gum cut into very small pieces; pour the turpentine into a long-necked matrafs, which must be placed in a sand bath; throw in the gum, not all at once, but by little and little according as it is perceived to dissolve: When it is entirely dissolved, pour into the matrafs a pint of nut or linseed oil, or oil of poppies, rendered defecative in the usual manner with litharge: Then let the whole boil for a quarter of an hour, and the preparation is finished. This would make an excellent varnish for air balloons, were it not too expensive on account of the price of the gum. Another method, invented by Mr Baldwin, is as follows. Take any quantity of the caoutchouc, as two ounces avoidupois: cut it into small bits with a pair of scissors. Put a strong iron ladle (such as plumbers or glaziers melt their lead in) over a common pit-coal or other fire. The fire must be gentle, glowing, and without smoke. When the ladle is hot, much below a red heat, put a single bit into the ladle. If black smoke issues, it will presently flame and disappear; or it will evaporate without flame: the ladle is then too hot. When the ladle is less hot, put in a second bit, which will produce a white smoke. This white smoke will continue during the operation, and evaporate the caoutchouc; therefore no time is to be lost; but little bits are to be put in, a few at a time, till the whole are melted. It should be continually and gently stirred with an iron or brass spoon. Two pounds, or one quart, of the best drying oil (or of raw linseed oil, which, together with a few drops of neats foot oil, has stood a month, or not so long, on a lump of quicklime, to make it more or less drying) is to be put into the melted caoutchouc, and stirred till hot: and the whole poured into a glazed vessel, through a coarse gauze, or fine sieve. When settled and clear, which will be in a few minutes, it is fit for use, either hot or cold. The abbé Clavigero informs us, that the elastic gum is called by the Mexicans Ollin or Olli, and by the Spaniards of that kingdom Ule: That it distills from the olquahuitl, which is a tree of moderate size; the trunk of which is smooth and yellowish, the leaves pretty large, the flowers white, and the fruit yellow and rather round, but angular; within which there are kernels as large as filberts, and white, but covered with a yellowish pellicle: That the kernel has a bitter taste, and the fruit always grows attached to the bark of the tree: That when the trunk is cut, the ole which distills from it is white, liquid, and viscid; afterwards it becomes yellow; and lastly of a leaden colour, though rather blacker, which it always retains. The tree, he adds, is very common in the kingdom of Guatemala. Different trees, it would appear, yield the elastic gum. Aublet, in his Histoire des Plantes de la Guiane (p. 871.), describes the tree, the fruit, and manner of collecting the juice; but never saw the flower: he calls it, however, Hevea Guianensis. In Jacquin's America, it is called Echites Corymbosa. The younger Linnæus, in his Supplementum Plantarum (p. 422), names it Jatropha Elastica; but acknowledges that he only gives it this name from the structure of the fruit having most resemblance to that genus, his dry species wanting the flowers. Of the above gum, it is said, the Chinese make e-

CAPACIO

Pages 168-168

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the hither Principato. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 18. N. Lat. 40. 40.

CAPACITY

Pages 169-169

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the ability of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body politic, to give or take lands or other things, or sue actions. Our law allows the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> two capacities; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>: in the first, he may purchase lands to him and his heirs; in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, to him and his successors. The clergy of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England have the like.

CAPARASON

Pages 169-169
or Caparison, the covering or clothing laid over a horse; especially a sumpter horse, or horse of state. The word is Spanish, being an augmentative of cape, caput, head. Anciently the caparasons were a kind of iron armour, wherewith horses were covered in battle.

CAPE

Pages 169-169

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> running out with a point into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, as Cape <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NORD">Nord</a>, Cape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, the Cape of Good Hope, &c. CAPE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELK">Elk</a>. See Cervus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CAPE Breton. See BRETON. CAPE <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">Coast</a> Castle. See COAST. CAPE of Good Hope. See GOOD HOPE. CAPE Verd. See VERD.

CAPELL

Pages 169-169

EDWARD, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> well known by his indefatigable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the works of Shakespeare, was a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the school of St Edmund's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a>. In the dedication of his edition of Shakespeare, in 1768, to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Grafton, he observes; that "his father and the grandfather of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, were friends, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the deceased nobleman he owed the leisure which enabled him to bestow the attention of 20 years on that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>." The office which his grace bestowed on Mr Capell was that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-inspector of the plays, to which a salary is annexed of £200 a-year. So early as the year 1745, as Mr Capell himself informs us, shocked at the licentiousness of Hanmer's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, he first projected an edition of Shakespeare, of the strictest accuracy, to be collated and published in due <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, ex fide codicum. He immediately proceeded to collect and compare the oldest and rarest copies; noting the original excellencies and defects of the rarest quartos, and distinguishing the improvements <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> variations of the first, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and third folios; and after many years labour produced a very beautiful small octavo, in 10 volumes, with an "Introduction." There is not, the authors of the Monthly Review observe, among the various publications of the present literary era, a more singular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> than that "Introduction." In style and manner it is more obsolete and antique than the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of which he treats. It is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Herbert of Cherbury, walking the new pavement in all the trappings of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>; but, like Lord Herbert, it displays many valuable qualities accompanying this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of extravagance, much found senfe, and appropriate erudition. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>-page of "Mr William Shakespeare, his Comedies, Histories, and Tragedies," it was also announced and promulgated, "Whereunto <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be added, in some other volumes, notes critical and explanatory, and a body of various readings entire." "The Introduction" likewise declared, that these "notes and various readings" would be accompanied with another work, disclosing the sources from which Shakespeare "drew the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his knowledge in mythological and classical matters, his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and even the seeming peculiarities of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>—to which," says Mr Capell, "we have given for title, The School of Shakespeare." Nothing surely could be more properly conceived than such designs; nor have we ever met with anything better grounded on the subject of "the learning of Shakespeare," than what may be found in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> to this part of Mr Capell's Introduction. It is more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> than even the popular "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>" on this topic. Certain quaintnesses of style, and peculiarities of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNCTUATION">punctuation</a>, attended the whole of this publication. The outline, however, was correct; and the critic, with unremitting toil, proceeded in his undertaking. But while he was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVING">diving</a> into the classics of Caxton (to continue the Reviewers account), and working his way underground, like the river <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a>, in order to emerge with all his glories; while he was looking forward to his triumphs, certain other <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> spirits went to work upon his plan; and, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> out the promised treasures, laid them prematurely before the public, defeating the effect of our critic's discoveries by anticipation. Steevens, Malone, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a>, Percy, Reed, and a whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> of literary ferrets, burrowed into every hole and corner of the warren of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> antiquity, and overran all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, whose map had been delineated by Edward Capell. Such a contingency nearly staggered the steady and unshaken perseverance of our critic, at the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of the completion of his labours, and as his editor informs us—for, alas! at the end of near 40 years, the publication was posthumous, and the critic himself no more!—he was almost determined to lay the work wholly aside. He persevered, however, by the encouragement of some noble and worthy persons; and to such their encouragement, and his perseverance, the public was, in 1783, indebted for three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volumes in 4to, under the title of "Notes and various readings of Shakespeare; together with the School of Shakespeare, or Extracts from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> English Books that were in print in the Author's time; evidently showing from whence his several Fables were taken, and some parcel of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a>. Also farther extracts, which contribute to a due understanding of his Writings, or give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to the History of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, or to the Dramatic History of his Time. By Edw. Capell."—Besides the works already mentioned, Mr Capell was the editor of a volume of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poems called "Prolusions;" and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of "Anthony and Cleopatra," as acted at Drury Lane in 1758. He died <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 24, 1781.

CAPELLA

Pages 169-169

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a bright fixed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the left shoulder of the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURIGA">Auriga</a>.

CAPELLE

Pages 169-169

a town of France, in Picardy, and in the Tierache, eight miles from Guise. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1616; but retaken the year after, E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 3. 59. N. Lat. 49. 58. CAPELLETS. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAPELLUS

Pages 169-170
LEWIS, an eminent French Protestant divine, born at Sedan in Champagne about the year 1579. He was the author of some learned works; but is chiefly known from the controversy he engaged in with the younger Buxtorf concerning the antiquity of Hebrew points, which Capellus undertook to disprove. His Critica Sacra was also an elaborate work, CAPER. See CAPPARIS, Botany Index.

CAPEQUIN

Pages 170-170

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, situated on the river Blackwater. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 50'. N. Lat. 52° 5'.

CAPER ALSO

Pages 170-170

r also denotes, a vessel used by the Dutch for cruising and taking prizes from the enemy; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, caper amounts to the same with privateer. Cappers are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> officered, and crowded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> even beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, because the thing chiefly in view is boarding the enemies.

CAPERNAUM

Pages 170-170

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> celebrated in the Gospels, being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> usually resided during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his ministry. This city is nowhere mentioned in the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> under this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other name like it; and therefore it is not improbable that it was one of those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> which the Jews built after their return from the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. It stood on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, i.e., on the coast of the sea of Galilee, in the borders of Zebulon and Naphtali (Matt. iv. 15.), and consequently towards the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof. It took its name no doubt from an adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute for its clear and limpid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and which, according to Josephus, was by the natives called Capernaum. As this spring might be some inducement to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the town in the place where it stood, so its being a convenient resting place from Galilee to any part on the other side of the sea, might be some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> for his moving from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAZARETH">Nazareth</a>, and making this the place of his most constant residence. Upon this account Capernaum was highly honoured, and said by our Lord himself to be exalted unto heaven; but because it made no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this signal favour, it drew from him the severe denunciation, that it should be brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a> (Matt. xi. 23.), which has certainly been verified: for, as Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a> observes, so far is it from being the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of all Galilee, as it once was, that it consists <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> since of no more than six <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> fishermen's cottages, and may perhaps be now totally desolate.

CAPEROLANS

Pages 170-170

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, so called from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Caperole their founder, in the 15th century. The Milanese and Venetians being at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the enmity occasioned thereby spread itself to the very cloisters. The superiors of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> brothers, which extended itself as far as the territories of the republic of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, carried it to haughtily over the Venetians, that those of the convent of Brescia resolved to shake off a yoke which was grown insupportable to them. The superiors, informed of this, expelled out of the province those whom they considered as the authors of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of whom were Peter Caperole, Matthew de Tharvillo, and Bonaventure of Brescia. Peter Caperole, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an enterprising genius, found means to separate the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of Brescia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERGAMO">Bergamo</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a>, from the province of Milan, and subject them to the conventuals. This occasioned a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>-general and these convents, which was determined in favour of the latter; and these convents, in 1475, by the authority of Pope Sixtus IV., were erected into a distinct vicariate, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of that of Brescia. This not satisfying the ambition of Caperole, he obtained, by the interposition of the doge of Venice, that this vicariate might be erected into a congregation, which was called from him Caperolans. This congregation still subsists in Italy, and is composed of 24 convents, situated in Brescia, Bergamo, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMA">Crema</a>.

CAPESTAN

Pages 170-170

a town of France, in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>, and near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> canal. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 5'. N. Lat. 43° 35'.

CAPH

Pages 170-170

a Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity for things, estimated by Kimchi at the 30th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the log, by Arbuthnot at the 16th part of the hin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 32d of the seah, amounting to five-eighths of an English pint. The caph does not occur in Scripture as the name of any measure.

CAPHAR

Pages 170-170

a duty which the Turks raised on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> who carry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> send merchandises from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> and other places in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. This duty of caphar was first imposed by the Christians themselves, when they were in possession of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, for the maintenance of the troops which were planted in difficult passes to observe the Arabs and prevent their incursions. It is still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, and much increased by the Turks, under pretence of defending the Christians against the Arabs; with whom, nevertheless, they keep a secret intelligence, favouring their excursions and plunders.

CAPHTOR

Pages 170-170
