in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> district of Higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; and hence the people called Caphtorim or Caphtorei.—Caphtor is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Egypt, Ai Caphtor, (Jeremiah); probably one of those in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a> supposes it to be Coptos, which stood in a small island. Thence came the Caphtorim or Caphtorei, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; who with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a> conspired to extirpate the Hevei; and whose name was swallowed up in that of the Philistines.

CAPI-AGA

Pages 170-170
or Capi-Agaff, a Turkish officer who is governor of the gates of the seraglio, or grand-master of the seraglio. The capi-aga is the first dignity among the white eunuchs; he is always near the person of the grand signior; he introduces ambassadors to their audience; nobody enters or goes out of the grand signior's apartment but by his means. His office gives him the privilege of wearing the turban in the seraglio, and of going everywhere on horseback. He accompanies the grand signior to the apartment of the sultanas, but stops at the door without entering. His appointment is very moderate; the grand signior bears the expense of his table, and allows him at the rate of about sixty French livres per day; but his office brings him in abundance of presents; no affair of consequence coming to the emperor's knowledge without passing through his hand. The capi-aga cannot be baffled when he quits his post.

CAPIAS

Pages 170-171

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ of two sorts; one before judgement in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and the other after. That before judgement is called capias <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> respondendum, where an original is issued ex t., to take the defendant, and make him answer the plaintiff. That after judgement is of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds; as, CAPIAS ad Satisfaciendum, a writ of execution that issues on a judgement obtained, and lies where any person recovers in a personal action, as for debt, damages, &c. in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> this writ issues to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, commanding him to take the body of him against whom the debt is recovered, who is to be kept in prison till he makes satisfaction. CAPLUS Pro Fine is a writ lying where a person is fined to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, for some offence committed against a statute, and he does not discharge the fine according to the judgement; therefore his body shall be taken by this writ, and committed to gaol till the fine is paid. CAPLUS Ullegatum, a writ which lies against any one outlawed, upon any action personal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> criminal, by which the sheriff is ordered to apprehend the party outlawed, for not appearing on the exigent, and keep him in safe custody till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of return, when he is ordered to present him to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to be there farther ordered for his contempt. CAPLUS in Withernam, a writ that lies for cattle in withernam: that is, where a distress taken is driven out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, so that the sheriff cannot make deliverance upon a replevin; then this writ issues, commanding the sheriff to take as many beasts of the distrainer, &c.

CAPIGI

Pages 171-171

a porter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> doorkeeper of the Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>. There are about five hundred capigis or porters in the seraglio, divided into two companies; one consisting of three hundred, under a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> called Capigi-Baffa, who has a stipend of three ducats per <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; the other consists of two hundred, distinguished by the name of Cuccicapigi, and their chief Cuccicapigi-Baffa; who has two ducats. The capigis have from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> to fifteen apers per day; some more, others less. Their business is to assist the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of the first and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> gates of the seraglio; sometimes all together; as when the Turk holds a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, receives an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, or goes to the mosque; and sometimes only in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; being ranged on either side to prevent people entering with arms; any tumults being made, &c. The word, in its original, signifies gate.

CAPILLAMENT

Pages 171-171

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>: whence the word is applied to several things, which on account of their length <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> their fineness resemble hairs: as, CAPILLAMENTS of the Nerves, in Anatomy, the fine fibres or filaments whereof the nerves are composed.

CAPILLARY

Pages 171-171

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, an appellation given to things on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> fineness <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resembling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. CAPILLARY Tubes, in Physics, are small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of glass, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are extremely narrow, their diameter being only a half, a third, or a fourth of a line. The ascent of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, &c. in capillary tubes, is a phenomenon that has <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> embarrassed the philosophers; for let one end of a glass tube open at both extremities be immersed in water, the liquor within the tube <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> rise to a considerable height above the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> surface: or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> two or more tubes are immersed in the same fluid, one a capillary tube, and the other of a larger bore, the fluid will ascend higher in the former than in the latter; and this will be in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> ratio of the diameters of the tubes. In order to account for this phenomenon, it will be necessary first to premise, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> between the particles of glass and water is greater than the attraction between the particles of water themselves: for if a glass tube be placed in a position <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, and a drop of water be applied to the under side of the tube, it will adhere to it: nor will it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the glass till its bulk and gravity are far increased, as to overcome the attraction of the glass. Hence it is easy to conceive how sensibly such a power must <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> on the surface of a fluid, not viscid, as water, contained within the small cavity or bore of a glass tube; as also that it will be proportionably stronger as the diameter of the bore is smaller; for it will be evident that the efficacy of the power is in the inverse proportion of the diameter, when it is considered, that such particles only as are in contact with the fluid, and those immediately above the surface, can effect it. Now these particles form a periphery contiguous to the surface, the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which attracts and raises the surface, while the lower part, which is in contact with it, supports it: so that neither the thickness nor length of the tube is of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> here; the periphery of particles only, which is always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the diameter of the bore, is the only acting power. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the fluid raised will therefore bear as the surface of the bore which it fills, that is, as the diameter; for otherwise the effect would not be proportional to the cause, since the quantities are always as the ratio of the diameters; the heights therefore to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> will rise in different tubes, will be inversely as the diameters. Some doubt whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> holds throughout, of the ascent of the fluid being always higher as the tube is smaller: Dr Hook's experiments, with tubes almost as fine as cobwebs, seem to show the contrary. The water in these, he observes, did not rise so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as one would have expected. The highest he ever found it, was at 21 inches above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the water in the basin; which is much short of what it ought to have been by the law above mentioned. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">Cohesion</a>. CAPILLARY Vessels. Many small vessels of animal bodies have been discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of injecting the vessels of animals, with a coloured fluid, which upon cooling grows hard. But though most anatomists know the manner of filling the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trunks, few are acquainted with the art of filling the capillaries. Dr Monro, in the Medical Essays, has given what after many trials he has found most successful. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJECTION">Injection</a>. CAPILLUS veneris. See ADIANTUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAPILUPI

Pages 171-171

Lachus, an Italian poet, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the former, made himself famous by some Centos of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. The manner in which he applied Virgil's expressions to represent things which the poet never dreamed of, is admired. His Cento against women is very ingenious, but too satirical. The poems of Capilupi are inserted in the Deliciæ Poetarum Italorum.

CAPISCOLUS

Pages 171-172

CAPISCOLUS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> CAPISCHOLUS, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> in certain cathedrals, who had the superintendency of the choir, or band of music, answering to what in other churches is called chanter or precentor. The word is also written cabicolus, and caputchole, q. d. the head of the school, or band of music. The capiscolus is also called scolasticus, as having the instruction of the young clerks and choristers, how to perform their duty.

CAPITA

Pages 172-172

DISTRIBUTION BY, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the appointing to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> an equal share of a personal estate; when all the claimants claim in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, as in equal degrees of kindred, and not jure representationis.

CAPITAL

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the uppermost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pilaster, serving as the head or crowning, and placed immediately over the shaft, and under the entablature. See ARCHITECTURE.

CAPITAL CITY

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, state, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>.

CAPITAL CRIME

Pages 172-172

such a one as subjects the criminal to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, that is, to loss of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

CAPITAL LETTERS

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> initial letters, wherein titles, &c. are composed; with which all periods, verses, &c. commence; and wherewith also all proper names of men, kingdoms, nations, &c. begin. The practice which, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, obtained among our printers, of beginning every substantive with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, is now justly fallen into disrepute; being a manifest perversion of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of capitals, as well as an offence against <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and distinctness.

CAPITAL PICTURE

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, denotes one of the finest and most excellent pieces of any celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>.

CAPITAL STOCK

Pages 172-172

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, and traders, signifies the sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which individuals bring to make up the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stock of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> when it is first formed. It is also said of the stock which a merchant at first puts into trade for his account. It likewise signifies the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of a trading <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> corporation, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the word stock is generally added to it. Thus we say, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> stock of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, &c. The word capital is opposed to that of profit or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, though the profit often increases the capital, and becomes of itself <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the capital, when joined with the former.

CAPITALAR

Pages 173-173
or CAPITULAR, denotes an act passed in a chapter, either of knights, canons, or religious. The capitularia or capitulars of Charlemagne, Charles the Bald, &c., are the laws, both ecclesiastical and civil, made by those emperors in the general councils or assemblies of the people; which was the way in which the constitutions of most of the ancient princes were made; each person present, though a plebeian, setting his hand to them. Some distinguish these from laws; and say, they were only supplements to laws. They had their name, capitulari, because divided into capitula, chapters, or sections. In these capitulars did the whole French jurisprudence anciently consist. In process of time, the name was changed for that of ordinances. Some distinguish three kinds of capitulars, according to the difference of their subject-matter; those on ecclesiastical affairs are really canons, extracted from councils; those on secular affairs, real laws; those relating to particular persons, or occasions, private regulations.

CAPITANA

Pages 172-172
or CAPTAIN GALLEY, the chief or principal galley of a state, not dignified with the title of a kingdom. The capitana was anciently the denomination of the chief galley of France, which the commander went on board of. But since the suppression of the office of captain general of the galleys in 1669, they have no capitana, but the first galley is called reale, and the second parone.

CAPITANATA

Pages 172-172

one of the 12 provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the east by the Terra di <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BASILICATA">Basilicata</a> and the Farther Principato, and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> di Molise and a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Hither Abruzzo. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, without trees; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> hot; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, however, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, is fertile in pastures. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANFREDONIA">Manfredonia</a>.

CAPITANEATE

Pages 172-172

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITANIA">capitania</a>. Capitaneates, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, are a kind of noble fiefs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> estates, which, besides their revenue, raise their owners to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. They are otherwise called baronies.

CAPITANEI

Pages 172-172
or CATANEI, in Italy, was a denomination given to all the dukes, marquises, and counts, who were called capitanei regis. The same appellation was also given to persons of inferior rank who were invested with fees, formerly distinguished by the appellation vallores majores.

CAPITANEUS

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> writers, denotes a tenant in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>.

CAPITANIA

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an appellation given to the 12 governments established by the Portuguese in the Brazils.

CAPITATION

Pages 172-172

a tax <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> imposition raised on each person, in proportion to his labour, industry, office, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, &c. It is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of tribute. The Latins call it tributum, by which taxes on persons are distinguished from taxes on merchandise, which were called vettigacia. Capitations are never practised among us but in exigencies of state. In France the capitation was introduced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in 1695; and is a tax very different from the taille, being levied from all persons, whether they be subject to the taille or not. The clergy pay no capitation, but the princes of the blood are not exempted from it.

CAPITE

Pages 172-172

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, (from caput, i.e. rex; whence tenere in capite is to hold of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, the head <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> paramount of all the lands in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>): An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, held immediately of the king, as of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, either by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> or by socage. It is now abolished. See TENURE.

CAPITE CENSU

Pages 172-172

in antiquity, the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of Roman citizens, who in public taxes were rated the least of all, being such as never were worth above 365 asses. They were supposed to have been thus called, because they were rather counted and marshalled by their heads than by their estates. The copite censi made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fifth class of citizens, being below the proletarii, who formed the other moiety of that class. They were not enrolled in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, as being judged not able to support the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; for in those days the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> maintained themselves. It does not appear that before <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Marius any of the Roman generals lifted the copite censi in their armies.

CAPITOL

Pages 172-173

CAPITOLIUM, in antiquity, a famous fort <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> castle, on the Mons Capitolinus at Rome, wherein was a temple dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, thence also denominated Capitolium, in which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> anciently assembled; and which still serves as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, or townhouse, for the meeting of the conservators of the Roman people.—It had its name capitoli, from copus, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s head," said to have been found fresh, and yet bleeding, upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> the foundation of the temple built in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Jupiter. Arnobius adds, that the man's name was Tulus, whence caput tolium. The first foundations foundations of the capitol were laid by Tarquin the Elder, in the year of Rome 139. His successor Servius raised the walls; and Tarquin the Proud finished it in the year 221. But it was not consecrated till the third year after the expulsion of the kings, and establishment of the consulship. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the dedication of the temple was performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Horatius in 246. The capitol consisted of three parts; a nave sacred to Jupiter, and two wings, the one consecrated to Juno, the other to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>: it was ascended to by stairs; the frontispiece and sides were surrounded with galleries, in which those who were honoured with triumphs entertained the senate at a magnificent banquet, after the sacrifice had been offered to the gods. Both the inside and outside were enriched with an infinity of ornaments, the most distinguished of which was the statue of Jupiter with his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> thunderbolt, his sceptre, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. In the capitol also were a temple to Jupiter the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>, and another to Juno, with the mint; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the hill was the temple of Concord. This beautiful edifice contained the most sacred depositories of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, such as the ancilia, the books of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBYLS">Sibyls</a>, &c. The capitol was burnt under Vitellius, and rebuilt under Vespasian. It was burnt a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> under Titus, and restored by Domitian. Anciently the name capitol was likewise applied to all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> in most of the colonies throughout the Roman empire; as at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>, &c.—That of Thoulouse has given the name of capitouls to the echevins or sheriffs.

CAPITOLINE GAMES

Pages 173-173

annual games instituted by Camillus, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Capitolinus, and in commemoration of the capitol's not being taken by the Gauls. Plutarch tells us that a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> consisted in the public criers putting up the Heturians to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> by auction: they also took an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and tying a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bulla about his neck, exposed him to the public derision. Festus says they also dressed him in a pretexta.—There was another kind of Capitoline games, instituted by Domitian, wherein there were rewards and crowns bestowed on the poets, champions, orators, historians, and musicians. These last Capitoline games were celebrated every five years, and became so famous, that, instead of calculating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by lustra, they began to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> by Capitoline games, as the Greeks did by Olympiads. It appears, however, that this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was not of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance.

CAPITOLINUS

Pages 173-173

Julius, an historian in the beginning of the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, under Diocletian, to whom he <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the Lives of Verus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, Claudius Balbinus, Macrinus, the Maximins, and the Gordians. He wrote other lives, which are most of them lost.

CAPITOUL

Pages 173-173
or CAPITOL, an appellation given to the chief magistrates of Thoulouse, who have the administration of justice and policy both civil and mercantile in the city. The capitouls at Thoulouse are much the same with the echevins at Paris, and with the consuls, bailiffs, burgomasters, mayors, and aldermen, &c., in other cities. In ancient acts they are called co-suleis, capitularii, or capitolini, and their body capitulum. From this last come the words capitularii and capitouls. The appellative capitolini arose hence, that they have the charge and custody of the townhouse, which was anciently called capitol. The office lasts only one year, and ennobles the bearers. In some ancient acts they are called capitulum nobilium totos. Those who have borne it style themselves afterwards burgesses. They are called to all general councils, and have the jus imaginum; that is, when the year of their administration is expired, their pictures are drawn in the townhouse; a custom which they have retained from the ancient Romans, as may be seen in Sigonius.

CAPITULATE

Pages 173-173

an appellation given to the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> districts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thoulouse, each under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a capitoul: much like the wards of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, under their aldermen. Thoulouse is now divided into eight capitulatures, or quarters, which are subdivided into moulans, each of which has its tithing-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose business is to inform the capitoul of what passes in his tithing, and to inform the inhabitants of the tithing of the orders of the capitoul.

CAPITULATION

Pages 173-174

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, was a transverse beam, wherein were holes through which passed the strings whereby the arms of huge engines, as balistae, catapultae, and scorpions, were played <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> worked.

CAPITULUM

Pages 174-174

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denoted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> read and explained. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they said, *ire <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> capitulum*, "to go to such a lecture." Afterwards the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment where such theological exercises were performed was denominated *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">domus</a> capituli*.

CAPNICON

Pages 174-174

in antiquity, chimney <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a tax which the Roman emperors levied for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, and which of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was due from all, even the poorest, who kept a fire. This was first invented by Nicephorus.

CAPNOMANCY

Pages 174-174

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> by means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> in their sacrifices. The words come from *καπνός*, smoke, and *φροντίζειν*, divination. The general rule was, when the smoke was thin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and rose straight up, it was a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the contrary, it was an ill one. There was also another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of capnomancy, consisting in the observation of the smoke rising from poppy and jasmine seed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon lighted coals.

CAPO D'ISTRIA

Pages 174-174

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Istria, on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRIESTE">Trieste</a>, with a bishop's see, and subject to the Venetians. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is wholesome and temperate; its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> revenue consists in wine and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. o. N. Lat. 45. 48.

CAPO DE ISTRIA

Pages 49-49

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Istria, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; and the see of a bishop. It is seated on a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice, and is joined to the main <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> by draw-bridges. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 22'. N. Lat. 45° 49'.

CAPO FINO

Pages 174-174

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> barren rock in the territory of the Genoese, which has a castle on its eastern peak. Near it is a small harbour of the same name, 13 miles east by south of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>.

CAPON

Pages 174-174

a cock chicken, gelded as soon as left by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as soon as he begins to crow. They are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> either to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> chickens, ducklings, pheasants, &c., and defend them from the kites and buzzards; or to feed for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, they being reckoned more delicate than either a cock or a hen.

CAPONIERE

Pages 174-174
or CAPONIERE, in Fortification, a covered lodgement sunk four or five feet into the ground, encompassed with a little parapet about two feet high, serving to support several planks covered with earth. The caponiere is large enough to contain 15 or 20 soldiers; and is usually placed in the glacis on the extremity of the counterscarp, and in dry moats; having little embrasures for the soldiers to fire through.

CAPPADOCIA

Pages 174-177

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; comprehending all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which lies between Mount Taurus and the Euxine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It was divided by the Persians into two satrapies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governments; by the Macedonians into two kingdoms, the one called Cappadocia <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Taurum; the other Cappadocia ad Pontum, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> Pontus; for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, &c. of which last, see the article PONTUS. CAPPADOCIA Magna, or Cappadocia properly so called, lies between the 38th and 41st degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It was bounded by Pontus on the north, Lycaonia and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> on the south, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a> on the west, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and part of Armenia <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> on the east. The first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Cappadocia we read of in history was Pharnaces, who was preferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, who gave him his sister Atossa in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. This is all we find recorded of him, except that he was killed in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Hyrcanians. After him came a succession of eight kings, of whom we know scarcely anything but that they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> faithful to the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, Cappadocia was governed by Ariarathes II., who, notwithstanding the vast conquests and fame of the Macedonian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, continued unshaken in his fidelity to the Persians. Alexander was prevented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> from invading his dominions; but Perdiccas, marching against him with a powerful and well-disciplined <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, dispersed his forces, and having taken Ariarathes himself prisoner, crucified him with all those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> blood whom he could get into his power. Diodorus tells us that he was killed in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. He is said to have reigned 82 years. His son Ariarathes III., having escaped the general slaughter of the royal family, fled into Armenia, where he lay concealed till the civil dissensions which rose among the Macedonians gave him a fair opportunity of recovering his paternal kingdom. Amyntas, at that time the governor of Cappadocia, opposed him; but being defeated in a pitched battle, the Macedonians were obliged to abandon all the strongholds. Ariarathes, after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and peaceable reign, left his kingdom to his son Ariarathes IV., who proved a very warlike <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and, having overcome Artaes, founder of the Parthian monarchy, considerably enlarged his own dominions. He was succeeded by Ariarathes V., who, marrying the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Antiochus the Great, entered into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with that prince against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; but Antiochus being defeated, the king of Cappadocia was obliged to sue for peace, which he obtained, after having paid 200 talents by way of fine, for taking up arms against the people of Rome. He afterwards assisted the republic with men and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> against Perseus king of Macedon, on which account he was by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the friend and ally of the Roman people. He left the kingdom in a very flourishing condition to his son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, who, on his accession, took the name of Ariarathes VI. This prince, (furnished Philopater, from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> respect and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> he showed his father from his very infancy,) immediately renewed the alliance with Rome. Out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, he restored Mithrobuzanes, son son to Ladriades, king of the Lesser Armenia, to his father's kingdom, though he foresaw that the Armenians would lay hold of that opportunity to join Artaxias, who was then on the point of invading Cappadocia. These differences, however, were settled before they came to an open rupture by the Roman legates; and Ariarathes seeing himself thus delivered from an impending war by the mediation of the republic, presented the senate with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> crown; and offered his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in whatever they thought proper to employ him. The senate in return sent him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>; which were presents usually bestowed on those only whom they looked upon as attached to their interest. Not long before this, Demetrius Soter king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> had offered Ariarathes his sister in marriage, the widow of Perseus king of Macedon: but this offer the king of Cappadocia was obliged to decline for fear of offending the Romans; and his doing so was in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> acceptable to the republic, who reckoned him among the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of her allies. Demetrius, however, being greatly incensed at the flight put upon his sister, set up a pretender to the throne, one Orophernes, a supposititious, or, as others call him, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of the deceased king. The Romans ordered <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a> to assist Ariarathes with all his forces; which he did, but to no purpose; for the confederates were overthrown by Demetrius, and Ariarathes was obliged to abandon the kingdom to his rival. This happened about 159 years before Christ, and the usurper immediately dispatched ambassadors to Rome with a golden crown. The senate declined accepting the present, till they heard his pretensions to the kingdom; and this Orophernes, by stubborn wittiness, made appear so plain, that the senate decreed that Ariarathes and he should reign as partners; but next year Orophernes was driven out by Attalus <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to Eumenes, and his successor to the kingdom of Pergamus. Ariarathes, being thus restored, immediately demanded of the Priennians 400 talents of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> which Orophernes had deposited with them. They honestly replied, that as they had been trusted with the money by Orophernes, they could deliver it to none but himself, or such as came in his name. Upon this, the king entered their territories with an army, destroying all with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The Priennians, however, still persevered in their integrity; and though their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was besieged by the united forces of Ariarathes and Attalus, not only made an obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, but found means to restore the sum to Orophernes. At last they applied to the Romans for assistance, who enjoined the two kings to raise the siege, under pain of being declared enemies to the republic. Ariarathes immediately obeyed; and marching his army into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, joined Alexander Epiphanes against Demetrius Soter, by whom he had been formerly driven out of his kingdom. In the very first engagement Demetrius was slain, and his army entirely dispersed, Ariarathes having on that occasion given uncommon proofs of his courage and conduct. Some years after, a war breaking out between the Romans and Ariftonicus who claimed the kingdom of Pergamus in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his father, Ariarathes joined the former, and was slain in the same battle in which P. Crassus proconsul of Asia was taken, and the Roman army cut in pieces. He left six sons by his wife Laodice, on whom the Romans bestowed Lycaonia and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>. But Laodice, fearing lest her children, when they came to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, should take the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> out of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, poisoned five of them, the youngest only having escaped her cruelty by being conveyed out of the kingdom. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> herself was soon after put to death by her subjects, who could not bear her cruel and tyrannical government. Laodice was succeeded by Ariarathes VII. who, soon after his accession, married another Laodice, daughter to Mithridates the Great, hoping to find in that prince a powerful friend to support him against Nicomedes king of Bithynia who laid claim to part of Cappadocia. But Mithridates, instead of afflicting, procured one Gordius to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> his unhappy son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and on his death, seized the kingdom, under pretence of maintaining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the Cappadocians against Nicomedes, till the children of Ariarathes were in a condition to govern the kingdom. The Cappadocians at first fancied themselves obliged to their new protector; but, finding him unwilling to resign the kingdom to the lawful heir, they rose up in arms, and driving out all the garrisons placed by Mithridates, placed on the throne Ariarathes VIII. eldest son of their deceased king. The new prince found himself immediately engaged in a war with Nicomedes; but, being assisted by Mithridates, not only drove him out of Cappadocia, but stripped him of a great part of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> dominions. On the conclusion of the peace, Mithridates, seeking for some pretence to quarrel with Ariarathes, inflicted upon his recalling Gordius, who had murdered his father; which being rejected with abhorrence, a war ensued. Mithridates took the field first, in hopes of overrunning Cappadocia before Ariarathes could be in a condition to make head against him; but, contrary to his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, he was met on the frontiers by the king of Cappadocia with an army no way inferior to his own. Hereupon he invited Ariarathes to a conference; and, in fight of both armies, stabbed him with a dagger, which he had concealed under his garment. This struck such terror into the Cappadocians, that they immediately dispersed, and gave Mithridates an opportunity of possessing himself of the kingdom without the least opposition. The Cappadocians, however, not able to endure the tyranny of his prefects, soon shook off the yoke; and recalling the king's brother, who had fled into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Asia, proclaimed him king. He was scarce seated on the throne, however, before Mithridates invaded the kingdom at the head of a very numerous army, and having drawn Ariarathes to a battle, defeated his army with great slaughter, and obliged him to abandon the kingdom. The unhappy prince soon after died of grief; and Mithridates bestowed the kingdom on his son, who was then but eight years old, giving him also the name of Ariarathes. But Nicomedes Philopater king of Bithynia, fearing lest Mithridates, having now got possession of the whole kingdom of Cappadocia, should invade his territories, suborned a youth to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> himself for the third son of Ariarathes, and to present to them a petition in order to be restored to his father's kingdom. With him he sent to Rome Laodice, sister of Mithridates, whom he had married after the death of her former husband Ariarathes. Laodice declared before the senate, senate, that she had three sons by Ariarathes, and that the petitioner was one of them; but that she had been obliged to keep him concealed, lest he should un- dergo the same fate with his brothers. The senate af- furred him that they would at all events reinstate him in his kingdom. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Mithridates, having notice of these transactions, dispatched Gordius to Rome, to undeceive the senate, and to persuade them that the youth to whom he had resigned the king- dom of Cappadocia was the lawful son of the late king, and grandson to Ariarathes who had lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the service of the Romans against Arioticus. This un- expected embassy put the senate upon enquiring more narrowly into the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, whereby the whole plot was discovered; upon which Mithridates was ordered to reign Cappadocia, and the kingdom was declared free. The Cappadocians, however, in a short time sent ambassadors to Rome, acquainting the senate that they could not live without a king. This greatly surprised the Romans, who had such an aversion to royal authority; but they gave them leave to elect a king of their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. As the family of Pharnaces was now extinct, the Cappadocians chose Ariobar- zanes; and their choice was approved by the senate, he having on all occasions shown himself a steady friend to the Romans. Ariobarzanes had scarce taken possession of his king- dom when he was driven out by Tigranes king of Ar- menia; who resigned Cappadocia to the son of Mithri- dates, in pursuance of an alliance previously concluded between the two parties. Ariobarzanes fled to Rome; and, having engaged the senate in his cause, he re- turned into Asia with Sylla, who was enjoined to re- store him to his kingdom. This was easily performed by Sylla, who, with a small body of troops, routed Gordius who came to meet him on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">Cap</a>- padocia at the head of a numerous army. Sylla, how- ever, had scarce turned his back, when Ariobarzanes was again driven out by Ariarathes the son of Mithri- dates, on whom Tigranes had bestowed the kingdom of Cappadocia. This obliged Sylla to return into A- sia, where he was attended with his usual success, and Ariobarzanes was again placed on the throne. After the death of Sylla, he was the third time forced by Mithridates to abandon his kingdom; but Pompey, having entirely defeated Mithridates near Mount Stel- la, restored Ariobarzanes to his throne, and rewarded him for his services during the war, with the provinces of Sophene, Gordicene, and great part of Cilicia. The king, however, being now advanced in years, and de- sirous of spending the remainder of his life in ease, resigned the crown to his son Ariobarzanes, in pre- sence of Pompey; and never afterwards troubled him- self with affairs of state. Ariobarzanes II. proved no less faithful to the Ro- mans than his father had been. On the breaking out of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, he sided with the latter; but, after the death of Pompey, he was received into favour by Caesar, who even bestowed upon him great part of Armenia. While Caesar was engaged in a war with the Egyptians, Pharnaces king of Pontus invaded Cappadocia, and stripped Ariobar- zanes of all his dominions; but Caesar, having defeated Pharnaces, restored the king of Cappadocia, and ho- noured him with new titles of friendship. After the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Caesar, Ariobarzanes, having refused to join Brutus and Cassius, was by them declared an enemy to the republic, and soon after taken prisoner and put to death. He was succeeded by his brother Ariobarza- nes III., who was by Mark Antony deprived both of his kingdom and his life; and in him ended the family of Ariobarzanes. Archelaus, the grandson of that general of the same name who commanded against Sylla in the Mithridatic war, was by Mark Antony placed on the throne of Cappadocia, though nowise related either to the fa- mily of Pharnaces or Ariobarzanes. His preferment was entirely owing to his mother Glaphyra, a woman of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, but of loose behaviour, who, in re- turn for her compliance with the desires of Antony, obtained the kingdom of Cappadocia for her son. In the war between Augustus and Antony, he joined the latter; but, at the intercession of the Cappadocians, was pardoned by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. He afterwards receiv- ed from him Armenia the lesser, and Cilicia Tra- chaea, for having assisted the Romans in clearing the seas of pirates, who greatly infested the coasts of Asia. He contracted a strict friendship with Herod the Great, king of Judea; and even married his daughter Glap- hyra to Alexander, Herod's son. In the reign of Tiberius, Archelaus was summoned to appear before the senate; for he had always been hated by that em- peror, because in his retirement at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> he had paid him no sort of respect. This had proceeded from no aversion in him to Tiberius, but from the warning gi- ven by Archelaus to his friends at Rome. For <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Caesar, the presumptive heir to the empire, was then alive, and had been sent to compose the differences of the east: whence the friendship of Tiberius was then looked upon as dangerous. But when he came to the empire, Tiberius, remembering the disrespect shown him by Archelaus, enticed the latter to Rome by means of letters from Livia, who promised him her son Tiberius's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, provided he came in person to im- plore it. Archelaus obeyed the summons, and hasten- ed to Rome; where he was received by the emperor with great wrath and contempt, and soon after accus- ed as a criminal in the senate. The crimes of which he was accused were mere fictions; but his concern at feeling himself treated as a malefactor was so great, that he died soon after of grief, or, as others say, laid vio- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> hands on himself. He is said to have reigned 50 years. On the death of Archelaus, the kingdom of Cappa- docia was reduced to a Roman province, and governed by those of the equestrian order. It continued subject to the Romans till the invasion of the eastern empire by the Turks, to whom it is now subject, but has no distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name. In what was an- ciently called Cappadocia, however, the Turks have four beglerbeglies, called Siras, Trebizond, Marajch, and Cogni. In the time of the Romans, the inhabitants of Cap- padocia bore so bad a character, and were reputed to vicious and lewd, that, among the neighbouring na- tions, a wicked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was emphatically called a Cappa- docian. In after ages, however, their lewd disposition was so corrected and restrained by the pure doctrines of Christianity, that no country whatever has produced greater champions of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, or given to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> prelates of more unblemished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. We have now no system of the Cappadocian laws, and scarce wherewithal to form any particular idea of them. As to their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, they carried on a considerable trade in horses, great numbers of which were produced in their country; and we read of them in Scripture as frequenting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> with this commodity. As Cappadocia abounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, brals, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, and afforded great store of alabaster, crystal, and jasper, it is probable that they might supply the neighbouring countries with these commodities. The religion of the ancient Cappadocians was much the same with that of the Persians. At Comana there was a rich and lately temple dedicated to Bellona; whose battles the priests and their attendants used to represent on fitted days, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> and wounding each other as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> feigned with an enthusiastic fury. No less famous and magnificent were the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> Catanius, and of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>: the last of which had 3000 sacred servants, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> votaries. The chief <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> was next in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> to that of Comana; and, according to Strabo, had a yearly revenue of 15 talents. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> Persica was worshipped in a city called Cabalalla, where women, devoted to the worship of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, were reported to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> barefooted on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals, without receiving any hurt. The temples of Diana at Diospolis, and of Anias at Zela, were likewise held in great veneration both by the Cappadocians and Armenians, who flocked to them from all parts. In the latter were tendered all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; and the chief among the priests was no way inferior in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, power, and wealth, to any in the kingdom; having a royal attendance, and an unlimited authority over all the inferior servants and officers of the temple. The Romans, who willingly adopted all the superstitions and superstitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the nations they conquered, greatly increased the revenues of this and other temples; conferring the priesthood on such as they thought most fit for carrying on their designs.—We are told that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sacrifices were offered at Comana; and that this barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was brought by Orestes and his sister Iphigenia from Taurica Scythica, where men and women were immolated to Diana. But this custom, if ever it obtained in Cappadocia, was abolished in the times of the Romans.

CAPPANUS

a name given by some authors to a worm that adheres to and gnaws the bottoms of hips; to which it is extremely pernicious, especially in the East and West Indies; to prevent this, several ships have lately been sheathed with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of which was made on his majesty's frigate the Alarm. CAPPARIS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The buds of this plant pickled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, &c., are brought to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> annually from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the Mediterranean. They are supposed to excite appetite and assist digestion; and to be particularly useful as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETERGENTS">detergents</a> and aperients in obstructions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> and spleen.

CAPRA

or Goat. See Mammalia Index. Capra Saltans, in Meteorology, a fiery meteor or exhalation sometimes seen in the atmosphere. It forms an inflected line, resembling in some measure the caperings of a goat; whence it has its name.

CAPRARA

Pages 177-177

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Corsica, on which it depends. It is pretty populous, and has a strong castle for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. It is about 15 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 5'. N. Lat. 43° 15'. CAPRARI. CAPRAROLA

Pages 177-177

one of the most magnificent palaces in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, seated on a hill, in Ronciglione, whose foot is watered by the river Tircia. It was built by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Farnese; and has five fronts, in the middle of which is a round <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, though all the rooms are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and well proportioned. It is 27 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Rome. CAPRAE. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRI">Capri</a>.

CAPRELUS

Pages 177-177

Elias, an excellent civilian, and learned historian, born at Brescia in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Brescia, and other works; died in 1519.

CAPRI

Pages 177-177

(anciently Capree), a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 50'. N. Lat. 40° 45'.—The island is only four miles long and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the city is a bishop's see, and situated on a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock at the west end of the island. Capree was anciently famous for the retreat of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Tiberius for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, during which he indulged himself in the most scandalous debaucheries*. Before Tiberius came hither, Capri had attracted the notice of Augustus, as a most eligible retreat, though in sight of populous cities, and almost in the centre of the empire. His successor preferred it to every other residence; and in order to vary his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and enjoy the advantages as well as avoid the inconveniences of each revolving season, built 12 villas in different situations, dedicated to the 12 greater gods; the ruins of some of them are still to be seen: at Santa <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> are extensive vaults and reservoirs; and on an adjoining brow are the remains of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>; two broken columns indicate the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. According to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius, this island was wild and barren before the Caesars took it under their immediate protection; at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of its surface is uncultivated and impracticable; but every spot that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit the hoe is industriously tilled, and richly laden with the choicest productions of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. The odium attached to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Tiberius proved fatal to his favourite abode; scarce was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> proclaimed at Rome, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> issued orders for the demolition of every fabric he had raised on the island, which by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> was thenceforward destined to be a state prison. The wife and sister of Commodus were banished to its inhospitable rocks, which were soon stained with their blood. In the middle ages Capri became an appendage of the Amalfitan republic, and after the downfall of that state, belonged to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Naples. There stood a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHAROS">pharos</a> on this island, which, a few days before the death of Tiberius, was overthrown by an earthquake.

CAPRIATA

Pages 177-177
Peter John, a civilian and historian, was born at Genoa. He wrote, in Italian, the history of the wars of Italy; an English translation of which was printed in London in 1663.

CAPRICORN

Pages 177-179

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, one of the 12 signs of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>. See Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> accounted Capricorn the tenth sign; and when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> arrived thereat, it made the winter solstice with regard to our hemisphere: but the stars having advanced a whole sign towards the east, Capricorn is now rather the 11th sign; and it is at the sun's entry into Sagittary that the solstice happens, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> manner of speaking is still retained. This sign is represented on ancient monuments, medals, &c., as having the forepart of a goat and the hind-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a fish, which is the form of an Ægipan; sometimes simply under the form of a goat. Tropic of Capricorn, a lesser circle of the sphere, which is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the equinoctial, and at 23° 30' distance from it southwards; passing through the beginning of Capricorn. Caprification, a method used in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, for ripening the fruit of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> fig tree, by means of insects bred in that of the wild fig tree. The most ample and satisfactory accounts of this curious operation in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, are those of Tournefort and Pontedra: the former, in his Voyage to the Levant, and in a Memoir delivered to the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1705; the latter, in his Anthologia. The substance of Tournefort's account follows: "Of the thirty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> varieties of the domestic fig tree which are cultivated in France, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, there are but two cultivated in the Archipelago. The first species is called ormos, from the old Greek erinos, which answers to caprificus in Latin, and signifies a wild fig-tree. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the domestic or garden fig tree. The former bears successively, in the same year, three sorts of fruit, called fornites, cratitires, and orni; which, though not good to eat, are found absolutely necessary towards ripening those of the garden fig. These <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> have a fleck even skin; are of a deep green <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and contain in their dry and mealy inside several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> placed upon distinct footstalks, the former above the latter. The fornites appear in August, and continue to November without ripening: in these are bred small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, which turn to a sort of gnats, nowhere to be seen but about these trees. In October and November, these gnats of themselves make a puncture into the second fruit, which is called cratitire. These do not show themselves till towards the end of September. The fornites gradually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> away after the gnats are gone; the cratitires, on the contrary, remain on the tree till May, and enclose the eggs deposited by the gnats when they pricked them. In May, the third sort of fruit, called orni, begins to be produced by the wild fig-trees. This is much bigger than the other two; and when it grows to a certain size, and its bud begins to open, it is pricked in that part by the gnats of the cratitires, which are strong enough to go from one fruit to another to deposit their eggs. It sometimes happens that the gnats of the cratitires are slow to come forth in certain parts, while the orni in those very parts are disposed to receive them. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the husbandman is obliged to look for the cratitires in another part, and fix them at the ends of the branches of those fig trees whose orni are in a fit disposition to be pricked by the gnats. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they miss the opportunity, the orni fall, and the gnats of the cratitires fly away. None but those that are well acquainted with the culture know the critical moment of doing this; and in order to know it, their eye is perpetually fixed on the bud of the fig; for that part not only indicates the caprification <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the prickers are to issue forth, but also when the fig is to be successfully pricked: if the bud is too hard and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, the gnat cannot lay its eggs; and the fig drops when the bud is too open. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of all these three sorts of fruit is to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> the fruit of the garden fig-tree, in the following manner: During the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the peasants take the orni, at the time their gnats are ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out, and carry them to the garden fig-trees; if they do not nick the moment, the orni fall; and the fruit of the domestic fig-tree, not ripening, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in a very little time fall in like manner. The peasants are so well acquainted with these precious moments, that, every morning, in making their inspection, they only transfer to their garden fig-trees such orni as are well conditioned, otherwise they lose their crop. In this case, however, they have one remedy, though an indifferent one; which is, to strew over the garden fig-trees another plant in whose fruit there is also a species of gnats which answer the purpose in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. The caprification of the ancient Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, described by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, Plutarch, Pliny, and other authors of antiquity, corresponds in every circumstance with what is practised at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the Archipelago and in Italy. These all agree in declaring, that the wild fig-tree, caprificus, never ripened its fruit; but was absolutely necessary for ripening that of the garden or domestic fig, over which the husbandmen suspended its branches. The reason of this success has been supposed to be, that by the punctures of these insects the vessels of the fruit are lacerated, and thereby a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of nutritious juice derived thither. Perhaps, too, in depositing their eggs, the gnats leave behind them some sort of liquor proper to ferment gently with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of the figs, and to make their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> tender. The figs in Provence, and even at Paris, ripen much sooner for having their buds pricked with a straw dipped in olive-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Plums and pears likewise, pricked by some insects, ripen much the faster for it; and the flesh round such puncture is better tasted than the rest. It is not to be disputed, that considerable changes happen to the cotyledons of fruits so pricked, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> the same as to parts of animals pierced with any sharp <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. Others have supposed that these insects penetrated the fruit of the tree to which they were brought, and gave a more free admission to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and to the sun. Linnaeus explained the operation, by supposing that the insects brought the farina from the wild fig, which contained male flowers only, to the domestic fig, which contained the female ones. Haffelquist, from what he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, seemed to doubt of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of fructification. M. Bernard, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, opposes it more decidedly. He could never find the insect in the cultivated fig; and, in reality, it appeared to leave the wild fig, after the stamina were mature, and their pollen dilated: besides, he adds, what they may have brought on their wings must be rubbed away, in the little aperture which they would form for themselves. At <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, where there are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight varieties of the domestic fig, this operation is only performed on those which ripen latest: the former are of a proper size, fine flavour, and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance without it; so that he thinks the caprification only hastens the ripening. He examined the parts of fructification of the fig; and he observes, if this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> be made previous to the ripening, that round the eye of the fig, and in the substance of its covering, may be seen triangular dentated leaves, pressed one against another; and under these leaves are the stamens, whose pollen is destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> of the grains, which fill the rest of the fruit. These male organs are much more numerous in the wild-fig than in the domestic; and the stamens are found to contain a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> dust, which may be collected when it is ripe. The wild figs, when ripe, are not succulent, and have no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, though the grains are disposed in the same manner as in the other kind. The pith of the grain of the wild fruit serves as food to a species of the cynips, whose larva is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, till the moment of its transformation; and it is by an opening, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the pitil, that the insect penetrates the grain. From this account it is thought probable that the insect is only communicated by accident to the domestic fig, and that the flowers of this genus are sometimes hermaphrodites. But the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hermaphrodite flowers being fewer on the cultivated than on the wild fig, the seeds are fecundated more certainly and quickly by the capriciousness; and every botanist knows, that when the impregnation is completed, the flower soon withers; while, if by any accident it is delayed, it continues in bloom much longer. This view of the subject, therefore, explains very completely the reason why, in Malta, the capriciousness is practised on the late kind of figs, because it hastens the formation and maturity of the fruit.

CAPRIOLLES

Pages 179-179

in the manege, leaps that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> makes in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> without advancing, in such a manner, that, when he is at the height of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>, he jerks out with his hinder legs even and near. It is the most difficult of all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> maneges. It differs from a croupade, in this, that, in a croupade, a horse does not throw his shoes; and from a ballotade, because in this he does not jerk out.
