To make a horse <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> well at caprioles, he must be put between two pillars, and taught to raise first his fore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and then his hind quarters while his fore ones are yet in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; for which reason you must give him the whip and the poinson.

CAPSA

Pages 179-179

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, situated amidst vast deserts, waste, uncultivated, and full of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, where Jugurtha kept his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. In his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was taken and razed by Marius the Roman general, who put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> all the citizens capable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> arms, and sold the rest for slaves. It was, however, afterwards rebuilt by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and strongly fortified; but, on the decline of their empire, was taken and demolished a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, by Occuba a famous Arab general. The walls of the citadel are still remaining, and are monuments of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and strength of Capsa. They are 24 fathoms in height, and five in thickness, built of large <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and have now acquired the solidity and firmness of a rock. The walls of the town were rebuilt by the inhabitants since their first demolition; but were afterwards destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Almanzor, who sent a governor and troops into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. In Marmol's time Capsa was very populous, and abounded with stately mosques and other structures of superb and elegant workmanship: but at present it is occupied by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and indigent people, fleeced and oppressed by the Tufitian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In the very centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> stands an enclosed fountain, which both supplies the people with drink, and affords them an agreeable bath. The adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is now cultivated, and produces several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is unhealthy. The inhabitants are remarkable for their peevishness of temper. Both men and women dress handsomely, except their feet, which they cover with coarse shoes of bungling workmanship, and made of the rough skins of wild beasts, equally inconvenient and unbecoming. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 9. 3. N. Lat. 33. 15.

CAPSARIUS

Pages 179-179

(from capa, satchel), in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> who attended the Roman youth to school, carrying a satchel with their books in it, sometimes also called liberarius. CAPSARIUS was also an attendant at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, to whom persons committed the keeping of their clothes. CAPSARIUS (from capa, "a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>") among the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, was he who had the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> chest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coffer.

CAPSICUM

Pages 179-180
or Guinea-pepper. See Botany Index. The bell-pepper produces fruit fit for pickling; for which purpose they must be gathered before they arrive at their full size, while their rind is tender. They must be slit down on one side to get out the seeds, after which they should be soaked two or three days in salt and water; when they are taken out of this and drained, boiling vinegar must be poured on them in a sufficient quantity to cover them, and closely stopped down for two months; then they should be boiled in the vinegar to make them green; but they want no addition of any spice, and are the wholesomest and best pickle in the world. Another species is used for making what is called cayen-butter or pepper-pots, by the inhabitants of America, and which they esteem the best of all the spices. The following is a receipt for making of a pepper-pot: "Take of the ripe seeds of this sort of capsicum, and dry them well in the sun; then put them into an earthen or stone pot, mixing flour between every stratum of pods; and put them into an oven after the baking of bread, that they may be thoroughly dried: after which they must be well cleansed from the flour; and if any of the stalks remain adhering to the pods, they should be taken off, and the pods reduced to a fine powder; to every ounce of this add a pound of wheat flour, and as much leaven as is sufficient for the quantity intended. After this has been properly mixed and wrought, it should be made into small cakes, and baked in the same manner as common cakes of the same size: then cut them into small parts, and bake them again, that they may be as dry and hard as biscuit; which being powdered and sifted, is to be kept for use." This is prodigiously hot and acrimonious, setting the mouth as it were on fire. It is by some recommended as a medicine for flatulences; but it is greatly to be doubted whether all those hot irritating medicines are not productive of more harm than good, in this country at least. If the ripe pods of capsicum are thrown into the fire, they will raise strong and noisome vapours, which occasion vehement sneezing. ing, coughing, and often vomiting, in those who are near the place, or in the room where they are burnt. Some persons have mixed the powder of the pods with snuff, to give to others for diversion; but where it is in quantity, there may be danger in using it; for it will occasion such violent fits of sneezing, as may break the blood-vessels of the head.

CAPSQUARES

Pages 180-180

strong plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> which come over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNNIONS">trunnions</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, and keep it in the carriage. They are fastened by a hinge to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-plate, that they may lift up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and form a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> in the middle to receive a third part of the thickness of the trunnions: for two-thirds are let into the carriage, and the other end is fastened by two iron wedges called the forelocks and keys.

CAPSTAN

Pages 180-180
or CAPSTERN, a strong massive column of timber, formed like a truncated cone, and having its upper extremity pierced with a number of holes to receive the bars or levers. It is let perpendicularly down through the decks of a ship; and is fixed in such a manner, that the men, by turning it horizontally with their bars, may perform any work which requires any extraordinary effort. A capstan is composed of several parts, where A is the barrel, b the whelps, c the drumhead, and d the spindle. The whelps rise out from the main body of the capstan like buttresses, to enlarge the sweep, so that a greater quantity of cable, or whatever rope encircles the barrel, may be wound about it at one turn, without adding much to the weight of the capstan. The whelps reach downwards from the lower part of the drumhead to the deck. The drumhead is a broad cylindrical piece of wood resembling a millstone, and fixed immediately above the barrel and whelps. On the outside of this piece are cut a number of square holes parallel to the deck, to receive the bars. The spindle or pivot d, which is shod with iron, is the axis or foot upon which the capstan rests, and turns round in the faucer, which is a sort of iron socket let into a wooden stock or standard called the flep, resting upon and bolted to the beams. Besides the different parts of the capstan above explained, it is furnished with several appurtenances, as the bars, the pins, the pawls, the swifter, and the faucer, already described. The bars are long pieces of wood, or arms, thrust into a number of square holes in the drumhead all round, in which they are as the radius of a circle, or the spokes in the nave of a wheel. They are used to heave the capstan round, which is done by the men setting their breasts against them, and walking about, like the machinery of a horse mill, till the operation is finished.—The pins e, are little bolts of iron thrust perpendicularly through the holes of the drumhead, and through a corresponding hole in the end of the bar, made to receive the pins when the bars are fixed. They are used to confine the bars, and to prevent them from working out as the men heave, or when the ship labours. Every pin is fastened to the drumhead with a small iron chain; and that the bars may exactly fit their respective holes, they are all numbered.—The pawls f, No. 1, are situated on each side the capstan, being two short bars of iron, bolted at one end through the deck to the beams close to the lower part of the whelps; the other end, which occasionally turns round on the deck, being placed in the intervals of the whelps, as the capstan turns round, prevents it from recoiling or turning back by any sudden jerk of the cable, as the ship rises on the sea, which might greatly endanger the men who heave. There are also hanging pawls g, No. 3, used for the same purpose, reaching from the deck above to the drumhead immediately below it. The swifter is a rope passed horizontally through holes in the outer end of the bars, and drawn very tight; the intent of this is to keep the men steady as they walk round when the ship rocks, and to give room for a greater number to assist by pulling upon the swifter itself. The most frequent use of the capstan is to heave in the cable, and thereby remove the ship or draw up the anchor. It is also used to wind up any weighty body, as the masts, artillery, &c. In merchant ships it is likewise frequently employed to discharge or take in the cargo, particularly when consisting of weighty materials that require a great exertion of ref="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical powers to be removed. There are commonly two capstans in a man of war, the main and the gear capstan; the former of which has two drumheads, and may be called a double one. This is represented in No. 3. The latter is represented in No. 2. Formerly the bars of the capstan went entirely through the head of it, and consequently were more than double the length of the present ones; the holes were therefore formed at different heights, as represented in No. 1. But this machine had several inconveniences, and has long been entirely disused in the navy. Some of these sort of capstans, however, are still retained in merchant ships, and are usually denominated crabs. The situation of the bars in a crab, as ready for heaving, is represented in No. 4. To rig the CAPSTERN, is to fix the bars in their respective holes, and thrust in the pins, in order to confine them.—Surge the CAPSTERN, is the order to slacken the rope heaved round upon it, of which there are generally two turns and a half about the barrel at once, and sometimes three turns.—To Heave the CAPSTERN, is to go round with it heaving on the bars, and drawing in any rope of which the purchase is created.—To come-up the CAPSTERN, is to let go the rope upon which they had been heaving.—To Pawl the CAPSTERN, is to fix the pawls to prevent it from recoiling during any pause of heaving.

CAPSULE

Pages 180-181

among botanists, a dry hollow seed-vessel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pericarpium, that cleaves or splits in some determinate manner. See PERICARPUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of seed-vessel is frequently fleshy and succulent, like a berry, before it has attained maturity; but, in ripening, becomes dry, and often so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> as to dart the seeds from their departments with considerable velocity. This elasticity is remarkably conspicuous in wood <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>; balm, impatiens; African <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, dioctria; fraxinella; justicia; ruellia; barleria; lathrea; and many others.—The general attitude or disposition of this species of seed-vessel to cleave or separate for the purpose of dispersing its seeds, distinguishes it not less remarkably than its texture from the pulpy or succulent <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the apple, berry, and cherry kind. This opening of the capsule for dischar- ging its seeds when the fruit is ripe, is either at the top, as in most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; at the bottom, as in triglochin; at the side, through a pore or small hole, as in campanula and orchis; horizontally, as in plantain, amaranthus, and anagallis; or longitudinally, as in convolvulus. All fruit that is jointed, opens at every one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, each of which contains a single seed. Capsules, in splitting, are divided, externally, into one or more pieces, called by Linnaeus valves. The internal divisions of the capsules are called cells, loculae, loculaments: these, in point of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, are exceedingly diversified; some having only one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, as the primrose; and others many, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> lily. Hence a capsule is termed unilocular, bilocular, trilocular, &c., according as it has one, two, three, &c., cells or cavities. CAPSULÆ Atrabiliariae, called also glandula renalis, and renes fucceuturianæ. See ANATOMY Index.

CAPTAIN

Pages 181-182

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> officer, whereof there are several kinds, according to their commands. CAPTAIN of a Troop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, an inferior officer who commands a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or a company of foot, under a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>. The duty of this officer is to be careful to keep his company full of able-bodied <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; to visit their tents and lodgings, to see what is wanting; to pay them well; to cause them keep themselves neat and clean in their clothes, and their arms bright. He has power in his own company of making sergeants, corporals, and lancepades. In the horse and foot guards, the captains have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of colonels. CAPTAIN-General, he who commands in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. CAPTAIN-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>, he who, with the rank of captain, but the pay of lieutenant, commands a troop or company in the name and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some other person who is dispensed with, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, from performing the functions of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. Thus the colonel being usually captain of the first company of his regiment, that company is commanded by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Captain-Lieutenant. So in England, as well as in France, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, duchess, princes, &c., have usually the title of captain of the guards, gens d'armes, &c.; the real duty of which offices is performed by captain-lieutenants. CAPTAIN Reformed, one who, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the forces, has his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> and company suppressed; yet is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> captain, either as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to another, or without any post or command at all. CAPTAIN of a Ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, the officer who commands a ship of the line of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, or a frigate carrying 20 or more cannon. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of a captain in his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> is very comprehensive, inasmuch as he is not only answerable for any bad conduct in the military <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and equipment of the ship he commands, but also for any neglect of duty or ill management in his inferior officers, whose several charges he is appointed to superintend and regulate. On his first receiving information of the condition and quality of the ship he is appointed to command, he must attend her constantly, and hasten the necessary preparations to fit her for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. So strict, indeed, are the injunctions laid on him by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, or commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, that he is forbid to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> out of his ship, from his arrival on board to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his discharge, unless by particular leave from the admiralty or from his commander in chief. He is enjoined to show a laudable example of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and virtue to the officers and men; and to discountenance all dissolute, immoral, and disorderly practices, and such as are contrary to the rules of subordination and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; as well as to correct those who are guilty of such offences as are punishable according to the usage of the sea. He is ordered particularly to survey all the military stores which are sent on board, and to return whatever is deemed unfit for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. His diligence and application are required to procure his complement of men; observing carefully to enter only such as are fit for the necessary duty, that the government may not be put to unnecessary expense. When his ship is fully manned, he is expected to keep the established <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men complete, and superintend the muster himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is no clerk of the check at the port. When his ship is employed on a cruising station, he is expected to keep the sea the whole length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> previously appointed; but if he is compelled by some unexpected accident to return to port sooner than the time limited, he ought to be very cautious in the choice of a good situation for anchoring, ordering the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> or other careful officers to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and discover the depths of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and dangers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. Previous to any possibility of an engagement with the enemy, he is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> the officers and men to the necessary stations according to their office and abilities, and to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> them in the management of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, that they may be more expert in time of battle. His station in the time of an engagement is on the quarter-deck: at which time he is expected to take all opportunities of annoying his enemy, and improving every advantage over him; to exhibit an example of courage and fortitude to his officers and crew; and to place his ship opposite to his adversary in such a position as that every cannon shall do effectual execution. At the time of his arrival in port, after his return from abroad, he is to assemble his officers, and draw up a detail of the observations that have been made during the voyage, of the qualities of the ship as to her <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a>, ballast, stowage, manner of sailing, for the information and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of those who may succeed him in the command; and this account is to be signed by himself and officers, and to be returned to the resident <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the navy at the port where the ship is discharged. CAPTAIN of a Merchant-ship, he who has the direction of the ship, her crew, and lading, &c. In small ships and short voyages, he is more ordinarily called the master. In the Mediterranean, he is called the patroon.—The proprietor of the vessel appoints the captain or master; and he is to form the crew, and choose and hire the pilots, mates, and seamen; though, when the proprietor and master reside on the same spot, they generally <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> together. CAPTAIN Bajshaw, or Capodan Bajshaw, in the polity of the Turks, signifies the Turkish high admiral. He possesses the third office of the empire, and is invested with the same power at sea that the vizir has on shore. Soliman II. instituted this office in favour of the famous Barbarossa, with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> authority over the officers of the marine and arsenal, whom he may punish, cashier, or put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as soon as he is with- <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">CAPTIVITY</a> pointed out in a manner almost as clear as that of Captivity the tribes of Benjamin and Judah: see Hosea, i. 10. 17. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a> ix. 14. The captivities of Judah are generally reckoned four; the fourth and last of which fell in the year of the world 3416, under Zedekiah; and from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> begins the 70 years captivity foretold by Jeremiah. Since the destruction of the temple by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the Hebrews boast that they have always had their heads or particular princes, whom they call princes of the captivity, in the east and west. The princes of the captivity in the east governed the Jews that dwelt in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; and the princes of the captivity in the west governed those who dwelt in Judaea, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in other parts of the Roman empire. He who resided in Judea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> took up his abode at Tiberias, and assumed the name of Rabbi, "head of the fathers or patriarchs." He presided in assemblies, decided in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, levied taxes for the expenses of his visits, and had officers under him who were despatched through the provinces for the execution of his orders. As to the princes of the captivity at Babylon, or the east, we know neither the original nor succession of them. It only appears that they were not in being before the end of the second century.

CAPTURE

Pages 182-182

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prey; particularly that of a ship taken at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Captures made at sea were formerly held to be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the captors after a possession of twenty-four hours; but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authorities require, that before the property can be changed, the goods must have been brought into port, and have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a night intra praefidia, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of safe custody, so that all hope of recovering them was lost.

CAPTURE ALSO

Pages 182-182

e also denotes an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZURE">seizure</a> of a criminal, debtor, &c. at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>.

CAPUA

Pages 182-183

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Campania, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that district. It is famous for the abode of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> the Carthaginian general after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae, where Livy accuses him, but unjustly, of having enervated himself with pleasures*. It still retains the name, and is the seat of an archbishop. It is seated on the river Volturno, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 5. N. Lat. 41. 7. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Capua is thus shortly deduced by Mr Swinburne. "It was a settlement of the Osci long before the foundation of Rome. As the amazing fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and a lucrative <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> poured immense wealth upon its inhabitants, it became one of the most extensive and magnificent cities in the world. With <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> excessive <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> crept in, and the Capuans grew insolent; but by their effeminacy they soon lost the power of repelling those neighbouring nations which their insolence had exasperated. For this reason Capua was continually exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of calling in foreign aid, and endangering its safety by the uncommon temptations it offered to needy auxiliaries. The Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> sent to defend Capua were on the point of making it their prey, and often the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the Roman people was loud for a removal from the barren unwholesome banks of the Tiber to the garden of Italy, near those of the Volturno. Through well-founded jealousy of the ambition of Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as Livy and other partial writers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> inconstancy, the Capuans warmly espoused the quarrel of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>: Hannibal made Capua his winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of Cannae; and there, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we are to believe historians, his rough and hitherto invincible soldiers were enervated by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and indolence. "When through a failure of supplies from Carthage Hannibal was under a necessity of remaining in Bruttium, and leaving the Capuans to defend themselves, this city, which had been long invested, was surrendered at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> to the consuls Appius Claudius and Q. Fulvius Flaccus. The senators were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> imprisoned for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and all the citizens sold and dispersed. Vibius, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of Hannibal's friends, avoided this ignominious fate, and escaped from the cruel vengeance of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, by a voluntary death. —When the mob inflicted upon the gates being thrown open to the enemy, Vibius assembled his steady associates, and sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with them to a superb banquet, after which each of the guests swallowed a poisonous draught, and expired in full possession of their freedom. The buildings were spared by the victor; and Capua was left to be merely a harbour for the husbandmen of the plain, a warehouse for goods, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> for corn; but so advantageous a situation could not long be neglected; colonies were sent to inhabit it, and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it regained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of importance. "Genferie the Vandal was more cruel than the Roman conquerors had been; for he massacred the inhabitants, and burnt the town to the ground. Narles rebuilt it; but in 841 it was totally destroyed by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Saracens, and the inhabitants driven into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Some time after the retreat of these <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> invaders, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a> ventured down again into the plain; but not deeming their force adequate to the defense of so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a circuit as the old city, they built themselves a smaller one on the river, and called it Capua.—They chose the site of Caflinum, famous in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, for the resistance made by its garrison against Hannibal. Since the foundation of the new city, Old Capua has remained in ruins. "In 876, Landulph formed here an independent earldom dismembered from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BENEVENTO">Benevento</a>, and in the course of a few generations Capua acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality. In the 11th century, the Normans of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVERSA">Aversa</a> expelled the Lombard <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of princes, and Richard their chief became <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Capua; the grandson of Tancred of Hauteville drove out the descendants of Richard, and united this state to the rest of his possessions. "Capua is at present a neat little city, fortified according to the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> art, and may be considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; though far removed from the frontier, it is the only fortification that really covers the approach to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>."

CAPUCHINS

Pages 183-183
religious of the order of St Francis in its strictest observance; deriving their name from capuce, or capuchon, a stuff cap, or cowl, wherewith they cover their heads. They are clothed with brown or gray; always barefooted; are never to go in a coach, nor ever shave their beard.—The Capuchins are a reform made from the order of Minors, commonly called Cordeliers, set on foot in the 16th century by Matthew Baschi, a religious observant of the monastery of Montefiascone; who, being at Rome, was advertised several times from heaven, to practice the rule of St Francis to the letter. Upon this he made application to Pope Clement in 1525; who gave him permission to retire into a solitude, with as many others as chose to embrace the strict observance. In 1528, they obtained the pope's bull. In 1529, the order was brought into complete form: Matthew was elected general, and the chapter made constitutions. In 1543, the right of preaching was taken from the Capuchins by the pope; but in 1545 it was restored to them again with honour. In 1578, there were already 17 general chapters in the order of Capuchins.

CAPUT

Pages 183-183

the head. See HEAD. CAPUT baronice, the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> customs, denotes the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> seat or castle of a nobleman, where he made his usual residence, and held his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; sometimes also called caput honoris, or the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. The caput baronice could not be settled in dowry; nor could it be divided among the daughters, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> there was no son to inherit; but was to descend entire to the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, ceteris filiabus aliunde satisfactis. CAPUT Gallinaginis, in Anatomy, is a kind of septum, or spongy border, at the extremities or apertures of each of the vesiculae seminales; serving to prevent the seed coming from one side, from rushing upon, and stopping, the discharge of the other. CAPUT Lupinum. Anciently an outlawed felon was said to have caput lupinum, and might be knocked on the head like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, by any one that should meet him; because, having renounced all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he was to be dealt with as in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, when every one that should find him might slay him; yet now, to avoid such inhumanity, it is holden that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is entitled to kill him wantonly and wilfully; but in so doing he is guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, unless it is done in the endeavour to apprehend him. CAPUT Mortuum, a Latin name given to fixed and exhausted residuum remaining in retorts after distillations. As these residua are very different, according to the substances distilled, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> employed, they are by the more accurate <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> chemists particularly specified by adding a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denoting their qualities; as earthly residuum, charry residuum, saline residuum, &c.

CARABINE

Pages 183-183

a fire arm shorter than a musket, carrying a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of 24 in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, borne by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, hanging at a belt over the left shoulder. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> is two feet and a half <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and is sometimes furrowed spirally within, which is said to add to the range of the piece.

CARABINEERS

Pages 183-183

regiments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, carrying longer carbines than the rest, and sometimes used on foot. CARABUS. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARACALLA

Pages 183-184

M. Antoninus Bassianus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> after his father Severus in 211, put the physicians to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for not dispatching his father, as he would have had them. He killed his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Geta; and put Papinianus to death, because he would not defend nor excuse his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARRICIDE">parricide</a>. In short, it is said that 20,000 persons were massacred by his order. He married Julia, his father's widow. Going to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, he slew the inhabitants, and applied to the magicians and astrologers. At last, going from Edfessa to Mesopotamia, one of his captains slew him, by order of Macrinus, who succeeded him. He died after he had reigned somewhat more than five years. Caracalla, in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> garment, having a sort of capuchin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hood a-top, and reaching to the heels; worn equally among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the men and the women, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. Spartan and Xiphilian represent the emperor Caracalla as the inventor of this garment, and hence suppose the appellation Caracalla was first given him. Others, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, make the caracalla originally a Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and only brought to Rome by the emperor above mentioned, who first enjoined the soldiery to wear it. The people call it anionian, from the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who had borrowed the name of Antoninus. The caracalla was a sort of caftock, or furtout. Salmasius, Scaliger, and after them Du Cange, even take the name caftoque to have been formed from that of caraque, for caracalla. This is certain from St Jerome, that the caracalla, with a retrenchment of the capuchin, became an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> garment. It is described as made of several pieces cut and sewed together, and hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the feet; but it is more than probable there were some made shorter, especially out of Rome, otherwise we do not see how it could have fitted the soldiery purposes.

CARACCAS

Pages 184-184

a district of Terra Firma in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, belonging to the Spaniards. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is rocky and mountainous, interspersed with small fertile valleys; subjected at certain seasons of the year to dry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west winds, but blest in general with a clear <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. A very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> illicit trade is carried on by the English and Dutch with this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, notwithstanding all the vigilance of the Spaniards, who have scouts perpetually employed, and breastworks raised in all the valleys. A vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CACAO">cacao</a> trees are cultivated in this province; and it is reckoned that the crop of cacao produced here amounts to more than 100,000 fanegas of 110 pounds each. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a> consumes 20,000; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> a little more; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a> a small cargo; and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from 50 to 60,000. The cultivation of the plant employs 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. Such of them as have obtained their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> have built a little town called Nirva, into which they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> people. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is likewise called Caracas, and is situated in N. Lat. 10.10. Dampier says it stands at a considerable distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, wealthy, and populous; and extremely difficult of access, by reason of the steep and craggy hills over which an enemy must take his route. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this town, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Guaira at two leagues distance serves for a harbour, was for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> open to all the subjects of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, and is still so to the Americans; but the Europeans are not so well treated. In 1728 a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was formed at St Sebastian, which obtained an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of maintaining connexions with this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the new world. Four or five ships which they dispatch every year, fail from thence, but they return to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>.

CARACCI

Pages 184-185
Lewis, Augustine, and Hannibal, three celebrated painters of the Lombard school, all of Bologna. Lewis was born in 1555; and was cousin-german to Augustine and Hannibal, who were brothers, the sons of a tailor, who was yet careful to give them a liberal education. They were both disciples of Caracci, their cousin Lewis. Augustine gained a knowledge of mathematics, ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy, music, poetry, and most of the liberal arts; but, though painting was his principal pursuit, he learned the art of engraving from Cornelius Cort, and surpassed all the masters of his time. Hannibal, again, never deviated from his pencil. These three painters, at length, having reaped all the advantages they could by contemplation and practice, formed a plan of association, continued always together, and laid the foundation of that celebrated school which has ever since been known by the name of Caracci's academy. Hither all the young students, who had a view of becoming masters, referred to be instructed in the rudiments of painting; and here the Caracci taught freely, and without reserve, all that came. Lewis's charge was to make a collection of antique statues and bas-reliefs. They had designs of the best masters, and a collection of curious books on all subjects relating to their art; and they had a skilful anatomist always ready to teach what belonged to the knitting and motions of the muscles, &c. There were often disputations in the academy; and not only painters, but men of learned professions, proposed questions, which were always decided by Lewis. Every body was well received; and though stated hours were allotted to treat of different matters, yet improvements might be made at all hours by the antiquities and the designs which were to be seen. The fame of the Caracci reaching Rome, the cardinal Farnese sent for Hannibal thither, to paint the gallery of his palace. Hannibal was the more willing to go, because he had a great desire to see Raphael's works, with the antique statues and bas-reliefs. The gusto which he took there from the ancient sculpture, made him change his Bolognian manner for one more learned but less natural in the design and in the colouring.—Augustine followed Hannibal, to assist him in his undertaking of the Farnese gallery; but the brothers not rightly agreeing, Farnese sent Augustine to the court of the duke of Parma, where he died in the year 1602, being only 45 years of age. His most celebrated piece of painting is that of the Communion of St Jerome, in Bologna. In the mean while, Hannibal continued working in the Farnese gallery at Rome; and, after inconceivable pains and care, finished the paintings in the perfection in which they are now to be seen. He hoped that the cardinal would have rewarded him in some proportion to the excellence of his work, and the time it took him up, which was eight years; but he was disappointed. The cardinal, influenced by an ignorant Spaniard, his domestic, gave him but a little above 200l. though it is certain he deserved more than twice as many thousands. When the money was brought him, he was so surprized at the injustice done him, that he could not speak a word to the person who brought it. This confirmed him in a melancholy to which his temper naturally inclined, and made him resolve never more to touch his pencil; which resolution he had undoubtedly kept if his necessities had not compelled him to break it. It is said, that his melancholy gained too much upon him, that at certain times it deprived him of the use of his senses. It did not, however, put a stop to his amours; and his debauches at Naples, whither he had retired for the the recovery of his health, brought a distemper upon him of which he died in 1609, when he was 49 years of age. His veneration for Raphael was so great, that it was his deathbed request to be buried in the same tomb with him; which was accordingly done, in the Pantheon or Rotunda at Rome. There are extant several prints of the blest Virgin, and some other subjects, etched by the hand of this incomparable artist. He is said to have been a friendly, plain, honest, and open-hearted man; very communicative to his scholars, and so extremely kind to them, that he generally kept his money in the same box with his colours, where they might have recourse to either as they had occasion. While Hannibal Caracci worked at Rome, Lewis was courted from all parts of Lombardy, especially by the clergy, to make pictures in their churches: and we may judge of his capacity and facility, by the great number of pictures he made, and by the preference that was given him to other painters. In the midst of these employments Hannibal solicited him to come and assist him in the Farnese gallery; and so earnestly, that he could not avoid complying with his request. He went to Rome; corrected several things in that gallery; painted a figure or two himself; and then returned to Bologna, where he died in 1619, aged 64.

CARACOL

Pages 185-185

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, denotes a staircase in a helix <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spiral form.

CARACOLI

Pages 185-185

a kind of metal of which the Caribbees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> natives of the Lesser Antilles, make a sort of ornament in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, which they also call caracoli.—This metal comes from the main <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, something like the Corinthian braids among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. These <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are so perfectly mixed and incorporated together, that the compound which results from them, it is said, has a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> that never alters, how <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> soever it remains in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or under ground. It is somewhat brittle; and they who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at it are obliged to mix a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of gold with it, to make the compound more tough and malleable.

CARACT

Pages 185-185
or CARAT, the name of that weight which expresses the degree of fineness that gold is of. The word is also written carract, carrat, karact, and karra. Its origin is contested: but the most probable opinion is that of Kennet, who derives it from carega, a term which antiently denoted any weight, and came not till of later days to be appropriated to that which expresses the fineness of gold, and the gravity of diamonds. These carats are not real determinate weights, but only imaginary. The whole mass, be the weight what it will, is conceived to be divided into 24 carats; and as many 24th parts as it contains of pure gold, it is called gold of so many carats, or so many carats fine. Thus, gold of 18 carats is a mixture, of which 18 parts are pure gold, and the other six an inferior metal, &c. This is the common way of reckoning in Europe, and at the gold mines in the Spanish West Indies, but with some variation in the subdivision of the carat: among us, it is divided into four grains; among the Germans, into 12 parts; and by the French, according to Mr Helot, into 32. The Chinese reckon by a different division called toucher, of which the highest number, or that which denotes pure gold, is 100; so that 100 touches correspond to our 24 carats, &c. CARACT is also a certain weight which goldsmiths and jewellers use wherewith to weigh precious stones and pearls.—In this sense, the word is by some supposed to be derived from the Greek καράτιον, a fruit which the Latins call filiqua, and we carob bean; each of which may weigh above four grains of wheat, whence the Latin filiqua has been used for a weight of four grains. This caraçt weighs four grains, but they are sometimes lighter than the grains of other weights. Each of these grains is subdivided into $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{4}$, $\frac{1}{8}$, $\frac{1}{16}$, &c.

CARACTACUS

Pages 185-185

a renowned <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> British people called Silures, inhabiting South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. Having valiantly defended his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, he was at length defeated; and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> to Cartimunda, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the Brigantes (inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>), was by her treacherously delivered up to the Romans, and led in triumph to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius; then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; where his noble behaviour, and heroic but pathetic speech, obtained him not only his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but the esteem of the emperor, A.D. 52.

CARAGROUTH

Pages 185-185

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the empire, weighing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> drachms. It goes at Constantinople for 120 apers. There are four sorts of them, which are all equally current and of the same value.

CARAITES

Pages 185-186

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Jews, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among that people, whereof there are still some subsisting in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, Russia, Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, and other places of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, whose distinguishing tenet and practice it is, to adhere closely to the words and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Scripture, exclusive of allegories, traditions, and the like. Leo of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, a rabbin of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, observes, that of all the heresies among that people, before the destruction of the temple, there is none now left but that of the Caraim, a name derived from Micra, which signifies the pure text of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, because of their keeping to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, observing it to the letter, and rejecting all interpretations, paraphrases, and constitutions of the rabbins. Aben <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>, and some other rabbins, treat the Caraites as Sadducees; but Leo de Juda calls them, more accurately, Sadducees reformed; because they believe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, paradise, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, &c., which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Sadducees denied. He adds, however, that they were doubtless originally real Sadducees, and sprung from among them. M. Simon, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, supposes them to have risen hence; that the more knowing among the Jews opposing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> and reveries of the rabbins, and using the pure texts of Scripture to refute their groundless traditions, had the name of Caraim given them; which signifies as much as the barbarous Latin Scripturarii; i.e., people attached to the text of Scripture. The other Jews gave them the odious name Sadducees, from their agreement with those sectaries on the head of traditions. Scaliger, Vossius, and Spanheim, Caraites, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> the Caraïtes among the Sabaeans, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANICHEES">Manichees</a>, and Mahommedans, but by mistake: Wolfgang, Fabricius, &c. say the Sadducees and Essenes were called Caraïtes, in opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; others take them for the doctors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> so often mentioned in the Gospel: but these are all conjectures, Josephus and Philo make no mention of them; which shows them to be more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> than either of those authors. In all probability, this sect was not formed till after the collection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Gemara; perhaps not till after the compiling of the Mishnah in the third century. The Caraïtes themselves pretend to be the remains of the ten tribes led captive by Shalmaneser. Wolfius, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Mardacheus, a Caraïte, refers their origin to a massacre among the Jewish doctors under Alexander Janneaus, their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, about 100 years before Christ: because Simon, son of Schetach, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, making his escape into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, there forged his pretended traditions; and, at his return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, published his visions; interpolating the law after his own fancy, and supporting his novelties on the notices which God, he said, had communicated by the mouth of Moses, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> he was: he gained many followers; and was opposed by others, who maintained, that all which God had revealed to Moses was written. Hence the Jews became divided into two sects, the Caraïtes and Traditionists: among the first, Juda, son of Tabbaï, distinguished himself; among the latter, Hillel. Wolfius reckons not only the Sadducees, but also the Scribes, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Caraïtes. But the addrets of the Pharisees prevailed against them all; and the number of Caraïtes decreased: Anan, indeed, in the eighth century, retrieved their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> a little; and Rabbi Schalom in the ninth. They succeeded pretty well till the fourteenth; but since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they have been declining. The Caraïtes are but little known; their works coming only into very few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, even among the greatest Hebraists. Buxtorf never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> more than one; Selden two; but Mr Trigland says, he has recovered enough to speak of them with assurance. He affirms, that soon after the prophets had ceased, the Jews became divided on the subject of works, and supererogation: some maintaining their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>; whilst others, keeping <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the written law, set them aside; and it was from these last that Caraitism commenced. He adds, that after the return from the Babylonian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, the observation of the law being to be re-established, there were several practices found proper for that end; and these once introduced, were looked upon as essential, and appointed by Moses; which was the origin of Pharisaïsm: as a contrary party, continuing to keep close to the letter, founded Caraitism. The modern Caraïtes, Leo of Modena observes, have their synagogues and ceremonies; they pretend to be the sole proper Jews, or observers of the laws of Moses; calling the rest by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Rabbinim, or followers of the Rabbins: these hate the Caraïtes mortally; refusing to ally or even to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with them, and treating them as mamzeim, bastards; because of their rejecting the constitutions of the rabbins relating to marriages, repudiations, purifications of women, &c. This aversion is so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a Caraïte should become a Rabbinit, he would never be received by the other Jews. The Caraïtes, however, do not absolutely reject all kinds of traditions; but only such as do not appear well grounded. Selden, who is very expert on this point, in his Uxor Hebraica, observes, that, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> text, they have certain interpretations, which they call <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, and which are proper traditions. Their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> only seems to differ from that of the other Jews, in that it is purer, and clearer of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; they give no credit to the explications of the Cabalists, chimerical allegories, nor to any constitutions of the Talmud, but what are conformable to the Scripture, and may be drawn from it by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and necessary consequences. Peringer observes of the Caraïtes in Lithuania, that they are very different, both in aspect, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and manners, from the Rabbinites, wherewith the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounds. Their mother tongue is the Turkish; and this they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and synagogues. In vogue they resemble the Mahometan Tartars. Their synagogues are placed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south; and the reason they give for it is, that Shalmaneser brought them northward: so that, in praying, to look to Jerusalem, they must turn to the south. He adds, that they admit all the books of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of many of the learned, who hold that they reject all but the Pentateuch. Calvin, a Caraïte, reduces the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them and the Rabbinites to three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>: 1. In that they deny the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-ORAL">oral</a> law to have come from Moses, and reject the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABALA">Cabala</a>. 2. In that they abhor the Talmud. 3. In that they observe the feasts, as the sabbaths, &c., much more rigorously than the Rabbins do. To this may be added, that they extend the degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a>, wherein <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> is prohibited, almost to infinity.

CARAMANIA

Pages 186-186

a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Anatolia. Bajazet united this province to his empire about the year 1488, and since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it has <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the possession of the Turks. Satalia was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but is now much decayed.

CARAMANTA

Pages 186-186

a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name in Terra Firme, and in the audience of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72. 35. N. Lat. 5. 18. The province of Caramanta is extended on both sides the river Cauca; and is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the district of Cartagena, on the east by New Grenada, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPAYAN">Popayan</a>, and on the west by Popayan and by the audience of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>. It is a valley surrounded on every side by very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>.

CARANGA

Pages 186-186

an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> in the East Indies. It affords nothing but some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, fowls, and goats, for that market.

CARANNA

Pages 186-186
or Karanna, a very scarce gum which comes from New Spain. It is said to possess many extraordinary medical virtues, but the present practice takes no notice of it.

CARANUS

Pages 186-186

the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon, and the seventh of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the Heraclidæ. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">MACEDONIA</a>.

CARARA

Pages 186-187

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, and in other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, used in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> and cod fish, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 60 pounds of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. CARAT. See CARACT.

CARAVAN

Pages 187-187
or KARAVANNE, in the east, signifies a company or assembly of travellers and pilgrims, and more particularly of merchants, who, for their greater security, and in order to assist each other, march in a body through the deserts, and other dangerous places, which are infested with Arabs or robbers. There are four regular caravans which go yearly to Mecca; the first from Damascus, composed of the pilgrims from Europe and Asia; the second from Cairo, from the Mahomedans of Barbary; the third from Zibith, a place near the mouth of the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red sea, where those of Arabia and India meet; the fourth from Babylon, where the Persians assemble. Most of the inland commerce of the east is carried on by caravans. The late czar Peter the Great established a trade between Russia and China by means of a caravan. M. Bougnon, geographer to the duke of Lorraine, has given a treatise of the caravans of merchants in Asia; wherein he shows of what they are composed, how many sorts there are; the several uses of the different sorts of animals in them; the prices given for them, the officers and men appointed to conduct them, and the pay of each, with their manner of marching, halting, fighting, retreating, &c. Caravans of this kind are large convoys of armed men, merchants, and travellers, with divers sorts of animals for the carriage of their provisions. There are commonly four chief officers of a caravan, viz. the caravan bachi, or chief; the captain guide; captain of rest; and captain of distribution. The first has absolute command over all the rest: the second is absolute in the march: the office of the third only commences when the caravan stops and makes a stay: to the fourth it belongs to dispose of every part of the corps, in case of an attack or battle; he has also the inspection over the distribution of provisions, which is made under him by several distributors, who give security to the master of the caravan, and have each of them a certain number of persons, elephants, dromedaries, &c., to take care of at their own peril. The treasurer of the caravan makes a fifth officer, who has under him several agents and interpreters, who keep journals of all that passes, for the satisfaction of those concerned in fitting out the caravan. Any dealer is at liberty to form a company, in order to make a caravan. He in whose name it is raised, is considered as the caravan bachi, or chief of the caravan, unless he appoint some other in his place. If there are several merchants equally concerned, they elect a caravan bachi; after which, they appoint officers to conduct the caravan, and decide all controversies that may arise during the journey. There are also sea caravans; established on the same footing, and for the same purpose: such is the caravan of vessels from Constantinople to Alexandria.

CARAVANSEKASKIER

Pages 187-187

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> keeper of a CARAVANSERA. He keeps an account of all the merchandises that are sold upon trust, and demands the payments of the sums due to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> for what has been sold in the caravansera, on the seller's paying two per cent. CARAVEL; thus they call a small vessel on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of France, which goes to fish for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> on the banks. They are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> from 25 to 30 tons burden. Those which are designed for the same fishery in the British channel are called by the French trimarins; these are from 12 to 15 tons burden. CARAWAY. See CARUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARAVANSERA

Pages 187-187
or KARAVANSERA, a place appointed for receiving and loading the caravans. It is commonly a large square building, in the middle of which there is a very spacious court; and under the arches or piazzas that surround it there runs a bank, raised some feet above the ground, where the merchants, and those who travel with them in any capacity, take up their lodgings as well as they can; the beasts of burden being tied to the foot of the bank. Over the gates that lead into the court, there are sometimes little rooms, which the keepers of the caravanseras let out at a very high price to such as have a mind to be private. The caravanseras in the east are something of the nature of the inns in Europe; only that you meet with little accommodation either for man or beast, but are obliged to carry almost every thing with you: there is never a caravansera without a well, or spring of water. These buildings are chiefly owing to the charity of the Mahometans: they are esteemed sacred dwellings, where it is not permitted to insult any person, or to pillage any of the effects that are deposited there. There are also caravanseras where most things may be had for money; and as the profits of these are considerable, the magistrates of the cities to whose jurisdiction they belong, take care to store them well. There is an inspector, who, at the departure of each caravan, fixes the price of the night's lodging, from which there is no appeal.

CARBONADE

Pages 187-187
or CARBONADO, in cookery; flesh, fowl, or the like, seasoned and broiled on the coals.

CARBUNCLE

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, consisting of eight radii, four whereof make a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and the other four a saltier. Some call these radii buttons, or flames, because round, and enriched with buttons, or pearly like pilgrims' flames, and frequently tipped or terminated with flower-de-luces.

CARCASSONE

Pages 187-188

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, with a bishop's see. It is divided into the upper and lower town. They are both surrounded with walls; and though their situations are different, they are both watered by the river Aude. The upper town is seated on a hill, with a castle that commands it as well as the lower town. It is strong, not only by its situation on a craggy rock, but also by several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> towers which are joined to its walls, and which render it of difficult access. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is remarkable for nothing but its antiquity. The lower town is large, and built after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The streets are very straight, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a large <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> in the middle, from whence may be seen the four gates of the town. There is here a manufacture of cloth. The neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is full of olive-trees; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> there is a fine marble, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called marble of Languedoc. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 25'. N. Lat. 43° 11'. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> bore a considerable share in that celebrated crusade undertaken against the Albigenses in the beginning of the 13th century, and which forms one of the most astonishing instances of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and of atrocious barbarity to be found in the annals of the world. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> power was nearly annihilated, during the reigns of the last kings of the Carolingian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> in France, most of the cities of Languedoc credited themselves into little independent states, governed by their own princes. Carcassone was then under the dominion of viceroys. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when Pope Innocent III. patronized and commanded the prosecution of hostilities against the Albigenses for the crime of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, Raymond the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> was included in that proscription. Simon de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>, general of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the church, invested the city of Carcassone in 1299. The inhabitants, terrified at the fate of several other places where the most dreadful massacres had been committed, demanded leave to capitulate; but this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of mercy was only extended to them under a condition equally cruel, incredible, and unparalleled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we are not compelled to believe it by the unanimous testimony of all the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> writers. The people found in the place were all obliged, without distinction of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, to evacuate it in a state of nudity; and Agnes the vicar was not exempted, though young and beautiful, from this ignominious and shocking <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. "On les fit fortir tout nus de la ville de Carcassone (says an ancient author) afin qu'ils receussent de la honte, en montrant ces parties du corps que la pureté de la langue n'exprime point, desquelles ils avoient abuse, et s'en estoient servis dans des crimes excrables." It seems by this imputation that the Albigois were accused by their enemies of some enormities, probably unjust, and similar to those which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> enmity and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> have attributed to the followers of Zinzendorf in the present century.

CARCERES

Pages 188-188

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Circenian games, were inclosures in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, wherein the horses were restrained till the signal was given for starting, when by an admirable contrivance, they all at once flew open.

CARCHEMISH

Pages 188-188

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town lying upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, and belonging to the Assyrians. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECHO">Necho</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> took it from the king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, 2 Chr. xxxv. 20.
