Necho left a garrison in it, which was taken and cut to pieces, in the fourth year of Jehoiachin king of Judah, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, 2 Kings xxiii. 29. Isaiah (x. 9.) speaks of Carchemish, and seems to say, that Tiglath-pileser made a conquest of it, perhaps from the Egyptians. This is thought to be the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> with that called Circeum by the Greeks and Latins.

CARCINOMA

Pages 188-188

in Medicine; the same with CANCER. See MEDICINE and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">SURGERY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARD

Pages 188-188

among artificers, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood, befit with sharp <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, serving to arrange the hairs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and the like; there are different kinds of them, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, stock-cards, &c. They are made as follows: A piece of thick <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, of the size intended for the card, is strained in a frame for that purpose; and then pricked full of holes, into which the teeth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wire are inserted. After which the leather is nailed by the edges to a flat piece of wood, in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, about a foot in length, and half a foot in breadth, with a handle placed in the middle of one of the longer sides. The teeth are made in the following manner. The wire being drawn of the size intended, a skin or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of wires are cut into proper lengths by means of a gauge, and then doubled in a tool contrived for that purpose; after which they are bent into the proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> by means of another tool; and then placed in the leather, as mentioned above.

CARDAMINE

Pages 189-189

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of the filiqua order, belonging to the tetradyamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 39th order Silicaceae. The filique parts adnate with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and the valves roll spirally backward; the stigma is entire, and the calyx a little gaping. Of this there are 15 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the most remarkable is the pratensis, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> purplish flower. This grows naturally in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and is also called cuckowflower. There are four varieties, viz. the single, with purple and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are frequently intermixed in the meadows; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, of both colours. The single sorts are not admitted into gardens; but the double deserve a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, as making a pretty appearance during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they are in flower. They <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive in a moist shady border; and are propagated by parting their roots, which is best performed in autumn. They delight in a soft loamy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, not too stiff. By some the plant is reckoned antifebrifuge.

CARDAN

Pages 189-190

JEROM, one of the most extraordinary geniuses of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a> on the 24th of September 1501. As his mother was not married, she tried every method to procure an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>, but without effect. She was three days in labour, and they were at last obliged to cut the child from her. He was born with his head covered with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> curled <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. When he was four years old, he was carried to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; his father being an advocate in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. At the age of 20, he went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at the university of that city; and two years afterwards he explained Euclid. In 1524, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>; and the same year he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts: in the end of the following year, he took the degree of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic. He married about the year 1531. For ten years before, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a> had hindered him from having knowledge of a woman; which was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mortification to him. He attributed it to the evil influences of his planet under which he was born. When he enumerates, as he frequently does, the greatest misfortunes of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, this ten years impotence is always one. At the age of 32, he became professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at Milan. In 1539, he was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians at Milan; in 1543, he read public lectures of medicine in that city, and at Pavia the year following; but discontinued them because he could not get payment of his salary, and returned to Milan. In 1552, he went into Scotland, having been sent for by the archbishop of St Andrew's, who had in vain applied to the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s physicians, and afterwards to those of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany. This prelate, then 40 years old, had for ten years been afflicted with a shortness of breath, which returned every eight days for the last two years. He began to recover from the moment that Cardan prescribed for him. Cardan took his leave of him at the end of six weeks. and three days, leaving him prescriptions which in two years wrought a complete cure. Cardan's journey to Scotland gave him an opportunity of visiting several countries. He crossed France in going thither; and returned through Germany, and the Low Countries, along the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. It was on this occasion he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and calculated King Edward's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. This tour took up about four months: after which, coming back to Milan, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there till the beginning of October 1552; and then went to Pavia, from whence he was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in 1562. He taught in this last city till the year 1570; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was thrown into prison; but some months after he was sent home to his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. He left Bologna in 1571; and went to Rome, where he lived for some time without any public employment. He was, however, admitted a member of the college of physicians, and received a pension from the pope. He died at Rome on the 21st of September 1575, according to Thuanus. This account might be sufficient to show the reader that Cardan was of a very fickle temper; but he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have a much better idea of his singular and odd turn of mind by examining what he himself has written concerning his own good and bad qualities. He paid himself congratulatory compliments for not having a friend in this world; but that in requital, he was attended by an aerial spirit, emanated partly from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and partly from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who was the constant guide of his actions, and teacher of every duty to which he was bound. He declared, too, that he was so <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> in his manner of walking the streets, as induced all beholders to point at him as a fool. Sometimes he walked very slowly, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> absorbed in profound meditation; then all on a sudden quickened his steps, accompanying them with very absurd attitudes. In Bologna his delight was to be drawn about in a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> vehicle with three <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>. When <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> did not visit him with any pain, he would procure to himself that disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> by biting his lips so wantonly, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pulling his fingers to such a vehement degree, as sometimes to force the tears from his eyes: and the reason he assigned for so doing, was to moderate certain impetuous fallacies of the mind, the violence of which was to him by far more insupportable than pain itself; and that the sure <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such a severe <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> was the enjoying the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. He says elsewhere, that, in the greatest tortures of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, he used to whip his legs with rods, and bite his left arm; that it was a great relief to him to weep, but that very often he could not; that nothing gave him more pleasure than to talk of things which made the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> uneasy; that he spoke on all subjects, in season and out of season; and he was so fond of games of chance, as to spend whole days in them, to the great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of his family and reputation, for he even staked his furniture and his wife's jewels. Cardanus makes no scruple of owning that he was revengeful, envious, treacherous, a dealer in the black-art, a backbiter, a calumniator, and addicted to all the foul and detestable excesses that can be imagined: yet notwithstanding (as one would think) so humbling a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, there was never perhaps a vainer mortal, or one that with less <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> expressed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> he had of himself, than Cardanus was known to do, as will appear by the following proofs. "I have been admired by many nations: an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of panegyrics, both in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, have been composed to celebrate my fame. I was born to release the world from the manifold errors under which it groaned. What I have found out could not be discovered either by my predecessors or my contemporaries; and that is the reason why those authors who write anything worthy of being remembered, scruple not to own that they are indebted to me for it. I have composed a book on the dialectic art, in which there is neither one superfluous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> nor one deficient. I finished it in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days, which seems a prodigy. Yet where is there a person to be found, that can boast of having become master of its doctrine in a year? And he that shall have comprehended it in that time, must appear to have been instructed by a familiar daemon." The same capriciousness observable in his outward conduct is to be observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of his works. We have a multitude of his treatises in which the reader is stopped almost every moment by the obscurity of his text, or his digressions from the point in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. In his arithmetical performances there are several discourses on the motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, and on the tower of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>. In his dialectic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, we find his judgement on the historians and the writers of epistles. The only apology which he makes for the frequency of his digressions is, that they were purposely done for the sooner filling up of his sheet, his bargain with the bookseller being at so much per sheet: and that he worked as much for his daily support as for the acquisition of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. The Lyons edition of his works, printed in 1663, consists of ten volumes in folio. It was Cardanus who revived in latter times all the secret <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the Cabbala or Cabalists, which filled the world with spirits; a likeness to whom, he asserted, we might attain by purifying ourselves with philosophy. He chose for himself, however, notwithstanding such reveries, this fine device, Tempus mea pofficio, tempus meus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">ager</a>: "Time is my sole possession, and the only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> I have to improve." In fact, when we consider the transcendent qualities of Cardan's mind, we cannot deny his having cultivated it with every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of knowledge, and his having made a greater progress in philosophy, in the medical art, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, in mathematics, &c. than the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his contemporaries who had applied their minds but to one of those sciences. Scaliger affirms, that Cardan, having fixed the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, abstained from food, that this prediction might be fulfilled, and that his continuance to live might not discredit his art. Cardan's father, who was a doctor of medicine, and a professor of civil and canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, died in the same manner in the year 1524, having abstained from all sustenance for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days. His son tells us that he had <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> eyes, and could see in the night time.

CARDASS

Pages 190-190

is also the name which, in the cloth manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, they give to a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> card, which is used for carding the dyed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, designed for making cloth of mixed colours.

CARDERS

Pages 190-191

in the woollen manufactory, are persons who prepare <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, &c., for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, &c. Carders, spinners, weavers, fullers, shearmen, and dyers, not performing their duty in their occupations, shall yield to the party grieved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> damages; to be committed until payment. One <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to hear and determine complaints. Carders, combers, sorters, spinners, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> weavers, conveying away, embezzling, or detaining any wool or yarn, delivered by the clothier, or any other person, shall give the party grieved such satisfaction, as two justices, mayor, &c., shall think fit; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not able or willing to make satisfaction, for the first offence to be whipped, or set in the stocks in some market-town, or in any other town where the offence is committed: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> offence to incur the like, or such further <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by whipping, &c., as justices shall think proper. Conviction by one witness on oath, or confession.

CARDIAC

Pages 191-191

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies all medicines beneficial to the heart, whether internally <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> externally applied. The word comes from the Greek word καρδία, cor; the heart being reputed the immediate seat of their operation.

CARDIACS

Pages 191-191

in a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denote medicines which raise the spirits and give present strength and cheerfulness; these amount to the same with what are properly called cordials. Cardiacs are medicines anxiously supposed to exert themselves immediately in comforting and strengthening the heart: but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> physicians rather suppose them to produce the effect by putting the blood into a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, whereby the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, before decayed, are repaired and invigorated, and the tone and elasticity of the fibres of the vessels restored; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which is a more easy and brisk circulation.

CARDIALGIA

Pages 191-191

in Medicine, a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> acrimony felt towards the upper or left orifice of the stomach, though seemingly at the heart; sometimes accompanied with palpitations of the heart, fainting, and a propensity to vomit: better known by the name of cardiac pallion, or heart-burn. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARDIFF

Pages 191-191

a town of Glamorganshire, in South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, seated on the river Tawe, in a rich and fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, well-built town, having a castle, a wall, and four gates, built by Robert Fitz-Hamon, a Norman, about the year 1100. It is governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of the castle, 12 aldermen, 12 burgesses, &c., and sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Here the assizes and sessions are held, besides several courts. There is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river, to which small vessels come to take in their lading. It has now only one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s having been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> since thrown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the undermining of the river. The castle, though much decayed, makes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> appearance even at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the walls of the town are very strong and thick. The church has a fine tower-steeple, and the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is a good structure. The magistrates are elected every year by the majority of the burgesses. W. Long. 3° 20'. N. Lat. 51° 30'. Cardiff gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a British baron to the family of Bute in Scotland.

CARDIGAN

Pages 191-191

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of Cardiganshire, in South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, is seated near the mouth of the river Teivy, on the Irish channel. It is indifferently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well-built, containing three wards, one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-gaol. It is governed by a mayor, 13 aldermen, 13 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men, &c. Here are the ruins of a castle which was built by Gilbert de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>, about the year 1100. It sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and has two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, held on Tuesdays and Saturdays. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 38'. N. Lat. 52° 15'.

CARDIGANSHIRE

Pages 191-191

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a> and Brecknockshire, on the west by the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAERMARTHENSHIRE">Caermarthenshire</a>. Its length from north-west to south-east is about 44 miles, and its breadth near 20. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as in other parts of Wales, varies with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which in the southern and western parts is more upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> than this principality generally is, which renders the air mild and temperate. But as the northern and eastern parts are mountainous, they are consequently more barren and bleak. However, there are cattle bred in all parts; but they have neither wood nor coals of their own for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>: they have rich <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and fish in plenty, with fowls both tame and wild. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Teivy, the Ridol, and the Iffith. This county hath five market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. Cardigan, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABERYSTWITH">Aberystwith</a>, Llanbadarnvawn, Llambedan, and Tregaron, with 77 parishes; and was formerly computed to have upwards of 3000 houses, and 520,000 acres of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; one for the county, and one for Cardigan.

CARDINAL

Pages 191-194

an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, being one who has a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the conclave at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a pope. Some say the cardinals were so called from the Latin incardinatio, which signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> in any church made of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of a foreign church, driven thence by misfortune; and add, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word commenced at Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>; the revenues of the churches of which cities being very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, they became the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> refuge of the unhappy priests of all other churches. The cardinals compose the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>: in the Vatican is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of Pope John, which regulates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and titles of the cardinals; and which declares, that as the pope represents Moses, so the cardinals represent the seventy elders, who, under the pontifical authority, decide private and particular differences. Cardinals, in their first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, were only the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> priests, or incumbents of the parishes of Rome. In the primitive church, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> priest of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, who immediately followed the bishop, was called prebyter cardinalis, to distinguish him from the other petty priests, who had no church nor preferment; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> was first applied to them in the year 150; others say, under Pope Silvester, in the year 300. These cardinal priests were alone allowed to baptize, and administer the eucharist. When the cardinal priests became <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, their cardinalate became vacant; they being then supposed to be raised to a higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>.—Under Pope Gregory, cardinal priests, and cardinal deacons, were only such priests and deacons as had a church or chapel under their particular care: and this was the original use of the word. Leo IV., in the council of Rome, held in 853, calls them prebyteros sui cardinis; and their churches, parochias cardinales. The cardinals <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on this footing till the eleventh century; but as the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and state of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> became then exceedingly augmented, he would have his council of cardinals make a better <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> priests had done. It is true, they still preserved their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>; but the thing expressed by it was no more. It was a good while, however, before they had the precedence over the bishops, or got the election of the pope into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>: but when they were once possessed of those privileges, they soon had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hat and purple; and growing still in authority, they became at length superior to the bishops, by the sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of being cardinals. Du Cange observes, that originally there were three kinds of churches: the first or genuine churches were properly called parishes; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> deanories, which were chapels joined to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and served by deacons; the third were simple oratories, where private masses were said, and were discharged by local and resident chaplains. He adds, that to distinguish the principal or parish churches from the chapels and oratories, the name cardinales was given to them. Accordingly, parish churches gave titles to cardinal priests; and some chapels also, at length, gave the title of cardinal deacons. Others observe, that the term cardinal was given not only to priests, but also to bishops and deacons who were attached to certain churches, to distinguish them from those who only served them en paupertate, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TITULAR">Titular</a> churches, or benefices, were a kind of parishes, i.e., churches, assigned each to a cardinal priest; with some stated district depending on it, and a font for administering of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the bishop himself could not administer it. These cardinals were subordinate to the bishops; and accordingly, in councils, particularly that held at Rome in 868, subscribed after them. It was not, however, only at Rome, that priests bore this name; for we find there were cardinal priests in France: thus, the curate of the parish of St John de Vignes is called in old charters the cardinal priest of that parish. The title of cardinal is also given to some bishops, quatenus binopos; e.g., to those of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>: the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a> is also, in ancient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, called cardinal; and the church of Bourges, a cardinal church. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of Vendome calls himself cardinalis natus. The cardinals are divided into three classes or orders; containing five bishops, fifty priests, and fourteen deacons; making in all seventy: which constitute what they call the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. The cardinal bishops, who are, as it were, the pope's vicars, bear the titles of the bishoprics assigned to them; the rest take such titles as are given them: the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cardinal bishops has been fixed; but that of cardinal priests and deacons, and consequently the sacred college itself, is always fluctuating. Till the year 1125, the college only consisted of fifty-two or fifty-three: the council of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a> reduced them to twenty-four; but Sixtus IV., without any regard to that restriction, raised them again to fifty-three, and Leo to sixty-five. Thus, as the number of cardinal priests was anciently fixed to twenty-eight, new titles were to be established, in proportion as new cardinals were created. As for the cardinal deacons, they were originally no more than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> for the fourteen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of Rome; but they were afterwards increased to nineteen, and after that were again diminished. According to Onuphrius, it was Pope Pius IV., who first enacted, in 1562, that the pope should be chosen only by the senate of cardinals; whereas, till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the election was by all the clergy of Rome. Some say, the election of the pope rested in the cardinals, excluding five of the clergy, in the time of Alexander III., in 1160. Others go higher still, and say, that Nicholas II., having been elected at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, in 1058, by the cardinals alone, occasioned the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of election to be taken from the clergy and people of Rome; only leaving them that of confirming him by their consent; which was at length, however, taken from them. See his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> for this purpose, issued in the Roman council of 1059, in Hardouin's Acta Conciliorum, tom. vii. pt. i. p. 1165. Whence it appears, that the cardinals who had the right of suffrage in the election of his successors, were divided by this pontiff into cardinal bishops and cardinal clerks; meaning by the former the seven bishops who belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and territory of Rome; and by the latter, the cardinal prebendaries, or ministers of the twenty-eight Roman parishes, or principal churches. To these were added, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, under Alexander III., and other pontiffs, new members, in order to appease the tumults occasioned by the edict of Nicholas II. At the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of a new cardinal, the pope performs the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of opening and shutting his mouth; which is done in a private confirmary. The shutting his mouth implies the depriving him of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of giving his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in congregations; and the opening his mouth, which is performed 15 days after, signifies the taking off his restraint. However, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the pope happens to die during the time a cardinal's mouth is shut, he can neither give his voice in the election of a new pope, nor be himself advanced to that dignity. The dress of a cardinal is a red fountaine, a rocket, a short purple mantle, and a red hat. The cardinals began to wear the red hat at the council of Lyons, in 1243. The decree of Pope Urban VIII, whereby it is appointed, that the cardinals be addressed under the title of eminence, is of the year 1630; till then, they were called illuftrifimi. When cardinals are sent to the courts of princes, it is in quality of legates à latere; and when they are appointed governors of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is called by the name of legation. Cardinal has also been applied to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> officers. Thus, the prime ministers in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius, are called cardinaler. Cassiodorus, lib. vii. formul. 31, makes mention of the cardinal prince of the city of Rome; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bretagne, in 1447, we meet with one Raoul de Thorel, cardinal of Quillart, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the vicount de Rohan: which shows it to have been an inferior quality. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDIOID">Cardioid</a>, in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, an algebraical curve, so called from its resemblance to a heart. Cardiospermum. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Cardium, or Cockle, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes testacea. The shell consists of two equal valves, and the sides are equal. There are 21 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus. Common on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> coasts, lodged a little beneath the sand; their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is marked by a depressed spot. They are wholesome and delicious food. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDONA">Cardona</a>, a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Catalonia, with a strong castle, and the title of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. Near it is an inexhaustible mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of several colours, as red, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, carnation, and green: but when washed, it becomes white. There are also vineyards which produce excellent wine, and very lofty pines. It is situated on an eminence, near the river Cardenero. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 26. N. Lat. 41. 42. Carduus. See Botany Index. Carduus Benedictus, Blest thistle. See Cnicus, Botany Index. Careening, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the bringing a ship to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on one side, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> and caulk the other side. A ship is said to be brought to the careen, when the most of her lading being taken out, she is hulled down on one side, by a small vessel, as low as necessary; and there kept by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the ballast, ordnance, &c., as well as by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, lest her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> should be strained too much; in order that her sides and bottom may be trimmed, seams caulked, or any thing that is faulty under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mended. Hence, when a ship lies on one side when she sails, she is said to fail on the careen. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">Career</a>, in the manege, a place inclosed with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, wherein they run the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>. The word is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> or course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> itself, provided it do not exceed 200 paces. In the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, the career was the space the bigae, or quadrigae, were to run at full speed, to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. See Circus. Career, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCONRY">falconry</a>, is a flight or tour of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, about 120 yards. If the mount more, it is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> career; if less, a semi-career. Carelia, the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>; divided into Swedish Carelia, and Muscovite Carelia. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the latter is Povenza, and of the former Weiburg. Carelsroon, a sea-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in Blekingia, or Bleking, on the Baltic sea, with a very good harbour defended by two forts. It was built in 1679; and is very populous, with arsenals for the marine: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>-general of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> is in this town, and here the Swedes lay up their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. E. Long. 15. 5. N. Lat. 66. 15. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARENTAN">Carentan</a>, a town of France in Lower Normandy, and in the Contentin, with an ancient castle. W. Long. 1. 14. N. Lat. 49. 20. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARET">Caret</a>, among grammarians, a character marked thus A, signifying that something is added on the margin, or interlined, which ought to come in where the caret stands. Carew, George, born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> in 1557, an eminent commander in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, was made <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; when, joining his forces with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Thomond, he reduced the Irish insurgents, and brought the earl of Desmond to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James made him governor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUERNSEY">Guernsey</a>, and created him a baron. As he was a valiant commander, he was no less a polite scholar; and wrote Pacata Hibernia, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the late wars in Ireland, printed after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 1633. He made several collections for a History of Henry V. which are digested into Speed's History of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Besides these, he collected materials of Irish history in four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> MSS. volumes, now in the Bodleian library, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Carew, Thomas, descended from the family of Carew in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the privy chamber to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. who always esteemed him one of the most celebrated wits of his court. He was much respected by the poets of his time, particularly by Ben Jonson and Sir William Davenant; and left behind him several poems, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASQUE">masque</a> called Calum Britannicum, performed at Whitehall on Shrove Tuesday night, 1633, by the king, and several of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> with their sons. Carew was assisted in the contrivance by Inigo Jones, and the music was set by Mr Henry Lawes of the king's chapel. He died in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, about the year 1639. Carew, Richard, author of the "Survey of Cornwall," was the eldest son of Thomas Carew of East Anthony, and was born in 1555. When very young, he became a gentleman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of Christ-church college, Oxford; and at 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of disputing, extempore, with the afterwards famous Sir <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a>, in the presence of the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. After spending three years at the university, he removed to the Middle Temple, where he resided the same length of time, and then travelled into foreign parts. Not long after his return to England, he married, in 1577, Juliana <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a>, of Trerice. In 1681, Mr Carew was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, and in 1586 was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cornwall; about which time he was likewise queen's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. In 1589, he was elected a member of the college of Antiquaries, a distinction to which he was entitled by his literary abilities and pursuits. What particularly engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was his native county, his "Survey" of which was published, in 4to, at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in 1602. It hath been twice reprinted, first in 1723, and next in 1769. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> Camden hath spoken in high terms, and acknowledges his obligations to the author. In the present improved state of topographical knowledge, and since Dr Borlase's excellent publications relative to the county of Cornwall, the value of Carew's "Survey" must have been greatly diminished. Mr Gough remarks, that the history and monuments of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> were faintly touched by Carew; but it is added, that he was a person extremely capable of describing them, if the infancy of those studies at that time had afforded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and materials. Another work of our author was a translation from the Italian, entitled, "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Men's Wits." In which, by discovering the variety of natures, is showed for what profession each one is apt, and how far he shall profit therein." This was published at London in 1594, and afterwards in 1604; and though Richard Carew's name is prefixed to it, hath been principally ascribed by some persons to his father. According to Wood, Carew wrote also, "The true and ready Way to learn the Latin Tongue," in answer to a query, whether the ordinary method of teaching the Latin by the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> be the best <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of instructing youths in that language? This tract is involved in Mr Hartlib's book upon the same subject, and with the same title. It is certain that Carew was a gentleman of considerable abilities and literature, and that he was held in great estimation by some of the most eminent scholars of his time. He was particularly intimate with Sir Henry Spelman, who extols him for his ingenuity, virtue, and learning. Carew, George, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the subject of the last article, was educated in the university of Oxford, after which he studied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the inns of court, and then travelled to foreign countries for farther improvement. On his return to his native country, he was called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and after some time was appointed secretary to Sir Christopher Hatton, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chancellor of England. This was by the special recommendation of Queen Elizabeth herself, who gave him a prothonotaryship in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, and conferred upon him the honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. In 1597, Sir George Carew, who was then a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in chancery, was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. In the next reign, he was one of the commissioners for treating with the Scotch concerning an union between the two kingdoms; after which he was appointed ambassador to the court of France, where he continued from the latter end of the year 1605 till 1609. During his residence in that country, he formed an intimacy with Thuanus, to whom he communicated an account of the transactions in Poland whilst he was employed there, which was of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to that admirable author in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up the 12th book of his history. After Sir George Carew's return from France, he was advanced to the important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of master of the court of wards, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> situation he did not long live to enjoy; for it appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written by Thuanus to Camden in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> 1613, that he was then lately deceased. Sir George Carew married Thomasine, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir Francis Godolphin, great grandfather of the lord <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Godolphin, and had by her two sons and three daughters. When Sir George Carew returned, in 1609, from his French embassy, he drew up, and addressed to James I., "A Relation of the State of France, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of Henry IV. and the principal persons of that Court." The characters are drawn from personal knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> observation, and might be of service to a general historian of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is perspicuous and manly, and entirely free from the pedantry which prevailed in the reign of James I.; but this is the less surprising, as Sir George Carew's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> had been formed in a better era, that of Queen Elizabeth. The valuable tract we are speaking of lay for a long time in MS.; till happily falling into the hands of the earl of Hardwicke, it was communicated by him to Dr Birch, who published it, in 1749, at the end of his "Historical View of the Negotiations between the Courts of England, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, from 1592 to 1617." That intelligent and industrious writer judiciously observes, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> upon which ambassadors may form and digest their notions and representations; and the late celebrated poet Mr Gray hath spoken of it as an excellent performance.

CARDS

Pages 188-189

among gamesters, little pieces of fine thin pasteboard of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, of several sizes; but most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, three inches and a half <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, on which are painted several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and figures. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> and blocks for making cards are exactly like those that were used for the first printed books. They lay a sheet of wet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> moist <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, which is very lightly done over with a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> diluted in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and mixed with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">starch</a> to give it a body. They afterwards rub it off with a round lift. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-cards are coloured by means of several patterns, styled <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>-files. These consist of papers cut through with a penknife; and in these apertures they apply feverally the various colours, as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, black, &c. These patterns are painted with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-colours, that the brushes may not wear them out; and when the pattern is laid on the pasteboard, they slightly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over it a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> full of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which, leaving it within the openings, forms the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> or figure of the card. Among sharpers, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sorts of false and fraudulent cards have been contrived; as, 1. Marked cards, where the aces, kings, queens, knaves, are marked on the corners of the backs with spots of different <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and order, either with clear water or water tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ink, that those in the secret may distinguish them. Aces are marked with single spots on two corners opposite diagonally; kings with two spots at the same corners; knaves with the same number transferred. 2. Breef cards, those which are longer or broader than the rest: chiefly used at whist and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIQUET">piquet</a>. The broad cards are usually for kings, queens, knaves, and aces; the long for the rest. Their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, to enable him in the secret to cut the cards disadvantageously to his adversary, and draw the person unacquainted with the fraud to cut them favourably for the sharper. As the pack is placed either endwise or sidewise to him that is to cut, the long or broad cards naturally <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to cut them. Breef cards are sometimes made thus by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a>; but, in defect of these, sharpeners pare all but the breefs with a penknife or razor. 3. Corner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, denotes four cards turned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> finely at one corner, to serve as a signal to cut by. 4. Middle bend, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, is where the tricks are bent two different ways, which causes an opening or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> in the middle, to direct likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>. Cards were invented about the year 1390, to divert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI. of France, who had fallen into a melancholy disposition. The inventor proposed, by the figures of the four suits or colours, as the French call them, to represent the four classes of men in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. By the coeurs (hearts) are meant the gens de coeur, choir-men, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>; and therefore the Spaniards, who certainly received the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of cards from the French, have copas, or chalices, instead of hearts. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, or prime <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdom, are represented by the ends or points of lances or pikes; and our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the meaning or the resemblance of the figure induced us to call them spades: The Spaniards have espadas, swords, in lieu of pikes, which are of similar import. By diamonds are designed the order of citizens, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, or tradesmen, carreaux, (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, tiles, or the like): The Spaniards have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, dineros, which answers to it; and the Dutch call the French word carreaux, "streenen," stones and diamonds, from the form. Trefoil, the trefoil-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, or clover-leafs (corruptly called clubs), alludes to the husbandmen and peasants. But how this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> came to be called clubs is not easily explained; unless borrowing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> from the Spaniards, who have bajos (slaves or clubs) instead of the trefoil, we give the Spanish signification to the French figure. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the four kings, which the French, in drollery, sometimes call the cards, are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Alexander, Caesar, and Charles; which names were then, and still are on the French cards. These respectable names represent the four celebrated monarchies of the Jews, Greeks, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Franks under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. By the queens are intended Argine, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>, Judith, and Pallas (names retained in the French cards), typical of birth, piety, fortitude, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, the qualifications residing in each person. Argine is an anagram for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. By the knaves were designed the servants to knights (for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a> originally meant only <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>); but French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> and valets, now indiscriminately used by various orders of persons, were formerly only allowed to persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, esquires (écuyers), shield or armour bearers. Others fancy that the knights themselves were designed by those cards; because Hogier and Lahire, two names on the French cards, were famous knights at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> cards were supposed to have been invented. Deceptions with Cards. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGERDEMAIN">Legerdemain</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. i.

CAREY

Pages 194-195

HARRY, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> distinguished by both <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and music, but perhaps more so by a certain facetiousness, which made him agreeable to every body. He published in 1720 a little collection of poems; and in 1732, six cantatas, written and composed by himself. He also composed sundry songs for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> comedies, particularly those in the "Provoked Husband;" he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> called "The Contrivances," in which were several little songs to very pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>; he also made two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three little dramas for Goodman's-fields <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, which were very favourably received. In 1729, he published by subscription his poems much enlarged: with the addition of one entitled "Namby Pamby," in which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> Philips is ridiculed. Carey's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, says his historian, lay in humour and unamiable satire: to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> the rant and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a> of modern tragedies he wrote one, to which he gave the strange <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Chrononhotonthologos;" acted in 1734. He also wrote a farce called "The Honest Yorkshireman." Carey was a thorough Englishman, and had an unsurmountable aversion to the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> and the fingers in it; he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> opera on the subject of the "Dragon of Wantley;" and afterwards a sequel to it, entitled, "The Dragonets;" both which were esteemed a true burlesque upon the Italian opera. His qualities being of the entertaining kind, he was led into more expenses than his finances could bear, and thus was frequently in distress. His friends, however, were always ready to assist him by their little subscriptions to his works: and encouraged by these, he republished, in 1740, all the songs he had ever composed, in a collection, entitled, "The Musical Century, in 100 English Ballads, &c." and, in 1743, his dramatic works, in a small volume, 4to. With all his mirth and good humour, he seems to have been at times deeply affected with the malevolence of some of his own profession, who, for reasons that no one can guess at, were were his enemies; and this, with the pressure of his circumstances, is supposed to have occasioned his untimely end; for, about 1744, in a fit of desperation, he laid violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on himself, and, at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Warner-street, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">Cold</a>-Bath Fields, put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which, says Sir John Hawkins, had been led without reproach. It is to be noted, and it is somewhat singular in such a character, that in all his songs and poems on wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and such kind of subjects, he seems to have manifested an inviolable regard for decency and good manners.

CARGADORS

Pages 195-195

a name which the Dutch give to those brokers whose business is to find freight for ships outward bound, and to give notice to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, who have commodities to send by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, of the ships that are ready to sail, and of the places for which they are bound.

CARGAPOL

Pages 195-195
or KARGAPOL, the capital of a territory of the same name, in the province of Dwina, in Muscovy. E. Long. 36° N. Lat. 63°.

CARGO

Pages 195-195

O denotes all the merchandises and effects which are laden on board a ship. Super-Cargo, a person employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to go a voyage, oversee the cargo, and dispose of it to the best advantage.

CARIA

Pages 195-195

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; whose limits are extended by some, while they are contracted by others. Mela and Pliny extend the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> Caria from Jafus and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>, to Calynda, and the borders of Lycia. The inland Caria <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> extends to the Meander and beyond. Car, Cariates, Cariatis, Carissa, and Caris, and Carra, are the gentilis names; Carius and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARICUS">Caricus</a> the epithets. In Care percivulum, was a proverbial saying on a thing exposed to danger, but of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value. The Cares being the Swils of those days, were hired and placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, (Cicero). Cum Care Carilla, denoted the behaviour of clowns. The Cares came originally from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to the continent, being formerly subject to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, and called Legeis: this the Cretans affirm, and the Cares deny, making themselves <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a>. They are of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> original with the Myfi and Lydi, having a common temple, of a very ancient standing, at Melasla, a town of Caria, called Jovis Carii Delubrum, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>). <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> calls the Carians, barbarians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>.

CARIATI

Pages 195-195

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, with a bishop's see, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality. It is two miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARANTO">Taranto</a>, and 37 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Cofenza. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 19' N. Lat. 30° 38'.

CARIBBEE ISLANDS

Pages 195-196

a cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> between 59 and 63 degrees of west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 11 and 18 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. They <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the form of a bow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, stretching almost from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a> north, to near the river Oronoque. Those that lie nearest the east have been called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">Windward</a> Islands, the others the Leeward, on account of the winds blowing generally from the eastern point in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Abbé Raynal conjectures them to be the tops of very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> formerly belonging to the continent, which have been changed into islands by some revolution that has laid the flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Caribbee islands, beginning from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOBAGO">Tobago</a>, is nearly north and N. N. W. This direction is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, forming a line somewhat curved towards the north-west, and ending at Antigua. In this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the line becomes at once curved; and extending itself in a straight direction to the west and north-west, meets in its course with Porto-Rico, St Domingo, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, known by the name of the Leeward Islands, which are separated from each other by channels of various breadths. Some of these are 6, others 15 or 20 leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; but in all of them the foundings are from 100 to 120 or 150 fathoms. Between Grenada and St Vincent's there is also a small archipelago of 30 leagues, in which the foundings are not above ten fathoms. The mountains in the Caribbee islands run in the same direction as the islands themselves. The direction is so regular, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we were to consider the tops of these mountains only, independent of their bases, they might be looked upon as a chain of hills belonging to the continent, of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a> would be the most northerly promontory. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of water which flow from the mountains in the Windward islands, run all in the western parts of these islands. The whole eastern coast is without any running water. No springs come <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> there from the mountains: and indeed they would have there been useless; for after having run over a very short tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity, they would have fallen into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>, St Domingo, and Cuba, there are a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that discharge themselves on the northern side, and whose sources rise in the mountains running from east to west, that is, through the whole length of these islands. From the other side of the mountains facing the south, where the sea, flowing with great impetuosity, leaves behind it marks of its inundations, several rivers flow down, the mouths of which are capable of receiving the largest ships. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the Caribbees consists mostly of a layer of clay or gravel of different thickness: under which is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or rock. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of some of these soils is better adapted to vegetables than others. In those places where the clay is drier and more friable, and mixes with the leaves and remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, a layer of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is formed of greater depth than where the clay is moister. The sand or gravel has different properties according to its peculiar nature; wherever it is less hard, less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and less porous, small pieces separate themselves from it, which, though dry, preserve a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of coolness useful to vegetation. This soil is called in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> a pumice-stone soil. Wherever the clay and gravel do not go through such modifications, the soil becomes barren, as soon as the layer formed by the decomposition of the original plants is destroyed.—By a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> concluded in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1660, between the French and English, the Caribs were confined to the islands of St Vincent's and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>, where all the scattered body of this people were united, and at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> did not exceed in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 6000 men. See St Vincent's and Dominica. As the Caribbee islands are all between the tropics, their inhabitants are exposed, allowing for the varieties resulting from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of situation and soil, to a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, which generally increases from the rising of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> till an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after noon, and then declines in proportion as the sun declines. The variations of the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> seem to depend rather on the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> than on the changes of the seasons. In those places... places where the wind does not blow, the air is excessively hot, and none but the easterly winds contribute to temper and refresh it; those that blow from the south and west afford little relief; but they are much less frequent and less regular than that which blows from the east. The branches of the trees exposed to the influence of the latter are forced round towards the west; but their roots are stronger, and more extended under the ground, towards the east than towards the west; and hence they are easily thrown down by strong west winds or hurricanes from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The easterly wind is scarce felt in the Caribbee islands before <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten o'clock in the morning, increases in proportion as the sun rises above the horizon, and decreases as it declines. Towards the evening it ceases entirely to blow on the coasts, but not on the open sea. It has also been observed, that it blows with more force and more regularity in the dog-days than at any other time of the year. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> also contributes to the temperature of the Caribbee islands, though not equally in them all. In those places where the easterly wind meets with nothing to oppose its progress, it dispels the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> as they begin to rise, and causes them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> either in the woods or upon the mountains. But whenever the storms are too violent, or the blowing of the easterly wind is interrupted by the changeable and temporary effect of the southerly or westerly ones, it then begins to rain. In the other Caribbee islands, where this wind does not generally blow, the rains are so frequent and plentiful, especially in the winter season, which lasts from the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to the middle of October, that, according to the most accurate observations, as much rain falls in one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> as in our climates in a year. Instead of these mild refreshing showers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the European climates, the rains of the Caribbee islands are torrents, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of which might be mistaken for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, were not that almost totally unknown under so <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> a sky. These showers indeed refresh the air; but they occasion a dampness, the effects of which are not less disagreeable than fatal. The dead must be interred within a few hours after they have expired. Meat <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not keep sweet above 24 hours. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> decay, whether they are gathered ripe or before their maturity. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> must be made up into biscuits, to prevent its growing mouldy. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> wines turn sour, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> turns rusty, in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s time. The seeds can only be preserved by constant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and care, till the proper season returns for sowing them. When the Caribbee islands were first discovered, the corn that was conveyed there for the support of the Europeans, was so soon damaged that it became necessary to send it out in the ears. This necessary precaution so much enhanced the price of it, that few were able to purchase it. Flour was then substituted in lieu of corn; which lowered indeed the expenses of transport, but had this inconvenience, that it was sooner damaged. It was imagined by a merchant, that if the flour were entirely separated from the bran, it would have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> advantage of being cheaper and keeping longer.
