He caused it therefore to be fitted, and put the finest flour into strong casks, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together with iron <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>, till it became so close a body that the air could scarcely penetrate it. This method was found to answer the purpose; and if, by it, the flour cannot be preserved as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as in our dry and temperate climates, it may be kept for six months, a year, or longer, according to the degree of care taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. However troublesome these effects of the rain may be, it is attended with some others still more formidable; namely, frequent and dreadful earthquakes. These happening generally during the time or towards the end of the rainy season, and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> are highest, some ingenious naturalists have supposed that there might be a connexion between them. The waters of the sky and of the sea undermine, dig up, and ravage the earth in several different ways. Among the various shocks to which the Caribbee islands are exposed from the fury of the boisterous ocean, there is one distinguished by the name of roas de maree, or whirlpool. It constantly happens once, twice, or thrice, from July to October, and always on the western coasts, because it takes place after the time of the westerly or southerly winds, or while they blow. The waves, which at a distance seem to advance gently within 400 or 500 yards, suddenly swell against the shore, as if acted upon in an oblique direction by some superior force, and break with the greatest impetuosity. The ships which are then upon the coast, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> beyond it, unable either to keep their anchors or to put out to sea, are dashed to pieces against the land, and all on board most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> perish. The hurricane is another terrible phenomenon in these islands, by which incredible damage is occasioned; but happily it occurs not often. The produce of the Caribbee islands is exceedingly valuable to the Europeans, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, rum, molasses, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, &c., a particular account of which is given under the names of the respective islands as they occur in the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>.

CARIBBIANA

Pages 196-196
or CARIBIANA, the north-east coast of Terra Firma, in South America, otherwise called New ANDALUSIA.

CARICA

Pages 196-196

the PAPAW. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The fruit of one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> eaten with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> as melons, but is much inferior to a melon in its native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but those which have ripened in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> were detectable: the only <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to which Mr Miller says he has known them put was, when they were about half grown, to soak them in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to get out the acrid juice, and then pickle them for orangos, to which they are a good substitute.

CARICATURA

Pages 196-196

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, denotes the concealment of real beauties, and the exaggeration of blemishes, but still so as to preserve a resemblance of the object. The word is Italian; formed of caric, a load, burden, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like.

CARICOUS

Pages 196-196

an epithet given to such tumours as resemble the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a fig. They are frequently found in the piles.

CARIES

Pages 196-196

the corruption <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mortification of a bone. See MEDICINE and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">SURGERY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARIGNAN

Pages 196-196

a fortified town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, situated on the river Po, about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 25' N. Lat. 44° 30'. It was taken in 1544 by the French; who demolished the fortifications, but spared the castle. It was also taken, and retaken, in 1691.

CARILLONS

Pages 196-197

CARILLONS, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of chimes frequent in the Low Countries, particularly at Ghent, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, and played on a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bells in a belfrey, forming a complete <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of tones and semitones, like those on the harpsichord and organ. There are pedals communicating with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bells, upon which the carillonist with his feet plays the bells to sprightly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, performed with the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> upon the upper series of keys. These keys are projecting sticks, wide enough to be struck with violence and velocity by either of the hands edgewise, without the danger of hitting the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>. The player is provided with a thick <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> covering for the little finger of each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the violence of the stroke. These carillons are heard through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town.

CARINA

Pages 197-197

a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, properly signifying the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> of a ship; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> running along the bottom of the ship from head to stern, upon which the whole structure is built or framed. Carina is also frequently used for the whole capacity or bulk of a ship; containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> or all the space below the deck. Hence the word is also sometimes used by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> for the whole ship. Carina is also used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gave the name carina to all buildings in form of a ship, as we still give the name nave to the middle or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> vault of our Gothic churches; because it has that figure. Carina, among anatomists, is used to denote the spina dorsi; as likewise for the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> or embryo of a chick appearing in an incubated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. The carina consists of the entire vertebrae, as they appear after ten or twelve days incubation. It is thus called, because crooked in form of the keel of a ship.—Botanists also, for the like reason, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word carina to express the lower petalum of a papilionaceous flower. Carinæ were also weepers or women hired among the ancient Romans to weep at funerals; they were thus called from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> whence most of them came.

CARINOLA

Pages 197-197

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and Terra di Lavoro. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 5'. N. Lat. 41° 15'.

CARINTHIA

Pages 197-197

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, bounded by the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a> and the Venetian territories on the south, on the west by Tyrol, and on the east by Styria. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was anciently called Carnia, and the inhabitants Carni; but the former afterwards obtained the name of Carinthia, and the latter Carantani <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Carinthi. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this country is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general mountainous and barren; but there are some fruitful dales and valleys in it, which produce wheat and other grain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, brooks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which are very numerous, abound with fish; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> yield <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and in many places are covered with woods. The river Drave, which runs across the country, is the most considerable in Carinthia. The inhabitants are partly descendants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans, and partly of the Slavonians or Wends. The states are constituted as in Austria, and their assemblies are held at Clagenfurt. The archbishop of Salzburg and the bishop of Bamberg have considerable territories in this country. Christianity was planted here in the 7th century. The only profession tolerated at present is the Roman Catholic. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> are those of Gurk and Lavant, who are subject to the archbishop of Salzburg. This duchy was formerly a part of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. In the year 1282, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Rudolph I. gave it to Maynard <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Tyrol, on condition that when his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue failed, it should revert to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Austria; which happened in 1331. Carinthia has its particular governor or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, as he is called; and contributes annually towards the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> establishment 637,695 florins. Only one regiment of foot is usually quartered in it.

CARIPHI

Pages 197-197

a kind of cavalry in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The cariphi to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of about 1000 are not slaves, nor bred up in the fraglio, like the rest; but are generally Moors <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> renegade <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who having followed adventures, being <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and having their fortune to seek by their dexterity and courage, have arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> guards to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signior. CARISSA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CARITAS.—The poculum caritatis, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> cup, was an extraordinary allowance of wine or other liquors, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> at festivals drank in commemoration of their founders and benefactors.

CARISBROOK CASTLE

Pages 197-197

a castle situated in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight, where <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. was imprisoned. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 30'. N. Lat. 50° 40'.

CARISTO

Pages 197-197

an episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGROPONT">Negropont</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Loro. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 24° 15'. N. Lat. 38° 6'.

CARKE

Pages 197-197

denotes the 30th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a sarplar of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. CARLE. See Churl.

CARLETON

Pages 197-197

SIR <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">DUDLEY</a>, was born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, 1573, and bred in Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He went as secretary to Sir Ralph Winwood into the Low Countries, when <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James resigned the cantonary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> to the States; and was afterwards employed for 20 years as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, Savoy, and the United Provinces. King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> created him Viscount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>, and appointed him one of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretaries of state; in which office he died in 1651. He was esteemed a good statesman, though an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and published several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> works.

CARLINE

Pages 197-197
or Caroline, a silver coin current in the Neapolitan dominions, and worth about 4d. of our money.

CARLINES

Pages 197-197
or CARLINGS, in a ship, two pieces of timber lying fore and aft, along from one beam to another, directly over the keel; serving as a foundation for the whole body of the ship. On these the ledges rest, whereon the planks of the deck and other matters of carpentry are made fast. The carlines have their ends let into the beams called culver-tail-ways. CARLINE Knees, are timbers going athwart the ship, from the sides to the hatchway, serving to sustain the deck on both sides.

CARLISLE

Pages 197-198

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, seated on the south of the river Eden, and between the Petterel on the east, and the Cauda on the west. It is surrounded by a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall, and has a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> castle in the western <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, as also a citadel in the eastern part, built by Henry VIII. It flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, as appears from the antiquities that are to be met with here, and the Roman coins that have been dug up. At the departure of the Romans this city was ruined by the Scots and Picts; and was not rebuilt till the year 680, by Egfrid, who encompassed it with a wall, and repaired the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the 8th and 9th centuries, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was again ruined, and the city laid desolate by the incursions of the Norwegians and Danes. In this condition it remained till the time of William Rufus; who repaired the walls and the castle, and caused the houses to be rebuilt. It was fortified by Henry I. as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against Scotland; he also placed a garrison in it, and made it an episcopal see. It was twice taken by the Scots, and afterwards burnt accidentally in the reign of Richard II. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, the suburbs, and 1500 houses, were destroyed at that time. It is at present in a good condition; and has three gates, the English on the south, the Scotch on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and the Irish on the west. It has two parishes, and as many churches, St Cuthbert's and St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s, the last of which is the cathedral, and is separated from the town by a wall of its own. The eastern part, which is the newest, is a curious piece of workmanship. The choir with the aisles is 71 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and has a stately east window 43 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and 30 broad, adorned with curious pillars. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is elegantly vaulted with wood; and is embellished with the arms of England and France quartered; as also with Percy's, Lucy's, Warren's, Mowbray's, and many others. In the choir are the monuments of three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> who are buried there. This see was erected in 1133 by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry I. and made suffragan to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. The cathedral church here had been founded a short time before by Walter, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> in these parts for King William Rufus, and by him dedicated to the Virgin Mary. He likewise built a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, and filled it with canons regular of St Augustine. This foundation <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of monasteries, when its lands were added to the see, and the maintenance of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, &c., placed here in their room. The church was almost ruined by the usurper Cromwell and his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; and has never since recovered its former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, although repaired after the Restoration. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> contains the greatest part of the counties of Cumberland and Westmorland, in which are only 93 parishes; but these (as all the northern are) exceeding large; and of them 18 are impropriations. Here is one archdeacon, viz. of Carlisle. The see is valued in the king's books at £32l. 4s. 11½d. but is computed to be worth annually 280l. The clergy's tenth amounts only to 16l. 1s. 7½d. To this cathedral belong a bishop, a dean, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, an archdeacon, four prebendaries, eight <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> canons, &c., and other inferior officers and servants. The Picts wall, which was built across the country from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, terminates near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Carlisle was a fortified place, and still has its governor and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor, but no garrison. It was taken by the rebels, Nov. 15, 1745; and was retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cumberland on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following, and deprived of its gates. It is governed by a mayor, twelve aldermen, two bailiffs, &c., and has a considerable market on Saturdays. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Carlisle are chiefly of printed linens, for which near 3000l. per annum is paid in duties. It is also noted for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> manufacture of whips, in which a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children are employed.—Salmons appear in the Eden in numbers, so early as the months of December and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and even Newcastle <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are supplied with early fish from this river; but it is remarkable, that they do not visit the Esk in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> till April; notwithstanding the mouths of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are at a small distance from each other.—Carlisle sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to a branch of the Howard family.

CARLOCK

Pages 198-198

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a fort of ironglass, made with the sturgeon's bladder, imported from Archangel. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it is for clarifying wine, but is also used by the dyers. The best carlock comes from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, where a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sturgeon is caught.

CARLOSTAD

Pages 198-198
or Carlstadt, a town of Hungary, capital of Croatia, and the usual residence of the governors of the province. It is seated on the river Kulph, in E. Long. 16. 5. N. Lat. 45. 34.

CARLOWITZ

Pages 198-198

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in Slavonia, remarkable for a peace concluded here between the Turks and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in 1669. It is seated on the west side of the Danube, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 5. N. Lat. 45. 25.

CARLSCRONA

Pages 198-199
or Carlscoorn, a sea-port town in the Baltic, belonging to Sweden. It derives its origin and name from Charles XI. who first laid the foundation of a new town in 1680, and removed the fleet from Stockholm to this place, on account of its advantageous situation in the centre of the Swedish seas, and the superior security of its harbour. The greatest part of Carlskrona stands upon a small rocky island, which rises gently in a bay of the Baltic; the suburbs extend over another small rock, and along the mole close to the basin where the fleet is moored. The way into the town from the mainland is carried over a dyke to an island, and from thence along two long wooden bridges joined by a barren rock. The town is spacious, and contains about 18,000 inhabitants. It is adorned with one or two handsome churches, and a few tolerable houses of brick; but the generality of the buildings are of wood. The suburbs are fortified towards the land by a stone wall. The entrance into the harbour, which by nature is extremely difficult from a number of shoals and rocky islands, is still further secured from the attack of an enemy's fleet by two strong forts built on two islands, under the batteries of which all vessels must pass. Formerly vessels in this port when careened and repaired, were laid upon their sides in the open harbour, Carmel, however, represent it as rather dry and barren; which perhaps may have happened from the neglect of agriculture common in all parts of the Turkish empire, especially where they are exposed to the incursions of the Arabs. Carmel is the name of the mountain, and of a city built on it: as well as of a heathen deity worshipped in it, but without either temple or statue: though anciently there must have been a temple, as we are told that this mountain was a favourite retreat of Pythagoras, who spent a good deal of time in the temple, without any person with him. But what hath rendered Mount Carmel most celebrated and revered both by Jews and Christians, is its having been the residence of the prophet Elijah, who is supposed to have lived there in a cave (which is there shown), before he was taken up into heaven.

CARMELITES

Pages 199-199

an order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, making one of the four tribes of mendicants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> begging friars; and taking its name from Mount Carmel, formerly inhabited by Elias, Elifha, and the children of the prophets; from whom this order pretends to descend in an uninterrupted succession. The manner in which they make out their antiquity has something in it too ridiculous to be rehearsed. Some among them pretend they are descendants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ: others go further, and make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> a Carmelite, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> regular branches of their order. Phocas, a Greek monk, speaks the most reasonably. He says, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> 1185, Elias's cave was still extant on the mountain; near which were the remains of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> which intimated that there had been anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>; that, some years before, an old monk, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, as he pretended, from the prophet Elias, fixed there, and assembled ten brothers. In 1229, Albert, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, gave the solitaries a rigid rule, which Papebroch has since printed. In 1217, or, according to others, 1226, Pope Honorius III. approved and confirmed it. This rule contained 16 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; one of which confined them to their cells, and enjoined them to continue <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; another prohibited the brethren having any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; another enjoined fasting from the feast of the holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> till Easter, except on Sundays; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> at all times from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> was enjoined by another article; one obliged them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> labour; another imposed a strict silence on them from vespers till the tierce the next day. The peace concluded by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic II. with the Saracens, in the year 1229, to disadvantageous to Christendom, and so beneficial to the infidels, occasioned the Carmelites to quit the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, under Alan the fifth general of the Order. He first sent some of the religious to Cyprus, who landed there in the year 1328, and founded a monastery in the forest of Fortania. Some Sicilians, at the same time, leaving Mount Carmel, returned to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where they founded a monastery in the suburbs of Messina. Some English departed out of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in the year 1240, to found others in England. Others of Provence, in the year 1244, founded a monastery in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Aigualates, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from Marfilles; and thus, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their monasteries increasing, they held their European general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> in the year 1245, at their monastery of Aylesford in England.—This order is so much increased, that it has, at present,

CARMEN

Pages 199-200

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> among the Latins, used in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; but more particularly to signify a spell, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exorcism, couched in a few words placed in a mystic order, on which its efficacy depended. Pezron derives the word *carmen* from the Celtic *carm*, the shout of joy, or the verses which the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BARDS">bards</a> sung to encourage the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>.—*Carmen* was anciently a denomination given also to precepts, laws, prayers, imprecatory, and all solemn formulæ couched in a few words placed in a certain order, though written in prose. In which sense it was that the elder Cato wrote a *Carmen de moribus*, which was not in verse but in prose.

CARMENTALIA

Pages 200-200

a feast among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, celebrated annually upon the 11th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Carmenta, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Carmentis, a prophetess of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, mother of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a>, with whom she came into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> 60 years before the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The solemnity was also repeated on the 15th of January, which is marked in the old <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> of *Carmentalia relata*. This feast was established on occasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fecundity among the Roman dames, after a general reconciliation with their husbands, with whom they had been at variance, in regard of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of coaches being prohibited them by an edict of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. This feast was celebrated by the women: he who offered the sacrifices was called *sacerdos carmentalis*.

CARMINATIVES

Pages 200-200

medicines used in colics, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other flatulent disorders, to dispel the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The word comes from the Latin *carminare*, to card or teaze <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and figuratively to attenuate and diffuse wind or vapours, and promote their discharge by perspiration. Though Dr Quincy makes it more mysterious: He says it comes from the word *carmen*, taking it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of an invocation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>; and makes it to have been a general name for all medicines which operated like charms, i.e., in an extraordinary manner. Hence, as the most violent pains were frequently those arising from pent-up wind, which immediately cease upon <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> *carminative* became in a peculiar sense applied to medicines which gave relief in windy <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they cured by enchantment: but this interpretation seems a little too far strained.

CARMINE

Pages 200-200

a powder of a very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> bordering upon purple; and used by painters in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>, though rarely, on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> price. The manner of preparing it is kept a secret by the colour-makers; neither do any of these receipts which have for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> been published concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of this and other colours at all answer the purpose. See COLOUR-making.

CARMONA

Pages 200-200

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>. The gate towards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> is one of the most extraordinary pieces of antiquity in all Spain. It is seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, 15 miles east of Seville. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 37'. N. Lat. 37° 34'. CARNATION. See DIANTHUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CARNATION <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>, among painters, is understood of all the parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, in general, which represent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> which are naked and without drapery. Titian and Correggio in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Rubens and Van-dyke in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, excelled in carnations.—In colouring for flesh, there is so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a variety, that it is hard to lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> any general rules for instructions therein; neither are there any regarded by those who have acquired a skill this way; the various colouring for carnations may be easily produced, by taking more or less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, blue, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BISTRE">bistre</a>, whether for the first colouring, or for the finishing; the colour for women should be bluish, for children a little red, both fresh and gay; and for men it should incline to yellow, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are old.

CARNATION

Pages 200-200

among dyers. To dye a carnation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> rose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, it is directed to take liquor of wheat bran a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> three pounds, tartar two ounces; boil them, and enter 20 yards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloth; after it has boiled three hours, cool and wash it: take fresh clear bran liquor a sufficient quantity, madder five pounds; boil and sodden according to art. —The Bow dyers know that the solution of tin, being put in a kettle to the alum and tartar, in another pot, makes the cloth, &c. attract the colour into it, so that none of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> is left, but the whole is absorbed by the cloth.

CARNEADES

Pages 200-200

a celebrated Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and founder of the third academy. He was so fond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, that he not only avoided all entertainments, but forgot even to eat at his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; his maid-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Melitta was obli-

CARNEDDE

Pages 200-201

in British antiquity, denotes heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, supposed to be druidical remains, and thrown together on occasion of confirming and commemorating a covenant, Gen. xxxi. 46. They are very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLESEY">Anglesey</a>, and were also used as sepulchral monuments, in the manner of tumuli; for Mr. Rowland found a curious urn in one of these carnedde. Whence it may be inferred, that the Britons had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of throwing stones on the deceased. From this custom is derived the Welsh proverb, Karn ardyben, "Ill betide thee."

CARNEIA

Pages 201-201

in antiquity, a festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, furnamed Carneus, held in most cities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, but especially at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, where it was first instituted. The reason of the name, as well as the occasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> is controverted. It lasted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days, beginning on the 13th of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Carneus. The ceremonies were an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the method of living and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>. CARNEL.—The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of ships first with their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and beams, and after bringing on their planks, is called carnel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, to distinguish it from clinch work. Vessels also which go with mizen sails instead of main sails are by some called carnels.

CARNELIAN

Pages 201-201

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of which there are three kinds, distinguished by three colours, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. The red is very well known among us; is found in roundish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> oval masses, much like our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pebbles; and is generally met with between an inch and two or three inches in diameter; it is of a fine, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> texture; of a glossy surface; and, in the several specimens, is of all the degrees of red, from the palest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the deepest blood-red. It is generally free from spots, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, or variegations: but sometimes it is veined very beautifully with an extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> red, or with white; the veins forming concentric circles, or other less regular figures, about a nucleus, in the manner of those of agates. The pieces of carnelian, which are all one colour, and perfectly free from veins, are those which our jewellers generally make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for seals, though the variegated ones are much more beautiful. The carnelian is tolerably hard, and capable of a very good polish: it is not at all affected by acid menstruums: the fire divests it of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of its colour, and leaves it of a pale red; and a strong and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> reduce it to a pale dirty gray. The finest carnelians are those of the East Indies; but there are very beautiful ones found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Silegia and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>; and we have some not despisable ones in England. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have recommended the carnelian as astringent, and attributed a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fanciful virtues to it, we know of no other use of the stone than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> seals on it; to which purpose it is excellently adapted, as being not too hard for cutting, and yet hard enough not to be liable to accidents, to take a good polish, and to separate easily from the wax.

CARNERO

Pages 201-201

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a name given to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> which extends from the western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Istria to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Grofia and the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORLACHIA">Morlachia</a>. CARNERO is likewise the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> to the west of the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Gibraltar.

CARNIFEX

Pages 201-201

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> executioner. By reason of the odiousness of his office, the carnifex was expressly prohibited by the laws from having his dwelling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers—carnifex also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>. Under the Anglo-Danish kings, the carnifex was an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; being ranked with the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Goodwin, and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>. Flor. Wigorn. ann. 1040, Rex Hardecanutus, Africum Ebor. Archiep. Goodwinum comitem, Edricum dispensa- A a 2

CARNIOLA

Pages 201-202

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany, bounded on the south by the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Istria possessed by the republic of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by Carinthia and Stiria; on the east, by Slavonia and Croatia; on the west, by Friuli, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Gorz <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Goritz, and a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice; extending in length about 110 miles, and in breadth about 50. It had its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name Carnia, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> one Carniola, from its ancient inhabitants, the Carni, a tribe of Scythians, otherwise called Japides, whence this and the adjacent countries were also called Japidia. Carniola is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, some of which are cultivated and inhabited, some covered with wood, others naked and barren, and others continually buried in snow. The valleys are very fruitful. Here are likewise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> must be had from the foreigner's magazines. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides many medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people are very hardy, going barefooted in winter through the snow, with open breasts, and sleeping on a hard <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> or bolster. Their food is also very coarse and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>. In winter, when the snow lies deep on the ground, the mountaineers bind either small baskets, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> thin narrow boards, like the Laplanders, to their feet, on which, with the help of a stout <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> or pole, they descend with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> velocity from the mountains. When the snow is frozen, they make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a sort of irons or skis. In different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> the inhabitants, especially the common sort, differ greatly in their dress, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and manner of living. In Upper and Lower Carniola they wear long beards. The languages chiefly in use are the Slavonian or Wendish, and German; the first by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>, and the latter by people of fashion. The duchy is divided into the Upper, Lower, Middle, and Inner Carniola. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> commodities exported hence are, iron, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, lead, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives, cattle, sheep, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and a kind of woollen stuff called mahalon, Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, walnuts, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; together with all manner of woodwork, as boxes, dishes, &c. Christianity was first planted here in the eighth century. Lutheranism made a considerable progress in it; but, excepting the Walachians or Ulkokes, who are of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and style themselves Staraverze, i.e. old <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>, all the inhabitants at present are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. Carniola was long a marquiseate or margravate; but in the year 1231 was erected into a duchy. As its proportion towards the maintenance of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, it pays annually 363,177 florins; but only two regiments of foot are quartered in it.

CARNIVAL

Pages 202-202
or CARNAVAL, a time of rejoicing, a season of mirth, observed with great solemnity by the Italians, particularly at Venice, holding from the twelfth day till Lent. The word is formed from the Italian Carnavalle; which M. Du Cange derives from Carn-a-val, by reason the flesh then goes to pot, to make amends for the season of abstinence then ensuing. Accordingly, in the corrupt Latin, he observes, it was called Carnele- vamen and Carnifrivium; as the Spaniards still denominate it carnes tollendas. Feasts, balls, operas, concerts of music, intrigues, marriages, &c., are chiefly held in carnival time. The carnival begins at Venice the second holiday in Christmas: Then it is they begin to wear masks, and open their playhouses and gaming houses; the place of St Mark is filled with mountebanks, jack-puddings, pedlars, whores, and such like mobs, who flock thither from all parts. There have been no less than seven foreign princes and 30,000 foreigners here to partake of these diversions.

CARNIVOROUS

Pages 202-203

an epithet applied to those animals which naturally feed and feed on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. It has been a dispute among naturalists, whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is naturally carnivorous. Those who take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> side of the question, insist chiefly on the structure of our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, which are mostly incisors <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> molars; not such as carnivorous animals are furnished with, and which are proper to tear flesh in pieces; to which it may be added, that, even when we do feed on flesh, it is not without a preparatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, roasting, &c. and even then that it is the hardest of digestion of all foods. To these arguments Dr Wallis subjoins another, which is, that all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> which feed on herbs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> have a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> colon, with a cæcum at the upper end of it, or somewhat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>, which conveys the food by a long and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> progress, from the stomach downwards, in order to its slower passage and longer stay in the intestines; but that, in carnivorous animals, such cæcum is wanting, and instead thereof there is a more short and slender gut, and a quicker passage through the intestines. Now in man, the cæcum is very visible: a strong presumption that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, who is still consistent with herself, did not intend him for a carnivorous animal. It is true, the cæcum is but small in adults, and seems of little or no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but in a fetus it is much larger in proportion: And it is probable, our customary change of diet, as we grow up, may occasion this shrinking. But to these arguments Dr Tyton replies, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> man had been by nature designed not to be carnivorous, there would doubtless have been found, somewhere on the globe, people who do not feed on flesh; which is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Neither are carnivorous animals always without a colon and cæcum; nor are all animals carnivorous which have these parts: the opossum, for instance, hath both a colon and cæcum, and yet feeds on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> and other flesh; whereas the hedgehog, which has neither colon nor cæcum, and so ought to be carnivorous, feeds only on vegetables. Add to this, that hogs which have both, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> feed upon flesh when they can get it; and rats and mice, which have large cæcums, will feed on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and cheese. Lastly, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> are furnished with teeth necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of all kinds of foods; from whence it would seem that nature intended we should live on all. And as the alimentary duct in the human body is fitted for digesting all kinds of foods, ought we not rather to conclude that nature did not intend to deny us any? It is not less disputed whether mankind were carnivorous before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. St Jerome, Chrysostome, Theodore, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, maintain, that all animal CARNOSITY is used by some authors for a little flethly excrecence, tubercle, or wen, formed in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>, the neck of the bladder, or yard, which stops the passage of the urine.—Carnosities are very difficult of cure: they are not easily known but by introducing a probe into the passage, which there meets with resistance. They usually arise from some venereal malady ill managed.

CARO

Pages 203-203

ANNIBAL, a celebrated Italian poet, was born at Civita Nuovo in 1507. He became secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Parma, and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Farnese. He was also made a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. He translated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Aeneid into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, with such propriety and elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, that he was allowed by the best judges to have equalled the original. He also translated <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, two oratories of Gregory Nazianzen, with a discourse of Cyprian. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>; and a miscellany of his poems was printed at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1584. He died at Rome in 1566.

CAROLINA

Pages 203-204

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, comprehending the most westerly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, and lying between 29 and 36 degrees of N. Lat. It is bounded on the east by the Atlantic, and on the west by the river <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and to the south of Georgia by the Floridas. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is seated between the extremities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, though the heat is more troublesome in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> than the cold in winter; their winters being very short, and the frosty mornings frequently succeeded by warm days. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is generally serene and clear the greatest part of the year; but in February and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> the inhabitants have a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the woods, which causes such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> as to strangers would seem to proceed from a fog <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thickness in the air. The smoke of the tar-kilns likewise deceives strangers, and gives them an ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the air of Carolina; to which also conduces a custom of the Indians of setting fire to the woods in their huntings, for many miles round. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rains are in winter, though they are not without heavy showers at midsummer; add to these the constant dews that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the night, which refresh the ground and supply the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> with moisture. In North Carolina, the northwest winds in the winter occasion very pinching <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; but they are not of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance. Westerly winds bring very pleasant weather; but the southerly are hot and unwholesome, occasioning fevers and other disorders. But this must be understood of summer, for in winter they are very comfortable. The depth of winter is towards the latter end of February, and then the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> is not strong enough to bear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. In August and September there are sometimes great storms and squalls of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which are so violent as to make lanes of 100 feet wide, more or less, through the woods, tearing up the trees by the roots. These storms generally happen once in about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years; and are attended with dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and heavy rains. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> happen about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the hurricanes which rage so fatally among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> between the tropics; and seem to be occasioned by them, or to proceed from the same cause; but by the time they reach Carolina, their force is much abated; and the farther north they proceed, so much the more do they decrease in fury. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; but farther up, the country is so fruitful that they have not yet been at the trouble to manure the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The grains most cultivated are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, though any sort <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> thrive well enough; they have also <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> of several sorts, little known in England. All kinds of garden stuff usual in England are cultivated here, and may be had in great plenty. They export <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities yearly of rice, pitch, tar, turpentine, deer-skins, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; cypress, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, sassafras, oak, walnut, and pine. Besides these, they also send out beef, pork, tallow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, furs, wheat, pease, potatoes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, bees-wax, myrtle-wax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, snakeroot, cotton, several sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> and medicinal drugs. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">Indigo</a> is also cultivated in this province, but of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that which comes from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee islands</a>. It hath been attempted in vain to cultivate vines, and produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, in this country; for though the frosts here do not continue long without intervals of warmer weather, they are sufficient to check the growth of the vine, as well as olives, dates, oranges, &c. The Univ. His. furs are bought of the Indians with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, xxvi. 88, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, coarse cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and spirituous liquors. As yet they have not a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of handicraftsmen; which renders labour very dear, and a supply of clothes from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> necessary. The aspect of the country is very fine, being adorned with beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and creeks, and the woods with lofty timber, which afford delightful and pleasant seats for the planters, and render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a> their lands very easy. And as they have plenty of fish, wild-fowl, and venison, besides other necessaries which this country produces naturally, they live easy and luxuriously. Their rivers are large, and navigable a great many miles up the country. They rise near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and abound with delicate fish, beside <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-fowl of different kinds. In some there are islands which yield good pasture, without the annoyance of wild beasts. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> mountains are the Cherokee or Alleghany mountains, which are situated north and northwest, five or six hundred miles distant from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. They are very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and abound with trees, plants, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and minerals, of different kinds. This country is divided into North and South Carolina, and Georgia; each of which, before the late revolution, was under a particular governor. The North is subdivided into four counties, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANVILLE">Granville</a>, Clinton, Berkeley, and Craven; and South Carolina into two, Clarendon and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>. This last is also divided into 14 parishes or townships, each of which has a brick or timber <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The former likewise has the same number of parishes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the whole country. Carolina was discovered by Sebastian Cabot about the year 1500, in the reign of Henry VII. But the settling of it being neglected by the English, a colony of French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, by the encouragement of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Coligny, were transported thither; and named the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their first settlement Arx Carolina, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX., of France; but in a short time that colony was destroyed by the Spaniards; and no other attempt was made by any European power to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there till the year 1664, when 800 English landed at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Fear in North Carolina, and took possession of the country. In 1672, Cha. II. of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> granted Carolina to the lords Berkeley, Clarendon, Albemarle, Craven, and Ashley, Sir George Carteret, Sir William Berkeley, and Sir John Colliton. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> for this new colony was drawn up by the famous Mr Locke, who very wisely proposed a universal toleration in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> matters. The only restriction in this respect was, that every person claiming the protection of that settlement, should, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 17, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> himself in some particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. To civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, however, our <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> was not so favourable; the code of Carolina gave to the eight proprietors who founded the colony, and to their heirs, not only all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of a monarch, but all the powers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which was composed of this sovereign body, and called the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> Court, was invested with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of nominating to all employments and dignities, and even of conferring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; but with new and unprecedented titles. They were, for instance, to create in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> two casiques, each of whom was to be possessed of 24,000 acres of land; and a landgrave, who was to have 80,000. The persons on whom these honours should be bestowed were to compose the upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and their possessions were made unalienable. They had only the right of farming or letting out a third part of them at most for three lives. The lower house was composed of the deputies from the several counties and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The number of this representative body was to be increased as the colony grew more populous. No tenant was to pay more than about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> per <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, and even this rent was redeemable. All the inhabitants, however, both slaves and freemen, were under an obligation to take up arms upon the first order from the Palatine court. It was not long before the defects of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> became apparent. The proprietary lords used every endeavour to establish an arbitrary government; and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the colonists exerted themselves with great zeal to avoid servitude. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this struggle, the whole province, distracted with tumults and dissensions, became incapable of making any progress, though great things had been expected from its particular advantages of situation. Though a toleration in religious matters was a part of the original constitution, dissensions arose likewise on that account. In 1705, Carteret, now <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Granville, who, as the oldest of the proprietors, was sole governor of the colony, formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of obliging all the non-conformists to embrace the ceremonies of the church of England; and this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of violence, though disavowed and rejected by the mother-country, inflamed the minds of the people. In 1720, while this animosity was still subsisting, the province was attacked by several bands of savages, driven to despair by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> course of the most atrocious violence and injustice. These unfortunate wretches were all put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but, in 1728, the lords proprietors having refused to contribute towards the expenses of an expedition, of which they were to share the immediate benefits, were deprived of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, except Lord Granville, who still retained his eighth part. The rest received a recompense of about 24,000l. The colony was taken under the immediate protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and from that time began to flourish. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into North and South Carolina now took place, and the settlement of Georgia commenced in 1732. See GEORGIA. CAROLINE. See CARLINE. CAROLINE-Books, the name of four books, composed by order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, to refute the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice. These books are couched in very harsh and severe terms, containing 120 heads of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against the council of Nice, and condemning the worship of images.

CAROLOSTADIANS

Pages 204-204
or CARLOSTADIANS, an ancient sect or branch of Lutherans, who denied the real presence of Christ in the eucharist. They were thus denominated from their leader Andrew Carolostadius, who having originally been archdeacon of Wittemberg, was converted by Luther, and was the first of all the reformed clergy who took a wife; but disagreeing afterwards with Luther, chiefly in the point of the sacrament, founded a sect apart. The Carolostadians are the same with what are otherwise denominated Sacramentarians, and agree in most things with the Zuingleans.

CAROLUS

Pages 204-204

a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, with a little silver mixed with it, struck under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VIII. of France. The carolus was worth 12 deniers when it ceased to be current. Those which are still current in trade in Lorraine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in some neighbouring provinces, go under the name of French fols.

CAROTIDS

Pages 204-204

in Anatomy, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> of the neck, which convey the blood from the aorta to the brain; one called the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and the other the left, carotid.

CARP

Pages 204-205

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cyprinus. See CYPRINUS, Ichthyology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The carp is the most valuable of all kinds of fish for stockfishing ponds. It is very quick in its growth, and brings forth the spawn three times a year, so that the increase is very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> does not begin to breed till eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years old; so that in breeding-ponds a supply must be kept of carp of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The best judges allow, that, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> a breeding-pond, four males should be allowed to twelve females. The usual growth of a carp is two or three inches in length in a year; but, in ponds which receive the fattening of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-fewers, they have been known to grow from five inches to 18 in one year. A feeding-pond of one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> very well feed 300 carp of three years old, 300 of two years, and 400 of one year old. Carp delight greatly in ponds that have marley sides; they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> also clay-ponds well sheltered from the winds and grown with weeds and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> grass at the edges, which they feed on in the hot months. Carp and tench thrive very fast in ponds and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is a little brackish; but they are not so well fed as those which live in fresh water. Grains, blood, chicken-guts, and the like, may at times times be thrown into carp-ponds, to help to fatten the fish. To make them grow <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and fat, the growth of grass under the water should by all means possible be encouraged. For this purpose, as the water decreases in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the sides of the pond left naked and dry should be well raked with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a>, to destroy all the weeds, and cut up the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; hay-feed should then be sown plentifully in these places; and more ground prepared in the same manner, as the water falls more and more away. By this means there will be a fine and plentiful growth of young grass along the sides of the pond to the water's edge; and when the rains fill up the pond again, this will be all buried under the water, and will make a feeding-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the fish where they will come early in the morning, and will fatten greatly upon what they find there.

CARPATES

Pages 205-205
or Alpes Bastarnicae, in Ancient Geography, a range of mountains, running out between Poland, Hungary, and Transylvania. Now called the Carpathian Mountains.

CARPATHUS

Pages 205-205

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, two hundred stadia in compass, and an hundred in length. Its name is said to be from its situation on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>.
