It lies between <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which, from this island, is called the Carpathian sea, and has to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> the Ionian, to the south the Egyptian, to the west the Cretan and African seas. It is two hundred furlongs in compass, and a hundred in length. It had anciently, according to Strabo, four cities; according to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCYLAX">Scylax</a>, only three. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> mentions but one, which he calls Posidium. This island is now called Scarpano. CARPÆA, a kind of dance anciently in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Athenians and Magnesians, performed by two persons, the one acting a labourer, the other a robber. The labourer, laying by his arms, goes to ploughing and sowing, still looking warily about him as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> afraid of being surprized; the robber at length appears; and the labourer, quitting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, betakes himself to his arms, and fights in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his oxen. The whole was performed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of flutes, and in cadence. Sometimes the robber was overcome and sometimes the labourer; the victor's reward being the oxen and plough. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> was to teach and accustom the peasants to defend themselves against the attacks of ruffians.

CARPENTER

Pages 205-205

a person who practices <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">Carpentry</a>. The word is formed from the French charpentier, which signifies the same, formed of charpente, which denotes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather from the Latin carpentarius, a maker of carpena, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. CARPENTER of a Ship, an officer appointed to examine and keep in order the frame of a ship, together with her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, yards, boats, and all other wooden machinery. It is his duty in particular to keep the ship tight; for which purpose he ought frequently to review the decks and sides, and to caulk them when it is necessary. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, he is to examine up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, with all possible <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, in the lower apartments of the ship, to stop any holes that may have been made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, with wooden plugs provided of several sizes.

CARPENTRAS

Pages 205-205

an episcopal town of France, in the department of Vaucluse, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Venailin. It is subject to the pope; and is seated on the river Aufion, at the foot of a mountain. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 6'. N. Lat. 44° 4'.

CARPENTRY

Pages 205-205

the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, framing, and joining <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces of wood, for the uses of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. It is one of the arts subservient to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and is divided into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-carpentry and ship-carpentry: the first is employed in rafting, roofing, flooring of houses, &c., and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in the building of ships, barges, &c. See Ship-building. The rules in carpentry are much the same with those of Joinery; the only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is, that carpentry is used in the larger and coarser <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and joinery in the smaller and curious. See Centre, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">Roof</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRENGTH_OF_MATERIALS">Strength of Materials</a>.

CARPENTUM

Pages 205-205

in Antiquity, a name <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sorts of vehicles, answering to coaches as well as waggons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even carts, among us. The carpentum was originally a kind of car or vehicle in which the Roman ladies were carried; though in after times it was also used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Some derive the word from carro; others from Carmenta the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a>, by a conversion of the m into p.

CARPET

Pages 205-205

a sort of covering of stuff, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other materials, wrought with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or on a loom, which is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the furniture of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> spread over tables, or laid on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. Persian and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> carpets are those most esteemed; though at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> there is a manufactory after the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, where they make them little inferior, not to say finer, than the true Persian carpets. They are velvety, and perfectly imitate the carpets which come from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. There are also carpets of Germany, some of which are made of woollen stuffs, as ferges, &c., and called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> carpets: others are made of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> also, but wrought with the needle, and pretty often embellished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; and, lastly, there are some made of dogs' <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. We have likewise carpets made in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which are used either as floor-carpets, or to cover chairs, &c. It is true, we are not arrived at the like perfection in this manufacture with our neighbours the French; but may not this be owing to the want of a like public encouragement?

CARPET-KNIGHT

Pages 205-205

a denomination given to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>-men and others, of peacable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, who, on account of their birth, office, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> merits to the public, or the like, are, by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. They take the appellation carpet, because they usually receive their honours from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, kneeling on a carpet. By which they are distinguished from knights created in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, or field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> prowess. Carpet-knights possess a medium between those called truck or dunghill knights, who only purchase or merit the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> by their wealth, and knights-bachelors, who are created for their services in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

CARPI

Pages 205-206

a principality of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, lying about four leagues from that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. It formerly belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Pio; the elder sons of which bore the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Princes of St Gregory. In the beginning of the 14th century, Monfroy was the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Carpi; but in the 16th, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. gave the principality to Alfonso <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>. This nobleman, in recompense, gave to Albert Pio, to whom the principality of Carpi belonged of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the town of Safiulola and some other lands. Albert was, however, at last obliged to retire to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where, being stripped of all his estates, he died in 1338, with the reputation of being one of the best and bravest men of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The family of Pio is yet in being, and continues attached to the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Some of them have even been raised to the purple, and still make a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Carpi, a town of Italy in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Modena, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the last mentioned principality. It has a strong castle, and is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 12. N. Lat. 44. 45. Carpi, a town of the Veronese in Italy, memorable for a victory gained by the Imperialists over the French in 1791. It is subject to the Venetians: and is situated on the river Adige, in E. Long. 11. 39. N. Lat. 45. 10. Carpi, Ugo da, an Italian painter, of no very considerable talents in that art, but remarkable for being the inventor of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of engraving on wood, distinguished by the name of chiaro-oscuro, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>. This is performed by using more blocks than one; and Ugo da Carpi usually had three; the first for the outline and dark shadows, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> shadows, and the third for the half tint. In that manner he struck off <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> after several designs, and cartoons of Raphael; particularly one of the Sibyl, a Defect from the Crofs, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Simon the Sorcerer. He died in 1550. This art was brought to a still higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection by Baltafar Peruzzi of Siena, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARMIGIANO">Parmigiano</a>, who published several excellent designs in that manner. Carpi, Girolamo da, history and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, was born at Ferrara in 1501, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Garofalo. When he quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he devoted his whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, thoughts, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the works of Correggio, and to copy them with a most critical care and observation; in which labour he spent several years at Parma, Modena, and other cities of Italy, where the best works of that exquisite painter were preserved. He acquired such an excellence in the imitation of Correggio's style, and copying his pictures, that many paintings finished by him were taken for originals, and not only admired, but were eagerly purchased by the connoisseurs of that time. Nor is it improbable that several of the paintings of Girolamo de Carpi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> for the genuine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Correggio himself. He died in 1556. Carpinus, the Hornbeam. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CarpoBalsam, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, the fruit of the tree which yields the true oriental balsam. The carpopallam is used in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, according to Proper Alpinus, in all the intentions in which the balsam itself is applied: but the only <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the Europeans make of it is in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> treacle and mithridate: and in these not a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, for cubebes and juniper-berries are generally substituted in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. CarpoCratians, a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Gnostics, so called from CarpoCrates, who in the second century revived and improved upon the errors of Simon Magus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>, Saturinos, and other Gnostics. He owned, with them, one sole principle and father of all things, whose name as well as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> was unknown. The word, he taught, was created by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, vastly inferior to the first principle. He opposed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; making him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, begotten carnally on the body of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, though possessed of uncommon gifts which set him above other creatures. He inculcated a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of women; and taught, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> could not be purified, till it had committed all kinds of abominations, making that a necessary condition of perfection. Carpoliti, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fruit-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> Rocks of the Germans, are composed of a kind of jasper, of the nature of the amygdaloides, or almond-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Bertrand affirms that the latter are those which appear to be composed of elliptical pieces like petrified almonds, though, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, they are only small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> pieces of calcareous stone rounded by attrition, and sometimes small mussel-shells connected by a stony concretion. The name of Carpolithi, however, is given in general by writers on fossils to all sorts of stony concretions that have any resemblance to fruit of whatever kind. Carpus, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">Wrist</a>. See Anatomy Index. Carr, a kind of rolling throne, used in triumphs, and at the splendid entries of princes. See Chariot. The word is from the ancient Gaulish, or Celtic, Carr; mentioned by Caesar, in his Commentaries, under the name Carrus. Plutarch relates, that Camillus having entered Rome in triumph, mounted on a carr drawn by four <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> horses, it was looked on as too haughty an innovation. Carr is also used for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> open chariot. The carr, on medals, drawn either by horses, lions, or elephants, usually signifies either a triumph or an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a>: sometimes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> of the images of the gods at solemn supplication, and sometimes of those of some illustrious family at a funeral. The carr covered, and drawn by mules, only signifies a consecration, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> done any one of having his image carried at the gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>. See Consecration, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRAC">Carrac</a>, or Carraca, a name given by the Portuguese to the vessels they send to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> and the East Indies; being very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, round built, and fitted for fight as well as burden. Their capacity lies in their depth, which is very extraordinary. They are narrower above than underneath, and have sometimes <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight floors; they carry about 2000 tons, and are capable of lodging 2000 men; but of late they are little used. Formerly they were also in use among the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, as well as among the Genoese, and other Italians. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> among the Portuguese, when the carracas returned from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, not to bring any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or sloop for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the ship beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Helena; at which place they sink them on purpose; in order to take from the crew all hopes or possibility of saving themselves, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of shipwreck. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRARA">Carrara</a> marble, among our artificers, the name of a species of white marble, which is called marmor tunecum, and liggurium by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>: it is distinguished from the Parian, now called the statuary marble, by being harder and less bright. Carraveira a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Europe,

CARRIAGE

Pages 206-207

a vehicle serving to convey persons, goods, merchandises, and other things, from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. For the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> principles of wheel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, see <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">MECHANICS</a>. CARRIAGE of a Cannon, the frame <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on which it is mounted, serving to point it for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a>, or to carry it from one place to another. It is made of two planks of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of one-half the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, and joined by three wooden trunions, strengthened with three bolts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. It is mounted on two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, but on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> has two fore-wheels with limbers added. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of a carriage are the cheeks, trunion, bolts, plates, trainbands, bridges, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, hooks, trunion holes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. Book-CARRIAGE, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a> made on purpose for carrying mortars and their beds from place to place. Truck-CARRIAGE, two short planks of wood, supported on two axletrees, having four trucks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> wood for carrying mortars or guns upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, where their own carriages cannot go. They are drawn by men.

CARRICK

Pages 207-207

the southern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the shire of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a> in Scotland. It borders on <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>; stretches 32 miles in length; and is a hilly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> fit for pasture. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Stinchar and Girvan, both abounding with salmon. Here are also several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and forests; and the people on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> employ themselves in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>-fishery, though they have no harbour of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of this district are Girvan and Ballantrae; the former at the mouth of the river of the same name, and the latter at the mouth of the Stinchar; and Maybole, an inland town. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, as prince of Scotland, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Carrick. CARRICK on the Sure, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIPPERARY">Tipperary</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. I. N. Lat. 52. 16. CARRICK-Fergus, a town of Ireland, in the county of Antrim and province of Ulster. It is a town and county in itself, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is very rich and populous, with a good harbour; and is governed by a mayor, recorder, and sheriffs.—It has, however, been of far greater consequence than at present, as appears from the mayor having been <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of coast in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> and Antrim, and the corporation enjoying the customs paid by all vessels within these bounds, the creeks of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> excepted. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> was repurchased, and the customhouse transferred to Belfast.—Here is the skeleton of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> built by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a> in the reign of James I, an old Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with many family monuments, and a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> old castle. The town was formerly walled round, and some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the walls is still remaining entire.—Carrick-fergus is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name in the Irish channel; and is noted for being the landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William in 1690. Here also Thurot made a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> in 1759, took possession of the castle, and carried away hostages for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of the town; but being soon after pursued by Commodore Elliot, his three ships were taken, and he himself was killed.

CARRIER

Pages 207-208

is a person that carries goods for others for hire. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> carrier, having the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> and carriage of goods, is to answer for the same, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the value, to the owner. And where goods are delivered to a carrier, and he is robbed of them, he shall be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> and answer for them, because of the hire. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a common carrier, who is offered his hire, and who has convenience, refuses to carry goods, he is liable to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, in the same manner as an innkeeper who refuses to entertain a guest. See ASUMPSIT. One brought a box to a carrier, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and the carrier demanded of the owner what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. Dix. was in it; he answered, that it was filled with silks, and such like goods: upon which the carrier took it, and was robbed, and adjudged to make it good; but a special <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>, as, provided there is no charge of money, would have excused the carrier.—A person delivered to a carrier's book-keeper two bags of money sealed up, to be carried from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and told him that it was 200l. and took his receipt for the same, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of delivery for 10s. per cent. carriage and risk: though it be proved that there was 400l. in the bags, if the carrier be robbed, he shall answer only for 200l. because there was a particular undertaking for that sum and no more; and his reward, which makes him answerable, extends no farther. If a common carrier loses goods which he is intrusted to carry, a special action on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> lies against him, on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the realm, and not trover; and so of a common carrier by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. An action <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> against a porter, carrier, or barge-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, upon his bare receipt of the goods, if they are lost through negligence. Also a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>-man spoiling goods he is to carry, by letting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> come to them, action of the case lies against him, on the common custom. CARRIER-Pigeon, or Courier-pigeon, a sort of pigeon used, when properly trained, to be sent with letters from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. See COLUMBA. Though you carry these birds hood-winked, 20, 30, nay, 60 or 100 miles, they will find their way in a very little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the place where they were bred. They are trained to this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; and are carried first, while young, short flights of half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, afterwards more, till at length they will return from the farthest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Every bawhaw has a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of these pigeons bred in the feraglio, which, upon any emergent occasion, as an infirmitie, or the like, he dispatches, with letters braced under the wings, to the feraglio; which proves a more speedy method, as well as a more safe one, than any other; he sends out more than one pigeon, however, for fear of accidents. Lithgow assures us, that one of these birds will carry a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, which is 30 days journey, in 48 hours. This is also a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> practice: Hirtius and Brutus, at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, held a correspondence with one another by means of pigeons. And Ovid tells us, that Taurophenes, by a pigeon stained with purple, gave notice to his father of his victory at the Olympic games, sending it to him at Ægina. In <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, the most noted were the pigeons of Aleppo, which served as couriers at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRETTA">Alexandretta</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>. But this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them has been laid aside for the last 30 or 40 years, because the Curd robbers kill... ed the pigeons. The manner of sending advice by them was this: they took pairs which had young ones, and carried them on horseback to the place from whence they wished them to return, taking care to let them have a full view. When the news arrived, the correspondent tied a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILLET">billet</a> to the pigeon's foot, and let her loose. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, impatient to see its young, flew off like <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and arrived at Aleppo in ten hours from Alexandretta, and in two days from Bagdad. It was not difficult for them to find their way back, since Aleppo may be discovered at an immense distance. This pigeon has nothing peculiar in its form, except its nostrils, which, instead of being smooth and even, are swelled and rough.

CARRON

Pages 208-209

a small but remarkable river in Scotland, rising about the middle of the isthmus between the friths of Forth and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>. Both its source, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it empties itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, are within the shire of Stirling, which it divides into two nearly equal parts. The whole length of its course, which is from west to east, is not above 14 miles. It falls into the frith of Forth about three miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a>. The stream thereof is but small, and scarcely deserves the notice of a traveller; yet there is no river in Scotland, and few in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, whose banks have been the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of so many memorable transactions. When the Roman empire was in all its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and had its eastern frontiers upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, the banks of Carron were its boundaries upon the north-west; for the wall of Antoninus*, which was raised to mark the limits of that mighty empire, stood in the neighbourhood of this river, and ran <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to it for several miles. Near the middle of its course, in a pleasant valley, stand two beautiful mounts, called the Hills of Dunipace, which are taken notice of by most of the Scottish historians as monuments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. The whole structure of these mounts is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but they are not both of the same form and dimensions. The more easterly one is perfectly round, resembling an oven, and about fifty feet in height: And that this is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> does not admit of the least doubt; but we cannot affirm the same, with equal certainty, of the other, though it has been generally supposed to be so too. It bears no resemblance to the eastern one either in shape <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> size. At the foundation it is nearly of a triangular form; but the superstructure is quite <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; nor does the height thereof bear any proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of its base. These mounts are now planted with firs, which, with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Dunipace standing in the middle between them, and the river running hard by, give this valley a very romantic appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> account given of those mounts is, that they were erected as monuments of a peace concluded in that place between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and the Caledonians, and that their name partakes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of both people; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">Dun</a> signifying a hill in the old language of this island, and Pae "peace" in the language of Rome. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> word, Dunipace, signifies "the hills of peace." And we find in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that no less than three treaties of peace were at different periods entered into between the Romans and Caledonians; the first by Severus about the year 210; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> soon after, by his son <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>; and the third, by the usurper Carausius, about the year 280; but of which of these treaties Dunipace is a monument, we do not pretend to determine. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the concurring testimony of historians and antiquaries did not agree in giving this original to these mounts, we would be tempted to conjecture that they are sepulchral monuments. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and urns have been discovered in earthen fabrics of this kind in many parts of this island, and the little mounts or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a> which are scattered in great numbers about <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> plain are generally supposed to have been the sepulchres of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons. See BARROWS. From the valley of Dunipace, the river runs for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a deep and hollow channel, with steep banks on both sides; here it passes by the foundations of the ancient Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; not far from which, as is generally thought, was the scene of the memorable conference betwixt the Scotch patriot William Wallace and Robert Bruce, father to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of that name, which first opened the eyes of the latter to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> view both of his own true <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and that of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. After the river has left the village and bridge of Larbert, it soon comes up to another smaller valley, through the midst of which it has now worn out to itself a straight channel, whereas, in former ages, it had taken a considerable compass, as appears by the track of the old <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> which is still visible. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and circling banks upon the south side give to this valley the appearance of a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>; and, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the country, there was once an harbour here; nor does the tradition seem altogether groundless, pieces of broken anchors having been found here, and some of them within the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of people yet alive. The stream <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> would still flow near the place, if they were not kept back by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>-head built across the river at Stenhouse; and there is reason to believe, that the frith flowed considerably higher in former ages than it does at present. In the near neighbourhood of this valley, upon the south, stand the ruins of ancient Camelon; which, after it was abandoned by the Romans, was probably inhabited, for some ages, by the natives of the country. Another ancient monument, called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>'s Oven, once stood upon the banks of the Carron; but was, with a spirit truly Gothic, entirely demolished about 40 years ago. The corner of a small inclosure between Stenhouse and the Carron <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-works, is pointed out as the place of its situation. This is generally supposed to have been a Roman work; though it is not easy to conceive what could be their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> for erecting such a fabric, at so great a distance from any other of their works, and in a spot which at that time must have been very remote and unfrequented. The form of it is said to have been perfectly round, and rising perpendicular for some yards at first, but afterwards gradually contracted, till it terminated in a narrow orifice at the top. Antiquaries are not agreed whether it had been a temple, or a trophy, or a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>; but the most common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is, that it had been a temple, and Buchanan thinks, a temple of Terminus. Hector Boetius says, that there were benches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> all around it upon the inside; and that there had been a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stone stone for sacrificing upon, or an altar, upon the south side. As the Carron extends over the half of the isthmus, and runs so near the ancient boundaries of the Roman empire, the adjacent country fell naturally to be the scene of many battles and encounters. Historians mention a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought near the river between the Romans and the confederate <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the Scots and Picts in the beginning of the 5th century. The scenes of some of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>'s poems were, in the opinion of the translator, upon the banks of this river. Here Fingal fought with Caracal, the son of the king of the world, supposed to have been the same with Caracalla, the son of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus. Here also young Oscar, the son of Ossian, performed some of his heroic exploits. Hereabout was the stream of Crona, celebrated in the ancient compositions of the Gaelic bard; possibly that now called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of Bonny, which runs in the neighborhood of the Roman wall, and discharges itself into the Carron at Dunipace. In those poems, mention is made of a green vale upon the banks of this river, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> standing in the middle of it, where young Oscar's party and the warriors of Caros met. We only take notice of this as it strengthens the conjecture hazarded above, that the mounts of Dunipace, especially the more easterly of them, were sepulchral monuments.—About the distance of half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the river, and near the town of Falkirk, lies the field of that battle which was fought by William Wallace and the English in the beginning of the 14th century. It goes by the name of Graham's mound, from the valiant John Graham, who fell there, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>-stone is still to be seen in the church-yard of Falkirk. The river Carron, though it has <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> since ceased to roll its stream amidst the din of arms, still preserves its fame, by lending its aid to trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; (see the next article.)—The river is navigable for some miles near its mouth, and a considerable trade is carried on upon it by small craft; for the convenience of which, its channel has of late years been straightened and much shortened, and the great Canal * has its entrance from it. Carron-Works, a large iron-foundery, two miles north from Falkirk in Scotland. They are conveniently situated on the banks of the Carron, three miles above its entry into the frith of Forth. Above 100 acres of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> have been converted into reservoirs and pools, for water diverted from the river, by magnificent dams built above two miles above the works, which, after <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> 18 large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> for the several purposes of the manufacture, falls into a tide-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> that conveys their castings to the sea. These works are the greatest of the kind in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and were established in 1760. At present, the buildings are of vast extent; and the machinery, constructed by Mr Smeaton, is the first in Britain, both in elegance and correctness: there are 1600 men employed, to whom is paid weekly above £500 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; which has greatly enriched the adjoining country; 6500 tons of iron are melted annually from the mineral with pit-coal, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into cannon, cylinders, &c.—In the founding of cannon, these works have lately arrived at such perfection, that they make above 5000 pieces a year, many of which are exported to foreign states; and their guns of new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> are the lightest and neatest now in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, not excepting <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> guns; the 32 pounder ship-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> weighing 42 hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, the 6 pounder 8 hundred-weight and one-half, and the other calibers in proportion. The present proprietors are a chartered <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of £50,000l. sterling, a common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, &c., but their stock is confined to a very few individuals.

CARRONADE

Pages 209-209

a short kind of ordnance, capable of carrying a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, and useful in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> engagements at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It takes its name from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRON">Carron</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where this sort of ordnance was first made, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the principle applied to an improved <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. See the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">GUNNERY</a>. CARROT. See Daucus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Deadly CARROT. See Thapsia, Botany Index.

CARROUSAL

Pages 209-209

a course of horses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a magnificent entertainment exhibited by princes on some public rejoicing. It consists in a cavalcade of several gentlemen, richly dressed and equipped after the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> cavaliers, divided into squadrons, meeting in some public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and practising jousts, tournaments, &c.—The last carousals were in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV.—The word comes from the Italian word carrofello, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of carro, "chariot." Tertullian ascribes the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of carousals to Circe; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have them instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, her father; whence some derive the word from carrus, or carrus folis. The Moors introduced ciphers, liveries, and other ornaments of their arms, with trappings, &c., for their horses. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> added <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>, plumes, &c.

CARRUCA

Pages 209-209
or Caruca, also was sometimes used for carrucata. See CARRUCATE.

CARRUCAGE

Pages 209-209

Carucage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Carugge, in husbandry, denotes the ploughing of ground, either ordinary, as for grain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>; or extraordinary, as for woad, dyers weed, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>, and the like.

CARRUCATE

Pages 209-209

(carucata), in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> laws and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as much arable ground as can be tilled in one year with one plough. In Doomsday <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>, the arable land is estimated in carrucates, the pasture in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> in acres. Skene makes the carrucata the same with hilda, or hilda terra; Littleton the same with foc. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of a carrucate appears to have differed in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. In the reign of Richard I., it was estimated at 60 acres, and in another <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of the same reign at 100 acres; in the time of Edward I., at 180 acres; and in the 23d of Edward III., a carrucate of land in Burcester contained 112 acres, and in Middleton 150 acres. By a statute under William III., for charging per-

CARRYING

Pages 210-210

among riding-masters. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is said to carry low, when having naturally an ill-shaped neck, he lowers his head too much. All horses that arm themselves carry low, but a horse may carry low without arming. A French branch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gigot is prescribed as a remedy against carrying low. A horse is said to carry well, when his neck is raised or arched, and he holds his head <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and firm, without constraint.

CARRYING WIND

Pages 210-210

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by our dealers in horses to express such a one as frequently tosses his nose as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as his ears, and does not carry handsomely. This is called carrying <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between carrying in the wind, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is this: that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> who beats upon the hand, shakes the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> and resists it, while he shakes his head; but the horse that carries in the wind puts up his head without shaking, and sometimes beats upon the hand. The opposite to carrying in the wind, is arming and carrying low: and even between these two there is a difference in wind.

CARSE

Pages 210-210
or Carse of Gowry, a district of Perthshire in Scotland. It lies on the north side of the Tay, and extends 14 miles in length from Dundee to Perth, and is from two to four in breadth. It is a rich plain country, cultivated like a garden, and producing as good harvests of wheat as any in Great Britain. It abounds with all the necessaries of life: but, from its low damp situation, the inhabitants are subject to agues, and the commonalty are in great want of firing. In this district, not far from the Tay, stands the house of Errol, which formerly belonged to the earls of that name, the chiefs of the ancient family of Hay, hereditary constables of Scotland.

CARSTAIRS

Pages 210-210

WILLIAM, an eminent Scots divine, whose merit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> called him to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> scenes, and to associate with men to whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> and intercourse his birth gave him few pretensions to aspire. A small village in the neighbourhood of Glasgow was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. His father, of whom little is known, exercised the functions of a clergyman. Young Carstairs turned his thoughts to the profession of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; and the persecutions and oppressions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, both in regard to civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, having excited his strongest indignation, it became a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> that he should prosecute his studies in a foreign university. He went accordingly to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; and his industry and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> being directed with skill, opened up and unfolded those faculties which he was about to employ with equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and himself. During his residence abroad, he became acquainted with Penfionary Fagel, and entered with warmth into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. On his return to Scotland to produce a licence to teach doctrines which he had studied with the greatest care, he became disgusted with the proud and insolent conduct of Archbishop Sharp, and prepared to revisit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; where he knew that religious liberty was respected, and where he hoped he might better his condition by the connections he had formed. His expectations were not vain. His prudence, his reserve, and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, were strong recommendations of him to the prince of Orange; and he was employed in personal negotiations in Holland, England, and Scotland. Upon the elevation of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to the English throne, he was appointed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s chaplain for Scotland, and employed in settling the affairs of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. William, who carried politics into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was solicitous that episcopacy should prevail there as universally as in England. Carstairs, more versed in the affairs of his native country, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> all the impropriety of this project, and the danger that would arise from the enforcing of it. His reasonings, his remonstrances, his intreates, overcame the firmness of King William. He yielded to considerations founded alike in policy and in prudence; and to Carstairs Scotland is indebted for the full establishment of its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the Presbyterian form of government. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of King William was a severe affliction to him; and it happened before that prince had provided for him with the liberality he deserved. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, however, in the office of chaplain for Scotland by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>; and he was invited to accept the principality of the University of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. He was one of the ministers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and four times moderator of the general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. Placed at the head of the church, he prosecuted its interest with zeal and with integrity. Nor were his influence and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> confined to matters of religion. They were exerted with success in promoting the culture of the arts and sciences. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Scotland owe him obligations of the highest kind. He procured, in particular, an augmentation of the salaries of their professors; a circumstance to which may be ascribed their reputation, as it enabled them to cultivate with spirit the different branches of knowledge. A zeal for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of moderation and order, prudence, and humility, distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">Principal</a> Carstairs in an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. His religion had no mixture of austerity; his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> transactions were attended with no imputation of artifice; and the versatility of his talents made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> with ease from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He was among the last who suffered torture before the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, in order to make him divulge the secrets intrusted to him, which he firmly refused; and after the revolution, that inhuman <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> the thumb-crew was given to him in a present by the council.—This excellent person died in 1715; and in 1774 his State papers and Letters, with an account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, were published in one vol. 4to, by the Rev. Dr M'Cormick.

CARSUGAI

Pages 210-211

RAINIER, a Jesuit, born at Citerna in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, in 1647, was the author of a Latin poem, entitled *Ars bene scribendi*, which is esteemed both for the elegance of the style and for the excellent precepts it contains. He also wrote some good epigrams. He died in 1709.

CART

Pages 211-211

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> carriage with two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, drawn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> by horses, to carry heavy goods, &c., from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another. The word seems formed from the French *charrette*, which signifies the same, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather the Latin *carreta*, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of *carrus*. See CARR. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Westminster carts shall not carry more than twelve packs of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hundred and fifty bricks, one chaldron of coals, &c., on pain of forfeiting one of the horses, (6 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6.) By the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, cart-men are forbidden to ride either on their carts or horses. They are to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or drive them on foot through the streets, on the forfeiture of ten shillings. (Stat. 1. Geo. I. cap. 57.) Criminals used to be drawn to execution on a cart. Bawds and other malefactors are whipped at the cart's tail. Scripture makes mention of a sort of carts or drags used by the Jews to do the office of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a>. They were supported on low thick wheels, bound with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which were rolled up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the sheaves, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them, and force out the corn. Something of the like kind also obtained among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, under the denomination of *playfra*, of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> makes mention, (Georg. I.) *Tardaque Eleusiae matris volventia playfra;* *Tribulaque, trahaeque.* On which Servius observes, that *trahea* denotes a cart without wheels, and *tribula* a fort of cart armed on all sides with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> for threshing corn. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and St Jerome represent these carts as furnished with saws, insomuch that their surface was beset with teeth. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> having taken Rabbah, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, ordered all the inhabitants to be crushed to pieces under such carts, moving on wheels set with iron teeth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Damascus is said to have treated the Israelites of the land of Gilead in the same manner. CART-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">Bole</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies wood to be employed in making and repairing instruments of husbandry. CARTS of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, a peculiar kind of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> anciently in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Scots. They are thus described in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, A.D. 1456: "It is thought expedient, that the king may require of certain of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> barons of the land that are of any might, to make carts of war, and in ilk cart twa gunnits, and ilk one to have two chalmers; with the remnant of the grain that effects thereto, and an cunning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to flout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAME">thame</a>." By another act, A.D. 1471, the prelates and barons are commanded to provide such carts of war against their old enemies the English.

CARTAMA

Pages 211-211

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Grenada, formerly very considerable. It is seated at the foot of a mountain, near the river Guadalu-Medina, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 28'. N. Lat. 36° 40'.

CARTE

Pages 211-211

THOMAS, the historian, was the son of Mr Samuel Carte prebendary of Lichfield, and born in 1686. When he was reader in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Bath, he took occasion in a 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> sermon, 1714, to vindicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. with respect to the Irish massacre, which drew him into a controversy with Mr Chandler the dissenting minister; and on the accession of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family, he refused to take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and put on a lay <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. He is said to have acted as a kind of secretary to Bishop Atterbury before his troubles: and in the year 1722, being accused of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, a reward of 1000l. was offered for apprehending him; but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Caroline, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> patroness of learned men, obtained leave for him to return home in security. He published, 1. An edition of Thuanus, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes, folio. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, three volumes, folio. 3. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England, four volumes, folio. 4. A Collection of original Letters and Papers concerning the affairs of England, two volumes octavo; and some other works. He died in April 1754. His History of England ends in 1654. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to have brought it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the Revolution; for which purpose he had taken great pains in copying every thing valuable that could be met with in England, Scotland, France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, &c.—He had (as he himself says, p. 43. of his Vindication of a full answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from a bystander), "read abundance of collections relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Charles II., and had in his power a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> from the beginning to the end of that reign, in which all those intrigues and turns at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, at the latter end of that king's life, which Bishop Burnet, with all his gout for tales of secret history, and all his genius for conjectures, does not pretend to account for, are laid open in the clearest and most convincing manner by the person who was most affected by them, and had the best reason to know them."—At his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, all his papers came into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of his widow, who afterwards married Mr Jernegan, a member of the church of Rome. They are now deposited in the Bodleian library, having been delivered by Mr Jernegan to the university, 1778, for a valuable consideration. Whilst they were in this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s possession, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Hardwick paid 200l. for the perusal of them. For a consideration of 300l. Mr Macpherson had the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them; and from these and other materials compiled his history and state-papers. Mr Carte was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and indefatigable application. When the studies of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> were over, he would eat heartily; and in conversation was cheerful and entertaining. CARTE-Blanche, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, signed at the bottom with a person's name, and sometimes affixed with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, giving another person power to superscribe what conditions he pleases. Much like this is the French *blanc signé*, a paper without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, except a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> at the bottom, given by contending parties to arbitrators <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> friends, to fill up with the conditions they judge reasonable, in order to end the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>.

CARTEL

Pages 211-212

l signifies also a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of defiance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a challenge to decide a controversy either in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a> or in a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">Duel</a>. CARTEL Ship, a ship commissioned in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> the prisoners of any two hostile powers; also to carry any particular request or proposal from one to another; Cartel Ship, another: for this reason the officer who commands her is particularly ordered to carry no cargo, ammunition, or implements of war, except a single <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> for the purpose of firing signals.

CARTES

Pages 212-212

RENE DES, descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Touraine in France, was one of the most eminent philosophers and mathematicians in the 17th century. At the Jesuit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> at La Flèche, he made a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in the learned languages and polite literature, and became acquainted with Father Marfenne. His father designed him for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but his tender <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> then not permitting him to expose himself to such fatigues, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he launched into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, in which he had prodigious success. Here Marfenne persuaded him to return to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; which he pursued till he went to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in May 1616, where he engaged as a volunteer among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>'s troops. While he lay in garrison at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>, he wrote a treatise on music, and laid the foundation of several of his works. He was at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> in 1628; returned to Paris; and, a few days after his return, at an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of men of learning in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Montigny Bagni, the pope's nuncio, was prevailed upon to explain his sentiments with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, when the nuncio urged him to publish his system. Upon this he went to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, and from thence to Franeker, where he began his metaphysical meditations, and drew up his discourse on meteors. He made a short tour to England; and not far from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, made some observations concerning the declination of the magnet. He returned to Holland, where he finished his treatise on the world. His books made a great noise in France; and Holland thought of nothing but discarding the old philosophy, and following his. Voetius being chosen rector of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, procured his philosophy to be prohibited, and wrote against him; but he immediately published a vindication of himself. In 1647, he took a journey into France, where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> settled a pension of 300 livres upon him. Christine, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, having invited him into that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, he went thither, where he was received with the greatest civility by her majesty, who engaged him to attend her every morning at five o'clock, to instruct her in philosophy, and desired him to revile and digest all his writings which were unpublished, and to form a complete body of philosophy from them. She likewise proposed to allow him a revenue, and to form an academy, of which he was to be the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>. But these designs were broken off by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1650. His body was interred at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, and 17 years afterwards removed to Paris, where a magnificent monument was erected to him in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Genevieve du Mont. The great Dr Halley, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> concerning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, observes, that though some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> mention refraction as an effect of transparent mediums, Des Cartes was the first who discovered the laws of refraction, and reduced dioptries to a science. As to his philosophy, Dr Keill, in his introduction to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Dr Burnet's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, says, that Des Cartes was so far from applying <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, that his whole system is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> blunder on account of his negligence in that point; the laws observed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in their revolutions round the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> not agreeing with his theory of vortices. His philosophy has accordingly given way to the more accurate discoveries and demonstrations of the Newtonian system.

CARTESIANS

Pages 212-212

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers, who adhered to the system of Des Cartes, founded on the two following principles, the one metaphysical, the other physical. The metaphysical one is, I think, therefore I am: the physical principle is, that nothing exists but substance. Substances he makes of two kinds; the one a substance that thinks, the other a substance extended; whence actual thought, and actual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, are the essence of substance. The essence of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> being thus fixed in extension, the Cartesians conclude that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> nor any possibility thereof in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but that the universe is absolutely full: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> space is excluded by this principle; because extension being implied in the idea of space, matter is so too. Upon these principles the Cartesians explained mechanically how the world was formed, and how the present celestial phenomena came to take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CARTHAGE

Pages 212-240

a famed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of antiquity, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> Propria; and which for many years, disputed with Rome the sovereignty of the world. According to Velleius Paterculus, this city was built when 65, according to Justin and Trogus 72, according to others 100 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 140 years before the foundations of Rome were laid. It is on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> agreed that the Phoenicians were the founders. The beginning of the Carthaginian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, like that of all other nations, is obscure and uncertain. In the 7th year of Pygmalion <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, his sister Elisa or Elisa, or Dido, is said to have fled, with some of her companions and vassals, from the cruelty and avarice of her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who had put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> her husband Sinther, in order to get possession of his wealth. She first touched at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, where she met with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, who was desirous of attending her; to which she readily consented, and fixed the priesthood in his family.
