The rope, therefore, being set at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, the spring must strike the darts with great violence, and send them, with surprising velocity, to a great distance. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> differs in some particulars from the description we have of that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; principally in the throwing of several darts at the same time, one only being thrown by theirs.

CATARACT

Pages 274-274

in Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a disorder of the humours of the eye, by which the pupilla, that ought to appear transparent and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, looks opaque, blue, gray, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, &c. by which vision is variously impeded, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> totally destroyed. See Surgery.

CATARACTES

Pages 274-274

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LARUS">Larus</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CATARO

Pages 274-274

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of the same name, with a strong castle, and a bishop's see. It is subject to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, and is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 19. N. Lat. 42. 25.

CATARRH

Pages 274-277

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> defluxion from the head upon the mouth and alptra arteria, and through them upon the lungs. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CATASTASIS

Pages 277-277

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> drama; being that wherein the intrigue, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, set forth in the epistle, is supported, carried on, and heightened, till it be ripe for the unravelling in the catastrophe. Scaliger defines it, the full growth of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, while things are at a stand in that confusion to which the poet has brought them.

CATASTROPHE

Pages 277-277

in Dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, the fourth and last <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> drama; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that immediately succeeding the catastasis; or, according to others, the third only; the whole drama being divided into prologue, epistle, and catastrophe; or in the terms of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, prologue, epilogue, and exode. The catastrophe clears up everything, and is nothing else but the discovery or winding up of the plot. It has its peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; for it ought entirely to be contained, not only in the last <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, but in the very conclusion of it; and, when the plot is finished, the play should be so also. The catastrophe ought to turn upon a single point, or start up on a sudden. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> art in the catastrophe is, that the clearing up of all difficulties may appear wonderful, and yet easy, simple, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. It is a very propitious artifice in some writers to show the catastrophe in the very <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the play. Mr Dryden thinks that a catastrophe resulting from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> change in the sentiments and resolutions of a person, without any other machinery, may be so managed as to be exceedingly beautiful. It is a dispute among the critics, whether the catastrophe should always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> out favourably on the side of virtue or not. The reasons on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> side seem the strongest. Aristotle prefers a shocking catastrophe to a happy one.—The catastrophe is either simple or complex. The first is that in which there is no change in the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons, nor any discovery or unravelling, the plot being only a mere passage out of agitation into quiet repose. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the principal persons undergo a change of fortune, in the manner already defined.

CATCH

Pages 277-277

in the musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, a fugue in unison, wherein, to humour some conceit in the words, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> is broken, and the sense interrupted in one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and caught again <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> supported by another; as in the catch in Shakespeare's play of the Twelfth Night, where there is a catch sung by three persons, in which the humour is, that each who sings, calls and is called known in turn: Or, as defined by Mr Jackson "a catch is a piece for three or more voices, one of which leads, and the others follow in the same notes. It must be so contrived, that rests (which are made for that purpose) in the music of one line be filled up with a word or two from another line; these form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> purpose, or catch, from whence the name." CATCH-Fly. See Lychnis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CATCH-Pole, (quasi one that catches by the pole), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used, by way of reproach, for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>'s follower or attendant. CATCH-Word, among printers, that placed at the bottom of each page, being always the first word of the following page.

CATECHESIS

Pages 277-277

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes an instruction given any person in the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of an art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> science; but more particularly of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, catechesis was an instruction given vivæ voce, either to children or adult heathens, preparatory to their receiving of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. In this sense, catechesis stands contradistinguished from mystagogica, which were a higher <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of instruction given to those already initiated, and containing the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Those who give such instructions are called catechists; and those who receive them, catechumens.

CATECHETIC

Pages 277-277
or Catechetical, something that relates to oral instruction in the rudiments of Christianity.—Catechetical schools were buildings appointed for the office of the catechist, adjoining to the church, and called catechumena: such was that in which Origen and many other famous men read catechetical lectures at Alexandria. See Catechumen.

CATECHISM

Pages 277-277

in its primary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, an instruction, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, in the principles of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, delivered vivæ voce, and so as to require frequent repetitions, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> or hearer, of what has been said. The word is formed from κατηχεῖν, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of κατὰ and ἐχεῖν, q. d., circumfondo; alluding to the noise or din made in this sort of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, or to the zeal and earnestness wherewith things are to be incultated over and over on the learners.—Anciently the candidates for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> were only to be instructed in the secrets of their religion by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, vivæ voce, without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; as had also been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> among the Egyptian priests, and the British and Gaulish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a>, who only communicated the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> by word of mouth. Catechism is more frequently used in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times for an elementary book, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of religion are summarily delivered in the way of question and answer.

CATECHIST

Pages 277-277

(κατηχητής, catecheta), he that catechises, i.e., he that instructs novices in the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

CATECHIST MORE PARTICULARLY

Pages 277-277

t more particularly denotes a person appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to instruct those intended for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, by word of mouth, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. The catechists of churches were ministers usually distinct from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and prebys ters, and had their auditory <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> catechumena apart. Their business was to instruct the catechumens, and prepare them for the reception of baptism. But the catechists did not constitute any distinct order of the clergy, but were chosen out of any other order. The bishop himself sometimes performed the office; at other times prebys ters, or even readers or deacons, were the catechists. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> seems to have had no higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in the church than reader, when he was made catechist at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, being only 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and consequently incapable of the deaconship.

CATECHU

Pages 277-277

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a name given to the extract otherwise known by the name of Terra Japonica, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. See Areca and Mimosa.

CATECHUMEN

Pages 277-278

CATECHUMEN, a candidate for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one who prepares himself for the receiving thereof. The catechumens, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, were the lowest order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in the primitive church. They had some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of Christian, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> above pagans and heretics, though not consummated by baptism. They were admitted to the state of catechumens by the imposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. The children of believing parents were admitted catechumens, as soon as ever they were capable of instruction; but at what <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> those of heathen parents might be admitted, is not so clear. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their continuance in this state, there were no general rules fixed about it; but the practice varied according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of times and places, and the readiness and proficiency of the catechumens themselves. There were four orders or degrees of catechumens; the first were those instructed privately without the church, and kept at a distance, for some time, from the privilege of entering the church, to make them the more eager and desirous of it. The next degree were the audientes, so called from their being admitted to hear sermons, and the Scriptures read in the church, but were not allowed to partake of the prayers. The third sort of catechumens were the genu-flectentes, so called because they received imposition of hands kneeling. The fourth order was the competentes et electi, denoting the immediate candidates for baptism, or such as were appointed to be baptized the next approaching festival; before which, strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> was made into their proficiency under the several stages of catechetical exercises. After examination, they were exercised for twenty days together, and were obliged to fasting and confession: some days before baptism they went veiled; and it was customary to touch their ears, saying, Ephatha, i.e., be opened; as also to anoint their eyes with clay; both ceremonies being in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of our Saviour's practice, and intended to shadow out to the catechumens their condition both before and after their admission into the Christian church.

CATEGORY

Pages 278-278

in Logic, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> order of all the predicates or attributes contained under any genus. The school philosophers distribute all the objects of our thoughts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> into certain genera or classes, not so much, say they, to learn what they do not know, as to communicate a distinct notion of what they do know; and these classes the Greeks called categories, and the Latins predicaments. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> made ten categories, viz., substance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, relation, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, situation, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, which are usually expressed by the following technical distich: Arbor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, servos, ardore, refrigerat, uflus, Rure eras flabo, nec tunicatus ero. CATEK. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">BENGAL</a>.

CATENARIA

Pages 278-278

in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the name of a curve line formed by a rope hanging freely from two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of suspension, whether the points be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">FLUXIONS</a>.

CATERPILLAR

Pages 278-290

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of all winged insects when in their reptile <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> worm state. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Method of Destroying CATERPILLARS on Trees.—Take a chafing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> with lighted <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, and placing it under the branches that are loaded with caterpillars, throw some pinches of brimstone upon the coals. The vapour of the sulphur, which is mortal to these insects, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not only destroy all that are on the tree, but prevent it from being infested with them afterwards. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of sulphur will clear as many trees as grow on several acres. This method has been successfully tried in France. In the Journal Oeconomique, the following is said to be infallible against the caterpillars feeding on cabbage, and perhaps may be equally serviceable against those that infest other vegetables. Sow with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> all the borders of the ground where you <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to plant your cabbage; and, although the neighbourhood is infested with caterpillars, the space enclosed with the hemp will be perfectly free, not one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> will approach it. CATERPILLAR-Eaters, a name given by some authors to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> bred in the body of the caterpillar, and which eat its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; these are owing to a certain kind of fly that lodges her eggs in the body of this animal, and they, after their proper changes, become flies like their parents. M. Reaumur has given us, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of insects, some very curious particulars in regard to these little worms. Every one of them, he observes, spins itself a very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a cylindric <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, made of a very strong sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>; these are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which this animal spends its state of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>; and they have a mark by which they may be known from all other animal productions of this kind, which is, that they have always a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> stripe or band surrounding their middle, which is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> when the rest of the case is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and white when that is black. M. Reaumur has had the pains and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> to find out the reason of this singularity, which is this: the whole shell is spun of a silk produced out of the creature's body; this at first runs all white, and towards the end of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> turns black. The outside of the case must necessarily be formed first, as the creature works from within: consequently this is truly white all over, but it is transparent, and shows the last spun or black silk through it. It might be supposed that the whole inside of the shell should be black; but this is not the case: the whole is fashioned before this black silk comes; and this is employed by the creature, not to line the whole, but to fortify certain parts only; and therefore is all applied either to the middle, or to the two ends omitting the middle; and so gives either a black band in the middle, or a blackness at both ends, leaving the white in the middle to appear. It is not unfrequent CATHERINE PARR. See PARR. CATHERINE I. Empress of Russia, a most extraordinary personage, whose history deserves to be given in detail. She was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> girl; and was born at Ringen, a small village upon the lake Virtschee, near Dorpt, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>. The year of her birth is uncertain; but, according to her own account, she came into the world on the 5th of April 1687. Her original name was Martha, which she changed for Catherine when she embraced the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Rosen, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> in the Swedish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, who owned the village of Ringen, supported, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the country, both the mother and the child; and was, for that reason, supposed by many persons to have been her father. She lost her mother when she was but three years old; and, as Count Rosen died about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, she was left in so destitute a situation, that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-clerk of the village received her into his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Soon afterwards Gluck, Lutheran minister of Marienburgh, happening, in a journey through those parts, to see the foundling, took her under his protection, brought her up in his family, and employed her in attending his children. In 1701, and about the 14th year of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, she espoused a dragoon of the Swedish garrison of Marienburgh. Many different accounts are given of this transaction: one author of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> affirms that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> and bridegroom remained together eight days after their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; another, of no less authority, affirms, on the contrary, that on the morning of the nuptials her husband being sent with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>, the marriage was never consummated. This much is certain, that the dragoon was absent when Marienburgh surrendered to the Russians, and Catherine, who was reserved for a higher fortune, never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him more. General Bauer, upon the taking of Marienburgh, saw Catherine among the prisoners; and, being smitten with her youth and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, took her to his house, where she superintended his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> affairs, and was supposed to be his mistress. Soon afterwards she was received into the family of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Menzikof, who was no less struck with the attractions of the fair captive. With him she lived until 1704; when, in the 17th year of her age, she became the mistress of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great, and won so much upon his affections, that he espoused her on the 29th of May 1711. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was secretly performed at Jawerow in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the presence of General Bruce; and on the 20th of February 1712, it was publicly solemnized with great pomp at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>. Catherine, by the most unwearied assiduity and unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, by the softness and complacency of her disposition, but above all by an extraordinary liveliness... Catherine's liveliness and gaiety of temper, acquired a wonderful ascendancy over the mind of Peter. The latter was subject to occasional horrors, which at times rendered him gloomy and suspicious, and raised his passions to such a height as to produce a temporary madness. In these dreadful moments Catherine was the only person who durst venture to approach him; and such was the kind of fascination she had acquired over his senses, that her presence had an instantaneous effect, and the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> composed his mind and calmed his agonies. From these circumstances she seemed necessary not only to his comfort, but even to his very existence; she became his inseparable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> on his journeys to foreign countries, and even in all his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> expeditions. The peace of Pruth, by which the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was relieved from certain destruction, has been wholly attributed to Catherine, though she was little more than an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in procuring the consent of Peter. The latter, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of 1711 against the Turks, having imprudently led his troops into a disadvantageous situation, took the desperate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> his way through the Turkish army in the night. With this resolution he retired to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> in an agony of despair, and gave positive orders that no one should be admitted under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. In this important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers and the vice-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Shafirov assembled in the presence of Catherine, and drew up certain preliminaries in order to obtain a truce from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> vizier. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this determination, plenipotentiaries were immediately dispatched without the knowledge of Peter, to the grand vizier, and a peace obtained upon more reasonable conditions than could have been expected. With these conditions Catherine, notwithstanding the orders issued by Peter, entered his tent, and prevailed upon him to sign them. Catherine, by her conduct on this occasion, acquired great popularity; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> particularly specifies her behaviour at Pruth as one of the reasons which induced him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> her publicly at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. This ceremony was performed in 1724; and although designed by Peter only as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his affection, was the principal cause of her subsequent elevation. Her influence <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> undiminished until a short time before the death of the emperor, when some circumstances happened which occasioned such a coldness between them as would probably have ended in a total rupture, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his death had not fortunately intervened. The original cause of this misunderstanding arose from the following discovery of a secret connection between Catherine and her first chamberlain, whose name was Mons. The emperor, who was suspicious of this connection, quitted Petersburgh under pretence of removing to a villa for a few days, but privately returned to his winter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. From thence he occasionally sent one of his confidential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> with a complimentary message to the empress, as if he had been in the country, and with secret orders to observe her motions. From the page's information the emperor, on the third night, surprized Catherine in an arbour of the garden with her favourite Mons; while his sister, Madame Balke, who was first lady of the bedchamber to the empress, was, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with a page, upon the watch without the arbour. Peter, whose violent temper was inflamed by this discovery, struck Catherine with his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, as well as the page, who endeavoured to prevent him from entering the arbour, and then retired without uttering a single word either to Mons or his sister. A few days after this transaction these persons were taken into custody, and Mons was carried to the winter palace, where no one had admission to him but Peter, who himself brought him his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. A report was at the same time circulated, that they were imprisoned for having received bribes, and making their influence over the empress subservient to their own mercenary views. Mons being examined by Peter, in the presence of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>-general Ushakov, and threatened with the torture, confessed the corruption which was laid to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. He was beheaded; his sister received five strokes of the knout, and was banished into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>; two of her sons, who were chamberlains, were also degraded, and sent as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> among the Russian troops in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> subsequent to the execution of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, Peter conveyed Catherine in an open carriage under the gallows to which was nailed the head of Mons. The empress, without changing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> at this dreadful sight, exclaimed, "What a pity it is that there is so much corruption among courtiers!" This event happened in the latter end of the year 1724; and as it was soon followed by Peter's death, and Catherine upon her accession recalled Madame Balke, it has been suspected that she shortened the days of her husband by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>. But notwithstanding the critical situation for Catherine in which he died, and her subsequent elevation, this charge is totally destitute of the least shadow of proof; for the circumstances of Peter's disorder were too well known, and the peculiar symptoms of his last illness sufficiently account for his death, without the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of recurring to poison. While Peter was yet lying in the agonies of death, several opposite parties were caballing to dispose of the crown. At a considerable meeting of many among the principal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, it was secretly determined, on the moment of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> Catherine, and to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Peter Alexievitch upon the throne. Bafflevitz, apprised of this resolution, repaired in person to the empress, although it was already night. "My grief and consternation," replied Catherine, "render me incapable of acting myself; do you and Prince Mensikof consult together, and I will embrace the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> which you shall approve in my name." Bafflevitz, finding Mensikof asleep, awakened and informed him of the pressing danger which threatened the empress and her party. As no time remained for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> deliberation, the prince instantly seized the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, secured the fortresses, gained the officers of the guards by bribes and promises, also a few of the nobility, and the principal clergy. These partizans being convened in the palace, Catherine made her appearance; she claimed the throne in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of her coronation at Moscow; she exposed the ill effects of a minority; and promised, that, "so far from depriving the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of the crown, she would receive it only as a sacred deposit, to be restored to him when she should be united, in another world, to an adored husband, whom she was now upon the point of losing." The pathetic manner with which she uttered this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, and the tears which accompanied it, added to the previous distribution of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and jewels, produced the desired effect; at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of this meeting the remainder of the night was employed in making the necessary preparations to ensure her accession in case of the emperor's death. Peter at length expired on the morning of the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1725. This event being made known, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, the generals, the principal nobility and clergy, hastened to the palace to proclaim the new sovereign. The adherents of the great duke seemed secure of success, and the friends of Catherine were avoided as persons doomed to destruction. At this juncture Baffevitz whispered one of the opposite party, "The empress is mistress of the treasure and the forts; she has gained over the guards and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, and many of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> nobility; even here she has more followers than you imagine; advise therefore your friends to make no opposition as they value their heads." This information being rapidly circulated, Baffevitz gave the appointed signal, and the two regiments of guards, who had been gained by a largess to declare for Catherine, and had already surrounded the palace, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to arms. "Who has dared (exclaimed Prince Repnin, the commander in chief), to order out the troops without my knowledge?" "I, (returned General Butterlin), without pretending to dispute your authority, in obedience to the commands of my most gracious mistress." This short reply was followed by a dead silence. In this moment of suspense and anxiety Menzikof entered, preceding Catherine, supported by the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. She attempted to speak, but was prevented by sobs and tears from giving utterance to her words; at length, recovering herself, "I come (she said), notwithstanding the grief which now overwhelms me, to assure you, that, submissive to the will of my departed husband, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> will be ever dear to me, I am ready to devote my days to the painful occupations of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, until <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> shall summon me to follow him." Then, after a short pause, she artfully added, "If the great duke will profit by my instructions, perhaps I shall have the consolation, during my wretched widowhood, of forming for you an emperor worthy of the blood and the name of him whom you have now irretrievably lost." "As this crisis (replied Menzikof) is a moment of such importance to the good of the empire, and requires the most mature deliberation, your majesty will permit us to confer, without restraint, that this whole affair may be transacted without reproach, as well in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the present age as in that of posterity." "Acting as I do (answered Catherine), more for the public good than for my own advantage, I am not afraid to submit all my concerns to the judgment of such an enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; you have not only my permission to confer with freedom; but I lay my commands upon you all to deliberate maturely on this important subject, and I <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to adopt whatever may be the result of your decisions." At the conclusion of these words the assembly retired into another apartment, and the doors were locked. It was previously settled by Menzikof and his party that Catherine should be empress; and the guards, who surrounded the palace with drums <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> and colours <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, effectually vanquished all opposition. Catherine: The only circumstance, therefore, which remained, was to give a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> colour to her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, by persuading the assembly that Peter intended to have named her his successor. For this purpose Menzikof demanded of that emperor's secretary, whether his late <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> had left any written <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of his intentions? The secretary replied, "That a little before his last journey to Moscow he had destroyed a will; and that he had frequently expressed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of making another; but had always been prevented by the reflection, that if he thought his people whom he had raised from a state of barbarism to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of power and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, could be ungrateful, he would not expose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> inclinations to the insult of a refusal; and that if they recollected what they owed to his labours, they would regulate their conduct by his intentions, which he had disclosed with more solemnity than could be manifested by any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>." An altercation now began in the assembly; and some of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> having the courage to oppose the accession of Catherine, Theophanes archbishop of Pleskoff called to their recollection the oath which they had all taken in 1722 to acknowledge the successor appointed by Peter; and added, that the sentiments of that emperor delivered by the secretary were in effect an appointment of Catherine. The opposite party, however, denied these sentiments to be so clear as the secretary chose to infirmate; and insisted, that as their late monarch had failed to nominate his heir, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of the new sovereign should revert to the state. Upon this the archbishop farther testified, that the evening before the coronation of the empress at Moscow, Peter had declared, in the house of an English merchant, that he should place the crown upon her head with no other view than to leave her mistress of the empire after his decease. This attestation being confirmed by many persons present, Menzikof cried out, "What need have we of any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>? A refusal to conform to the inclination of our great sovereign, thus authenticated, would be both unjust and criminal. Long live the empress Catherine!" These words being instantaneously repeated by the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of those who were present, Menzikof, saluting Catherine by the title of empress, paid his first obeisance by kissing her hand; and his example was followed by the whole assembly. She next presented herself at the window to the guards and to the people, who shouted acclamations of "Long live Catherine!" while Menzikof scattered among them handfuls of money. Thus (says a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>) the empress was raised to the throne by the guards, in the same manner as the Roman emperors by the pretorian cohorts, without either the appointment of the people or of the legions. The reign of Catherine may be considered as the reign of Menzikof, that empress having neither inclination or abilities to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the helm of government; and she placed the most implicit confidence in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had been the original author of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, and the sole instrument of her elevation to the throne. During her short reign her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; she was extremely averse to business; would frequently, when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was fine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> whole nights in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and was particularly intemperate in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOKAY">tokay</a> wine. These irregularities, joined to a cancer and a droopy, hastened her end; and she expired on the 17th of May 1727, a little more than two years after her accession to the throne, and in about the 46th year of her age. As the deaths of sovereigns in despotic countries are seldom imputed to natural causes, that of Catherine has also been attributed to poison; as if the disorders which preyed upon her frame were not sufficient to bring her to her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. Some assert that she was poisoned in a glass of spirituous liquor; others by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a> given her by General Diever. Suspicion also fell upon Prince Menzikof, who, a short time before her decease, had a trifling misunderstanding with her, and who was accused of hastening her death, that he might reign with still more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> power during the minority of Peter II. But these reports deserve not the least credit, and were merely dictated by the spirit of party, or by popular rumour. Catherine was in her person under the middle size, and in her youth delicate and well formed, but inclined to corpulency as she advanced in years. She had a fair <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, dark eyes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which she was always accustomed to dye with a black colour. She could neither read nor write; her daughter <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> usually signed her name for her, and particularly to her last will and testament; and Count Ostroff generally put her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> to the public decrees and dispatches. Her abilities have been greatly exaggerated by her panegyrists. Gordon, who had frequently seen her, seems of all writers to have represented her character with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, when he says, "She was a very pretty well-looking woman, of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, but not of that sublimity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, or rather that quickness of imagination, which some people have believed. The great reason why the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> was so fond of her, was her exceeding good temper; she never was seen peevish or out of humour; obliging and civil to all, and never forgetful of her former condition; withal, mighty grateful." Catherine maintained the pomp of majesty with an air of ease and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> united; and Peter used frequently to express his admiration at the propriety with which she supported her high station, without forgetting that she was not born to that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The following anecdotes will prove that she bore her elevation meekly; and, as Gordon affirms, was never forgetful of her former condition. When Wurm, who had been <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to Gluck's children at the time that Catherine was a domestic in that clergyman's family, presented himself before her after her marriage with Peter had been publicly announced, she recollected and addressed him with great complacency, "What, thou good man, art thou still alive! I will provide for thee." And she accordingly settled upon him a pension. She was no less attentive to the family of her benefactor Gluck, who died a prisoner at Moscow; she pensioned his widow; made his son a page; portioned the two eldest daughters; and advanced the youngest to be one of her maids of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. If we may believe Weber, she frequently inquired after her first husband; and, when she lived with Prince Menzikof, used secretly to send him small sums of money, until, in 1705, he was killed in a skirmish with the enemy. But the most noble part of her character was her peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and compassion for the unfortunate. Motraye has paid a handsome tribute to this excellence. "She had, in some sort, the government of all his (Peter's) passions; and even saved the lives of a great many more persons than Le Fort was able to do: she inspired him with that humanity which, in the opinion of his subjects, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> seemed to have denied him. A word from her mouth in favour of a wretch, just going to be sacrificed to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, would disarm him; but if he was fully resolved to satisfy that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, he would give orders for the execution when she was absent, for fear she should plead for the victim." In a word, to use the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the celebrated Munich, "Elle estoit proprement la médiateur entre le monarque et ses sujets." Catherine II., empress of Russia, whose original name was Sophia Augusta Frederica, was the daughter of Christian Augustus of Anhalt Zerbitz, a small district in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and was born in the castle of Zerbitz, on the 23rd of May 1729. She was educated under the eye of her parents, along with her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Prince Frederic Augustus, and at an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> displayed a masculine spirit. Elegant, majestic, and handsome in her person, her complexion exhibited the union of the lily and the rose, while a native dignity was tempered by a smile of benevolence. But it was early observed, that the concealed under this a certain austerity of disposition, and an ambition, which was even then considered as excessive, and proved afterwards to be infatuated. She soon learned all the fashionable accomplishments of that day. In addition to her native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, she wrote and conversed in French; of music she acquired a competent knowledge, and excelled particularly in needlework, which she did not disdain to practice after her elevation to the throne. The empress Elizabeth, who had pitched upon her nephew the duke of Holstein Gottorp Oldenburg for her successor, was also desirous to choose a consort for him, and the princess of Anhalt Zerbitz was selected upon this occasion, when only fourteen years of age. She was chiefly indebted for so unexpected an honour to the tender regard which her imperial majesty always entertained for the memory of her uncle, who had been her lover; and in an evil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> she united the fate of the prince, better known afterwards by the name of Peter III. to that of the princess of Anhalt Zerbitz. In consequence of a special invitation, the future empress repaired to St. Petersburg, accompanied by her mother, and being admitted into the bosom of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a> of marriage, after some delay, took place; on which these august personages were formally acknowledged, by her imperial majesty and the senate, as grand duke and duchess of Russia. Elizabeth, at the same time, presented them with the palace of Oranienbaum, delightfully situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a>, as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> residence; this had formerly belonged to Menzikof, the favourite of Peter the Great, who, in this capricious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, had been by turns a pie-boy, a prince, and an exile. The grand duke was far from being handsome; on the contrary, his person was disagreeable, and almost disfiguring. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> had been greatly neglected, and he was passionately fond of military parade. Frederick Catherine, derick of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> was at once his friend and his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>; he kept up a secret correspondence with that monarch, at the time when Russia was at open <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with him; he was accustomed in his cups to kneel before a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>; and, after quaffing a bumper, he would exclaim, "My brother! we shall conquer the world together." The first moments of this union seemed to be peculiarly auspicious. The illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> were accustomed to withdraw themselves daily, as if desirous to enjoy the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of each other's company, in preference to the giddy dissipation of a court. It was perceived at last, that grandeur was not incompatible with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, and that nuptial felicity was not confined to plebeian life. The empress hoped that the name and pretensions of Prince Ivan would be obliterated by the issue of the grand duke, and the whole empire impatiently wished for and now expected an heir to the throne of Peter the Great. It has since been discovered, that this young couple occupied their time in a far different manner than was then suspected! His highness, it seems, retired from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> on purpose to perfect himself in the Prussian exercises, and his comfort on these occasions participated in his diversions, for he was accustomed to make her stand for hours together, as a centinel, with a musket at her shoulder. This species of entertainment did not altogether <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the disposition of a young princess of an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>, and her highness accordingly began, in her own language, to think "that she was made for something else." Although she did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, she at this period governed her husband, and even concealed his foibles; imagining at first that he could not reign but by means of him, she wisely determined to make him appear worthy of a throne. A marriage of eight years was not productive of any issue, and strange suspicions began to be entertained. This alarmed the court, for a formidable rival, who possessed a superior claim to the throne, still existed; it is true, he was in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>, but in a country like Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> might not be long between a dungeon and a throne. The birth of a son and daughter, soon after this, put an end to all apprehensions of this kind, and tended not a little to give stability to the empire. The grand duke, who at times discovered noble, and even magnanimous sentiments, had about this period formed a most unfortunate connexion with Elizabeth Voronoff, a lady of high <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, but neither celebrated for her beauty nor her talents. He seldom saw his comfort in private, and all the hours that were not occupied either by military exhibitions, or the pleasures of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, were entirely devoted to his mistress. The grand duchess, on the other hand, is said to have spent much of her time in company with a young Pole, whose history, like that of Catherine's, has since been interwoven with the annals of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. This was Count Poniatowski, afterwards known as Stanislaus Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Poland. He was the third son of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANDEE">grandee</a> of the same name, the favourite of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, by the princess Ezatoryska, who boasted the possession of the noblest blood in Poland, as she traced her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the Jagellon, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sovereigns of Lithuania. His person was of exquisite symmetry, his air noble, his manners agreeable; in short, he possessed a charming exterior, and his mind, a circumstance extremely rare, was no less graceful than his person. At this period he was in no higher station, than a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in the suite of the minister plenipotentiary from England, who had formed an intimacy with his family during a former mission at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a>. Being now taught to look higher, he returned to his native country, and appeared soon after at Petersburgh, as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from the king of Poland. In this new capacity he did not forget to pay his respects at the little court of Oranienbaum, and the young plenipotentiary, with a view of ingratiating himself with the grand duke, smoked, drank, and praised the king of Prussia. At length Paul Petrovitch received the Polish minister with coolness, and he was actually forbidden to visit at the palace. This, however, it is said, did not deter him from concealing the order of the white eagle, and disguising himself as a mechanic, under which assumed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> he repaired one summer's evening to the gardens, in the neighbourhood of the gulf of Cronstadt; but he was discovered by his highness, who ordered him to be brought before him, and, after affecting to reprimand the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> for his disrespect to the representative of a crowned head, told him he was at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to depart. From this moment the grand duchess is said to have changed both her system and her conduct. She had formerly aspired only to direct the councils of the future emperor; she now resolved, if possible, to obtain the crown for her son, and the regency for herself. Such a task would have discouraged a common mind, for it was impossible to achieve this without prevailing on the empress to consent to dethrone her own nephew. Beluchef, the grand chancellor, who hated the heir apparent, joined cordially in their scheme; and Elizabeth, who herself had obtained the crown by means of a revolution, was taught to tremble for her life, in consequence of the designs of her successor, who was represented as having resolved to shorten her days by poison. But a sudden and unexpected revolution in the ministry put an end to these intrigues; for Beluchef was driven into exile, and Poniatowski recalled. A long and melancholy interval now ensued, during which the ambition of the grand duchess was rather frustrated than annihilated. She, however, had recourse to, and soothed her anguish by means of books; it was in her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> that she laid the foundation of her future greatness, and rendered herself in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> deserving of a throne. During her leisure moments she found means to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> partisans, and she acquired the favour of the soldiery, who did duty around her person, by means of her liberality and condescension. Peter, on the other hand, to the personal exertions of a common soldier, added the orgies of a debauchee. Surrounded by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> favourites, he consumed whole days and nights in intoxication, and forgot that he was a prince. There were some few moments, however, when he appeared great, and even magnanimous, but unfortunately they were of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; and it was his misfortune to have a weak woman for his mistress, and an able and ambitious one for his wife. Such was the situation of the court when Elizabeth died, on the 5th of January 1762. This event, so productive of interesting effects, had been long foreseen. Catherine, by Catherine, who now began to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> a more conspicuous part on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of public affairs. Her sorrow, which appeared unbounded, was only equalled by her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. She was constantly employed either at her prayers in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, or occupied in public processions, during which she fervently adhered to all the ceremonious practices of the Greek church. The courtiers were astonished at the sudden change, and affected to survey it with contempt; but it imposed on the populace, and the priests were highly gratified with the zeal of the empress, more especially as her consort had always treated their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> with indignity. Another design, meditated with no less art, proved unsuccessful. She is said to have made use of all her eloquence to persuade Peter, that he ought to leave off the barbarous custom of being proclaimed emperor by the army, in the same manner as his predecessors: instead of this, she proposed that his title should be recognized by the senate alone, and produced a speech which she herself had composed for the occasion; but Godowitz, one of the favourites, and the only friend of the new sovereign, perceived the snare, and partly owing to his entreaties, and partly from an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to everything military, the soldiery were as usual gratified with the ceremony of saluting the czar. The grand duke now ascended the throne, by the name of Peter III, and the commencement of the new reign appeared to be peculiarly auspicious. The catastrophe, which terminated a short reign of six months, may be attributed to three apparently trifling, but, in reality, irretrievable errors; for it is allowed on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, that if they did not constitute the original cause, they at least afforded the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for his dethronement and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. The first of these was, the sudden peace with, and marked predilection for, the king of Prussia, certainly the greatest monarch of his age; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, an attempt to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> a barbarous and fanatical clergy, whose power Peter I. had curbed, but whose persons he still affected to consider as sacred; the third was, the war against <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. Let it be recollected, however, in honour to his memory, that the young monarch, immediately after his elevation, threw open the state <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, recalled Munich, Biron, Lefort, and several others, who had offended him during the late reign, from Siberia; that he limited the despoticism of his officers, abridged his own power, by abolishing a state <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, exercised under the name of the Secret <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>; and that he framed the memorable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> which enfranchised the nobles from compulsive service in the army, and permitted them to travel without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> permission. The following answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the king of Prussia, who had requested him to be on his guard against the plot then meditating, conveys no unfavourable opinion of his heart. "Touching the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a> you express for my safety, I request you will rest contented. I am called the father of my soldiers—they prefer a male to a female government. I walk alone constantly in St Petersburg—if any mischief is meditated, it would have been affected long since; but I am a general benefactor. I repose myself on the protection of heaven; trusting to that, I have nothing to fear." This false security proved his ruin. While his mind was occupied with plans of reform, and he aspired to Catherine's rival, and even to excel, his illustrious predecessor, whose name he had assumed, a person who had sworn fidelity to him at the altar, and who owed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> ties of a wife and a subject, was actually employed in planning a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>, and organizing a revolt, against him. It has been said that he intended to have shut up his consort and son in a convent. But did a meditated imprisonment justify treachery, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and murder? On the other hand, it is known that, far from this being the intention of Peter, he was preparing for a journey to Holstein, and had actually empowered his consort to act as regent during his absence. The mistakes of the emperor did not escape the eagle eyes of his enemies. He purposed to carry his guards into Holstein, with a view to recover the possessions wrested from his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The regiments that had hitherto done duty at the palace, and were incurred to the indulgences of the capital, revolted at the idea of a foreign war; they had been accustomed to be governed by women, and they were taught to fix their eyes on the comfort of the czar. It is not the least wonderful part of her conduct, that, previously to the great catastrophe now meditating, Catherine contrived to appear abandoned by all the world. She knew how interesting a female, and more especially an empress, appeared while in distress; and she took care to heighten the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of the public, by bursting at times into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> of tears. This artful woman had found means to attach many persons to her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>: it must be owned, however, that her adherents were neither so powerful, nor so numerous as to afford her any well founded hopes of success. She had gained several favourites, and some privates, of the guards; but her principal partisans consisted of the princess D'Aschevski, niece to the new chancellor; Prince Rozamouki, who had risen from obscurity, having been originally a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>; Odart, an intriguing Italian; and Panin, governor to the grand duke. The arrest of Pafliak, one of the conspirators, seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a discovery, which would have proved fatal to the malcontents; but this very circumstance induced them to declare instantly, and in the end crowned an apparently rash attempt with success. The empress, who was asleep at the castle of Petershoffer, received intimation of their design by a common soldier, who soon after returned with a carriage and eight horses. On the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of this man, and accompanied only by a few peasants, a German female domestic, and a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre, she arrived at eight o'clock in the morning in the capital, and stopped opposite the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> of the regiment of Ilmaioff. There she addressed the soldiers in an eloquent speech, intermingled with sighs and tears, and actually found means to persuade them that she and her son had but that moment escaped from the hands of assassins, sent by the emperor to murder them. This story, by agitating the passions of the troops, had a wonderful effect on them, and they all swore, with the exception of only one regiment, to die in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of her and the young archduke. On this the empress ordered a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> to be brought, and commanded the priests to administer a new oath of allegiance. She afterwards repaired to one of the principal churches, where she was met by the bishop of Novgorod and the clergy, and, having returned thanks to Almighty God, ascended a balcony, and presented her son to the people. In a few hours she was again seen, draped in the uniform of the guards, riding at the head of a numerous and well-appointed army against her husband. That unfortunate prince first made a show of resistance, and manned his Lilliputian batteries, at Oranienbaum, with his Holstein guards, in order to oppose what appeared to him to be a contemptible sedition. When it was too late, he attempted to get possession of Cronstadt. He might still have escaped to Revel, but the women in his galley were apprehensive of danger, and the courtiers shuddered at the proposition of old Munich, who wished them to assist the sailors in rowing. On the first intelligence of the plot this intrepid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> had repaired to his benefactor, and advised him to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> directly to the capital, at the head of his German troops. "I shall precede you," (said the generous veteran,) "and my dead body shall be a rampart to your sacred person." But, on the other hand, the emissaries of the empress, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> their hands in their crocodile tears, deprecated resistance, magnified the danger, and invited him to repose in the inviolable fidelity of his comfort. In short, on the 14th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, 1762, he was taken prisoner by the orders of his own wife, to whom he had been married 14 years, prevailed on by the threats and entreaties of Count Panin to renounce his crown, conveyed to the cattle of Robocha, and three days afterwards put to death. Of the titled minions, who perpetrated this daring murder, one carried the guilty marks of the czar's icemiter on his forehead to the grave, and another, tortured for years by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of the last bloody <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> in the tragedy of his expiring sovereign, exhibited a shocking spectacle of insanity and remorse. The empress, on her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> of the new vacant crown, notified the event to all the courts of Europe, under her new name of Catherine Alexievna II. But there was still a competitor for the empire, and suspicion never flutters near a throne. This was Prince Ivan, son to the princes of Mecklenburg, and grand nephew to Peter the Great and the empress <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> Ivanovna, who had destined him for her successor; but, in consequence of a former revolution, he was seized while yet an infant, and doomed to lead a life of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. During 18 years of precarious existence, he had been shut up in the castle of Schluffelbourg, and never in all that time did he breathe the open air, or behold the sky, but once. This prince was visited by Peter III., who finding him in an arched room, 20 feet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, determined to set him at liberty; but, alas! the youth, in consequence of his long and solitary confinement, had been deprived of his senses. In this situation, the emperor determined to build a house for him, with a convenient terrace, where he might take the air daily within the fortress. Such, however, are the changes of fortune, that, in three weeks, he himself was also precipitated from a throne, and exposed to a violent death. This event was but the prelude to that of Ivan; for, as orders had been given, in case of an attempt to rescue him, that an end should be put to his life, and a real or pretended plot having been hatched for this purpose, the motives and details of which have hitherto been involved in the most profound obscurity, the unhappy prince experienced the same fate as his generous protector. Catherine being now firmly seated on the throne, wisely determined to divert the thoughts of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> from the late horrid scenes, and fix them on more agreeable objects. Having foothold Prussia, acquired a preponderance in the cabinet of Denmark, long become an absolute <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, and entered into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with the popular party in Sweden, not yet bereft of its liberties, she <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> her eyes on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, then governed by Prince Charles of Saxony, the second son of Augustus III., king of Poland; and, finding that country admirably situated for the increase of her present, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of her future power, the, in 1762, expelled the lawful sovereign, and invested Biron, a creature of her own, with the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. Not content with this, the new duke, soon reduced to the most abject dependence, was prevented from resigning his precarious power, and the states assembled at Mitau were actually interdicted from nominating a successor. This, however, was only a prelude to far greater scenes, for she had hardly dethroned one sovereign before she undertook to create another. Augustus II., or, as he is called by some, Augustus III., of Poland, having died at Dresden, in 1763, her imperial majesty did not let slip so fair an opportunity for interfering in the appointment to the vacant throne, and even placing one of her dependents on it. Count Poniatowski, on the elevation of Catherine, had sent a friend to Petersburgh, to sound the disposition of the empress about his return to that capital, where he naturally hoped to participate in her power, and bask in the sunshine of the royal smiles. But the more prudent German, who was at this very moment meditating a splendid provision for him elsewhere, prohibited the journey from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> motives. Accordingly, notwithstanding the opposition of the grand chancellor Belotcheff, and indeed of all her ministers, she determined to invest him with the ensigns of royalty. The head of the house of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, swayed by his hatred to Saxony and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, or, what is still more likely, the Prussian eagle having perhaps, even now, scented his future prey, Catherine was enabled to send 10,000 men into Poland, who, encamping on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>, overawed the deliberations of the diet, assembled on the 9th of May 1764, and placed Stanislaus Augustus on the throne. Thus, by the appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> filled with Russian mercenaries, was violated one of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> laws of the commonwealth, established ever since the time of Sigismund-Augustus, two centuries before, in consequence of which the election of a king is deemed void while there are any foreign troops within the territories of the republic; and so justly jealous were the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> of their national independence, that the marshal of the diet, on those occasions, was accustomed to request all ambassadors to absent themselves, as he could not be answerable for the safety of their persons. Having conferred the crown of Poland, September 7, 1764, on an amiable and accomplished prince, who, on account of his youth, his poverty, and even his dependence on Russia, would have been excluded from that painful pre-eminence had the free suffrage of the nation been collected; and who was, in consequence... Catherine, of the hatred of his countrymen, still more subjected to the dominion of the empress, she began to prepare for a war against the Turks, which was accordingly declared in 1768. During this contest the Greek cause was triumphant both by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. On the first of these elements her fleet, under Count Orloff, entered the straits of Gibraltar, and carried terror and devastation among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Archipelago, and throughout the defences of shores of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; on the second, her armies, under Galitzin and Romanoff, achieved many important victories, seized on the fortresses of Choczim, and prevailed on the Greek inhabitants of Wallachia and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a> to acknowledge her as their sovereign. In the meantime, however, a dangerous insurrection broke out in the heart of her dominions, instigated by a Cossack of the name of Pugatscheff, who pretended to be Peter III. After displaying great valour and considerable talents, which had enabled him, at the head of raw and undisciplined levies, to contend against veteran troops and experienced generals, this unfortunate man was at length seized, enclosed in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cage, and beheaded at Moscow on the 21st of January 1775. A peace had been concluded on the 21st of July, in the preceding year, with the Porte, which proved highly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to Russia; but it was productive of little benefit, for the liberty of navigating the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA">Black Sea</a>, and a free trade with all the ports of the Turkish empire, which would have afforded inestimable advantages to a civilized people, was scarcely of any consequence to a nation unacquainted alike with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. Accordingly, we find her imperial majesty still unsatisfied.
