Ambition, which in a female bosom is ever insatiable, stimulated her to attempt new acquisitions, and we learn with astonishment that her diplomatic artifices proved infinitely more hostile to the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, than even her victorious arms. Scarcely had four years elapsed, when, after an armed negociation, a new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of pacification was agreed to by the reluctant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, on the 21st of March 1780, in consequence of which the Crimea was declared independent: an event not calculated to close ancient jealousies, but, on the contrary, to produce fresh dissensions, as it afforded an opening into the very heart of the Turkish empire, and a ready pretext for future interference. New claims and new concessions immediately followed. Russia insisted on establishing consuls in the three provinces of Moldavia, Wallachia, and Bessarabia, which she was accordingly permitted to do by the treaty of 1781. Mortifying as this compliance was, it produced but a short respite. The emperor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> was now brought upon the political stage, and the Roman and Russian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, after hovering over the carcass of the Turkish empire, and meditating to devour the whole, were at last content with a part of the prey. The empress, as it may be readily believed, was not inattentive to her own interests; and by the treaty of Constantinople, signed January 9, 1784, to Russia was ceded the entire sovereignty of the Crimea, which then received its ancient name of Taurica, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TAMAN">Taman</a>, and part of Cuban. It was now in the 58th year of her age, and the 25th of her reign, that Catherine may be said to have attained the very summit of her wishes. There was no one who pretended to the throne, unless her son Paul Petrovitch, an amiable prince, who had attained his 33rd year, without displaying the least symptom of ambition, and who besides was superintended with the most watchful jealousy. She had triumphed over a nation, supposed to be the natural enemy of Russia, both by arms and negotiations, and she dazzled her barbarous subjects with the blaze of her glory, for they were eager to forget her errors, in order to contemplate a grandeur which soothed their national vanity. Knowing the effect of splendour upon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, she ushered in the year 1787 with a brilliant journey to Chernov. Accompanied thither at once by a court and an army, with foreign ambassadors, an emperor and a king in her train, she intended to have assumed the high-founding titles of Empress of the East, and Liberator of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. At Kiow, where she remained during three months, she was received under triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, and having heard the petitions of the deputies from distant nations, and extended the walls of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, she <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>, with an arrogant anticipation, the following motto, in Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> next to Constantinople: "Through this gate lies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Byzantium." Scarcely, however, had the empress, after visiting Molcow, returned to her capital, than the Turk thought proper to declare war. Her majesty, long since prepared for an event which was far from being displeasing, called forth the stipulated succours of her ally the emperor; and the combined army under the Prince de Cobourg made itself master of Choczim, at the end of a siege of three months. Oczzakow, after a still more obstinate resistance, was taken by storm, by the Russians alone. A diversion, however, was made by the king of Sweden, who, subsidized with Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and directed by Prussian counsels, fought his own battles at the expense of his ally. But the exertions of this monarch were principally confined to the indecisive naval actions of Stoogland, in which both parties claimed the victory, and this was soon after followed by a convention for peace. Disembarrassed from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, if not a powerful enemy, the empress no longer confined her conquests to the course of the Danube, but crowned the campaign with the capture of Imael, which was taken by storm on the 22nd of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. On this occasion Suvarrow, one of her favourite generals, displayed a horrid mixture of courage and cruelty, and thus proved, to a demonstration, that personal bravery is far from being incompatible with the deadliest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. Incensed at the gallant resistance of the Turks, like Caesar, he snatched a standard from a subaltern, and planted it with his own hand on the walls of the city; like Sylla, he doomed the vanquished to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> a bloody proscription, and upwards of 30,000 men, women, and children, if we are to credit the boastful account of the barbarians themselves, perished by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and bayonet of the unsparing Russians. Instead of regaining the Crimea, as had been expected by the sultan, the fortresses of Oczzakow, and all the territories between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Bog and Dniefter, were assigned to the empress, who now found herself nearer Having concluded a final treaty of peace with the Turk, on the 9th of January 1792, by which the river Dnieper became the boundary of the two empires, and was to be navigated by both, the empress had more time to apply her attention to European politics. Part of Poland had been dismembered and partitioned during the year 1772, not only in contravention to the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of nations, but in direct opposition to the most solemn treaties on the part of Russia, Prussia, and Austria. The revolution which took place in that ill-fated country on May 3, 1791, and which afforded the prospect of a happy and stable government to the remains of the republic, was the signal of its annihilation. The imperial and royal spoilers seized this opportunity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> once more in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> on their prey, which they forced to expire under their talons, and they have since cut it into shares, and attempted to disfigure it by new names, lest it should one day be reclaimed by the lawful owners. After this insult to humanity, Stanislaus, whom posterity may acknowledge as an unfortunate, but surely not as a great king, was forced soon after to abdicate, and allowed to retire into obscurity with his mistresses, his children, and a pension. Another great object had for some time engaged the attention of Catherine and her cabinet. This was the French revolution; an event pregnant with consequences that involved the claims, or, more properly speaking, the existence of all the sovereigns of Europe. With a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> nearly exhausted by the war with the Ottoman Porte, which was not then terminated, and at a distance from the scene of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, the empress could not well engage in the contest; but she readily entered into the coalition, and soon after subsidized her late enemy the king of Sweden; but that enterprising prince met his fate, on the night of the 16th of March 1792, by the hand of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSASSIN">assassin</a>. Notwithstanding this sinister event, the head of the Greek church, compassionating the fate of the pretended father of the Christian world, promised to exert herself for the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a> to the holy see. She also launched forth a menacing manifesto against France, and prepared for a new war. The empress has hitherto been contemplated in her public character. It may not be amiss now to fix our eyes on the individual; to pay some attention to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> of the sovereign, and, viewing majesty as it were in an undress, behold the woman lurking behind the princes. It might have been supposed, that in the neighbourhood of the Hyperborean regions, the passions, if not dormant would be at least moderate, and that the men would consequently be temperate, and the women chaste. The contrary, however, is the case: and it is left to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> to determine, whether the double windows and heated rooms of St. Petersburg, added to an affectation of oriental manners, be not to the full as critical, in respect to female virtue, as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. Certain it is, however, that, during the reign of Catherine II, no remarkable increase of indecorum took place, and that any occasion- al indiscretions appear to have made but little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the public mind. Count Gregory Orloff, distinguished in Russia by the appellation of Gregorevitch, was one of the handsomest men in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">Gratitude</a> and affection both conspired to procure him a favourable reception at court; and from an obscure condition he soon rose to the highest offices of the state, which he, in fact, governed. His opinion in the cabinet was listened to with deference, and he was invested with the supreme military command. Still higher honours awaited him. The empress-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> was solicited to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> him a diploma of prince of the empire; it was next in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> to decorate him with the titles of duke of Ingria and Carelia, and the chancellor Beftuchoff actually proposed to the empress that he should be admitted as the partner of her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> and throne. But this scheme was blasted by the interference of Count Panin; who, not content with his own remonstrances, invoked the intervention of Razumofsky and Vorontzoff, and found means to divert Catherine from her purpose. Soon after this the conduct of Orloff began to give dissatisfaction: for he absented himself from court; went but seldom to the palace; resided principally in the country; and, being extremely addicted to hunting, dedicated whole weeks to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> of the bear. Panin, who had frequently experienced his arrogance, deemed this a happy opportunity to procure his disgrace. He accordingly introduced a young officer named Vasilchikoff, who, being directed by the artful minister, behaved in such a manner as to give reason to believe that he would soon reign uncontrolled. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">Pride</a>, however, on this occasion supplied the place of affection, and Orloff suddenly altering his conduct, his rival was dismissed with superb presents, and invested with an employment that required his residence in a remote <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. A new favourite soon after made his appearance in the person of Vasilchikoff, a fubaltern in the guards, and advantage was taken of the absence of Orloff to introduce him at the hermitage. This officer was young and handsome; but nature, which had been lavish to his person, seems to have been at no pains with his mind. He was immediately appointed chamberlain to the empress, enriched with splendid presents, and treated with the most flattering attention. In the mean time Gregorevitch, who had been appointed to treat with the Turkish plenipotentiaries relative to a peace, on hearing of this unexpected event, instantly returned to the capital from Fokhiani, but was arrested at the gates of Peterburgh, and stripped of all his employments. He, however, experienced the imperial bounty, and received, as a recompense for his submission, the sum of 100,000 rubles in hand, a pension of 150,000 more, a magnificent service of plate; and, to crown the whole, an estate, with 6000 peasants upon it, was made over to him. Vasilchikoff, during 22 months, enjoyed all the distinction belonging to the reigning favourite; but at the end of that period he also found occasion to lament the inconstancy of fortune. This young man had conducted himself with great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, for he had never abused his influence. He possessed none of that haughtiness so common to upstarts; and he did not ap- Catherine, pear eager to increase his own fortune, or to diminish that of his rivals. Such was his moderation, that, as his elevation excited no envy, so his disgrace was unaccompanied by exultation. His faults are still unknown; and most probably he had ceased to please. His retreat, however, was accompanied by every mark of respect; and, as he repaired to Moscow, the place of his destined exile, he received presents, on his journey, which might be styled imperial on account of their magnificence. No sooner was this change made public than Orloff appeared once more on the scene, and was readmitted to all his former influence. Supposing Panin to be the cause of his late exile, he extorted a promise from his royal mistress to dismiss him from his employments. Her afflent was given with reluctance; and the prayers of the grand duke, who was too generous to suffer his preceptor to fall a prey to the suspicions of a man he did not love, induced her to revoke her intentions. In the mean time the manly air and elegant appearance of Potemkin make a great impression on an illustrious personage. This officer had been bred in the guards; and, perceiving on that memorable day when the empress, mounted on a fine charger and dressed in regimentals, exhibited herself at the head of the troops, that she had forgotten to place a plume in her hat, he snatched this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> from his own, and presented it to the new sovereign. Neither this action, nor the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> with which it was performed, had escaped unnoticed; and the time was now arrived when his attachment was to receive an ample remuneration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of favourite is almost peculiar to Russia, and was during many years considered an official employment. Ever since 1730 the nation had been governed by women, except during the short and unfortunate reign of Peter III. In fine, it seemed to be sanctioned, if not by a fundamental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the empire, at least by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>; as four empresses had successively consecrated it by their practice, and the age of the last Elizabeth made it be considered in some measure as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> appendage to imperial grandeur. Potemkin soon grew giddy with success, and his pride and presumption keeping pace with his elevation, he accordingly exposed himself to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disagreeable events. Boasting one day of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his power in presence of Count <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Orloff, the brother of his predecessor, he received a blow which deprived him of an eye; and Prince Gregory Orloff having requested his dismission, he was forced to repair to Smolensk, at once the place of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> and exile. Such was his vexation, partly from the loss of his eye, and partly from his disgrace, that he actually entertained some idea of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> monk; but a submissive letter produced his recall; and from that moment he seemed to have dropped all thoughts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COWL">cowl</a>. Ambition now appears to have taken complete possession of the bosom of Potemkin; and this was amply gratified, for his influence soon extended to every department of the state, and he himself, after procuring the dismission of Count Zachar Chernicheff, became vice-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> at war, with a seat in the council. But his aspiring hopes were not yet gratified, for he entertained still higher expectations. With a view to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of these, he affected to be once more seized with a fit of religion; and kept <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> with great strictness, living upon roots Catherine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> during that holy season. He also wearied all the saints in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> with his prayers; went daily to confession; and, having selected on this occasion the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> that afforded <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTION">absolution</a> to a great personage, he besought him to inform her, that his alarmed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> could no longer permit him to indulge in an intercourse, which, by marriage alone, would cease to be criminal. This project, however, failed of success; and, soon after the empress's return to Petersburg (for it was at Moscow that it had been first conceived), a young man from the Ukraine, of the name of Zavadofsky, was honoured with the imperial countenance, while the haughty Potemkin received the customary intimation, "that he must prepare to travel." Potemkin did not dare to disobey, but he evaded the order; for, setting out in great form, he proceeded a few miles towards the place indicated for his exile, but returned in the course of next day, and placed himself in the evening exactly opposite to the empress as she was about to sit <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to dinner. Every one expected to behold some signal mark of the imperial displeasure; but, on the contrary, Catherine, handing him a pack of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, desired the ex-favourite to cut in, observing that he had always been a fortunate player. His posts, his honours, his influence, were all restored to him, and he now occupied a new situation about the person of her imperial majesty, for he became her friend. In the mean time the bosom of the humble Zavadofsky began to catch the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of ambition; and, as he was jealous of the grandeur of Potemkin, he aimed a deadly blow at his consequence. But the minister at war, become wily in his turn, warded it off, and made it recoil on the head of his rival. Perceiving a handsome young Servian officer of hussars, of the name of Zoritch, who had repaired to Petersburg in search of promotion, he presented him with a captain's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and in a few days he was perceived behind the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of the empress. A large estate, the rank of major-general, and an immense sum of money, soon became the appanage of this fortunate youth; but the empress perceiving that he was ignorant, and being disgusted at his want of accomplishments, recommended, as he could speak no language but that of the Russian boors, that he should be sent abroad for improvement. Fortune seems to have been in a playful mood when she elevated Rimsky Korzakoff to the post of chamberlain, and successor to the Servian. This man had actually been a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> in the guards; he was now declared aide-de-camp general to the empress and presented with the palace of Vassiltchikoff. He proved to be a vain upstart, whose dress exhibited a profusion of diamonds, and whose conduct was such as could not fail to involve him in ruin. This speedily occurred; for, being detected in a secret correspondence with a lady, he was banished from court, and he was obliged to repair to Moscow. The same day that beheld his disgrace, witnessed the good fortune of Lukoi, a Pole by descent, and an officer of the body-guards by profession. The education of this young man had been neglected; but this defect was in some measure remedied by the zeal and attachment of an illustrious personage, who superintended Catherine tended his improvement; and in a short time he became as remarkable for the superior elegance of his manners, as the graces of his person: but, while in the flower of his youth, and the very height of his favour, he was attacked by a mortal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which cut him off after a short illness. He died in the arms of his mistress, who was inconsolable on the occasion, and refused to take any suifrance during three whole days. A <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of which was sketched out by an English <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, attested the respect of the empress, who burst into tears on seeing it two years after. His fortune he had bequeathed to her imperial majesty, but she presented it, with her accustomed generosity, to the sister of this handsome youth. The next person who aspired to the post of favourite was a young man educated in Scotland, and who had become a fellow of the Royal Society of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. This was Prince Dalmatoff, son to the celebrated princes of the same name, who had participated in the memorable revolution that levelled Peter III. with the dust. A lieutenant of the name of Yermoloff anticipated him, however, in this post, to which he was raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Potemkin; but, proving ungrateful to his benefactor, he was suddenly disgraced, being replaced by Momonoff, who attended her imperial majesty during her journey to the Crimea. He fell in love, however, with a lady of the court; and no sooner was the empress informed of this circumstance, than she insisted on his marrying her immediately; after which they were sent into exile at Moscow. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> Zuboff, an officer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-guards, supplied his place. This aspiring young man, not content with wealth and honours, affected public employments; and it is asserted that the idea of the second <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Poland originated with him. In a short time he became omnipotent at Peterburgh. He was decorated with the title of prince; received the post of grand master of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>; all the admirals, generals, and ministers of the empire, were to be seen at his levee, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> lowly before him, and, if we are to believe the author of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of some reputation, paying their compliments at the same time, in great form, to his favourite monkey. Catherine hitherto had only afforded empty promises to the enemies of France; but, at the instigation of Zuboff, she now formed the design of giving effectual assistance to the confederated kings; and, as a proof of her intentions, issued orders for a squadron of men of war to join the English fleet, and commanded a levy of 60,000 troops. She at the same time prosecuted a war on the frontiers of Persia, where her army, under the command of a near relation of the grand master of the artillery, had experienced a most humiliating defeat; and she was now preparing to send fresh succours to his assistance. Such were the projects that occupied the mind of Catherine, the overthrow of the French republic, and the subjugation of the distant Persians, when she was smitten by the hand of death. This fortunate princess had hitherto enjoyed an almost uninterrupted state of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> during the whole of her long reign. She was sometimes, indeed, subject to a colic, and her legs were now and then observed to swell; but neither of these symptoms were alarming. On the morning of the 9th of November she rose at her usual hour, and breakfasted on coffee according to Catherine's custom. Some time after she retired to her closet; and her long absence affording cause of suspicion to her attendants, they entered the apartment, and found her lying speechless. Dr Robertson, her physician, being sent for, he treated her disease as an apoplexy, and considerable relief seemed to ensue after the application of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCET">lancet</a>. But the empress never entirely recovered her senses; and did not utter a single word during the remainder of her life, which was prolonged till ten o'clock in the evening of November 10, 1797. Thus, with her usual good fortune, after a very short illness, died Catherine II., empress of all the Russias. During her youth she had been extremely handsome, but she got fat as she increased in years; she, however, preferred a certain air of gracefulness, intermingled with dignity, until the last moment of her life. Her majesty in person was not above the middle size; but, being well proportioned, and carrying her head high, she appeared tall. Her forehead was open, her nose aquiline, her mouth agreeable, and her chin, without being ugly, was rather long. Her hair, in which she took great delight, was auburn, and her eye-brows dark and thick. Her eyes, according to some, were blue, whilst others insist that they were of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> hue. Upon the whole, her physiognomy was not deficient in expression; but she had such a command of her countenance, that no one could there discover the secrets of her heart. Her imperial majesty was accustomed, on great occasions, to dress in a splendid manner, and to wear a profusion of jewels. Being particularly fond of diamonds, she possessed a prodigious number; and one in particular was the largest that ever had been seen in Europe. Catherine, however, was accustomed in general to affect the ancient Russian fashions, for the most part wearing green, out of compliment to the nation. Her hair was powdered but slightly. On the other hand, her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> was covered with rouge; and as her imperial majesty, like the ladies in the French court, wore it in proportion to her rank, it is not to be wondered if it was of a high colour. The strictest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> was regularly preserved by Catherine, in a country, and at a court, where a little deviation would not have given occasion to much scandal. A slight breakfast, a moderate dinner, and two or three glasses of wine (for she never indulged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>), constituted her usual diet. It is far more easy to describe the empress than the woman. The acts of the former have now become history, but those of the latter must be left to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of genius, that can analyze the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> action. It must be confessed that both she and the empire appear to have been frequently a prey to favouritism; and this part of her conduct, by being connected with the happiness of millions of her subjects, is highly censurable. As a sovereign she stands conspicuous. She increased the extent of Russia, and added not only new countries, but new nations, to that mighty empire. As a conqueror, her victories were numerous and brilliant; she triumphed equally by sea and by land, and had she lived but ten years longer, might have realized Catherine, the proud dream of her ambition, and beheld her grandson Constantine sitting on the throne of the Ottomans. Her merit as a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, too, is great; but she would have been far more worthy of our admiration, had she effected the generous idea of enfranchising all the peasantry of her immense dominions. She was the only sovereign of Russia who ever exhibited a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for letters. This was not all; she was an author herself, and did not disdain to compose little treatises for her grandchildren, whose education she superintended. For music she also possessed an exquisite relish, and brought Gabrielli, and a number of fingers of great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, allowing them liberal salaries, and treating them with great attention. Throughout the whole of her long reign Catherine also evinced a marked predilection for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. In the midst of a war with the Turks she purchased pictures in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, to the amount of 60,000 rubles, all of which were lost in consequence of a ship's being wrecked on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>. This, however, rather served to stimulate her to fresh exertions, and her agents accordingly procured whatever was to be found in Italy worthy of notice. The Houghton collection from England was also transferred, by an act of her munificence, to the shores of the Baltic; and, while it added to her glory, disgraced this nation in the eyes of foreigners. Her conduct to learned men was truly worthy of a woman of genius. She was proud of the correspondence and friendship of Voltaire; she invited Diderot to her court, and lived with him, while there, in habits of the utmost familiarity; to D'Alembert she looked up as to a superior being, and endeavoured, although in vain, to seduce him to reside at St Petersburg; but he possessed a haughty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, was devoted to liberty, and would not consent to degrade the mind of a freeman, by residing among a nation of slaves. To the honour of Catherine, she was extremely attentive to the education of her people, and instituted a prodigious number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> for their instruction. To remove their prejudices against <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a>, she herself submitted to the operation, and thus hazarded her life for her nation. Amidst the schemes of grandeur, the allurements of power, and the gratification of the passions, she found leisure to civilize and instruct her subjects: this added not a little to her glory, as it contributed to the benefit of so large a portion of the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; but it will infensibly operate against a despotic government, by rendering the boors unfit for their chains, which they will some day <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, perhaps, on the heads of the boyars, who at once enslave and oppress them. No woman could so easily forgive; and in this point of view her conduct must be allowed to have possessed a great share of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>. She generously pardoned old Munich and Godowitz, the one the counsellor, the other the favourite of Peter III. She even admitted the former of these into her confidence, and would have conferred honours and preferments on the latter; but he loved his late sovereign, and with a noble scorn spurned at the proffered friendship of his successor. To the misfortunes of Peter III., although her own rival, she granted her life, restored her fortune, and at length admitted her daughters to honourable situations at court. No personage in our own times has attracted a greater share of censure and eulogium than Catherine; and no woman in any age ever exhibited more of the masculine greatness of one sex, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a> weakness of another. As a female, she appears at times the slave of passion, and the puppet of her courtiers; but while we behold her diminishment, in this point of view, into insignificance, we look again, and contemplate the sovereign, towering like an immense colossus, and with one foot placed on Cherbon, and another at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>, waving her iron sceptre over the subject nations, and regulating the destiny of a large portion of mankind. The frailties, however, of the woman will soon be forgotten, while the glory that encircles the brows of the legislator and conqueror will long continue to dazzle the eyes of an admiring world. The present age, however, flutters at the untimely fate of Peter and of Ivan, and posterity will not easily <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of Stanislaus, the partition of Poland, and the massacres of Iznailow and of Praga.

CATETUS

Pages 290-290

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a perpendicular line, supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the middle of a cylindrical body, as a balluster, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, &c. CATHNESS. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAITHNESS">CAITHNESS</a>.

CATHERINE

Pages 290-290

St., Order of, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, belongs to ladies of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. It was instituted in 1714 by Catherine wife of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his signal escape from the Turks in 1711. The emblems of this order are a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, supported by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of St Catherine, and fastened to a scarlet string edged with silver, on which are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the name of St Catherine, and the motto, Pro fide et patria.

CATHERLOUGH

Pages 290-290

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, about 28 miles in length, and eight in breadth; bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WICKLOW">Wicklow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEXFORD">Wexford</a>, on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN_S_COUNTY"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s county, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a>, and on the south and south-west by Wexford. It contains 5600 houses, 42 parishes, five baronies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> boroughs, and sends six members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. two for the county, two for Catherlough, and two for Old Leighlen.

CATHETER

Pages 290-290

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a fitful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, usually made of silver, to be introduced into the bladder, in order to search for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discharge the urine when suppressed. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CATHOLIC

Pages 290-292

CATHOLIC, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes any thing that is universal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> general. Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>. The rise of heresies induced the primitive Christian church to assume to itself the appellation of catholic, being a characteristic to distinguish itself from all sects, who, though they had party names, sometimes sheltered themselves under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. The Roman church distinguishes itself now by the name of Catholic, in opposition to all those who have separated from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, and whom she considers as heretics and schismatics, and herself only as the true and Christian church. In the strict sense of the word, there is no Catholic church in being, that is, no universal Christian communion. Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> which has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. Mariana pretends, that Reccared first received this title after he had destroyed Arianism in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and that it is found in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> for the year 589. Vafe attributes the origin of it to Alphonsus in 738. Some allege that it has been used only since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Ferdinand and Isabella. Colombiere says, it was given them on occasion of the expulsion of the Moors. The Bollandists pretend it had been borne by their predecessors the Visigoth kings of Spain; and that Alexander VI. only renewed it to Ferdinand and Isabella. Others say that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> de Valois first bore the title; which was given him after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, on account of his favouring their interests. In some epistles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> popes, the title catholic is given to the kings of France and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, as well as to several patriarchs and primates. Catholicon, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a kind of soft purgative electuary, so called, as being supposed an universal purger of all humours. Catiline, Lucius, a Roman of a noble family, who, having spent his whole fortune in debauchery, formed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of oppressing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, destroying the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, seizing the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, setting Rome on fire, and usurping a sovereign power over his fellow-citizens. In order to succeed in this design, he drew some young noblemen into his plot; whom he prevailed upon, it is said, to drink <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood as a pledge of their union. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>, however, was discovered by the vigilance of Cicero, who was then <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. Upon which, retiring from Rome, he put himself at the head of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, with several of the conspirators, and fought with incredible valour against Petreius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> to Antony, who was colleague with Cicero in the consulship; but was defeated and killed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) Rome.—Sallust has given an excellent history of this conspiracy. Cato, Marcus Porcius, the censor, one of the greatest men among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was born at Tusculum in the year of Rome 519, about the 232d before Christ. He began to bear arms at 17; and, on all occasions, showed extraordinary courage. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sobriety, and reckoned no bodily <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> unworthy of him. He had but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> for himself and his baggage, and he looked after and dressed it himself. At his return from his campaigns, he took himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> his ground; not that he was without slaves to do it, but it was his inclination. He dressed also like his slaves, sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with them, and partook of the same fare. He did not in the meanwhile neglect to cultivate his mind, especially in regard to the art of speaking; and he employed his talents, which were very great, in generously pleading causes in the neighbouring cities without fee or reward. Valerius Flaccus, who had a country seat near Cato, conceiving an esteem for him, persuaded him to come to Rome; where Cato, by his own merits, and the influence of so powerful a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, was soon taken notice of, and promoted. He was first of all elected tribune of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; he was next made quæstor in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> under Scipio. Having in this last office reproved him for his profuseness to his soldiers, the general answered, that "he did not want to exact a quæstor, but would make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> at what expense he pleased; nor was he to give an account to the Roman people of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he spent, but of his enterprises, and the execution of them." Cato, provoked at this answer, left Sicily, and returned to Rome. Afterwards Cato was made praetor, when he fulfilled the duties of his office with the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. He conquered <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, governed with admirable moderation, and was created consul. Being tribune in the war of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, he gave distinguished proofs of his valour against Antiochus the Great; and at his return stood candidate for the office of censor. But the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, who not only envied him as a new man, but dreaded his severity, set up against him <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> powerful competitors. Valerius Flaccus, who had introduced him into public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and had been his colleague in the consulship, was a ninth candidate, and these two united their interests. On this occasion Cato, far from employing soft words to the people, or giving hopes of gentleness or complaisance in the execution of his office, loudly declared from the rostra, with a threatening look and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, "That the times required firm and vigorous magistrates to put a stop to that growing <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> which menaced the republic with ruin; censors who would cut up the evil by the roots, and restore the rigour of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>." It is to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the people of Rome, that notwithstanding these terrible intimations, they preferred him to all his competitors, who courted them by promises of a mild and easy administration; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> also appointed his friend Valerius to be his colleague, without whom he had declared that he could not hope to compass the reforms he had in view. Cato's merit, upon the whole, was superior to that of any of the great men who stood against him. He was temperate, brave, and indefatigable; frugal of the public money, and not to be corrupted. There is scarce any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> requisite for public or private life which he had not received from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, or acquired by industry. He was a great soldier, an able statesman, an eloquent orator, a learned historian, and very knowing in rural affairs. Yet, with all these accomplishments, he had very great faults. His ambition being poisoned with envy, disturbed both his own peace and that of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> as long as he lived. Though he would not take bribes, he was unmerciful and unconscionable in amassing wealth by all such means as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> did not punish. The first <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of Cato in his new office, was naming his colleague to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the senate: after which the censors struck out of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the senators the names of seven persons; among whom was Lucius the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of T. Flaminius. Lucius, when consul, and commanding in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, had with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> murdered a Boian of distinction, a defector to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and he committed this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> purely to gratify the curiosity of his pathetic, a young Carthaginian, who longing to see somebody die a violent death, had approached the general for bringing him away from Rome <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> when there was going to be a fight of gladiators. Titus Flamininus, full of indignation at the dishonour done to his brother, brought the affair before the people; and insisted upon Cato's giving the reason of his proceeding. The censor related the story; and when Lucius denied the fact, put him to his oath. The accused, refusing to swear, was deemed guilty; and Cato's censure was approved. But no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the censor's conduct seemed so cruel to the nobles and their wives as the taxes he laid upon luxury in all its branches; dyes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture, women's toilette, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, slaves, and equipage. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> were all taxed at three per cent. of the real value. The people, however, in general, were pleased with his regulations; inasmuch that they ordered a statue to be erected to his honour in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>, with an inscription that mentioned nothing of his victories or triumphs, but imported only, that by his wife ordinances in his censorship he had reformed the manners of the republic. Plutarch relates, that before this, upon some of Cato's friends expressing their surprise, that when many persons without merit or reputation had <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, he had none; he answered, "I had much rather it should be asked why the people have not erected a statue to Cato, than why they have." Cato was the occasion of the third Punic war. Being dispatched to Africa to terminate a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the Carthaginians and the king of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, on his return to Rome he reported that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> was grown excessively rich and populous, and he warmly exhorted the senate to destroy a city and republic, during the existence of which Rome could never be safe. Having brought from Africa some very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> figs, he showed them to the conscript fathers in one of the lapses of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>. "The country (says he) where this fine fruit grows is but a three days' voyage from Rome." We are told, that from this time he never spoke in the senate upon any subject, without concluding with these words, "I am also of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that Carthage ought to be destroyed." He judged, that for a people debauched by prosperity, nothing was more to be feared than a rival state, always powerful, and now from its misfortunes grown wise and circumspect. He held it necessary to remove all dangers that could be apprehended from without, when the republic had within so many distempers threatening her destruction. From the censor, dignified and severe, the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not perhaps be displeased to turn his view upon Cato sociable and relaxed. For we should have a false notion of him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we imagined that nothing but a sad austerity prevailed in his speech and behaviour. On the contrary, he was extremely free; and often with his friends at table intermixed the conversation with lively discourses and witty sayings. Of these Plutarch has collected a pretty large <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; we shall relate but one, and make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of Balzac's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> with which he introduces it. "The very censors, though sardonic seemed to be one of the functions of their office, did not altogether lay aside railing. They were not always bent upon severity; and the first Cato, that troublesome and intolerable honest man, ceased sometimes to be troublesome and intolerable. He had some glimpses of mirth, and some intervals of good humour. He dropped now and then some words that were not unpleasant, and you may judge of the rest by this. He had married a very handsome wife; and history tells us that she was extremely afraid of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, and loved her husband well. These two passions prompted her to the same thing; she always pitched upon her husband as a sanctuary against thunder, and threw herself into his arms at the first noise she fancied she heard in the sky. Cato, who was well pleased with the storm, and very willing to be careless, could not conceal his joy. He revealed that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> secret to his friends; and told them one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, speaking of his wife, "that she had found out a way to make him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> bad <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and that he never was so happy as when <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> was angry." It is worth observing, that this was during his censorship; when he degraded the senator Manlius, who would probably have been consul the year after, only for giving a kiss to his wife in the daytime, and in the presence of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. Cato died in the year of Rome 624, aged 85. He wrote several works. 1. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman History</a>. 2. Concerning the art of war. 3. Of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>. 4. A treatise of Husbandry. Of theft, the last only is extant.

CATIVELLAUNI

Pages 301-302

anciently a people of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, seated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which is now divided into the counties of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol10.html#article-HERTFORD">Hertford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>. The name of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> British people is written in several different ways by Greek and Roman authors, being sometimes called Catti, Caffii, Catticulcani, Cattidudani, Catticladani, &c. That they were of Belgic origin cannot be doubted; and it is not improbable that they derived their name of Catti from the Belgic word Katten, which signifies illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> noble, and that the addition of Vellauni, which means on the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, might be given them after their arrival in Britain, as descriptive of the situation of their country. However this may be, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATTIVELLAUNI">Cattivellauni</a> formed one of the most brave and warlike of the ancient British nations when Caesar invaded Britain, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after. Cassibelanus, their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, was made commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the confederated Britons, not only on account of his own personal qualities, but also because he was at the head of one of their bravest and most powerful tribes. In the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the departure of Caesar and the next invasion under Claudius, the Cattivellauni had reduced several of the neighbouring states under their obedience; and they again took the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in opposition to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> at their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> invasion, under their brave but unfortunate Prince Caractacus. The country of the Cattivellauni was much frequented and improved by the Romans, after it came under their obedience. Verulamium, their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which stood near where St Albans now stands, became a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> consideration, was honoured with the name and privileges of a municipium or free <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and had magistrates after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the city of Rome. This place was taken and almost destroyed by the insurgents under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOADICEA">Boadicea</a>; but it was afterwards rebuilt, restored to its former splendour, and surrounded with a strong wall, some vestiges of which are still remaining. Durobrivae and Magiaevintum, in the second iter of Antoninus, were probably <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNSTABLE">Dunstable</a> and Fenny <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRATFORD">Stratford</a>, at which places there appear to have been Roman stations. The Salones of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, a town in the country of the Cattivellauni, was perhaps situated at Sandly in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, where several Roman antiquities have been found. There were, besides these, several other Roman forts, stations, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in this country, which it would be tedious to enumerate. The territories of the Cattivellauni made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> called Britannia Prima.

CATO

Pages 292-294

Marcus Porcius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Cato <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cato of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>-grandson of Cato the Censor. It is said, that from his infancy he discovered by his speech, by his countenance, and even his childhood sports and recreations, an inflexibility of mind; for he would force himself to go through with whatever he had undertaken, though the task was ill-fitted to his strength. He was rough towards those that flattered him, and quite untractable when threatened; was rarely seen to laugh, or even to smile; was not easily provoked to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> once incensed, hard to be pacified. Sylla having had a friendship for the father of Cato, sent often for him and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, and talked familiarly with them. Cato, who was then about 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, seeing the heads of great men brought there, and observing the figs of those that were present, asked his preceptor, "Why does nobody kill this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>?" Because, said the other, he is more feared than he is hated. The boy replied, Why then did you not give me a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> when you brought me hither, that I might have stabbed him, and freed my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>? He learned the principles of the Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which so well suited his character, under Antipater of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, and applied himself diligently to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of it. Eloquence he likewise studied, as a necessary means to defend the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and he made a very considerable proficiency in that science. To increase his bodily strength, he insured himself to suffer the extremes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; and used to make journeys on foot and bare-headed in all seasons. When he was sick, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> were his only remedies: he flung himself up, and would see nobody till he was well. Though remarkably sober in the beginning of his his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, making it a rule to drink but once after <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, and then retire, he infensibly contracted a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of drinking more freely, and of sitting at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> till morning. His friends endeavoured to excuse this, by saying that the affairs of the public engrossed his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and that, being ambitious of knowledge, he passed the night in the conversation of philosophers. Cæsar wrote, that Cato was once found dead drunk at the corner of a street, early in the morning, by a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people who were going to the levee of some great man; and that when, by uncovering his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, they perceived who it was, they blushed for shame: "You would have thought (added Cæsar), that Cato had found them drunk, not they him." Pliny observes, that by this reflection Cæsar praises his enemy at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that he blames him. And Seneca, his extravagant panegyrist, ventures to assert, that it is easier to prove drunkards to be a virtue, than Cato to be vicious. He affected singularity; and in things indifferent, to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> directly contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and fashions of the age. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">Magnanimity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> are generally ascribed to him; and Seneca would fain make that haughtiness and contempt for others which, in Cato, accompanied those virtues, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of praise. Cato, says Seneca, having received a blow in the face, neither took <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> nor was angry; he did not even <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> the affront, but denied that he had received it. His virtue raised him so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that injury could not reach him. He is reputed to have been chaste in his youth. His first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> was Lepida; but when the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was upon the point of being concluded, Metellus Scipio, to whom he had been promised, interfered, and the preference was given to him. This affront extremely exasperated our Stoic. He was for going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> with Scipio; and when his friends had diverted him from that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, by showing him the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of it, he revenged himself by making verses upon his rival. When this first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> subsided, he married Attilia the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Serranus, had two children by her, and afterwards divorced her for her very indirect conduct. He served as a volunteer under <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of Spartacus; and when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> rewards were offered him by the commander, he refused them, because he thought he had no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to them. Some years after, he went a legionary tribune into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> under the praetor Rubrius: in which station he appeared, in his dress and during a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, more like a private soldier than an officer: but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his manners, the elevation of his sentiments, and the superiority of his views, set him far above those who bore the titles of generals and proconsuls. It is said, that Cato's design in all his behaviour was to engage the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to the love of virtue; whose affections he engaged thereby to himself, without his having that in his intention. "For the sincere love of virtue (adds Plutarch) implies an affection for the virtuous. Those who praise the worthy without loving them, pay homage to their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; but are neither admirers nor imitators of their virtues." When the time of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> expired, and he was leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the soldiers were all in tears; so effectually had he gained their hearts by his condescending manners and sharing in their labours. After his return home, he was chosen to the quæstorship; and had scarce entered on his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, when he made a great reformation in the quæstor's office, and particularly with regard to the registers. These registers, whose places were for life, and through whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> passed incessantly all the public accounts, being to act under young magistrates unexperienced in business, assumed an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of importance; and, instead of asking orders from the quæstors, pretended to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and govern as if they themselves were the quæstors. Cato reduced them to their proper sphere. One thing, by which Cato extremely pleased the people, was his making the assassins to whom Sylla had given considerable rewards out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> for murdering the proscribed, disgorge their gains. Plutarch tells us, that Cato was so exact in discharging the duties of a senator, as to be always the first who came to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the last who left it; and that he never quitted Rome during those days when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> was to sit. Nor did he fail to be present at every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people, that he might awe those who, by an ill-judged facility, bestowed the public <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in largesses, and frequently, through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> favour, granted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of debts due to the state. At first his austerity and stiffness displeased his colleagues; but afterwards they were glad to have his name to oppose to all the unjust solicitations, against which they would have found it difficult to defend themselves. Cato very readily took upon him the task of refusing. Cato, to keep out a very bad man, put in for the tribunate. He sided with Cicero against Catiline, and opposed Cæsar on that occasion. His enemies sent him to recover Cyprus, which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> had forfeited, thinking to hurt his reputation by so difficult an undertaking; yet none could find fault with his conduct. Cato laboured to bring about an agreement between Cæsar and Pompey; but seeing it in vain, he sided with the latter. When Pompey was slain he fled to Utica; and being pursued by Cæsar, advised his friends to be gone, and throw themselves on Cæsar's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>. His son, however, remained with him; and Statilius, a young man, remarkable for his hatred to Cæsar. The evening before the execution of the purpose he had formed with regard to himself, after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>, he supped with his friends and the magistrates of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. They sat late at table, and the conversation was lively. The discourse falling upon this maxim of the Stoics, that "the wise man alone is free, and that the vicious are slaves," Demetrius, who was a Peripatetic, undertook to confute it from the maxims of his school. Cato, in answer, treated the matter very amply; and with so much earnestness and vehemence of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, that he betrayed himself, and confirmed the suspicions of his friends that he designed to kill himself. When he had done speaking, a melancholy silence ensued; and Cato perceiving it, turned the discourse to the present situation of affairs, expressing his concern for those who had been obliged to put to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, as well as for those who had determined to make their escape by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and had a dry and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY_DESERT"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. After supper, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> being dismissed, he walked for some time with a few friends, and gave his orders to the officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>; and going into his chamber, he embraced his son and his friends with more than usual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CATOPTRICS">CATOPTRICS</a> CATOPTRICS is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> which explains the properties of reflected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and particularly that which is reflected from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>. As this and the other branches of Optics <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be fully treated under the collective word, we shall, in the present article, 1st, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> give a summary of the principles of the branch, in a few plain aphorisms, with some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> definitions; and, 2dly, Insert a set of entertaining experiments founded upon them. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I. Definitions. 1. Every polished body that reflects the rays of light is called a mirror, whether its surface be <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, spherical, conical, cylindric, or of any other form whatever. 2. Of mirrors there are three principally used in optical experiments: The plane mirror, GHI, (fig. I.)

CATOPTRICS

Pages 294-296

1. The spherical convex mirror, GHI, (fig. 2.) and the spherical concave mirror, GHI, (fig. 3.) 3. The point K, (fig. 2, 3.) round which the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is described, is called its centre. The line KH, drawn from its centre perpendicular to its two surfaces, is the axis of the mirror; and the point H, to which that line is drawn, is its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a>. 4. The distance between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> AG and BG, (fig. 1.) is called the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INCIDENCE">incidence</a>, and the distance between BG and CG is the angle of reflection. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">SECT</a>. II. Aphorisms. 1. The image DF, (fig. 1.) <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear as far behind the mirror as the object AC is before it. 2. The image will appear of the same size, and in the same position as the object. 3. Every such mirror will reflect the image of an object of twice its own length and breadth. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the object be an opaque body, and its rays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the mirror nearly in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> lines, there will be only one image visible, which will be reflected by the inner surface of the glass. But, 5. If the object be a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> body, and its rays fall very obliquely on the mirror, there will appear to an eye, placed in a proper position, several images; the first of which, reflected from the outer surface of the glass, will not be so bright as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, reflected from the inner surface. The following images, that are produced by the repeated reflections of the rays between the two surfaces of the glass, will be in proportion less vivid, to the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenth, which will be scarcely visible. 1. The image DF, (fig. 2.), will always appear behind it. 2. The image will be in the same position as the object. 3. It will be less than the object. 4. It will be curved, but not, as the mirror, spherical. 5. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">Parallel</a> rays falling on this mirror will have the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> or image at half the distance of the centre K from the mirror. 6. In converging rays, the distance of the object must be equal to half the distance of the centre, to make the image appear behind the mirror. 7. Diverging rays will have their image at less than half the distance of the centre. If the object be placed in the centre of the mirror, its image will appear at one eighth of that distance behind it. 1. That point where the image appears of the same dimensions as the object, is the centre of that mirror. 2. Parallel rays will have their focus at one half the distance of the centre. 3. Converging rays will form an image before the mirror. 4. In diverging rays, if the object be at less than one-half the distance of the centre, the image will be behind the mirror, erect, curved, and magnified, as DEF, (fig. 3.) but if the distance of the object be greater, the image will be before the mirror, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> and diminished, as DEF, (fig. 4.) 5. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays falling on a concave mirror, and being parallel, will be collected in a focus at half the distance of its centre, where their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> will be augmented in proportion of the surface of the mirror to that of the focal spot. 6. If a luminous body be placed in the focus of a concave mirror, its rays being reflected in parallel lines, will strongly enlighten a space of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> with the mirror, at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. If the luminous object be placed nearer than the focus, its rays will diverge, and consequently enlighten a larger space. It is on this principle that reverberators are constructed. IV. In all <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> and spherical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a> the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. SECT. III. Entertaining Experiments. I. Of all our senses the sight is certainly subject to the greatest illusion. The various writers on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> illusions have described a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of instances in which it deceives us, and have constantly endeavoured to investigate the causes, to explain their effects, and to reconcile appearance with reality. We every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> discover new phenomena, and doubtless many more are reserved for posterity. It frequently happens, moreover, that a discovery which at first seemed of little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> has led to matters of the highest importance. Take a glass bottle A (fig. 14.) and fill it with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the point B; leave the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> BC empty, and cork it in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> manner. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> this bottle opposite a concave mirror, and beyond its focus, that it may appear reversed, and before the mirror (see Sect. II. aph. 3. 4. of a spherical concave mirror,) place yourself still further distant from the bottle, and it will appear to you in the situation a, b, c, (fig. 15.) Now it is remarkable in this apparent bottle, that the water, which, according to all the laws of catoptrics, and all the experiments made on other objects, should appear at a b, appears on the contrary at b c, and consequently the part a b appears empty. If the bottle be inverted and placed before the mirror (as in fig. 16.), its image will appear in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> erect position; and the water, which is in reality at BC, will appear at a b. If while the bottle is held inverted, and partly empty, some drops of water fall from the bottom A towards BC, it seems in the image as if there were formed at the bottom of that part a b, bubbles of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> that rose from a to b; which is the part that seems full of water. All these phenomena constantly appear. The remarkable circumstances in this experiment are, first, not only to see an object where it is not, but also where the image is not; and secondly, that of two objects which are really in its same place, as the surface at one place, and the other at another; and to see the bottle in the place of its image, and the water where neither it nor its image are.
