II. Construct a box <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, of about a foot <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, eight inches II. Appearance of a boundless vista. On the inside of this box, and against each of its opposite ends A and B, place a mirror of the same size. Take off the quicksilver from the mirror that you place at B, for about an inch and a half, at the part C, where you are to make a hole in the box of the same size, by which you may easily view its inside. Cover the top of the box with a frame, in which must be placed a transparent glass, covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, on the side next the inner part of the box. Let there be two grooves at the parts E and F to receive the two painted scenes hereafter mentioned. On two pieces of cut pasteboard let there be skilfully painted on both sides (see fig. 6 and 7) any subject you think proper; as woods, gardens, bowers, colonnades, &c., and on two other pasteboards, the same subjects on one side only; observing that there ought to be on one of them some object relative to the subject placed at A, that the mirror placed at D may not reflect the hole at C on the opposite side. Place the two boards painted on both sides in the grooves E and F; and those that are painted on one side only against the opposite mirrors C and D; and then cover the box with its transparent top. This box should be placed in a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to have a good effect. When the eye is placed at C, and views the objects on the inside of the box, of which some, as we have said, are painted on both sides, they are successively reflected from one mirror to the other; and if, for example, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> consists of trees, they will appear like a very long vista, of which the eye cannot discern the end: for each of the mirrors repeating the objects, continually more faintly, contribute greatly to augment the illusion. III. Take a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> box ABCD, of about six inches long, and twelve <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; cover the inside of it with four plane mirrors, which must be placed perpendicular to the bottom of the box CHFD. Place certain objects in relief on the bottom of this box; suppose, for example, a piece of fortification, (as fig. 9.) with tents, foldiers, &c. or any other subject that you judge will produce an agreeable effect by its disposition when repeatedly reflected by the mirrors. On the top of this box place a frame of glass, in form of the bottom part of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, whose base AGEB is equal to the size of the box: its top ILN must form a square of six inches, and should not be more than four or five inches higher than the box. Cover the four sides of this frame with a gauze, that the inside may not be visible but at the top ILN, which should be covered with a transparent glass. When you look into this box through the glass LN, the mirrors that are diametrically opposite each other, mutually reflecting the figures enclosed, the eye beholds a boundless <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, completely covered with these objects; and if they are properly disposed, the illusion will occasion no small surprize, and afford great entertainment. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>. The nearer the opening ILN is to the top of the box, the greater will be the apparent extent of the subject. The same will happen if the four mirrors placed on the sides of the box be more elevated. The objects, by either of these dispositions, will appear to be repeated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, twenty-five, forty-nine times, &c., by taking always the square of the odd numbers of the arithmetical progression 3, 5, 7, 9, &c., as is very easy to conceive, if we remember that the subject enclosed in the box is always in the centre of a square, composed of several others, equal to that which forms the bottom of the box. Other pieces of the same kind (that is, viewed from above) may be contrived, in which mirrors may be placed perpendicular on a triangular, pentagon, or hexagon (that is, a three, five, or six-sided) plane. All these different dispositions, properly directed, as well with regard to the choice as position of the objects, will constantly produce very remarkable and pleasing illusions. If instead of placing the mirrors perpendicular, they were to incline equally, so as to form part of a reversed pyramid, the subject placed in the box would then have the appearance of a very extensive globular or many-sided <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. IV. On the hexagonal or six-sided plane ABCDEFIV. Sur draw six semidiameters GA, GB, GC, GD, GE, GF; and on each of these place perpendicularly two plane mirrors, which must join exactly at the centre G, and fig. 10, which placed back to back must be as thin as possible. Decorate the exterior boundary of this piece (which is at the extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the hexagon) with six columns, that at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> serve to support the mirrors, by grooves formed on their inner sides. (See the profile H). Add to these columns their entablatures, and cover the edifice in such a manner as you shall think proper. In each one of these six triangular spaces, contained between two mirrors, place little figures of pasteboard, in relief, representing such objects as when seen in a hexagonal form will produce an agreeable effect. To these add small figures of enamel; and take particular care to conceal, by some object that has relation to the subject, the place where the mirrors join, which, as we have said before, all meet in the common centre G. When you look into any one of the six openings of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the objects there contained being repeated six times, will seem entirely to fill up the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. This illusion will appear very remarkable; especially if the objects made choice of are properly adapted to the effect that is to be produced by the mirrors. Note. If you place between two of these mirrors part of a fortification, as a curtain and two demi-batons, you will see an entire citadel, with six battions. Or if you place part of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>-room, ornamented with chandeliers and figures in enamel, all those objects being here multiplied, will afford a very pleasing prospect. V. Within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> ABCD, place your mirrors, O, P, Q, R, so disposed that they may each of them bodies make an angle of forty-five degrees, that is, that they may be half way inclined from the perpendicular, as transparent in the figure. In each of the two extremities A.B, fig. 11, make a circular overture, in one of which fix the tube.

CATOPTROMANCY

Pages 298-301

Κατοπτρομαντική, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; so called, because consisting in the application of a mirror. The word is formed from κατοπτρος, σφυρίς, "mirror," and σφυρίς, σφυρίς, "divination." Pausanias says, it was in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Achaeans; where those who were sick, and in danger of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a mirror, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> looking glass fastened by a thread, into a fountain before the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>; then looking in the glass, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a ghastly disfigured <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, they took it as a sure sign of death; on the contrary, if the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> appeared fresh and healthy, it was a token of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. Sometimes glasses were used without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the images of things future represented in them. See GASTROMANCY.

CATROU

Pages 301-301

FRANCIS, a famous Jesuit, born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1659. He was engaged for 12 years in the Journal de Trevoux, and applied himself at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to other works, which distinguished him among the learned. He wrote a general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Mogul empire, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman History</a>, in which he was assisted by Father Rouille, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Jesuit. Catrou died in 1737; and this last history was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by Rouille, who died in 1740.

CATTERTHUN

Pages 301-301

a remarkable Caledonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> a few miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BRECHIN">Brechin</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a> in Scotland. Mr Pennant describes it as of uncommon strength. "It is (says he) of an oval form, made of a stupendous dike of loose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, whose convexity, from the base within to that without, is 122 feet. On the outside a hollow, made by Catterthun, the disposition of the stones, surrounds the whole. Round the base is a deep ditch, and below that about 100 yards, are vestiges of another, that went round the hill. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> within the flinty mound is flat; the axis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> length of the oval, is 436 feet, the transverse diameter 200. Near the east side is the foundation of a rectangular <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; and on most parts are the foundations of others small and circular: all which had once their superstructures, the shelter of the poftellors of the post: there is also a hollow, now almost filled with stones, the well of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>." There is another fortification, but of inferior strength, in the neighbourhood. It is called the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a> Catterthun, from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the ramparts, which are composed only of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It is of a circular form, and consists of various concentric dikes. On one side of this rises a small rill, which, running <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the hill, has formed a deep gully. From the side of the fortrefs is another rampart, which extends <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the rill, and then reverts, forming an additional post or retreat. The meaning of the word Catter-thun is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>-town; and Mr Pennant thinks thee might probably be the posts occupied by the Caledonians before their engagement at the foot of the Grampian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> with the celebrated Agricola. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) SCOTLAND.

CATTI

Pages 301-301

a people of Germany, very widely spread, on the east reaching to the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALA">Sala</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to Westphalia; occupying, besides <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, the Wetterau, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the tract on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and on the banks

CATTLE

Pages 302-302

a collective word, which signifies the four-footed animals, which serve either for tilling the ground, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> for food to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. They are distinguished into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle; and into small cattle: of the former are horses, bulls, oxen, cows, and even calves, and heifers; amongst the latter are rams, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a>, sheep, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, goats, kids, &c. Cattle are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> flock of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>: they who <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in cattle are styled graziers.

CATULLUS

Pages 302-302
CAIUS VALERIUS, a Latin poet, born at Verona, in the year of Rome 666. The harmony of his numbers acquired him the esteem and friendship of Cicero, and other great men of his time. Many of his poems, however, abound with gross obsequies. He wrote satirical verses against Caesar, under the name of Marmoro. He spent his whole life in a state of poverty; and died in the flower of his age and the height of his reputation. Joseph Scaliger, Passerat, Muret, and Isaac Vollius, have written learned notes on this poet.

CATZ

Pages 302-302

JAMES, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> civilian, politician, and Dutch poet, was born at Browerhaven, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, in the year 1577. After having made several voyages, he fixed at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLEBURG">Middleburg</a>; and acquired by his pleadings such reputation, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> chose him for its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a>; as did also, some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, that of Middleburg. In 1634, he was nominated pensionary of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and West Friesland; and in 1648, he was elected keeper of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the same state, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> of the fiefs: but some time after, he resigned these employments, to enjoy the repose which his advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> demanded. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> pensionary had been fatal to almost all those who had enjoyed it, from the beginning of the republic till that time, Catz delivered up his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, before the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states, weeping for joy, and thanking God for having preserved him from the inconveniences that seemed attached to the duties of that office. But though he was resolved to spend the rest of his days in repose, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> engaged him to comply with the desires of the states, who importuned him to go on an embassy to England, in the delicate conjuncture in which the republic found itself during the protectorate of Cromwell. At his return, he retired to his fine country seat at Sorgvliet, where he lived in tranquillity till the year 1660, in which he died. He wrote a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of poems in Dutch; most of which are on moral subjects, and so esteemed, that they have been often printed in all the different sizes; and, next to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, there is no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> so highly valued by the Dutch.

CATZENELLIBOGEN

Pages 302-302

a town of Germany, in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the upper circle of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, with a strong castle. It is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 38. N. Lat. 50. 20.

CAUCASUS

Pages 303-303

the name of a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, being one of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ridge which runs between the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> and Caspian seas. Sir John Chardin describes this as the highest mountain, and the most difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, of any he had seen. It has frightful precipices, and in many places the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> are cut out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he passed it, the mountain was entirely covered with snow; so that, in many places, his guides behoved to clear the way with shovels. The mountain is 36 leagues over, and the summit of it eight leagues in breadth. The top is perpetually covered with snow; and our traveller relates, that the two last days he seemed to be in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and was not able to see 20 paces before him. Excepting the very top, however, all the parts of Mount-Caucasus are extremely fruitful; abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, hogs, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cattle. The vines twine about the trees, and rise so high, that the inhabitants cannot gather the fruit from the uppermost branches. There are many streams of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages. The inhabitants are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the Georgian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. They have fine complexions, and the women are very beautiful.—In the winter they wear snow shoes in the form of rackets, which prevent their sinking in the snow, and enable them to run upon it with great swiftness.

CAUDEBEC

Pages 303-303

a rich, populous, and trading town, in Normandy, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Caux. It is seated at the foot of a mountain near the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 46. N. Lat. 40. 30.

CAUDEX

Pages 303-304

by Malpighi and other botanists, is used to signify the stem <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree; by Linnaeus, the stock or body of the root, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which ascends, part descends. The ascending part raises itself gradually above ground, serving frequently for a trunk, and corresponds in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to the caudex of former writers: the descending part strikes gradually downward into the ground, and puts forth radicles or small fibres, which are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and essential part of every root. The descending caudex Caudex therefore corresponds to the radix of other botanists. Agreeably to this idea, Linnaeus considers trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> as roots above ground; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which is confirmed by a well-known fact, that trees, when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, put forth leaves from the descending caudex, and radicles or roots from the ascending. For the varieties in the descending caudex, see the article Radix.

CAUDIUM

Pages 304-304

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Samnium, on the Via Appia, between Calatia and Beneventum; Caudinus, the epithet. The Caudine Furcae, Furcatae, were memorable by the disgrace of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; being spears disposed in the form of a gallows under which prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> were made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, and gave name to a defile <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> narrow pass near Caudium (Livy); where the Samnites obliged the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> and the two consuls to lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their arms and pass under the gallows, or yoke, as a token of submission.

CAUING

Pages 307-307
or CAULKING of a Ship, is driving a quantity of oakum, or old ropes untwisted and drawn together, into the seams of the planks, or into the intervals where the planks are joined together in the ship's decks or sides, in order to prevent the entrance of water. After the oakum is driven very hard into these seams, it is covered with hot melted pitch or rosin, to keep the water from rotting it. Among the ancients, the first who made use of pitch in caulking, were the inhabitants of Phæacia, afterwards called Corfica. Wax and rosin appear to have been commonly used previous to that period; and the Poles at this time use a sort of unctuous clay for the same purpose on their navigable rivers. CAULKING Irons, are iron chisels for that purpose. Some of these irons are broad, some round, and others grooved. After the seams are stopped with oakum, it is done over with a mixture of tallow, pitch, and tar, as low as the ship draws water.

CAUL

Pages 307-307

in Anatomy, a membrane in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, covering the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the guts; called, from its structure, Reticulum, but most frequently Omentum. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Caul is likewise a little membrane, found on some children, encompassing the head when born. Drelincourt takes the caul to be only a fragment of the membranes of the fetus; which ordinarily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> at the birth of the child. Lampadius tells us, that the midwives sold this caul at a good price to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> and pleaders of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; it being an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that while they had this about them, they should carry with them a force of persuasion which no judge could withstand: the canons forbid the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it; because some witches and sorcerers, it seems, had abused it.

CAULIFLOWERS

Pages 307-307

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a much esteemed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cabbage. See Brassica.

CAURIS

Pages 307-307

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by some to the genus of shells called, by the generality of writers, porcellana and concha veneris. It is from a false <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> of this word cauris that these shells are called cowries. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>-Shell, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CAURSINES

Pages 307-307

were Italians that came into England about the year 1235, terming themselves the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, but driving no other trade than letting out <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; and having <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> banks in England, they differed little from Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> (as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> says) they were rather more merciless to their debtors. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have them called Courfines, quasi Caufa Urfin, bearish, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cruel in their causes; others Caorfini or Corfini, as coming from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Corfica; but Cowell says, they have their name from Caorium, Caorsi, a town in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, where they first practised their arts of usury and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTORTION">extortion</a>; from whence spreading themselves, they carried their infamous trade through most parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and were a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> to every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> where they came. The then bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> excommunicated them; and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry III. banished them from this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in the year 1240. But, being the pope's solicitors and money changers, they were permitted to return in the year 1250; though in a very short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they were again driven out of the kingdom on account of their intolerable exactions. CAUSA MATRIMONII PRÆLOCUTI, in common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a writ that lies where a woman gives lands to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in fee to the intent he shall marry her, and he refuses to do it in a reasonable time, being thereupon required by the woman; and in such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, for not performing the condition, the entry of the woman into the lands again has been adjudged lawful. The husband and wife may sue this writ against another who ought to have married her.

CAUSALITY

Pages 307-307

among miners, denotes the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, fulphurous, earthy parts of ores, carried off in the operation of washing. This, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, they throw in heaps upon banks, which in six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years they find it worth their while to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> over again.

CAUSE

Pages 307-310

that from whence any thing proceeds, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by virtue of which any thing is done: it stands opposed to effect. We get the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of cause and effect from our observation of the vicissitude of things, while we perceive some qualities or substances begin to exist, and that they receive their existence from the due application and operation of other beings. That which produces, is the cause; and that which is produced, the effect: thus, fluidity in wax is the effect of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, which we observe to be constantly produced by the application of such heat. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, and the schoolmen after him, distinguished four kinds of causes; the efficient, the material, the formal, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a>. This, like many of Aristotle's distinctions, is only a distinction of the various meanings of an ambiguous word: for the efficient, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, the form, and the end, have nothing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, by which they may be accounted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the same genus; but the Greek word, which we translate translate cause, had these four different meanings in Aristotle's days, and we have added other meanings. We do not indeed call the matter or the form of a thing its cause; but we have final causes, instrumental causes, occasional causes, and many others. Thus the word cause has been so hackneyed, and made to have so many different meanings in the writings of philosophers, and in the discourse of the vulgar, that its original and proper meaning is lost in the crowd. With regard to the phenomena of nature, the important end of knowing their causes, besides gratifying our curiosity, is, that we may know when to expect them, or how to bring them about. This is very often of real importance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and this purpose is served, by knowing what, by the course of nature, goes before them and is connected with them; and this, therefore, we call the cause of such a phenomenon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a magnet be brought near to a mariner's compass, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, which was before at rest, immediately begins to move, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> its course towards the magnet, or perhaps the contrary way. If an unlearned sailor is asked the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the needle, he is at no loss for an answer. He tells you it is the magnet; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> is clear: for, remove the magnet, and the effect ceases; bring it near, and the effect is again produced. It is, therefore, evident to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, that the magnet is the cause of this effect. A Cartesian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> enters deeper into the cause of this phenomenon. He observes, that the magnet does not touch the needle, and therefore can give it no impulse. He pities the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the sailor. The effect is produced, says he, by magnetic effluvia, or subtle matter, which passes from the magnet to the needle, and forces it from its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. He can even show you, in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, where these magnetic effluvia issue from the magnet, what round they take, and what way they return home again. And thus he thinks he comprehends perfectly how, and by what cause, the motion of the needle is produced. A Newtonian philosopher inquires what proof can be offered for the existence of magnetic effluvia, and can find none. He therefore holds it as a fiction, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>; and he has learned that hypotheses ought to have no place in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of nature. He confesses his ignorance of the real cause of this motion, and thinks that his business as a philosopher is only to find from experiment the laws by which it is regulated in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. These three persons differ much in their sentiments with regard to the real cause of this phenomenon; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who knows most is he who is sensible that he knows nothing of the matter. Yet all the three speak the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and acknowledge that the cause of this motion is the attractive or repulsive power of the magnet. What has been said of this, may be applied to every phenomenon that falls within the compass of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy. We deceive ourselves, if we conceive that we can point out the real efficient cause of any one of them. The grandest discovery ever made in natural philosophy, was that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, which opens such a view of our planetary system, that it looks like something divine. But the author of this discovery was perfectly aware that he discovered no real cause, but only the law or rule according to which the unknown cause operates. Natural philosophers, who think accurately, have a precise meaning to the terms they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the science; and when they pretend to show the cause of any phenomenon of nature, they <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> by the cause, a law of nature of which that phenomenon is a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The whole object of natural philosophy, as Newton expressly teaches, is reducible to these two heads: first, by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> induction from experiment and observation, to discover the laws of nature; and then to apply those laws to the solution of the phenomena of nature. This was all that this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> philosopher attempted, and all that he thought attainable. And this indeed he attained in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, with regard to the motions of our planetary system, and with regard to the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. But supposing that all the phenomena which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> within the reach of our senses were accounted for from general laws of nature justly deduced from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; that is, supposing natural philosophy brought to its utmost perfection; it does not discover the efficient cause of any one phenomenon in nature. The laws of nature are the rules according to which the effects are produced; but there must be a cause which operates according to these rules. The rules of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> never navigated a ship. The rules of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> never built a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Natural philosophers, by great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the course of nature, have discovered many of her laws, and have very happily applied them to account for many phenomena; but they have never discovered the efficient cause of any one phenomenon; nor do those who have distinct notions of the principles of the science make any such pretence. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of nature we see innumerable effects which require an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> endowed with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> power: but the agent is behind the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. Whether it be the Supreme cause alone, or a subordinate cause or causes; and if subordinate causes be employed by the Almighty, what their nature, their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and their different offices may be; are things hid, for wise reasons, without doubt, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> eye. Cause, among civilians, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. See Action. Cause, among physicians. The cause of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is defined by Galen to be that during the presence of which we are ill, and which being removed, the disorder immediately ceases. The doctrine of the causes of diseases is called Etiology. Physicians divide causes into procatarectic, antecedent, and continent. Procatarectic Cause, (κατά προκαταρεξιν), called also primitive and incipient cause, is either an occasion which of its own nature does not beget a disease, but happening on a body inclined to diseases breeds a fever, gout, &c. (such as are watching, fasting, and the like); or an evident and manifest cause, which immediately produces the disease, as being sufficient thereto, such as is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in respect of a wound. Antecedent Cause, (κατά προερχομένων), a latent disposition of the body, from whence some disease may arise; such as a plethora in respect of a fever, a caco-chymia in respect of a scurvy. Continent, Conjunct, or Proximate Cause, that principle in the body which immediately adheres to the disease, and which being present, the disease is also present; or, which being removed, the disease is taken away: such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in a nephritic patient. Causeway, or Causey, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, flanks, and fascines; or an elevation of fat viscid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, well beaten; serving either as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> in wet marshy places, or as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> to retain the waters of a pond, or prevent a river from overflowing the lower grounds. See Road.—The word comes from the French chausse, anciently wrote chaulfée; and that from the Latin calceata, or calceata; according to Sonner and Spelman, à calcaro. Bergier rather takes the word to have had its rise à pediment calcei, quibus terratur. Some derive it from the Latin calce, or French chaux, as supposing it primarily to denote a way paved with chalk stones. Causeway, (calceatum or calcea), more usually denotes a common hard raised way, maintained and repaired with stones and rubbish. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a>'s Causeway, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this kind, which ranges through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> supposed to be Roman, though Mr Hersley suspects it to be of later times. Giant's Causeway, is a denomination given to a huge pile of stony columns in the district of Coleraine in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. See Giant's Causeway. Causin, Nicholas, surnamed the Jesuit, a French Jesuit, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TROYES">Troyes</a> in Champagne, in the year 1580; and entered into the Jesuits order when he was 26 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> in several of their colleges, and afterwards began to preach, by which he gained very great reputation. He increased this reputation by publishing books, and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was preferred to be confessor to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. But he did not discharge this office to the satisfaction of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Richelieu, though he discharged it to the satisfaction of every honest man; and therefore it is not to be wondered at that he came at length to be removed. He died in the Jesuits convent at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1611. None of his works did him more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> than that which he entitled La Cour Sainte. It has been printed a great many times; and translated into Latin, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, German, and English. He published several other books both in Latin and French. Causticity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> belonging to several substances, by the acrimony of which the parts of living animals may be corroded and destroyed. Bodies which have this quality, when taken internally, are true poisons. The causticity of some of these, as of arsenic, is so deadly, that even their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> use is prohibited by prudent physicians. Several others, as nitrous acid, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> infernalis or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> caustic, common caustic, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, are daily and successfully used to consume fungous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, to open ulcers, &c. They succeed very well when properly employed and skilfully managed. The causticity of bodies depends entirely on the state of the saline, and chiefly of the acid, matters they contain. When these <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> happen to be at the same time much concentrated, and slightly attached to the matters with which they are combined, they are then capable of acting, and are corrosive or caustic. Thus fixed and volatile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, although they are themselves caustic, become much more so by being treated with quicklime; because this substance deprives them of causticity, all their fixed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or carbonic acid to which they owe their mildness. By this treatment, then, the saline principle is more disengaged, and rendered more capable of action. Also all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of metallic matters with acids form salts more or less corrosive, because these acids are deprived of all their superabundant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and are besides but imperfectly saturated with the metallic matters. Nevertheless, some other circumstance is necessary to constitute the causticity of these saline metallic matters. For the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of marine acid, which, when pure and diluted with a certain quantity of water, would be productive of no harm, shall, however, produce all the effects of a corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, when it is united with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> in corrosive sublimate, although the sublimate shall be dissolved in so much water that its causticity cannot be attributed to the concentration of its acid. This effect is, by some chemists, attributed to the great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the metallic matters, with which the acid is united; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is very probable, seeing its causticity is nothing but its dissolving power, or its disposition to combine with other bodies; and this disposition is nothing else than <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>. On this subject Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> observes, that the compounds produced by the union of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> with acids are in general corrosive. Many of them applied to the skin destroy it almost as fast as the mineral acids; and some of the most powerful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">potential</a> cauteries are made in this way. Some are reckoned more acid than the pure acids themselves; and they have more powerful effects when taken internally, or at least seem to have. Thus we can take 10 or 12 drops of a fossil acid, diluted with water, without being disturbed by it; but the same quantity of acid previously combined with silver, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, or regulus of antimony, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> throw the body into violent disorders, or even prove a poison, if taken all at once. This increased <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> was, by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> philosophers, supposed to arise from the weight of the metallic particles. They imagined that the acid was composed of minute particles of the shape of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> or wedges; by which means they were capable of entering the pores of other bodies, separating their atoms from each other, and thus dissolving them. To these acid spiculae the metallic particles gave more force; and the momentum of each particular needle or wedge was increased in proportion to its increase of gravity by the additional weight of the metallic particle. But this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> is entirely fanciful, and does not correspond with facts. The activity of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> is not in proportion to the weight of the metal; nor are the compounds always possessed of any great degree of acrimony: neither is it true that any of them have a greater power of destroying animal substances than the pure acids have. There is a material <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the powers called stimuli and corrosives. Let a person apply to any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the skin a small quantity of lunar caustic, and likewise a drop of strong nitrous acid, and he will find that the acid acts with more violence than the caustic; and the disorders that are occasioned by the compounds of metals and acids do not proceed from a causticity in them, but from the metal afflicting and proving a stimulus to the nerves; and that this is the Cauticity appears from their affecting some particular nerves of the body. Thus the compounds of antimony and mercury with the vegetable acids, do not show the smallest degree of acrimony; but, taken internally, they produce violent convulsive motions over the whole body, which are occasioned by the metallic matter having a power of producing this effect; and the acid is only the means of bringing it into a dissolved state, and making it capable of acting on the nervous system. In general, however, the compounds of metallic substances with acids may be considered as milder than the acids in a separate state; but the acid is not so much neutralized as in other compounds, for it is less powerfully attracted by the metal; so that alkaline salts, absorbent earths, or even heat alone, will decompose them; and some of the inflammable substances, as spirit of wine, aromatic oils, &c., will attract the acid, and precipitate the metal in its metallic form; and the metals can be employed to precipitate one another in their metallic form; so that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of these compounds is much weaker than those formed of the same acids with alkaline salts or earths.

CAUSTICS

Pages 310-310

is an appellation given to substances of so hot and fiery a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that, being applied, they consume, and as it were burn, the texture of the parts, like hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Cautics are generally divided into four sorts; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stronger caustic, the common milder caustic, the antimonial caustic, and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> caustic. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CAUSTIC Curve, in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, a curve formed by the concurrence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coincidence of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> reflected from some other curve.

CAUSUS

Pages 310-310
or Burning Fever, a species of continual fever, accompanied with a remarkable inflammation of the blood.

CAUTERIZATION

Pages 310-310

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> searing some morbid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, by the application of fire either actual or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">potential</a>. In some places they cauterize with burning tow, in others with cotton or moxa, in others with live coals; some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> Spanish wax, others pyramidal pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, others <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver; Severinus recommends <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> blown through a pipe; but what is usually preferred among us is a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Cauterizing irons are of various figures; some flat, others round, some curved, &c., all of which we find draughts in Albucafs, Scultetus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and others. Sometimes a cautery is applied through a capfula, to prevent any terror from the sight of it. This method was invented by Placentinus, and is described by Scultetus. In the use of all cauteries, care is to be taken to defend the neighbouring parts, either by a lamina, defensive platter, or lint moistened in oxycrate. Sometimes the hot iron is transmitted through a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> cannula, for the greater safety of the adjoining parts. The degrees and manners of cauterizing are varied according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and the part affected.

CAUTERY

Pages 310-310

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a medicine for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, scarring, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> corroding any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body. Cauteries are distinguished into two classes; actual and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIAL">potential</a>: by actual cauteries are understood <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot instruments, usually of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and by potential cauteries are understood certain kinds of corroding medicines. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>.

CAUTION

Pages 310-310

in the Civil and Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes much the same with what, in the law of England, is called Bail.

CAUTIONER

Pages 310-310

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, that person who becomes bound for another to the performance of any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> obligation. As to the different kinds and effects of cautionry, see Law, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. No. clxxv. 19. CAWK. See CAUK.

CAVAILLAN

Pages 302-302

a town of France, in the department of Vaucluse, and formerly a bishop's see. It is situated on the river Durance, in a fertile and pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and 20 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 17. N. Lat. 43. 52.

CAVALCADE

Pages 302-302

a formal pompous <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> of horsemen, equipages, &c. by way of parade or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> a triumph, public entry, or the like.

CAVALCADOUR

Pages 302-302
or CAVALCADEUR, anciently denoted a riding master; but at present is diffused in that sense, and only employed to denote a sort of equerries or officers who have the direction of princes stables. The French say, ecuyer cavalcadeur of the king, the duke of Orleans, &c. Menage writes it cavalcadour, and derives it from the Spanish cavalgador, a horfeman.

CAVALCANTE

Pages 302-303

GUIDO, a nobleman of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in the 13th century, who having followed the party of the Guelphs, experienced the changeableness of fortune. He showed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength of mind in his misfortunes, and never neglected to improve his talents. He wrote a treatise in Italian concerning style, and some verses which are esteemed. His poem on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of this world has been commented on by several learned men.

CAVALIER

Pages 303-303

in the manege, one that understands horses, and is practised in the art of riding them.

CAVALIERI

Pages 303-303

BONAVENTURE, an eminent mathematician in the 17th century, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and a friar of the order of the Jesuits of St Jerome, was professor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, where he published several mathematical books, particularly the "Method of Indivisibles." He was a scholar of Galileo. His "Dilectiorum generale Uranometricum" contains <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of most useful practices in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. His trigonometrical tables in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> are excellent.

CAVALRY

Pages 303-303

a body of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> on horseback. The word comes from the French, cavalerie, and that from the corrupt Latin, caballus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. The Roman cavalry consisted wholly of those called equites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> knights, who were a distinct order in the distribution of citizens.—The Greek cavalry were divided into cataphractae and non cataphractae, i.e., into heavy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> armed.—Of all the Greeks, the Thessalians excelled most in cavalry. The Lacedemonians, inhabiting a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, were but meanly furnished with cavalry, till, carrying their arms into other countries, they found <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> occasion for horses to support and cover their foot. The Athenian cavalry, for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, consisted only of 96 horsemen: after expelling the Persians out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, they increased the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to 300; and afterwards to 1000, which was the highest pitch of the Athenian cavalry. The Turkish cavalry consists partly of Spahis, and partly of horsemen raised and maintained by the Zaims and Timariots. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the cavalry is to make frequent excursions to disturb the enemy, intercept his convoys, and destroy the country: in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to support and cover the foot, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through and disorder the enemy; also to secure the retreat of the foot. Formerly, the manner of fighting of the cavalry was, after firing their pistols or carbines, to wheel off, to give opportunity for loading again. Gustavus Adolphus is said to have first taught the cavalry to charge through, to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> straight up to the enemy, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> drawn in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> having fired his piece, at the proper distance, to take himself to his sword, and charge the enemy as was found most advantageous.

CAVAN

Pages 303-303

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 32. N. Lat. 54. 0. Cavan, a county of Ireland, 47 miles in length and 23 in breadth; is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONAGHAN">Monaghan</a>, and on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGFORD">Longford</a>, West-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, and East-Meath. It has but two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, viz. Cavan and Kilmore. It sends five members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; two for the county, two for Cavan, and one for Kilmore. It contains upwards of 8000 houses, 37 parishes, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> baronies, and two boroughs.

CAVE

Pages 304-305

Edward, printer, celebrated as the projector of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>,—the first publication of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and since The fruitful mother of a thousand more, was born in 1691. His father being disappointed of some small family expectations, was reduced to follow the trade of shoemaker at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUGBY">Rugby</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>. The free school of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in which his son had, by the rules of its foundation, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to be instructed, was then in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation, under the Rev. Mr Holyoak, to whose care most of the neighbouring families, even of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, intrusted their sons. He had judgement to discover, and for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> generosity to encourage, the genius of young Cave; and was so well pleased with his quick progress in the school, that he declared his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to breed him for the university, and recommend him as a servitor to some of his scholars of high rank. But prosperity which depends upon the caprice of others, is of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Cave's superiority in literature exalted him to an invidious familiarity with boys who were far above him in rank and expectations; and, as in unequal affections it always happens, whatever unlucky prank was played was imputed to Cave. When any mischief, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> small, was done, though perhaps others boasted of the stratagem when it was successful, yet upon detection or miscarriage, the fault was sure to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> Cave. The harsh treatment he experienced from this source, and which he bore for a while, made him at last leave the school, and the hope of a literary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, to seek some other means of gaining a livelihood. He was first placed with a collector of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>; but the influence of his mistress, who employed him in servile drudgery, quickly disgusted him, and he went up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in quest of more suitable employment. He was recommended to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> merchant at the Bankside; and while he was there on liking, is said to have given hopes of great mercantile abilities; but this place he soon left; and was bound apprentice to Mr Collins, a printer of some reputation, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. This was a trade for which men were formerly qualified by a literary education, and which was pleasing to Cave, because it furnished some employment for his scholastic attainments. Here, therefore, he resolved to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>, though his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and mistress lived in perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was therefore no comfortable habitation. From the inconveniences of these <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> tumults he was soon released, having in only two years attained so much skill in his art, and gained so much the confidence of his master, that he was sent without any superintendant to conduct a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> house at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, and publish a weekly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. In this undertaking he met with some opposition, which produced a public controversy, and procured young Cave the reputation of a writer. His master died before his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> was expired, and he was not able to bear the perverseness of his mistress. He therefore quitted her house upon a stipulated allowance, and married a young widow, with whom he lived at Bow. When his apprenticeship was over, he worked as a journeyman at the printing-house of Mr Barbar, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> much distinguished and employed by the Tories, whose principles had at that time so much prevalence with Cave, that he was for some years a writer in Mill's Journal. He afterwards obtained by his wife's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> a small place in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST_OFFICE"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-office; but still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, at his intervals of attendance, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his trade, or to employ himself with some typographical business. He corrected the Gradus <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Parnassum; and was liberally rewarded by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>. Company of Stationers. He wrote an Account of the Criminals, which had for some time a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; and published many little pamphlets that accident brought into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, of which it would be very difficult to recover the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. By the correspondence which his place in the post-office facilitated, he procured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> newspaper, and told their intelligence to a journalist in London for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> a-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. He was afterwards raised to the office of the clerk of the franks, in which he acted with great spirit and firmness; and often stopped franks which were given by members of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to their friends, because he thought such <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of a peculiar right illegal. This raised many complaints; and the influence that was exerted against him procured his ejectment from office. He had now, however, collected a sum sufficient for the purchase of a small printing-office, and began the Gentleman's Magazine; an undertaking to which he owed the influence in which he passed the last 20 years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortune which he left behind him. When he formed the project, he was far from expecting the success which he found; and others had so little prospect of its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, that though he had for several years talked of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> among printers and bookellers, none of them thought it worth the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. That they were not (says Dr Johnson) restrained by their virtue from the execution of another man's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, was sufficiently apparent as soon as that design began to be gainful; for, in a few years, a multitude of magazines arose, and perished; only the London Magazine, supported by a powerful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of bookellers, and circulated with all the art and all the cunning of trade, exempted itself from the general fate of Cave's invaders, and obtained though not an equal, yet a considerable sale. Cave now began to aspire to popularity; and being a greater lover of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> than any other art, he sometimes offered subjects for poems, and proposed prizes for the best performers. The first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> was £50, for which, being but newly acquainted with wealth, and thinking the influence of £50 extremely great, he expected the first authors of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to appear as competitors, and offered the allotment of the prize to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. But, when the time came, no name was seen among the writers that had been ever seen before; and the universities and several private men rejected the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of affixing the prize. The determination was then left to Dr Cromwell Mortimer and Dr Birch; and by the latter the award was made, which may be seen in Gent. Mag. vol. vi. p. 59. Mr Cave continued to improve his Magazine, and had the satisfaction of seeing its success proportionate to his diligence, till in 1754, his wife died of an asthma. He seemed not at first much affected by her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, but in a few days lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> and his appetite, which he never recovered. After having lingered about two years, with many vicissitudes of amendment and relapse, he fell by drinking acid liquors into a diarrhoea, and afterwards into a kind of lethargic insensibility; and died Jan. 10. 1754, having <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> concluded the 23rd annual collection. CAVEARE. See CAVIARE.

CAVEAT

Pages 305-305

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in the spiritual courts, to stop the proving of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, the granting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> of administration, &c. to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of another. It is also used to stop the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of a clerk to a benefice.

CAVEATING

Pages 305-305

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, is the shifting the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> from one side of that of your adversary to the other.

CAVEDO

Pages 305-305

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, equal to 27.56.4 English inches.

CAVENDISH

Pages 305-306

William, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, grandson of Sir William Cavendish, was born in 1592. In 1610, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the Bath; in 1620, raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a peer, by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Ogle, Cavendish, Ogle, and Viscount <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>; and in the third year of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Newcastle upon Tyne, and Baron Cavendish of Bolefever. He was after this made governor to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, afterwards Charles II. When the first troubles broke out in Scotland, and the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> was but indifferently provided, he contributed ten thousand pounds, and also raised a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, consisting of about two hundred knights and gentlemen, who served at their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, were commanded by the earl, and honoured with the title of the prince's troop. He had after this the command of the northern counties; and was constituted general and commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of all the forces that might be raised <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, and of several counties south of that river. He afterwards raised an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of eight thousand horse, foot, and dragoons; with which he took some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and gained several important victories. On this he was advanced to the dignity of marquis of Newcastle; but his majesty's affairs being totally ruined by the ruffians of Prince Rupert, he, with a few of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers of the army, went abroad, and stood for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where, notwithstanding the vast estate he had when the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> broke out, his circumstances were now so bad, that himself and wife were reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of pawning their clothes for a dinner. He afterwards removed to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, that he might be nearer his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and there, though under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulties, resided for several years; but, notwithstanding his distresses, he was treated, during an exile of eighteen years, with extraordinary marks of distinction. On his return to England at the Restoration, he was advanced to the dignity of earl of Ogle, and duke of Newcastle. He spent his time in a country retirement, and was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of men of merit. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> died in 1670, aged 84. He wrote a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>, which is esteemed; and some comedies, which are not. Mr Granger observes, that he was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of many accomplishments, and was much better qualified for a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; that he understood horsemanship, music, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; but was a better horseman than musician, and a better musician than poet. Cavendish, Margaret, duchess of Newcastle, famous for her voluminous productions, was born about the latter end of the reign of James I. and was the youngest sister of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lucas of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>. She married the duke of Newcastle abroad in 1645; and on their return after the Restoration, spent the remainder of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> plays, poems, with the life of her husband, to the amount of about a dozen of folios. "What gives the best idea of her unbounded <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for scribbling (says Mr Walpole), was her seldom revising the copies of her works, left, as she said, it should disturb her following conceptions. She died in 1673. Cavendish, William, the first duke of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and one of the most distinguished patriots in the British annals, was born in 1640. In 1677, being then member for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, he vigorously opposed the venal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the court; and, the following year, was one of the committee appointed to draw up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of impeachment against the lord-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Danby. In 1679, being re-elected to serve for Derby in a new <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, Charles II. thought fit to make him a privy counsellor; but he soon withdrew from the board, with his friend Lord Ruffel, when he found that Popish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> prevailed. He carried up the articles of impeachment to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, against Lord-chief-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> Scroggs, for his arbitrary and illegal proceedings in the court of king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>; and when the king declared his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> not to sign the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> for excluding the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> (afterwards James II.) he moved the house of commons, that a bill might be brought in for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of all his majesty's Protestant subjects. He also openly named the king's evil counsellors, and voted for an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to remove them from his presence and councils for ever. He nobly appeared at Lord Ruffel's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of that great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, at a time when it was scarce more criminal to be an <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a> than a witness for him. The same fortitude, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his country, animated this illustrious patriot to oppose the arbitrary proceedings of James II.; and when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> there was no other method of saving the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> from impending <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, he was the foremost in the association for inviting over the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and the first nobleman who appeared in arms to receive him at his landing.
