Be that as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, the island of Ceos became so populous, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> prevailed there, commanding all persons upwards of sixty to be poisoned, that others might be able to subsist; so that none above sixty were to be seen in the island, being obliged, after they arrived at that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, either to submit to the law, or abandon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, together with their effects. Ceos had, in former times, four famous cities, viz. Julis, Carthaea, Coreflus, and Prae-essa. The two latter were, according to Pliny, swallowed up by an earthquake. The other two flourished in Strabo's time. Carthaea stood on a rising ground, at the end of a valley, about three miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The situation of it agrees with that of the present town of Zea, which gives name to the whole island. The ruins both of Carthaea and Julis are still remaining; those of the latter take up the whole mountain, and are called by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> inhabitants Polis, that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> are the ruins of a flatly temple, with many pieces of broken pillars, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of most exquisite workmanship. The walls of the city were of marble, and some pieces are still remaining above 12 feet in length. Julis was, according to Strabo, the birthplace of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHYLIDES">Bacchylides</a>, Eratosthenes, and Aristo. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> marbles tell us, that Simonides, the son of Leopropis, invented a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, the principles of which he explained at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; and add, that he was descended of another Simonides, who was a poet no less renowned than himself. One of these two poets invented those melancholy verses which were sung at funerals, and are called by the Latins naniae. Strabo says, that the Athenians, having besieged the city of Julis, raised the siege, upon advice that the inhabitants had resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> all the children under a certain age, that useful persons might not be employed in looking after them. Ceos was, with the other Greek islands, subdued by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and bestowed upon the Athenians by Mark Antony the triumvir, together with Aegina, Tinos, and some other adjoining islands, which were all reduced to one Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> by Vespasian. The island is now called Zea.

CEPHALENIA

Pages 346-346
or CEPHALLENIA, an island of the Ionian sea, between Ithaca and Zacynthus, known in Homer's time by the names of Same and Epirus Melena, is about eighty miles in length, forty in breadth, and a hundred and thirty in compass. It had anciently four cities, one of which bore the name of the island. Strabo tells us, that in his time there were only two cities remaining; but Pliny speaks of three; adding, that the ruins of Same, which had been destroyed by the Romans, were still in being. Same was the metropolis of the island, and is supposed to have stood in the place which the Italians call Porto Guiccardo. The names of the four cities were, according to Thucydides, Same, Prone, Cranii, and Pala. This island was subdued by the Thebans, under the conduct of Amphitryon, who is said to have killed Pelopidas, who then reigned here. While Amphitryon was carrying on the war in Cephalenia, then called Samos, one Cephalus, a man of great distinction at Athens, having accidentally killed his wife Procris in shooting at a deer, fled to Amphitryon, who, pitying his case, not only received him kindly, but made him governor of the island, which henceforth was called Cephalenia. After it had been long in subjection to the Thebans, it fell under the power of the Macedonians, and was taken from them by the Aetolians, who held it till it was reduced by M. Fulvius Nobilior, who having gained the metropolis after a four months' siege, sold all the citizens for slaves, adding the whole island to the dominions of the republic. Now called CEPHALONIA.

CEPHALIC

Pages 346-346

in a general meaning, signifies anything belonging to the head. CEPHALIC Medicines, are remedies for disorders of the head. Cordials are comprehended herein, as are also whatever promotes a free circulation of the blood through the brain. Except when the disorder arises from excess of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an inflammatory disposition in the head, moist tinctures should never be used, but always dry ones. To rub the head after it is shaved proves an instantaneous cure for a cephalgia, a fluffing of the head, and a weakness of the eyes, arising from a weak and relaxed state of the fibres. And as by every fresh evacuation of the humours their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is not only lessened, but also their recreementitious parts derived thither, the more frequently the head is shaved, the larger quantity of humour is discharged; so that the frequent shaving of the head and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> is likewise a perpetual blister; and in as much as it is useful, it is a cephalic. CEPHALIC Vein, in Anatomy, creeps along the arm between the skin and the muscles, and divides it into two branches; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> goes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, where it joins the basilica, and turns up to the back of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; the internal branch, together with a small one of the basilica, makes the mediana. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used to open this vein for disorders of the head, for which reason it bears this name; but a better acquaintance with the circulation of the blood informs us that there is no foundation for such a notion.

CEPHALONIA

Pages 346-346

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name, situated in the Mediterranean, near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Epirus, and subject to the Venetians. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21. N. Lat. 30. 30.

CEPHEUS

Pages 346-346

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the northern hemisphere. See Astronomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERAM

Pages 346-347

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, between the Molucca <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and those of Ambonaya and Banda on the south, lying between E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 126. and 129. in S. Lat. 3. It is about 150 miles long, and 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and here the Dutch have have a fortress, which keeps the natives in subjection.

CERAMBYX

Pages 347-347

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects, of the beetle kind, belonging to the order of insecta coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERASTES

Pages 347-347

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Anguis and Coluber. See Ophiology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CERASTIUM

Pages 347-348

Mouse-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>.** See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **CERASUS.** See Prunus, Botany Index. **CERATE,** in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a thickish kind of ointment, applied to ulcerations, excoriations, &c. See Pharmacy Index. **CERATION,** the name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to the small seeds of ceratonia, used by the Arabian physicians as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to adjust the doses of medicines; as the grain weight with us took its rise from a grain of barley. **Ceration,** <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ceratium, was also a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, equal to one-third of an obolus. **CERATOCARPUS.** See Botany Index. **CERATONIA,** the Carob Tree, or St John's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. See Botany Index. The pods of this plant are called St John's bread, from an ill founded assertion of some writers on Scripture, that these were the locusts which St John ate with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> in the wilderness. **CERATOPHYLLUM.** See Botany Index. **CERAUNIA,** Ceraunias, or Ceraunius Lapit, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a sort of flinty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of no certain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, but of a pyramidal or wedge-like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; popularly supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>-storms, and to be possessed of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> notable virtues, as promoting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, preserving from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, &c. The word is from the Greek θύρανος, thunderbolt. The ceraunia is the same with what is otherwise called the thunder-stone, or thunder-bolt; and also sometimes sagitta or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>'s head, on account of its shape. The ceraunia are frequently confounded with the ombrice and brontiae, as being all supposed to have the same origin. The generality of naturalists take the ceraunia for a native stone, formed among the pyrites, of a saline, concrete, mineral juice. Mercatus and Dr Woodward assert it to be <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, and to have been fashioned thus by tools. The ceraunia, according to these authors, are the heads of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> weapons of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; which, upon the introduction of that metal, growing into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a>, were dispersed in the fields through this and the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Some of them had possibly served in the early ages for axes, others for wedges, others for chisels; but the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> for arrow-heads, darts, and lances. The ceraunia is also held by Pliny for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or crystal coloured gem, that attracted lightning in itself. What this was, is hard to say. Prudentius also speaks of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> ceraunia; by which he is supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a> or pyropus. **CERBERA.** See Botany Index. **CERBERUS,** in fabulous history, a dreadful three-headed mastiff, born of Typhon and Echidna, and placed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the gates of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. He fawned upon those who entered, but devoured all who attempted to get back. He was, however, mastered by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, who dragged him up to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, when, in struggling, a foam dropped from his mouth, which produced the poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> called aconite or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>'s bane. Some have supposed that Cerberus is the symbol of the earth, or of all-devouring time; and that its three mouths represent the present, past, and future. The victory obtained by Hercules over this monster denotes the conquest which this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> acquired over his passions. Dr Bryant supposes that Cerberus was the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and that it signified the temple of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>; deriving it from Kir Alor, the place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. This temple was called also Tor-Caph-El, which was changed to τερκαπλος; and hence Cerberus was supposed to have had three heads. It was likewise called Tor-Keren, Turris Regia; whence τρικεφαλος, from τρεις, three, and κεφαλη, head. **CERCLE,** in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> cercle is a cross which, opening at the ends, turns round both ways like a ram's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. See Cross. **CERCIS,** the Judas tree. See Botany Index. **CERCOPITHECI,** in Natural History, the name given by Mr Ray to monkeys, or the clats of apes with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> tails. See Simia, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. **CERDA,** JOHN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">LEWIS</a> DE LA, a learned Jesuit of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, wrote <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> commentaries on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, which have been much esteemed; also several other works. He died in 1643, aged 80. **CERDONIANS,** ancient heretics, who maintained most of the errors of Simon Magus, Saturninus, and the Manichæes. They took their name from their leader Cerdon, a Syrian, who came to Rome in the time of Pope Hyginus, and there abjured his errors; but in appearance only; for he was afterwards convicted of perfuming in them, and accordingly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> again. Cerdon asserted two principles, the one good and the other evil; this last, according to him, was the creator of the world, and the god that appeared under the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The first, whom he called unknown, was the father of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; who, he taught, was incarnate only in appearance, and was not born of a virgin; nor did he suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> but in appearance. He denied the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, and rejected all the books of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, as coming from an evil principle. Marcion, his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, succeeded him in his errors. **CEREALIA,** in antiquity, feasts of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, instituted by Triptolemus, son of Celeus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Eleusine in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for his having been instructed by Ceres, who was supposed to have been his nurse, in the art of cultivating corn and making bread. There were two feasts of this kind at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; the one called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSINIA">Eleusinia</a>, the other Thesmophoria. See the article Eleusinia. What both agreed in, and was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all the cerealia, was, that they were celebrated with a world of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and purity; so that it was deemed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pollution to meddle, on those days, in conjugal matters. It was not Ceres alone that was honoured here, but also <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The victims offered were hogs, by reason of the waste they make in the products of the earth: whether there was any wine offered or not, is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of much debate among the critics. Plautus and Macrobius seem to countenance the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> side; Cato and Virgil the positive. Macrobius says, indeed, they did not offer wine to Ceres, but xviilum, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of wine and honey boiled up together: that the fa- CER crifice made on the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> and Hercules, was a pregnant fow, together with cakes and mullum; and that this is what Virgil means by Mili Baccho. The cerealia passed from the Greeks to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who held them for eight days successively; commencing, as generally held, on the fifth of the ides of April. It was the women alone who were concerned in the celebration, all dressed in white; the men, likewise in white, were only spectators. They ate nothing till after sunset; in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Ceres, who in her search after her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> took no repast but in the evening. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae, the defolation was so great at Rome, that there were no women to celebrate the feast, by reason they were all in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; so that it was omitted that year. CEREA利亚, in Botany, from Ceres, the goddess of corn; Linnaeus's name for the larger <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESCULENT">esculent</a> seeds of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>; these are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, wheat, rye, barley, oats, millet, panic grass, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> millet, holcus, zizania, and maize. To this head may be likewise referred darnel (clodium); which, by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, is rendered esculent.

CEREBRUM

Pages 348-348

the Brain. Its structure and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> are not so fully known as some other parts of the body; and different authors consider it in various manners. However, according to the observations of those most famed for their accuracy and dexterity in anatomical inquiries, its general structure is as given in Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Dr Hunter observes, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of the medullary substance of the brain in idiots and madmen, such as the thalami nervorum opticorum, and medulla oblongata, are found entirely changed from a medullary to a hard, tough, dark-colored substance, sometimes resembling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONIAL">CEREMONIAL</a> (ceremoniale) a book in which is prescribed the order of the ceremonies to be observed in certain actions and occasions of solemnity and pomp. The ceremonial of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is called ordo Romanus. It was published in 1516 by the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORCYRA">Corcyra</a>; at which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of cardinals were so scandalized, that some of them voted to have the author as well as book burnt, for his temerity in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the sacred ceremonies to the eyes of profane people.

CEREMONIAL

Pages 348-348

in a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes the manner in which princes and ambassadors used to receive and to treat one another. There are endless disputes among sovereigns about the ceremonial: some endeavouring to be on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, and others to be superior; inasmuch that numerous schemes have been proposed for settling them. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> are, 1. To accommodate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> by compromise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alternation; so that one shall precede now, the other the next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; or one in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the other in another: 2. By seniority; so that an elder <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in years shall precede a younger, without any other distinction. These expedients, however, have not yet been accepted by any, except some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> princes, as they are called, in Germany. CEREMONIAL is more particularly used in speaking of the laws and regulations given by Moses relating to the worship of God among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews. In this sense it amounts to much the same with what is called the Levitical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and stands contradistinguished from the moral as well as judicial law.

CEREMONY

Pages 348-348

an assemblage of several actions, forms, and circumstances, serving to render a thing more magnificent and solemn. In 1646, M. Ponce published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ceremonies, tracing the rise, growth, and introduction of each rite into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and its gradual advancement to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> therein. Many of them were borrowed from Judaism; but more seemingly from Paganism. Dr Middleton has given a fine discourse on the conformity between the Pagan and Popish ceremonies, which he exemplifies in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of incense, holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, lamps, and candles, before the shrines of saints, votive gifts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> offerings round the shrines of the deceased, &c. In effect, the altars, images, crosses, processions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, and legends; nay, even the very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>, pontificate, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders, &c., of the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, he shows, are all copied from their heathen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>.—We have an ample and magnificent account of the religious ceremonies and customs of all nations in the world, represented in figures designed by Picart, with historical explanations, and many curious dissertations. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of the CEREMONIES, an officer instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I., for the more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reception of ambassadors and strangers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. He wears about his neck a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with a medal under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, having on one side an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of peace, with this motto, Beati pacifici; and on the other, an emblem of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, with Dieu et mon droit; his salary is 300l. per annum. Assistant Master of the CEREMONIES, is to execute the employment in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, whensoever the master of the ceremonies is absent. His salary is 14l. 13s. 4d. per annum. Marshal of the CEREMONIES, is their officer, being subordinate to them both. His salary is 100l. per annum.

CERENZA

Pages 348-348

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, with a bishop's see. It is seated on a rock, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 5' N. Lat. 39° 23'.

CERES

Pages 348-349

a pagan deity, the inventor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of corn; in like manner as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> was of wine. According to the poets, she was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Ops, and the mother of Proserpine, whom she had by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. Pluto having stolen away Proserpine, Ceres travelled all over the world in quest of her daughter, by the help of a torch, which she had lighted in Mount Aetna. As Ceres was thus travelling in search of her daughter, she came to Celeus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, and undertook to bring up his infant son Triptolemus. Being desirous to render her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> immortal, she fed him in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and in the night covered him with fire. Celeus observing an unusual improvement in his son, resolved to watch his nurse. to which end he hid himself in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> where she used to cover the child with fire: but when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> her put the infant under the embers, he cried out and discovered himself. Ceres punished the curiosity and indiscretion of the father with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Afterwards she taught the youth the art of sowing corn and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and mounted him in a chariot drawn by winged dragons, that he might <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the world, and teach mankind the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of corn and fruits. After this, having discovered, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Arethusa, that Proserpine was in the infernal regions, she applied to Jupiter, and obtained of him that Proserpine should be restored, on condition that she had tasted nothing during her stay in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: but it being discovered, by the information of Ascalaphus, that, as she was walking in Pluto's orchard, she had gathered an apple, and had tasted of some of the seeds, she was forever forbidden to return. Ceres, out of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, turned Ascalaphus into an owl. At length, Jupiter, to mitigate her grief, permitted that Proserpine should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> one half of the year in the infernal regions with Pluto, and the other half with her mother on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Cicero speaks of a temple of Ceres at Catanea in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, where was a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statue of that goddess, but entirely concealed from the sight of men, everything being performed by matrons and virgins.

CERET

Pages 349-349

a town of France in Roussillon, with a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of a single <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>. It is seated near the river Tec, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 46. N. Lat. 42. 23.

CERIGO

Pages 349-349

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, anciently called Cytherea; noted for being the birthplace of Helen, and, as the poets say, of Venus. At present there is nothing very delightful in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is mountainous, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> dry. It abounds in hares, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUAIL">quail</a>, turtle, and excellent falcons. It is about 50 miles in circumference, and had formerly good <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; but there is now none remaining but that which gives name to the island. This is strong both by art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, it being seated on a craggy rock. The inhabitants are Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and subject to the Venetians, who keep a governor there, whom they change every two years.

CERINES

Pages 349-349

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, with a good castle, a harbour, and a bishop's see. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 33. 35. N. Lat. 35. 22.

CERINTHIANS

Pages 349-349
ancient heretics, who denied the deity of Jesus Christ.—They took their name from Cerinthus, one of the first heresiarchs in the church, being contemporary with St John. See CERINTHUS. They believed that Jesus Christ was a mere man, born of Joseph and Mary; but that, in his baptism, a celestial virtue descended on him in form of a dove; by means whereof he was consecrated by the Holy Spirit, and made Christ. It was by means of this celestial virtue, therefore, that he wrought so many miracles; which, as he received it from heaven, quitted him after his passion, and returned to the place whence it came; so that Jesus, whom they called a pure man, really died, and rose again; but that Christ, who was distinguished from Jesus, did not suffer at all. It was partly to refute this fact that St John wrote his gospel. They received the gospel of St Matthew, to countenance their doctrine of circumcision, from Christ's being circumcised; but they omitted the genealogy. They discarded the epistles of St Paul, because that apostle held circumcision abolished.

CERINTHUS

Pages 349-349

a heresiarch, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with the apostles, ascribed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> not to God, but to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. He taught that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, and that circumcision ought to be retained under the gospel. He is looked upon as the head of the converted Jews, who raised in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Antioch the tumult of which St Luke has given the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the 15th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Acts. Some authors ascribe the book of the Apocalypse to Cerinthus; adding, that he put it off under the name of St John, the better to authorize his reveries touching Christ's reign upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>: and it is even certain that he published some works of this kind under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Apocalypse. See APOCALYPSE. CEROPEGIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

CERTHIA

Pages 349-349

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, the Creeper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> OX-EYE, a genus belonging to the order of picae. See ORNITHOLOGY.

CERTIFICATE

Pages 349-350
Trial by, in the law of England, a species of trial allowed in such cases where the evidence of the person certifying is the only proper criterion of the point in dispute*. For when the fact in question lies out of the cognizance of the court, the judges must rely on the solemn averment or information of persons in such a station as affords them the most clear and competent knowledge of the truth. As Blackstone therefore such evidence, if given to a jury, must have been conclusive, the law, to save trouble and circuitry, permits the fact to be determined upon such certificate merely. Thus, 1. If the issue be whether A was absent with the king in his army out of the realm in time of war, this shall be tried by the certificate of the marshal of the king's host in writing under his seal, which shall be sent to the justices. 2. If, in order to avoid an outlawry, or the like, it was alleged that the defendant was in prison, ultra mare, at Bordeaux, or in the service of the mayor of Bordeaux, this should have been tried by the certificate of the mayor, and the like of the captain of Calais. But when this was law, those towns were under the dominion of the crown of England. And therefore, by a parity of reason, it should now hold, that in similar cases arising at Jamaica or Minorca, the trial should be by certificate from the governor of those islands. We also find that the certificate of the queen's messengers, sent to summon home a prelate of the realm, was formerly held a sufficient trial of the contempt in refusing to obey such summons. 3. For matters within the realm; the customs of the city of London shall be tried by the certificate of the mayor and aldermen, certified by the mouth of their recorder, upon a summons from the party alleging it, that the custom ought to be thus tried; else it must be tried by the country: As, the custom of distributing the effects of freemen deceased; of enrolling apprentices, or that he who is free of one trade may use another; if any of these, or other similar points come in issue. 4. The trial of all customs and practice of the courts shall be by certificate from the proper officers of those courts respectively. CERTIFICATE and when returned was made on a writ by the sheriff or under sheriff, shall be only tried by his own certificate.

CERTIORARI

Pages 350-350

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ which issues out of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, directed to an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to call up the records of a cause there depending, in order that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> may be done. And this writ is obtained upon complaint, that the party who seeks it has received hard usage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is not likely to have an impartial <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in the inferior court. A certiorari is made returnable either in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, or in chancery. It is not only used out of the court of chancery, but likewise out of the king's bench; in which last mentioned court it lies where the king would be certified of a record. Indictments from inferior courts, and proceedings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions of the peace, may also be removed into the king's bench by a certiorari: and here the very record must be returned, and not a transcript of it; thought usually in chancery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a certiorari be returnable there, it removes only the tenor of the record.

CERTITUDE

Pages 350-350

considered in the things <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> which are the objects of our understanding, is a necessary agreement or disagreement of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our knowledge with another: as applied to the mind, it is the perception of such agreement or disagreement; or such a firm well-grounded assent, as excludes not only all manner of doubt, but all conceivable possibility of a mistake. There are three sorts of certitude, or assurance, according to the different natures and circumstances of things. 1. A physical or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> certitude, which depends upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; so that I see such or such a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, or hear such or such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; nobody questions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this, where the organs, the medium, and the object, are rightly disposed. 2. Mathematical certitude, is that arising from mathematical evidence; such as, that the three <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of a triangle are equal to two <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ones. 3. Moral certitude is that founded on moral evidence, and is frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a mathematical one; as that there was formerly such an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> as Julius Cæsar, and that he wrote the commentaries which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under his name; because the historians of these times have recorded it, and no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has ever disproved it since: this affords a moral certitude, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sense so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that one would be thought a fool or madman for denying it.

CERTOSA

Pages 350-350

a celebrated Carthusian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, in the territory of the Pavese, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, four miles from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>: its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a> is surrounded with a wall 20 miles in circumference; but there are several small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages therein. CERVANTES. See SAAVEDRA.

CERUMEN

Pages 350-350

a thick, viscid, bitter, excrementitious humour, separated from the blood by proper glands placed in the meatus auditorius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> outer passage of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>.

CERUS

Pages 350-350
WHITE LEAD, a sort of calx of lead made by exposing plates of that metal to the vapour of vinegar. See Chemistry Index. Ceruss as a medicine, is used externally, either mixed in ointments or by sprinkling in on old gleeting and watery ulcers, and in many diseases of the skin. If, when it is reduced into a fine powder, it is received with the breath in inspiration, and carried down into the lungs, it causes incurable asthmas. Instances of the very pernicious effects of this metal are too often seen among those persons who work lead in any form, but particularly among the workers in white lead. The painters use it in great quantities; and that it may be afforded cheap to them, it is generally adulterated with common whitening.

CERVA

Pages 350-350

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in Romagna, with a bishop's see, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 5. N. Lat. 44. 16.

CERVERA

Pages 350-350

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in Catalonia, seated on a small river of the same name, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 9. N. Lat. 41. 28.

CERVICAL NERVES

Pages 350-350

are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of nerves, so called, as having their origin in the cervix, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> neck.

CERVICAL VESSELS

Pages 350-350

among anatomists, denote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, veins, &c. which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the vertebrae and muscles of the neck up to the skull.

CERVIX

Pages 350-350

in Anatomy, properly denotes the hind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck; as contradistinguished from the fore part, which is called jugulum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the throat. CERVIX of the Scapula, denotes the head of the shoulder blade, or that upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> whose sinus receives the head of the humerus. CERVIX of the Uterus, the neck of the uterus, or that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> canal or passage between the internal and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> orifices, which receives and encloses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> like a fleath, whence it is also called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">Vagina</a>.

CERVUS

Pages 350-350
or DEER, in Zoology, a genus of quadrupeds belonging to the order of Pecora. See MAMMALIA Index. SERVUS Volans, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History, a name given by authors to the stag-fly, or horned beetle, a very large species of beetle with horns flopped, and something like those of the stag.

CERYX

Pages 350-350

in antiquity. The ceryces were a sort of public crier appointed to proclaim <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> publish things aloud in assemblies. The ceryx among the Greeks answered to the praeco among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Our criers have only a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their office and authority. There were two kinds of ceryces, civil and sacred. The former were those appointed to call assemblies, and make silence therein; also to go on messages, and do the office of our heralds, &c. The sacred ceryces were a sort of priests, whose office was to proclaim silence in the public games and sacrifices, publish the names of the conquerors, proclaim feasts, and the like. The priesthood of the ceryces was annexed to a particular family, the descendants of Ceryx, son of Eumolpus. To them it also belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> solemn victims to slaughter. Before the ceremonies began, they called silence in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, by the formula, Ευφραντεῖς ὁρᾶτε πρὸς τὸ λέγειν; answered to the favete linguis of the Romans. When the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was over, they dismissed the people with this formula, Δαιμῶν αὐτοῖς, Ἰε, μῆλα εἰ.

CESARE

Pages 350-350

among logicians, one of the modes of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of syllogisms; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> proposition of which is an universal affirmative, and the other two universal negatives: thus, CE No immoral books ought to be read; SA But every obscene book is immoral; RE Therefore no obscene books ought to be read.

CESENNA

Pages 350-351
CESENA, a town of Romagna in Italy, with a bishop's see, subject to the pope, and situated on the river Savio, in E. Long. 12° 46'. N. Lat. 44° 8'. CESPITOSÆ PLANTÆ (from cespæ, turf or sod), are those plants which produce many stems from one root, and thence form a close thick carpet on the surface of the earth. CESPITOSÆ Paludes, turf bogs.

CESSATION

Pages 351-351

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of intermitting, discontinuing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> interrupting, the course of any thing, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, or the like. CESSATION of Arms, an armistice or occasional truce. See Truce. When the commander of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> finds things reduced to an extremity, so that he must either surrender, or sacrifice the garrison and inhabitants to the mercy of the enemy, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>, or beats the chamade; on which a cessation of arms and hostilities commences, to give room for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>.

CESSIO BONORUM

Pages 351-351

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the name of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> by which an insolvent debtor may apply for liberation from prison, upon making over his whole real and personal estate to his creditors.

CESSION

Pages 351-351

in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is when an ecclesiastical person is created a bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> when a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> takes another benefice, without dispensation, or being otherwise qualified. In both these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> their first benefices became void by cession, without any resignation; and to these livings that the person had, who was created bishop, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> may present for that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whoever is patron of them; and in the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the patron may present: but by dispensation of remainder, a bishop may retain some or all the preferments he was entitled to before he was made bishop.

CESTUI

Pages 351-351

a French word, signifying he <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> him, frequently used in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> writings. Thus, Cestui qui trust, a person who has lands, &c., committed to him for the benefit of another; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such person does not perform his trust, he is compellable to it in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. Cestui qui vie, one for whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> any lands, &c., are granted. Cestui qui ufe, a person to whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> any one is inclosed of lands or tenements. Formerly the feoffees to ufe were deemed owners of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but now the possession is adjudged in cestui qui ufe.

CESTUS

Pages 351-351

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, a fine embroidered girdle said to be worn by Venus, to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> ascribes the power of charming and conciliating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. The word is also written cestium and ceston: it comes from κεστος, a girdle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other thing embroidered or wrought with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>; derived, according to Servius, from κεστον, pungere; whence also incestus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used at first for any indecency by undoing the girdle, &c., but now restrained to that between persons near akin. See <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-INCEST">Incest</a>.

CETACEOUS

Pages 351-351

an appellation given to the fishes of the whale kind. See Cetology.

CETERACH

Pages 351-351

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Asplenium. See Asplenium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CETOLOGY

Pages 387-388
Sense of seeing, 166 Sucking, mode of 166 T. Teeth, 112-114 U. Unicorn-fish, 53-60 Ureter, 139 W.
