Cape of Good Hope a convenient station for, Dutch early engaged in, extent of their, ships employed and produce of it from 1661 to 1788, 220 Attempt of the French to revive, other nations engage in, time of the, mode practised by the Europeans, by the people of Kamchatka, their previous ceremonies, by the people of the Kurile islands, of Iceland, of Greenland, Astonishing mode by the Floridan Indians,

CETUS

Pages 388-388

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the whale; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> constellation of the southern hemisphere, under Piscis, and next the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUARIUS">Aquarius</a>. The stars in the constellation Cetus, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are twenty-two; in Tycho's twenty-one; in Hevelius's forty-five; in the Britannic catalogue ninety-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. Cetus is represented by the poets as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-monster which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the nymphs, sent to devour <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of her mother, and which was killed by Perseus. In the mandible of Cetus is a variable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> which appears and disappears periodically, passing through the several degrees of magnitude, both increasing and diminishing, in about 333 days. See ASTRONOMY.

CEU CETTE

Pages 388-388

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, seated at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were the canal of Languedoc begins, between Montpelier and Agde, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Maguelona, in the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 15' N. Lat. 43° 25'.

CEUTA

Pages 388-388

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of Barbary in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, seated on the straits of Gibraltar, opposite that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 25' N. Lat. 36° 35'. John <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> took it from the Moors in 1415, but it now belongs to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. In 1697, it sustained a vigorous siege by the Moors.

CEVENNES

Pages 388-388
mountains of Languedoc in France, remarkable for the frequent meetings of the Protestants there as a place of security against the tyranny of their governors. In Queen Anne's reign there was an attempt made to assist them by an English fleet in the Mediterranean; but no purpose, for the French had occupied the passages.

CEYLON

Pages 388-393

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the East Indies, which lies between 5° 40' and 10° 30' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude; and between 79° and 82° east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is situated at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, by which it is bounded on the north. On the north-west it is separated from the Coromandel <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Mannar, a narrow strait full of shoals, and impassable by large ships; and is distant about 60 leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Comorin, the southern point of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. Its circumference is computed to be about 900 miles; and its length from Point Pedro at the northern extremity to Dondarhead at the southern is about 300 miles. Its breadth is very unequal, being in some parts only from 40 to 50 miles, while in others it extends to 60, 70, and even 100. The appearance of the eastern coast is bold and rocky, and a few reefs of rocks run out into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the south-east between Point de Galle and Batocolo. The deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on the eastern shores admits the approach of the largest vessels in safety; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that side of the island be the least fertile, its other defects are amply compensated by the harbours of Trincomalee and Batocolo. The north and north-west coast from Point Pedro to Columbo is flat, and everywhere indented with inlets of the sea. The largest of them extends almost quite across the island from Mullipati to Jafnapatam on the north-west point of the island; and forms the peninsula of Jafnapatam. Several of these inlets form small harbours. The interior of the island abounds with steep and lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, covered with thick forests, and full of of almost impenetrable jungles. The woods and mountains completely surround the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDY">Candy</a>, and seem destined by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to defend him against those foreign enemies, whose superior skill and power have deprived him of the open tracts on the sea-coast. The most lofty range of mountains divides the island nearly into two parts, and so completely separates them from each other, that both the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> and seasons on either side are essentially different. These mountains also obstruct completely the effect of the monsoons, which set in periodically from opposite sides of them; so that not only the opposite sea-coast, but the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the interior, suffers very little from these storms. The monsoons in Ceylon are connected with those on the Coromandel and Malabar coasts; but they set in much sooner on the western than the eastern side of the island. On the west side, where Columbo lies, the rains prevail in the months of May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the season when they are felt on the Malabar coast. This monsoon is usually extremely violent, being accompanied with dreadful storms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, together with vast torrents of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and violent south-west winds. During its continuance, the northern parts of the island are very little affected, and are even generally dry. In the months of October and November, when the opposite monsoon sets in on the Coromandel coast, it is the north of Ceylon which is affected, and scarcely any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of it is felt in the southern parts. These monsoons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> slightly over the interior, and seldom occasion any considerable inconvenience. But this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island is not altogether freed from the dreadful storms which so terribly ravage the tropical climates. During its own periodical season, which happens in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and April, the rain pours <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in torrents, and the thunder and lightning are terrible. From the situation of this island, so near the equator, the days and nights are nearly of equal length; the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> during the two seasons not exceeding 15 minutes. The seasons are more regulated by the monsoons than the course of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; for although the island lies to the north of the line, the coolest season is during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice, while the western monsoon prevails. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> commences in October; and the hottest season is from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> to the beginning of April. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, is nearly the same throughout the whole year; the rainy season, however, renders the nights much cooler, from the dampness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the prevalence of winds during the monsoons. The climate, upon the whole, is much more temperate than on the continent of India. This temperate climate, however, is chiefly confined to the coast where the sea-breezes have room to circulate. In the interior of the country, owing to the thick and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> woods, and the hills which crowd upon each other, the heat is many degrees greater than on the sea-coast, and the climate often extremely sultry and unhealthy. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> harbours in the island for large ships are Trincomalee and Point de Gallo; they also come to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, and at certain seasons of the year moor securely, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> of Columbo. There are several other inferior ports round the island, which afford shelter to the smaller <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> vessels. The two principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Malivagonga and the Mulivaddy. The former takes its rise among the hills to the south-east of Candy, and nearly surrounds that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. After a variety of circuitous windings among the mountains, it at last discharges itself into the sea at Trincomalee. This river is so deep as to be fordable only towards the source; but the rocks, which everywhere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> its course, prevent it from being navigated. The Mulivaddy rises from the foot of a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, known to Europeans by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>'s Peak, and situated about sixty miles to the north-east of Columbo. This river falls into the sea by several branches: the largest of these empties itself about three miles from the fort of Columbo, after having nearly surrounded a large tract of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> country, of which it forms a peninsula. Besides the rivers with which Ceylon abounds, there are many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> communicating with them, particularly in the neighbourhood of Columbo and Nigumbu. They are often of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> utility to the inhabitants in their neighbourhood, who have thus an opportunity of readily transporting their several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of trade; and it is by this means also that the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the coast are supplied with the greatest abundance of fresh-water fish. The internal communications by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> through the island have scarcely passed the first stage of improvement. Along the sea-coasts indeed there are roads and stations for travellers: but these roads are in many places rugged and steep. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, with a small mixture of clay. In the south-west parts, particularly about Columbo, there is a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of marshy ground very rich and productive. This tract, however, is chiefly occupied with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> plantations, and the rest of the island, in its present state of cultivation, does not produce a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> for the consumption of its inhabitants. Ceylon was originally divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of distinct petty kingdoms, separated by the several rivers and mountains which are dispersed over the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the island, and subject each to its own independent sovereign. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, the whole country was reduced under the dominion of the king of Candy, and divided by him into a few great provinces, from which several of the numerous titles he still retains were derived. These provinces were Candy, Coitu, Matura, Dambadar, and Sittivacca, which included the rich districts on the west coast. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of these provinces was Candy, situated in the centre of the island, and honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence. The king holds his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> there to this day; and though all the other provinces have been more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less encroached upon, no part of Candy has ever been reduced to permanent subjection under a foreign power. The great divisions of the island now are reduced to two; the one comprehending those parts under the dominion of Europeans, and the other those which still remain to the natives. Little was known of the island of Ceylon previous to the arrival of the Portuguese in 1505, who were admitted by the king of the country in a friendly manner, and received from him an annual tribute for their protection against <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> invasion, particularly against the attacks of the Arabs, who had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> harried and opprested oppressed the Ceylonese. The inhabitants at that time, as at present, consisted of two distinct races, the Bedahs, who lived in the forests, particularly in the northern parts, and the Cingalese, who inhabited the sea coast. Columbo, now the European <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> at Ceylon, was at that time the royal residence. Cinnamon was even then the chief product and staple commodity of the country. Two hundred and fifty thousand pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> were annually delivered by the king to the Portuguese in name of tribute. The inhabitants suffered great cruelties and oppression under the Portuguese, and were glad of an opportunity of throwing off the yoke and putting themselves under the protection of the Dutch. In 1632, a strong armament was sent out by the latter to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with the native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and, after a bloody struggle, the Portuguese were at last expelled from the island. Columbo surrendered to the Dutch arms in 1656, and this terminated the dominion of the Portuguese in the island. In the year 1795, a body of British troops was sent for the conquest of Ceylon, and after various <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations, this valuable possession was added to the British colonies. The chief towns in Ceylon are Trincomalee and Columbo. Trincomalee lies in latitude $8^\circ 30'$. It runs in a north-east <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> along one branch of the bay. The country around it is mountainous and woody; the soil uncultivated and rather barren, and the whole appearance wild. Trincomalee, from its situation and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, is naturally strong. It occupies more ground than Columbo, but contains a much smaller number of houses, and those inferior in size and appearance to those which are to be met with in several towns on the south-west coast. The circumference of Trincomalee, within the walls, is about three miles; within this space is also included a hill or rising point, immediately over the sea, and covered with brushwood. The fort is strong, and commands the principal bays; and, in particular, the entrance into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> harbour, or inner bay, which affords at all seasons, and in every variety of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, a secure shelter to ships of all descriptions, being land-locked on all sides, and sufficiently deep and capacious to receive any number of the largest vessels. This harbour, from its nature and situation, is that which stamps Ceylon one of our most valuable acquisitions in the East Indies. As soon as the violent monsoons commence, every vessel which is caught by them in any other part of the bay of Bengal, is obliged immediately to put to sea to prevent inevitable destruction. At these seasons Trincomalee and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> alone, of all the ports on the different coasts of the peninsula of India, are capable of affording a safe retreat. The incalculable advantages to be derived from such a harbour, are increased by its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> and easy access to our settlements in the bay of Bengal. Columbo is the capital of Ceylon and the seat of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Although Trincomalee, on account of its situation and harbour, be of more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to retain, yet Columbo in every other respect is greatly superior. The number of its inhabitants is much greater; its fort and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> town are much larger; the country where it is situated is far more fertile, and the rich district depending upon it much wider, being not less than 20 leagues in length, and 10 in breadth. It is situated in the west, or rather towards the south-west part of the island, in about $7^\circ$ north latitude and $78^\circ$ east longitude from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of Columbo is regular. It is nearly divided into four equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> by two principal streets, which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> each other, and extend the whole length of the town. To these, smaller ones run <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, with connecting lanes between them. At the foot of the ramparts on the inside is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> street or way, which goes round the whole fort, and communicates with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>' barracks; and also affords, at the different <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, open spaces for their private parading. Beside the European inhabitants of Ceylon, the natives are quite distinct from each other in manners and civilization. The Cingalese, who inhabit the low lands and parts contiguous to the coasts, live entirely under the dominion of whatever European nation has been able to acquire possession of that part of the island. The nature of the country they inhabit indeed leaves them hardly any alternative but unconditional submission, unless they could either meet the Europeans in open <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, or consent to quit their plentiful fields for the barren mountains of the interior. They are a quiet, inoffensive people; exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, temperate, and frugal. Their bodies partake of the indolence of their minds, and it is with reluctance they are roused to any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> exertion. When, however, they are obliged to apply themselves to any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, such as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, they are capable of undergoing a great deal of labour. The milder virtues form the most prominent features of the Cingalese character. They are gentle, charitable, and friendly, and have scarcely any of the false, treacherous, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> arts which are often found among the Canarians. With much less smoothness and courtlyness of face and manner than the latter, they have much finerer hearts. On examining the countenances and carriage of these two classes of Ceylonese, it is easy to perceive the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arising from the respective circumstances in which they are placed. The countenance of the Canarian is erect, his look haughty, his mein lofty, and his whole carriage marked by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of independence. The looks of the Cingalese even denote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of effeminacy and cowardice, which excites the contempt of the Canarians; although the latter, with all their boasted spirit, can never venture to attack an European but by the tame method as the Cingalese, and are equally cautious in waiting the convenient moment of assaulting him from the bushes, in which they have concealed themselves. The most singular part of the inhabitants of Ceylon are the Bedahs or Vaddahs. The origin of the Bedahs or Vaddahs, who inhabit the deep forest recesses of the Ceylonese forests, has never been traced, as no other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> can be found in the eastern world which corresponds with them. Conjecture has, indeed, been busy on the occasion, as it usually is where real information is wanting. The Bedahs are generally supposed to have been the aboriginal inhabitants of the island, who, upon being overwhelmed by their Cingalese invaders, preferred the independence of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> to a tame submission. A current <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, how- ever, assigns them a different origin. It is related that they were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away on the island, and chose to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there; but refusing, upon a certain occasion, to assist the king in his wars against some foreign enemies, they were driven out from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of the natives, and forced to take up their abode in the most unfrequented forests. Some imagine that the Bedahs are merely a part of the native Candians, who chose to retain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> savage freedom, when their brethren of the plains and valleys submitted to the cultivation of the earth, and the restraints of society. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> rests entirely on those Bedahs, who are most known, speaking a broken dialect of the Cingalese. It is, however, by no means ascertained that this is the universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Bedahs; nor is any account of their origin supported by the slightest shadow of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Among the animals of Ceylon, and at the head of the class of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, is the elephant, which is considered as superior to those found in any other part of the world. The oxen are of very small size, scarcely exceeding that of calves of a year old. They are of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> which have the hump on the shoulder; but are inferior in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as well as in size, to any found on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> continent. The beef is sometimes of a good quality, and forms the chief food of the European soldiers. Buffaloes are found in great numbers in the island, both in a wild and tame state. They are wild and untractable; and even when tamed and trained to the draught, for which, being stronger and larger than the oxen, they are well adapted, they retain a good deal of their original manners. A variety of deer and elks are found in Ceylon; especially the gazelle, a very small species, about the size of our hare, which is caught by the natives and brought to market in cages, where they are sold for about 1s. piece. Hares, similar to the European, abound in every part of the island; a small species of tyger, the tyger cat, the leopard, the jackal, porcupines, racoons, squirrels, and sometimes, but rarely, the hyena and the bear, are found in Ceylon. Birds, insects, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, and other reptiles, such as are usually to be met with in the larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Indian ocean, or on the neighbouring continent, are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> on this island. Ceylon abounds in all the vegetables and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> which are found within the tropical regions. But among the vegetable productions of Ceylon, the most valuable, and what may be reckoned the staple commodity of the island, is the cinnamon. The principal woods, or gardens, as they are called, where the cinnamon is procured, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the neighbourhood of Columbo. The grand garden near the town is so extensive as to occupy a tract of country from 10 to 15 miles in length, and stretching along from the north-east to the south of the district. Nature has here concentrated both the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the island. Nothing can be more delightful to the eye than the prospect which stretches around Columbo. The low cinnamon trees which cover the plain allow the view to reach the groves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, interspersed with tall clumps, and bounded everywhere with extensive ranges of cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a> and other large trees. The whole is diversified with small lakes and green marshes, skirted all around with rice and pasture fields. In one part the intertwining cinnamon trees appear completely to clothe the face of the plain; in another, the openings made by the intersecting footpaths <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> serve to show that the thick underwood has been penetrated. The soil best adapted for the growth of the cinnamon is a loose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> land. Such is the soil of the cinnamon gardens around Columbo, as well as in many parts around Nigumbo and Cultura, where this spice is found of the same superior quality. Of late years little is procured from the interior; and what is brought thence is coarser and thicker in the appearance, and of a hot pungent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. As this spice constitutes the wealth of Ceylon, great pains are taken to ascertain its quality, and to propagate the choicest kinds. The prime sort, and that which grows in the gardens around Columbo, is procured from the *Laurus cinnamomum*. This is a tree of a small size, from four to ten feet in height: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> is slender, and like several of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, a number of branches and twigs shoot out from it on every side. The wood is soft, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and porous, in appearance much resembling that of our oifer; and when barked it is chiefly fit for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, to which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> converted. It is, however, sometimes sawed into planks, and manufactured into caddies and other pieces of furniture; but its scent does not secure it from the attacks of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. The cinnamon tree produces a species of fruit resembling an acorn, but not so large, which ripens about the latter end of autumn, and is gathered by the natives for the purpose of extracting the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The process they employ is to bruise the fruit, boil it, and skim off the oil: this they use for their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and body on great occasions, and also for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> in their lamps. When mixed with cocoa-nut oil, it gives extremely good light. The kings of Candy use it for this purpose, and formerly commanded their subjects to bring them a certain quantity as a yearly tribute. When any ambassadors are sent to these princes, they always burn this oil during the time of audience. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-fishery in the bay of Condatchy, during the season, exhibits one of the most interesting scenes in Ceylon. The banks, where it is carried on, extend several miles along the coast from Manar southward, off Arippo, Condatchy, and Poo-pario. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> is opposite to Condatchy, and lies out at sea about 20 miles. The first step, previous to the commencement of the fishery, is to have the different oyster banks surveyed, the state of the oysters ascertained, and a report made on the subject to government. If it has been found that the quantity is sufficient, and that they are arrived at a proper degree of maturity, the particular banks to be fished that year are put up for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> to the highest bidder, and are usually purchased by a black merchant. Government sometimes judges it more advantageous to fish the banks on its own account, and to dispose of the pearls afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. When this plan is adopted, boats are hired for the season on account of government, from different quarters; the price varies considerably, according to circumstances; but is usually from 500 to 800 pagodas for each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>. As neither the season, nor the convenience of the persons attending, would permit the whole of the banks to be fished in one year, they are divided into three or four different portions, which are fished one portion annually in succession. The different portions are completely distinct, and are set up separately to sale, each in the year in which it is to be fished. By this means a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> is given to the oysters to attain their proper growth; and as the portion first used has generally recovered its maturity by the time the last portion has been fished, the fishery becomes almost regularly annual, and may thus be considered as yielding a yearly revenue. The oysters are supposed to attain their completest state of maturity in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years; for, if left too long, it is said that the pearl becomes so large and inconvenient to the fish, that it throws it out of the shell. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> season commences in February, and ends about the beginning of April. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> allowed to the merchant to fish the banks is six weeks, or two months at the utmost; but there are several interruptions, which prevent the fishing days from exceeding more than about thirty. If it happens to be a very bad season, and many stormy days intervene during the period allotted, the purchaser of the fishery is often allowed a few days more as a favour. During the season, all the boats regularly sail and return together. A signal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> is fired at Arippo, about ten o'clock at night, when the whole fleet sets sail with the land breeze. They reach the banks before daybreak; and at sunrise commence fishing. In this they continue busily occupied till the sea breeze, which arises about noon, warns them to return to the bay. As soon as they appear within sight, another gun is fired, and the colours hoisted, to inform the anxious owners of their return. When the boats come to land, their cargoes are immediately taken out, as it is necessary to have them completely unloaded before night. Whatever may have been the success of their boats, the owners seldom wear the looks of disappointment; for, although they may have been unsuccessful one day, they look with the most complete assurance of better fortune to the next; as the Brahmins and conjurers, whom they implicitly trust in defiance of all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, understand too well the liberality of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in hopes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, not to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> them all they can desire. Each of the boats carries 20 men, with a tidal or chief boatman, who acts as pilot. Ten of the men row and assist the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> in reascending. The other ten are divers; they go down into the sea by five at a time; when the first five come up the other five go down, and by this method of alternately <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVING">diving</a>, they give each other time to recruit themselves for a fresh plunge. In order to accelerate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the divers, large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are employed; five of these are brought in each boat for the purpose; they are of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, common in this country, and of a pyramidal shape, round at top and bottom, with a hole perforated through the smaller end sufficient to admit a rope. Some of the divers use a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> shaped like a half-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, which they fasten round the belly when they <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to descend, and thus keep their feet free. The people are accustomed to dive from their very infancy, and fearlessly descend to the bottom in from four to ten fathom water, in search of the oysters. The diver, when he is about to plunge, seizes the rope, to which one of the stones we have described is attached, with the toes of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> foot, while he takes hold of a bag of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>-work with those of his left; it being customary among all the Indians to use their toes in working or holding as well as their fingers, and such is the power of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> that they can pick up even the smallest thing from the ground with their toes as nimbly as an European could do with his fingers. The divers thus prepared, seizes another rope with his right <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and holding his nostrils shut with the left, plunges into the water, and by the assistance of the stone speedily reaches the bottom. He then hangs the net round his neck, and with much dexterity, and all possible dispatch, collects as many oysters as he can while he is able to remain under water, which is usually about two minutes. He then resumes his former position, makes a signal to those above by pulling the rope in his right hand, and is immediately by this means drawn up and brought into the boat, leaving the stone to be pulled up afterwards by the rope attached to it. The exertion undergone during this process is so violent, that upon being brought into the boat, the divers discharge water from their mouth, ears, and nostrils, and frequently even blood. But this does not hinder them from going down again in their turn. They <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> often make from 40 to 50 plunges in one day; and at each plunge bring up about 100 oysters. Some rub their bodies over with oil, and stuff their ears and noses to prevent the water from entering; while others use no precautions whatever. Although the usual time of remaining under water does not much exceed two minutes, yet there are instances known of divers who could remain four and even five minutes. The longest instance ever known was that of a diver who came from Anjango in 1797, and who absolutely remained under water full six minutes. The boat-owners and merchants are very apt to lose many of the best pearls while the boats are on their return to the bay from the banks, as the oysters when alive and left for some time undisturbed frequently open their shells of their own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>; a pearl may then be easily discovered, and the oyster prevented by means of a bit of grass or soft wood from again closing its shell, till an opportunity offers of picking out the pearl. Those fellows who are employed to search among the fish also commit many depredations, and even swallow the pearls to conceal them; when this is suspected, the plan followed by the merchants is to lock the fellows up, and give them strong emetics and purgatives, which have frequently the effect of discovering the stolen goods. As soon as the oysters are taken out of the boats, they are carried by the different people to whom they belong, and placed in holes or pits dug in the ground to the depth of about two feet, or in small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> places cleared and fenced round for the purpose; each person having his own separate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. Mats are spread below them to prevent the oysters from touching the earth; and here they are left to die and rot. As soon as they have passed through a state of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, and have become dry, they are easily opened without any danger of injuring the pearls, which might be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> if they were opened fresh, as at that time to do so requires great force. On the shell being opened, the oyster is minutely examined for the pearls: it is usual even to boil the oyster, as the pearl, though commonly found in the shell, is not unfrequently contained in the body of the fish itself. The pearls found at this fishery are of a whiter <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> than those got in the gulf of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> on the Arabian... bian coast, but in other respects are not accounted so pure or of such an excellent quality; for though the white pearls are most esteemed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the natives prefer those of a yellowish or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> cast. Off Tutucoreen, which lies on the Coromandel coast, nearly opposite to Condatchy, there is another fishery; but the pearls found there are much inferior to the two species now mentioned, being tainted with a blue or grayish tinge. In preparing the pearls, particularly in drilling and stringing them, the black people are wonderfully expert. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> they employ in drilling, is a machine made of wood, and of a shape resembling an obtuse <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> cone, about six inches in length, and four inches in breadth, which is supported upon three feet, each twelve inches long. In the upper flat surface of this machine, holes or pits are formed to receive the larger pearls, the smaller ones being beaten in with a little wooden hammer. The drilling instruments are spindles of various sizes according to that of the pearls; they are turned round in a wooden head by means of a bow-handle to which they are attached. The pearls being placed in the pits which we have already mentioned, and the point of the spindle adjusted to them, the workman presses on the wooden head of the machine with his left hand, while his right is employed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round the bow-handle. During the process of drilling, he occasionally moistens the pearl by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> the little finger of his right hand in a cocoa-nut filled with water, which is placed by him for that purpose; this he does with a dexterity and quickness which scarcely impedes the operation, and can only be acquired by much practice. They have also a variety of other instruments, both for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> and drilling the pearls. To clean, round, and polish them to that state in which we see them, a powder made of the pearls themselves is employed. These different operations in preparing the pearls occupy a great number of the black men in various parts of the island. In the black town of Columbo, in particular, many of them may every day be seen at this work. Putallom is remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-pans. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, before the arrival of Europeans on the island, supplied the natives with salt; and on account of its convenient situation, was pitched upon by the Dutch for manufacturing the salt with which they supplied the king of Candy's dominions, according to the articles of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with him. The salt-pans are formed by an arm of the sea which overflows part of the country between Putallom and Calpenteen. A very large quantity of salt was manufactured here by the Dutch; they looked upon it as of the highest importance to their interests in the island, and the most formidable weapon which it was in their power to employ against the native king, as it was impossible for him to procure any but through their means. The Dutch enacted severe laws to prevent individuals from manufacturing or trading in this article, the government taking upon itself the management of the works and the care of supplying both its own subjects and the Candians. In order to keep a constant check on the latter, the Dutch were careful not to allow them too great a quantity at once; and whatever remained at Putallom after supplying the demands of each year they destroyed, that it might not be seized upon by surprize. But this manufacture has been greatly neglected, it is said, since the island came into the possession of the British. CHACE. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">Chase</a>.

CHACO

Pages 393-393

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated between 16° and 37° S. Lat. It belongs to the Spaniards, by whom it was conquered in 1536. It is not naturally fruitful; but abounds in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which are so much the more valuable that they are easily worked. The works are carried on by about 8000 blacks, who deliver every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to their masters a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gold; and what they can collect above this belongs to themselves; as well as what they find on those days that are consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and rest, upon condition that during the festival they maintain themselves. This enables many of them to purchase their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; after which they intermarry with the Spaniards.

CHADCHOD

Pages 393-394

in Jewish antiquity. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> mentions chadchad among the several merchandises which were brought to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>. The old interpreters, not very well knowing the meaning of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it in their translation. St Jerome acknowledges that he could not discover the interpretation of it. The Chaldee interprets it pearls; others think that the onyx, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUBY">ruby</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a>, crystal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, is meant by it. CHÆRONEA, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the last town, or rather the last village, of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, towards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>; the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Plutarch; famous for the fatal defeat of the confederate Greeks by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon. This place was considered by Philip as well adapted to the operations of the Macedonian phalanx; and the ground for his encampment, and afterwards the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, were chosen with equal sagacity; having in view on one side a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, whom the Macedonians regarded as the author of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> protector of their fortune; and on the other the banks of the Thermodon, a small river flowing into the Cephissus, announced by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> as the destined <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of desolation and woe to their unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The generals of the confederate Greeks had been much less careful to avail themselves of the powerful sanctions of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. Unrestrained by inauspicious sacrifices, the Athenians had left the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> at the exhortation of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, to wait no other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a> but the cause of their country. Regardless of oracles, they afterwards advanced to the ill-fated Thermodon, accompanied by the Thebans, and the scanty reinforcements raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and states of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a> which had joined their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> amounted to 32,000 men, animated by the noblest cause for which men can fight, but commanded by the Athenians Lysicles and Charis; the first but little, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> unfavourably known; and by Theagenes the Theban, a person strongly suspected of treachery: all three creatures of cabal and tools of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, slaves of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> or voluptuousness, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> (especially as they had been appointed to command the only states whose shame, rather than virtue, yet opposed the public enemy) are alone sufficient to prove that Greece was ripe for ruin. When the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> approached for abolishing the tottering independence of those turbulent republics, which their own internal vices, and the arms and intrigues of Philip, Philip had been gradually undermining for 22 years, both armies formed in battle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a> before the rising of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing of the Macedonians was headed by Philip, who judged it proper to oppose in person the dangerous fury of the Athenians. His son Alexander, only 19 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, but surrounded by experienced officers, commanded the left wing, which faced the Sacred Band of the Thebans. The auxiliaries of either army were posted in the centre. In the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, the Athenians <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with impetuosity, and repelled the opposing divisions of the enemy; but the youthful ardour of Alexander obliged the Thebans to retire, the Sacred Band being cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The young <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> completed their disorder, by pursuing the scattered multitude with his Thessalian cavalry. Meantime the Athenian generals, too much elated with their first advantage, lost the opportunity to improve it; for having repelled the centre and right wing of the Macedonians, except the phalanx, which was composed of chosen men, and immediately commanded by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, they, instead of attempting to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> this formidable body by attacking it in flank, pressed forward against the fugitives, the insolent Lyceids exclaiming in vain triumph, "Pursue, my brave countrymen! let us drive the cowards to Macedon." Philip observed this rash folly with contempt; and saying to those round him, "Our enemies know not how to conquer," commanded his phalanx, by a rapid <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> an adjacent eminence, from which they poured down, firm and collected, on the advancing Athenians, whose confidence of success had rendered them totally insensible to danger. But the irresistible shock of the Macedonian spear converted their fury into despair. Above a thousand fell, two thousand were taken prisoners; the rest escaped by a precipitate and shameful flight. Of the Thebans more were killed than taken. Few of the confederates perished, as they had little share in the action, and as Philip, perceiving his victory to be complete, gave orders to spare the vanquished, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> unusual in that age, and not less <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to his understanding than his heart; since his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> thus subdued the minds, and gained the affections of his conquered enemies. According to the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, the battle was followed by an entertainment; at which the king, presiding in person, received the congratulations of his friends, and the humble supplications of the Athenian deputies, who craved the bodies of their slain. Their request, which served as an acknowledgment of their defeat, was readily granted; but before they availed themselves of the permission to carry off their dead, Philip, who with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> intemperance had prolonged the entertainment till morning, issued forth with his licentious companions to visit the field of battle; their heads crowned with festive garlands, their minds intoxicated with the insolence of wine and victory; yet the sight of the slaughtered Thebans, which first presented itself to their eyes, and particularly the sacred band of friends and lovers, who lay covered with honourable wounds on the spot where they had been drawn up to fight, brought back these insolent spectators to the sentiments of reason and humanity. Philip beheld the awful scene with a mixture of admiration and pity; and, after an affecting silence, denounced a solemn curse against those who basely suspected the friendship of such brave men to be tainted with criminal and infamous passions. But this furious temper of mind did not last <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; for having proceeded to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the field where the Athenians had fought and fallen, the king abandoned himself to all the levity and littleness of the most petulant joy. Instead of being impressed with a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his recent danger, and with dutiful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to Heaven for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his escape, and the importance of his victory, Philip only compared the boastful pretensions with the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> performances of his Athenian enemies; and, struck by this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>, rehearsed, with the insolent mockery of a buffoon, the pompous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> lately drawn up by the ardent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> and too sanguine hopes of Demosthenes. It was on this occasion that the orator <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMADES">Demades</a> at once rebuked the folly, and flattered the ambition of Philip, by asking him, Why he assumed the character of Therites when fortune assigned him the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Agamemnon? Whatever might be the effect of this sharp reprimand, it is certain that the king of Macedon indulged not, on any future occasion, a vain triumph over the vanquished. When advised by his generals to advance into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, and to render himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, he only replied, "Have I done so much for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and shall I destroy the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of that glory?" His subsequent conduct corresponded with the moderation of this sentiment. He restored without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> the Athenian prisoners; who, at departing, having demanded their baggage, were also gratified in this particular; the king pleasantly observing, that the Athenians seemed to think he had not conquered them in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a>. Soon afterwards he dispatched his son Alexander, and Antipater the most trusted of his ministers, to offer them peace on such favourable terms as they had little reason to expect. They were required to send deputies to the isthmus of Corinth, where, to adjust their respective contingents of troops for the Persian expedition, Philip purposed assembling early in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> a general convention of all the Grecian states: they were ordered to surrender the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, which actually formed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> station of their fleet, and the main bulwark and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of all their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> or insular possessions; but they were allowed to enjoy, unmolested, the Attic territory, with their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. CHÆTODON. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This fish is a native of the East Indies, where it frequents the sides of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in search of food; from its singular manner of obtaining which it receives its name. When it spies a fly sitting on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> that grow in shallow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it swims to the distance of four, five, or six feet; and then, with a surprising dexterity, it ejects out of its tubular mouth a single drop of water, which never fails striking the fly into the water, where it soon becomes its prey.

CHAFF

Pages 394-395

in Husbandry, the husks of the corn, separated by screening <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> winnowing it. It signifies also the rind of corn, and straw cut small for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of cattle. CHAFF-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTER">Cutter</a>, a machine for making chaff to feed horses. The advantages of an easy and expeditious method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> straw into chaff, by an engine which could be used by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> labourers, have been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> acknowledged; and various attempts have been made to bring such an engine to perfection. But the objections to most of them have been their complicated structure, their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> price, and the noise they make in working; all which inconveniences seem to have been lately removed by an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Mr James Pike, watchmaker at Newton <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">Abbot</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. Of his engine, which is of a simple and cheap <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> referred to, are extracted from the Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Arts, for 1787. The engine is fixed on a wooden frame, which is supported with four legs, and on this frame is a box for containing the straw, four feet six inches long; and about ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; at one end is fixed across the box two rollers inlaid with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, in a diagonal line about an eighth of an inch above the surface; on the ends of these rollers are fixed two strong <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, which take one into the other. On one of these wheels is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> wheel, whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> take in a worm on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> arbor; on the end of this arbor is fixed a wooden wheel, two feet five inches diameter and three inches thick; on the inside <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this wheel is fixed a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and every revolution of the wheel the knife passes before the end of the box and cuts the chaff, which is brought forward between the rollers, which are about two inches and a half asunder; the straw is brought on by the worm taking one tooth of the wheel every round of the knife; the straw being so hard pressed between the rollers, the knife cuts off the chaff with so great ease, that 22 bushels can be cut within the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and makes no more noise than is caused by the knife passing through the chaff. A is the box into which the straw is put. B, the upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, with its diagonal projecting ribs of iron, the whole moving by the revolution of the brass wheel C on the axis of which it is fixed. D, a brass wheel, having upon it a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> wheel, whose teeth take into the endless screw on the arbor E, while the teeth on the edge of this wheel enter between those on the edge of the wheel C. On the axis of the wheel D is a roller, with iron ribs similar to B, but hid within the box. E, the arbor, one of the ends of which being made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and passing through a mortise in the centre of the wooden wheel F, is fastened by a strong screw and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a>; the other end of this arbor moves round in a hole within the wooden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> G. H, the knife, made fast by screws to the wooden wheel F, and kept at the distance of nearly three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch from it by means of a strip of wood of that thickness, of the form of the blade, and reaching to within an inch of the edge. I, the handle mortised into the outside of the wooden wheel F.

CHAFFER

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of beetle. See Scarabaeus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHAFFERCONNERS

Pages 395-395

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, printed linens manufactured in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul's dominions. They are imported by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, and are of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those linens prohibited in France.

CHAFFERY

Pages 395-395

in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> works, the name of one of the two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> forges. The other is called the finery. When the iron has been brought at the finery into what is called an ancony, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, hammered into a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> in its middle, but with its two ends rough, the business to be done at the chaffery is reducing the whole to the same shape, by hammering <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> these rough ends to the shape of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>.

CHAFFINCH

the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Fringilla. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHAGRE

a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>, at the mouth of a river of the same name. It has been taken several times by the Buccaneers, and last of all by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a> in 1740. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 82° 7'. N. Lat. 9° 50'.

CHAIN

Pages 395-396

in surveying, is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, consisting of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of links of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wire, usually a hundred; serving to take the dimensions of fields, &c. This is what Mercenne takes to be the arvipedium of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The chain is of various dimensions, as the length <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> number of links varies: that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in measuring <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, called Gunter's chain, is in length four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> or perches; or sixty-five feet, or a hundred links; each link being <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches $\frac{9}{10}$$. Whence it is easy to reduce any number of those links to feet, or any number of feet to links. This chain is entirely adapted to English measure; and its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> convenience is in finding readily the numbers contained in a given field. Where the proportions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> feet and acres differ, the chain, to have the same advantages as Gunter's chain, must also be varied. Thus, in Scotland, the chain ought to be of 74 feet, or 24 Scotch ells, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> no regard be had to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the Scotch and English foot; but if regard be had to this difference, the Scotch chain ought to consist of 74$\frac{3}{4}$ English feet, or 74 feet four inches and $\frac{3}{4}$ of an inch. This chain being divided into an hundred links, each of these <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be $\frac{9}{100}$ inches. That ordinarily used for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> distances, is in length 100 feet; each link one foot. For small parcels, as gardens, &c. is sometimes used a small chain of one pole, or 16 feet and a half length; each link one inch $\frac{9}{10}$. Some in lieu of chains <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>; but these are liable to several irregularities, both from the different degrees of moisture, and of the force which stretches them. Schwenterus, in his Practical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, tells us, he has observed a rope sixteen feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> reduced to fifteen in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> falling of a hoar-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. To obviate these inconveniences, Wolfius directs, that the little strands whereof the rope consists be twisted contrariwise, and the rope dipped in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> hot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and when dry, drawn through melted wax. A rope thus prepared will not get or lose any thing in length, even though kept under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. CHAIN <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">Pump</a>. See Pump. CHAIN-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">Shot</a>, two bullets with a chain between them. They are used at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to shoot <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> yards or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and to cut the throats or rigging of a ship. Top CHAIN, on board a ship, a chain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLING">sling</a> the sail yards in time of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, in order to prevent them from falling down when the ropes by which they are hung happen to be shot away or rendered incapable of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. CHAIN <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, or Channels, of a ship, (porteboîffres), are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and thick planks projecting horizontally from the ship's outside, abreast of and somewhat behind the masts. They are formed to extend the throats from each other, and from the axis or middle line of the ship, so as to give a greater security and support to the masts, as well as to prevent the throats from damaging the gunwale, or being hurt by rubbing against it. Every mast has its chain wales, which are either built above and below the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> deck ports in a ship of the line; they are strongly connected to the side by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, bolts, and standards, besides being confined thereto by the chains, whose upper ends <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through notches on the outer edge of the chain wales, so as to unite with the throats above.

CHAIN ALSO

Pages 395-395

n also denotes a kind of string, of twisted wire; serving to hang watches, tweeter <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and other valuable toys upon. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of this piece of curious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is owing to the English; whence, in foreign countries, it is denominated the English chain. These chains are usually either of silver <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, some of gilt <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; the thread or wire of each kind to be very fine.—For the fabric, or making of these chains; a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the wire is folded into little links of an oval form; the longest diameter about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>; the shortest one. These, after they have been exactly soldered, are again folded into two; and then bound together or interwoven, by means of several other little threads of the same thickness; some whereof, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from one end to the other, imitate the warp of a stuff; and the others, which pass transverse, the woof. There are at least four thousand little links in a chain of four pendants; which are by this means bound so equally, and withal so firmly together, that the eye is deceived, and takes the whole to consist of one entire piece. Chain is also a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> in France, in the trade of wood for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. There are chains for wood by tale, for wood by the rope, for faggots, for cleft wood, and for round sticks. There are also chains for measuring the sheaves of all sorts of corn, particularly with regard to the payment of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>; for measuring pottles of hay, and for measuring horses. All these are divided into feet, inches, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, &c. according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> they are designed for.

CHAINS

Pages 396-396

in Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, are strong links <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, the lower ends of which are bolted through the ship's side to the timbers. Hanging in CHAINS, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>. By stat. 25 Geo. I. c. 37, the judge shall <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> such to be executed on the next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> but one, unless <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> intervene; and their bodies to be delivered to the surgeons to be dissected and anatomized; and he may direct them afterwards to be hung in chains. During the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> and execution, the prisoner shall be kept alone, and fed only with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The judge, however, hath power to reprieve the execution, and relax the other restraints of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. CHAIN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, an island lately discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Wallis in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It seemed to be about five miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, lying in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west and south-east. It appeared to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> range of woody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> joined together by reefs, so as to compose one island of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, with a lake in the middle. The trees are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> that issued from the woods, it appeared to be inhabited. W. Long. 145° 54'. S. Lat. 17° 23'.

CHAIR

Pages 396-397

(Cathedra), was anciently used for the pulpit, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suggestum, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> spoke to the people. It is still applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where professors and regents in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> deliver their lectures, and teach the sciences to their pupils; thus, we say, the professor's chair, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s chair, &c. Curule CHAIR, was an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> seat placed on a car, wherein were seated the prime magistrates of Rome, and those to whom the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a triumph had been granted. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a> CHAIR, a vehicle supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, wherein persons are carried; borne by two men. There are 200 chairs allowed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>: and no person is obliged to pay for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HACKNEY">hackney</a> chair more than the rate allowed by the act for a hackney <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a> driven two-thirds parts of the said distance. 9 Ann. c. 23, § 8. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is since increased by 10 Ann. c. 19, and 12 Geo. I. c. 12, to 400. See Hackney COACHES. CHAIR is also applied by the Romanists to certain seats, held anciently in commemoration of the translation of the see, or seat, of the vicarage of Christ, by St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. The perforated chair, wherein the new elected pope is placed, T. Mabillon observes, is to be seen at Rome; but the origin thereof he does not <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a>, as is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> done, to the adventure of Pope Joan; but says there is a mystery in it; and it is intended, tended, forsooth, to explain to the pope those words of Scripture, that God draws the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> from out of the dust and mire.

CHAIRMAN

Pages 397-397
