the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> speaker of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, &c. We say, the chairman of a committee, &c.

CHAISE

Pages 397-397

a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> open chariot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> calash. Aurelius Victor relates, that Trajan first introduced the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-chaises; but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> is generally ascribed to Augustus; and was probably only improved by Trajan and succeeding emperors.

CHAJOTLI

Pages 396-396
or Chayoti, a Mexican fruit of a round shape, and similar in the husk with which it is covered to the chestnut, but four or five times larger, and of a much deeper green colour. Its kernel is of a greenish white, and has a large stone in the middle, which is white, and like it in substance. It is boiled, and the stone eaten with it. This fruit is produced by a twining perennial plant, the root of which is also good to eat.

CHAL

Pages 443-443

a town of the East Indies, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGLANA">Baglana</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Vizapour. Its river affords a good harbour for small vessels. The town is fortified, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the south side of the harbour. It had formerly a good trade, but is now miserably <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. It was taken by the Portuguese in 1557, to whom it still belongs. It is 15 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, and five miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72. 45. N. Lat. 18. 30.

CHALAZA

Pages 397-397

among naturalists, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> knotty sort of a string at each end of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, formed of a plexus of the fibres of the membranes, whereby the yolk and white are connected together. CHALCAS. Sec <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHALCEDON

Pages 397-397
or CALCEDON, anciently known by the names of Procerastis and Colbysa; a city of Bithynia, situated at the mouth of the Euxine, on the north extremity of the Thracian Bosphorus, over against Byzantium. Pliny, Strabo, and Tacitus, call it, The City of the Blind; alluding to the answer which the Pythian Apollo gave to the founders of Byzantium, who, consulting the oracle relative to a place where to build a city, were directed to choose that spot, which lay opposite "to the habitation of the blind;" that is, as was then understood, to Chalcedon: the Chalcedonians well deserving that epithet for having built their city in a barren and sandy foil, without seeing that advantageous and pleasant spot on the opposite shore, which the Byzantines afterwards chose.—Chalcedon, in the Christian times, became famous on account of the council which was held there against Eutyches. The emperor Valens earled the walls of this city to be levelled with the ground for siding with Procopius, and the materials to be conveyed to Constantinople, where they were employed in building the famous Valentinian aqueduct. Chalcedon is at present a poor place, known to the Greeks by its ancient name, and to the Turks by that of Cadiaci, or, "the judges town."

CHALCEDONY

Pages 397-397

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of the semipellucid gems. They are of an even and regular, not tabulated structure; of a semi-opaque crystal-line basis, and variegated with different colours, but those ever disposed in form of mists <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> nicely examined, found to be owing to an admixture of various coloured earths, but imperfectly blended in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, and often visible in distinct molecules. It has been doubted by some whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were at all acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> we call chalcedony; they having described a Chalcedonian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>, neither of which can at all agree with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of our stone; but we are to consider that they have also described a Chalcedonian jasper, which seems to have been the very same stone as they describe by the word turbida, which extremely well agrees with our chalcedony. There are four known <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the chalcedony. 1. A bluish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> one. This is the most <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> of all, and is found in the shape of our flints and pebbles, in masses of two or three inches or more in diameter. It is of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a faint cloud of blue diffused all over it, but always in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> near the surface. This is a little less hard than the oriental onyx. The oriental chalcedonies are the only ones of any value; they are found in vast abundance on the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in all parts of the East Indies, and frequently come over among the ballast of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> ships. They are common in Silesea and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> also; but with us are less hard, more opaque, and of very little value. 2. The dull milky-veined chalcedony. This is a stone of little value; and is sometimes met with among our lapidaries, who mistake it for a kind of nephritic stone. It is of a somewhat yellowish white or cream colour, with a few <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-white veins. This is principally found in New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. 3. The third is a brownish, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, dull, and cloudy one, known to the ancients by the name of smoky jasper, or jaspis capnitis. This is the least beautiful stone of all the clasps: it is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> brownish white, clouded all over with a blackish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a>, as the common chalcedony is with a blue. It is common both in the East and West Indies, and in Germany; but is very little valued, and is seldom worked into anything better than the handles of knives. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> chalcedony is greatly superior to all the rest in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; and is in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, though very little known among us. It is naturally composed of an admixture of red and yellow only, on a clouded crystalline basis; but is sometimes found blended with the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of common chalcedony, and then is mixed with blue. It is all over of the milky hue of the common chalcedony. This is found only in the East Indies, and there not plentifully. The Italians make it into beads, and call these calcidones; but they are not determinate in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word, but call beads of several of the agates by the same name. All the chalcedonies readily give fire with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, and make no effervescence with aquafortis.

CHALCIDE

Pages 397-398

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, taken in a larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, included <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>; as in the prophecies of Jeremiah and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>. In a restricted sense, it denoted a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Babylonia, towards <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deserta; called in Scripture, The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the Chaldeans. Named from Chaled the fourth son of Nahor. See BABYLONIA.

CHALCIDENE

Pages 397-397
or CHALCIDICE, in Ancient Geography, an inland country of Syria, having Antiochia or Seleucia to the west, Cyrrhescia to the north, to the south Apamene and Coelozyria, and to the east Chalybonites; being so called from its principal city Chalcis. This province, one of the most fruitful in Syria, was seized by Ptolemy the son of Memnaeus during the troubles of Syria, and by him made a separate kingdom. Ptolemy himself is styled by Josephus and Hegesippus only prince of Chalcis, but his son Lyfanias is honoured both by Josephus and Dio with the title of king. Upon the death of Antiochus Dionysius king of Syria, Ptolemy attempted to make himself master of Damascus and all Coelozyria; but the inhabitants having an utter aversion to him on account of his cruelty and wickedness, chose rather to submit to Arcas king of Arabia, by whom Antiochus and his whole army had been cut off. He opposed Pompey on his entering Syria; but was by him defeated, taken prisoner, and sentenced to death; which, however, he escaped by paying a thousand talents, and was left also in possession of his kingdom. After Aristobulus king of Judea had been poisoned by the friends of Pompey, and Alexander his son beheaded at Antioch, he sent Philippion his son to Antioch, whither the widow of Aristobulus had retired with her other children, to bring them all to Chalcis; proposing, as he was in love with one of the daughters named Alexandra, to maintain them in his own kingdom in a manner suitable to their rank; but Philippion likewise be-

CHALCIS

Pages 443-443

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Chauci, a people of Germany: divided into the Minores, now East Friesland, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Oldenburg; and into the Majores, now the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Bremen and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a>.

CHALDEE LANGUAGE

Pages 398-398

that spoken by the Chaldeans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> people of Chaldea. It is a dialect of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>.

CHALDEE PARAPHRASE

Pages 398-398

in the rabbinical style, is called TARGUM. There are three Chaldee paraphrases in Walton's Polyglot; viz. that of Onkelos, that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> son of Uzziel, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>.

CHALDRON

Pages 398-398

a dry English <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, consisting of thirty-six bushels, heaped up according to the sealed bushel kept at Guildhall, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>: but on shipboard, twenty-one chaldrons of coals are allowed to the score. The chaldron should weigh two thousand pounds.

CHALICE

Pages 398-398

the cup <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessel used to administer the wine in the sacrament, and by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the chalice, or communicanting in both kinds, is by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome denied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>, who communicate only in one kind, the clergy alone being allowed the privilege of communicating in both kinds.

CHALK

Pages 398-401

is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> found plentifully in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, said to have been anciently dug chiefly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and thence to have received its name of Creta. They have a very easy way of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> chalk in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England. It is there found on the sides of hills; and the workmen undermine it so far as appears proper; then digging a trench at the top, as far distant from the edge as the undermining goes at bottom, they fill this with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which soaks through in the space of a night, upon which the whole flake falls <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at once. In other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, chalk generally lies deeper, and they are forced to dig for it at considerable depths, and draw it up in buckets. Chalk is of two kinds; hard, dry, and firm, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soft and unctuous; both of which are adapted to various purposes. The hard and dry kind is much the properest for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> into lime; but the soft and unctuous chalk is the best for using as a manure for lands. Chalk, whether burnt into lime or not, is in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> an excellent manure. Pure chalk melts easily with alkali and flint into a transparent colourless glass. With alkaline salts it melts somewhat more difficulty, and with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a> somewhat more easily, than with flint or sand. It requires about half its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of borax and its whole weight of alkali to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> it. Sal mirabile, and sandiver, which do not vitrify at all with the crystalline earths, form, with half their weight of chalk, the first a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, the latter a greenish glass. Nitre, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> fluxes for flint, does not perfectly vitrify with chalk. This earth notably promotes the vitrification of flint; a mixture of the two requiring less alkali than either of them separately. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> glasses made from flint and alkali is further saturated with the flint, so as to be incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>... bearing any further addition of that earth without becoming opaque and milky, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> still in a strong fire take up a considerable proportion, one-third or one-fourth of its weight, of chalk, without injury to its transparency: hence chalk is sometimes made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in compositions for glaas, as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> may then be spared. Chalk likewise has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> effect in melting the stony matters intermixed with metallic ores, and hence might be of use in melting ores; as indeed <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> is used for that purpose. But it is remarkable, that chalk, when deprived of its fixed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and converted into limestone, loses much of its disposition to vitrify. It is then found to melt very difficultly and imperfectly, and to render the glaas opaque and milky. Chalk readily imbibes water: and hence masses of it are employed for drying precipitates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, earthy powders that have been leagued with water, and other moist preparations. Its economical uses in cleaning and polishing metallic or glaas utensils are well known. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is powdered and washed from any gritty <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> it may contain, and is then called whitening.—In medicine it is one of the most useful absorbents, and is to be looked upon simply as such. The astringent virtues which some have attributed to it have no foundation, unless in so far as the earth is saturated with an acid, with which it composes a saline concrete manifestly subastringent. For the further properties of chalk, see <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Black Chalk, a name given by painters to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of earth with which they draw on blue <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, &c. It is found in pieces from two to ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and from four inches to twenty in breadth, generally flat, but somewhat rising in the middle, and thinner towards the edges, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> lying in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities together. While in the earth, it is moist and flaky: but being dried, it becomes considerably hard and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, but always breaks in some particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; and if attentively examined when first broken, appears of a striated texture. To the touch it is soft and smooth, stains very freely, and by virtue of its smoothness makes very neat marks. It is easily reduced into an impalpable soft powder without any diminution of its blackness. In this state it mixes easily with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> into a smooth paste; and being diffused through water, it slowly settles in a black slimy or muddy form; properties which make its use very convenient to the painters, both in oil and water colours. It appears to be an earth quite different from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> chalk, and rather of the flat bituminous kind. In the fire it becomes white with a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, and very friable, retaining its flaky structure, and looking much like the white flaky masses which some sorts of pitcoal leave in burning. Neither the chalk nor these ashes are at all affected by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> shops are supplied with this earth from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> or Germany; though some parts of England afford substances nearly, if not entirely, of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and which are found to be equally serviceable both for marking and as black paints. Such particularly is the black earth called kilow, said by Dr Merret, in his Pinax Rerum Britannicarum, to be found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, and by Mr Da Costa, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Fossils, to be plentiful near the top of Cay-Avon, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Chalk, an earth much used by painters and artists, and common in the colour shops. It is properly an indurated clayey ochre, and is dug in Germany, Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and France, but in greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. It is of a fine, even, and firm texture; very heavy, and very hard; of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> red on the outside, but of a deep dark chocolate colour within. It adheres firmly to the tongue, is perfectly infusible to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and makes no effervescence with acids. Chalk <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. Barley and wheat will succeed very well on the better sort of chalky land, and oats generally do well on any kind of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> produce of this sort of land in weeds, is that sort of small vetch called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TINE">tine</a>-tare, with poppies, may-weed, &c. Sainfoin and hop-clover will generally succeed tolerably well on these lands; and where they are of a better sort, the great clover will do. The best manure is dung, old rags, and the sheep dung left after folding them. Chalk-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">Stones</a>, in Medicine, signify the concretions of calcareous matter in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet of people violently afflicted with the gout. Leeuwenhoek has been at the pains of examining these by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. He divides them into three parts. The first is composed of various small parcels of matter looking like white grains of sand; this is harder and drier, and also whiter, than the rest. When examined with large magnifiers, those are found to be composed of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> particles laid closely and evenly together: though the whole small stones are opaque, these component parts of them are pellucid, and resemble pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> cut short, only that they are somewhat pointed at both ends. These are so extremely thin, that Mr Leeuwenhoek computes that 1000 of them placed together would not amount to the size of one hair of our heads. The whole stones in this harder part of the chalk are not composed of these particles, but there are confusedly thrown in among them some broken parts of other substances, and in a few places some globules of blood and small remains of other juices. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind of chalky matter is less hard and less white than the former, and is composed of fragments or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> parts of those oblong bodies which compose the first or hardest kind, and these are mixed among tough and clear matter, and interspersed with the small broken globules of blood discoverable in the former, but in much greater quantity. The third kind appears red to the naked eye; and, when examined with glaases, is found to be a more tough and clammy white matter, in which a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of globules of blood are interspersed; these give it the red appearance it has. Challenge, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTEL">cartel</a> or invitation to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a> or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>*. A challenge either by word or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, or to be the bearer of such a challenge, is punishable by fine and imprisonment on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> or information. Challenge, among hunters. When hounds or beagles, at first finding the scent of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, presently open and cry, they are said to challenge. Challenge, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a> of England, is an exception made to jurors†; and is either in civil or criminal cases. I. In civil cases challenges are of two sorts; challenges to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>, and challenges of the poll. 3 A 2. Challenges Challenges. 1. Challenges to the array are at once an exception to the whole panel, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> are arrayed, or set in order by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> in his return; and they may be made upon account of partiality or some default in the sheriff or his under-officer who arrayed the panel. Also, though there be no personal objection against the sheriff, if yet he arrays the panel at the nomination, or under the direction of either party, this is good cause of challenge to the array. Formerly, if a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> had a cause to be tried, and no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> was returned upon the jury, it was a cause of challenge to the array: also by the policy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law, the jury was to come de vicineto, from the neighbourhood of the vill or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was laid in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>: and therefore some of the jury were obliged to be returned from the hundred in which such vill lay; and, if none were returned, the array might be challenged from defect of hundredders. For, living in the neighbourhood, these were supposed to know beforehand the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the parties and witnesses; and therefore they better knew what <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to give to the facts alleged in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. But this convenience was over-balanced by another very natural and almost unavoidable inconvenience; that jurors, coming out of the immediate neighbourhood, would be apt to intermix their prejudices and partialities in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. And this the law was so sensible of, that it for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> has been gradually relinquishing this practice; the number of necessary hundredders in the whole panel, which in the reign of Edward III. was constantly fixed, being in the time of Fortescue reduced to four; afterwards by statute 26 Eliz. c. 6. to two; and at length, by statute 4 and 5 <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, c. 16. it was entirely abolished upon all civil actions, except upon penal statutes, and upon those also by the 24 Geo. II. c. 18. the jury being now only to come de corpore co-stitutis, from the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> at large, and not de vicineto, or from the particular neighbourhood. The array by the ancient law may also be challenged, if an alien be party to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, and upon a rule obtained by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> for a jury de medietate linguae, such a one be not returned by the sheriff pursuant to the statute 28 Edward III. c. 13. enforced by 8 Hen. VI. c. 29. which enacts, that where either party is an alien born, the jury shall be one half denizens and the other aliens (if so many be forthcoming in the place), for the more impartial trial; a privilege indulged to strangers in no other country in the world; but which is as ancient in England as the time of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>, in whose statute de monticolis Walliae (then aliens to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England), c. 3. it is ordained, that "duodenii legales homines, quorum <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> Walli et sex Angli erunt, Anglicis et Wallis jus ducunt." 2. Challenges to the polls, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a>, are exceptions to particular jurors; and seem to answer to the recusatio judicis in the civil and canon laws; by the constitutions of which a judge might be refused upon any suspicion of partiality. By the laws of England also, in the times of Bracton and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLETA">Fleta</a>, a judge might be refused for good cause; but now the law is otherwise, and it is held that judges or justices cannot be challenged. For the law will not suppose a possibility of bias or favour in a judge who is already sworn to administer impartial <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and whose authority greatly depends on that presumption and idea. And, should the fact at any time prove flagrantly such, as the delicacy of the law will not presume beforehand, there is no doubt but that such misbehaviour would draw down a heavy censure from those to whom the judge is accountable for his conduct. But challenges to the polls of the jury (who are judges of fact) are reduced to four heads by Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>: propter honores respectum; propter defectum; propter affectum; and propter delictum. 1. Propter honores respectum; as, if a lord of parliament be impannelled on a jury, he may be challenged by either party, or he may challenge himself. 2. Propter defectum; as, if a jurymen be an alien born, this is defect of birth; if he be a slave or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol3.html#article-BONDMAN">bondman</a>, it is defect of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and he cannot be a liber et legalis homo. Under the word homo also, though a name common to both sexes, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is however excluded, propter defectum fæcis: except when a widow feigns herself with child in order to exclude the next heir, and a supposititious birth is suspected to be intended; then upon the writ de ventre inspiciendo, a jury of women is to be impannelled to try the question whether with child or not. But the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> deficiency is defect of estate sufficient to qualify him to be a juror, which depends upon a variety of statutes *. 3. Jurors may be challenged propter affectum, for suspicion of bias or partiality. This may be either a principal challenge, or to the favour. A principal challenge is such, where the cause assigned carries with it, prima facie, evident marks of suspicion either of malice or favour; as, that a juror is of kin to either party within the ninth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; that he has an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the cause; that there is an action depending between him and the party; that he has taken <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for his verdict, &c., which if true cannot be overruled; for jurors must be omni exceptione majoris. Challenges to the favour are where the party hath no principal challenge; but objects only some probable circumstances of suspicion, as acquaintance, and the like; the validity of which must be left to the determination of triors, whose office is to decide whether the juror be favourable or unfavourable. 4. Challenges propter delictum, are for some crime or misdemeanour that affects the juror's credit, and renders him infamous: As for a conviction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, felony, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>; or if for some infamous offence, he hath received judgement of the pillory or the like. II. In criminal cases, challenges may be made either on the part of the king, or on that of the prisoner; and either to the whole array, or to the separate polls, for the very same reasons that they may be in civil causes. For it is here at least as necessary as there, that the sheriff or returning officer be totally indifferent; that, where an alien is indicted, the jury should be de medietate, or half foreigners, if so many are found in the place (which does not indeed hold in treasons, aliens being very improper judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; nor yet in the case of Egyptians under the statute 22 Hen. VIII. c. 10.) that on every panel there should be a competent number of hundredders; and that the particular jurors should be omni exceptione majoris, not liable to objections either propter honores respectum, propter defectum, propter affectum, or propter delictum. Challenges Challenges on any of the foregoing accounts are styled challenges for cause; which may be without stint in both civil and criminal trials. But in criminal cases, or at least in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> ones, there is, in favorem vitae, allowed to the prisoner an arbitrary and capricious species of challenge to a certain number of jurors, without flowing any cause at all; which is called a peremptory challenge: a provision full of tenderness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to prisoners for which our laws are justly famous. This is grounded on two reasons: 1. As everyone must be sensible what sudden impressions and unaccountable prejudices we are apt to conceive upon the bare looks and gestures of another; and how necessary it is that a prisoner, when put to defend his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, should have a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his jury, the want of which might totally disconcert him; the law wills not that he should be tried by any one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> against whom he has conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> even without being able to assign a reason for such his dislike. 2. Because upon challenges for cause shown, if the reason assigned prove insufficient to set aside the juror, perhaps the bare questioning his indifference may sometimes provoke a resentment; to prevent all ill consequences from which, the prisoner is still at liberty, if he pleases, peremptorily to set him aside. This privilege of peremptory challenges, though granted to the prisoner, is denied to the king by the statute 33 Edward I. stat. 4, which enacts, that the king shall challenge no jurors without assigning a cause certain, to be tried and approved by the court. However, it is held that the king need not assign his cause of challenge till all the panel is gone through, and unless there cannot be a full jury without the persons so challenged. And then, and not sooner, the king's counsel must show the cause, otherwise the juror shall be sworn. The peremptory challenges of the prisoner must, however, have some reasonable boundary, otherwise he might never be tried. This reasonable boundary is settled by the common law to the number of 35; that is, one under the number of three full juries. For the law judges, that 35 are fully sufficient to allow the most timorous man to challenge through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> caprice; and that he who peremptorily challenges a greater number, or three full juries, has no intention to be tried at all. And therefore it deals with one who peremptorily challenges above 35, and will not retract his challenge, as with one who stands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a> or refuses his trial; by sentencing him to the peine forte et dure in felony, and by attainting him in treason. And so the law stands at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with regard to treason of any kind. But by statute 22 Hen. VIII. c. 14. (which, with regard to felonies, stands unrepealed), no person arraigned for felony can be admitted to make more than 20 peremptory challenges. CHALONS-SUR-SAÔNE, an ancient town of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and capital of the Chalonnais, with a citadel and bishop's see. It is seated on the river Saône, in E. Long. 5° 7' N. Lat. 46° 47'.

CHALONER

Pages 401-402

Sir Thomas, the younger, though inconsiderable as an author, deserves to be recorded as a skilful naturalist, in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> wherein <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was very little understood in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and particularly as the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> works in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, which have since proved so exceedingly advantageous. vantageous to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He was the only son of Sir Thomas Chaloner mentioned in the last article, and was born in the year 1559. Being very young at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Burleigh, taking <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, sent him to St Paul's school, and afterwards to Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where, like his father, he discovered extraordinary talents for Latin and English <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. About the year 1585, he made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and returned to England before 1584; for in that year, we find him a frequent attendant in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. About this time he married the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir William Fleetwood, recorder of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. In 1591 he was knighted; and, some time after, discovered the alum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> on his estate at Gibborough, near the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEES">Tees</a> in Yorkshire (A). Towards the latter end of the queen's reign, Sir Thomas visited Scotland; and returning to England in the retinue of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. found such favour in the sight of his majesty, that he was immediately appointed governor to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry, whom he constantly attended, and, when his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> pupil visited Oxford, was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. How he was employed after the death of the prince is not known. Some years before that event, he married a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife, the daughter of Mr William Blount of London, by whom he had some children. He died in the year 1615, and was buried at Chiswick in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>. His eldest son William was created a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARONET">baronet</a> in the 18th of James, anno 1640. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was extinct in 1681. He wrote, 1. Dedication to Lord Burleigh of his father's poetical works, dated 1579. 2. The virtue of nitre, wherein is declared the sundry cures by the same effect. Lond. 1584, 4to.

CHALONS-SUR-MARNE

Pages 401-401

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> episcopal town of France, in Champagne. It carries on a considerable trade in flannels and other woollen stuffs. It is seated between two fine meadows on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, Mau, and Nau, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 37' N. Lat. 48° 57'.

CHALYBEAT

Pages 402-402

in Medicine, an appellation given to any liquid, as wine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, impregnated with particles of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. See MINERAL WATERS.

CHALYBES

Pages 402-402

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an ancient people of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Their situation is differently assigned; Strabo placing them in Paphlagonia, to the east of Synope; Apollonius Rhodius and Stephanus, on the east of the Thermodon, in Pontus; called Halizones, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. They either gave their name to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> took it from, their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> (Xenophon, Val. Flaccus), their only support, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> being barren and ungrateful, (Dionysius Periegetes).

CHAM

Pages 402-402
or KHAN, the title given to the sovereign princes of Tartary. The word, in the Persian, signifies mighty lord; in the Sclavonic, emperor. Sperlingus, in his dissertation on the Danish term of majesty, koning, king, thinks the Tartarian cham may be well derived from it; adding, that in the north they say kan, kommen, konge, kon- ring, &c. The term cham is also applied, among the Persians, to the great lords of the court, and the governors of provinces.

CHAMA

Pages 402-402

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of shell fish belonging to the order of vermes tellaccae. The shell is thick, and has two valves; it is an animal of the oyster kind. Linnaeus enumerates 14 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, principally distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of their shells.

CHAMADE

Pages 402-402

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> of a drum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, which is given the enemy as a signal to inform them of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> to be made to the commander, either to capitulate, to have leave to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead, make a truce, or the like.—Ménage derives the word from the Italian chiamata, of clamare, "to cry." CHAMÆDRYS. See VERONICA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. CHAMÆPITYS. See TEUCRIUM, Botany Index. CHAMÆROPS. See Botany Index. This plant the Americans call thatch, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to which the leaves are applied.—Under the name of palmetto, however, Mr Adanson describes a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of palm which grows naturally at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> rises from 50 to 60 feet in height: from the upper end of the trunk issues a bundle of leaves, which, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> off, form a round head: each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> represents a fan of five or six feet in expansion, supported by a tail of the same length. Of these trees some produce <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which are consequently barren; others are <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, and loaded with fruit, which succeed each other uninterruptedly almost the whole year round. The fruit of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> palmetos, Mr Adanson affirms to be of the bigness of an ordinary melon, but rounder: it is enveloped in two skins, as tough as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and as thick as strong <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>; within the fruit is yellowish, and full of filaments, fastened to three large kernels in the middle. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> are very fond of this fruit, which, when baked under the ashes, is said to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> like a quince.

CHAMANIM

Pages 402-402

in the Jewish antiquities, is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> name for that which the Greeks call Pyreia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pyrateria; and St Jerome in Leviticus has translated simulacra, in Ifaiah, delubra. These chamanim were, according to Rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, idols exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> upon the tops of houses. Abenezoa says they were portable chapels or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> made in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the sun. What the Greeks call Pyreia were temples consecrated to the sun and fire, wherein a perpetual fire was kept up. They were built upon eminences; and were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enclosures without (A) Sir Thomas, during his residence in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, being particularly fond of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, spent some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Puzzoli, where he was very attentive to the art of producing <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> proved infinitely serviceable to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, though of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> benefit to himself or his family, his attempt being attended with much difficulty and expense. It was begun about the year 1600, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; but was not brought to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection till some time in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. by the assistance of one Ruffel a Walloon, and two other workmen brought from the alum works at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>. By one of the arbitrary acts of Charles, it was then deemed a mine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and granted to Sir Paul <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> adjudged it a monopoly, and justly restored it to the original proprietors.

CHAMARIN

Pages 402-403

a word which occurs in several places of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, and is generally translated the priests of the idols, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the priests clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, because chamar signifies "black," or "blackness." St Jerome, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of Kings, renders it aruspicer. In Hosea and Zephaniah, he translates it aditut or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-wardens. But the best commentators are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that by this word we are to understand the priests of the false gods, and in particular the worshippers of fire; because they were, as they say, drest in black; or perhaps the Hebrews gave them this name in derision, because, as they were continually employed in taking care about the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and keeping up the fire, they were always as black as smiths or colliers. We find priests, among those of Isis, called melanephoroi, that is to say, that wear black; but whether this may be by reason of their dressing in black, or whether it were because they wore a certain thinning black veil in the processions of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, is not certain. Camar, in Arabic, signifies the "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>." Isis is the same deity. Grotius thinks the Roman priests, called camilli, came from the Hebrew chamarin. Those among the heathens who sacrificed to the infernal gods were drest in black.

CHAMBER

Pages 403-404

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, a member of a lodging, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piece of an apartment, ordinarily intended for sleeping in; and called by the Latins cubiculum. The word comes from the Latin camera; and that, according to Nicod, from the Greek καμάρα, vault or curve; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> chamber being originally confined to places arched over. A complete apartment is to consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, antechamber, chamber, and cabinet. Privy Chamber. Gentlemen of the privy chamber, are servants of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, who are to wait and attend on him and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in their diversions, &c. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is forty-eight, under the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chamberlain, twelve of whom are in quarterly waiting, and two of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the privy chamber. In the absence of the lord chamberlain, or vice chamberlain, they execute the king's orders: at coronations, two of them personate the dukes of Aquitain and Normandy; and fix of them, appointed by the lord chamberlain, attend ambassadors from crowned heads to their audiences, and in public entries. The gentlemen of the privy chamber were instituted by Henry VII. Chamber, in Policy, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where certain assemblies are held, also the assemblies themselves. Of these some are established for the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, others for commercial affairs. Of the first kind are, 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">Star</a> chamber, so called because the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> was painted with stars; the authority, power, and jurisdiction of which, are absolutely abolished by the statute 17 Car. I. 2. Imperial chamber of Spire, the supreme court of judicature in the empire, erected by Maximilian I. This chamber has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of judging by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>; and is the last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of all civil affairs of the states and subjects of the empire, in the same manner as the aulic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. Chamber. Nevertheless it is restrained in several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>: it takes no notice of matrimonial causes, these being left to the pope; nor of criminal causes, which either belong to particular princes or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in their respective territories, or are cognizable by all the states of the empire in a diet. By the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Osnaburg, in 1648, fifty assessors were appointed for this chamber, whereof 24 were to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and 26 Catholics; besides five presidents, two of them Protestants, and the rest Catholics. 3. Chamber of accounts, a sovereign court in France, where accounts are rendered of all the king's revenues, inventories and avowals thereof registered, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of fidelity taken, and other things relating to the finances transacted. There are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in France: that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; it registers proclamations, treaties of peace, naturalizations, titles of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, &c. All the members wear <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> gowns of velvet, of fatin, or damask, according to their places. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> chambers in France, which judge by appeal of differences about collecting the tythes. 5. Chamber of audience, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> chamber, a jurisdiction in each <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of France, the counsellors of which are called jugeurs, or judges, as those of the chamber of inquests are called raporteurs, reporters of proceedings by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. 6. Chamber of the edict, or mipyarty, a court established by virtue of the edict of pacification in favour of those of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. This chamber is now suppressed. 7. Apostolical chamber of Rome, that wherein affairs relating to the revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and the pope are transacted. This council consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> camerlinga, the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTA">rota</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, an auditor, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, one advocate-general, a solicitor-general, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>, and twelve clerks. 8. Chamber of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, an apartment in Guildhall, where the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is deposited. Of the last sort are, the chambers of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; the chambers of assurance; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> or syndical chamber of bookellers in France. 1. The chamber of commerce is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and traders, where the affairs relating to trade are treated of. There are several established in most of the chief cities of France; and in our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> we have lately seen chambers of this kind erected, particularly in London, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and Glasgow. 2. Chamber of assurance in France, denotes a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of merchants and others for carrying on the business of insuring: but in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> it signifies a court of justice, where causes relating to insurances are tried. 3. Chamber of bookellers in Paris, an assembly consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNDIC">syndic</a> and assistants, elected by four delegates from the printers, and twelve from the bookellers, to visit the books imported from abroad, and to search the houses of sellers of marbled <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, print-sellers, and dealers in printed paper for hangings, who are prohibited from keeping any letters proper for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> books. In the visitation of books, which ought to be performed by three persons at least from among the syndic and assistants, all libels against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of God, and the welfare of the state, and all books printed either within or without the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of their regulations and privileges, are to be, even with the merchandises that may happen to be in the bales with such libels or other prohibited books. Chamberlain. The days appointed for this chamber to meet are Tuesdays and Fridays, at two o'clock in the afternoon. Chamber, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs. 1. Powder chamber, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a> chamber; a place sunk under ground for holding the powder, or bombs, where they may be out of danger, and secured from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. 2. Chamber of a mine; the place, most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of a cubical form, where the powder is confined. 3. Chamber of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>; that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the chafe, much narrower than the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, where the powder lies. It is of different forms; sometimes like a reversed cone; sometimes globular, with a neck for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the cylinder, whence it is called a bot-tled chamber; but most commonly cylindrical, that being the form which is found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to carry the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> to the greatest distance.

CHAMBERLAIN

Pages 404-404

an officer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the management and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a chamber. See Chamber, in Policy. There are almost as many kinds of chamberlains as chambers; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> whereof are as follows: <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> CHAMBERLAIN of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the sixth great officer of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; to whom belong <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> and lodging in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and there are certain fees due to him from each archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bishop when they perform their homage to the king, and from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> at their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> or doing their homage. At the coronation of every king, he is to have forty ells of crimson velvet for his own robes. This officer, on the coronation <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, is to bring the king his shirt, coif, and wearing clothes; and after the king is drested, he claims his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and all the furniture of his chamber, for his fees: he also carries, at the coronation, the coif, gloves, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, to be used by the king on that occasion; also the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and scabbard; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to be offered by the king, and the robes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> and crown: he dresses and undresses the king on that day, waits on him before and after dinner, &c. To this officer belongs the care of providing all things in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; to him also belongs the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Westminster: he dispenses likewise of the sword of state, to be carried before the king, to what lord he pleases. The great chamberlain of Scotland was ranked by King Malcolm, as the third great officer of the crown, and was called Camerarius Domini Regis. Before a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> was appointed, it was his duty to collect the revenue of the crown; and he disbursed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> necessary for the king's expenses, and the maintenance of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. From the time that a treasurer was appointed, his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was limited to the boroughs throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, where he was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> general, as he had a power for judging of all crimes committed within the borough, and of the crime of foretelling. He was to hold chamberlain ayres every year. He was supreme judge; nor could any of his decrees be questioned by any inferior judiciary. His sentences were put in execution by the magistrates of the boroughs. He also regulated the price of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> within the borough, and the fees of the workmen in the mint house. His salary was only 200l. a-year. The smallness of his salary, and his great powers, had no doubt been the causes of much oppression in this officer, and the chamberlain ayre was called rather a legal robbery than a court of justice; and when the combined lords feigned King James VI. August 24, 1584, and carried him to Ruthven Castle, they issued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> in the king's name, discharging the chamberlain ayres to be kept. The chamberlain had great fees arising from the profits of elecheats, fines, tolls, and customs. This office was granted heritably to the family of Stuart <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lenox; and when their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> line failed, King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. conferred it in like manner upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son, whom he created duke of Monmouth, and on his forfeiture it went to the duke of Lenox; but that family surrendered the office to the crown in 1703. Lord CHAMBERLAIN of the Household, an officer who has the oversight and direction of all officers belonging to the king's chambers, except the precinct of the king's bedchamber. He has the oversight of the officers of the wardrobe at all his majesty's houses, and of the removing wardrobes, or of beds, tents, revels, music, comedians, hunting, messengers, &c. retained in the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He moreover has the oversight and direction of the sergeants at arms, of all physicians, apothecaries, surgeons, barbers, the king's chaplains, &c. and administers the oath to all officers above stairs. Other chamberlains are those of the king's court of exchequer, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, &c. in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> this officer is generally the receiver of all rents and revenues belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> whereof he is chamberlain. In the exchequer there are two chamberlains, who keep a controlment of the pells of receipts and exitus, and have certain keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, records, &c. CHAMBERLAIN of London keeps the city money, which is laid up in the chamber of London; he also presides over the affairs of masters and apprentices, and makes free of the city, &c. His office lasts only a year; but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> usually obtains to re-choose the same person, unless charged with any misdemeanor in his office.

CHAMBERLAYNE

Pages 404-406

JOHN, son to the author of "The Present State of England," and continuator of that useful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, was admitted into Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, 1685; but it doth not appear that he took any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Beside the Continuation <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, he was author of "Dissertations historical, critical, theological, and moral, on the most memorable events of the Old and New Testaments, with Chronological Tables;" one vol. that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for science and learning which accompanied Chambers through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and directed all his pursuits. It was even at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> work, the "Cyclopaedia;" and some of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of it were written behind the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>. Having conceived the idea of so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> an undertaking, he justly concluded that the execution of it would not confit with the avocations of trade; and therefore he quitted Mr Senex, and took chambers at Gray's Inn, where he chiefly resided during the rest of his days. The first edition of the Cyclopaedia, which was the result of many years intense application, appeared in 1728, in two vols. folio. It was published by subscription, the price being 4l. 4s.; and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of subscribers was very respectable. The dedication, which was to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, is dated October 15, 1727. The reputation that Mr Chambers acquired by his execution of this undertaking, procured him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being elected F.R.S. November 6, 1729. In less than 10 years time a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition became necessary; which accordingly was printed, with corrections and additions, in 1738; and was followed by a third the very next year. Although the Cyclopaedia was the grand business of Mr Chambers's life, and may be regarded as almost the sole foundation of his fame, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was not wholly confined to this undertaking. He was concerned in a periodical publication, entitled, "The Literary <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>," which was begun in 1735. In this work he wrote a variety of articles, and particularly a review of Morgan's "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>." He was engaged likewise, in conjunction with Mr John Martyn, F.R.S. and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, in preparing for the press a translation and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the "Philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an Abridgment of all the Papers relating to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Philosophy, which have been published by the Members of that illustrious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>." This undertaking, when completed, was comprised in five volumes, 8vo, which did not appear till 1742, some time after our author's decease, when they were published under the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> names of Mr Martyn and Mr Chambers. Mr Martyn, in a subsequent publication, hath passed a severe censure upon the share which his fellow-labourer had in the abridgment of the Parisian papers. The only work besides, that we find ascribed to Mr Chambers, is a translation of the Jesuit's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">Perspective</a>, from the French; which was printed in 4to, and hath gone through several editions. Mr Chambers's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and unremitting attention to his studies at length impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and obliged him occasionally to take a lodging at Canonbury-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, Illington. This not having greatly contributed to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, he made an excursion to the south of France, but did not reap that benefit from it which he had himself hoped, and his friends wished. Returning to England, he died at Canonbury-house, and was buried at Westminster; where the following inscription, written by himself, is placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the cloisters of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>: Multis pervulgatis, Paucis notus; Qui vitam, inter lucem et umbram, Nec cruditus, nec idiota, Literis After the author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> two more editions of his Cyclopaedia were published. A supplement, which extended to two volumes more, was afterwards compiled; and in the year 1778 was published an edition of both, incorporated into one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REES">Rees</a>, which was completed in four volumes folio. Another edition which is now (1803) going on, and is to extend to 20 vols. 4to, has been undertaken by the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>.

CHAMBRE

Pages 406-406

MARTIN CUREAU DE LA, physician in ordinary to the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, was distinguished by his knowledge in medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and polite learning. He was born at Mons, and was received into the French academy in 1635, and afterwards into the academy of sciences. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of works; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the passions. 2. The art of knowing men. 3. On the knowledge of beasts, &c. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1669. CHAMELEON. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">Lacerta</a>, Erpetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHAMFERING

Pages 406-406

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a phrase used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> any thing aforesaid on the under side.

CHAMIER

Pages 406-406

DANIEL, an eminent Protestant divine, born in Dauphiny. He was many years preacher at Montellimart; from whence he went in 1612 to Montaubon, to be professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and was killed by a cannon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> during the siege in 1621. The most considerable of his works is his Pantheologia Catholica, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, "Wars of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>," in four volumes folio; in which he treats very learnedly of the controversies between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>.

CHAMOIS

Pages 406-406
or Chamois Goat, in Zoology. See Capra, Mammalia Index. CHAMOMILE. See Anthemis, Botany Index.

CHAMOS

Pages 406-406
or Chemosh, the idol or god of the Moabites. The name of chamos comes from a root which, in Arabic, signifies to make haste; for which reason many believe Chamos to be the sun, whose precipitate course might well procure it the name of swift or speedy. Others have confounded Chamos with the god Hammon, adored not only in Libya and Egypt, but also in Arabia, Ethiopia, and the Indies. Macrobius shows that Hammon was the sun; and the horns, with which he was represented, denoted his rays. Calmet is of opinion that the god Hamonos, and Apollo Chomeus, mentioned by Strabo and Ammianus Marcellinus, was the very same as Chamos or the sun. These deities were worshipped in many of the eastern provinces. Some who go upon the resemblance of the Hebrew term chamos to that of the Greek cosmos, have believed Chamos to signify the god Bacchus, the god of drunkenness, according to the signification of the Greek cosmos. St Jerome, and with him most other interpreters, take Chamos and Peor for the same deity. But it seems that Baal Peor was the same as Tammuz or Adonis; so that Chamos must be the god whom the heathens call the sun.

CHAMOUNI

Pages 406-408

one of the elevated valleys of the Chamoun <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, situated at the foot of Mont Blanc. See Alps and Blanc. The first strangers whom a curiosity to visit the glaciers drew to Chamouni (M. Sauflure observes), certainly considered this valley as a den of robbers; for they came armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>-a-pie, attended with a troop of domestics armed in the same manner: they would not venture into any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; they lived in tents which they had brought along with them; fires were kept <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, and sentinels on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, the whole night over. It was in the year 1741 that the celebrated traveller Pocock, and another English <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> called Wyndham, undertook this interesting journey.
