or Chauntry, was anciently a church or chapel endowed with lands, or other yearly revenue, for the maintenance of one or more priests, daily fasting or fingering mass for the souls of the donors, and such others as they appointed. Hence chantry-rents are rents paid to the crown by the tenants or purchasers of chantry-lands.

CHAOLOGY

Pages 415-415

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>. See Chaos. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, in his chaology, sets forth the different alterations, secrétions, and diverse forms, which <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> went through till it became inhabitable; which amounts to the same with what we otherwise call cosmogony. Dr Burnet, in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, represents the chaos as it was at first, entire, undivided, and universally rude and deformed; or the tohu bohu; then shows how it came to be divided into its respective regions; how the homogeneous matter gathered itself apart from all of a contrary principle; and, lastly, how it hardened and became a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> habitable globe. See Earth.

CHAOS

Pages 415-417

that confusion in which <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> lay when newly produced out of nothing at the beginning of the world, before God, by his almighty word, had put it into the order and condition wherein it was after the six days <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>. Chaos is represented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> as the first principle, ovum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seed of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and the world. All the sophists, sages, naturalists, philosophers, theologues, and poets, held that chaos was the eldest and first principle, το ἀρχαιότατον κύριον. The Barbarians, Phoenicians, Egyptians, Persians, &c. all refer the origin of the world to a rude, mixed, confused <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of matter. The Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, and the writers of the Cyclical Poems, all speak of the first chaos; the Ionic and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophers build the world out of it. The Stoics hold, that as the world was first made of a chaos, it shall at last be reduced to a chaos; and that its periods and revolutions in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> are only transitions from one chaos to another. Lastly, the Latins, as Ennius, Varro, Ovid, Lucretius, Statius, &c., are all of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Nor is there any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> whatever that does not derive their *diacereon*, the structure of the world, from a chaos. The opinion first arose among the Barbarians, whence it spread to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and other nations. Dr Burnet observes, that besides <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and a few other Pseudo-Pythagoreans, nobody ever asserted that our world was always from eternity of the same nature, form, and structure, as at present; but that it had been the standing opinion of the wise men of all ages, that what we now call the terrestrial earth, was originally an unformed, indigested mass of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matter, called *chaos*; and no more than the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> and materials of the present world. It does not appear who first broached the notion of a chaos. Moses, the eldest of all writers, derives the origin of this world from a confusion of matter, dark, void, deep, without form, which he calls *rosh bohu*; which is precisely the chaos of the Greek and Barbarian philosophers. Moses goes no further than the chaos, nor tells us whence it took its origin, or whence its confused state; and where Moses stops, there precisely do all the rest. Dr Burnet endeavours to show that as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, &c., who wrote of the cosmogony, acknowledged a chaos for the principle of their world; so the divines, or writers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOGONY">theogony</a>, derive the origin or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of their fabled gods from the same principle. Mr Whiston supposed the ancient chaos, the origin of our earth, to have been the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> of a comet; which, though new, yet, all things considered, is not the most improbable assertion. He endeavours to make it out by many arguments, drawn from the agreement which appears to be between them. So that, according to him, every planet is a comet, formed into a regular and lasting <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and placed at a proper distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, revolving in a nearly circular orbit: and a comet is a planet either beginning to be destroyed or re-made; that is, a chaos or planet unformed or in its primeval state, and placed as yet in an orbit very eccentric. **Chaos**, in the phrase of Paracelsus, imports the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It has also some other significations amongst the alchemists. **Chaos**, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of vermes zoophyta. The body has no shell or covering, and is capable of reviving after being dead to appearance for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time: it has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. There are five <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, mostly obtained by infusions of different vegetables in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and only discoverable by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. See **Animalcula**. **Chapeau**, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> worn by dukes, being scarlet-coloured velvet on the outside, and lined with a fur. It is frequently borne above a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> instead of a wreath, under gentlemen's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>. **Chapel**, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of divine worship so called. The word is derived from the Latin *capella*. In former times, when the kings of France were engaged in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, they always carried St Martin's hat into the field, which was kept in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> as a precious relic: from whence the place was called *capella*; and the priests, who had the custody of the tent, *capellani*. Afterwards the word *capella* became applied to private oratories. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> there are several sorts of chapels. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a> chapels: these differ from parish churches only in name; they are generally small, and the inhabitants within the district few. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there be a presentation <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> ecclesiam instead of capellam, and an admission and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> upon it, it is no longer a chapel, but a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. 2. Chapels, which adjoin to, and are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the church; such were formerly built by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> persons, as burying places for themselves and their families. 3. Chapels of ease: these are usually built in very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> parishes, where all the people cannot conveniently repair to the mother church. 4. Free chapels; such as were founded by kings of England. They are free from all episcopal jurisdiction, and only to be visited by the founder and his successors; which is done by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>: yet the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> may license any subject to build and endow a chapel, and by letters patent exempt it from the visitation of the ordinary. 5. Chapels in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, belonging to particular colleges. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">Domestic</a> chapels, built by noblemen or gentlemen for the private <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of God in their families. See **Chaplain**. **Chapel** is also a name given to a printer's workshop; because, according to some authors, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> was first actually performed in chapels or churches; or, according to others, because Caxton, an early printer, exercised the art in one of the chapels in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they say, *the orders or laws of the chapel, the secrets of the chapel*, &c. **Knights of the Chapel**, called also <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">Poor</a> knights of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, were instituted by Henry VIII. in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was at first thirteen, but has been since augmented to twenty-six. They assist in the funeral services of the kings of England: they are subject to the office of the canons of Windsor, and live on pensions assigned them by the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">Garter</a>. They bear a blue or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cloak, with the arms of St George on the left shoulder. **Chaplain**, James, an eminent French poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1595, and often mentioned in the works of Balzac, Menage, and other learned men. He wrote several works, and at length distinguished himself by a heroic poem called *La Pucelle, ou France Deliverée*, which employed him several years; and which, raising the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the public, was as much decried by some as extolled by others. He was one of the king's counsellors; and died in 1647, very rich, but was very covetous and fond. **Chapelet**, in the manege, a couple of stirrup-leathers, mounted each of them with a stirrup, and joined atop in a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> buckle, called the head of the chapelet, by which they were made fast to the pommel of the saddle, after being adjusted to the rider's length and bore. They are used both to avoid the trouble of taking up or letting <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the stirrups every time that a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> mounts on a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and saddle, and to supply the place of the academy saddles, which have no stirrups to them. **Chapelle**, Claudius Emanuel Luillier, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Francis Luillier, took the name of Chapelle from a village between Paris and St Denis, where he was born. He distinguished himself by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> small pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, in which he discovered <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> delicacy, delicacy, an easy turn, and an admirable felicity of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. He was the friend of Gassendi and Molière; and died in 1686.

CHAPERON

Pages 417-417

CHAPERONNE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> CHAPEROON, properly signifies a sort of hood or covering for the head, anciently worn both by men and women, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> and the populace, and afterwards appropriated to the doctors and licentiates in colleges, &c. Hence the name passed to certain little shields, and other funeral devices, placed on the foreheads of the horses that drew the hearse in pompous funerals, and which are still called chaperoons or jafferoons; because such devices were originally fastened on the chaperonnes, or hoods, worn by those horses with their other coverings of state. CHAPERON of a bit-mouth, in the manege, is only used for catch-mouths, and all others that are not cannon-mouths, signifying the end of the bit that joins to the branch <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> by the banquet. In catch-mouths the chaperon is round, but in others it is oval; and the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> that in catch and other mouths is called chaperon, is in cannon-mouths called fronceau.

CHAPITERS

Pages 417-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, formerly signified a summary of such matters as were inquired of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> presented before justices in eyre, justices of assize, or of the peace, in their sessions. Chapters, at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, denotes such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as are delivered by the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> to the inquest.

CHAPLAIN PROPERLY

Pages 417-417

N properly signifies a person provided with a chapel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who discharges the duty thereof. CHAPLAIN is also used for an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> person, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, or a person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, who officiates in their chapels, &c. In England there are 48 chaplains to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, who wait four each <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, preach in the chapel, read the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the family, and to the king in his private oratory, and say <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> in the absence of the clerk of the closet. While in waiting they have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> and attendance, but no salary. In Scotland the king has six chaplains, with a salary of £50 each, three of them having in addition the deanery of the chapel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> divided between them, making up above £100 to each. The only duty at present is to say prayers at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> for Scotland to fit in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.—According to a statute of Henry VIII., the persons vested with a power of retaining chaplains, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> each is allowed to qualify, is as follows: An archbishop, eight; a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> or bishop, six; marquis or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, five; viscount, four; baron, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, three; a duchess, marchioness, countess, baroness, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> and comptroller of the king's house, clerk of the closet, the king's secretary, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the chapel, almoner, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the rolls, each of them two; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, and warden of the cinqueports, each one. All these chaplains may purchase a licence or dispensation, and take two benefices with cure of souls. A chaplain must be retained by letters testimonial under <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; for it is not sufficient that he serve as chaplain in the family. The first chaplains are said to have been those instituted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings of France, for preserving the chape, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a>, with the other relics of St. Martin, which the kings kept in their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and carried out with them to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The first chaplain is said to have been Gul. de Mefmes, chaplain to St. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>. CHAPLAIN in the order of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, is used for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or class in that order; otherwise called diaco. The knights make the first class, and the chaplains the second. CHAPLAINS of the Pope, are the auditors, or judges of cause in the sacred palace; so called, because the pope anciently gave audience in his chapel, for the decision of causes sent from the several parts of Christendom. He hither summoned as afterlong the most learned lawyers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and they hence acquired the appellation of copellani, chaplains. It is from the decrees formerly given by these that the body of decrets is composed: their number Pope Sixtus IV. reduced to twelve. Some say, the shrines of relics were covered with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>-cape, or capella, i.e. little cape; and that hence the priests, who had the care of them, were called chaplains. In time these relics were repolished in a little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, either contiguous to a larger or separate from it; and the same name, capella, which was given to the cover, was also given to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it was lodged: and hence the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> who superintended it came to be called chaplain.

CHAPLET

Pages 417-417

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ornament for the head, like a garland <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wreath: but this word is frequently used to signify the circle of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. There are instances of its being borne in a coat of arms, as well as for <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a>; the paternal arms for Lafelettes are argent, three chaplets, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULES">gules</a>.

CHAPLET ALSO

Pages 417-423

t also denotes a string of beads used by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their prayers. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of it is ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the hermit, who probably learned it of the Turks, as they owe it to the East Indians. Chaplets are sometimes called pater-nothers; and are made of coral, of diamonds, of wood, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAPLET">chaplet</a> contains 50 ave-marias, and five pater-nothers. There is also a chaplet of our Saviour, consisting of 33 beads, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his 33 years living on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, instituted by Father Michael the Camaldulian. The Orientals have a kind of chaplets which they call chains, and which they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in their prayers, reciting one of the perfections of God on each link <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bead. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul is said to have 18 of these chains, all precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; some diamonds, others rubies, pearls, &c. The Turks have likewise chaplets, which they bear in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or hang at the girdle: but Father Dandini observes, they differ from those used by the Romanists, in that they are all of the same signification, and have not that distinction into decades, though they consist of six decades, or 60 heads. He adds, that the Musselmans run over the chaplet almost in an instant, the prayers being extremely short, as containing only these words, "praise to God," or "<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to God," for each bead. Besides the common chaplet they have likewise a larger one consisting of 100 beads, where there is some distinction, as being being divided by little threads into three parts; on one of which they repeat 32 times "subhan Allah," i.e., "God is worthy to be praised;" on another, "allah Allah," "Glory be to God;" and on the third, "Allah echer," "God is great." These thrice thirty times making only 96; to complete the number 100, they add other prayers for the beginning of the chaplet.—He adds, that the Mahometan chaplet appears to have had its rise from the mea beracoth, or "hundred benedictions," which the Jews are obliged to repeat daily, and which we find in their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> books; the Jews and Mahometans having this in common, that they scarce do anything without pronouncing some laud or benediction. Menage derives the word chaplet from chapeau, "hat." The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Latins call it chapellina, the Italians more frequently corona. Chaplet, or Chapelet, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a little moulding, cut or carved into round beads, pearls, olives, or the like. Chapman, George, born in 1557, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> highly esteemed in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for his dramatic and poetical works. He wrote 17 plays; translated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets; and was thought no <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> genius. He died in 1634; and was buried in St Giles's in the Fields, where his friend Inigo Jones erected a monument to him. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPPE">Chappe</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the dividing an escutcheon by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> drawn from the centre of the upper edge to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> below, into three parts, the sections on the sides being of different metal or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from the rest. Chapel, in Frith, a market-town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, about 26 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 50'. N. Lat. 53° 22'. Chappel, William, a learned and pious bishop of Cork, Cloyne, and Ross in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a> in 1582. When the troubles began under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. he was persecuted by the puritan party in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and retired to Derby, where he devoted himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1649. He wrote Methodus Concionandi, i.e., "the Method of Preaching;" and he is one of those to whom the Whole Duty of Man has been attributed. He left behind him also his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> written by himself in Latin, which has been twice printed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">Chapter</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> polity, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of clergymen belonging to the cathedrals and collegiate churches. It was in the eighth century that the body of canons began to be called a chapter. The chapter of the canons of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> were a standing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> to the bishop, and, during the vacancy of the see, had the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. In the earlier ages, the bishop was head of the chapter; afterwards abbots and other dignitaries, as deans, provosts, treasurers, &c. were preferred to this distinction. The deans and chapters had the privilege of choosing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> in England; but Henry VIII. got this power vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and as the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> expelled the monks from the cathedrals, and placed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> canons in their room, those he thus regulated were called deans and chapters of the new foundation; such are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, Carlisle, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a>. Chapter, in matters of literature, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> in a book for keeping the subject treated of more clear and distinct. Char, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Salmo. Chara. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Charabon, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> in the East Indies. E. Long. 10° 8'. S. Lat. 6'. Characene, the most southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Susiana, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, lying on the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, between the Tigris and the Euileus. It was so named from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Chorax, called first <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, from its founder Alexander the Great; afterwards Antiochia, from Antiochus V. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, who repaired and beautified it; and lastly, Chorax Spafnae, or Pafnae, that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a> of the Spafnes, an Arabian king of that name having secured it against the overflowing of the Tigris, by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> or mole, extending three miles, which served as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> to all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Dionysius Periegetes, and Isidorus, author of the Parthicae Maniones, were both natives of this city. The small district of Characene was seized by Pafnes, the son of Sogdonacus, king of the neighbouring Arabs, during the troubles of Syria, and erected into a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Lucian calls him Hypspafnes, and adds, that he ruled over the Characeni and the neighbouring people: he died in the 85th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The other kings of this country we find mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are, Tcaeus, who died in the 92nd year of his age, and after him <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTABAZUS">Artabazus</a> the seventh, as Lucian informs us, who was driven from the throne by his own subjects, but restored by the Parthians. And this is all we find in the ancients relating to the kings of Characene. Character, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies a mark or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, drawn on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, metal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, graver, chisel, or other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, to signify or denote any thing. The word is Greek, \(\chiαραγμα\), formed from the verb, \(\chiαραγω\), inficulpero, "to engrave, impress," &c. The various kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> may be reduced to three heads, viz. Literal Characters, Numerical Characters, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">Abbreviations</a>. I. Literal Character, is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, serving to indicate some articulate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, expressive of some idea or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the mind. See Alphabet. 1. These may be divided, with regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and use, into Nominal Characters, or those we properly call letters; which serve to express the names of things: See Letter. Real Characters; those that instead of names express things and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>: See Idea, &c. Emblematical or Symbolical Characters; which have this in common with real ones, that they express the things themselves; but have this further, that they in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> personate them, and exhibit their form: such are the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> of the ancient Egyptians. See Hieroglyphic, Symbol, &c. 2. Literal Characters may be again divided, with regard to their invention and use, into particular and general or universal. Particular Characters, are those peculiar to this or that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Such are the Roman, Italic, Greek, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Arabic, Gothic, Chinese, &c. characters.—See Hebrew, Gothic, Chinese, &c. Universal Universal characters are also real characters, and make what some authors call a Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>. That diversity of characters used by the several nations to express the same idea, is found the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> obstacle to the advancement of learning: to remove this, several authors have taken occasion to propose plans of characters that should be universal, and which each people should read in their own language. The character here is to be real, not nominal: to express things and notions; not, as the common ones, letters or sounds: yet to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, like letters, and arbitrary; not emblematical, like hieroglyphics. Thus, every nation should retain its own language, yet every one understand that of each other, without learning it; only by seeing a real or universal character, which should signify the same things to all people, by what sounds forever each expresses it in their particular idiom. For instance, by seeing the character defined to signify to drink, an Englishman should read to drink; a Frenchman, boire; a Latin, bibere; a Greek, πίνω; a Jew, נא; a German, trinken; and so of the rest; in the same manner as seeing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, each people expresses it after their own manner; but all mean the same animal. This real character is no chimera; the Chinese and Japanese have already something like it. They have a common character, which each of those nations understand alike in their several languages; though they pronounce them with such different sounds, that they do not understand one another in speaking. The first and most considerable attempts for a real character, or philosophical language, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, are those of Bishop Wilkins and Dalgarno: but these, with how much art forever they were contrived, have yet proved ineffectual. M. Leibnitz had some thoughts the same way; he thinks those great men did not <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> method. It was probable, indeed, that by their means, people who do not understand one another might easily have a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> together; but they have not hit on true real characters. According to him, the characters should resemble those used in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>; which, in effect, are very simple, yet very expressive; without any thing superfluous or equivocal; and contain all the varieties required. The real character of Bishop Wilkins has its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> applause: Dr Hook recommends it on his own knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, as a most excellent scheme; and to engage the world to the study thereof, publishes some fine inventions of his own therein. M. Leibnitz tells us, he had under consideration an alphabet of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> thoughts; in order to a new philosophical language, on his own scheme: but his death prevented its being brought to maturity. M. Lodwig, in the Philosophical Transactions, gives us a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of an universal alphabet or character of another kind: this was to contain an enumeration of all such single sounds, or letters, as are used in any language; by means whereof, people should be enabled to pronounce truly and readily any language; to describe the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> of any language that shall be pronounced in their hearing, so as others accustomed to this language, though they had never heard the language pronounced, shall at first be able truly to pronounce it; and, lastly, this character to serve as a standard to perpetuate the sounds of any language. In the Journal Litteraire, au. 1729, we have a very ingenious project for an universal character. The author, after obviating the objections that might be made against the feasibility of such schemes in the general, proposes his own: his characters are to be the common Arabic, or numeral figures. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of these <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> are sufficient to express distinctly an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of numbers, much more than we shall need terms to signify our actions, goods, evils, duties, passions, &c. Thus is all the trouble of framing and learning any new character at once saved; the Arabic figures having already all the universality required. The advantages are immense. For, 1mo, We have here a stable, faithful interpreter; never to be corrupted or changed, as the popular languages continually are. 2do, Whereas the difficulty of pronouncing a foreign language is such as usually gives the learner the greatest trouble, and there are even some sounds which foreigners never attain to, in the character here proposed this difficulty has no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: every nation is to pronounce them according to the particular pronunciation that already obtains among them. All the difficulty is, the accustoming the pen and the eye to affix certain notions to characters that do not, at first sight, exhibit them. But this trouble is no more than we find in the study of any language whatever. The inflections of words are here to be expressed by the common letters. For instance, the same character shall express a filly or a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLT">colt</a>, a horse or a mare, an old horse or an old mare, as accompanied with this or that distinctive letter, which shall show the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, youth, maturity, or old age; a letter also to express the bigness or size of things; thus v.g. a man with this or that letter, to signify a great man, or a little man, &c. The use of those letters belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>; which, once well understood, would abridge the vocabulary exceedingly. An advantage of this grammar is, that it would only have one declension and one conjugation: those numerous anomalies of grammarians are exceeding troublesome; and arise hence, that the common languages are governed by the populace, who never reason on what is best: but in the character here proposed, men of sense having the introduction of it, would have a new ground, whereon to build regularly. A new universal character has been proposed by Mr Northmore of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by which different nations may communicate their sentiments to each other. His original plan was, to make the same numerical figure represent the same word in all languages. But he found afterwards that it might be improved, by using a figure not for every word, but every useful word. And even these he thinks might be abbreviated by adopting certain uniform fixed signs, the number of which would not exceed 20, for the various parts of speech. Words of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>, he proposed, to be expressed by a prefixed sign. A few instances <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> explain the author's meaning. Suppose the number 5 to represent the word see, | Number | Meaning | |--------|---------| | 6 | a man | | 7 | happy | | 8 | never | | 9 | I | "I" Characters. "I would then (says he) express the tenses, genders, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, &c., in all languages, in some such uniform manner as the following: (1) $5 = \text{present tense},$ (2) $5 = \text{perfect tense},$ (3) $5 = \text{perfect participle},$ (4) $5 = \text{present participle},$ (5) $5 = \text{future},$ (6) $5 = \text{substantive},$ (7) $5 = \text{personal substantive},$ (8) $6 = \text{nominative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>},$ (9) $6 = \text{genitive},$ (10) $6 = \text{dative},$ (11) $6 = \text{<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a>},$ (12) $+6 = \text{plural},$ (13) $7 = \text{positive},$ (14) $7 = \text{comparative},$ (15) $7 = \text{superlative},$ $7 = \text{as above, No. 6}.$ "From the above specimen, I should find no difficulty in comprehending the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, though it were written in the language of the Hottentots: 9, 8, .5, — 7, 6. I never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a more unhappy woman. "Those languages which do not use the pronoun prefixed to the verb, as the Greek and Roman, &c., may apply it, in a small character, simply to denote the person; thus, instead of 9, 8, .5, I never saw; they may write, 8, .5, which will signify that the verb is in the first person, and will still have the same meaning." Our author thinks, that according to this scheme of an universal character, about 20 signs, and less than 10,000 chosen words (synonyms being set aside), would answer all the ends proposed; and that foreigners, by referring to their numerical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, would easily comprehend each other. He proceeds next to show how appropriate sounds may be given to his signs, and an universal living language formed from the universal characters. To attain this end, he proposes to distinguish the ten numerals by ten monosyllabic names of easy pronunciation, and such as may run without difficulty into one another. To illustrate his scheme, however, he calls them, for the present, by their common English names; but would pronounce each number made up of by uttering separately its component parts, after the manner of accountants. Thus, let the number 6943 represent the word horse, he would not, in the universal language, call a horse six thousand nine hundred and forty-three, but six, nine, four, three, and so on for all the words of a sentence, making the proper stop at the end of each. In the same manner, a distinct appellation must be appropriated to each of the prefixed signs, to be pronounced immediately after the numeral to which it is an appendage. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> plu be the appellation or the sign of the plural number, six, nine, four, three, plu will be horses. "Thus (says our author), I hope, it is evident that about 30 or 40 distinct syllables are sufficient for the above purpose; but I am much mistaken if eleven only will not answer the same end. This is to be done by substituting the first 20 or 30 numerals for the signs, and saying, as in algebra, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is in the power of such a number, which may be expressed by the simple word under. Ex. gr. Let 6943 represent the word horse; and suppose 4 to be the sign of the plural number, I would write the word thus $\frac{6}{943}$; and pronounce it, fix, nine, four, three, in the power of or under four. By these means eleven distinct appellations would be sufficient, and time and use would much abbreviate the pronunciation." But the difficulty is not in inventing the most simple, easy, and commodious character, but in engaging the several nations to use it; there being nothing they agree less in, than the understanding and pursuing their common <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. 3. Literal characters may again be divided, with respect to the nations among whom they have been invented, into Greek characters, Roman characters, Hebrew characters, &c. The Latin character now used through all Europe, was formed from the Greek, as the Greek was from the Phoenician; and the Phoenician, as well as the Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic characters, were formed from the ancient Hebrew, which subsisted till the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>; for after that event the character of the Assyrians, which is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> Hebrew now in use, prevailed, the ancient being only found on some Hebrew medals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Samaritan medals. It was in 1091 that the Gothic characters, invented by Ulphilas, were abolished, and the Latin ones established in their room. Medallists observe, that the Greek character, consisting only of majuscule letters, has preserved its uniformity on all medals, as low as the time of Gallienus, from which time it appears somewhat weaker and rounder: from the time of Constantine to Michael we find only Latin characters: after Michael, the Greek characters recommence; but from that time they began to alter with the language, which was a mixture of Greek and Latin. The Latin medals preserved both their characters and language as low as the translation of the seat of the empire to Constantinople: towards the time of Decius the character began to lose its roundness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; some time after, it retrieved and subsisted tolerably till the time of Justin, when it degenerated gradually into the Gothic. The rounder, then, and better formed a character is upon a medal, the fairer pretence it has to antiquity. II. Numerical Characters, or characters used to express numbers, are either letters or figures. The Arabic character, called also the common one, because it is used almost throughout Europe in all sorts of calculations, consists of these ten digits, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0. The Roman numeral character consists of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> majuscule letters of the Roman alphabet, viz. I, V, X, L, C, D, M. The I denotes one, V five, X ten, L fifty, C a hundred, D five hundred, and M a thousand. The I repeated twice makes two, II; thrice, three, Four is expressed thus, IV. as I before V or X takes an unit from the number expressed by these letters. To express five, an I is added to a V, VI.; for seven, two, VII.; and for eight, three, VIII. Nine is expressed by an I before X, thus, IX. The same remark may be made of the X before L or C, except that the diminution is by tens; thus, XL denotes forty, XC ninety, and LX sixty. The C before D or M diminishes each by a hundred. The number five hundred is sometimes expressed by an I before a C <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, thus, IO; and instead of M, which signifies a thousand, an I is sometimes used between two C's the one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, and the other inverted, thus, CIO. The addition of C and O before or after raises CIO by tens; thus, CCICIO expresses ten thousand, CCCICIO a hundred thousand. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> also expressed any number of thousands by a line drawn over any numeral less than a thousand; thus, V denotes five thousand, LX sixty thousand; so likewise MM is one million, MMM is two millions, &c. The Greeks had three ways of expressing numbers: 1. Every letter, according to its place in the alphabet, denoted a number, from α, one, to ω, twenty-four. 2. The alphabet was divided into eight units, α one, β two, γ three, &c.; into eight tens, ι ten, κ twenty, λ thirty, &c.; and eight <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, ε one hundred, σ two hundred, τ three hundred, &c. 3. I stood for one, II five, Δ ten, Η a hundred, Χ a thousand M ten thousand; and when the latter Π enclosed any of these, except I, it showed the enclosed letter to be five times its value; as, [α] fifty, [ι] five hundred, [ξ] five thousand, [μ] fifty thousand. The French CHARACTERS used in the chamber of accounts, and by persons concerned in the management of there venue, is, properly speaking, nothing else than the Roman numerals, in letters that are not majuscule: thus, instead of expressing fifty-five by LVII, they denote it by smaller characters, lvj. III. CHARACTERS of Abbreviations, &c., in several of the arts, are symbols contrived for the more concise and immediate conveyance of the knowledge of things. For the CHARACTERS used in Algebra, see ALGEBRA, Introduction. CHARACTERS used in Music, and of Musical Notes with their proportions, are as follows: | Character | Proportion | |-----------|------------| | a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> | 8 | | a long | 4 | | a breve | 2 | | a semibreve | 1 | | a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIM">minim</a> | ½ | * character of a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>; this character, at the beginning of a line or space, denotes that all the notes in that line are to be taken a semitone higher than in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>; and the same affects all the octaves above and below, though not marked: but when prefixed to any particular note, it shows that note alone to be taken a semitone higher than it would be without such a character. b or b, character of a flat note: this is the contrary to the other above; that is, a semitone lower. h character of a natural note: when in a line or series of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> notes, marked at the beginning b or *, the natural note happens to be required, it is denoted by this character. & character of the treble cliff. C C D characters that distinguish the movements of common time, the first implying slow, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> quick, and the third very quick. ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, ⅓, characters of simple triple time, the measure of which is equal to three semibreves, or to three minims. ⅔, ⅔, or ⅔, characters of a mixed triple time, where the measure is equal to fix crotchets, or fix quavers. ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, characters of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> triple time. ⅔, ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, or ⅔, characters of that species of triple time called the measure of twelve times. Character, in human life, that which is peculiar in the manners of any person, and distinguishes him from all others. Good Character, is particularly applied to that conduct which is regulated by virtue and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; in an inferior but very common sense, it is understood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> honesty of dealing between man and man. The importance of a good character in the commerce of life seems to be universally acknowledged.—To those who are to make their own way either to wealth or honours, a good character is usually no less necessary than <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and abilities. To transcribe the observation of an elegant moralist: though human nature is degenerate, and corrupts itself still more by its own inventions; yet it usually retains to the last an esteem for excellence. But even if we are arrived at such an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> degree of depravity as to have lost our native reverence for virtue; yet a regard to our own interest and safety, which we seldom lose, will <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to apply for aid, in all important transactions, to men whose character integrity is unimpeached. When we choose an assistant, a partner, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, our first inquiry is concerning his character. When we have occasion for a counselor or attorney, a physician or apothecary, whatever we may be ourselves, we always choose to trust our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and persons to men of the best character. When we fix on the tradesmen who are to supply us with necessaries, we are not determined by the sign of the lamb, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, or the fox, nor by a shop fitted up in the most elegant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but by the fairest reputation. Look into a daily newspaper, and you will see, from the highest to the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, how important the characters of the employed appear to the employers. After the advertisement has enumerated the qualities required in the person wanted, there constantly follows, that none need apply who cannot bring an undeniable character. Offer yourself as a candidate for a seat in parliament, be promoted to honour and emolument, or in any respect attract the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of mankind upon yourself, and if you are vulnerable in your character, you will be deeply wounded. This is a general testimony in favour of honesty, which no writings and no practices can possibly refute. Young men, therefore, whose characters are yet unfixed, and who consequently may render them just such as they wish, ought to pay great attention to the first steps which they take on entrance into life. They are usually careless and inattentive to this object. They pursue their own plans with ardour, and neglect the opinions which others entertain of them. By some thoughtless <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, they suffer a mark to be impressed upon them, which scarcely any subsequent merit can entirely erase. Every man will find some persons, who, though they are not professed enemies, yet view him with an envious or jealous eye, and who will gladly revive any tale to which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> has given the slightest foundation. In this turbulent and confused <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, where our words and actions are often misunderstood, and often misrepresentated, it is indeed difficult even for innocence and integrity to avoid reproach, abuse, contempt, and hatred. These not only hurt our interest and impede our advancement in life, but forcibly afflict the feelings of a delicate and tender mind. It is then the part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> first to do every thing in our power to preserve an irreproachable character, and then to let our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> depend chiefly on the approbation of our own consciences, and on the advancement of our interest in a world where liars shall not be believed, and where flatterers shall receive countenance from none but him who, in Greek, is called by way of eminence, Diabolus, or the calumniator. Character, in Poetry, particularly the epopee and drama, is the result of the manners or peculiarities by which each person is distinguished from others. The poetical character, says M. Boiflu, is not properly any particular virtue or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, but a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of several which are mixed together, in a different degree, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> and the unity of the action: there must be one, however, to reign over all the rest; and this must be found, in some degree, in every part. The first quality in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, is wrath; in Ulysses, dissimulation; and in Aeneas, Character, Æneas, mildness; but as these characters cannot be alone, they must be accompanied with others to embellish them, as far as they are capable, either by hiding their defects, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> of Achilles, which is palliated by extraordinary valour; or by making them centre in some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> virtue, as in Ulysses, whose diffimulation makes a part of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>; and in Æneas, whose mildness is employed in a submission to the will of the gods. In the making up of which union, it is to be observed, the poets have joined together such qualities as are by nature the most compatible; valour with anger, piety with mildness, and prudence with diffimulation. The fable required prudence in Ulysses, and piety in Æneas; in this, therefore, the poets were not left to their choice: but Homer might have made Achilles a coward without abating any thing from the justness of his fable; so that it was the necessity of adorning his character, that obliged him to make him valiant: the character, then, of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in the epic poem, is compounded of three sorts of qualities: the first essential to the fable; the second, embellishments of the first; and valour, which fulfils the other two, makes the third. Unity of character is as necessary as the unity of the fable. For this purpose a person should be the same from the beginning to the end: not that he is always to betray the same sentiments, or one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; but that he should never speak nor <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> inconsistently with his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> character. For instance, the weak may sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into a warmth, and the breath of the passionate be calm, a change which often introduces in the drama a very affecting variety: but if the natural disposition of the former was to be represented as boisterous, and that of the latter mild and soft, they would both act out of character, and contradict their persons. True characters are such as we truly and really see in men, or may exist without any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to nature: no man questions but there have been men as generous and as good as Æneas, as passionate and as violent as Achilles, as prudent and wise as Ulysses, as impious and atheistical as Mezentius, and as amorous and passionate as Dido; all these characters, therefore, are true, and nothing but just imitations of nature. On the contrary, a character is false when an author so feigns it, that one can see nothing like it in the order of nature wherein he feigns it shall stand: these characters should be wholly excluded from a poem, because transgressing the bounds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> and reason, they meet with no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> from the readers; they are fictions of the poet's brain, not imitations of nature; and yet all poetry confits of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of nature. Character is also used for certain visible qualities, which claim respect or reverence to those veiled therewith.—The majesty of kings gives them a character which procures respect from the people. A bishop should sustain his character by learning and solid piety, rather than by worldly lucre, &c. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS">law of nations</a> secures the character of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from all insults. Character, among naturalists, is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of the genera of animals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, &c. Characteristic, in general, is that which characterizes a thing or person, i.e., constitutes its character, whereby it is distinguished. See Characteristic. Characteristic, is peculiarly used in grammar, for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> letter of a word: which is preferred in most of its tenses and moods, its derivatives and compounds. Characteristic of a Logarithm, is its index or exponent. See Logarithm. Characteristic Triangle of a Curve, in the higher geometry, is a rectilinear right-angled triangle, whose hypotenuse makes a part of the curve, not sensibly different from a right line. It is so called, because curve lines are used to be distinguished hereby. See Curve. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARADE">Charade</a>, the name of a new species of composition or literary amusement. It owes its name to the idler who invented it. Its subject must be a word of two syllables, each forming a distinct word: and these two syllables are to be concealed in an enigmatical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, first separately, and then together. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of charades, if not greatly instructive, is at least innocent and amusing. At all events, as it has made its way into every fashionable circle, and has employed even Garrick, it will scarcely be deemed unworthy of attention. The fillings indeed of most that have appeared in the papers under this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, are not only destitute of all pleasantry in the stating, but are formed in general of words utterly unfit for the purpose. They have therefore been treated with the contempt they deserved. In trifles of this nature, inaccuracy is without excuse. The following examples therefore are at least free from this blemish. I. My first, however here abused, Designs the fox alone; In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIA">Cambria</a>, such is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>'s pow'rs, 'Tis Jenkin, John, or Joan. My second oft is loudly call'd, When men prepare to fist it: Its name delights the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>; Its force, may none resist it: It binds the weak, it binds the strong. The wealthy and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; Still 'tis to joy a pallport deem'd, For fullic fame a cure. It may ensure an age of bliss, Yet miseries oft attend it; To fingers, ears, and noses too, Its various lords commend it. My whole may chance to make one drink, Though vended in a fish shop; 'Tis now the monarch of the seas, And has been an archbishop. Her-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>. II. My first, when a Frenchman is learning English, Serves him to swear by. My second, is either hay or corn. My whole, is the delight of the present age; and will be the admiration of posterity. Gar-rick.

CHARAG

Pages 424-424

the tribute which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> and Jews pay to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> sionior. It consists of ten, twelve, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fifteen francs per annum, according to the estate of the party. Men begin to pay it at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or at fifteen years old; women are dispensed with, as also priests, rabbins, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>.

CHARAIMS

Pages 424-424

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Jews in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. They live by themselves, and have a separate synagogue; and as the other Jews are remarkable for their eyes, so are those for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> noses, which run through all the families of this sect. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Effones. They strictly observe the five books of Moses, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>; and receive no written traditions. It is said that the other Jews would join the Charaims; but those not having observed the exact rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> with regard to divorces, these think they live in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>. CHARANTIA. Sec Momordica, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHARBON

Pages 424-424

in the manege, that little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mark which remains after a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> spot in the cavity of the corner <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>: about the seventh or eighth year, when the cavity fills up, the tooth being smooth and equal, it is said to be rated.

CHARCAS

Pages 424-424

the southern <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, remarkable for the silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Potosi.

CHARCOAL

Pages 424-426

a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> coal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, consisting of wood half burnt; chiefly used where a clear strong fire, without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, is required; the humidity of the wood being here mostly dissipated, and exhaled in the fire wherein it is prepared. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> discovers a surprising <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Char pores in charcoal: they are disposed in order, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> it lengthwise; so that there is no piece of charcoal, how <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> forever, but may be easily blown through. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a piece be broken pretty short, it may be seen through with a microscope. In a range the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an inch long, Dr Hook reckoned 150 pores; whence he concludes, that in a charcoal of an inch diameter, there are not less than 5,724,000 pores. It is to this prodigious number of pores that the blackness of charcoal is owing: for the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> striking on the charcoal, are received and absorbed in its pores, instead of being reflected; whence the body must of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> appear <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, blackness in a body being no more than a want of reflection. Charcoal was anciently used to distinguish the bounds of estates and inheritances; as being incorruptible, when let very deep within ground. In effect, it preserves itself so long, that there are many pieces found entire in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tombs of the northern nations. M. Dodart says, there is charcoal made of corn, probably as old as the days of Caesar: he adds, that it has kept so well, that the wheat may be still distinguished from the rye; which he looks on as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of its incorruptibility. The operation of charring wood is performed in the following manner: The wood intended for this purpose is cut into proper lengths, and piled up in heaps near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the charcoal is intended to be made: when a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wood is thus prepared, they begin constructing their stacks, for which there are three methods. The first is this: They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> a proper spot of ground, of about 12 or 15 feet in diameter, near the piles of wood; in the centre of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILLET">billet</a> of wood, split across at one end and pointed at the other, is fixed with its pointed extremity in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and two pieces of wood inserted through the clefts of the other end, forming four <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; against these <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> pieces four other billets of wood are placed, one end on the ground, and the other leaning against the angles. This being finished, a number of large and straight billets are laid on the ground to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, each being as it were the radius of the circular area: on this floor a proper quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> or small wood is fired, in order to fill up the interstices, when the floor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be complete; and in order to keep the billets in the same order and position in which they were first arranged, pegs or flumes are driven into the ground in the circumference of the circle, about a foot distant from one another: upon this floor a stage is built with billets set upon one end, but something inclining towards the central billet; and on the tops of these another floor is laid in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, but of shorter billets, as the whole is, when finished, to form a cone. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> method of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the stacks for making charcoal is performed in this manner: A long pole is erected in the centre of the area above described, and several small billets ranged round the pole on their ends: the interstices between these billets and the pole is filled with dry brushwood, then a floor is laid on that stage, in a reclining position, and on that a second floor, &c. in the same manner as described above; but in the lower floor there is a billet larger and longer than the rest, extending from the central central pole to some distance beyond the circumference of the circle. The third method is this: A chimney, or aperture of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> form, is built with billets in the centre, from the bottom to the top; and round these, floors and inclined slates are erected, in the same manner as in the stacks above described, except that the base of this, instead of being circular like the others, is square; and the whole stack, when completed, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. The stack of either form being thus finished, is coated over with turf, and the surface plastered with a mixture of earth and charcoal dust well tempered together. The next operation is the setting the stack on fire. In order to this, if it be formed according to the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, the central billet in the upper stage is drawn out, and some pieces of very dry and combustible wood are placed in the void space, called, by workmen, the chimney, and fire set to these pieces. If the stack be built according to the second construction, the central pole is drawn out, together with the large horizontal billet above described; and the void space occupied by the latter being filled with pieces of very dry combustible wood, the fire is applied to it at the base of the stack. With regard to the third construction, the square aperture or chimney is filled with small pieces of very dry wood, and the fire applied to it at the top or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> of the pyramidal stack. When the stack is set on fire, either at the top or bottom, the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is necessary in the workman; for in the proper management of the fire the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> difficulty attending the art of making good charcoal consists. In order to this, care is taken, as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> begins to issue some height above the chimney, that the aperture he covered with a piece of turf, but not so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as to hinder the smoke from passing out; and whenever the smoke appears to issue very thick from any part of the pile, the aperture must be covered with a mixture of earth and charcoal dust. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as it is necessary that every part of the stack should be equally burnt, it will be requisite for the workman to open vents in one part and shut them in another. In this manner the fire must be kept up till the charcoal be sufficiently burnt, which will happen in about two days and a half if the wood be dry; but if green, the operation will not be finished in less than three days. When the charcoal is thought to be sufficiently burnt, which is easily known from the appearance of the smoke, and the flames no longer issuing with impetuosity through the vents; all the apertures are to be closed up very carefully with a mixture of earth and charcoal dust, which, by excluding all access of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, prevents the coals from being any further consumed, and the fire goes out of itself. In this condition it is suffered to remain, till the whole is sufficiently cooled; when the cover is removed, and the charcoal is taken away. If the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is skilfully managed, the coals will exactly retain the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the pieces of wood: some are said to have been so dexterous as to char an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> without altering even the figure of the feather. There are considerable differences in the coals of different vegetables, in regard to their habitu to fire: the very light coals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, some fungi, &c., readily catch fire from a spark, and soon burn out; the more dense ones of woods and roots are set on fire more difficultly, and burn more slowly: the coals of the black berry-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> alder, of the hazel, the willow, and the lime tree, are said to answer best for the making of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> and other pyrotechnical compositions, perhaps from their being easily inflammable: for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of metallic calces those of the heavier woods, as the oak and the beech, are preferable, these seeming to contain a larger proportion of the phlogistic principle, and that, perhaps, in a more fixed state; considered as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fuel, those of the heavy woods give the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and require the most plentiful supply of air to keep them <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>; those of the light woods preserve a glowing heat, without much draught of air, till the coals themselves are consumed; the bark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> crackles and flies about in burning, which the coal of the wood itself very seldom does. Mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> makers, engravers, &c., find charcoal of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to polish their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> plates after they have been rubbed clean with powdered pumice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Plates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> are polishable in the same way, and a glost may be afterwards given with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">tripoli</a>. The coals of different substances are also used as pigments; hence the bone-black, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>-black, &c., of the shops.
