Most of the paints of this kind, besides their incorruptibility, have the advantage of a full <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> freely in all the forms in which powdery pigments are applied; provided they have been carefully prepared, by thoroughly burning the subject in a close vessel, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> the coal into a powder of due fineness. Pieces of charcoal are used also in their entire state for tracing the outlines of drawings, &c.; in which intention they have an excellence, that their mark is easily wiped out. For these purposes, either the finer pieces of common charcoal are picked out and cut to a proper shape; or the pencils are formed of wood, and afterwards burnt into charcoal in a proper vessel well covered. The artists commonly make choice of the smaller branches of the tree freed from the bark and pith; and the willow and vine are preferred to all others. This choice is confirmed by the experiments of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, who has found that the wood of the trunks of trees produces charcoal of a harder <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> than their small twigs or branches; and the hard woods, such as box and guaiacum, produced coals very sensibly harder than the softer woods. Willow he prefers to all others. The shells and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> yielded coals so hard that they would scarcely mark on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> at all; while the coals of the kernels of fruits were quite soft and mellow. The several coals produced by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s experiments were levigated into fine powder, mixed both with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and applied as paints both thin and thick, and diluted with different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. All of them, when laid on thick, appeared of a strong full black, nor could it be judged that one was of a finer colour than another; diluted with white, or when spread thin, they had all somewhat of a bluish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. Horns, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> both of fishes and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> animals, gave coals rather glossier and deeper coloured than vegetables; and which, in general, were very hard, so as difficultly, or not at all, to stain paper. Here also the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the coal seemed to depend on that of the subject from whence it was prepared; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, blood, and the flaky parts of animals, yielded soft coals. Some of these differed from others very sensibly in colour; that of ivory is superior to all the rest, and indisputably the finest of all the charcoal blacks. The animal coals had much less of the bluish cast in them than the vegetable, many of them inclining rather to a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. Charred pit coal, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, seemed to have this blueness in a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. For the chemical properties of charcoal see <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHARDIN

Pages 426-426

Sir John, a celebrated traveller, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1643. His father, who was a jeweller, had him educated in the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; after which he travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. He traded in jewels, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1713. The account he wrote of his travels is much esteemed.

CHARENTON

Pages 426-426

the name of two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of France, the one upon the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a> and the Bourbnois; the other in the Ille de France, near the confluence of the Marne with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">CHARLES</a> the Lydian, a celebrated statuary, was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Lyfippus; and made the famous Colossus of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>. Flourished 288 years before Christ.

CHARGE

Pages 426-426
or rather Overcharge, in Painting, is an exaggerated representation of any person; wherein the likeness is preferred, but at the same time ridiculed. Few painters have the genius necessary to succeed in these charges: the method is, to select and heighten something already amiss in the face, whether by way of defect, or redundancy: thus, e.g., if Nature hath given a man a nose a little larger than ordinary, the painter falls in with her, and makes the nose extravagantly long: or if the nose be naturally too short, in the painting it will be a mere stump; and thus of the other parts.

CHARGED

Pages 426-426

in electrical experiments, is when a phial, pane of glass, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other electric substance, properly coated on both sides, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> communicated to it; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the one fide is always electrified positively, and the other negatively.

CHARIOT

Pages 426-427

a half <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, having only a seat behind, with a stool before. See Coach. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, were called by the several names of bigae, trigae, &c., according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of horses applied to draw them. Every chariot carried two men, who were probably the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> and the charioteer; and we read of several men of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> and valour employed in driving the chariot. When the warriors came to encounter in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> fight, they alighted out of the chariot, and fought on foot; but when they were weary, which often happened by reason of their armour, they retired into their chariot, and thence annoyed their enemies with darts and missile weapons. These chariots were made so strong, that they lasted for several generations. Besides this sort, we find frequent mention of the currus falcati, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those chariots armed with hooks or scythes, with which whole ranks of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were cut off together, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had not the art of avoiding the danger; these were not only used by the Persians, Syrians, Egyptians, &c., but we find them among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Chariot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a>.

CHARISIA

Pages 427-427

in the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a wake, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> night festival, instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Graces. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the whole night, most of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was spent in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>; after which, cakes made of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flour mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and other sweetmeats, were distributed among the attendants.—Charisia is also sometimes used to signify the sweetmeats used on such occasions.

CHARISIUS

Pages 427-427

in the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> given to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. The word is derived from ἡμέρας γρατίας, "<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>" <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "favour;" he being the god by whose influence men obtain the favour and affection of one another. On which account the Greeks used at their meals to make a libation of a cup to Jupiter Charisius.

CHARISTIA

Pages 427-427

a festival of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, celebrated in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February, wherein the relations by blood and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> met, in order to preserve a good correspondence; and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there happened to be any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> among them, it might be the more easily accommodated by the good humour and mirth of the entertainment. Ovid, Fasti, i. 617.

CHARISTICARY

Pages 427-427

commendatory, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> donatory, a person to whom is given the enjoyment of the revenues of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, or benefice. The Charisticaries among the Greeks, were a kind of donatories, or commendatories, who enjoyed all the revenues of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> and monasteries, without giving an account thereof to any person.—The original of this abuse is referred to the Iconoclastæ, particularly Constantine Copronymus, the avowed enemy of the monks, whose monasteries he gave away to strangers. In after times, the emperors and patriarchs gave many to people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, not by way of gift to reap any temporal advantage from them, but to repair, beautify, and patronize them. At length avarice crept in, and those in good condition were given away, especially such as were rich; and at last they were all given away, rich and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, those of men and of women, and that to laymen and to married men.

CHARITY

Pages 427-434

among divines, one of the three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> theological virtues, consisting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of God and of our neighbour, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and disposition of loving God with all our heart, and our neighbour as ourselves. Charity is also used for the effect of a moral virtue, which consists in supplying the necessities of others, whether with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, counsel, assistance, or the like. As pecuniary relief is generally the most efficacious, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that from which we are most apt to execute ourselves, this branch of the duty merits particular illustration; and a better cannot be offered than what is contained in the following extracts (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may be permitted to make them) from the elegant Moral System of Archdeacon Paley. Whether pity be an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> or a habit, it is in fact a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which God appointed; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> cause for which it was appointed, is to afford to the miserable, in the compassion of their fellow-creatures, a remedy for those inequalities and distresses which God foretold that many must be exposed to, under The Christian Scriptures are more copious and explicit upon this duty than almost any other. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> which Christ hath left us of the proceedings of the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, establishes the obligation of bounty beyond controversy. "When the Son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> shall come in his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and all the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory, and before him shall be gathered all nations; and he shall separate them one from another. Then shall the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> say unto them on his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Come ye blessed of my Father, inherit the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was hungry, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink; I was a stranger, and ye took me in; naked, and ye clothed me; I was sick, and ye visited me; I was in prison, and ye came unto me. And inasmuch as ye have done it to one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." It is not necessary to understand this passage as a literal account of what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> actually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> on that day. Supposing it only a metaphorical description of the rules and principles by which the Supreme Arbiter of our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> will regulate his decisions, it conveys the same lesson to us: it equally demonstrates how <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value and importance these duties in the sight of God are, and what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARES">tares</a> will be laid upon them. The apostles also describe this virtue as propitiating the divine favour in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. And their recommendations have produced their effect. It does not appear that, before the times of Christianity, an infirmary, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, or public charity of any kind, existed in the world; whereas most countries in Christendom have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> abounded with these institutions. To which may be added, that a spirit of private liberality seems to flourish amidst the decay of many other virtues: not to mention the legal provision for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, which obtains in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and which was unknown and unthought of by the most polished nations of antiquity. St Paul adds upon the subject an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; and which is practicable by all who have anything to give. "Upon the first day of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> (or any other stated time) let every one of you lay by in store, as God hath prospered him." By which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> may be understood to recommend, what is the very thing wanting with most men, the being charitable upon a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; that is, from a deliberate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of our fortunes with the reasonable expenses and expectations of our families, to compute what we can spare, and to lay by so much for charitable purposes, in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> or other. The mode will be a consideration afterwards. The effect which Christianity produced upon some of its converts, was such as might be looked for from a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> coming with full force and miraculous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> upon the consciences of mankind. It overwhelmed all worldly considerations in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of a more important existence. "And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; neither said any of them that aught of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>.—Neither was there any among them that lacked; for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at the apostles feet; and distribution was made unto every man according as he had need," Acts iv. 32. Nevertheless, this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of goods, however it manifested the sincere zeal of the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, is no precedent for our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. It was confined to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> not long there; was never enjoined upon any (Acts v. 4.); and, although it might <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with the particular circumstances of a small and select <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, is altogether impracticable in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and mixed community. The conduct of the apostles upon the occasion deserves to be noticed. Their followers laid down their fortunes at their feet; but so far were they from taking advantage of this unlimited confidence to enrich themselves or establish their authority, that they soon after got rid of this business as inconsistent with the main object of their mission, and transferred the custody and management of the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> to deacons elected to that office by the people at large (Acts vi.). There are three kinds of charity, our author observes, which prefer a claim to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. 1. The first, and apparently one of the best, is to give stated and considerable sums, by way of pension or annuity to individuals or families, with whose behaviour and distresses we ourselves are acquainted. In speaking of considerable sums, it is meant only, that five pounds, or any other sum, given at once, or divided amongst five or fewer families, will do more good than the same sum distributed amongst a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in drillings or half crowns; and that, because it is more likely to be properly applied by the persons who receive it. A poor fellow who can find no better <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> than to drink his benefactor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and purchase half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s recreation for himself, would hardly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> for any such purpose, or be so improvident as not to lay it by for an occasion of importance, for his rent, his clothing, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, or stock of winter's provision. It is a still greater recommendation of this kind of charity, that pensions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>, which are paid regularly, and can be expected at the time, are the only way by which we can prevent one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a poor man's sufferings, the dread of want. 2. But as this kind of charity supposes that proper objects of such expensive benefactions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> within our private knowledge and observation, which does not happen to all, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> method of doing good, which is in every one's power who has the money to spare, is by subscription to public charities. Public charities admit of this argument in their favour, that your money goes farther towards attaining the end for which it is given, that it can do by any private and separate benevolence. A guinea, for example, contributed to an infirmary, becomes the means of providing one patient, at least, with a physician, surgeon, apothecary, with medicine, diet, lodging, and suitable attendance; which is not the tenth part of what the same assistance, if it could be procured at all, would cost to a sick person or family in any other situation. 3. The last, and compared with the former, the lowest exertion of benevolence, is in the relief of beggars. Nevertheless, the indiscriminate rejection of all who implore our alms, in this way, is by no means approved. proved. Some may perish by such a conduct. Men are sometimes overtaken by distress; for which all other relief would come too late. Besides which, resolutions of this kind compel us to offer such violence to our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, as may go near, in a little while, to suffocate the principle itself; which is a very serious consideration. A good man, if he do not surrender himself to his feelings without reserve, will at least lend an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to importunities which come accompanied with outward attestations of distress; and after a patient hearing of the complaint, will <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> himself by the circumstances and credibility of the account that he receives. There are other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of charity well contrived to make the money expended go far; such as keeping down the price of fuel or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a monopoly or temporary scarcity, by purchasing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> at the best market, and retailing them at prime cost, or at a small loss; or the adding a bounty to a particular species of labour, when the price is accidentally depressed. The proprietors of large estates have it in their power to facilitate the maintenance, and thereby encourage the establishment of families (which is one of the noblest purposes to which the rich and great can convert their endeavours), by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> cottages, splitting farms, erecting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, cultivating wastes, embanking the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, draining marshes, and other expedients, which the situation of each estate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out. If the profits of these undertakings do not repay the expense, let the authors of them <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> to the account of charity. It is true of almost all such projects, that the public is a gainer by them, whatever the owner be. And where the loss can be spared, this consideration is sufficient. It is become a question of some importance, Under what circumstances works of charity ought to be done in private, and when they may be made public without detracting from the merit of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>? If indeed they ever may, the Author of our religion having delivered a rule upon this subject, which seems to enjoy universal fealty. "When thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth; that thy alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret, himself shall reward thee openly." (Matt. vi. 3, 4). From the preamble to this prohibition it is plain, that our Saviour's sole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to forbid ostentation, and all publishing of good works which proceeds from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>. "Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them; otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven; therefore, when thou doest thine alms, do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a> before thee, as the hypocrites do, in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto thee, they have their reward," v. 2. There are motives for the doing our alms in public besides those of ostentation; with which therefore our Saviour's rule has no concern: such as to testify our approbation of some particular species of charity, and to recommend it to others; to take off the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> which the want, or, which is the same thing, the suppression, of our name in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of contributors, might excite against the charity or against ourselves. And so long as these motives are free from any mixture of vanity, they are in no danger of invading our Saviour's prohibition: they rather seem to comply with another direction which he has left us: "Let your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." If it be necessary to propose a precise distinction upon the subject, there can be none better than the following: When our bounty is beyond our fortune or station, that is, when it is more than could be expected from us, our charity should be private, if privacy be practicable: when it is not more than might be expected, it may be public: for we cannot hope to influence others to the imitation of extraordinary generosity, and therefore want, in the former case, the only justifiable reason for making it public. The pretences by which men excuse themselves from giving to the poor are various; as, 1. "That they have nothing to spare;" i.e., nothing, for which they have not some other use; nothing, which their plan of expense, together with the savings they have resolved to lay by, will not exhaust; never reflecting whether it be in their power, or that it is their duty, to retrench their expenses, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> their plan, "that they may have to give to them that need;" or rather that this ought to have been part of their plan originally. 2. "That they have families of their own, and that charity begins at home." A father is no doubt bound to adjust his economy with a view to the reasonable demands of his family upon his fortune; and until a sufficiency for these is acquired, or in due time probably will be acquired (for in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> is enough, he is justified in declining expensive liberality; for to take from those who want, in order to give to those who want, adds nothing to the stock of public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. Thus far, therefore, and no farther, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> in question is an excuse for parsimony, and an answer to those who solicit our bounty. 3. "That charity does not consist in giving money, but in benevolence, philanthropy, love to all mankind, goodness of heart," &c. Hear St James. "If a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled, notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful for the body, what doth it profit?" (James ii. 15, 16.). 4. "That giving to the poor is not mentioned in St Paul's description of charity, in the 13th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the first epistle to the Corinthians." This is not a description of charity, but of good nature; and it is not necessary that every duty be mentioned in every place. 5. "That they pay the poor <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>." They might as well allege that they pay their debts; for the poor have the same right to that portion of a man's property which the laws assign them, that the man himself has to the remainder. 6. "That they employ many poor persons;"—for their own sake, not the poor's—otherwise it is a good plea. 7. "That the poor do not suffer so much as we imagine; that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and habit have reconciled them to the evils of their condition, and make them easy under it." Habit can never reconcile human nature to the extremities of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, and thirst, any more than it can reconcile the hand to the touch. Charity of Hippolitus, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> founded about the end of the 16th century, by one Bernardino Alvarez, a Mexican, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St Hippolitus the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>; and approved by Pope Gregory XIII. Charity of our Lady, in church <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a religious order in France, which, though charity was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> motive of their union, grew, in length of time so disorderly and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, that their order dwindled, and at last became extinct. There is still at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, a religious order of women, called nuns hospitaliers of the charity of our lady. The religious of this hospital are by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> obliged to administer to the necessities of the poor and sick, but those only women. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLATAN">Charlatan</a>, or Charletan, signifies an empiric or quack, who retails his medicines on a public stage, and draws people about him with his buffooneries, feats of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, &c. The word, according to Calepine, comes from the Italian, ceretano; of Caretum, a town near Spoleto in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where these impostors are said to have first risen. Menage derives it from ciarlatano, and that from circulatorius or circulator, a quack. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., king of France by succession, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the west by conquest in 800 (which laid the foundation of the dynasty of the western Franks, who ruled the empire 472 years till the time of Rodolphus Auspurgensis, the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>). Charlemagne was as illustrious in the cabinet as in the field; and, though he could not write his name, was the patron of men of letters, the rector of learning, and a wise <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>; he wanted only the virtue of humanity to render him the most accomplished of men; but when we read of his beheading 4500 Saxons, solely for their loyalty to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, in opposing his conquests, we cannot think he merits the extravagant encomiums bestowed on him by some historians. He died in 814, in the 74th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and 47th of his reign. France had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> sovereigns of this name, of whom Charles V. merited the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the wise (crowned in 1364, died in 1380); and Charles VIII., signalized himself in the field by rapid victories in Italy; (crowned in 1483, died in 1498). The rest do not deserve particular mention in this place. See History of France. Charlemont, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a> in the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, about eighteen miles south of Namur. E. Long. 4. 40. N. Lat. 50. 10. Charlemont is also the name of a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated on the river Blackwater, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>, and province of Ulster, about six miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNGANNON">Dungannon</a>. W. Long. 6. 50. N. Lat. 50. 16. Charleroy, a strong town in the province of Namur in the Austrian Netherlands, situated on the river Sambre, about 19 miles west of Namur. E. Long. 46. 20. N. Lat. 50. 30. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES_MARTEL">Charles Martel</a>, a renowned conqueror in the early annals of France. He deposed and restored Childeric Childebert king of France; and had the entire <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the kingdom, first with the title of mayor of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and afterwards as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of France; but he would not accept the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. He died regretted, in 741. Charles le Gros, emperor of the west in 881, king of Italy and Swabia, memorable for his reverse of fortune; being dethroned at a diet held near <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, by the French, the Italians, and the Germans, in 887: after which he was obliged to submit on the bounty of the archbishop of Mentz. He died in 888. Charles V. (emperor and king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>) was son of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> I. archduke of Austria, and of Jane <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Castile. He was born at Ghent, February 24, 1500, and succeeded to the crown of Spain in 1517. Two years afterwards he was chosen emperor at Frankfort after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Maximilian his grandfather. He was a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> and politician: and his ambition was not satisfied with the many kingdoms and provinces he possessed; for he supposed, with reason, to have aspired at universal empire. He is said to have fought 60 battles, in most of which he was victorious. He took the king of France (Francis I.) prisoner, and sold him his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> on very hard terms; yet afterwards, when the people of Ghent revolted, he asked leave to pass through his dominions: and though the generous king thus had him in his power, and had an opportunity of revenging his ill treatment, yet he received and attended him with all pomp and magnificence. He sacked Rome, and took the pope prisoner; and the cruelties which his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> exercised there are said to have exceeded those of the northern barbarians. Yet the pious emperor went into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> on account of this conquest: forbade the ringing of bells; commanded processions to be made, and prayers to be offered up for the deliverance of the pope his prisoner; yet did not inflict the least <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> on those who treated the holy father and the holy see with such inhumanity. He is accused by some Roman writers of favouring the Lutheran principles, which he might easily have extirpated. But the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, he found his account in the divisions which that fact occasioned; and he forever made his advantage of them, sometimes against the pope, sometimes against France, and at other times against the empire itself. He was a great traveller, and made 50 different journeys into Germany, Spain, Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, France, England, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. Though he had been successful in many unjust enterprises, yet his last attempt on <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>, which he besieged with an army of 100,000 men, was very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, and very unsuccessful. Vexed at the reverse of fortune which seemed to attend his latter days, and oppressed by sickness, which unfitted him any longer for holding the reins of government with steadiness, or to guide them with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, he resigned his dominions to his brother Ferdinand and his son Philip; and retreated to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Justus near <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a> in Etruria. When Charles entered this retreat, he formed such a plan of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for himself as would have suited a private <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of moderate fortune. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> was neat, but plain; his domestics few; his intercourse with them familiar; all the cumbersome and ceremonious forms of attendance on his person were entirely abolished, as destructive of that social ease and tranquillity which he courted in order to soothe the remainder of his days. As the mildness of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, together with his deliverance from the burdens and cares of government, procured him at first a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> from the acute pains of the gout, with which he had been long tormented, he enjoyed perhaps more complete satisfaction in this humble solitude than all his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> had ever yielded him. The ambitious thoughts and projects which had so long engrossed and disquieted him were quite effaced from his mind. Far from taking any part in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> transactions of the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he restrained his curiosity even from an inquiry concerning them; and he seemed to view the busy <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> which he had abandoned with all the contempt and indifference arising from his thorough <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of its vanity, as well as from the pleasing reflection of having disentangled himself from its cares. Other amusements, and other subjects, now occupied him. Sometimes he cultivated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in his garden with his own hand; sometimes he rode out to the neighbouring wood on a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, the only one that he kept, attended by a single <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> on foot. When his infirmities confined him to his apartment, which often happened, and deprived him of these more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> recreations, he either admitted a few gentlemen who resided near the monastery to visit him, and entertained them familiarly at his table; or he employed himself in studying <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> principles, and in forming curious works of mechanism, of which he had always been remarkably fond, and to which his genius was peculiarly turned. With this view he had engaged Turriano, one of the most ingenious artists of that age, to accompany him in his retreat. He laboured together with him in framing models of the most useful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, as well as in making experiments with regard to their respective powers; and it was not seldom that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the monarch assisted or perfected the inventions of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. He relieved his mind at intervals with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> and more fantastic works of mechanism, in fashioning puppets, which, by the structure of internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, mimicked the gestures and actions of men, to the no small astonishment of the ignorant monks, who, beholding movements which they could not comprehend, sometimes distrusted their own senses, and sometimes suspected Charles and Turriano of being in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> with invisible powers. He was particularly curious with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of clocks and watches; and having found, after repeated trials, that he could not bring any two of them to go exactly alike, he reflected, it is said, with a mixture of surprise as well as regret, on his own folly, in having bestowed so much time and labour in the more vain attempt of bringing mankind to a precise uniformity of sentiment concerning the intricate and mysterious doctrines of religion. But in what manner forever Charles disposed of the rest of his time, he constantly reserved a considerable portion of it for religious exercises. He regularly attended divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the chapel of the monastery, every morning and evening; he took great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> books of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, particularly the works of St Augustine and St Bernard; and conversed much with his confessor, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of the monastery, Thus did Charles pass the first year of his retreat in a manner not unbecoming a man perfectly disengaged from the affairs of this present life, and standing on the confines of a future world, either in innocent amusements which soothed his pains, and relieved a mind worn out with excessive application to business; or in devout occupations, which he deemed necessary in preparing for another state. But, about six months before his death, the gout, after a longer intermission than usual, returned with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> increase of violence. His shattered <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> had not strength enough remaining to withstand such a shock. It enfeebled his mind as much as his body; and from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> we hardly discern any traces of that sound and masculine understanding which distinguished Charles among his contemporaries. An illiberal and timid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> depressed his spirit. He had no relish for amusements of any kind. He endeavoured to conform, in his manner of living, to all the rigour of monastic austerity. He defied no other society than that of monks, and was almost continually employed in chanting with them the hymns of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. As an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> for his sins, he gave himself the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> in secret, with such severity, that the whip of cords which he employed as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of his punishment, was found, after his decease, tinged with his blood. Nor was he satisfied with these acts of mortification, which, however severe, were not unexampled. The timorous and distrustful solicitude which always accompanies superstition, still continued to disquiet him, and depreciating all that he had done, prompted him to aim at something extraordinary, at some new and singular <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of piety, that would display his zeal, and merit the favour of heaven. The act on which he fixed was as wild and uncommon as any that superstition ever suggested to a disordered fancy. He resolved to celebrate his own obsequies before his death. He ordered his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> to be erected in the chapel of the monastery. His domestics marched thither in funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> tapers in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. He himself followed in his shroud. He was laid in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> with much solemnity. The service for the dead was chaunted; and Charles joined in the prayers which were offered up for the rest of his soul, mingling his tears with those which his attendants shed, as if they had been celebrating a real funeral. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> closed with sprinkling holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on the coffin in the usual form, and, all the assistants retiring, the doors of the chapel were shut. Then Charles rose out of the coffin, and withdrew to his apartment, full of those awful sentiments which such a singular solemnity was calculated to inspire. But either the fatiguing length of the ceremony, or the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> which this image of death left on his mind, affected him so much, that next day he was seized with a fever. His feeble frame could not long resist its violence; and he expired on the 21st of September, after a life of 58 years 6 months and 21 days. Charles I. Kings of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. See Britain, Charles II. No 49—254. Charles XII, king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, was born in 1682. By his father's will, the administration was lodged in the hands of the queen dowager Eleonora, with five senators, till the young prince was 18; but he was declared <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> at 15, by the states convened at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>. The beginning of his administration raised no favourable ideas of him, as he was thought both by Swedes and foreigners to be a person of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> capacity. But the difficulties that gathered round him, soon afforded him an opportunity to display his real character. Three powerful princes, Frederick king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, Augustus king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Muscovy, presuming on his youth, confinded his ruin almost at the same instant. Their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> alarming the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, they were for diverting the storm by negotiations; but Charles, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> that astonished them, said, "I am resolved never to enter upon an unjust <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, nor to put an end to a just one but by the destruction of my enemies. My resolution is fixed: I will attack the first who shall declare against me; and when I have conquered him, I may hope to strike a terror into the rest." The old counsellors received his orders with admiration; and were still more surprized when they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him on a sudden renounce all the enjoyments of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, reduce his table to the utmost frugality, dress like a common soldier, and, full of the ideas of Alexander and Caesar, propose these two conquerors for his models in everything but their vices. The king of Denmark began by ravaging the territories of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. Upon this Charles carried the war into the heart of Denmark, and made such progress that the king of Denmark thought it best to accept of peace, which was concluded in 1700. He next resolved to advance against the king of Poland, who had blocked up <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>. He had no sooner given orders for his troops to go into winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, than he received advice that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Horne was governor, was besieged by an army of 100,000 Muscovites. This made him alter his measures, and move towards the czar; and at Narva he gained a surprising victory, which cost him not above 2000 men killed and wounded. The Muscovites were forced to retire from the provinces they had invaded. He pursued his conquests, till he penetrated as far as where the diet of Poland was sitting; when he made them declare the throne of Poland vacant, and elect Stanislaus their king; then making himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Saxony, he obliged Augustus himself to renounce the crown of Poland, and acknowledged Stanislaus by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of congratulation on his accession. All Europe was surprized with the expeditious finishing of this great negotiation, but more at the disinterestedness of the king of Sweden, who satisfied himself with the bare reputation of this victory, without demanding an inch of ground for enlarging his dominions. After thus reducing the king of Denmark to peace, placing a new king on the throne of Poland, having humbled the emperor of Germany, and protected the Lutheran religion, Charles prepared to penetrate into Muscovy, in order to dethrone the czar. He quickly obliged the Muscovites to abandon Poland, pursued them into their own country, and won several battles over them. The czar, disposed to peace, ventured to make some proposals; Charles only answered, "I will treat with the czar at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>." When this haughty answer was brought to Peter, he said, "My brother Charles still affects to act the Alexander, but I flatter myself..." The event justified him: for the Muscovites, already beaten into discipline, and under a prince of such talents as Peter, entirely destroyed the Swedish army at the memorable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Pultowa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 8, 1709; on which decisive day, Charles lost the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of nine years labour, and of almost 150 battles! The king, with a small troop, pursued by the Muscovites, passed the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORISTHENES">Boristhenes</a> to Oczakow in the Turkish territories; and from thence, through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> countries, arrived at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENDER">Bender</a>; where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, when informed of his arrival, sent orders for accommodating him in the best manner, and appointed him a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. Near Bender Charles built a house, and entrenched himself; and had with him 1800 men, who were all clothed and fed, with their horses, at the expense of the grand signior. Here he formed a design of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the Ottoman arms upon his enemies; and is said to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> from the vizir of being sent into Muscovy with 200,000 men. While he remained here, he insensibly acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for books; he read the tragedies of Corneille and Racine, with the works of Defreux, whose satires he relished, but did not much admire his other works. When he read that passage in which the author represents Alexander as a fool and a madman, he tore out the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>. He would sometimes play at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>; but when he recovered from his wounds, he renewed his fatigues in exercising his men: he tired three horses a-day; and those who courted his favour were all day in their boots. To dispose the Ottoman Porte to this war, he detached about 800 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> and Cossacks of his retinue, with orders to pass the Nester, that runs by Bender, and to observe what passed on the frontiers of Poland. The Muscovite troops, dispersed in those quarters, fell immediately upon this little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and pursued them even to the territories of the grand signior. This was what the king expected. His ministers at the Porte excited the Turks to vengeance; but the czar's money removed all difficulties, and Charles found himself in a manner prisoner among the Tartars. He imagined the sultan was ignorant of the intrigues of his grand vizir. Poniatowski undertook to make his complaints to the grand signior. The sultan, in answer, some days after, sent Charles five Arabian horses, one of which was covered with a saddle and houing of great richness; with an obliging letter, but conceived in such general terms, as gave reason to suspect that the minister had done nothing without the sultan's consent: Charles therefore refused them. Poniatowski had the courage to form a design of deposing the grand vizir, who accordingly was deprived of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and wealth, and banished. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the empire was given to Numan Cuproughly; who persuaded his master, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> forbade him to invade the czar, who had done him no injury; but to succour the king of Sweden as an unfortunate prince in his dominions. He sent his majesty 800 purses, every one of which amounted to 500 crowns, and advised him to return peaceably to his own dominions. Charles rejected this advice, threatening to hang up the bailiffs, and shave the beards of any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a> who brought him such messages, and sent word that he should depend upon the grand signior's promise, and hoped to re-enter Poland as a conqueror with an army of Turks. After various intrigues at the Porte, an order was sent to attack this head of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, as he was called, and to take him either alive or dead. He stood a siege in his house, with 40 domestics, against the Turkish army; killed no less than 20 janizaries with his own hand; and performed prodigies of valour on a very unnecessary and unwarrantable occasion. But the house being set on fire, and himself wounded, he was at last taken prisoner, and sent to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a>, where the grand signior gave him audience, and promised to make good all the damages he had sustained. At last, after a stay of above five years, he left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; and, having disguised himself, traversed Wallachia, Transylvania, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and Germany, attended only by one person; and in fifteen days' riding, during which time he never went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, came to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STRALSUND">Stralsund</a> at midnight, November 21, 1714. His boots were cut from his swollen legs, and he was put to bed; where, when he had slept some hours, the first thing he did was to review his troops, and examine the state of the fortifications. He sent out orders that very day to renew the war with more vigour than ever. But affairs were now much changed: Augustus had recovered the throne of Poland; Sweden had lost many of its provinces, and was without money, trade, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, or troops. The kings of Denmark and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> seized the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Rugen; and besieged him in Stralsund, which surrendered; but Charles escaped to Carlisle. When his country was threatened with invasion by so many princes, he, to the surprize of all Europe, marched into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> with 20,000 men. A very few Danes might have stopped the Swedish army; but such a quick invasion they could not foresee. Europe was yet more at a loss to find the czar so quiet, and not making a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon Sweden, as he had before agreed with his allies. This inaction was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of one of the greatest designs, and at the same time the most difficult of any, that were ever formed by the imagination of man. In short, a scheme was set on foot for a reconciliation with the czar; for replacing Stanislaus on the throne of Poland; and setting James II.'s son upon that of England, besides restoring the duke of Holstein to his dominions. Charles was pleased with these grand ideas, though without building much upon them, and gave his minister leave to act at large. In the mean time, Charles was going to make a second attempt upon Norway in 1718; and he flattered himself with being master of that kingdom in six months; but while he was examining the works at Frederickshall, a place of great strength and importance, which is reckoned to be the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of that kingdom, he was killed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from the enemy, as has been generally believed, though it has been also reported that he fell by the treachery of one of his own officers, who had been bribed for that purpose. This prince experienced the extremes of prosperity and of adversity, without being softened by the one or disturbed for a moment at the other; but was a man rather extraordinary than great, and fitter to be admired than imitated. He was honoured by the Turks for his rigid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from wine, and his regularity in attending public devotion. As to his person, he was tall and of a noble mien, had a fine open forehead, large blue eyes, flaxen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, fair Charles had a fair <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, a handsome nose, but little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, and a laugh not agreeable. His manners were harsh and austere, not to say <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>; and as to religion, he was indifferent towards all, though exteriorly a Lutheran, and a strong believer in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>. A few anecdotes will illustrate his character. No dangers, however great, made the least impression upon him. When a horse or two were killed under him at the battle of Narva, in 1702, he leaped nimbly upon fresh ones, saying, "These people find me <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>." One day, when he was dictating letters to a secretary, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a> fell through the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> into the next room of the house where they were sitting. The secretary, terrified left the house should come down upon them, let his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> drop out of his hand: "What is the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>?" says the king calmly. The secretary could only reply, "Ah, Sir, the bomb." "The bomb (says the king) what has the bomb to do with what I am dictating to you! Go on." He preferred more humanity than is usually found among conquerors. Once, in the middle of an action, finding a young Swedish officer wounded and unable to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, he obliged the officer to take his horse, and continued to command his infantry on foot. The princess Lubomirski, who was very much in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and good graces of Augustus, falling by accident into the hands of one of his officers, he ordered her to be set at liberty: saying, "That he did not make war with women." One day, near Leipzig, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> threw himself at his feet, with a complaint against a grenadier, that he had robbed him of certain eatables provided for himself and his family. "Is it true (said Charles sternly), that you have robbed this man?" The soldier replied, "Sir, I have not done near so much harm to this man as your majesty has done to his master; for you have taken from Augustus a kingdom, whereas I have only taken from this poor scoundrel a dinner." Charles made the peasant amends, and pardoned the soldier for his firmness: "However, my friend (says he to him), you will do well to recollect that if I took a kingdom from Augustus, I did not take it for myself." Though Charles lived hardly himself, a soldier did not fear to remonstrate to him against some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, which was very black and mouldy, and which yet was the only provision the troops had. Charles called for a piece of it, and calmly ate it up; saying, "that it was indeed not good, but that it might be eaten." From the danger he was in in Poland, when he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the Saxon troops in 1702, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> was exhibited at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARIENBURG">Marienburg</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> was represented to the disadvantage of the Swedes. "Oh, (says Charles, hearing of it), I am far from envying them this pleasure. Let them beat me in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> as long as they will, provided I do but beat them in the field." He wrote some observations on war, and on his own campaigns from 1700 to 1709: but the MS. was lost at the unfortunate battle of Pultowa.

CHARLES'S CAPE

Pages 434-434

a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, forming the northern headland of the strait that enters the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Chesapeake.

CHARLES'S FORT

Pages 434-434

a fortress in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated at the mouth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINSALE">Kinsale</a> harbour. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 20' N. Lat. 51° 21'.

CHARLESTON

Pages 434-435

the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of South Carolina, is the most considerable town in the state; situated in the district of the same name, and on the tongue of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> formed by the confluent streams of Ashley and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">Cooper</a>, which are short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and navigable. These waters unite immediately below the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and form a spacious and convenient harbour; which communicates with the ocean <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> below Sullivan's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which it leaves on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles south-east of Charleston. In these rivers the tide rises, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, about 6½ feet; but uniformly rises 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 inches more during a night tide. The fact is certain; the cause unknown. The continual agitation which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> occasion in the waters which almost surround Charleston, the refreshing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-breezes which are regularly felt, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> arising from so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>, render this city more healthy than any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the southern states. On this account it is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of gentlemen, invalids from the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and of the rich planters from the country, who come here to spend the sickly months, as they are called, in quest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and of the social enjoyments which the city affords. And in no part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> are the social blessings enjoyed more rationally and liberally than here. Unaffected hospitality, affability, ease of manners and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, and a disposition to make their guests welcome, easy, and pleased with themselves, are characteristics of the respectable people of Charleston. In speaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, it ought to be observed, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the people of Carolina in general, that when in common with the other colonies, in the contest with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, they resolved against the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of certain luxuries, and even necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, which improve the mind, enlarge the understanding, and correct the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, were excepted; the importation of books was permitted as formerly. The land on which the town is built is flat and low, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> brackish and unwholesome. The streets are pretty regularly cut, and open beautiful prospects, and have subterranean <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> to carry off filth and keep the city clean and healthy; but are too narrow for so large a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and so warm a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. Their general breadth is from 35 to 66 feet. The houses which have been lately built, are brick, with tiled roofs. The buildings in general are elegant, and most of them are neat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a>, and well furnished. The public buildings are, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, a state-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, an armory, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-house, and an orphan's house. Here are several respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>. Part of the old <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> has been handsomely fitted up, and converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and there are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of students; but it can only be called as yet a respectable academy. Here are two banks, a branch of the national <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, and the South Carolina bank, established in 1792. The houses for public worship are two Episcopal churches, two for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>, one for Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, one for Baptists, one for German Lutherans, two for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, one for French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, a meeting-house for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, a Roman Catholic chapel, and a Jewish synagogue. Little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to the public <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>; a great proportion of the more wealthy inhabitants having plantations from which they receive supplies of almost every article of living. The country abounds Charleston with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> and wild ducks. Their beef, mutton and veal are not generally of the best kind; and few fish are found in the market. In 1787, it was computed that there were 1600 houses in this city, and 15,000 inhabitants, including 5400 slaves; and what evinces the healthiness of the place, upwards of 200 of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> inhabitants were above 60 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In 1791, there were 16,359 inhabitants, of whom 7684 were slaves. This city has often suffered much by fire: the last and most destructive happened as late as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1796. Charleston was incorporated in 1783, and divided into three wards, which choose as many wardens, from among whom the citizens elect an intendant of the city. The intendant and wardens form the city-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, who have power to make and enforce bye-laws for the regulation of the city. The value of exports from this port, in the year ending November 1787, amounted to £55,278.19s. 3d. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The number of vessels cleared from the customhouse the same year, was 947, measuring 62,118 tons; 735 of these, measuring 41,531 tons, were American; the others belonged to Great Britain, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, France, and the United <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>'s Wain, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, seven stars in the constellation called Ursae Majoris, or the Great Bear. Charleton, an island at the bottom of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, in North America, subject to Great Britain. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80°. O. N. Lat. 53°. 30'. Charleton, Walter, a learned English physician, born in 1619, was physician in ordinary to Charles I. and Charles II. One of the first members of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the college of physicians. He wrote on various subjects; but at last his narrow circumstances obliged him to retire to the island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, where he died in 1707. Charlock, the English name of the Raphanus. It is a very troublesome weed among corn, being more frequent than almost any other. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> kinds of it: the one with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> flower, the other with a white. Some fields are particularly subject to be overrun with it, especially those which have been manured with cow-dung alone, that being a manure very favourable to the growth of it. The farmers in some places are so sensible of this, that they always mix <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> dung with their cow dung, when they use it for arable land. When barley, as is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, is infested with this weed to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as to endanger the crop, it is a very good method to mow <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the charlock in May, when it is in flower, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it so low as just to take off the tops of the leaves of barley with it: by this means the barley <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> get up above the weed: and people have got four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of grain from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of such land as would have scarce yielded anything without this expedient. Where any land is particularly subject to this weed, the best method is to sow it with grass seed, and make a pasture of it; for then the plant will not be troublesome, it never growing where there is a coat of grass upon the ground. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Charlotte's Island, an island in the South sea, first discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Wallis in the Dolphin, in 1767, who took possession of it in the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> George III. Here is good water, and plenty of cocoa nuts, palm nuts, and scurvy grass. The inhabitants are of a middle stature and dark <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, with long <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hanging over their shoulders; the men are well made, and the women handsome; their clothing is a kind of coarse cloth, or matting, which they fasten about their middle. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUEEN_CHARLOTTE_S_ISLANDS">Queen Charlotte's Islands</a>, a cluster of South sea islands, discovered in 1767 by Captain Carteret. He counted seven, and there were supposed to be many more. The inhabitants of these islands are described as extremely nimble and vigorous, and almost as well qualified to live in the water as upon land: they are very warlike; and, on a quarrel with some of Captain Carteret's people, they attacked them with great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; mortally wounded the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and three of the sailors; were not at all intimidated by the firearms; and at last, notwithstanding the aversion of Captain Carteret to shed blood, he was obliged to secure the watering places by firing grape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> into the woods, which destroyed many of the inhabitants. These islands <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in S. Lat. 11°. E. Long. 164°.
