They are supposed to be the Santa Cruz of Mandana, who died there in 1595. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">Charm</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> derived from the Latin carmen, "a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>;" and used to denote a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> power, or spell, by which, with the assistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, sorcerers and witches were supposed to do wonderful things, far surpassing the power of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARNEL">Charnel</a>, or Charnel-house, a kind of portico, or gallery, usually in or near a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, over which were anciently laid the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the dead, after the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> was wholly consumed. Charnel-houses are now usually adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a>, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOX">Nox</a>, whose office was to ferry the souls of the deceased over the waters of Acheron, for which each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> was to pay a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. For this reason the Pagans had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of putting a piece of money into the mouth of the dead, in order that they might have something to pay Charon for their passage. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARONDAS">Charondas</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of the Thracians, and a native of Catanea, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, flourished 446 before Christ. He forbade any person's appearing armed in the public assemblies of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> going thither in haste, without thinking of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, he was no sooner made to observe his mistake than he ran it through his body. Charost, a town of France, in Berry, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is seated on the river Arnon. E. Long. 2°. 15'. N. Lat. 46°. 56'. Charoux, a town of France, in the Bourbonnais, seated on an eminence, near the river Sioule. It has two parishes, which are in different dioceses. E. Long. 3°. 15'. N. Lat. 46°. 10'. Charpentier, Francis, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the French academy, was born in 1620. His early capacity inclined his friends to educate him at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>; but he was much more delighted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of languages and antiquity than of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and preferred repose to tumult. M. Colbert made use of him in establishing his new academy of medals and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>; and no person of that learned society contributed more than himself toward that noble <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of medals which were struck on the considerable events that distinguished the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. He published several works,

CHARRON

Pages 435-437
Peter, the author of a book entitled *Of Wisdom*, which gained him great reputation, was born at Paris in the year 1541. After being advocate in the parliament of Paris for five or six years, he applied himself to divinity; and became so great a preacher, that the bishops of several dioceses offered him the highest dignities in their gift. He died at Paris, suddenly in the street, November 16, 1632. **Chart**, or **Sea Chart**, an hydrographical map, or a projection of some part of the s="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth's superficies in *plano*, for the use of navigators. Charts differ very considerably from geographical or land maps, which are of no use in navigation. Nor are sea charts all of the same kind, some being what we call plane charts, others Mercator charts, and others globular charts. **Plane Chart**, is a representation of some part of the superficies of the terraqueous globe, in which the meridians are supposed parallel to each other, the parallels of latitude at equal distances, and consequently the degrees of latitude and longitude everywhere equal to each other. See **Plane Chart**. **Mercator's Chart**, is that where the meridians are straight lines, parallel to each other, and equidistant; the parallels are also straight lines, and parallel to each other; but the distance between them increases from the equinoctial towards either pole, in the ratio of the secant of the latitude to the radius. See **Navigation**. **Globular Chart**, a meridional projection, wherein the distance of the eye from the plane of the meridian, upon which the projection is made, is supposed to be equal to the sine of the angle $45^\circ$. This projection comes the nearest of all to the nature of the globe, because the meridians therein are placed at equal distances; the parallels also are nearly equidistant, and consequently the several parts of the earth have their proper proportion of magnitude, distance, and situation, nearly the same as on the globe itself. See **Globular Projection**. **Hydrographic Charts**, sheets of large paper, wherein several parts of the land and sea are described, with their respective coasts, harbours, sounds, flats, rocks, shelves, sands, &c., together with the longitude and latitude of each place, and the points of the compass. See **Mercator's Chart**. **Selenographic Charts**, particular descriptions of the spots, appearances, and maculae of the moon. See **Astronomy Index**. **Topographic Charts**, draughts of some small parts of the earth only, or of some particular place, without regard to its relative situation, as London, York, &c. **Charta**, or **Carta**, primarily signifies a sort of paper made of the plant *papyrus* or *biblius*. See **Paper** and **Charter**. **Charta Emporetica**, in **Pharmacy**, &c., a kind of paper made very soft and porous, used to filter withal. See **Filtration**, &c. **Charta** is also used in our ancient customs for a charter, or deed in writing. See **Charter**. **Magna Charta**, the great charter of the liberties of Britain, and the basis of our laws and privileges. This charter may be said to derive its origin from King Edward the Confessor, who granted several privileges to the church and state by charter: these liberties and privileges were also granted and confirmed by King Henry I., by a celebrated great charter now lost; but which was confirmed or re-enacted by King Henry II. and King John. Henry III., the successor of this last prince, after having caused 12 men make inquiry into the liberties of England in the reign of Henry I., granted a new charter; which was the same as the present magna charta. This he several times confirmed, and as often broke; till, in the 37th year of his reign, he went to Westminster Hall, and there, in presence of the nobility and bishops, who held lighted candles in their hands, magna charta was read, the king all the time holding his hand to his breast, and at last solemnly swearing faithfully and inviolably to observe all the things therein contained, &c. Then the bishops extinguishing the candles, and throwing them on the ground, they all cried out, "Thus let him be extinguished, and sink in hell who violates this charter." It is observed that, notwithstanding the solemnity of this confirmation, King Henry, the very next year, again invaded the rights of his people, till the barons entered into a war against him; when, after various sucessefs, he confirmed this charter, and the charter of the forest, in the 52d year of his reign. This charter confirmed many liberties of the church, and redressed many grievances incident to feudal tenures, of no small moment at the time; though now, unless considered attentively and with this retrospect, they seem but of trifling concern. But, besides these feudal provisions, care was also taken therein to protect the subject against other oppressions, then frequently arising from unreasonable amercements, from illegal distresses or other proceedings for debts or services due to the crown, and from the tyrannical abuse of the prerogative of purveyance and pre-emption. It fixed the forfeiture of lands for felony in the same manner as it still remains; prohibited for the future the grants of exclusive fisheries; and the erection of new bridges to as to oppress the neighbourhood. With respect to private rights, it established the testamentary power of the subject over part of his personal estate, the rest being distributed among his wife and children; it laid down the law of dower, as it hath continued ever since; and prohibited the appeals of women, unless after the death of their husbands. In matters of public police and national concern, it enjoined an uniformity of weights and ="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures; gave new encouragements to commerce, by the protection of merchant strangers; and forbade the alienation of lands in mortmain. With regard to the administration of justice, besides prohibiting all denials or delays of it, it fixed the court of common pleas at Westminster, that the suitors might no longer be harassed with following the king's person in all his progresses; and at the same time brought the trial of issues home to the very doors of the freeholders, by directing affizes to be taken in the proper counties, and establishing annual circuits: it also corrected some abuses then incident to the trials by wager of law and of battle; directed the regular awarding ing of inquests for life or member; prohibited the king's inferior ministers from holding places of the crown, or trying any criminal charge, whereby many forfeitures might otherwise have unjustly accrued to the exchequer; and regulated the time and place of holding the inferior tribunals of justice, the county-court, sheriff's torn, and court-leet. It confirmed and established the liberties of the city of London, and all other cities, boroughs, towns, and ports of the kingdom. And lastly (which alone would have merited the title that it bears, of the great charter), it protected every individual of the nation in the free enjoyment of his life, his liberty, and his property, unless declared to be forfeited by the judgment of his peers, or the law of the land. This excellent charter, so equitable, and beneficial to the subject, is the most ancient written law in the kingdom. By the 25th Edward I. it is ordained, that it shall be taken as the common law; and by the 43d Edward III. all statutes made against it are declared to be void.

CHARTER

Pages 437-437

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a written <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of things acted between one person and another. The word charter comes from the Latin *charia*, anciently used for a public and authentic <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, a donation, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, or the like, from the Greek *χάρτης*, "thick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>" or "pasteboard," whereon public acts were wont to be written. Britton divides charters into those of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and those of private persons. 1. Charters of the king, are those whereby the king passeth any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to any person or body politic, as a charter of exemption, of privilege, &c.; charter of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is forgiven a felony, or other offence committed against the king's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; charter of the forest, wherein the laws of the forest are comprised, such as the charter of Canutus, &c. 2. Charters of private persons, are deeds and instruments for the conveyance of lands, &c. And the purchaser of lands shall have all the charters, deeds, and evidences, as incident to the same, and for the maintenance of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. **CHARTER-Governments** in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. See COLONY. **CHARTER-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>**, such land as a person holds by charter; that is, by evidence in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; otherwise called freehold.

CHARTERPARTY

Pages 437-437

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of freightage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of agreement for the hire of a vessel. See FREIGHT, &c. The charterparty is to be in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; and to be signed both by the proprietor or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the ship, and the merchant who freights it. It is to contain the name and the burden of the vessel; the names of the master and the freighter; the price or rate of freight; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of loading and unloading; and the other conditions agreed on. It is properly a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, or policy, whereby the master or proprietor of the vessel engages to furnish immediately a tight found vessel, well equipped, caulked, and flopped, provided with anchors, sails, cordage, and all other furniture to make the voyage required, as equipage, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, victuals, and other munitions; in consideration of a certain sum to be paid by the merchant for the freight. Lastly, the ship with all its furniture, and the cargo, are respectively subjected to the conditions of the charterparty. The charterparty differs from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of lading, in that the first is for the entire freight, or lading, and that both for going and returning; whereas the latter is only for a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the freight, or at most only for the voyage one way. Boyer says, the word is derived from hence, that *per medium charia incidebatur, et sic fiebat charia parititia*; because, in the time when notaries were less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, there was only one instrument made for both parties; they cut it in two, and gave each his portion; joining them together at their return, to know <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> each had done his part. This he observes to have been practised in his time; agreeable to the method of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who, in their stipulations, used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, each party retaining a moiety thereof as a mark.

CHARTOPHYLAX

Pages 437-437

the name of an officer of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Constantinople, who attends at the door of the rails when the sacrament is administered, and gives notice to the priests to come to the holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. He represents the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, tries all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> causes, keeps all the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> registers, assists at the consecration of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and presents the bishop elect at the solemnity, and likewise all other subordinate clergy. This office resembles in some shape that of the *bibliothecarius* at Rome.

CHARTRES

Pages 437-437

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Orleanois, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EURE">Eure</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 32. N. Lat. 48. 47. It is a bishop's see.

CHARTREUSE

Pages 437-437
or **CHARTREUSE-GRAND**, a celebrated monastery, the capital of all the convents of the Carthusian monks, situated on a steep rock in the middle of a large forest of fir trees, about seven miles north-east of Grenoble, in the province of Dauphiny in France, E. Long. 5. 5. N. Lat. 45. 20. See CARthusians. From this mother convent, all the others of the same order took their name; among which was the Chartreuse of London, corruptly called the *charterhouse*, now converted into a hospital, and endowed with a revenue of 600l. per annum. Here were maintained 80 decayed gentlemen, not under 50 years of age; also 40 boys are educated and fitted either for the university or trades. Those sent to the university have an exhibition of 20l. a-year for eight years; and have an immediate title to nine church-livings in the gift of the governors of the hospital, who are sixteen in number, all persons of the first distinction, and take their turns in the nomination of pensioners and scholars.

CHARTULARY

Pages 437-437

*Chartularius*, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> officer in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who had the care of charters and papers relating to public affairs. The chartulary presided in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> judgments, in lieu of the pope. In the Greek church the chartulary was called *chartophylax*; but his office was there much more considerable; and some even distinguisht the chartulary from the chartophylax in the Greek church. See CHARTOPHYLAX.

CHARYBDIS

Pages 437-438

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a whirlpool in the straits of Messina, according to the poets; near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a>, a rock on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> makes it to be only a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and reflux in the strait, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a violent reciprocation of the tide, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> sets south. But on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVING">diving</a> into the Charybdis, there are found vast gulfs... Charybdis, and whirlpools below, which produce all the commotion on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Charybdis is used by Horace to denote a rapacious prostitute.

CHASE

Pages 438-438

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is to pursue a ship; which is also called giving chase. Stern-CHASE, is when the chaser follows the chased after directly upon the same point of the compass. To <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> with a ship's fore-foot in a CHASE, is to fail and meet with her by the nearest distance; and to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> her in her way, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to come across her fore-foot. A ship is said to have a good chase, when she is so built forward on, or aft, that she can carry many guns to shoot forwards or backwards; according to which she is said to have a good forward or good stern chase.

CHASE GUNS

Pages 438-440

are such whose ports are either in the head (and then they are used in chafing of others); <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the stern, which are only useful when they are pursued or chased by any other ship. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">CHASE</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>, is the whole bore or length of a piece taken withinside. Wild-geese CHASE, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACING">racing</a> on horseback used formerly, which resembled the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> of wild geese; those birds generally going in a train one after another, not in confused flocks as other birds do. In this sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> the two horses, after running twelve score yards, had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> forever could take the leading, to ride what ground the jockey pleased, the hindmost horse being bound to follow him within a certain distance agreed on by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, or else to be whipped in by the tryers and judges who rode by; and whichever horse could distance the other won the race. This sort of racing was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; for it was found inhuman, and destructive to good horses, when two such were matched together. For in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> neither was able to distance the other till they were both ready to sink under their riders; and often two very good good horses were both spoiled, and the wagers forced to be drawn at last. The mischief of this sort of racing soon brought in the method now in use, of running only for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ground, and determining the plate or wager by the coming in first at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. **CHASING of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, Silver, &c.** See **ENCHASING.** **CHASTE TREE.** See **VITEX**, **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.** **CHASTITY;** Purity of the body, or freedom from obscenity.—The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> justifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a> in defense of the chastity either of one's self or relations; and so also, according to Selden, stood the law in the Jewish republic. Our law likewise justifies a woman for killing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who attempts to ravish her. So the husband or father may justify killing a man who attempts a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> upon his wife or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>; but not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he takes them in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> by consent; for the one is forcible and felonious, but not the other. Chastity is a virtue universally celebrated. There is indeed no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> that can supply its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Without it, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> is unlovely, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> is contemptible; good breeding degenerates into wantonness, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> into impudence. Out of the numerous instances of eminent chastity recorded by authors, the two following are selected on account of the lesson afforded by the different modes of conduct which they exhibit. Lucretia was lady of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> beauty and noble <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>; she married Collatinus, a relation of Tarquinius Superbus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Rome. During the siege of Ardea, which lasted much longer than was expected, the young princes passed their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in entertainments and diversions. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> as they were at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>* at Sextus Tarquin's, the king's eldest son, with Collatinus, Lucretia's husband, the conversation turned on the merit of their wives: every one gave his own the preference. "What signify so many words?" says Collatinus; "you may in a few hours, if you please, be convinced by your own eyes, how much my Lucretia excels the rest. We are young; let us mount our horses, and go and surprize them. Nothing can better decide our dispute than the state we shall find them in at a time when most certainly they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not expect us." They were a little warmed with wine: "Come on, let us go," they all cried together. They quickly galloped to Rome, which was about twenty miles from Ardea, where they find the princesses, wives of the young Tarquins, surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and every circumstance of the highest mirth and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. From thence they rode to Collatia, where they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Lucretia in a very different situation. With her maids about her, she was at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the inner <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, talking of the dangers to which her husband was exposed. The victory was adjudged to her unanimously. She received her guests with all possible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> and civility. Lucretia's virtue, which should have commanded respect, was the very thing which kindled in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of Sextus Tarquin a strong and detestable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. Within a few days he returned to Collatia; and upon the plausible excuse he made for his visit, he was received with all the politeness due to a near relation, and the eldest son of a king. Watching the fittest opportunity, he declared the passion she had excited at his last visit, and employed the most tender entreaties, and all the artifices possible to touch a woman's heart; but all to no purpose. He then endeavored chastity to extort her compliance by the most terrible threatenings. It was in vain. She still persisted in her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; nor could she be moved even by the fear of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. But when the monster told her that he would first dispatch her, and then having murdered a slave, would lay him by her side, after which he would spread a report, that having caught them in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of adultery, he had punished them as they deserved; this seemed to shake her resolution. She hesitated, not knowing which of these dreadful alternatives to take, whether, by consenting to dishonor the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of her husband, whom she tenderly loved; or, by refusing, to die under the odious character of having prostituted her person to the lust of a slave. He saw the struggle of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; and seizing the unlucky moment, obtained an inglorious conquest. Thus, Lucretia's virtue, which had been <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against the fear of death, could not hold out against the fear of infamy. The young <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> having gratified his passion, returned home as in triumph. On the morrow, Lucretia overwhelmed with grief and despair, sent early in the morning to defile her father and her husband to come to her, and bring with them each a trusty friend, assuring them there was no time to lose. They came with all speed, the one accompanied with Valerius (so famous after under the name of Publicola), and the other with Brutus. The moment she saw them come, she could not command her tears; and when her husband asked her if all was well? "By no means," said she, "it cannot be well with a woman after she has lost her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. Yes, Collatinus, thy bed has been defiled by a stranger; but my body only is polluted; my mind is innocent, as my death shall witness. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">Promise</a> me only not to suffer the adulterer to go unpunished: it is Sextus Tarquinius, who last night, a treacherous guest, or rather cruel foe, offered me violence, and reaped a joy fatal to me; but, if you are men, it will be still more fatal to him." All promised to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> her; and at the same time, tried to comfort her with representing, "That the mind only sins, not the body; and where the consent is wanting, there can be no guilt." "What Sextus deserves," replies Lucretia, "I leave you to judge; but for me, though I declare myself innocent of the crime, I exempt not myself from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. No immaculate woman shall plead Lucretia's example to outlive her dishonor." Thus saying, she plunged into her breast a dagger she had concealed under her robe, and expired at their feet. Lucretia's tragic death has been praised and extolled by Pagan writers, as the highest and most noble act of heroism. The Godf thinks not so: it is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, even according to Lucretia's own principles, since she punished with death an innocent person, at least acknowledged as such by herself. She was ignorant that our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is not in our own power, but in his disposal from whom we receive it. St Austin, who carefully examines, in his book De Civitate Dei, what we are to think of Lucretia's death, considers it not as a courageous <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> flowing from a true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of chastity, but as an infirmity—a woman too sensible of worldly fame and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; and who, from a dread of appearing in the eyes of men an <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a> of the violence she abhorred, and of a crime to which she was entirely a stranger, commits a real crime upon herself voluntarily and designedly. But what cannot Chastity be sufficiently admired in this Roman lady, is her abhorrence of adultery, which she seems to hold so detestable as not to bear the thoughts of it. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, she is a noble example for all her sex. Chiomara, the wife of Ortigagon, a Gaulish prince, was equally admirable for her beauty and chastity. During the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> and the Gauls, A. R. 563, the latter were totally defeated on Mount Olympus. Chiomara, among many other ladies, was taken prisoner, and committed to the care of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">centurion</a>, no less passionate for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> than women. He at first endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> her consent to his infamous desires; but not being able to prevail upon her, and subvert her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, he thought he might employ force with a woman whom misfortune had reduced to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Afterwards, to make her amends for that treatment, he offered to restore her liberty: but not without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>. He agreed with her for a certain sum, and to conceal this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> from the other Romans, he permitted her to send any of the prisoners she should choose to her relations, and assigned a place near the river where the lady should be exchanged for gold. By accident there was one of her own slaves among the prisoners. Upon him she fixed; and the centurion soon after carried her beyond the advanced posts, under cover of a dark night. The next evening two of the relations of the princess came to the place appointed, whither the centurion also carried his captive. When they had delivered him the Attic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> they had brought, which was the sum they had agreed on, the lady, in her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, ordered those who came to receive her to draw their swords and kill the centurion, who was then amusing himself with weighing the gold. Then, charmed with having revenged the injury done her chastity, she took the head of the officer, which she had cut off with her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and hiding it under her robe, went to her husband Ortigagon, who had returned home after the defeat of his troops. As soon as he came into his presence, she threw the centurion's head at his feet. He was strangely surprised at such a sight: and asked her whose head it was, and what had induced her to do an act so uncommon to her sex? With her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> covered with a sudden blush, and at the same time expressing her fierce indignation, she declared the outrage which had been done her, and the revenge she had taken for it. During the rest of her life, she steadfastly retained the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> for the purity of manners which constitutes the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> glory of the sex, and nobly sustained the honour of so glorious, bold, and heroic an action.—This lady was much more prudent than Lucretia, in revenging her injured honour by the death of her ravisher, rather than by her own. Plutarch relates this fact, in his treatise upon the virtue and great actions of women; and it is from him we have the name of this, which is well worthy of being transmitted to posterity. The above virtue in men is termed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a>. See Continence.

CHATEAU-BRIANT

Pages 440-440

a town of France in Brittany, with an old castle. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 20. N. Lat. 47. 40. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATEAU_CHINON">CHATEAU-<a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHINON">Chinon</a>, a town of France in Nivernois, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Morvan, with a considerable manufactory of cloth. E. Long. 3. 48. N. Lat. 47. 2. CHATEAU-Dauphin, a very strong castle of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, situated in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and in the marquisate of Saluces, belonging to Dauphin, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>. It was taken by the combined <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in 1744, and was restored by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATEAU_DU_LOIRE">CHATEAU-du-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, a town of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, famous for sustaining a siege of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of Mans. It is seated on the river Loire, in E. Long. 0. 25. N. Lat. 47. 40. CHATEAU-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">Dun</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of France, and capital of the Dunois, with a castle and rich <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>; seated on an eminence near the river Loire, in E. Long. 1. 26. N. Lat. 48. 4. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHATEAU_NEUF">CHATEAU-Neuf</a>, the name of several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of France, viz. one in Perche; another in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a>, on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, near Angoulême; a third in Berry, seated on the river Cher; and several other small places. CHATEAU-Portien, a town of France, in Champagne, and in a district called Portien, with a castle built on a rock, near the river Aifne. E. Long. 4. 23. N. Lat. 49. 35. CHATEAU-Renaud, a town of France, in the Gatinois, where clothes are made for the army, and where there is a trade in saffron. E. Long. 4. 25. N. Lat. 48. 0. This is also the name of a town of Touraine, in France, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquisate. E. Long. 2. 41. N. Lat. 47. 22. CHATEAU-Roux, a town of France, in Berry, with the title of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It has a cloth manufacture, and is seated in a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pleasant plain on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDRE">Indre</a>, in E. Long. 1. 47. N. Lat. 46. 49. CHATEAU-Thiery, a town of France, in Champagne, with the title of a duchy, and a handsome castle on an eminence, seated on the river Maine, in E. Long. 3. 23. N. Lat. 49. 12. CHATEAU-Vilain, a town of France, in Champagne, with a castle, and the title of a duchy; seated on the river Anjou. E. Long. 2. 59. N. Lat. 48. 0.

CHATEL

Pages 440-440
or CHATEL, a town of Lorraine, in the Vosque, seated on the river Moselle, eight miles from Mirecourt. CHATEL-Allow, a maritime town of France, in Saintonge, five miles from Rochelle; formerly very considerable, but now greatly decayed. CHATEL-Chalon, a town of France, in Franche Comté, remarkable for its abbey of Benedictine nuns. E. Long. 5. 25. N. Lat. 46. 50.

CHATELET

Pages 440-440

the name of certain courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> established in several cities in France. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> chatelet at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the presidial <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of justice of the provost of Paris is kept; consisting of a presidial, a civil chamber, a criminal chamber, and chamber of policy. The little chatelet is an old fort, now serving as a prison.

CHATELLERAULT

Pages 440-440

a town of France, in Poitou, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>; seated in a fertile and pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 40. N. Lat. 46. 34.

CHATHAM

Pages 440-441

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, adjoining to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, and seated on the river Medway. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> principal station of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>; and the yards and magazines are furnished with all kinds of naval stores, as well as materials for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and rigging the largest men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The entrance into the river Medway is defended by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> and other forts; notwithstanding which, the Dutch fleet burnt several ships of war here in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. after the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a> had been agreed upon. In the year 1757, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, several additional fortifications were begun at Chatham; so that now the ships are in no danger of an insult either by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a chapel of ease, and a ship used as a church for the sailors. It has likewise about 500 houses, mostly low, and built with brick; the streets are narrow, and paved; and it contains about 3000 inhabitants. The principal employment of the labouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> is ship-building in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s yard and private docks. This town gave <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> statesman William Pitt in the reigns of George II. and III. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 40'. N. Lat. 51°.

CHATIGAN

Pages 441-441

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, on the most easterly branch of the river Ganges. It is but a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though it was the first the Portuguese settled in these parts, and who still keep a sort of possession. It has but a few cotton <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; but affords the best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of any place about it. The inhabitants are so suspicious of each other, that they always go armed with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, pistol, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLUNDERBUSS">blunderbuss</a>, not excepting the priests. It is subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 91° 10'. N. Lat. 23° 0'. CHATILLON sur <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, a town of France, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, divided into two by the river Seine. It is 32 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGRES">Langres</a>, and 40 from Dijon; and has <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> works in its neighbourhood. E. Long. 4° 33'. N. Lat. 47° 45'.

CHATRE

Pages 441-441

a town of France, in Berry, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDRE">Indre</a>, 37 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>. It carries on a considerable trade in cattle. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 55'. N. Lat. 46° 35'.

CHATTELS

Pages 441-441

a Norman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, under which were anciently comprehended all moveable goods; those immoveable being termed seif <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> see. Chattels, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, are all sorts of goods, moveable or immoveable, except such as are in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of freehold. CHATTERER. See Ampelis, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

CHATTERTON

Pages 441-442

Thomas, a late unfortunate poet, whose fate and performances have excited in no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the public <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, as well as given rise to much literary controversy. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, Nov. 20, 1752; and educated at a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> school on St Augustine's Back, where nothing more was taught than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, and accounts. At 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was articled clerk to an attorney at Bristol, with whom he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> about three years; yet, though his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was thus confined, he discovered an early turn towards <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and English antiquities, and particularly towards <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>. How soon he began to be an author is not known. In the Town and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1769, are two letters, probably from him, as they are dated from Bristol, and subscribed with his usual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a>, D. B. that is, Dunhelmus Chatterton. Britfoliensis. The former contains short extracts from two MSS. "written 300 years ago by one Rowley a monk," concerning dyes in the age of Henry II.; the latter, "Ethelgar, a Saxon poem," in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a> prose. In the same magazine for May 1769, are three communications from Bristol, with the same signature D. B., one of them entitled, "Observations upon Saxon Heraldry, with drawings of Saxon Achievements;" and in the subsequent months of 1769 and 1770, there are several other pieces in the same magazine, which are undoubtedly of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. In April 1770, he left Bristol, disgusted with his profession, and irreconcilable to the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in which he was placed; and coming to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in hopes of advancing his fortune by his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, he sunk at once from the sublimity of his views to an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> dependence on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a>. Things, however, seem soon to have brightened up a little with him; for, May 14, he writes to his mother, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> spirits, upon the change of his situation, with the following sarcastic reflections upon his former patrons at Bristol. "As to Mr ____, Mr ____, Mr ____, &c. &c. they rate literary lumber so low, that I believe an author, in their estimation, must be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> indeed: but here matters are otherwise. Had Rowley been a Londoner instead of a Briton, I could have lived by copying his works." In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to his sister, May 30, he informs her that he is to be employed in writing a voluminous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of London, to appear in numbers the beginning of next winter. Meanwhile, he had written something in praise of Beckford, then <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor, which had procured him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being presented to his lordship; and, in the letter <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, he gives the following account of his reception, with certain observations upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writing. "The lord mayor received me as politely as a citizen could: but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is, there is no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to be got on this side of the question.—However, he is a poor author who cannot write on both sides.—Essays on the patriotic side <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fetch no more than what the copy is sold for. As the patriots themselves are searching for places, they have no gratuity to spare.—On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, unpopular essays will not even be accepted, and you must pay to have them printed; but then you seldom lose by it, as courtiers are so sensible of their deficiency in merit, that they generously reward all who know how to daub them with the appearance of it." He continued to write incessantly in various periodical publications. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 11, he tells his sister that he had pieces last <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> in several magazines; in The Gospel Magazine, The Town and Country, The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">City</a>, The London, The Political <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a>, &c. But all these exertions of his genius brought in so little profit, that he was soon reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> indigence; so that at last, oppressed with poverty and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, in a fit of despair, he put an end to his existence, August 1770, with a dose of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>. This unfortunate person, though certainly a most extraordinary genius, seems yet to have been a most ungracious composition. He was violent and impetuous to a strange degree. From the first of the above cited letters he seems to have had a portion of ill humour and spleen more than enough for a lad of 17; and the editor of his his Miscellanies records, "that he possessed all the vices and irregularities of youth, and that his profligacy was at least as conspicuous as his abilities." In 1777 were published in one volume 8vo, "Poems, supposed to have been written at Bristol, by Thomas Rowley and others, in the 15th century: the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> now first published from the most authentic copies, with an engraved specimen of one of the MSS. To which are added, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">Preface</a>, an introductory Account of the several Pieces, and a Glossary." And in 1778, were published, in one volume 8vo, "Miscellanies in Prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">Verse</a> by Thomas Chatterton, the supposed author of the Poems published under the names of Rowley, &c." Of Rowley's poems, we have the following account in the preface, given in the words of Mr George Catcot of Bristol, to whom, it is said, the public is indebted for them. "The first discovery of certain MSS. having been deposited in Redclift <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> above three centuries ago, was made in the year 1768, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of opening the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> at Bristol; and was owing to a publication in Farley's Weekly Journal, Oct. 1, containing an account of the ceremonies observed at the opening of the old bridge, taken, as it was said, from a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> MS. This excited the curiosity of some persons to inquire after the original. The printer, Mr Farley, could give no account of it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the person who brought the copy; but, after much inquiry, it was discovered that this person was a youth between 15 and 16 years of age, whose name was Thomas Chatterton, and whose family had been sextons of Redclift church for near 150 years. His father, who was now dead, had also been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the free school in Pile-street. The young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was at first very unwilling to discover from whence he had the original: but, after many promises made to him, was at last prevailed on to acknowledge that he had received this, together with many other MSS. from his father, who had found them in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> in an upper room over the chapel, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of Redclift church." It is added, that soon after this Mr Catcot commenced an acquaintance with Chatterton, and partly as presents, partly as purchases, procured from him copies of many of his MSS. in prose and verse; as other copies were disposed of in like manner to others. It is concluded, however, that whatever may have been Chatterton's part in this very extraordinary transaction, whether he was the author, or only (as he constantly affected) the copier of all these productions, he appears to have kept the secret entirely to himself, and not to have put it in any one's power to bear certain testimony either of his fraud or of his veracity. This affair, however, hath since become the foundation of a mighty controversy among the critics, which hath yet scarcely subsided. The poems in question, published in 1777, were republished in 1778, with an "Appendix, containing some observations upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; tending to prove that they were written, not by any ancient author, but entirely by Chatterton." Mr Warton, in the third volume of his History of English Poetry, hath espoused the same side of the question. Mr Walpole also obliged the world with a Letter on Chatterton, from his pres at Strawberry-hill. On the other hand have appeared, "Observations" upon these poems, "in which their authenticity is ascertained," by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Bryant, Esq.; 1781, 2 vols. 8vo; and another edition of the "Poems, with a Comment, Chatterton," by Jeremiah Miles, D.D., <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, 1782, 4to. In answer to these two works, we have had three pamphlets: 1. "Curious Observations on the Poems, and Remarks on the Commentaries of Mr Bryant and Dr Miles; with a salutary proposal addressed to the friends of these gentlemen." 2. "An Archaeological Epistle to Dean Miles, editor of a superb edition of Rowley's Poems, &c." 3. "An Inquiry into the authenticity of the Poems attributed to Thomas Rowley, in which the Arguments of the dean of Exeter and Mr Bryant are examined, by Thomas Warton?" and other pieces in the public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> and magazines: All preparatory to the complete settlement of the business in "A Vindication of the Appendix to the Poems called Rowley's, in reply to the Answers of the dean of Exeter, Jacob Bryant, Esq. and a third Anonymous Writer; with some further Observations upon these Poems, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">Examination</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">Evidence</a> which has been produced in support of their Authenticity. By Thomas Tyrwhitt, 1782," 8vo.

CHAUCER

Pages 442-443

Sir Geoffrey, an eminent English poet in the 14th century, born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1328. After he left the university, he travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, France, and other countries. Upon his return he entered himself in the Inner Temple, where he studied the municipal laws of England. His first station at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> was page to Edward III, and he had a pension granted him by that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> till he could otherwise provide for him. Soon after we find him <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s privy chamber; next year, field-bearer to the king. Esteemed and honoured, he spent his younger days in a constant attendance at court, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> living near it, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>-gate at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a>, still called Chaucer's House. Soon after, having got the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> for his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, Chaucer began every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to rise in greatness. In 1373, he was sent with other persons to the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> to hire ships for the king's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> (our want of shipping in those times being usually supplied by such means); and the king was so well satisfied with his negotiation, that, on his return, he obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of a pitcher of wine daily in the port of London, to be delivered by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">butler</a> of England; and soon after was made comptroller of the customs for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, wool fells, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>; an office which he discharged with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diligence and integrity. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, Chaucer's income was about 100l. a-year; a sum which in those days might well enable him to live, as he says he did, with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in office, and hospitality among his friends. It was in this meridian blaze of prosperity, in perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of body and peace of mind, that he wrote his most humorous poems. His satires against the priests were probably written to oblige his patron the duke of Lancaster, who favoured the cause of Wickliff, and endeavoured to expose the clergy to the indignation of the people. In the last year of Edward III, our poet was employed in a mission to treat with the French; and in the beginning of King Richard's reign, he was in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of favour at court. The duke of Lancaster at last finding his views checked, began to abandon Wickliff's party: upon which which Chaucer likewise, how much sooner he had espoused that divine's opinions, thought it prudent to conceal them more than he had done. With the duke's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> that of Chaucer entirely sunk; and the former passing over <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, his friends felt all the malice of the opposite party. These misfortunes occasioned his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> that excellent treatise, *The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>*, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> on the Consolation of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. Being much reduced, he retired to Woodstock, to comfort himself with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, which produced his admirable treatise of the *Astrolabe*. The duke of Lancaster at last surmounting his troubles, married Lady Catherine Swynford, sister to Chaucer's wife; so that Thomas Chaucer, our poet's son, became allied to most of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and to several of the kings of England. Now the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> began to shine upon Chaucer with an evening ray; for by the influence of the duke's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, he again grew to a considerable share of wealth. But being now 75, he retired to Dunnington castle near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWBURY">Newbury</a>. He had not enjoyed this retirement <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before Henry IV. son of the duke of Lancaster, assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and in the first year of his reign gave our poet marks of his favour. But however pleasing the change of affairs might be to him at first, he afterwards found no small inconveniences from it. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> and grants of the late king were annulled: and Chaucer, in order to procure fresh grants of his pensions, left his retirement, and applied to court; where, though he gained a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of some grants, yet the fatigue of attendance, and his great <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, prevented him from enjoying them. He fell sick at London: and ended his days in the 72nd year of his age, leaving the world as though he despised it, as appears from his song of *Flie from the Prefe*. The year before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> it might be so called, to see the son of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> (Hen. IV.) seated on the throne. He was interred in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>; and in 1556, Mr Nicholas Bingham, a gentleman of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, at his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, erected a handsome monument for him there. Caxton first printed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> Tales; but his works were first collected and published in one volume folio, by William Thynne, London, 1542. They were afterwards reprinted in 1561, 1598, 1602, Oxford, 1721. Chaucer was not only the first, but one of the best poets which these kingdoms ever produced. He was equally great in every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> which he attempted; and his poems in general possess every kind of excellence, even to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> reader, except <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> and accuracy of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>; defects which are to be attributed to the imperfect state of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and the infancy of the art in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at the time when he wrote. "As he is the father of English poetry (says Mr Dryden), so I hold him in the same degree of veneration as the Grecians did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. He is a perpetual fountain of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, learned in all sciences, and therefore speaks properly on all subjects. As he knew what to say, so he knows also when to leave off; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a> which is practised by few writers, and scarcely by any of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, except Virgil and Horace." This character Chaucer certainly deserved. He had read a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>; and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the world, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgement. He was the first English poet who wrote *poetically*, as Dr Johnson observes in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, and (he might have added) who wrote like a gentleman. He had also the merit of improving our language considerably, by the introduction and naturalization of words from the Provencal, at that time the most polished dialect in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

CHAUD MEDLEY

Pages 443-443

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is of much the same import with **CHANCE Medley**. The former in its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> signifies an affray in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of blood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>: the latter, a casual affray. The latter is in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> speech too often erroneously applied to any manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a> by misadventure; whereas it appears by the flat. 24 Hen. VIII. c. 5. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> books (Standf. P. C. 16.), that it is properly applied to such killing as happens in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-<a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> upon sudden encounter.

CHAULIEU

Pages 443-443

William Amfryede, Abbé d'Amale, one of the most polite and ingenious of the French poets, was born in 1629, and died at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 84. The most complete edition of his poems is that printed in two vols. 8vo, in 1733.

CHAUMONT

Pages 443-443

a town of France, in Champagne, and in the district of Bassigni, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It is seated on a mountain near the river <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 15. N. Lat. 48. 6.

CHAUNE

Pages 443-443

a town of France, in Picardy, and in the district of Santerre, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 55. N. Lat. 49. 45. **CHAUNTRY**. See **CHANTRY**.

CHAUNY

Pages 443-443

a town of France, in Picardy, seated on the river Oise, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANTILLY">Chantilly</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 17. N. Lat. 49. 37.

CHAUVIN

Pages 443-443

Stephen, a celebrated minister of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, born at Nîmes, left France at the revocation of the edict of Nantes, and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, where he began a new *Journal des Savans*; and afterwards removing to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it there three years. At this last <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he was made professor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and discharged that office with much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and reputation. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is a philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, in Latin, which he published at Rotterdam in 1602; and gave a new edition of it much augmented, at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in 1703, in folio. He died in 1725, aged 85.

CHAVEZ

Pages 443-443

a strong town of Tralos-Montes in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, seated at the foot of a mountain on the river Tamega. It has two suburbs, and as many forts; one of which looks like a citadel. Between the town and suburb of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MAGDALENA">Magdalena</a>, is an old Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> about 92 geometrical paces <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. W. Long. 7. 1. N. Lat. 41. 45.

CHAZELLES

Pages 443-444

CHAZELLES, Jean Matthew, a celebrated French mathematician and engineer, was born at Lyons in 1677. M. du Hamel, with whom he got acquainted, finding his genius incline towards <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, presented him to M. Cassini, who employed him in his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>. In 1684, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Mortemar made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of Chazelles to teach him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and, the year after, procured him the preferment of hydrography professor for the galleys of Marseille, where he set up a school for young pilots <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> to serve aboard the galleys. In 1686, the galleys made four little campaigns <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather four courses, purely for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. Chazelles went on board every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with them, kept his school upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and showed the practice of what he taught. In the years 1687 and 1688, he made two other sea campaigns, in which he drew a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many plans of ports, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and forts, which were lodged with the ministers of state. At the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which ended with the peace of Ryswick, some marine officers, and Chazelles among the rest, fancied the galleys might be so contrived as to live upon the ocean; that they might serve to tow the men of war when the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> failed or proved contrary, and also help to secure the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of France upon the ocean. Chazelles was sent to the west coasts in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1689, to examine the practicability of this scheme; and in 1690, fifteen galleys new built set sail from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHEFORT">Rochefort</a>, and cruised as far as Torbay, in England, and proved serviceable at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon Tintmouth. After this, he digested into order the observations he had made on the coasts of the ocean; and drew distinct maps, with a portolan to them, viz. a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of every haven, of the depth, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, the dangers and advantages discovered, &c. These maps were inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> Francoise, published in 1692, in which year Chazelles was engineer at the descent at Oenelle. In 1693, Monsieur de Pontchartrain, then secretary of state for the marine, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of France, resolved to get the Neptune Francoise carried on to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume, which was also to take in the Mediterranean. Chazelles desired that he might have a year's voyage on this sea, for making astronomical observations; and the request being granted, he passed through <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, with his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. When he was in Egypt, he measured the pyramids: and finding the sides of the largest precisely facing the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, naturally concluded this position to have been intended, and also that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and meridians had not since deviated. Chazelles likewise made a report of his voyage in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, and gave the academy all the satisfaction they wanted concerning the position of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; upon which he was made a member of the academy in 1695. He died in 1710.

CHAZINZARIANS

Pages 444-444

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics who rose in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> in the seventh century. The word is formed of the Armenian chazur, "crofs." They are also called flouralatre, which in Greek signifies the same as Chazinzarians in Armenian, viz. adorers of the crofs; they being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with paying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> to the crofs alone. In other respects they were Nestorians; and admitted two persons in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ: Nicaephorus attributes other singularities to them; particularly their holding an annual feast in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the dog of their false prophet Sergius, which they called Chazinartzbartzes.

CHE-KYANG

Pages 446-447
or Tche-kiang, a maritime province of China, and one of the most considerable in the empire; is bounded on the south by Fo-kien; on the north and west by Kiang-nan and Kiang-si; and on the east by the sea. The air is pure and healthful, and the soil fertile, being watered by a number of rivers and canals, as well as springs and lakes. The chief produce is silk; a vast quantity of which is cultivated Che-kyang, tivated here, and for which the whole country is covered with mulberry trees. These are purposely checked in their growth by the natives, experience having taught them, that the leaves of the smallest trees produce the best silk. The stuffs made in this province, which are embroidered with gold and silver, are reckoned the best in the empire; and notwithstanding a vast exportation to Japan and Philippine s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands, as well as to every part of China, and to Europe, such an abundance is left in the province, that a complete suit of silk may be bought here as cheap as one of the coarsest woollen in France.
