His family finding him a hopeful youth, sent him early to Rome, where he soon engaged in a friendship with the marquis Pallavicini, who recommended him so effectually to Pope Urban VIII. that he procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of inquisitor at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. He was sent vice-legate to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and afterward nuncio into Germany; there he had an opportunity of displaying his intriguing genius; for he was mediator at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> conference held to conclude a peace with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarin had some resentment against Chigi, who was soon after made a cardinal and secretary of state by Innocent X. but his resentment was sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> views. In 1665, when a pope was to be chosen, Cardinal Sacchetti, Mazarin's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> friend, finding it was impossible for him to be raised into St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, because of the powerful opposition made by the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, desired Cardinal Mazarin to consent to Chigi's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a>. His request was granted, and he was elected pope by the votes of all the 64 cardinals who were in the conclave; an unanimity of which there are but few instances in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of popes. He showed uncommon humility at his election, and at first forbade all his relations to come to Rome without his leave; but he soon became more favourable to his nephews, and loaded them with favours. It is asserted that he had once a mind to turn Protestant. The newspapers in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> bestowed great encomiums upon him; and acquainted the world that he did not approve of the cruel persecutions of the Waldenses in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. There is a volume of his poems extant. He loved the Belles-Lettres, and the conversation of learned men. He was extremely fond of stately buildings: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> Della Sapienza, which he finished, and adorned with a fine library, remains a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. He died in 1667.

CHILBLAIN

Pages 822-823

in Medicine, a tumor affecting the feet and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; accompanied with an inflammation, pains, and sometimes an ulcer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> solution of of continuity: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it takes the denomination of chaps on the hands, and of kibes on the heels. Chilblain is compounded of chill and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLAIN">blain</a>; q. d. a blain or sore contracted by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. Pernio is the Latin name adopted by physicians; and is derived by Voßius from perna, "a gammon of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a>," on account of some resemblance. Chap alludes to gape, both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and appearance. Kibes, in Welch kibw, may be derived from the German kerben, "to cut;" the skin, when broke, appearing like a cut. Chilblains are occasioned by excessive cold stopping the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the blood in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>. See the article PERNIO.

CHILD

Pages 823-823

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. See Parent and CHILDREN. Bartholine, Parè, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LICETUS">Licetus</a>, and many other writers, give an account of a petrified child, which has seemed wholly incredible to some people. The child, however, which they describe, is still in being; and is kept as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rarity in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. The woman who was big with this, lived at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENS">Sens</a> in Champagne in the year 1582; it was cut out of her belly, and was universally supposed to have lain there about 20 years. That it is a real <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> fetus, and not <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, is evident to the eyes of any observer; and the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, when examined, is found to be of a substance resembling the gypsum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> whereof they made the platter of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>: the lower part is much harder, the thighs and buttocks being a perfect stone of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and as hard as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> stone: the grain and surface of this part appears exactly like that of the calculi or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> taken out of human bladders: and the whole substance, examined even so nearly, and felt ever so carefully, appears to be <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> stone. It was carried from Sens to Paris, and there purchased by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; and Frederic III. king of Denmark purchased it of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> at Venice for a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum, and added it to his collection of rarities. CHILD-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">Bed</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">MIDWIFERY</a>. CHILD-Birth. A power to take a fine of a bond-woman unlawfully gotten with child, that is, without consent of her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>. Every reputed father of a base child got within the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Writtle in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, pays to the lord a fine of 3s. 4d.; where, it seems, childwit extends to free as well as bond-women.

CHILDERMAS-DAY

Pages 823-823
or INNOCENTS DAY, an anniversary held by the church of England on the 28th of December, in commemoration of the children of Bethlehem massacred by order of Herod.

CHILDREN

Pages 823-823

the plural of CHILD. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> computes, that marriages, one with another, produce four children not only in England but in other parts also. In the genealogical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, written by Gamarini, mention is made of a nobleman of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, named Pichi, who of three wives had 150 children; and that, being sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the pope and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, he had 48 of his sons in his retinue. In a monument in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard of St Innocent, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, erected to a woman who died at 88 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; it is recorded, that she might have seen 268 children directly issued from her. This exceeds what Hakewell relates of Mrs Honeywood, a gentlewoman of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, born in the year 1527, and married at 16 to her only husband R. Honeywood of Charing, Esq. and died in her 93rd year. She had 16 children of her own body; of which three died young, and a fourth had no issue; yet her grandchildren, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, amounted to 114; in the third, to 228; though in the fourth they fell to 9. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> she might have seen in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, being 367. 16 + 14 + 228 + 9 = 367. So that she could say the same as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a> does of one Dalburgh's family at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>: \[ \begin{align*} 1 & \quad 2 & \quad 3 & \quad 4 \\ Mater ait natae, die natae filia natam, \\ Ut noncat, natae plangere, filiolam. \end{align*} \] Management of CHILDREN. See INFANT. Overlaying of CHILDREN, is a misfortune that frequently happens; to prevent which, the Florentines have contrived an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called arcuccio. See ARCUCCIO. CHILDREN are, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s issue begotten on his wife. As to illegitimate children, see <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">BASTARD</a>. For the legal duties of parents to their children, see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">PARENT</a> and BASTARD. As to the duties of children to their parents, they arise from a principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and retribution. For those who gave us existence, we naturally owe subjection and obedience during our minority, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and reverence ever after; they who protected the weakness of our infancy, are entitled to our protection in the infirmity of their age; they who by sustenance and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> have enabled their offspring to prosper, ought, in return, to be supported by that offspring, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they stand in need of assistance. Upon this principle proceed all the duties of children to their parents, which are enjoined by positive laws. And the Athenian laws carried this principle into practice with a scrupulous kind of nicety, obliging all children to provide for their father when fallen into poverty; with an exception to spurious children, to those whose chastity had been prostituted with consent of their father, and to those whom he had not put in any way of gaining a livelihood. The legislature, says Baron Montesquieu, considered, that, in the first case, the father, being uncertain, had rendered the natural obligation precarious; that, in the second case, he had fulfilled the life he had given, and done his children the greatest of injuries, in depriving them of their reputation; and that, in the third case, he had rendered their life (so far as in him lay) an insupportable burden, by furnishing them with no means of subsistence. Our laws agree with those of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, with regard to the first only of these particulars, the case of spurious issue. In the other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the law does not hold the tie of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to be dissolved by any misbehaviour of the parent; and, therefore, a child is equally justifiable in defending the person, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> maintaining the cause or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, of a bad parent as of a good one; and is equally compellable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> of sufficient ability, to maintain and provide for a wicked and unnatural progenitor, as for one who has shown the greatest tenderness and parental piety. See further the article <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">FILIAL</a> Affection.

CHILI

Pages 823-825

CHILI, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the province of La Plata on the east, by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATAGONIA">Patagonia</a> on the south, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a> on the west, lying between 75 and 85 degrees of west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; and between 25 and 45 of south latitude; though some comprehend in this province Patagonia and Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a>. The first attempt of the Spaniards upon this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was made by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMAGRO">Almagro</a> in the year 1535, after he and Pizarro had completed the conquest of Peru. He set out on his expedition to Chili with a considerable body of Spaniards and auxiliary Indians. For 200 leagues he was well accommodated with every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> by the Indians, who had been subjects of the emperors of Peru; but reaching the barren country of Charcas, his troops became discontented through the hardships they suffered; which determined Almagro to climb the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called Cordilleras; in order to get the sooner into Chili; being ignorant of the invaluable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Potosi, contained in the province of Charcas, where he then was. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Cordilleras were covered with snow, the depth of which obliged him to dig his way through it. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> made such an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on his naked Indians, that it is computed no less than 10,000 of them perished on these dreadful mountains, 150 of the Spaniards sharing the same fate; while many of the survivors lost their fingers and toes through the excess of cold. At last, after encountering incredible difficulties, Almagro reached a fine, temperate, and fertile plain on the opposite side of the Cordilleras, where he was received with the greatest kindness by the natives. These <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> savages taking the Spaniards for deputies of their god Virachoca, immediately collected for them an offering of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver worth 200,000 ducats; and soon after brought a present to Almagro worth 300,000 more. These offerings only determined him to conquer the whole country as soon as possible. The Indians among whom he now was, had acknowledged the authority of the Peruvian incas, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> emperors, and consequently gave Almagro no trouble. He therefore marched immediately against those who had never been conquered by the Peruvians, and inhabited the southern parts of Chili. These savages fought with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and disputed every inch of ground; but in five months' time the Spaniards had made such progress, that they must infallibly have reduced the whole province in a very short time, had not Almagro returned to Peru, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> sent him from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. In 1540, Pizarro having overcome and put Almagro to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, sent into Chili, Baldivia or <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-VALDIVIA">Valdivia</a>, who had learned the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and was reckoned one of the best officers in the Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. As he penetrated southwards, however, he met with much opposition; the confederated caziques frequently gave him <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and displayed great courage and resolution; but could not prevent him from penetrating to the valley of Maipocho, which he found incredibly fertile and populous. Here he founded the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of St Jago; and, finding gold mines in the neighbourhood, forced the Indians to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in them; at the same time <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a castle for the safety and protection of his new colony. The natives, exasperated at this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, immediately took up arms; attacked the fort; and though defeated and repulsed, set fire to the outworks, which contained all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of the Spaniards. Nor were they discouraged by this and many other defeats, but still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to carry on the war with vigour. At last, Valdivia, having overcome them in many battles, forced the inhabitants of the vale to submit; upon which he immediately set them to work in the mines of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUILLOTA">Quillota</a>. This indignity offered to their countrymen redoubled the fury of those who remained at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Their utmost efforts, however, were as yet unable to stop Valdivia's progress. Having crossed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Mauile and Hata, he traversed a vast tract of country, and founded the city of La Concepcion on the South-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. He erected fortresses in several parts of the country, in order to keep the natives in awe; and built the city called Imperial, about 40 leagues to the southward of Concepcion. The Spanish writers say, that the neighbouring valley contained 80,000 inhabitants of a peaceable disposition; and who were even so tame as to suffer Valdivia to parcel out their lands among his followers, while they themselves remained in a state of inactivity. About 16 leagues to the eastward of Imperial, the Spanish general laid the foundation of the city Villa Rica, so called on account of the rich gold mines he found there. But his ambition and avarice had now involved him in difficulties from which he could never be extricated: He had extended his conquests beyond what his strength was capable of maintaining. The Chileans were still as zealous as ever of recovering their liberties. The horses, fire-arms, and armour of the Spaniards, indeed, appeared dreadful to them; but thoughts of endless slavery were still more so. In the course of the war they had discovered that the Spaniards were vulnerable and mortal men like themselves; they hoped, therefore, by dint of their superiority in numbers, to be able to expel the tyrannical usurpers. Had all the nations joined in this resolution, the Spaniards had certainly been exterminated; but some of them were of a pacific and fearful disposition, while others considered servitude as the greatest of all possible calamities. Of this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> were the Araucans, the most intrepid people in Chili, and who had given Valdivia the greatest trouble. They all rose to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and chose Capaulican, a renowned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> among them, for their leader. Valdivia however received notice of their revolt sooner than they intended he should, and returned with all expedition to the vale of Aracce; but before he arrived, 14,000 of the Chileans were there assembled under the conduct of Capaulican. He attacked them with his cavalry, and forced them to retreat into the woods; but could not obtain a complete victory, as they kept continually falling out and harassing his men. At last Capaulican, having observed that fighting with such a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of undisciplined troops only served to contribute to the defeat and confusion of the whole, divided his forces into bodies of 1000 each. These he directed to attack the enemy by turns; and, though he did not expect that a single thousand would put them to flight, he directed them to make as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> a stand as they could; when they were to be relieved and supported by another body; and thus the Spaniards would be at last wearied out and overcome. The event fully answered his expectations. The Chileans maintained a fight for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight hours, until the Spaniards, growing faint for want of refreshment, retired precipitately. Valdivia ordered them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at some distance from the field, to stop the pursuit; but this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> being discovered to the Chileans by the treachery of his page, who was a native of that country, the Spaniards were surrounded on all sides, and cut in pieces by the Indians. The general was taken and put to death; some say with the tortures usually inflicted by those savages on their prisoners; others that he had melted gold poured <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his throat; but all agree, that the Indians made flutes and other instruments of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and preserved his skull as a monument of their victory, which they celebrated by an annual festival. After this victory the Chileans had another engagement with their enemies; in which also they proved victorious, defeating the Spaniards with the loss of near 3000 men; and upon this they bent their whole force against the colonies. The city of Concepcion, being abandoned by the Spaniards, was taken and destroyed; but the Indians were forced to raise the siege of Imperial; and their progress was at last stopped by Garcia de Mendoza, who defeated Capuican, took him prisoner, and put him to death. No defeats, however, could dispirit the Chileans. They continued the war for 50 years; and to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> they remain unconquered, and give the Spaniards more trouble than any other American <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Their most irreconcilable enemies are the inhabitants of Arauco and Tucapel, those to the south of the river Bobia, or whose country extends towards the Cordilleras. The manners of these people greatly resemble those of North America, which we have already described under the article AMERICA; but they seem to have a more warlike disposition. It is a constant rule with the Chileans never to sue for peace. The Spaniards are obliged not only to make the first overtures, but to purchase it by presents. They have at last been obliged to abandon all thoughts of extending their conquests, and reduced to cover their frontiers by erecting forts at proper distances. The Spanish colonies in Chili are dispersed on the borders of the South-sea. They are parted from Peru by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of 80 leagues in breadth; and bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Chiloe, at the extremity next the straits of Magellan. There are no settlements on the coast, except those of Baldivia, Concepcion island, Valparaiso, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COQUIMBO">Coquimbo</a> or La Serena, which are all sea-ports. In the inland country is St Jago, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the colony. There is no culture nor habitation at any distance from these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The buildings in the whole province are low, made of unburnt brick; and mostly thatched. This practice is observed on account of the frequent earthquakes; and is properly adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, as well as the indolence of the inhabitants. The climate of Chili is one of the most wholesome in the whole world. The vicinity of the Cordilleras gives it such a delightful temperature as could not otherwise be expected in that latitude. Though gold mines are found in it, their richness has been too much extolled; their produce never exceeds 218,750l. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is prodigiously fertile. All the European <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> have improved in that happy climate. The wine would be excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> nature were properly assisted by art: and the corn-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> is reckoned a bad one when it does not yield a hundred fold. With all these advantages, Chili has no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> intercourse with the mother-country. Their trade is confined to Peru, Paraguay, and the savages on their frontiers. With these last they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> their less valuable commodities, for oxen, horses, and their own children, whom they are ready to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with for the most trifling things. This province supplies Peru with great plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, dried fruit, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-meat, horses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, wheat, and gold. In exchange it receives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, cocoa, earthen-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, woollen cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, made at Quito, and every article of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> brought from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The ships sent from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALLAO">Callao</a> on this traffic were formerly bound to Concepcion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, but now come to Valparaiso. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> between this province and Paraguay is carried on by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, though it is a journey of 300 leagues, 40 of which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> through the snows and precipices of the Cordilleras; but if it was carried on by sea, they must either pass the straits of Magellan or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, which the Spaniards always avoid as much as possible. To Paraguay are sent some woollen stuffs called poncho, which are used for cloaks; also wines, brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and chiefly gold. In return they receive wax, a kind of tallow fit to make <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, European goods, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. Chili is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who is <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> in all civil, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, and is also independent of the viceroy. The latter has no authority except when a governor dies; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he may appoint one in his room for a time, till the mother-country names a successor. If, on some occasions, the viceroy has interfered in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Chili, it was when he has been either authorized by a particular trust reposed in him by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, or by the deference paid to the eminence of his office; or when he has been actuated by his own ambition to extend his authority. In the whole province of Chili there are not 20,000 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> men, and not more than 60,000 negroes, or Indians, able to bear arms. The military establishment amounted formerly to 2000 men; but the maintaining of them being found too expensive, they were reduced to 500 at the beginning of this century.

CHILIAD

Pages 825-825

an assemblage of several things ranged by thousands. The word is formed of the Greek χιλίας, milles, "a thousand."

CHILIARCHA

Pages 825-825
or CHILIARCHUS, an officer in the armies of the ancients, who had the command of a thousand men.

CHILLAGON

Pages 825-825

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a regular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of 100 sides and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. Though the imagination cannot form the idea of such a figure, yet we may have a very clear notion of it in the mind, and can easily demonstrate that the sum of all its angles is equal to 1996 <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ones: for the internal angles of every plane figure are equal to twice as many right ones as the figure hath sides, except those four which are about the center of the figure, from whence it may be resolved into as many triangles as it has sides. The author of l'Art de Penier, p. 44, has brought this instance to show the distinction between imagination and conceiving.

CHILLINGWORTH

Pages 825-826

WILLIAM, an eminent divine. vine of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1602, and bred there. He made early <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> proficiency in his studies, being of a very quick genius. He was an expert mathematician, as well as an able divine, and a very good poet. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">Study</a> and conversation at the university <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> upon the controversy between the church of England and that of Rome, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Henrietta <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to Henry IV. king of France, Mr Chillingworth forsook the church of England, and embraced the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Dr Laud, then bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, hearing of this, and being greatly concerned at it, wrote Mr Chillingworth; who expressing a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of candour and impartiality, that prelate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to correspond with him. This set Mr Chillingworth on a new inquiry; and at last determined him to return to his former religion. In 1634 he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a> of the arguments which had induced him to go over to the church of Rome. He spoke freely to his friends of all the difficulties that occurred to him; which gave occasion to a groundless report, that he had turned Papist a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and then Protestant again. His return to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the church of England made a great noise, and engaged him in several disputes with those of the Roman persuasion. But in 1635 he engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which gave him a far greater opportunity to confute the principles of the church of Rome, and to vindicate the Protestant religion, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "The religion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> a safe Way to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">Salvation</a>." Sir Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> keeper of the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, offering him preferment, Mr Chillingworth refused to accept it on account of his scruples with regard to the subscription of the 39 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. However, he at last surmounted these scruples; and being promoted to the chancellorship of the church of Sarum, with the prebend of Brixworth in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a> annexed to it, he complied with the usual subscription. Mr Chillingworth was zealously attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> party; and, in August 1643, was present in King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, where he advised and directed the making certain engines for assaulting the town. Soon after, having accompanied the lord Hopton, general of the king's forces in the west, to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARUNDEL">Arundel</a> castle in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, he was there taken prisoner by the parliamentary forces under the command of Sir William Waller, who obliged the castle to surrender. But his ill-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> increasing, he obtained leave to be conveyed to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, where he was lodged at the bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; and, after a short sickness, died in 1644. He hath left several excellent works behind him. CHILMINAR. See Persepolis.

CHILOE

Pages 826-826

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lying near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, under the 43d <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of an archipelago of 40 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is Castro. It rains here almost all the year, infomuch that nothing but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some such grain, that requires but little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> it, can ever come to perfection. They have excellent shell-fish, very good wild-fowl, hogs, sheep, and bees; as also a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wax. They carry on a trade with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> and Chili; whither they send boards of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, of which they have vast forests.

CHILTERN

Pages 826-826

a chain of chalky hills forming the southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Buckinghamshire, the northern part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, being distinguished by the name of the Vale. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> on these heights is extremely healthful: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, though stony, produces good crops of wheat and barley; and in many places it is covered with thick woods, among which are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of beech.—Chiltern is also applied to the hilly parts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, and it is believed has the same meaning in some other counties. Hence the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">Hundreds</a> lying in those parts are called the Chiltern Hundreds. CHILTERN Hundreds, stewards of. Of the hundreds into which many of the English counties were divided by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred for the better <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the jurisdiction was originally vested in peculiar courts; but came afterwards to be devolved to the county courts, and so remains at present; excepting with regard to some, as the chilterns, which have been by privilege annexed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. These having still their own courts, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of those courts is appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer, with a salary of £20. and all fees, &c. belonging to the office: and this is deemed an appointment of such profit, as to vacate a seat in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. CHIMÆRA, a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, situated at the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Epirus, about 32 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Corfu, near which are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Chimæra, which divide Epirus from Thessaly. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20° 40'. N. Lat. 40° 20'. CHIMÆRA, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated monster, sprung from Echidna and Typhon. It had three heads; that of a lion, a goat, and a dragon; and continually vomited flames. The forc parts of its body were those of a lion, the middle was that of a goat, and the hinder parts were those of a dragon. It generally lived in Lycia, about the reign of Jobates, by whose orders Bellerophon, mounted on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> Pegasus, overcame it. This fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> is explained by the recollection that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mountain in Lycia, whose top was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of lions on account of its defoliate wilderness; the middle which was fruitful, was covered with goats; and at the bottom the marshy ground abounded with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>. Bellerophon is said to have conquered the Chimæra, because he destroyed the wild beasts on that mountain, and rendered it habitable. Plutarch says that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of some pirates who adorned their ships with the images of a lion, a goat, and a dragon. By a chimæra among the philosophers, is understood

CHILTONHAM

Pages 826-826

a town in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, five miles from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>; noted for its purgative chalybeate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, which has rendered it of late years a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of fashionable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which operates with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ease, is deemed excellent in scrofulous complaints, and has been used with success in the gravel.

CHIMES

Pages 826-829

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> creature of the imagination, composed of such contradictions and absurdities as cannot possibly anywhere exist but in thought. CHIMES OF A CLOCK, a kind of periodical music, produced at equal intervals of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, by means of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, added to a clock. In order to calculate numbers for the chimes, and adapt the chime-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, it must be observed, that the barrel must turn round in the same time that the tune it is to play requires in singing. As for the chime-barrel, it may be made up of certain bars that run athwart it with a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of holes punched in them to put in the pins that are to draw each hammer; and these pins, in order to play the time of the tune rightly, must stand uprightly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hang <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, some more, some less. To <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the pins rightly, you may proceed by the way of changes on bells; viz. 1, 2, 3, 4; or rather make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the musical notes. Observe what is the compass of your tune, and divide the barrel accordingly from end to end. Thus, in the examples on Plate CXLIV, each of the tunes is eight notes in compass; and accordingly the barrel is divided into eight parts. These divisions are struck round the barrel; opposite to which are the hammer-tails. We speak here as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there were only one hammer to each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, that it may be more clearly apprehended; but when two notes of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> came together in a tune, there must be two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a> to the bell to strike it; so that if in all the tunes you intend to chime of eight notes compass, there should happen to be such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> notes on every bell, instead of eight you must have sixteen hammers; and accordingly you must divide the barrel, and strike sixteen strokes round it, opposite to each hammer tail; then you are to divide it round about into as many divisions as there are musical bars, semibreves, minims, &c. in the tune. Thus the hundredth-psalm tune has 20 semibreves, and each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of it is a semibreve: the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of it also is a semibreve; and, therefore, on the chime-barrel must be a whole division, from five to five; as you may understand plainly, if you conceive the surface of a chime-barrel to be represented by the above figures, as if the cylindrical superficies of the barrel were stretched out at length, or extended on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>: and then such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, so divided, if it were to be wrapped round the barrel, would show the places where all the pins are to stand in the barrel; for the dots running about the table are the places of the pins that play the tune. Indeed, if the chimes are to be complete, you ought to have a set of bells to the gamut notes; so as that each bell having the true sound of sol, la, mi, fa, you may play any tune with its flats and sharps; nay, you may by this means play both the base and treble with one barrel: and by setting the names of your bells at the head of any tune, that tune may easily be transferred to the chime-barrel, without any skill in music: but it must be observed, that each line in the music is three notes distant; that is, there is a note between each line, as well as upon it.

CHIMNEY

Pages 829-831

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a particular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where the fire is made, having a tube <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> funnel to carry off the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. The word chimney comes from the French cheminée; and that from the Latin caminata, "a chamber wherein is a chimney;" caminata, again, comes from caminos; and that from the Greek καμίνος, "chimney;" of καίω, uro, "I burn." <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">Chimneys</a> are usually supposed a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> only making <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of stoves: but Ostavio Ferrari endeavours to prove chimneys in use among the ancients. To this end, he cites the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Et jam summa procul villarum culmina fumant: and that of Appian, who says, "That of those persons proscribed by the triumvirate, some hid themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEWERS">sewers</a>, and some on the tops of houses and chimneys;" for so he understands κατακλεισθεῖς ὑπόγειοι, fumaria sub teeto poista. Add, that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, in one of his comedies, introduces his old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, Polycleon, shut up in a chamber, whence he endeavours to make his escape by the chimney. Chimneys, in Professor Beckman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, are comparatively of modern invention. We shall lay before our readers some observations from his elaborate dissertation on this subject. He thus explains the above passage of Virgil. "When the triumviri, says Appian*, caused those * De bello who had been proscribed by them to be sought for by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, some of them, to avoid the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of their persecutors, hid themselves in wells, and others, as Ferrarius translates the words, in fumaria sub teeto, qua feliciet fumus et teeto evolviatur (A). The true translation, however, (says Mr Beckman) is fumosa cenacula. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons of Rome endeavoured to conceal themselves in the smoky apartments of the upper story under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, which in general, were inhabited only by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people; and this seems to be confirmed by what Juvenal † expressly says, Rarus venit ‡ Sat. x. in cenacula miles. ver. 17. "Those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the ancients which speak of smoke rising up from houses, have with equal impropriety been supposed to allude to chimneys, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the smoke could not make its way through doors and windows. Seneca † writes, 'Last evening I had some friends with me, and on that account a stronger smoke was raised; not such a smoke, however, as bursts forth from the kitchens of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and which alarms the watchmen, but such a one as signifies that guests are arrived.' Those whose judgements are not already warped by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> undoubtedly find the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of these words to be, that the smoke forced its way through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> windows. Had the houses been built with chimney-funnels, one cannot conceive why the watchmen should have been alarmed when they observed a stronger smoke than usual arising from them; but as the kitchens had no convenience of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of fire, when extraordinary entertainments... ments were to be provided in the houses of the rich for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> companies, seems to have been well founded; and on such occasions people appointed for that purpose were stationed in the neighbourhood to be constantly on the watch, and to be ready to extinguish the flames in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a fire should happen. There are many other passages to be found in Roman authors of the like kind, which it is hardly necessary to mention; such as that of Virgil*, * Eclog. i. ver. 83. Et jam summa procul villarum culmina fumant. † Aen. vii. sc. 4. and the following words of Plautus†, descriptive of a mifer: Quin divum atque hominum clamat continuo fides, Suam rem persifle, legae eradicariet, De suo tigillo fumus si qua <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a> foras. "The passage of Aristophanes above alluded to however, (says the professor) which, according to the usual translation, seems to allude to a common chimney, can, in my opinion, especially when we consider the illustration of the scholiasts, be explained also by a simple hole in the roof, as Reiske has determined; and indeed this appears to be more probable, as we find mention made of a top or covering (τηλία) with which the hole was closed." It has been said that the instances of chimneys remaining among the ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> buildings are few, and the rules given by Vitruvius for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> them are obscure; but it appears that there exists no remains of ancient chimneys; and that Vitruvius gives no rules, either obscure or perspicuous, for building what, in the modern acceptation of the word, deserves the name of a chimney. "The ancient mason-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> still to be found in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, does not determine the question. Of the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, amphitheaters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, and bridges, there are some though very imperfect remains, in which chimneys cannot be expected; but of common dwelling houses none are to be seen, except at Herculaneum, and there no traces of chimneys have been discovered. The paintings and pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> which are preserved, afford us little information; for nothing can be perceived in them that bears the smallest resemblance to a modern chimney. "If there were no funnels in the houses of the ancients to carry off the smoke, the directions given by Columella, to make kitchens so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> that the roof should not catch fire, was of the utmost importance. An accident of the kind, which that author seems to have apprehended, had almost happened at Beneventum, when the landlord who entertained Maecenas and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was making a strong fire in order to get some birds sooner roasted. ubi fedulus holpes Pane arsit, macros dum turdos versat in igne; Nam vaga per veterem dilapsa flamma culinam Vulcano fumum properabat lambere teclam †. Had there been chimneys in the Roman houses, Vitruvius certainly would not have failed to describe their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, which is sometimes attended with considerable difficulties, and which is intimately connected with the regulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the whole edifice. He does not, however, say a word on this subject; neither does Julius <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, who has collected with great care the Greek names of every part of a dwelling-house; and Grapaldus, who in later times made a collection of the Latin terms, has not given a Latin word expressive * Francisci of a modern chimney *." "Camenis signified, as far as I have been able to learn, first a chemical or metallurgic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, in which a crucible was placed for melting and refining <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; secondly, a smith's forge; and, thirdly, a hearth on which portable stoves or fire-panes were placed for warming the apartment. In all these, however, there appears no trace of a chimney." <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> relates (lib. viii. c. 137.), that a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, when one of his servants asked for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, offered him in jest the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> shone into the house through an opening in the roof, under which the fire was perhaps made in the middle of the edifice. If such a hole must be called a chimney, our author admits that chimneys were in use among the ancients, especially in their kitchens; but it is obvious that such chimneys bore no resemblance to ours, through which the sun could not dart his rays upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of any apartment. "However imperfect may be the information which can be collected from the Greek and Roman authors respecting the manner in which the ancients warmed their apartments, it nevertheless shows that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used for that purpose a large fire-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a> or portable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, in which they kindled wood, and, when the wood was well lighted, carried it into the room, or which they filled with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals. When Alexander the Great was entertained by a friend in winter, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and raw, a small fire before was brought into the apartment to warm it. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, observing the size of the vessel, and that it contained only a few coals, desired his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> in a jeering manner, to bring more wood or frankincense; giving him thus to understand that the fire was fitter for burning perfumes than to produce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Anacharsis, the Scythian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, though displeased with many of the Grecian customs, praised the Greeks, however, because they shut out the smoke and brought only fire into their houses *. We * Plutarch, are informed by Lampridius, that the extravagant He-Sympofliogabalus caused to be burned in these stoves, instead lib. vi. 7. of wood, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> spices and costly perfumes †. It is p. 692. also worthy of notice, that coals were found in some of † Eul Lam. the apartments of Herculaneum, as we are told by prid. Vita Winkelmann, but neither stoves nor chimneys. It is well known to every scholar, that the useful arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were invented in the east, and that the customs, manners, and furniture of eastern nations, have remained from time immemorial almost unchanged. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, which the late Sir William Jones seems to have considered as the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of mankind, the methods employed by the inhabitants, for warming themselves have a great resemblance to those employed by the ancient Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for the same purpose. According to De la Valle, the Persians make fires in their apartments, not in chimneys as we do, but in stoves in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which they call tenor. "These stoves consist of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> or round hole, two spans or a little more in depth, and in shape not unlike an Italian cauldron. That this hole may throw out heat sooner, and with more strength, there is placed in it an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> vessel..." Chimney of the same size, which is either filled with burning coals, or a fire of wood and other inflammable substances is made in it. When this is done, they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> over the hole or stove a wooden top, like a small low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and spread above it a large coverlet quilted with cotton, which hangs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on all sides to the floor. This covering condenses the heat, and causes it to warm the whole apartment. The people who eat or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> there, and some who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in it, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> down on the floor above the carpet, and lean, with their shoulders against the wall, on square cushions, upon which they sometimes also sit; for the tenor is constructed in a place equally distant from the walls on both sides. Those who are not very cold only put their feet under the table or covering; but those who require more heat can put their hands under it, or creep under it altogether. By these means the stove diffuses over the whole body, without causing uneasiness to the head, so penetrating and agreeable a warmth, that I never in winter experienced anything more pleasant. Those, however, who require less heat, let the coverlet hang down on their side to the floor, and enjoy without any inconvenience from the stove the moderately heated <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the apartment. They have a method also of stirring up or blowing the fire when necessary, by means of a small pipe united with the tenor or stove under the earth, and made to project above the floor as high as one chooses; so that the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, when a person blows into it, because it has no other vent, acts immediately upon the fire like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of bellows. When there is no longer occasion to use this stove, both holes are closed up, that is to say, the mouth of the stove and that of the pipe which conveys the air to it, by a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> made for that purpose. Scarcely any appearance of them is then to be perceived, nor do they occasion inconvenience, especially in a country where it is always customary to cover the floor with a carpet, and where the walls are plastered. In many parts these ovens are used to cook victuals, by placing kettles over them. They are employed also to bake <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and for this purpose they are covered with a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> metal plate, on which the cake is laid; but if the bread is thick and requires more heat, it is put into the stove itself.* The professor farther observes, the oldest account of them which he finds is an inscription at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, which relates, that in the year 1347 a great many chimneys were thrown down by an earthquake. It would appear, however, that in some places they had been in use for a considerable time before that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; for De Gataris, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, relates, that Francesco de Carraro, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Padua, came to Rome in 1368, and finding no chimneys in the inn where he lodged, because at that time fire was kindled in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in the middle of the floor, he caused two chimneys like those which had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been used at Padua to be constructed by masons and carpenters, whom he had brought along with him. Over these chimneys, the first ever seen at Rome, he affixed his arms, which were still remaining in the time of De Gataris, who died of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> in 1405. Method of Building Chimneys that will not smoke. Chimney Workmen have different methods of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up the funnels of chimneys, generally according to their own fancies and judgments, and sometimes according to the customs of places. They are seldom directed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and rational principles. It will be found for the most part, that the smoking of chimneys is owing to their being carried up narrower near the top than below, or zig-zag, all in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, indeed, it is owing to accidental causes; but, for the most part to those two above mentioned. Where they are carried up in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> or tapering form, especially if the house be of a considerable height, it is ten to one but they sometimes smoke. The air in the rooms, being rarefied, is forced into the funnel of the chimney, and receives from the fire an additional force to carry up the smoke. Now it is evident, that the further up the smoke flies, the less is the force that drives it, the slower it must move, and consequently the more room in proportion it should have to move in; whereas in the usual way it has less, by the sides of the chimney being gathered closer and closer together. The method here proposed of carrying up chimneys will be objected to by some, thus: The wider a chimney is at the top, say they, the more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> has the wind to blow down. Very true; but is it not resisted in going down, both by the form of the chimney and other evident causes, so that it must return again? In the other way, when the wind blows down, the resistance being less, the wind and smoke are, if we may use the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, imprisoned, and make the smoke puff out below. This method has proved effectual after all others had failed; and that in a house placed in the worst situation possible, namely, under a high mountain to the southward, from which strong blasts blow down upon it. A vent was carried up without angles, as perpendicular as possible; and was made about three or four inches wider at top than at the bottom: the funnel was gathered in a throat directly above the fire-place, and so widening upwards. Since that time the house has not only ceased to smoke, but when the doors stand open, the draught is so strong that it will carry a piece of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> out at the chimney head. See more on this subject and the improvements by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Rumford under the article SMOKE. CHIMNEY-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>, otherwise called Hearth-money, a duty to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on houses. By stat. 14, Char. II, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2, every fire-hearth and stove of every dwelling or other house, within England and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> (except such as pay not to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and poor), was chargeable with 2s. per annum, payable at Michaelmas and Lady-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to the king and his heirs and successors, &c.; which payment was commonly called chimney-money. This tax, being much complained of as burdensome to the people, has been since taken off; and others imposed in its stead; among which that on windows has by some been esteemed almost equally grievous.
