in the other the tube MF, and observe that in each of these is to be inserted another tube, as H and I (A). Furnish the first of these tubes with an object-glass at G, and a concave eye-glass at F. You are to observe, that in regulating the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of these glasses, with regard to the length of the tube, you are to suppose it equal to the line G, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> visual pointed ray, which entering at the aperture G, is reflected by the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>, and goes out at the other aperture F, where the ocular glass is placed. Put any glass you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> into the two ends of the moveable tubes H and I; and, lastly, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the machine on a stand E, moveable at the point S, that it may be elevated or depressed at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. When the eye is placed at F, and you look through the tube, the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> that proceed from the object T, passing through the glass G, are successively reflected by the mirrors O, P, Q, and R, to the eye at F, and there paint the object T in its proper situation; and these rays appear to proceed directly from that object. The two moveable tubes H and I, at the extremities of each of which a glass is placed, serve only the more to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> the illusion, for they have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the interior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the machine. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> being moveable on the stand E, may be directed to any object; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> furnished with proper glasses will answer the purpose of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>. The two moveable tubes H and I being brought together, the machine is directed toward any object, and defining a person to look at the end F, you ask him if he sees distinctly that object. You then separate the two moveable tubes, and leaving a space between them sufficient to place your <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, or any other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body; you tell him that the machine has the power of making objects visible through the most opaque body; and as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> you define him then to look at the same object, when, to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> surprize, he will see it as distinct as when there was no solid body placed between the tubes. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, This experiment is the more extraordinary, as it is very difficult to conceive how the effect is produced. The two arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> appearing to be made to support the perspective glass; and to whatever object it is directed, the effect is still the same. VI. In the partition <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, make two apertures, CD, and EF, of a foot <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and ten inches wide, and about a foot distant from each other. Let them be at the common height of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s head; and in each of them place a transparent glass, surrounded with a frame, like a common mirror. Behind this partition place two mirrors H and I, inclined to it in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of forty-five degrees; that is, half way between a line drawn perpendicular to the ground and its surface; let them be both 18 inches <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>: let all the space between them be inclosed by boards or pasteboard painted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and well closed, that no light may enter: let there be also two curtains to cover them, which may be drawn aside at pleasure. When a person looks into one of these supposed mirrors, instead of seeing his own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, he will perceive the object that is in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the other; so that if two persons present themselves at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before these mirrors, instead of each one seeing himself, they will reciprocally see each other. Note, There should be a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> placed on each side of the two glasses in the window, to enlighten the faces of the persons who look in them, otherwise this experiment will have no remarkable effect. This experiment may be considerably improved by placing the two glasses in the partition in adjoining rooms, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons being previously placed in one room, when a stranger enters the other, you may tell him his face is dirty; and desire him to look in the glass, which he will naturally do; and on seeing a strange face he will draw back; but returning to it, and seeing another, another, and another, like the phantom kings in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, what his surprize will be is more easy to conceive than express. After this, a real mirror may be privately let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the back of the glass; and if he can be prevailed to look in it once more, he will then, to his further astonishment, see his own face; and may be told, perhaps persuaded, that all he thought he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> before was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> effect of imagination. How many tricks, less artful than this, have passed in former times for sorcery, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at this time in some countries for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a>! Note, When a man looks in a mirror that is placed perpendicular to another, his face will appear entirely deformed. If the mirror be a little inclined, so as to make an angle of 80 degrees (that is, one-ninth part from the perpendicular), he will then see all the parts of his face, except the nose and forehead. If it be inclined to 60 degrees (that is, one-third part), he will appear with three noses and six eyes: in short, the apparent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> will vary at each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of inclination; and when the glass comes to 45 degrees (that is, half way down), the face will vanish. If, instead of placing the two mirrors in this situation, they are so disposed that their junction may be vertical, their different inclinations will produce other effects; as the situation of the object relative to these mirrors is quite different. The effects of these mirrors, though remarkable enough, occasions but little surprize, as there is no method of concealing the cause by which they are produced. VII. Make a box of wood, of a cubical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, ABCD, of about 15 inches every way. Let it be fixed to the pedestal P, at the usual height of a man's head. In each side of this box, let there be an opening. (A) These four tubes must terminate in the substance of the case, and not enter the inside, that they may not hinder the effect of the mirrors. The fourfold reflection of the rays of light from the mirrors, darkens in some degree the brightness of the object; some light is also lost by the magnifying power of the perspective. If, therefore, instead of the object-glass at G, and concave eye-glass at F, plain glasses were substituted, the magnifying power of the perspective will be taken away, and the object appear brighter. ing of an oval form, of ten inches high, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wide. In this box place two mirrors A, D, with their backs against each other; let them <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the box in a diagonal line, and in a vertical position. Decorate the openings in the sides of this box with four oval frames and transparent glaïs, and cover each of them with a curtain, so contrived that they may all draw up together. Place four persons in front of the four sides, and at equal distances from the box, and then draw up the curtains that they may see themselves in the mirrors; when each of them, instead of his own figure, will see that of the person who is next to him, and who, at the same time, will seem to him to be placed on the opposite side. Their confusion will be the greater, as it will be very difficult for them to discover the mirrors concealed in the box. The reason of this phenomenon is evident; for though the rays of light may be turned aside by a mirror, yet as we have before said, they always appear to proceed in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. VIII. Provide a box ABCD of about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 15 inches wide, and 12 inches high. At the end AC place a concave mirror, the focus of whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> rays is at 18 inches from the reflecting surface. At IL place a pâteboard blacked, in which a hole is cut sufficiently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> to see on the mirror H the object placed at BEFD. Cover the top of the box, from A to I, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, that the mirror H may be entirely darkened. The other part IB must be covered with a glaïs, under which is placed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>. Make an aperture at G, near the top of the side EB; beneath which, on the inside, place, in succession, paintings of different subjects, as vistas, landscapes, &c., so that they may be in front of the mirror H. Let the box be so placed that the object may be strongly illuminated by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, or by wax lights placed under the enclosed part of the box AI. By this simple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> the objects placed at GD will be thrown into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> perspective; and if the subjects be properly chosen, the appearance will be altogether as pleasing as in optical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> of a much more complicated form. Note. A glaïs mirror should be always here used, as those of metal do not represent the objects with equal vivacity, and are beside subject to tarnish. It is also necessary that the box be sufficiently large, that you may not be obliged to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a mirror whose focus is too short; for in that case, the right lines near the border of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> will appear bent in the mirror, which will have a disagreeable effect, and cannot be avoided. IX. To set fire to a combustible body by the reflection of concave fire to a combustible body. IX. The rays of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> body placed in the focus of a concave mirror being reflected in parallel lines, if a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> mirror be placed diametrically opposite the first, it will, by collecting those rays in its focus, set fire to a combustible body. Place two concave mirrors, A and B, at about 12 or 15 feet distance from each other, and let the axis of each of them be in the same line. In the focus C of one of them, place a live coal, and in the focus D of the other some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. With a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> bellows, which make a continual blast, keep constantly blowing the coal, and notwithstanding the distance between them, the powder will presently take fire. It is not necessary that these mirrors be of metal or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, those made of wood or pâteboard gilded will produce the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>, which has sometimes taken effect at the distance of 50 feet, when mirrors of 18 inches, or two feet diameter, have been used. This experiment succeeds with more difficulty at great distances; which may proceed from the mixture in a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It would doubtless take effect more readily, if a tin tube, of an equal diameter with the mirrors, were to be placed between them. X. Behind the partition AB, place, in a position something oblique, the concave mirror EF, which must appear to be at least ten inches in diameter, and its distance from the partition equal to three fourths of the distance of its centre. In the partition make an opening of seven or eight inches, either square or circular: it must face the mirror, and be of the same height with it. Behind this partition place a strong light, so disposed that it may not be seen at the opening, and may illuminate an object placed at C, without throwing any light on the mirror. Beneath the aperture in the partition place the object C, that you intend shall appear on the outside of the partition, in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> position; and which we suppose to be a flower. Before the partition, and beneath the aperture, place a little flowerpot D, the top of which should be even with the bottom of the aperture, that the eye, placed at G, may see the flower in the same position as if its stalk came out of the pot. Take care to paint the space between the back part of the partition and the mirror black, to prevent any reflections of light from being thrown on the mirror; in a word, so dispose the whole that it may be as little enlightened as possible. When a person is placed at the point G, he will perceive the flower that is behind the partition, at the top of the pot at D; but on putting out his hand to pluck it, he will find that he attempts to grasp a shadow. If in the opening of the partition a large double convex <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENS">lens</a> of a short focus be placed, or, which is not quite so well, a bottle of clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the image of the flower reflected thereon will appear much more vivid and distinct.
